They honor him with light,
And the brightness of heaven teaches
What the charity of John is.

Grant, O everlasting Trinity,
That goodness may be steadfast;
Or let rivers of tears
Submerge the sins of those who fall.
Amen.

The just wrath of the Creator,
With the avenging flood of waters,
Submerged the criminal world,
Noah being saved in the ark;
At last the wondrous power of love
Washed the world with blood.

The blessed earth, happily watered
By so salutary a rain,
Which before had abounded with thorns,
Put forth little flowers;
And wormwood was transformed
Into the taste of nectar.

At once the grim serpent laid down
Its deadly venom,
And the bloody ferocity of beasts
Ceased;
This was the victory
Of the mild wounded Lamb.

O depth of heavenly knowledge
Unfathomable!
O sweetness of the gracious breast
To be proclaimed!
The servant deserved death;
The best of kings paid the penalty.

When by our sins we provoke
The vengeance of the judge,
May we then be protected
By the presence of the speaking Blood;
May the armies of encroaching evils
Then withdraw.

May the redeemed world praise you,
Guarding your grateful gifts,
O renowned Leader and Author
Of everlasting salvation,
Who hold the blessed kingdom
With the Father and the Spirit.
Amen.

This Confessor of the Lord, whom
The people devoutly praise and worship
Throughout the world, rejoicing
On this day, has merited the wounds of Christ.

Who, devout, prudent, humble, and modest,
Led a sober life without stain,
Until the breath of life
Quickened his human frame.

By reason of whose outstanding merit,
The afflicted limbs that lay
Here and there in sickness,
The power of disease overcome, are restored to health.

Our choir therefore sings
Obedient praise and renowned palms to him,
That we may be aided by his devout prayers
For all eternity.

May salvation, honor, and power be to him
Who, gleaming above on the throne of heaven,
Guides the order of the whole world,
Three and one.
Amen.

This one, whom we the faithful joyfully honor,
Whose lofty triumphs we celebrate,
On this day Joseph has merited
The joys of everlasting life.

O all too happy, O all too blessed,
At whose last hour as he watched,
Both Christ and the Virgin together stood by
With serene countenance.

Hence, conqueror of the underworld,
Freed from the snare of the flesh,
He passes in gentle sleep
To the eternal dwelling places, and girds his temples
With gleaming garlands.

Therefore let us all implore him as he reigns,
That he may be present to us
And, obtaining pardon for our sins,
Bestow upon us the gifts of heavenly peace.

May applause be to you, may honor be to you,
O triune God who reign, and
Bestow golden crowns upon your faithful servant
For every age.
Amen.

The noble Crown of Christ
Is depicted in the figures of the Law;
The Victim encircled with thorns
And the burning bush bear witness.

A crown had encircled the Ark,
And the sacred circle of the table
And the altar smoking with incense;
A crown binds them, encompassing.

Hail, Crown of glory,
Knowing the sufferings of Christ.
Fairer than gems and gold,
You will surpass the crowns of the stars.

Strength, honor, praise, and glory
To God the Father with the Son,
And the Holy Paraclete together,
For ages of ages.
Amen.

O gracious light of minds, O Jesus,
As you refresh our hearts,
You put to flight the darkness of sin
And fill us with sweetness.

How happy is he whom you visit!
Sharer in the Father's right hand,
You are the sweet light of the homeland,
Denied to the senses of the flesh.

Splendor of the Father's glory,
Incomprehensible charity,
Lavish upon us an abundance of love
By your presence.

Jesus, to you be glory,
Who reveal yourself to the little ones,
With the Father and the gracious Spirit,
For everlasting ages.
Amen.

O light and glory of our homeland,
Friendly to the Slavic peoples,
Hail, brothers: with the year's own hymn
We lift you up in song.

Whom Rome, applauding, welcomes,
A mother embracing her sons,
The crown of bishops grows
And is confirmed with new strength.

To the farthest barbarian lands
You press on to bring Christ;
How many the vain error had mocked,
You fill with nurturing light.

Hearts freed from their offenses
Are caught up by heavenly ardor;
The terror of thorns is changed
Into the blossoms of holiness.

And now, received in the serene court
Of the heavenly ones, be present
To our suppliant prayer: keep
The Slavic peoples for the Lord.

May those plunged in error
Be gathered into Christ's one fold;
May faith, rivaling ancestral deeds,
Flourish ever more beautiful.

O Blessed Trinity, kindle us
With heavenly love,
And make us, children of our fathers,
Follow their glorious footsteps.
Amen.

Charity burns deep within mortal breasts
With inward fire,
By which Christ graciously raises
The faithful to heavenly things.

Charity burns deep within mortal breasts
With inward fire,
By which Christ graciously raises
The faithful to heavenly things.

The Queen of the world, ever watchful,
Stands lovingly by her children,
Beating back the wiles of the enemy
And bringing the help of salvation.

Conrad exalts Jesus and his Mother
With fervent praises,
And by the bond of sweet love
Is joined to them forever.

Having attained the joys of heaven,
Singing blessed hymns,
May he, we pray, obtain for us
The divine gifts of grace.

May he wisely drive back
The shadows of error from our borders:
A company consecrated to the Virgin,
Let us wage the battles of Christ.

We exiles, drawing out our life
Beneath the wings of shining peace,
May we at last in our homeland
Praise God at all times.

Jesus, to you be glory,
Divine offspring of the Virgin,
Who through Mary has bestowed
Upon his servant so many gifts.

Mary with chaste lips
Kisses the feet of God,
Bathes them with weeping, wipes them with her hair,
And anoints the feet she has dried with nard.

Glory be to God the Father,
And to his only Son,
With the Holy Spirit the Comforter,
Now and through all ages.
Amen.

Mary, who lovingly receive
The prayers of mortal men,
Behold, we pray as suppliants:
Be ever present to us.

Be present, if the dreadful chain
Of sins holds us bound;
Swiftly loose the shackles
That bind our hearts in their offenses.

Succor us, if the deceitful image
Of this world entices us,
Lest the soul, forgetting heaven,
Abandon the path of salvation.

Be also a shield to your sons
At the hour of death,
That, aided by you, they may be granted
To attain the everlasting reward.

Jesus, to you be glory,
Who were born of the Virgin,
With the Father, and the nurturing Spirit,
Through ages everlasting.
Amen.

Applaud the glorious name of Martina,
O citizens of Rome, applaud her glory:
Call her a Virgin eminent in merit,
Call her a Martyr of Christ.

While she, born of illustrious parents,
Amid delights, amid the pleasing
Allurements of luxury, abounded
In the gifts of a prosperous house,

Despising the comforts of life, she dedicates
Herself to the Lord of all things, and with generous hand
Distributing her wealth among the poor of Christ,
She seeks the rewards of the heavenly ones.

Neither the torturing claw, nor wild beasts,
Nor the horrible blow of rods moves her;
Hence Angels, descended from the dwellings of the Most High,
Refresh her with heavenly food.

Moreover, the lion, his savagery laid aside,
Casts himself at her feet with a gentle muzzle:
Yet the sword consigns you, Martina, to death
And inserts you into the assemblies of heaven.

The smoking altar, fragrant with incense vapors,
Incessantly invokes you in prayer,
And, destroying the false omen, blots it out
With the portent of your name.

Drive far from us the allurements of sin,
You, O God, who stand by Martyrs on the right,
One and Three: give your servants the light
With which in mercy you gladden souls.
Amen.

The Martyr of God, Venantius,
Light and glory of Camerino,
Having overcome his torturer and judge,
Joyfully sings his triumph.

A boy in years, after bonds,
After prisons, after stripes,
He is given as food to lions
Growling with prolonged hunger.

But the ferocity of the lions
Spares his innocence:
They lick the feet of the Martyr,
Forgetful of wrath and hunger.

With head turned downward
He is forced to breathe in smoke;
A burning lamp scorches
His ribs on both sides and his entrails.

Praise be to the Father, praise to the Son,
And to you, Holy Spirit:
Grant us, through Venantius's prayers,
Blessed joys.
Amen.

Suddenly freed by wondrous means, Peter
Sheds the iron chains at Christ's command:
That Shepherd and Ruler of the flock,
He opens the pastures of life and sacred fountains,
Keeps the sheep entrusted to him, and drives off wolves.

To the Father let there be perennial glory through all ages;
And let us sing praises renowned to you,
Eternal Son; let there be, O Spirit from above,
Honor and glory to you: let the holy Trinity
Be praised forever through all ages.
Amen.

A wondrous mystery is made manifest
To us on this day:
The true Son of God
Endures a blood-soaked death.

Defending the cause of his servant,
And putting on the form of the guilty,
The Master is hung in place of the slave,
The Just One is punished in place of the guilty.

The marks of death remain,
Imprinted on the Sacred Shroud,
Which after the noble triumph
Had wrapped the bloodied body.

These are the marks of death, of hell,
And of the world conquered:
These are the glorious trophies
Of an unconquered general.

We therefore owe this debt of gratitude
To the Avenger of our salvation,
That we may do battle with this sign
Against the snares of the devil.

Dead to the old life
Let us rise to new life,
Following Christ: through the Cross
Of Christ we shall enjoy glory.

Grant this, most loving Father,
And you the Only-Begotten, equal to the Father,
With the Holy Spirit the Comforter,
Reigning through all ages. Amen.

No father's blandishments draw you away,
You are not captured by the ease of a wealthy life,
Nor by the gleam of gems,
Nor by the desire to reign.

The dreadful threats of the sword
Do not terrify you, nor does the fatal fury
Of the executioner:
For you prefer the lasting joys of heaven to passing things.

Now protect us from the dwellings of the Most High,
Merciful one, and receive with willing ears
Our prayers, as we sing of
Your palm won through death.

Let the Lord, the eternal Master of creation, have lasting honor,
And may our lips in prayer celebrate the Son,
And extol the divine Spirit
With the highest praises.
Amen.

O how blessed, how lofty in merit,
Unknowing of the stain of snow-white chastity,
O mighty Martyr, dweller of the groves,
Greatest of Prophets.

Garlands crown others thirtyfold,
Increased in growth, others doubled,
But a triple, a hundredfold increase of fruit
With its bonds adorns you.

Now mighty in your rich merits,
Root out the hard stones of our heart,
Making the rough way smooth, and guiding
The crooked paths.

That the merciful Creator and Redeemer of the world
May worthily deign, coming to minds
Pure from the stain of sin,
To plant his blessed steps.

Let the citizens of heaven celebrate you
With praises, O God, simple and yet threefold,
And we suppliants also beg pardon:
Spare those you have redeemed.
Amen.

O first of all, Virgin, brought forth
From the Spirit of the Creator,
Predestined by the Most High
To carry the Son in your womb;

You, woman foretold as the perpetual enemy
Of the demon,
Are filled with grace alone,
Untouched in your origin.

You conceive Life in your womb,
And the life lost by Adam,
By ministering the flesh for the divine Victim
To be offered, you restore.

Death, the wage owed to the atonement,
Defeated, abandons you,
And you, sharer in your nurturing Son,
Are borne in body to the stars.

Radiant with such great glory,
All nature is exalted,
Called in you to touch the summit
Of all beauty.

To us, triumphant, turn
Your eyes, O Queen, upon us exiles,
That we may attain the blessed homeland
Of heaven, with you as our guide.

Jesus, to you be glory,
Who were born of the Virgin,
With the Father and the nurturing Spirit,
Through ages everlasting.
Amen.

In how many floods of tears,
In what grief does she turn,
The sorrowful Mother, mourning,
When, torn from the bloody stake,
She sees her Son lying
In her arms!

O sweet mouth, gentle breast
And most sweet side,
And the wounded right hand
And the wounded left,
And the feet red with blood—
She bathes them, ailing, with her tears.

A hundred times and a thousand times
She clasps to close embrace
That breast and those arms,
She fixes her lips upon those wounds:
And so she wholly melts
In kisses of grief.

Come, Mother, we beseech you
By these your tears,
And by your Son's sorrowful death,
And the crimson of his wounds,
This grief of your heart
Lay deep within our hearts.

Be to the Father, and to the Son,
And to the coeternal Spirit,
Be to the supreme Trinity
Sempiernal glory,
And perennial praise and honor
In this age and in all ages.
Amen.

O Bethlehem, greater than the great cities,
To whom it fell
To bring forth, incarnate from heaven,
The leader of salvation.

Whom a star, surpassing the disc of the sun
In beauty and in light,
Announces to have come to the earth
As God in earthly flesh.

After the Magi had seen him,
They bring forth gifts from the East:
And prostrate in their vows they offer
Frankincense, myrrh, and royal gold.

Treasure and fragrant odor
Of Sabean incense proclaim
King and God, and myrrh-dust
Foreshadows a tomb.

Jesus, to you be glory,
Who appeared to the nations,
With the Father and the nurturing Spirit,
Through ages everlasting.
Amen.

O bright star of Jacob,
O resplendent like the sun,
Dawn, than whom nothing purer
Shines among the stars.

Clad in white robes,
Thronging companies of the heavenly ones
Applaud you, and holy virgins
Sing ceaseless praises.

Moreover, in willing service they offer
Privet and white lilies;
But the whiteness of these is surpassed
By the whiteness of a chaste heart.

Our lowly earth, echoing
The praises of Angels,
Let it lift its voice to the stars,
And proclaim the glories of the Virgin.

Jesus, to you be glory,
Who were born of the Virgin,
With the Father and the nurturing Spirit,
Through ages everlasting.
Amen.

You had left behind the wealth and the royal splendor,
Elizabeth, consecrated to God's divinity:
Now received, you are blessed among the Angels;
Willingly shield us from the snares of the enemy.

Go before, and as guide of salvation show the way:
We will follow: O may the faithful be of one mind,
May every action be a good fragrance—this
Your charity, hidden beneath its roses, indicates.

Blessed charity, powerful to place us
In the stronghold of the stars through all ages:
To the Father and to the Son be supreme glory,
And to you, nurturing Spirit, praise everlasting.
Amen.

O Father of the light from above,
When you look upon Magdalene,
You kindle flames of love
And melt the ice of her heart.

Wounded with love, she runs
To anoint the blessed feet,
To bathe them with weeping, to dry them
With her hair, and to kiss them with her lips.

She does not fear to stand at the Cross,
She clings anxious to the sepulcher,
She does not shrink from the brutal soldiers:
Charity drives out fear.

O true Charity, O Christ,
Cleanse our sins,
Fill our hearts with grace,
Restore to us the rewards of heaven.

To the Father and likewise to the Son,
And to you, Holy Spirit,
As it was, so let it be forever
Glory through all ages.
Amen.

Be appeased, O Christ, toward your servants,
For whom the Virgin, as patroness,
Seeks the Father's clemency
At the tribunal of your grace.

Be present to us, O Archangel,
You who bear the name of God's strength:
Increase the strength of the weak,
Bring consolation to the sorrowful.

And you, blessed companies
Ranked through nine orders,
Ward off against things past and present
The damages yet to come.

Drive away the faithless people
From the borders of believers,
That one shepherd may rule us all,
One flock together.

To God the Father be glory,
Who may guard through Angels
Those whom the Son has redeemed
And the Holy Spirit has anointed.
Amen.

Be appeased, O Christ, toward your servants,
For whom the Virgin, as patroness,
Seeks the Father's clemency
At the tribunal of your grace.

And you, blessed companies
Ranked through nine orders,
Ward off against things past and present
The damages yet to come.

Apostles together with Prophets,
Before the stern Judge,
Obtain pardon
Through the true tears of sinners.

You, clad in purple, O Martyrs,
You, made bright by the reward
Of confession, O exiles,
Call us into the homeland.

O chaste choir of Virgins,
And those whom the desert
Has sent on to the stars, set us
In the dwellings of the heavenly ones.

Drive away the faithless people
From the borders of believers,
That one Shepherd may rule us all,
One flock together.

To God the Father be glory,
And to the Father's only Son,
With the Holy Spirit the Comforter,
Through ages everlasting.
Amen.

Illustrious guardian of Virgins,
Untouched Mother of God,
Gateway of the heavenly court,
Our hope, the joy of heaven,

A lily among thorns,
Most beautiful dove,
A shoot budding from the root,
Bringing healing to our wounds.

A tower impregnable to the dragon,
A friendly star to the shipwrecked,
Protect us from deceptions,
And guide us with your light.

Dispel the shadows of error,
Remove deceitful shoals,
Amid so many waves, open
A safe path for those who stray.

Jesus, to you be glory,
Who were born of the Virgin,
With the Father and the nurturing Spirit,
Through ages everlasting.
Amen.

What tongue, O Lance, is fit
To repay you with due thanks for your merit?
For you open the life-giving side of Christ,
Whence the Church is born.

This is Eve coming forth from the side of man
While deep sleep weighs upon him;
The second Adam truly begets her from the heart's
Overflowing water and blood.

O Nails! Equal grace remains for you also,
When, planted in the sacred limbs of Christ,
You fix to the Cross the written bond of death
Blotted out by the blood of the Lord.

Let the heavenly ones exalt you with praises, O Jesus,
Who retain in heaven the apertures of the Nails
And the marks of the Lance, where you live and reign
With the Father and the Comforter.
Amen.

All you who seek Christ,
Lift your eyes on high:
There you may see
The sign of eternal glory.

We behold something resplendent
That knows no end,
Sublime, exalted, without boundary,
More ancient than heaven and the deep.

Here is that King of the nations
And King of the Jewish people,
Promised to Abraham our father
And to his seed forever.

Him, with the prophets as witnesses
And as signators of the same,
The Father as testator commands
Us to hear and to believe.

Jesus, to you be glory,
Who reveal yourself to little ones,
With the Father and the nurturing Spirit,
Through ages everlasting.
Amen.

Whatever you bind on earth with bonds,
O Peter, shall be bound in the stronghold of the stars:
And what the power entrusted here resolves,
Shall be loosed at the high summit of heaven;
At the end of the world you shall judge the age.

To the Father let there be perennial glory through all ages;
And let us sing renowned praises to you,
Eternal Son; let there be, O Spirit from above,
Honor and glory to you: let the holy Trinity
Be praised forever through all ages.
Amen.

Hermenegild, radiance and glory of Martyrs,
Powerful on the royal throne of Spain,
Whom the love of Christ inserts
Into the blessed companies of heaven.

How patient you stand, keeping
The service pledged to God! before which
You set nothing as preferable,
Warily shunning what is harmful yet pleasing.

How you restrain the impulses that prepare
The nourishment of growing vice, walking
With unwavering steps
Along the way where truth directs!

Let the Lord, the eternal Master of creation, have lasting honor,
And may our lips in prayer celebrate the Son,
And extol the divine Spirit
With the highest praises.
Amen.

Hermenegild, radiance and glory of Martyrs,
Powerful on the royal throne of Spain,
Whom the love of Christ inserts
Into the blessed companies of heaven.

How patient you stand, keeping
The service pledged to God! before which
You set nothing as preferable,
Warily shunning what is harmful yet pleasing.

How you restrain the impulses that prepare
The nourishment of growing vice, walking
With unwavering steps
Along the way where truth directs!

Let the Lord, the eternal Master of creation, have lasting honor,
And may our lips in prayer celebrate the Son,
And extol the divine Spirit
With the highest praises.
Amen.
No father's blandishments draw you away,
You are not captured by the ease of a wealthy life,
Nor by the gleam of gems,
Nor by the desire to reign.

The dreadful threats of the sword
Do not terrify you, nor does the fatal fury
Of the executioner:
For you prefer the lasting joys of heaven to passing things.

Now protect us from the dwellings of the Most High,
Merciful one, and receive with willing ears
Our prayers, as we sing of
Your palm won through death.

Let the Lord, the eternal Master of creation, have lasting honor,
And may our lips in prayer celebrate the Son,
And extol the divine Spirit
With the highest praises.
Amen.

Messenger of the King of heaven,
You leave your father's home,
Teresa, to bring Christ
To barbarian lands, or your blood.

But a sweeter death awaits you,
A more welcome suffering demands you:
Struck in the wound by the lance
Of divine love, you shall fall.

O victim of charity!
Set our hearts on fire,
And the peoples entrusted to you
Deliver from the fire of hell.

Praise be to the Father with the Son
And the Holy Spirit the Comforter,
And to you, O holy Trinity,
Now and through all ages.
Amen.

O best Creator of things,
Our Ruler, look upon us:
Free us, plunged in harmful rest,
From sleep's depths.
We lift our minds and our hands,
As the Prophet commands us to do
In the night watches,
And Paul judged by his deeds.
We beseech you, O holy Christ,
Forgive all our sins:
We rise to make confession,
And break the delay of night.
Jesus, to you be glory,
Who were born of the Virgin,
With the Father and the nurturing Spirit,
Through ages everlasting.
Amen.

At the highest summit of creation,
O Virgin, you stand as Queen,
Enriched abundantly with the beauty
Of all things.

More beautiful than any created work,
You shine before the creating Word,
Predestined to bear the Son
Who brought you forth.

As Christ, made King crimson with blood
Upon the lofty tree,
So you, a sharer in his Passion,
Are the Mother of the living.

Adorned with such great praises,
Look upon us as we rejoice,
And receive with gladness
The praise we pour out to you.

Jesus, to you be glory,
Who were born of the Virgin,
With the Father and the nurturing Spirit,
Through ages everlasting.
Amen.

O glorious King of bishops,
Crown of confessors,
Who lead those who reject earthly things
To heavenly ones.

Bend your gracious ear at once
To our voices:
We sing your sacred trophies:
Forgive what we have done amiss.

You conquer in the Martyrs,
By sparing the Confessors:
Conquer also our sins,
By granting pardon.

To God the Father be glory,
And to his only Son,
With the Holy Spirit the Comforter,
Both now and forever.
Amen.

Proclaim, O faithful, the twin athletes
Received into the bright seats of heaven;
Proclaim the twofold pillar and glory
Of the Slavic people.

One love joined these brothers together,
And one devotion led them to the desert,
To hasten to bring to many
The pledges of blessed life.

With the light that shines in the heavenly temples,
They fill Bulgars, Moravians, Bohemians;
Soon, numerous as troops, they lead
Thronging companies to Peter.

Girt with the crown owed to their merits,
O continue to be moved by the tears of those who pray;
The primordial gifts given to the Slavs
You must maintain as their protectors.

May the noble land that calls upon you
Keep the brightness of the eternal faith:
What Rome as prince bestowed, Rome herself
Will ever give: salvation.

O Creator and Redeemer of the human race,
Who in your goodness grant us all good things,
To you be thanksgiving, to you be glory
Through all ages.
Amen.

Often while the people of Christ
Were hard pressed by the blood-stained arms
Of a hostile enemy,
The gracious Virgin came as helper,
Descending from the serene heaven.

So the ancient memorials of the Fathers narrate,
Templates bear witness, made glorious
With abundant spoils, repeated each year
In the festal cult of vows.

Behold, let us offer to Mary the thanks
Of a new canticle in joyful measures
For her new gifts, with the resounding applause
Of city and world.

O happy day, worthy of the calendar,
When the Chair of Peter received, blessed,
The teacher of the faith returned after five
Sorrowful years!

Chaste virgins and pure boys,
The joyful clergy and the people
With grateful heart: let all strive
To celebrate the gifts of the Queen of heaven.

O Virgin of Virgins, blessed Mother of Jesus,
Increase these blessings; grant, we pray,
That the Good Shepherd may lead his flock
To the pastures of salvation.

May we venerate you through eternal years,
O Trinity, to be celebrated with the highest applause:
May minds praise you in faith, and tongues
With their resounding song. Amen.

O Savior of the human race,
Jesus, delight of hearts,
Founder of the redeemed world,
And chaste light of those who love:

By what clemency were you conquered
That you would bear our sins?
To undergo death, though innocent,
That you might lift us from death?
Let your indulgence move you
To repair our losses,
And enrich those who behold your face
With blessed light.
Jesus, to you be glory,
Who were born of the Virgin,
With the Father and the nurturing Spirit,
Through ages everlasting.
Amen.

O giver of eternal salvation,
Jesus, assist those you have redeemed:
O Virgin, Mother of clemency,
Grant salvation to your servants.

You, thousands of Angels,
And companies of the Fathers, the melodious
Troops of Prophets; intercede, for sinners,
To obtain pardon.

The forerunner of Christ, the Baptist,
And the Keybearer of the highest heaven,
With the other Apostles,
May they loose the bonds of our sins.

May the triumphant band of Martyrs,
The gracious choir of Priests,
And virginal chastity
Wash away our offenses.

Whoever you are who reign as princes
In the high court of the stars,
Look favorably on the vows of suppliants
Who seek the gifts of heaven.

Virtue, honor, praise, and glory
To God the Father, with the Son,
With the Holy Spirit the Comforter,
Through ages of ages.
Amen.

Hail, O wounds of Christ,
Pledges of immense love,
From which perennial streams
Flow of reddening blood.

You surpass the stars in splendor,
The roses and balms in fragrance,
The gems of India in worth,
The honeycomb in sweetness.

Through you a most welcome refuge
Is open to our souls;
The fury of threatening enemies
Never penetrates here.

How many stripes does Jesus
Bare receive in the praetorium!
How many drops of blood
Drip from his lacerated skin on every side!

His beautiful brow, alas,
Is stung by the crown of thorns,
The blunted point of nails
Pierces hands and feet.

But after he, loving and willing,
Had given up the spirit,
The breast is struck by a lance,
And a twin stream gushes forth.

That the redemption might be complete,
He is pressed under the wine-press;
And Jesus, forgetful of himself,
Reserves not a drop of blood for himself.

Come, all you whom the deadly stain
Of sins infects;
Whoever bathes in this cleansing bath
Shall be made clean.

Thanks must be given to the one
Who sits at the right hand of the Most High Father,
Who redeemed us with his blood
And strengthens us with the Holy Spirit.
Amen.

Hail, flowers of Martyrs,
Whom on the very threshold of the light
The persecutor of Christ cut off,
As a storm wind tears budding roses.

You, the first victims of Christ,
A tender flock of those immolated,
At the very foot of the altar
You play simply with palm and crown.

Jesus, to you be glory,
Who were born of the Virgin,
With the Father and the nurturing Spirit,
Through ages everlasting.
Amen.

Hail, nails and lance,
Lately covered with filth,
Which, plunged into Christ's body,
Grow red with his nurturing blood.

The treacherous Jewish people
Had chosen you for crime;
But God from heaven turned you
Into ministers of grace.

For however many wounds you once
Engraved upon the sacred limbs,
From so many opened fountains
Heavenly gifts flow forth.

O piercing nails and lance,
Jesus, to you be glory,
With the Father and the nurturing Spirit,
Now and through all ages.
Amen.

Thus the Fathers lead their life in shadow,
As seven lilies of snowy beauty,
Gladly pleasing to the exalted Virgin,
Were seen to shine for Peter.

And now, seized by the divine flame,
They hasten through cities, wander every place,
If they might plant deep in all hearts
The sorrows of the Mother.

Hence they prevail to tame blind wrath,
And join savage hearts that knew no peace,
And the words of the devout raise the downcast
And call back the guilty.

But the Virgin, escorting her own Servants,
Lifts them at last to the heights above;
And adorns the blessed ones for all ages
With garlands of gems.

Come now, let the sighing of those who pray
Be heard and their hard toils be seen:
And let them always favor our vows
With a kindly light.

Glory be to the Father, and to the Son born of him,
And to you, equal in power to both,
O Spirit, ever God, one through
All ages of time.
Amen.

O Virgin, clothed with the rays of the sun,
With your head encircled twice by six stars,
The moon furnishing a footstool for your feet,
You shine forth in glory.

Conqueress of death, hell, and sin,
You sit close by Christ, zealous for us,
And earth and heaven celebrate you
As their powerful Queen.

But the dire serpent persists in threatening harm
To the offspring once entrusted to you;
Mother, come mercifully here, and crush
The neck of the evil one.

Protect the followers of the divine faith,
Bring back the wanderers to the holy fold,
Gather together the peoples long covered
By the shadow of death on every side.

Beg pardon for the guilty with gentleness,
Aid those who weep, and the poor and the sick,
A certain gleam of hope of salvation
For all in life's sharp trials.

Let praise be everlasting to the exalted Trinity,
Who bestowed upon you, O Virgin, the crown,
And in her providence established you
As our Queen and Mother.
Amen.

Behold how the Word of the Father
From the heavenly seats, merciful and burning with love,
Presses on to heal those born
Lost through the sin of Adam.

Taking pity on the world's lamentable ruin,
And willing to repair our failures,
The Master prays and with bowed forehead
Begs pardon.

He wavers within himself, turning over such bitter things:
This cup of sorrow, he says, a suppliant,
My Father, take from me; but let your will,
Not mine, be done.

When sad dread weighs upon the depths of his heart,
The Lord faints, exhausted; through his limbs
Flows a sweat of blood, and the earth
Is moistened with drops.

But swiftly, coming from highest Olympus,
An Angel refreshes Jesus as he lies:
Strength returns to his body, and with new
Vigor he rises.

Praise and honor to the Father and to the begotten Son,
To whom is given the name above every name,
And to the Comforter glory and power,
Through all ages.
Amen.

O God of supreme clemency,
Grant that we may duly meditate
On the seven sorrows of the Virgin
And the wounds of Jesus her Son.

May the many tears of the Mother of God
Bring us salvation—
Tears sufficient to wash
The sins of the whole world.

May the bitter contemplation
Of Jesus's five wounds,
And the sorrows of the Virgin,
Be eternal joy for all.
Jesus, to you be glory,
Who suffered for your servants,
With the Father and the nurturing Spirit,
Through ages everlasting.
Amen.

O Only-Begotten of the most high Father,
Look upon us with your merciful face,
Calling to the heights of glory
Magdalene's penitent heart.

The lost coin has been returned
To the royal treasury,
And the gem, cleansed of its mud,
Surpasses the stars in splendor.

Jesus, healing of wounds,
Only hope of penitents,
Through Magdalene's tears
Wash away our sins.

O most merciful Mother of God,
Bear the weeping children of Eve
From the thousand floods of life
Into the harbor of salvation.

To the one God be glory,
For his manifold grace,
Who forgives the sins
Of sinners, and grants rewards.
Amen.

O Bride of the heavenly Prince,
Intercessor for mankind,
Mary, royal Virgin,
Full of grace, you are praised.

Restrain the fuel of the flesh
And the rage of the cruel enemy;
Grant us to despise earthly things
And to desire heavenly things.

Protection of Bavaria!
Grant strength, bring help;
Rain down grace from heaven
Upon this your family.

Bind us close in
Your gentle embrace, O Mother;
Make us pleasing to your Son
And fill us with holy joy.

Jesus, to you be glory,
Who were born of the Virgin,
With the Father and the nurturing Spirit,
Through ages everlasting. Amen.

Arise! For now the harsh winter has left the earth,
All the beauty of flowers smiles in the meadows,
You who were the gracious Mother of Life,
Arise, O Mary!

As a shining lily among the thorns,
You alone tread upon the author of death, plucking
For sinners the fruit denied to our fathers
From the tree of life.

Ark fashioned not of rotting wood,
You preserve the manna, from which flows power,
By which the bones that were laid in tombs
Shall rise again animated.

A ready servant of the governing mind,
The flesh is not allowed to dissolve in corruption;
The spirit, sharer without end in the depths,
Strives toward the stars.

Arise! Seek heaven, leaning upon your Beloved,
Receive the diadem woven among the stars,
And receive the canticle resounding to your blessedness,
You who are called blessed by your sons.

Let praise be everlasting to the exalted Trinity,
Who bestowed upon you, O Virgin, the crown,
And in her providence established you
As our Queen and Mother.
Amen.

The eternal gifts of Christ,
And the glory of Bishops,
Singing the praises that are due,
Let us sing with joyful hearts.

Princes of the Churches,
Triumphant leaders in battle,
Soldiers of the heavenly court,
And true lights of the world.

The devoted faith of the Saints,
The unconquered hope of believers,
The perfect charity of Christ
Triumphs over the prince of this world.

In them is the glory of the Father,
In them is the will of the Spirit,
In them the Son exults,
And heaven is filled with joy.

You, O Redeemer, we now beseech,
That you would join to their fellowship
These servants who pray to you,
Through ages everlasting.
Amen.

O Eternal Image of the Most High,
Light, God from Light,
To you, O Redeemer, be glory,
Honor and royal power.

You alone before all ages,
The hope and center of the times,
To whom the Father by right
Entrusted the supreme scepter of the nations.

You the flower of the chaste Virgin,
The head of our lineage,
A stone falling from the summit
And by its mass covering the earth.

The condemned race of mortals,
Subject to the terrible tyrant,
Through you has broken its chains
And claims heaven for itself.

Doctor, Priest, and Lawgiver,
You bear, marked with blood,
Upon your garment: "Prince of princes
And King of kings Most High."

We willingly submit to you,
Who by right reign over all:
This is the blessedness of citizens,
To be subject to your laws.
Jesus, to you be glory,
Who govern the scepters of the world,
With the Father and the nurturing Spirit,
Through ages everlasting.
Amen.

O Eternal Ruler of the stars,
Who created whatever exists
By your great power, and govern it
With no lesser providence:

Be present to the assembled throng
Of sinners who supplicate you,
And at the coming of the twilight
Give new light to our minds.

And may your Angel, chosen
To guard us,
Be present here; that he may protect us
From the contagion of sins.

May he drive away from us
The cunning of the rival dragon;
Lest his net of deception
Ensnare unwary hearts.

May he drive far from our borders
The dread of enemies;
May he obtain peace for citizens,
And banish pestilence.

To God the Father be glory,
Who may guard through Angels
Those whom the Son has redeemed
And the Holy Spirit has anointed.
Amen.

We declare you with our proclamation,
Untouched Mother of God,
Kindly repay with your grace
Our praises to you.

We, the guilty offspring of Adam,
Are born as an infected generation;
You alone, O Virgin, are believed
Unknowing of the ancestral stain.

You crush the head of the envious dragon
Under your foot,
And you alone bring back the glory
Of an origin unstained.

O glory of the human race,
Who takes away the reproach of Eve,
Protect us suppliants,
Raise us up as we stumble.

Powerfully blunt the cunning
And assaults of the ancient serpent,
That through you we may enjoy forever
The joys of the heavenly ones.

Jesus, to you be glory,
Who were born of the Virgin,
With the Father and the nurturing Spirit,
Through ages everlasting.
Amen.

At your intercession, the blight
Of bodily sickness departs, wicked
Diseases are driven away, and the original
Gifts of health return.

Those brought by consumption, fever, and ulcer
To a dreadful death,
Victims consecrated to death,
You snatch from its jaws.

At your intercession, goods swept away
By the swollen river,
Drawn back by the power of God,
Flow upward against their course.

Since you have such power, seated
In the dwellings of heaven, we beseech you:
Answer the vows of suppliants,
And come to the aid of those who call upon you.

O Trinity ever one,
O Unity ever threefold:
Grant, through the intercession of Cantius,
Eternal rewards to us.
Amen.

Let the armies of the heavenly ones celebrate you, O Joseph,
Let all the choirs of Christians resound your name,
You who, glorious in merit, were joined
To the renowned Virgin in a chaste covenant.

When, admiring your wife swelling
With the nurturing child, you are touched with anxious doubt,
An Angel, by the breath of the Spirit from above,
Teaches you of the Child conceived.

You clasp the newborn Lord, you follow him
As a refugee to the distant regions of Egypt;
You seek and find him when lost in Jerusalem,
Mixing your joys with tears.

After death, a holy lot consecrates the rest,
And glory receives those who have earned their palm:
You, living, equal to those above, enjoy God,
Blesseder by a wondrous lot.

Spare us, O supreme Trinity, as we pray to you,
Grant that by Joseph's merits we may climb to the stars:
That at last it may be permitted us to offer you forever
A canticle of grateful praise.
Amen.

O gracious Mother of God,
We all pray to you as suppliants,
That under your shadow you may protect us
From the deceit of the devil.

Because of the ruin of our race
Through the sin of the first parent,
The supreme King raised you
To the renowned honor of Mother.

Therefore look with clemency
Upon the fallen children of Adam:
May your Son, moved by your prayer,
Lay aside his avenging wrath.
Jesus, to you be glory,
Who were born of the Virgin,
With the Father and the nurturing Spirit,
Through ages everlasting.
Amen.

O father Joseph, craftsman to be revered,
Happily hidden in obscurity in Nazareth,
With great voices and full hearts
We shall sing to you in the night.

You bear with even temper and carry silently
A royal lineage and a humble livelihood,
While with the great labor of your hands
You nourish the holy pledges.

O Craftsman, holy mirror for craftsmen,
What great examples of life you give to the people,
That toiling labor and also the workshop
May be sanctified.

Be a comfort to those who lack food in their misery;
Restraint the unbridled and put down quarrels;
May the mystical Christ grow under the shelter
Of the shadow of the homeland.

O God, three and yet one,
Who are the Father and Craftsman of all things,
Grant that we may imitate father Joseph in life,
And imitate him in death. Amen.

We call you the Mother of our Redeemer and Lord,
O beautiful Virgin,
The glory and comfort of Christians —
In time of need.

Even though the gates of hell may rage,
The ancient enemy roar, and as against God
Suggesting wrathful threats to devastate
The sacred company,

The fierce furies can do no harm
To chaste souls, upon whom the gracious Virgin,
Called upon in prayer and consenting,
Looks with favor and strengthens with heavenly might.

If so great a Patroness favors us,
The tumult of warlike crime ceases,
A thousand are laid low, and companies of thousands
Flee.

As the holy tower rises its head in Zion,
A citadel built with a firm wall,
The city of David, safe with shields
And sharp-edged soldiers;

So the mighty Virgin, by the Lord's powerful
Right hand, heaped with gifts of heaven,
Drives far from devoted servants
The blows of the demon.

May we venerate you through eternal years,
O Trinity, to be celebrated with the highest applause,
May minds praise you in faith, and tongues
With their resounding song. Amen.

You, O Christ, Prince of peace,
We confess the one Arbiter
Of minds, of hearts,
As Prince of ages and King of nations.

The wicked crowd cries out:
We do not want Christ to reign:
We, rejoicing, proclaim you
Supreme King of all.

O Christ, Prince of peace,
Subdue rebellious minds:
And gather those who have strayed from your love
Into one fold.

For this, you hang from the blood-stained tree
With arms stretched wide,
And display your heart pierced
By the dreadful lance, blazing with fire.

For this, on the altars you are hidden
Under the appearance of wine and food,
Pouring salvation upon your children
From your pierced breast.

Let the rulers of nations
Honor you publicly,
Let teachers and judges pay homage,
Let laws and arts reflect you.

May the submitted insignia of kings
Shine dedicated to you:
And with your gentle scepter subdue
The homeland and the homes of citizens.
Jesus, to you be glory,
Who govern the scepters of the world,
With the Father and the nurturing Spirit,
Through ages everlasting.
Amen.

O you, O Father's splendor and power,
O you, Jesus, life of hearts,
We who hang upon your lips
Praise you among the Angels.

A thousand dense thousands
Of leaders fight as your crown;
But Michael, the standard-bearer of salvation, victorious,
Untfurls the Cross.

He drives the dire head of the dragon
Down into the lowest tartarus,
And thunders their leader with the rebels
From the heavenly citadel.

Against the leader of pride
Let us follow this prince,
That from the throne of the Lamb
May be given us the crown of glory.

To God the Father be glory,
Who may guard through Angels
Those whom the Son has redeemed
And the Holy Spirit has anointed.
Amen.

Turn therefore the lance dipped in the blood of Christ
Against me:
Pierce heart, feet, hands,
Exact punishment from the guilty.

But I pray that the stripes
You rightly inflict for my sins,
Smeared with the divine blood,
May become healings for the spirit.

May my steps be powerless toward evil,
May my hands cease to do harm,
And may every profane ardor depart
From my wounded heart.

O piercing nails and lance,
Jesus, to you be glory,
With the Father and the nurturing Spirit,
Now and through all ages.
Amen.

Protect the land of our birth, grant
The peace of rest to the lands of Christians;
Drive the clatter of arms and the savage battles
To the Thracian borders.

And joining the forces of kings under the standard
Of the Cross, free Jerusalem from its chains,
And as avenger of innocent blood, overthrow
The strength of the enemy utterly.

You are our support, you our illustrious glory,
Look upon the service of our minds;
Willingly receive the vows of Rome, which
In pious rite sings of you and honors you.

Drive far from us the allurements of sin,
You, O God, who stand by Martyrs on the right,
One and Three: give your servants the light
With which in mercy you gladden souls.
Amen.

Let the East and West that hear
Sing your praises and your celebrated palms,
O Bishop Emygdius, pillar
And glory of your people,
Who presides over the coming of emperors.

O light adorned with the rays of heaven,
O mighty in signs, happy in merits,
Whom God was wont to employ
In great deeds of old.

Born first of a pagan father,
You immediately gave your name to the Most High,
Setting aside your ancestral riches,
Seeking the blessed Kingdom.

Enrolled then as a soldier of the heavenly Trinity,
You carry sacred warfare to the Italian lands,
You teach with the word and bestow the wondrous
Gifts of salvation.

Victor and rich with spoils, you overthrow
The temples of the gods and the images and altars,
And soon you render savage peoples
As numerous companies to Christ.

Let salvation, glory, and power be to him
Who, enthroned on the seat of heaven,
Governs the order of the whole world,
Three and One.
Amen.

That the servants of your wonders
Might be able to sing with full voice,
Free the offense of our defiled lips,
O holy John.

A messenger coming from high Olympus
Set forth to your father that you would be born great,
Your name and the course of life to be led
In order.

He, doubting the heavenly promise,
Lost the capacity for ready speech;
But you, being born, restored
The organs of the lost voice.

Lying hidden in the closed dwelling of the womb
You had sensed the King dwelling in the bridal chamber;
Hence each parent, by the merit of the child,
Reveals hidden things.

Glory be to the Father and to the begotten Son,
And to you, equal in power to both,
O Spirit, ever God, one through
All ages of time.
Amen.

The Mediator comes from high heaven,
Whom the holy prophets long sang of:
Cease mourning and bitter tears,
O daughter of Sion.

The ancient garden brought death, from which
Sin sprang forth: this new garden
Behold now brings life, where Jesus
Remains praying through the night.

He appeases the avenging wrath of the Father:
He restrains with his strong right hand
The thunderbolts that were to be hurled:
The Redeemer willingly meets suffering to expiate sin.

Thus he will tread down the hard snares of hell,
And will open the long-closed court,
Calling us back to the blessed joys
Of the eternal kingdom.

Praise and honor to the Father and to the begotten Son,
To whom is given the name above every name,
And to the Comforter glory and power,
Through all ages.
Amen.

Christ the conqueror spreads abroad
His glorious banners afar:
Come, peoples, as suppliants,
And applaud the King of kings.

Not by disasters did he subdue kingdoms;
Not by force and fear did he subject them:
Raised on high upon the tree,
By love he drew all things to himself.

O thrice blessed city
Over which Christ rightly reigns,
Which presses on to carry out
The decrees proclaimed to the world from heaven!

No impious arms blaze,
Peace ever confirms its bonds,
Concord smiles upon all,
Civic order stands secure.

Faith keeps its marriage bonds,
Youth grows up pure,
Chaste homes flourish
With domestic virtues.

May this longed-for light shine for us,
O most sweet King:
May the world in submission, when white peace is obtained,
Adore you.
Jesus, to you be glory,
Who govern the scepters of the world,
With the Father and the nurturing Spirit,
Through ages everlasting.
Amen.

Scarcely is John buried in the tomb
When signs declare him;
Through the bars of the grating
Miracles flash forth.

Here his enemies are at once
Struck with public shame,
By the avenging right hand of God
And pay penalties for their crime.

Here, to those weeping for loss of property
Or complaining about their reputation,
The thing taken away is returned,
The reputation taken away is given back.

Here the body flees sicknesses,
Time flees its vicissitudes,
Danger flees into security,
Mortality flees from death.

Here the living tongue of the Martyr,
But with the mute voice of blood
Crying, like Abel, reproves,
And reproaches the king for his crime.

O grant, O Trinity of One,
Simple Unity of Three,
That those who supplicate John
May obtain what they ask.
Amen.

Appointed by Blessed Gregory X to govern the Church of Lyon, he quickly and happily settled the grave and long-standing disputes of clergy and people. Enrolled among the Senate of the Purple-robed Fathers, he diligently prepared all things for the Ecumenical Council to be celebrated at Lyon; and then in that same Council, by the command of the Pontiff, he moderated together with Saint Bonaventure the matters of greater importance. It was especially through his efforts that the union of the Greeks with the Latins was ratified, the complaints of the secular clergy against the regulars resolved, and the statutes of the Conclave established for future elections of Roman Pontiffs.

Assailed by the devil with ambushes and deadly assaults, this valiant woman, having detected the enemy by his words, repelled him once and again, unconquered. To elude the enticement of vainglory by which she was tempted by the evil spirit, she did not cease to accuse her past conduct aloud through the streets and public squares, crying out that she deserved every punishment and shameful penalty. Restrained only by her confessor, she refrained from inflicting harm upon her own fair face, once the cause of impure love, yet chafing that her beauty could not be abolished by long mortification of the flesh. Cleansed of the stain of her sins by these and other works of great penance, and thus triumphant over herself, keeping all her senses wholly guarded against the allurements of the world, she was found worthy to enjoy frequent intimacy with the Lord. Made also a sharer in the sufferings of Christ and of his Virgin Mother — a thing she had ardently desired — she was at times deprived of all her senses and appeared truly dead. To her, therefore, as to a mistress of perfection, very many came from distant regions as well; and she, illumined by a heavenly light, discerning the secrets of hearts, the consciences of men, and even sins committed against God in remote places, with grief and tears, and burning with the greatest charity toward God and neighbor, brought forth an immense harvest of souls. She obtained healing for the sick who came to her, and liberation from demonic possession for the oppressed. She restored to life a dead child at his mother's grief. She quieted imminent tumults of war by her unceasing prayers. Finally, by works of the most eminent piety she merited grace for both the living and the dead.

Appointed by Paul IV — to whom he was most dear for his outstanding virtues — to the bishopric of Nepi and Sutri, and after two years enrolled among the cardinal priests of the Roman Church, he was then transferred by Pius IV to the church of Monreale in Piedmont. When he learned that many abuses had crept in there, he visited the entire diocese; and having set things in order, he returned to Rome. Engaged in the most weighty affairs, he rendered his decisions with apostolic freedom and constancy. After the death of Pius, elected Pontiff beyond all expectation, he changed nothing in his manner of life except his external dress. In him there was a perpetual zeal for the propagation of religion, tireless labor in restoring ecclesiastical discipline, assiduous vigilance in rooting out errors, unfailing generosity in relieving the needs of the poor, and invincible strength in vindicating the rights of the Apostolic See.
From his first novitiate, ...

Brought up from childhood in the patriarchate of the Lateran basilica, before the eyes of the Pontiffs, he advanced so greatly in every kind of virtue, learning, and ecclesiastical discipline that, once initiated into holy orders, Leo III — perceiving his virtue — placed him over the monastery of Saint Stephen; in which he was both an example to the monks subject to him and so received the pilgrims who came in crowds to the thresholds of the Apostles as to supply all their necessities and, in imitation of Christ, even to render them the most lowly services; by which offices of piety and charity he was judged most worthy to govern the Lord's flock and the whole Church.

Instructed by Saint Francis de Sales — whose spiritual direction she enjoyed — in the divine will, she left, with unconquered constancy, her own father, her father-in-law, and finally her son himself — whom, as he resisted her vocation, she did not hesitate to tread underfoot with her feet as she went forth from her house — and laid the foundations of the sacred institute of the Visitation of Holy Mary. She kept the rule of that institute with complete integrity, and was so devoted to poverty that she rejoiced when even necessities were lacking to her. She showed herself a most perfect example of Christian humility of soul and obedience, and indeed of all virtues. Setting her heart upon ever higher ascents, she bound herself by vow to the most demanding resolve always to do what she understood to be more perfect. Finally, the sacred institute of the Visitation having been spread far and wide chiefly through her efforts, and having stirred her sisters to piety and charity by word, example, and writings filled with divine wisdom as well, she departed to the Lord at Moulins, on the thirteenth day of December in the year sixteen hundred and forty-one, laden with merits and having duly received the sacraments; and Saint Vincent de Paul, at a distance, beheld her soul being carried into heaven, with Saint Francis de Sales coming forth to meet it. Her body was afterwards translated to Annecy; and Benedict XIV numbered her among the Blessed for her miracles before and after death, while Clement XIII, Supreme Pontiff, added her to the catalogue of the Saints. Clement XIV, Supreme Pontiff, commanded that her feast be celebrated by the universal Church on the twelfth day before the Kalends of September.

Sought for the episcopal office by Saint Willibrord, he declined it so as to be more free to devote himself to the salvation of unbelievers. Setting out for Germany, he drew many thousands of the Hessians away from the superstition of the devil. Summoned to Rome by Gregory the Pontiff, he was consecrated bishop after a remarkable profession of faith. Returning thence to the Germans, he thoroughly purged Hesse and Thuringia from the remnants of idolatry. For such great merits, Boniface was raised by Gregory III to the dignity of archbishop, and on his third journey to Rome was appointed legate of the Apostolic See by the Supreme Pontiff. Armed with this authority, he established four bishoprics and celebrated various synods, among which the memorable Council of Leptines is noteworthy, celebrated among the Belgians in the diocese of Cambrai, at which time he contributed greatly to the increase of faith in Belgium. Created archbishop of Mainz by Pope Zachary, at the command of the Pontiff himself he anointed Pepin as king of the Franks. After the death of Saint Willibrord, he undertook the governance of the church of Utrecht, first through Eoban and then through himself, when he had been released from the church of Mainz and resided at Utrecht. Setting out again to preach the Gospel to the Frisians who had relapsed into idolatry, while engaged in his pastoral duty he was slain in a bloody massacre near the river Borne together with Eoban his co-bishop and many others, and was crowned with the palm of martyrdom. The body of Saint Boniface was translated to Mainz and, as he himself had requested while living, was laid to rest in the monastery of Fulda which he had built, where it became illustrious by many miracles. Pius IX, Supreme Pontiff, extended his Office and Mass to the universal Church.

Called to Rome by Supreme Pontiff Urban IV, he composed by his command the ecclesiastical Office to be celebrated on the solemnity of Corpus Christi; but he refused the honors offered to him and the archbishopric of Naples, even when it was tendered by Clement IV. He did not cease from the preaching of the divine word; and while doing so through the octave of Easter in the basilica of Saint Peter, he freed from a flow of blood a woman who had touched the hem of his garment. Sent by Blessed Gregory X to the Council of Lyon, he fell ill in the monastery of Fossanova, where, though sick, he expounded the Song of Songs. There he died at the age of fifty, in the year of salvation twelve hundred and seventy-four, on the Nones of March. He was also renowned by miracles after death; and upon their verification, he was numbered among the Saints by John XXII, in the year thirteen hundred and twenty-three, his body having afterwards been translated to Toulouse at the command of Blessed Urban V. Compared with the holy angelic spirits no less in innocence than in genius, he rightly obtained the name of Angelic Doctor, confirmed to him by the authority of Saint Pius V. And Leo XIII, most gladly receiving the petitions and desires of nearly all the sacred pastors of the Catholic world — especially to repel the blight of so many philosophical systems straying from truth, for the advancement of the sciences and the common benefit of the human race — declared and established him, by apostolic letters and on the advice of the Congregation of Sacred Rites, as the heavenly patron of all Catholic schools.

Courteously receiving Irenaeus, a most learned man, as the bearer of letters from the Church of Lyon on certain questions addressed to him, he laid open for him the apostolic traditions which the Roman Church had kept inviolate. He condemned the superstitious xerophagies of the Montanists; he prescribed the best laws for the proper conduct of ecclesiastical trials; and he expelled from the Church entirely Marcion and Valentinus, who had repeatedly relapsed.

He most steadfastly shrank from the ecclesiastical dignities offered to him; but, compelled by the authority of Clement XIII, he undertook the governance of the church of Sant'Agata dei Goti. As bishop, he changed only his outward dress, but not his austere manner of life. The same frugality, the utmost zeal for Christian discipline, intense dedication to restraining vices and warding off errors, and diligence in discharging the other pastoral duties continued unchanged. Liberal toward the poor, he distributed all the revenues of the church to them, and, when the price of grain rose sharply, he gave even his household furniture to feed the hungry. Made all things to all men, he brought religious women to a more perfect form of life and arranged for the founding of a monastery of the nuns of his congregation. Having resigned the episcopate on account of grave and habitual illnesses, he returned poor to his students, from whom he had departed poor. At last, though broken in body by old age, labors, long-standing arthritis, and other most grave illnesses, yet ever more joyful in spirit, he never ceased to discuss or write of heavenly things, until, at ninety years of age, on the Kalends of August, in the year seventeen hundred and eighty-seven, at Nocera dei Pagani, amid the tears of his students, he breathed his last most peacefully. Renowned after this for virtues and miracles, Pius VII, Supreme Pontiff, enrolled him in the catalogue of the Blessed in the year eighteen hundred and sixteen; and Gregory XVI, resplendent with new signs, solemnly added him to the catalogue of the Saints on the Feast of the Most Holy Trinity, in the year eighteen hundred and thirty-nine. Finally, Pius IX, Supreme Pontiff, on the advice of the Congregation of Sacred Rites, declared him a Doctor of the universal Church.

Invited by him, Victorinus — a native of Aquitaine — composed with most careful inquiry the Paschal cycle. Most zealous for ecclesiastical discipline, he wished no bishop to be consecrated in any church without the consent of his Metropolitan, nor any bishop to be transferred from his own church to another, nor the boundaries established by the Fathers to be overstepped. He appointed Leontius, bishop of Arles, as his vicar over the Gauls, delegating to him the care of assembling the bishops each year. He forbade the alienation of church properties that were neither desolate nor useless — by which the needs of many might be supplied — unless the reason for the alienation had first been set forth before a council; and he enacted many other holy decrees in the synod which he convened at Santa Maria Maggiore.

Called to Rome by the same Gregory and honored with the offices of chaplain, penitentiary, and confessor, he at Gregory's command reduced the decrees of the Roman Pontiffs, scattered through various councils and epistles, into a single volume of Decretals. He most steadfastly refused the archbishopric of Tarragona when it was offered to him by the Pontiff himself, and he voluntarily resigned the general mastership of the entire Order of Preachers, which he had administered most holily for two years. He was the one who urged King James of Aragon to establish the office of the Holy Inquisition in his kingdoms. He performed many miracles, among which the most celebrated was that, wishing to return from the island of Majorca to Barcelona, he spread his cloak upon the waters and covered one hundred and sixty miles in six hours, and entered his monastery with its doors closed. At last, nearly a hundred years of age and laden with virtues and merits, he fell asleep in the Lord, in the year of salvation twelve hundred and seventy-five. Clement VIII numbered him among the Saints.

Designated bishop of his homeland by Eugene IV — an honor he had resisted with great determination — he bore it with still greater distinction. For, having changed little in his accustomed manner of life, he retained at table, in furnishings, and in bed the poverty he had always cultivated. He kept a small household at home, saying that he had a large one elsewhere — meaning the poor of Christ. At whatever hour he was approached, he was ready for all, lifting everyone with fatherly charity, not refusing even to burden himself with debt lest the needs of the poor go unmet. Asked in what hope he did so, he answered: 'In my Lord's, who can easily repay for me.' That this hope was not put to shame, divine providence declared continually by sending unforeseen aid. He built several monasteries of virgins, whom he also guided to a more perfect manner of life by his watchful care. He was most earnestly devoted to drawing matrons away from worldly pomp and the vanity of ornament, and to the reform of ecclesiastical discipline and morals — worthy indeed to be called by that same Eugene, in the presence of the cardinals, the glory and ornament of bishops, and to be named by his successor Nicholas V, once the title had been transferred from the city of Grado, the first Patriarch of Venice.

From the most holy Pontiff Phocas he obtained the noble temple of Rome known as the Pantheon; having consecrated it with Christian rites, he converted it into a church dedicated to the Virgin Mother of God and the holy Martyrs. To lend it greater sanctity, he arranged for an incredible quantity of sacred relics, brought up from various catacombs, to be carried in and laid to rest beside the high altar. Finally, renowned for virtue and merits under Heraclius, he fell asleep in the Lord on the eighth day before the Kalends of June, and was buried in the Vatican.

From his very first novitiate, he seemed already to have attained something perfect and complete. He endured with unconquered heart the adversities stirred up against him by the devil. Meanwhile, Jesus was enriching his victorious bride with the most abundant gifts of his grace. It is attested by many witnesses that she was marked with the sacred stigmata, likewise adorned with a crown of deeply implanted thorns and the emblems of the Passion upon her heart, and refreshed by almost unceasing ecstasies. All these things brought Veronica an abundant harvest of troubles; for there were those who attributed everything to evil arts and declared her most deserving of every penalty and infamous punishment. The most valiant virgin bore all this joyfully, desiring indeed that still crueler things should daily be heaped upon her to be endured for her Spouse fixed to the Cross. Cast into a dark prison, she was made subject to the lowest of the sisters, who was commanded to treat her harshly; nor did she love life unless it were continually harassed by the greatest tribulations: even though at times she lamented that she had been abandoned and as it were forsaken by her Spouse, which was for her the most bitter of all torments.

Abdon and Sennen, Persians, were accused under the Emperor Decius of having buried in their own estate the bodies of Christians that had been cast out unburied. By order of the emperor they were seized and commanded to sacrifice to the gods. When they neglected to do so and most steadfastly proclaimed Jesus Christ as God, they were handed over into close custody; and Decius, on his return to Rome, led them bound in his triumphal procession. When in the City they were dragged before the idols, they detested and spat upon them. For this reason, they were cast to bears and lions; but the wild beasts did not dare to touch them. Finally, slain by the sword, they were dragged by their feet bound before the statue of the sun. Their bodies, secretly carried away from there, were buried by the deacon Quirinus in his own house.

Having completed his novitiate with great fervor of spirit and having been ordained a priest, he was sent by the Apostolic See to the northern provinces of Europe. After establishing the first house of his Congregation in Warsaw, Poland, and associating several companions with himself, it is marvelous with what copious fruit he fulfilled his priestly duties there for more than twenty years, refusing no labor — whether to call Catholics back to good morals and the practice of piety, or to bring heretics and Jews to the true faith. He also did much for the religious formation of youth. Moved with pity for the condition of orphans, he built a hospice where he nourished the most wretched with fatherly charity; at times seen begging alms on their behalf, and not even turning his face from those who rebuked and spat upon him. Yet amid all these cares, ever walking before God, singularly devoted to the Virgin Mother of God — whose Rosary he recited without cease — upright, simple, humble, affable and kind to all, he continually shone before everyone as a model of holiness.

He was of admirable abstinence and continence; he was content with one tunic; most diligent in observing fasts; assiduous in prayer, in which he often spent entire nights. He preserved his virginity perpetually. Having built monasteries, he so ordered the monastic life that he admirably united at once the advantages of the solitary and the active life. He wrote many things learnedly; and no one, as Gregory of Nazianzus testifies, explained the books of Holy Scripture more truly or more abundantly. He died on the Kalends of January, by then alive only in spirit, and seeming to consist of nothing besides bones and skin, with no other bodily substance remaining.

He was of admirable abstinence; he fasted very frequently, content only with bread and water, sometimes with lupins alone. He subdued his body by night vigils, the harshest hair-shirt, and constant scourgings. He was most devoted to humility and meekness. He never interrupted prayer and the preaching of God's word, however much occupied by the most grave cares. He built many churches, monasteries, and colleges. He wrote many works, most useful especially for the instruction of bishops; and through his efforts also the Catechism for parish priests was produced. Finally, he withdrew to the solitude of Mount Varallo, where the mysteries of the Lord's Passion are represented to the life in sculpted images; and there, spending some days in voluntary mortification — a harsh life made sweet by meditation on the sufferings of Christ — he fell into a fever. Returning to Milan, with his illness growing worse, covered with ashes and sackcloth and with his eyes fixed upon the image of the Crucified, he passed to heaven at the age of forty-seven, in the year of the Lord fifteen hundred and eighty-four, on the third day before the Nones of November. Paul V, Supreme Pontiff, renowned for miracles, enrolled him in the catalogue of the Saints.

He was of such great abstinence and continence that, by the constancy of his fasting, all sense of food seemed to be almost extinguished in him. For having spent the daytime in monastic exercises, in teaching, and in answering various questions on religion, he took from the remainder of the night the sleep that was due, so as to refresh his mind with divine meditations, which he watered with a perpetual flood of tears. Elected prior of the monastery, he so won over the envious brethren by charity, humility, and prudence that those whom he had received as rivals he restored as friends to himself and to God, with the greatest benefit to regular observance. The abbot having died, and he himself — though unwilling — elected in his place, he shone everywhere with such fame for learning and holiness that not only kings and bishops held him in reverence, but also Saint Gregory VII held him dear; the latter, then assailed by great persecutions, sent him letters full of affection, commending himself and the Catholic Church to his prayers.

Having received from Constantine Pogonatus letters written to his predecessor Donus for the convening of an ecumenical council — to resolve the long-standing schism afflicting the Church and to define the controversies of faith, which had aroused the greatest storms and ruin throughout nearly the whole East — he took care to hold provincial synods in the West, in which the cause of the Monothelites might be examined and their errors condemned.

She therefore approached not the head of the Lord, but his feet. And she who had long walked ill was now seeking the righteous path. First she poured forth tears from her heart, and washed the Lord's feet with the tribute of confession; she dried them with her hair, kissed them, anointed them. In silence she spoke; she brought forth not words, but showed devotion. Because, therefore, she touched the Lord by pouring, kissing, wiping, and anointing his feet, the Pharisee who had invited the Lord Jesus Christ — being of that race of proud men of whom the prophet Isaiah says: 'Who say, Depart far from me; do not touch me, for I am clean' — supposed that the Lord did not know the woman.

Receive another lesson. The Magi came by one road and returned by another. For those who had seen Christ and understood Christ returned certainly better than they had come. There are indeed two roads: one that leads to destruction; the other that leads to the kingdom. The former belongs to sinners, and leads to Herod; the latter is Christ, by which one returns to the homeland. For this sojourning is temporal, as it is written: My soul has been a sojourner for a long time.

6 And when Herod was ready to produce him, in that same night, Peter was sleeping between two soldiers, and was bound with two chains. And the guards before the door were keeping watch over the prison.
7 And behold, an Angel of the Lord stood near, and a light shined forth in the cell. And tapping Peter on the side, he awakened him, saying, 'Rise up, quickly.' And the chains fell from his hands.
8 Then the Angel said to him: 'Dress yourself, and put on your boots.' And he did so. And he said to him, 'Wrap your garment around yourself and follow me.'

9 And going out, he followed him. And he did not know this truth: that this was being done by an Angel. For he thought he was seeing a vision.
10 And passing by the first and second guards, they came to the iron gate which leads into the city; and it opened for them by itself. And going out, they passed through one street, and immediately the Angel withdrew from him.
11 And Peter, returning to himself, said: 'Now I know, truly, that the Lord sent his Angel, and that he rescued me from the hand of Herod and from all the expectation of the people of the Jews.'

48 Then the Gentiles, upon hearing this, were gladdened, and they were glorifying the Word of the Lord. And as many as believed were preordained to eternal life.
49 Now the word of the Lord was disseminated throughout the entire region.
50 But the Jews incited some devout and honest women, and the leaders of the city. And they stirred up a persecution against Paul and Barnabas. And they drove them away from their parts.
51 But they, shaking the dust from their feet against them, went on to Iconium.
52 The disciples were likewise filled with gladness and with the Holy Spirit.

5 And when they had arrived at Salamis, they were preaching the Word of God in the synagogues of the Jews. And they also had John in the ministry.
6 And when they had traveled throughout the entire island, even to Paphos, they found a certain man, a magician, a false prophet, a Jew, whose name was Bar-Jesu,
7 who was with the proconsul, Sergius Paulus, a prudent man. This man, summoning Barnabas and Saul, wanted to hear the Word of God.
8 But Elymas the magician (for so his name is translated) stood against them, seeking to turn the proconsul away from the Faith.

9 Then Saul, who is also called Paul, having been filled with the Holy Spirit, looked intently at him,
10 and he said: 'So full of every deceit and of all falsehoods, son of the devil, enemy of all justice, you never cease to subvert the righteous ways of the Lord!
11 And now, behold, the hand of the Lord is upon you. And you will be blinded, not seeing the sun for a length of time.' And immediately a mist and darkness fell upon him, and going about, he sought someone to lead him by the hand.
12 Then the proconsul, when he had seen what was done, believed, being in wonder over the doctrine of the Lord.
13 And when Paul and those who were with him had sailed from Paphos, they arrived at Perga in Pamphylia. Then John departed from them and returned to Jerusalem.

1 Now it happened in Iconium that they entered together into the synagogue of the Jews, and they spoke in such a way that a copious multitude of both Jews and Greeks believed.
2 Yet truly, the Jews who were unbelieving had incited and enflamed the souls of the Gentiles against the brothers.
3 And so, they remained for a long time, acting faithfully in the Lord, offering testimony to the Word of his grace, providing signs and wonders done by their hands.

11 Then, as he held on to Peter and John, all the people ran to them at the portico, which is called Solomon's, in astonishment.
12 But Peter, seeing this, responded to the people: 'Men of Israel, why do you wonder at this? Or why do you stare at us, as if it were by our own strength or power that we caused this man to walk?
13 The God of Abraham and the God of Isaac and the God of Jacob, the God of our fathers, has glorified his Son Jesus, whom you, indeed, handed over and denied before the face of Pilate, when he was giving judgment to release him.
14 Then you denied the Holy and Just One, and petitioned for a murderous man to be given to you.
15 Truly, it was the Author of Life whom you put to death, whom God raised from the dead, to whom we are witnesses.
16 And by faith in his name, this man, whom you have seen and known, has confirmed his name. And faith through him has given this man complete health in the sight of you all.'

Feeling himself called for a long time to the most austere manner of life, he had grown accustomed to passing his days in rigid fasting or on hard bread alone, to giving his weary limbs brief rest on bare planks with a pillow of wooden fragments, to scourging himself with a discipline, and to spending several hours in prayer on bended knee before the most august Sacrament of the Eucharist. Moreover, reckoning that God was calling him to some stricter cenobitic institute, he betook himself first to the Trappists, then to the Carthusians, and finally to the Cistercians. But on account of his slight bodily constitution and the ailments he had contracted, he was compelled to depart from each in turn; for God so disposed it that the blessed young man should become a spectacle to the world, to Angels, and to men, of a stricter following of the Cross of Christ in the midst of the people. For when, by more fervent prayer, he had implored the divine light, he understood through a most clear interior locution that he must follow the arduous footsteps of Saint Alexis and lead a most harsh life in holy pilgrimages. With the approval therefore of the director of his conscience, at the age of twenty-two, he undertook holy and very lengthy journeys — on foot, covered with a worn garment and a rough little cap, girded with a cord and poorly shod, without money and destitute of all things, living only on alms offered to him, and carrying a sack loaded with stones, that he might make the toils of pilgrimage heavier for himself. In this manner he traversed many regions of Europe several times, visiting the holier places everywhere, never changing his garments, enduring heat, cold, and rain, sleeping at night most often under the open sky, and keeping away from the main road and from inns so as to avoid dangers and to turn his mind more freely toward God.

To him, together with Venerius, a priest of the Church of Milan, the African synod sent a bishop as legate, so that the same African Church, which was in the greatest need of sacred ministers, might be assisted, lest in the various nearly lifeless communities — in which not so much as a single deacon or literate person was to be found — innumerable souls should perish. To this likeness of little children, most beloved, the mystery of today's feast invites you; and this form of humility the child Savior, adored by the Magi, instills in you — who, to show his imitators what glory he was preparing for them, at the time of his birth consecrated those brought forth to martyrdom; so that those born in Bethlehem, where Christ was born, might become, through the fellowship of age, sharers in his Passion. Let humility therefore be loved, and let all pride be shunned by the faithful. Let each prefer the other to himself, and let no one seek what is his own, but what belongs to another; so that, when the impulse of goodwill shall have abounded in all things, the venom of envy may be found in none — since he who exalts himself shall be humbled, and he who humbles himself shall be exalted, as Jesus Christ our Lord himself testifies, who lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit, God for ever and ever. Amen.

Summoned to the Council of Lyons by Blessed Gregory X and created Cardinal Bishop of Albano, he rendered outstanding service in the difficult affairs of the council; through which both the dissensions of the schism were resolved and the dogmas of the Church were vindicated. In the midst of these labors, in the fifty-third year of his age, and in the year of salvation one thousand two hundred and seventy-four, he departed to the great grief of all, honored with funeral rites by the entire council, the Roman Pontiff himself being present. Sixtus IV, who had declared him illustrious by very many and very great miracles, enrolled him in the number of the Saints. He wrote many works, in which, joining the highest learning with the ardor of devotion, he moves the reader by his teaching; wherefore by Sixtus V he was deservedly honored with the title of Seraphic Doctor.
