Though still a novice, not yet having made solemn vows, he already seemed to have attained the summit of religious perfection. A diligent cultivator of obedience, he was ready at not only the word but even the nod of his superior; and calling himself the beast of burden of the monastery, he always seized upon the most menial services, and received mockeries and insults with a cheerful countenance. How zealous he was for poverty, God himself declared by a striking proof. For as he went begging from door to door through streets and squares to feed his brothers — a service he performed for forty years with feet almost always bare — when one day he felt himself weighed down by an unusual burden, he searched his sack and found a coin secretly thrown in; which he threw away and trod upon, not without indignation, and departed thence brisk and light. The chastity which he preserved unblemished until death — he was therefore called holy in body and spirit by Paul V — he safeguarded by watchful custody of his eyes and voluntary bodily chastisement, bloodying himself daily with the harshest discipline, bound with an iron hairshirt, and also repeatedly visiting the seven basilicas of the City. He sometimes added to the fasts of the Order by total abstinence. His bed was a place of pain rather than of rest: for he took his brief sleep with bare knees bent upon a plank, and a bundle of twigs placed under his head.

He added bodily affliction to the custody of his senses. He bore three fasts each week, enduring them most often on a little bread and water, though the fasting of that period could appear to have been continual, since his meals scarcely amounted to an ounce. Often he also bloodied himself three times a day with ropes or chains: he supplemented his disciplines at times with dogs' leashes, his hairshirts with horses' spurs. He secretly roughened his soft bed by inserting fragments of planks, also so that he might be more quickly roused to prayer; for he passed a great part of the night — even in the depth of winter — covered only with a linen shift, his knees placed on the ground, or lying prone from weakness, in the contemplation of heavenly things. During the day also he remained immovable in that contemplation for three, four, five hours at a time, until he had completed at least one hour with his mind nowhere distracted. The reward of this constancy was a stability of mind that during prayer wandered nowhere else, indeed was fixed on God as in a perpetual ecstasy. That finally he might cleave to him alone, having overcome his father after three years of most bitter struggle, and having transferred the right to his ancestral principality to his brother, he joined the Society of Jesus at Rome, to which he had been summoned by a heavenly voice at Madrid.

The men he had gathered to himself in this grave and arduous work he first received in his own house; then, having established them in a more suitable dwelling, he formed them excellently in his discipline by those laws and wise constitutions that were afterward confirmed by Benedict XIII. Out of humility of spirit and love of poverty he first renounced his canonry and distributed all his goods to the poor; and later, what he had several times tried in vain, he voluntarily laid down the governance of the institute he had founded. Yet, remitting nothing meanwhile of his solicitude for the brothers, and with the schools opened by him now in several places, he began to devote himself more intensely to God. Afflicting himself continually with fasts, scourgings, and other austerities, he spent his nights in prayer. Until at last, conspicuous in all virtues — especially obedience, zeal for fulfilling the divine will, and love and devotion toward the Apostolic See — laden with merits, having duly received the Sacraments, he fell asleep in the Lord at the age of sixty-eight. Leo XIII, Supreme Pontiff, enrolled him in the catalogue of the Blessed; and Pius XII appointed him the principal heavenly Patron before God of all teachers engaged in the instruction of boys and young people.

Afra, therefore, well known for the fame of her past life, was herself also summoned to examination among the other Christians; and she replied undauntedly to Gaius the judge, who was striving to turn her away from the profession of the Christian faith — first by flatteries and promises, then also by threats, to induce her to return to the worship of Venus — that she would by no means be received by Christ because of the sins she had committed; that she was ready to subject her body, with which she had long sinned against the injury of Almighty God, to all the atrocity of torments; and that Christ did not will the death of sinners, but that in his goodness and mercy he easily pardons anyone returning to a better way of life. When the judge heard these words, understanding that she could by no reason be led away from such great confidence of soul toward God, he condemned her to the flames. The ministers therefore dragged her to the island of the Licus river and bound her to a stake: there, with faggots piled on all sides, by the very brief torment of fire she was translated to the eternal joys of the heavenly homeland. Her body, unharmed by the fire and resplendent with miracles, rests at Augsburg in the church of Saint Ulrich.

Afra, given to the worship of idols and sunk in the filth of shameful deeds, received as her guest the Bishop Narcissus, who was fleeing to Augsburg of the Vindelici; and when she saw him spending the night with his deacon in psalms and prayers, moved by so great an example and wearied by her own impurity, she immediately threw herself at the feet of Narcissus and obtained from him the sacred washing of Baptism. Then she also enkindled her mother Hilaria and three handmaids with the same zeal for the Christian faith; these Narcissus illumined at the sacred font, having first appointed a fast of seven days. When, however, Afra was advancing day by day in the faith she had received, she was seized by the prefect Gaius and taken to the temple of Venus, and commanded to sacrifice to the gods. When she declared that she rendered worship not to demons but to the one true God, at the command of the prefect she was led together with her mother and handmaids to an island of the river called the Licus, bound to a stake, and burned with a slow fire. Her body, honorably buried, is preserved at Augsburg.

Let us therefore put off the old man with his deeds; and having obtained a share in the birth of Christ, let us renounce the works of the flesh. Acknowledge, O Christian, your dignity; and having been made a sharer in the divine nature, do not return by a degenerate manner of life to the old baseness. Remember whose head and whose body you are a member of. Remember that you have been rescued from the power of darkness and translated into the light and kingdom of God.

Agapitus of Palestrina, fifteen years old, under the Emperor Aurelian, most ardently desirous of martyrdom, after having been beaten for a very long time with cords by command of the emperor on account of his steadfast adherence to the faith, and then thrown into a foul prison so that he might taste nothing at all for four days, was brought out from custody. And, with burning coals placed on his head, giving thanks to God, he was beaten again, then suspended naked by his feet so that a great smoke from a fire beneath overpowered his mouth. Then boiling water was poured over his belly, and his jaws were broken. At that time the judge fell from his tribunal and died shortly after. When the emperor was enraged by this, and commanded the holy young man to be thrown to the wild beasts — which did not dare to touch him — he was beheaded at Palestrina.

Agatha, born of noble parents in Sicily, under the persecution of the Emperor Decius achieved a glorious martyrdom at Catania. For when Quintianus, the praetor of Sicily, had tried in every way in vain to assault her chastity, Agatha, taken up on the charge of the Christian superstition, was first struck with blows, then stretched on the rack with burning plates applied, then had her breast cut off. Soon after, cast into prison, she was healed by the Blessed Apostle Peter, who appeared to her by night. Summoned again by the praetor and persevering in the confession of Christ, she was rolled over sharp potsherds and burning coals placed beneath her. But when the city was violently shaken by a great earthquake, Quintianus, fearing the uproar of the people, secretly ordered her to be carried back half-dead to the prison; where shortly afterward she passed to heaven, on the Nones of February.

Agatha the Virgin, born of noble parents in Sicily — whom the people of Palermo and Catania each claim as their citizen — under the persecution of the Emperor Decius obtained the crown of a glorious martyrdom at Catania. For when she was commended equally for the praise of beauty and chastity, Quintianus the praetor of Sicily was seized with love for her. But when, having assaulted her chastity in every way, he could not bring Agatha to his opinion, he handed her over, taken up on the charge of the Christian superstition, to a certain woman named Aphrodisia to be corrupted. When she could not by the association of Aphrodisia be removed from her constancy in keeping the Christian faith and preserving her virginity, that woman reported to Quintianus that she was wasting her effort on Agatha. Wherefore he ordered the Virgin to be brought before him; and said: "Are you not ashamed, born of noble birth, to lead the humble and servile life of Christians?" To which Agatha replied: "Far more excellent is Christian humility and servitude than the riches and pride of kings."

Alexius, most noble of the Romans, out of an exceptional love for Jesus Christ, on the first night of his marriage, by a particular warning of God, left his spouse untouched and undertook a pilgrimage to the most illustrious churches of the world. Having spent seventeen years unknown in these journeys, at Edessa, a city of Syria, when his name was made known through an image of the most holy Virgin Mary, he departed thence by ship. Having arrived at the port of Rome, he was received by his father as an unknown poor stranger; and with him, unknown to all, after he had lived for seventeen years, leaving behind a written account of his name, family, and the whole course of his life, he passed to heaven, under Innocent I, the Supreme Pontiff.

Albert, surnamed the Great on account of his singular learning, born at Lauingen on the Danube in Swabia, was diligently educated from boyhood. Departing from his homeland for the sake of his studies and staying at Padua, he sought to be enrolled in the Dominican Order at the urging of Blessed Jordan, the Master General of the Order of Preachers, while his uncle fruitlessly opposed him. Admitted among the brothers, he excelled in religious observance and devotion, most deeply loved the Blessed Virgin Mary, and burned with zeal for souls. He was sent to Cologne to complete his studies. Afterward he was appointed lector at Hildesheim, Freiburg, Regensburg, and Strasbourg. He won great renown at the chair in Paris. He had Thomas Aquinas as a beloved disciple, and was the first to perceive and proclaim the greatness of his mind. At Anagni, before the Supreme Pontiff Alexander IV, he refuted William, who was attacking the mendicant Orders with impious audacity, and was afterward appointed Bishop of Regensburg. He conducted himself admirably in offering counsel and composing discord, so that he was rightly called a peacemaker. He wrote very many works in almost every branch of learning, especially sacred learning, and composed outstanding pieces on the admirable Sacrament of the Altar. Most illustrious in virtues and miracles, he died in the Lord in the year one thousand two hundred and eighty. Pius XI increased the veneration long rendered to him in several dioceses and in the Order of Preachers by the authority of the Roman Pontiffs, and willingly accepting the vote of the Congregation of Sacred Rites, extended his feast — with the added title of Doctor — to the universal Church; and Pius XII appointed him as heavenly Patron before God of all those who cultivate the natural sciences.

Albert, surnamed the Great on account of his singular learning, born at Lauingen on the Danube in Swabia, was diligently educated from boyhood. Departing from his homeland for the sake of his studies and staying at Padua, he sought to be enrolled in the Dominican Order, the fruitless opposition of his uncle notwithstanding, at the urging of Blessed Jordan, Master General of the Order of Preachers. Admitted among the brothers, dedicated to God in all things, he excelled in religious observance and devotion, burning with filial and most tender devotion toward the Blessed Virgin Mary. He so ordered the whole pattern of his life — by preceding study with prayer — that, having professed the apostolic religious life, he might become a fit minister for preaching the Word of God and procuring the salvation of souls. Soon sent to Cologne to complete his studies, he made such progress that he investigated and advanced almost all the secular sciences more diligently than any of his contemporaries; and from the fountain of the divine law, as Alexander IV testifies, he drank such healthful streams of doctrine that its fullness thrived in his breast.

Alexander the Roman, son of a father named Alexander from the village of Caput Tauri, young indeed in age but incomparable in holiness and most illustrious in faith, obtained the Apostolic See after Evaristus. In memory of the Passion of Christ, he was the first to add to the sacrifice of the Mass: "Who the day before he suffered," up to the words "This is my Body." He instituted that only bread and wine should be offered in the mystery, and that in the consecration of the Body and Blood of the Lord the wine should be mixed with water, on account of the blood and water which flowed from the side of Jesus Christ. He likewise decreed that blessed water mixed with salt, with sacred prayers intervening, should perpetually be kept both in churches and in rooms, for the driving away of demons. Moreover, being a most fervent preacher of the Christian faith, during his lifetime he was wondrously diligent in this, that by his teaching and the example of his life he might lead to the true religion of Christ as many as he could.

Alexander the Roman, governing the Church under the Emperor Hadrian, converted a great part of the Roman nobility to Christ. He instituted that only bread and wine should be offered in the mystery; and commanded that wine should be mixed with water, on account of the blood and water which flowed from the side of Jesus Christ; and in the Canon of the Mass he added, "Who the day before he suffered." He likewise decreed that blessed water, mixed with salt, should be perpetually kept in the church, and used in rooms to drive away demons. He held his see for ten years, five months, and twenty days, illustrious for the holiness of his life and his salutary ordinances. He was crowned with martyrdom together with the priests Eventius and Theodulus, and was buried on the Via Nomentana, at the third milestone from the City, in the same place where he had been beheaded; having ordained at different times in December six priests, two deacons, and five bishops in various places. Their bodies, afterward translated to the City, were deposited in the church of Saint Sabina. On the same day falls the blessed death of Saint Juvenal, Bishop of Narni; who, having won many for Christ in that city by his holiness and learning, rested in peace, renowned for miracles, and was honorably buried there.

Alexius the Roman, son of the senator Euphemianus, educated most devoutly and generously in his father's house from his tender years, and so inflamed by the assiduous exercise of Christian virtues with love for Jesus Christ, that he resolved to set aside the nobility of his family, the extent of his patrimony, and the allurements and pleasures of the world for the sake of imitating him. Therefore on the first night of his marriage, by a particular warning of God, he left untouched the wife taken according to his parents' wishes.

Alphonsus Maria de Liguori, born of noble parents at Naples, had scarcely grown up when he delighted in serving the sick in public hospitals and in devoting himself to unceasing prayer in churches. Obeying his father, he undertook the advocacy of cases; but, having experienced the dangers of the forum, he voluntarily gave up that manner of life. Having renounced the ancestral right of primogeniture and been ordained a priest, he rushed with such zeal against vices that he accomplished the conversion of great numbers of lost souls. Having taken pity especially on the poor and country folk, he founded the Congregation of the Most Holy Redeemer for their evangelization. And lest he should ever turn aside from his purpose, he bound himself by a perpetual vow to waste no time. A constant contemplator of the Lord's Passion and of the Holy Eucharist, and an outstanding devotee of the Mother of God, he was more than once refreshed by the signs of her heavenly protection. He published many works filled with sacred learning and devotion, by which he strove to win souls for Christ. He most steadfastly shrank from ecclesiastical dignities offered to him; yet, compelled by apostolic authority, he undertook the governance of the church of Sant'Agata dei Goti. Generous to the poor, made all things to all men, he brought religious women to a more perfect manner of living. Having resigned his episcopate on account of grave and habitual illnesses, he returned to his own. At last, a nonagenarian, resplendent in innocence of life and penance, he passed away most peacefully in the year one thousand seven hundred and eighty-seven. Pius IX declared him Doctor of the universal Church, and Pius XII appointed him the heavenly Patron before God of all confessors and moralists.

Alphonsus Maria de Liguori, born of noble parents at Naples, gave from his earliest age unmistakable signs of holiness. When his parents, while he was still an infant, brought him to Saint Francis de Girolamo of the Society of Jesus, the latter, having prayed over him, declared that he would live to the age of ninety, would be raised to episcopal dignity, and would be of the greatest benefit to the Church. From his very boyhood, averse to games, he drew noble young men to Christian modesty by word and example. As a youth, having enrolled in pious confraternities, he delighted in serving the sick in public hospitals, in devoting himself to unceasing prayer in churches, and in frequenting the sacred mysteries. He so joined devotion to literary studies that, scarcely sixteen years of age, he obtained the doctorate of both laws at his native university. Obeying his father, he undertook the advocacy of cases; and though he had gained great praise in that function, yet having experienced the dangers of the forum, he voluntarily gave up that manner of life. Having therefore spurned the distinguished marriage proposed to him by his father, having renounced the ancestral right of primogeniture, and having hung his sword at the altar of Our Lady of Mercy, he dedicated himself to the divine ministries. Ordained a priest, he rushed with such zeal against vices that, fulfilling the apostolic duty and flying hither and thither, he accomplished the conversion of great numbers of lost souls. Having taken pity especially on the poor and country folk, he founded the Congregation of the Most Holy Redeemer, who, following the Redeemer himself, might evangelize the poor through fields, villages, and hamlets.

The precious death of other Martyrs earned praise in the confession; that of these pleased in its completion; because at the very outset of a life just beginning, the very one who put the end to their present life gave them its end as the beginning of glory. Those whom the impiety of Herod tore from their mothers' nursing breasts; who are rightly called the flowers of the Martyrs, whom, springing up in the midst of the cold of unbelief like the first bursting buds of the Church, a certain frost of persecution nipped.

One mother was crying out, when the exacting robber was not compelling the mother to be slain along with her little child: "Why do you send me away empty? If there is fault, it is mine: if there is no crime, join death, and set the mother free." Another was saying: "What do you seek? You seek one, and you kill many, and you cannot reach the one who is the only One." Still another was crying against this: "Come now, come, Savior of the world, how long shall you be sought? You fear no one: let the soldier see you and not kill our infants." The lamentation of the mothers was mingled together, and the offering of the little ones was passing to heaven.

Some wish this man to be Zechariah, who was slain by King Joash of Judah between the temple and the altar, as the Book of Kings relates. But it must be noted that Zechariah is not the son of Barachiah, but the son of the priest Jehoiada; wherefore Scripture also records: Joash did not remember the kindness that Jehoiada his father had done to him. Since therefore we hold that it is Zechariah and the place of the slaying agrees, we ask: why is he said to be the son of Barachiah and not of Jehoiada? Barachiah in our language means "Blessed of the Lord," and the justice of the priest Jehoiada is indicated by the Hebrew name. In the Gospel used by the Nazarenes, instead of "son of Barachiah" we find written "son of Jehoiada."

When other monasteries were then established, the holiness of William, growing more illustrious day by day, drew many men to him from all sides, attracted by the fragrance of his sanctity and the fame of his miracles. For the mute received speech, the deaf hearing, the withered their vigor, and those suffering from various and incurable diseases recovered their health through his intercession. He changed water into wine, and performed many other wonders; among which this is not to be passed over in silence, that a little woman sent to tempt his chastity rolled herself unharmed on burning coals spread on the ground. When King Roger of Naples was informed of this matter, he was moved to the deepest veneration for the man of God. At last, after having foretold to the king and to others the time of his death, he fell asleep in the Lord, illustrious in innumerable virtues and miracles, in the year of salvation one thousand one hundred and forty-two.

On another occasion as well, when the same venerable man was washing glass lamps in the oratory, one fell from his hands and, drawn by the impact, shattered into countless pieces. Fearing the most violent anger of the father of the monastery, he gathered all the fragments of the lamp and placed them before the altar, and gave himself to prayer with deep groaning. And when he raised his head from prayer, he found the lamp whole which he had anxiously gathered up piece by piece.

Finally, with the relics of Saint Maximilian, Bishop of Lorch, brought in, under the rule of Rudolph, King of the Romans, Gottfried the First of that name, Bishop of Passau, had the bodies of Saints Valentine and Maximilian placed in an honorable tomb in the same basilica of Passau outside the choir, lest they should fall into disrepair placed in a lowlier location, in about the year of the Lord one thousand two hundred and eighty-five.

Aloysius, son of Ferdinand Gonzaga, Marquis of Castiglione delle Stiviere, baptized in haste on account of danger to his life, and seeming to be born for heaven before he was born for earth, so steadfastly preserved that first grace that he was believed to have been confirmed in it. At nine years of age he vowed perpetual virginity before the altar of the Blessed Virgin in Florence, whom he always held in the place of a parent; and he preserved it untouched by any struggle of mind or body — a singular gift of God — so that he was deservedly called a man without flesh, or an angel in flesh. Having transferred the right to his ancestral principality to his brother, he joined the Society of Jesus at Rome. Even in his novitiate he began to be regarded as a master of all virtues. In him the love of God was so ardent that it gradually consumed even his body. Embracing his neighbors also with a marvelous charity, he contracted a contagious plague in the public hospitals where he served with alacrity. Slowly consumed by it, on the eleventh day before the Kalends of July, at the beginning of his twenty-fourth year, he passed to heaven. Benedict XIII enrolled him among the Saints and gave him as an example and patron of innocence and chastity above all to studious youth.

Aloysius, son of Ferdinand Gonzaga, Marquis of Castiglione delle Stiviere, baptized in haste on account of danger to his life, and seeming to be born for heaven before he was born for earth, so steadfastly preserved that first grace that he was believed to have been confirmed in it. From the first use of reason, by which he immediately offered himself to God, he led a life each day more holy. At nine years of age he vowed perpetual virginity before the altar of the Blessed Virgin in Florence, whom he always held in the place of a parent; and he preserved it untouched by any struggle of mind or body, a singular gift of God. The remaining disturbances of the soul he began at that very age to suppress with such force that he was not thereafter stirred by even the first movement of them. He also so restrained his senses, and his eyes above all, that he not only never directed them to the face of Mary of Austria, whom for several years he greeted almost daily among the honorary pages of the Prince of Spain, but also kept them away from his own mother's face: a man therefore deservedly called without flesh, or an angel in flesh.

Altmann was born of noble parents in that part of Saxony which afterward received the name of Westphalia. Formed in sacred and human letters, he was enrolled among the canons at Paderborn and for many years directed the schools there. Later placed over the canons at Aachen, he also served as chaplain to the Emperor Henry III. At the death of that emperor he undertook a devout and danger-laden pilgrimage to Jerusalem; on his return from that journey he was chosen as the bishop of the diocese of Passau, which at that time extended beyond the part that is now Bavaria to Upper and Lower Austria. There, renowned for his learning and religious life, he was received with the greatest acclaim of clergy and people, and was consecrated by Blessed Gebhard, Archbishop of Salzburg.

Ambrose, Bishop of Milan, son of Ambrose, a Roman citizen, was educated at Rome in the liberal arts. Appointed by the prefect Probus over Liguria and Emilia, he came to Milan by his command and with his authority; where, on the death of Auxentius the Arian bishop, the people were at odds over the choice of a successor. Ambrose therefore, having entered the church in the performance of his official duty to quiet the stirring of sedition, when he had spoken admirably at length on the peace and tranquility of the commonwealth, suddenly at the cry of a child, "Ambrose for bishop!" the voice of the entire people burst forth demanding Ambrose as bishop. Wherefore, having been baptized — for he was a catechumen — initiated into the sacred rites, and having received all the grades of orders according to the custom of the Church, he was raised to episcopal dignity. In that office he vigorously defended Catholic truth and ecclesiastical discipline both by word and by his writings, and converted many Arians and other heretics to the faith, among whom he begot Saint Augustine for Jesus Christ. Having discharged so many labors and cares for the Church of God, he died on the day before the Nones of April, in the year three hundred and ninety-seven.

Ambrose, Bishop of Milan, son of Ambrose, a Roman citizen, was born when his father was prefect of Gaul. It is said that a swarm of bees settled on the mouth of this infant, which portended the divine eloquence of the man. He was educated at Rome in the liberal arts. Afterward he was appointed by the prefect Probus over Liguria and Emilia; and from there, later, by the same Probus's command, he came with authority to Milan; where, on the death of Auxentius the Arian bishop, the people were at odds over the choice of a successor. Ambrose therefore, having entered the church in the performance of his official duty to quiet the stirring of sedition, when he had spoken admirably at length on the peace and tranquility of the commonwealth, suddenly at the cry of a child, "Ambrose for bishop!" the voice of the entire people burst forth demanding Ambrose as bishop.

Anacletus the Athenian governed the Church under the Emperor Trajan. He decreed that a bishop should be consecrated by three bishops and no fewer; that clerics should be publicly ordained to sacred orders by their own bishop; and that at Mass, after the consecration was completed, all should receive Communion. He adorned the sepulcher of Blessed Peter and assigned a place for the burial of the Pontiffs. He held two ordinations in December, at which he created five priests, three deacons, and six bishops. He held his see for nine years, three months, and ten days. Having been crowned with martyrdom, he was buried in the Vatican.

Anacletus, a Greek by birth, from Athens, son of Antiochus, most celebrated for his many distinguished deeds, after an interregnum of the pontificate of four months and ten days, having obtained the supreme pontificate of the Christian religion, was substituted for Clement who had been taken away by martyrdom, on the third of the Nones of April, and held the chair of Peter for nine years, three months, and ten days, having created five priests, three deacons, and six bishops in two ordinations, under the Emperor Trajan.

Anastasius, a Roman, son of Maximus, after the death of Siricius, was ordained Bishop of the Roman Church; and while he governed it admirably, from the regions of the East a fierce storm of the heretics the Origenists attempted to pollute and undermine the simplicity of the faith which the Apostle had praised. But Anastasius, a man of richest poverty and apostolic solicitude, immediately struck down the noxious head and suppressed the hissing mouths of the hydra, and pursuing the heretics lurking in their dens, condemned in his letters in the West what had been condemned in the East. Nor did care ever fail him to guard the faith of the Gospel among his own peoples, and to communicate as much as he could by letters with those parts of his people spread over all the various spaces of the lands, lest any origin of profane interpretation should creep in to disturb with its darkness the souls devoted to God.

Anastasius the Persian, a monk, under the Emperor Heraclius, having visited the holy land of Jerusalem, at Caesarea of Palestine steadfastly endured chains and scourgings for the religion of Christ. Soon afterward, afflicted by the Persians with various torments for the same cause, he was beheaded by King Chosroes together with seventy other Christians. His relics were first brought to Jerusalem, to the monastery in which he had professed the monastic life, and then to Rome, where they were placed in the monastery at the Aquae Salviae.

Andrew of Corsini, born at Florence from the noble family of the Corsini, was obtained by his parents from God by prayer and was vowed by them to the Mother of God. Educated devoutly as a youth, but gradually inclining toward vices, he was often rebuked by his mother. When, however, he came to know that he had been dedicated to the Blessed Virgin by his parents' vow, enkindled by the love of God, he embraced the Carmelite institute, and was appointed to govern it in Tuscany. Meanwhile the Church of Fiesole, widowed of her shepherd, chose him as her bishop; which office he at last accepted, lest he should contradict the divine will, and fulfilled it with the greatest zeal for souls and pastoral solicitude. Sent by Urban V as legate to quell the disturbances at Bologna, he extinguished the deadly hatreds of the citizens with the greatest prudence. Spent by unceasing labors and penances, he rested in peace in the year one thousand three hundred and seventy-three, in the seventy-first year of his age. Urban VIII enrolled him in the number of the Saints.

Andrew the Apostle, born at Bethsaida, a village of Galilee, brother of Peter, a disciple of John the Baptist, when he heard him speak of Christ, saying: "Behold the Lamb of God," followed Jesus and also led his own brother to the same Lord. Afterward, when he was fishing with his brother in the sea of Galilee, both were called before the other Apostles by Christ the Lord as he passed by, with these words: "Come after me, I will make you fishers of men"; and without any delay, leaving their nets, they followed him. After the Lord's Passion and Resurrection, Andrew, having come into Scythia of Europe — the province allotted to him for the sowing of the faith of Christ — and then having traversed Epirus and Thrace, converted innumerable men to Christ by his teaching and miracles. Going afterward to Patras in Achaia, and having led very many in that city to the evangelical truth, he freely rebuked Aegeas the proconsul, who was resisting the preaching of the Gospel, because one who wished to be considered a judge of men did not recognize Christ the Judge of all, being deceived by demons.

Andrew Avellino, previously called Lancellotto, born at Castronuovo in Lucania, having obtained the doctorate of jurisprudence at Naples and been ordained a priest, began to conduct the advocacy of cases, but only in the ecclesiastical forum. But when on a certain occasion a slight lie escaped him in the course of pleading a case, and he happened upon those words of Scripture: "A mouth that lies kills the soul," seized with grief at that fault he bade farewell to forensic pursuits and humbly petitioned to be enrolled among the Clerks Regular. Having obtained his wish, on account of his immense love for the Cross that burned in him, he obtained by prayer that the name of Andrew be given him. He excelled most greatly in abstinence and patience, as well as in self-abasement and self-hatred. He wonderfully propagated the Order of the Clerks Regular. He venerated the Virgin Mother of God with singular love and devotion. After heroic examples of virtue, weighed down by years and broken by labors, as he was about to celebrate Mass, at the thrice-repeated words: "I will go to the altar of God," he was stricken by apoplexy and, soon having received the Sacraments, passed away peacefully.

Andrew of Corsini, born at Florence from the noble family of the Corsini, was obtained by his parents from God by prayer and was vowed by them to the Blessed Virgin. And what he was to be was shown by divine presage before he was born: for his mother, while pregnant, saw in a dream that she had given birth to a wolf, which, making its way to the Carmelite church, was immediately changed into a lamb in the very vestibule of the temple. Educated devoutly and simply as a youth, as he gradually declined toward vices, he was often rebuked by his mother. When, however, he came to know that he had been dedicated to the Virgin Mother of God by his parents' vow, enkindled by the love of God and admonished by the vision of his mother, he embraced the Carmelite institute; in which, vexed by various temptations from the devil, he could never be moved from his religious purpose. Soon sent to Paris, and having completed the course of studies and received his doctorate, he was recalled to his homeland and placed over the governance of his Order in Tuscany.

Andrew Avellino, previously called Lancellotto, born in the village of Castronuovo in Lucania, gave from the very beginnings of his infancy unmistakable signs of future holiness. As a youth, having left his father's house to pursue studies, he passed the slippery path of that age among the studies of the good arts in such a manner that he never ceased to keep chiefly before his eyes the beginning of wisdom, which is the fear of the Lord. He also joined to his outstanding beauty an exceptional love of chastity, by which he frequently eluded the shameless snares of women, and at times even repelled open violence. Already long enrolled in the clerical state, he betook himself to Naples to devote himself to legal studies; and there, having obtained the doctorate of jurisprudence and being in the meantime raised to the priestly dignity, he began to conduct the advocacy of cases only in the ecclesiastical forum and on behalf of certain private persons, in accordance with the prescriptions of the sacred canons. But when on a certain occasion a slight lie escaped him in the course of pleading a case, and he then fortuitously happened upon those words of Holy Scripture: "A mouth that lies kills the soul," he was seized with such grief and repentance for that fault that he immediately judged he must withdraw from that manner of life. And so, having given up forensic pursuits, he devoted himself wholly to divine worship and the sacred ministries. And when he was distinguished by examples of ecclesiastical virtue, he was placed over the governance of nuns by the archbishop of Naples then in office. When in that duty he had incurred the hatred of evil men, he first escaped the danger of an attempt on his life; but then, having received three wounds on his face from an assassin, he bore the atrocity of the injury with equanimity. Then, burning with desire for a more perfect life, he humbly petitioned to be enrolled among the Clerks Regular; and having obtained his wish, on account of his immense love for the Cross that burned in him, he obtained by prayer that the name of Andrew be given him.

Angela Merici, born of devout parents at Desenzano, a town of the diocese of Verona on Lake Garda in the Venetian dominion, from her earliest age she diligently guarded the lily of virginity which she had resolved to preserve perpetually. Shrinking from all feminine adornment, she studiously disfigured her fine features and beautiful hair, that she might please only the heavenly Spouse of souls. Bereft of her parents in the very flower of adolescence, she attempted from desire for a stricter life to flee to a desert place; but, prevented by her uncle, she knew how to achieve at home what was not permitted in solitude. She frequently wore a hairshirt and used the discipline, eating meat only when ill and wine only at the feasts of the Lord's Nativity and Resurrection; and for many days she tasted nothing at all. Devoted to prayer, she took the briefest sleep on the ground. She recognized at once a demon attempting to delude her under the appearance of a shining angel, and put him to flight. At last, having renounced her paternal goods and having embraced the habit and rule of the Third Order of Saint Francis, she joined evangelical poverty to the praise of virginity.

Angela Merici, born of devout parents, gave from her earliest age great proofs of virtue, making frequent use of the hairshirt and the discipline, and devoted herself unceasingly to prayer. Having renounced her paternal goods and embraced the rule of the Third Order of Saint Francis, she joined evangelical poverty to the praise of virginity, and omitted no work of devotion toward her neighbors. Refreshed most frequently by the Holy Eucharist, she was borne with such power of charity toward God that she was often rapt beyond her senses. At Brescia she established a new society of virgins under a certain discipline and holy rules of life, which she distinguished with the patronage and name of Saint Ursula. At last, nearly seventy years of age, she flew to heaven in the year of the Lord one thousand five hundred and forty, on the sixth of the Kalends of February. Clement XIII solemnly confirmed and ratified the devotion long paid to her by formal decree. And Pius VII enrolled her in the catalogue of holy Virgins.

Enriched with angelic virtues, she cared with solicitous charity not only for her own salvation but also for the public good. Therefore, with God inspiring and Pius IV approving, she proposed the stricter rule of the ancient Carmelites to be observed, first by women and then by men. The all-powerful blessing of the merciful Lord flourished in this undertaking; for that indigent virgin was able to build more than thirty-two monasteries, destitute of all human help and even with the princes of the world most often opposing her. She wept with perpetual tears over the darkness of unbelievers and heretics, and dedicated the voluntary afflictions of her own body to God for their salvation as a means of appeasing the wrath of divine justice. Moreover, the fire of divine love so inflamed her heart that she deservedly saw an Angel transfixing her breast with a fiery dart, and heard Christ say to her, giving her his right hand: "From now on, as a true spouse, you shall jealously guard my honor." At his counsel she made the most arduous vow of always doing what she understood to be more perfect. She wrote many documents of heavenly wisdom, by which the minds of the faithful are greatly stirred to desire the heavenly homeland.

He had Angels as guardians of his body. For when he was going to single combat against Radislav, Duke of Kourim, with the purpose of providing for the safety of his people, Angels were seen to provide him with arms and to say to the adversary: "Do not strike." The terrified enemy, prostrating himself in veneration, begged pardon. When he had gone into Germany, the emperor, beholding two Angels adorning him with a golden cross as he approached, leaped from his throne, embraced him in his arms, honored him with royal insignia, and gave him the arm of Saint Vitus. Nevertheless his impious brother, urged by his mother, received him at a banquet and afterward slew him in the church while he was praying and already aware of the death prepared for him, with the help of his accomplices in crime. The blood sprinkled on the walls is still to be seen; and by God's vengeance the unnatural mother was swallowed by the earth, and the murderers perished miserably in various ways.

The Angel, declaring the prayer heard, immediately promises the birth of his wife. Not that he who had entered to offer for the people, having left aside the public prayers, could have been able to pray for the receiving of sons, especially since no one prays for what he despairs of receiving. But indeed he, already mindful of his own age and of his barren wife, so despaired that sons would be born to him that he did not believe even the Angel who was promising this. But what he says: "Your prayer has been heard," signifies the redemption of the people; and "Your wife shall bear you a son" unfolds the order of that same redemption — namely, that the son born to Zechariah would go before the Redeemer of that people by his preaching. For since he had said that Zechariah, as he was interceding for the people, had been heard, he teaches the order in which that same people should be saved and perfected — namely, by repenting at the preaching of John and believing in Christ.

Anicetus the Syrian, under the Emperor Marcus Aurelius Antoninus, presided over the Church. He decreed that clerics should not wear long hair. He held ordinations five times in December, at which he ordained seventeen priests, four deacons, and nine bishops in various places. He lived in his pontificate eight years, eight months, and twenty-four days. Having been crowned with martyrdom for the faith of Christ, he was buried on the Appian Way in the cemetery that was afterward called that of Callistus, on the fifteenth of the Kalends of May.

Burning with zeal for souls, he spared no labor and no expense in order to establish rest homes for young boys on feast days, hospices for orphans, schools for working boys, houses for the raising and educating of children, and temples to God far and wide throughout the world. At the same time he did not cease to foster the faith of Christ in Piedmont by word and example, to protect it throughout all Italy by compiling, publishing, and disseminating the best books, and to propagate it by repeatedly sending preachers of the Gospel to unbelieving peoples. A simple and upright man of God, equipped for every good work, he flourished in virtues of every kind, which were nourished by the ardor of his most burning charity. With his mind steadfastly raised toward God and heaped with heavenly gifts, that most holy man appeared to be terrified by no threats, wearied by no labors, oppressed by no anxieties, and disturbed by no adversities. Three works of devotion he most strongly commended to his own: that they should approach the sacrament of Confession and the holy Synaxis as frequently as possible, that they should venerate Mary Help of Christians with great love, and that they should be submissive to the Supreme Pontiff as most devoted sons. Nor should it be passed over in silence that in the most difficult circumstances he was at the service of the Roman Pontiff more than once, to temper the evils flowing from the laws against the Church enacted at that time. He completed the course of his life, filled with so many and such great works and labors, on the day before the Kalends of February in the year of salvation one thousand eight hundred and eighty-eight, in the seventy-third year of his age. Pius XI, Supreme Pontiff, declared him illustrious for many miracles and enrolled him in the number of the Blessed in the year one thousand nine hundred and twenty-nine; and five years later, on the solemn day of Easter, with the peoples from the whole world flocking to the City on the nineteenth centenary of the completion of the Redemption of the human race, he enrolled him in the ranks of the Saints.

In the year one thousand six hundred and forty-eight, on the fourth day of July, Anthony Daniel, who had charge of the village of Saint Joseph among the Hurons, fearlessly defending his flock against the invading Iroquois, was pierced with arrows and burning bullets and laid down his life at the doors of the church as a good shepherd for his sheep. The following year, on the sixteenth day of March, John de Brebeuf, deservedly called the Apostle of the Hurons, together with Gabriel Lalemant, was taken by the Iroquois, and after prolonged and most cruel torments — the very barbarians marveling at the invincible fortitude of the champion of Christ — died gloriously in the village of Saint Ignatius in what is today called the Canadian province of Ontario; Gabriel Lalemant followed him on the next day by the same bloody path and with the same virtue. In the month of December of that same year one thousand six hundred and forty-nine, on the vigil of the Immaculate Conception of the Blessed Virgin Mary, Charles Garnier, pierced with wounds and struck with a hatchet, concluded his most innocent life with a glorious end. On the very next day, Natalis Chabanel, treacherously assailed by an apostate Huron and cast into a river, in the beloved Mission to which he had bound himself by a heroic vow to serve perpetually — nature fruitlessly protesting — attained the longed-for palm of martyrdom. These eight foremost Martyrs of North America, Pius XI, Supreme Pontiff, in the holy year one thousand nine hundred and twenty-five enrolled in the number of the Blessed, and five years later enrolled them in the rolls of the Saints.

In the fourth year after the dogmatic definition of the Immaculate Conception of the Blessed Virgin, on the bank of the Gave river near the town of Lourdes in the diocese of Tarbes in France, when a certain girl named Bernadette asserted that she had several times seen the Immaculate Mother of God in the hollow of a rock, so many and such great wonders were wrought that any prudent and devout member of the faithful could easily understand that the finger of God was there. Among these the following is celebrated: that the sick who draw water from the spring then first miraculously gushing forth in the grotto very often and repeatedly receive health. As the fame of the favors reported to have been received in the sacred grotto spread widely and the gathering of people grew daily, the Bishop of Tarbes, after a judicial inquiry into the facts, permitted the cult of that same Immaculate Virgin in that same grotto. Soon, a church having been built, innumerable crowds of the faithful come there every year, and the name of the Immaculate Mother of God grows more famous day by day throughout the world; the more so because every year, during the procession of the Most Blessed Sacrament, among the sick borne there from all sides, some who are seeking healing from the Lord through the intercession of the Immaculate Mother recover forthwith. Rightly moved by these events, the Supreme Pontiff Pius X extended to the universal Church the feast which Leo XIII had granted to certain places.

In the fourth year after the dogmatic definition of the Immaculate Conception of the Blessed Virgin, on the bank of the Gave river near the town of Lourdes in the diocese of Tarbes in France, the Virgin herself in the hollow of a rock above the grotto of Massabielle presented herself several times to be seen by a certain girl, called Bernadette in the vernacular, who was of most humble circumstances but of simple and devout character. The Immaculate Virgin appeared of a youthful and kindly aspect, clothed in a white robe and white cloak, and girded with a blue sash; a golden rose adorned her bare feet. On the first day of the apparition, which was the eleventh of February in the year one thousand eight hundred and fifty-eight, she taught the girl to make the sign of the Cross properly and devoutly, and aroused her to the recitation of the holy Rosary by her own example, rolling the beads between her fingers — which had hitherto hung from her arm — and doing the same in the subsequent apparitions as well. On the second day of the apparition, the girl, in the simplicity of her heart and fearing diabolical deception, poured holy water on the Virgin; but the Blessed Virgin, smiling gently, showed her a kinder face. When she appeared the third time, she invited the girl to come to the grotto for fifteen days. From that time she spoke to her more frequently, urged her to pray for sinners, to kiss the earth, and to do penance; then she commanded her to inform the priests that a chapel was to be built there, and that solemn processions were to be held in that manner. She also commanded her to drink of the spring that was still hidden under the sand but was soon to gush forth, and to wash herself with it. Finally, on the feast of the Annunciation, when the girl earnestly inquired the name of her whose sight she had so often been granted, the Virgin, joining her hands to her breast and raising her eyes to heaven, answered: "I am the Immaculate Conception."

When he was about in his forty-fifth year, having made solemn profession in the Order of Friars Preachers, as a new soldier he exercised himself in every kind of virtue, but especially in charity toward the needy, and most of all toward captives held by unbelievers. Therefore when, at his urging, Saint Peter Nolasco — whose confessions he himself heard — was contributing his resources to this most devout work, the most Blessed Virgin appeared both to him and to Blessed Raymond and to James I, King of Aragon, and said that it would be most pleasing to her and to her only-begotten Son if there were founded in her honor an Order of religious men whose care it would be to free captives from the tyranny of the unbelievers. Therefore, having taken counsel together, they founded the Order of Blessed Mary of Mercy for the Redemption of Captives: for which Blessed Raymond prescribed certain rules of life most suited to the vocation of that same Order, the approval of which he obtained from Gregory IX several years later, and with his own hands clothed and appointed the said Saint Peter as the first Master General of the Order.

Anselm, born at Aosta on the borders of Italy of noble and Catholic parents, as a young man, having left his homeland and all his goods, made his regular profession in the monastery of Bec of the Order of Saint Benedict and made wonderful progress in the pursuit of letters and virtues. He was held in veneration by kings and bishops, and was also dear to Saint Gregory VII, who at that time, harassed by persecutions, sent him letters full of affection, commending himself and the Church to his prayers. When Lanfranc, his former teacher, Archbishop of Canterbury, had died, he was called to govern that same church, and by word and example, by his writings, and by councils he held, restored ancient piety and ecclesiastical discipline. But when King William soon attempted by force and threats to usurp the rights of the Church, and he himself had invincibly resisted, having suffered the plundering of his goods and exile, he betook himself to Rome to Urban II. Received by him with honor and adorned with the highest praises, at the Council of Bari he defended, against the error of the Greeks, with innumerable testimonies from the Scriptures and the holy Fathers, that the Holy Spirit proceeds also from the Son. After the death of William, recalled to England by his brother King Henry, he fell asleep in the Lord.

Anselm, born at Aosta on the borders of Italy of Gundulph and Ermemberga, noble and Catholic parents, from his tender years gave by his assiduous study of letters and desire for a more perfect life no obscure indication of his future holiness and learning. And although in youthful ardor he was at times drawn to the allurements of the world, yet soon called back to the right path, having left his homeland and all his goods, he betook himself to the monastery of Bec of the Order of Saint Benedict: where, having made his regular profession under the most observant Abbot Herluino, and under the most learned man Lanfranc, he made such progress with ardor of soul and unceasing study in the pursuit of letters and virtues that he was in a wonderful manner regarded by all as a model of holiness and learning.

Anthony the Egyptian, when he had entered a church and heard from the Gospel: "If you wish to be perfect, go and sell all that you have and give to the poor," judged that he ought to obey Christ the Lord in this, as though the words had been addressed to him. And so, having sold his estate, he distributed the price to the poor, and himself withdrew into the vast solitude of Egypt. He was so enkindled with the pursuit of all virtues that he strove to imitate whoever he saw excelling in any praise of virtue. There was therefore nothing more continent, nothing more watchful than he. He was such a terror to demons that many throughout Egypt who were tormented by them were freed upon the name of Anthony being invoked over them. Thus, illustrious in holiness and miracles, when he had innumerable imitators of his manner of life, he departed this life in the one hundred and fifth year of his age, on the sixteenth of the Kalends of February.

Anthony Mary Claret, born of devout and honorable parents at Sallent in Spain, as a young man practiced the trade of weaving; but afterward, having been ordained a priest, he first cultivated parish ministry, then came to Rome to be sent to foreign missions by the Congregation for the Propagation of the Faith. But, God so disposing, returning to Spain, he journeyed as an apostolic missionary through Catalonia and the Canary Islands. A prolific writer of good books, he also founded the Congregation of the Sons of the Immaculate Heart of Mary. Having been placed over the archiepiscopal see of Santiago in Cuba, he shone admirably with the virtues of a zealous Pastor; he restored the seminary, promoted the learning and discipline of the clergy, founded social works, and established the Teaching Sisters of Mary Immaculate for the Christian education of girls. Having been summoned at last to Madrid to serve as confessor to the Queen of Spain and as counselor in the gravest ecclesiastical affairs, he furnished an outstanding example of austerity and all virtues. At the Vatican Council he vigorously defended the infallibility of the Roman Pontiff. He wonderfully propagated devotion toward the Most Blessed Sacrament and the Immaculate Heart of Mary and her Rosary. At last, in exile at Fontfroide in France, he died in the year one thousand eight hundred and seventy. Pius XI enrolled him, illustrious in miracles, in the number of the Blessed, and Pius XII enrolled him in the rolls of the Saints.

Anthony Mary Zaccaria, born of noble family at Cremona, shone from his boyhood in purity of character and mercy toward the poor. In the pursuit of the humanities, philosophy, and medicine, he surpassed his peers in integrity of life and keenness of mind. At God's prompting he diligently cultivated learning; then, having been ordained a priest, he so distinguished himself that he deserved to be called by his fellow citizens father of the homeland and an angel. At Milan, together with Bartholomew Ferrari and James Morigia, most holy men, he founded the congregation of the Clerks Regular, named after Saint Paul, and the society of the Angelic Sisters. A devoted worshiper of the Holy Eucharist, he wonderfully promoted the public exposition of the Most Blessed Sacrament. Enriched by God with heavenly gifts and oppressed by great labors, when he had contracted a grave illness, he died most holily at Cremona on the third of the Nones of July, in the year one thousand five hundred and thirty-nine. Leo XIII ratified and confirmed the devotion paid to him, and enrolled him in the catalogue of the Saints.

Anthony, born of honorable parents at Lisbon in Portugal and educated devoutly by them, as a young man entered the institute of the Canons Regular. But when the bodies of the Blessed Five Martyrs of the Order of Friars Minor were being transferred to Coimbra — they had suffered shortly before at Morocco for the faith of Christ — inflamed with desire for martyrdom he transferred to the Franciscan Order. Soon impelled by the same ardor, he set out to go to the Saracens; but, afflicted by adverse health and compelled to return, when the ship was heading for the shores of Spain, he was driven by the force of winds to Sicily.

Anthony, born of honorable and devout parents at Lisbon in Portugal, as a young man entered the institute of the Canons Regular; but, enkindled by desire for martyrdom, he transferred to the Franciscan Order. Sent to the Saracens and compelled by adverse health to return, he was driven by the force of winds to Sicily. Soon ordained to holy orders and fulfilling the office of preacher, he aroused such admiration of himself that he was called to interpret the sacred letters at Bologna and elsewhere, was placed over the studies of his brothers, and merited to be called the Ark of the Testament and the Hammer of heresies. Having traversed many provinces, he came the year before his death to Padua, where he left outstanding monuments of his holiness. Illustrious in merits and miracles, he fell asleep in the Lord on the Ides of June in the year of salvation one thousand two hundred and thirty-one, in the thirty-sixth year of his age, and by the Supreme Pontiff Pius XII was declared Doctor of the universal Church.

"Before they came together, she was found to be with child of the Holy Spirit." She was found by no other than Joseph, who, by the near license of a husband, knew all things of his future wife. But the fact that it says, "Before they came together," does not follow that they came together afterward; but Scripture shows what did not happen.

When the Emperor Anthemius, with Philotheus the Macedonian — relying on his familiarity with the emperor — was attempting to introduce into the City new conventicles of various sects, he restrained him by openly rebuking him before Blessed Peter the Apostle that it should not be done: to such an extent that the emperor promised under oath that these things would not be introduced. He built four oratories in the baptistery of the Constantinian basilica: namely of the Holy Cross, of Saint John the Baptist, of Saint John the Evangelist, and of Saint Stephen; and in addition two libraries. He constructed a monastery together with a bath and a praetorium at Saint Lawrence outside the walls, and another in the City at the Luna. He contributed many and magnificent ornaments of gold, silver, and precious stones besides to the sacred places. He appointed in the City officials to carry out the assigned duties. He was solicitously concerned for the common concord of the priests of the Lord, that they should not dare to seek their own, but should strive to obtain what belongs to Christ. At last, freed from his body, he departed to heaven to reign with Christ, on the fourth of the Ides of September, under the Emperors Leo and Anthemius; and his body was buried at Saint Lawrence in the crypt next to the body of Blessed Sixtus. In a single ordination in December he created twenty-five priests, six deacons, and twenty-two bishops in various places. He held the governance of the Apostolic See for six years, nine months, and twenty-eight days.

Anterus, a Greek by birth, son of Romulus, was ordained Bishop of Rome after Saint Pontian. He diligently gathered the acts of the martyrs by means of notaries and deposited them in the Church. For that cause he was crowned with martyrdom by the prefect Maximus on the third of the Nones of January, and was buried in the cemetery of Callistus on the Appian Way, under the Prince Maximinus. In a single ordination in December he ordained a Bishop of the city of Fondi in Campania. He held the pontificate for one month and twelve days.

Antoninus, born at Florence of honorable parents, displayed from his very boyhood a remarkable token of his future holiness. In his sixteenth year he embraced the Order of Preachers and thenceforth began to shine with the greatest virtues. He was distinguished by singular abstinence and preserved his virginity with perfect integrity at all times. So great was his skill in giving counsel that he was called Antoninus of the Counsels. Appointed Archbishop of Florence by Eugene IV, he nevertheless consented only with great reluctance, and only after being terrified by apostolic threats, to accept the episcopate. In that office he excelled in prudence, piety, charity, meekness, and priestly zeal. He mastered nearly all the sciences without any teacher, and wrote many books of distinguished learning. He died in the Lord on the sixth day before the Nones of May, in the year one thousand four hundred and fifty-nine, and was enrolled among the Saints by Adrian VI.

Antoninus, born at Florence of honorable and devout parents, displayed from his very boyhood a remarkable token of his future holiness. In his sixteenth year he embraced the Order of Preachers and thenceforth began to shine with the greatest virtues. He declared perpetual war against idleness. After a brief sleep at night, he was the first to be present at the morning prayers; when these were finished, he devoted the remainder of the night to prayer, or at least to reading and writing books; and if at times a more importunate sleep crept over his weary limbs, he would lean his head briefly against the wall, and, having shaken off his sleep, would return all the more eagerly to the sacred night watches.

Antony the Egyptian, born of noble and Christian parents, whom he lost in his adolescence, when he had entered the church and heard the Gospel passage: If you wish to be perfect, go and sell all that you have and give to the poor — as though these words were addressed to him — resolved that he must obey Christ the Lord in this manner. Accordingly, having sold his property, he distributed all the money to the poor. Freed from these encumbrances, he undertook to follow the form of heavenly life on earth. But when he entered upon that perilous combat, he judged that to the defense of faith with which he was armed he must add the assistance of the remaining virtues; and so great was the ardor with which he was inflamed for these virtues, that he strove to imitate whoever he saw excelling in any praiseworthy virtue.

Anthony Mary Zaccaria, born at Cremona in Lombardy of a noble family, seemed from boyhood to give promise of the holiness he was to possess. For the marks of extraordinary virtues shone out early in him: piety toward God and the Blessed Virgin; and a notable mercy toward the poor, for whose want he was more than once at hand to relieve, even stripping himself of a costly garment. Educated in the humanities in his native city, he applied himself at Pavia to the study of philosophy and at Padua to medicine; and as he excelled all others in integrity of life, so also did he easily surpass his contemporaries in sharpness of intellect. Having obtained his degree and returned home, when he understood through God's prompting that he was called to heal souls rather than bodies, he applied himself diligently to the sacred disciplines. In the meantime he never ceased to visit the sick, to instruct boys in Christian doctrine, to cultivate the piety of groups of young men, and frequently to exhort even those of advanced age to amend their ways. When ordained and offering his first Mass, he is said to have appeared to the astonished people surrounded by a crown of Angels amid a heavenly light that suddenly arose. From then on, it was his care to attend ever more earnestly to the salvation of souls and to oppose corrupt morals with all his strength. Moreover, he embraced strangers, the needy, and the afflicted with fatherly affection, comforting them when refreshed by pious words and assistance, so that his house was regarded as a refuge for the wretched, and he himself merited to be called by his fellow citizens father of the fatherland and an angel.

Summoned to Antwerp, he there overthrew the wicked heresy of Tanchelm. He was renowned for prophetic spirit and miracles. Finally created Archbishop of Magdeburg (though reluctantly), he steadfastly defended ecclesiastical discipline and especially celibacy. At Reims, in council, he gave distinguished assistance to Innocent II, and journeying to Rome with other bishops, he suppressed the schism of Peter of Leon. At last, this man of God, full of merits and of the Holy Spirit, fell asleep in the Lord at Magdeburg, in the year of salvation one thousand one hundred and thirty-four, on the sixth day of June.

Apollonia, a virgin of Alexandria, in the reign of the Emperor Decius, when she was already of advanced age and was brought before the idols to offer them veneration, despised them and proclaimed that Jesus Christ, the true God, was to be worshipped. For this reason all her teeth were broken out and pulled; and the impious executioners threatened to burn her alive unless she renounced Christ and worshipped the gods. She replied to them that she was prepared to undergo any death whatsoever for the faith of Jesus Christ. And so, when she was seized to be burned, after standing for a moment as if deliberating what she should do, she slipped from their hands and, with a greater flame of the Holy Spirit burning within her, threw herself with alacrity into the fire prepared for her. Whereupon, her body being swiftly consumed, her most pure spirit flew up to heaven to the eternal crown of martyrdom.

Apollinaris came to Rome from Antioch with the Prince of the Apostles, by whom he was ordained bishop and sent to Ravenna to preach the Gospel of Christ the Lord; where, having converted very many to the faith of Christ, he was seized by the priests of the idols and severely beaten. And when, at his prayer, a noble man named Boniface, who had long been mute, began to speak, and his daughter was freed from an unclean spirit, sedition was again stirred up against him. For this reason he endured manifold and varied punishments. Afterward, preaching the Gospel through Aemilia, he brought very many back from the worship of idols. Returning to Ravenna, exhorting the Christians to steadfastness in the faith, he consummated his glorious martyrdom. His body was buried near the wall of the city.

Apollinaris came to Rome from Antioch with the Prince of the Apostles, by whom he was ordained bishop and sent to Ravenna to preach the Gospel of Christ the Lord; where, having converted very many to the faith of Christ, he was seized by the priests of the idols and severely beaten. And when, at his prayer, a noble man named Boniface, who had long been mute, began to speak, and his daughter was freed from an unclean spirit, sedition was again stirred up against him. Accordingly, beaten with rods, he was forced to tread burning coals with bare feet; but when the fire beneath did him no harm, he was driven outside the city.

The Apostles, disciples of Christ, are held to be teachers of believers: schooled by them, Confessors fight most valiantly, Martyrs perfect triumph, and the Christian army, ever armed by God, defeats the devil. In these men the virtues are ever equal, the combats unlike, the victories glorious. Hence, O Christian, you are a soft soldier if you think you can conquer without a fight, triumph without a contest. Stretch forth your strength, fight bravely, contend fiercely in this battle. Consider the pact, attend to the condition, know the service: the pact you pledged; the condition on which you enlisted; the service to which you gave your name.
