Before John VIII, who had succeeded Adrian, once again accused of suspected faith and of violating ancestral custom, and commanded to come to Rome, Methodius appeared before John and certain bishops and the city clergy, and easily prevailed in showing that he had steadfastly retained a thoroughly Catholic faith and had diligently taught it to others: and that as for the use of the Slavonic language in the celebration of sacred rites, he had done so with good reasons, by permission of Pope Adrian and without contradiction of the sacred Scriptures, and therefore lawfully. Wherefore, the Pope embraced Methodius as he stood before him, and commanded by formal letters that his archiepiscopal authority and his Slavonic mission were to be ratified. Accordingly, Methodius returned to Moravia and persevered more vigilantly in fulfilling the office assigned to him, for which he also willingly endured exile. He led the prince of the Bohemians and his wife to the faith, and spread the Christian name far and wide among that people. He brought the light of the Gospel to Poland, and, as certain writers record, having founded an episcopal see at Lviv, he went in his own name to Muscovy and established the pontifical throne of Kyiv. At length he returned to his own people in Moravia; and now sensing that he was being snatched away to his human end, he himself designated his successor, and having exhorted the clergy and people with his final precepts to virtue, he passed most peacefully from that life which had been for him the way to heaven. As Rome had honored Cyril at his departure, so Moravia honored Methodius. Their feast, which had long been celebrated among the peoples of Slavonia, Pope Leo XIII commanded to be observed throughout the universal Church each year with a proper Office and Mass.

Aquilinus, the prefect of the place, first trying his steadfastness by a beating with clubs, and despairing of being able to beat out of him the name of Christ, commanded him to be cast headlong into the river Anausum or Anisus; and the executioner who carried out his impious orders was punished with sudden blindness. An eagle guarded his lifeless body when it was driven against the rocks, until it could be honorably buried. For he himself roused the religious woman Valeria to perform the last rites over his body, and rewarded her devotion with a spring of healthful waters that proved beneficial to the sick who drank of it.

John is himself the Eagle, the preacher of sublime things, and the contemplator with fixed gaze of the inward and eternal light. For it is said that the young of eagles are tested by their parents in this way: namely, that they are suspended from their father's talon and held up before the rays of the sun. Whoever gazes steadfastly is acknowledged as a true son; if his sight wavers, he is let fall from the talon as a bastard. Consider then how sublime must be the utterances of one who is compared to the eagle; and yet even we, creeping on the ground, weak, and of scarcely any account among men, dare to handle these things and to expound them — and we think we can grasp them when we reflect or be grasped by them when we speak.

Tiridates at first shut Gregory up in close confinement; then he commanded his hands to be bound to his sides so that his elbows protruded, a gag to be inserted in his mouth, masses of cut salt to be laid on his back, and with a strap tightly bound around his chest he was to be suspended in the highest place. He remained thus suspended for seven days; after which, since he persisted in his resolve, he was hung from one foot and forced to inhale smoke raised from foul dung, while all the while he was beaten hard with wet rods. Amid these torments he earnestly besought God in prayer for the salvation of all, especially of the Armenian people, and that steadfastness in the faith might be granted him. The king, though he admired this, yet raged more cruelly and commanded logs of wood to be brought and boards to be laid against the front part of his feet, and to be tightly bound with knotted ropes until blood ran down from the tips of his toes. He was also beaten with blows of the fist, his head was placed in an intricate vice, and a pipe was applied to his nostril through which salt, alkali, and vinegar mixed together were poured in. He suffered many similar and worse kinds of cruelty, so that the king himself marveled greatly that he had remained alive and had made nothing of his intense pains.

Bound by these closer fetters and given over to the ministry of the sick, it is marvelous with what alacrity he watched over their needs day and night until his last breath, broken by no labors, deterred by no perils of life. Made all things to all men, he took up even the most menial services with the most humble submission and with knees frequently bent — as if he beheld Christ himself in the sick — with a cheerful and ready spirit; and in order to be at hand for the needs of all, he willingly relinquished the general governance of the order and the delights of heaven with which he was flooded as he remained fixed in contemplation. His fatherly love for the wretched shone out most of all when the City was first afflicted with a contagious disease and then with extreme scarcity of food, and a dreadful plague was raging at Nola in Campania. So great at last was the charity with which he burned toward God and neighbor that he merited to be called an angel, and in various perils of his journeys to experience the help of Angels. Gifted with the gift of prophecy and the grace of healing, he also penetrated the secrets of hearts; and at his prayers food was multiplied and water was turned into wine. At last, worn out by vigils, fasts, and unceasing labors, when he seemed to consist of nothing but skin and bones, having bravely endured five troublesome and long illnesses, which he called the mercies of the Lord, fortified with the sacraments, at Rome, amid the most sweet names of Jesus and Mary, at the words: May the face of Christ Jesus, meek and glad, appear to you — at the hour he had foretold, he fell asleep in the Lord on the day before the Ides of July, in the year of salvation one thousand six hundred and fourteen, in the sixty-fifth year of his age. Benedict XIV enrolled him among the Saints with solemn rite, illustrious as he was by many miracles; and Leo XIII, at the request of the bishops of the Catholic world and with the advice of the Congregation of Rites, declared him the heavenly patron of all hospitals and of the sick wherever they dwell, and commanded that his name be invoked in the litanies for the dying.

Having entered with eager zeal upon the course of a stricter life, he applied himself especially to those exercises of virtue to which he had bound himself by the making of arduous vows: one, of continually resisting his own will; the other, of always advancing further on the way of Christian perfection. He was an assiduous observer of regular discipline, and most zealous in promoting it when he held authority over others. Whatever time remained beyond what was prescribed by the duties of his institute and its rule, he devoted to prayer and the salvation of souls. His admirable piety and prudence shone forth in receiving confessions; he frequently traversed the villages and towns near Naples with evangelical ministries, to the great profit of souls. The Lord also illustrated by signs the burning charity of this holy man toward his neighbors. For when, at dead of night, he was returning home after hearing the confession of a sick man, and the violence of rain and wind had extinguished the torch that gave him light, not only he and his companions were not wetted in the midst of the most copious rains, but by an unusual splendor marvelously radiating from his body, he showed the way to his companions through the deepest darkness. He excelled supremely in abstinence and patience, as well as in self-abasement and self-hatred. He bore with undisturbed soul the murder committed against his nephew, and restrained his own from all desire of vengeance; indeed, he also implored mercy and clemency of judgment even for the murderers.

On the death of Blessed Gregory X at Arezzo, he was raised to the Chair of Peter by the unanimous vote of all the Cardinals. Pursuing the plans of his magnanimous predecessor, he labored tirelessly to liberate the Eastern peoples from the yoke of the infidels: he reconciled Charles, King of Sicily, with the Italian cities in friendship; he repelled Rudolph the Emperor, who was threatening the dominions of the Roman Church from the Alps; against the Saracens invading Spain, he quickly organized an army of crusaders; he laid down the norms by which the religious reconciliation of the Greeks with the Latins was to be accomplished, norms carefully retained by his successors. Having accomplished such great things in the brief space of five months, while the Church still hoped for still greater things from him, he was seized by fever at Rome in the fifty-first year of his age and passed most devoutly to those above. He was renowned by many miracles in his life and after his death. Wherefore, an ecclesiastical cult was rendered to the blessed Pontiff immediately upon his departure, which, never having been interrupted, was confirmed by Pope Leo XIII, at the advice of the Congregation of Sacred Rites.

Porphyry and the Emperor Julian here charge either the ignorance of a lying historian or the foolishness of those who immediately followed the Savior, as if they followed without reason any man who called them; yet so many mighty works and so many signs had preceded, which without doubt the Apostles had seen before they believed. Certainly the very radiance and majesty of the Divinity hidden within him, which shone forth even in his human countenance, could from the very first draw to himself those who looked upon him. For if this power is said to belong to the loadstone and to amber, that they attach rings, straws, and bits of straw to themselves, how much more could the Lord of all creatures draw to himself those whom he called?

The Arians also spread abroad that the bishop Arsenius had been murdered by Athanasius; and while they kept him secretly hidden, they brought the dead man's hand into the court, alleging that Athanasius had cut it off from Arsenius for use in the magic arts. But Arsenius, having fled by night, when he presented himself in the sight of the whole council, disclosed the most shameless wickedness of Athanasius's enemies. Yet these men, attributing it nonetheless to the magic arts of Athanasius, did not cease to plot against his life. For this reason he was driven into exile and lived as an exile in Gaul at Trier. Then, tossed by severe and long-lasting storms under the Emperor Constantius, a favorer of the Arians, and having endured incredible calamities, he traversed a great part of the world; and often expelled from his church, he was often also restored to it by the authority of Julius, Bishop of Rome, and by the patronage of the Emperor Constans, brother of Constantius, and by the decrees of the councils of Sardica and Jerusalem, while the Arians were ever hostile to him; and fleeing their persistent wrath and extreme danger to his life, he hid himself for five years in a dry cistern, with only one friend of Athanasius knowing of this, who secretly sustained him.

Jesus ascended from the water, drawing up and elevating with him the world that had in some manner been submerged with him; and he saw the heavens not divided but opened — that very heaven which Adam of old had shut against both himself and us who came after him, just as paradise had been shut with the flaming sword. The Holy Spirit bears witness; for like things concur with like. Witness is borne from heaven; for from heaven was he to whom witness was borne.

This one ascended while the Jews were stoning him, because that One descended while the Angels were rejoicing. Glory to God in the highest — yesterday the holy Angels sang out in exultation; today they received Stephen with joy into their fellowship. Yesterday the Lord came forth from the womb of the Virgin; today the soldier went forth from the prison of the flesh. Yesterday Christ was wrapped in swaddling clothes for our sake; today Stephen was clothed by him in the robe of immortality. Yesterday the narrow confines of the manger held Christ as an infant; today the immensity of heaven received Stephen in triumph. The Lord descended alone, that he might raise up many; our King humbled himself, that he might exalt his soldiers.

Stanislaus at last excommunicated Boleslaus, who had been fruitlessly admonished many times. The king, raging with anger, sent soldiers into the church to cut down the holy bishop; who, having tried three times, were three times repelled by a hidden divine power. At last the impious king slew with his own hand the priest of God as he was offering the spotless Victim at the altar. Eagles wondrously defended the body, which had been cut limb from limb and thrown across the fields, from the wild beasts. Soon the canons of Cracow, guided by a nocturnal heavenly radiance, gathered together the scattered members and arranged them fitly in their places; and these were suddenly joined together so that no trace of wounds remained. Moreover, God declared the holiness of his servant by many miracles after his death: moved by which, Innocent IV, the Supreme Pontiff, enrolled him among the number of the Saints. And Clement VIII, Pope, having placed the feast of Saint Stanislaus in the Roman Breviary, commanded that the memory of the glorious Martyr be celebrated everywhere with a double Office.

But the wisdom of the just is this: to feign nothing for the sake of show, to open one's meaning in words, to love the truth as it is, to avoid falsehood; to render good things freely, to endure evil things more willingly than to do them; to seek no revenge for injury, to count reproach a gain for the sake of truth. But this simplicity of the just is mocked; for by the wise of this world the virtue of purity is deemed folly. For whatever is done in innocence is undoubtedly reckoned foolish by them; and whatever truth approves in deed sounds stupid to carnal wisdom. For what seems more foolish to the world than to show one's mind in words, to simulate nothing by cunning contrivance, to return no insults for injuries, to pray for those who speak ill of us, to seek poverty, to abandon possessions, to offer no resistance to one who takes, to turn the other cheek to one who strikes?

But though the human race is by nature inferior to those blessed minds, it strives with all its strength and purpose, so far as is possible, to attain them. How? Angels do not marry; but neither does the virgin. Standing always before God, they serve him; and the virgin does likewise. And if virgins, so long as they are weighed down by the burden of the body, cannot ascend to heaven as Angels do, they compensate for this with the very great consolation that, being holy in both spirit and body, they receive the King of heaven. Do you see the excellence of virginity? How it so affects the dwellers on earth that it makes those clothed in a body equal to the incorporeal minds?

And they said to him: In Bethlehem of Judea. This is a copyist's error. For we believe that the Evangelist first wrote, as we read in the Hebrew itself, of Judah, not of Judea. For what other Bethlehem is there belonging to other peoples, that this one should be distinguished as of Judea? But Judah is written because there is another Bethlehem in Galilee. John, soothing the minds of the citizens by his preaching and by private conversations, reduced the city to tranquility. He deeply offended a local ruler because he had rebuked his cruelty toward his subjects. For this reason the ruler sent two horsemen to run him through on the road, and they had already drawn near to him, when, struck with a stupor sent from God, they stood motionless together with their horses, until, casting themselves at the feet of the holy man, they begged pardon for their crime. The ruler himself also, struck with sudden terror, had already despaired of his life, when, recalling John and repenting of what he had done, he was restored to health. Likewise, factious men who attacked him with clubs had their arms grow stiff, and their strength was not restored until they begged pardon for their offense. He was accustomed to behold Christ the Lord present while he celebrated Mass, and to draw from that very source of divinity the heavenly mysteries. To perceive the secrets of hearts and to foresee future events of rare occurrence were frequent gifts of his; and he raised to life a seven-year-old niece of his brother who had died. Finally, having foretold the day of his death and having most devoutly received the sacraments of the Church, he closed his last day, glorious for many miracles before and after his death. These being duly proved, Alexander VIII enrolled him in the number of the Saints.

It seems to me that for this reason also kindness and mercy toward the poor are necessary for us: that we may stop the mouths of those who hold such views of them, and not yield to empty words, enacting against ourselves the law of cruelty. But above all let us be moved by the divine commandment and example. And what is this commandment? Look, I pray you, how firm and sincere it is. For those inspired by the Holy Spirit were not content to speak of the poor once or twice; nor did only some speak of these matters while others did not, or some more fully, others more briefly, as of a thing not of great importance or very necessary: but all, universally, and each one diligently, among the first or among the foremost things, urge us to this, now admonishing, now threatening, now reproving, sometimes also extolling with praise those who perform the duty of this virtue — surely to bring us by the frequency of admonition to the point of carrying out this commandment.

But the envious devil strove to disturb his monks with various terrors, attacking the doors of the monastery by night in a hostile manner. But the man of God so repressed the enemy's assault that the monks were more confirmed in the holy way of life and came to know their father's holiness. He shone with the spirit of prophecy and other gifts. As he always preserved these with deep humility, so he drew upon himself the devil's envy; cast headlong down a stairway of the oratory by him, and on the point of being killed, he was restored to safety by the most swift assistance of the Virgin. He commended this benefit by a perpetual and singular devotion toward her up to the very last breath of his life, which, at nearly ninety years of age, renowned for holiness and miracles, he rendered to God in the year of salvation one thousand two hundred and sixty-seven, on the sixth day before the Kalends of December. Leo XIII, Supreme Pontiff, extended his Office and Mass to the universal Church.

Terentianum, fearing lest, if they were put to death publicly, the people might be stirred up, caused their heads to be struck off at home, where they then were, on the sixth day before the Kalends of July, and arranged for them to be buried in secret; and he spread the rumor that John and Paul had been sent into exile. But their death was made known by unclean spirits, which vexed the bodies of many; among them was Terentianum's own son, himself likewise afflicted by a demon, who was led to the tomb of the Martyrs and set free. Moved by this miracle, he himself came to believe in Christ, as did his father Terentianum; by whom also the life of these blessed Martyrs is said to have been written.

Venantius was brought before the prefect, and when he was tried once more in vain to make him abandon the faith of Christ, he was cast into prison; to which Attalus, a herald, was sent, to tell him that he too had been a Christian but had renounced that name because he had come to know that the doctrine of faith, by which Christians renounce present things for a vain hope of future goods, was a mere fiction. But the noble athlete of Christ, not ignorant of the snares of the cunning enemy, utterly rejected the minister of the devil. And so, when he was brought before the prefect again, all his teeth were knocked out and his jaws broken; and thus beaten, he was thrown onto a dung heap. But having been rescued from there by an Angel as well, he stood again before the judge; who, while Venantius was still speaking, fell from the tribunal and, crying out in these words, The God of Venantius is true — destroy our gods — expired.

But the holy men, since they had learned this pattern also from the Savior (for by him all men were taught at all times and before), fled in order to contend legitimately against their persecutors, and hid themselves when sought by them. For since they did not know the end of the time appointed for them by divine providence, they were unwilling rashly to give themselves over to those who were plotting against them: but on the contrary, since they knew what is written, that the lots of men are in the hands of God, and that the Lord kills and makes alive, they persevered rather to the very end, wandering, as the Apostle says, in sheepskins and goatskins, needy, afflicted, wandering in deserts, and hiding in caves and caverns of the earth, until either the appointed time of death should come, or God himself who had appointed that time should speak with them and restrain those who were plotting against them, or at least deliver them over to their persecutors, as it might please him.

Athanasius, Bishop of Alexandria, the most ardent defender of the Catholic religion, having as a deacon suppressed the impiety of Arius in the Council of Nicaea, incurred such hatred from the Arians that from that time they never ceased to plot against him. Driven into exile, he lived as an exile in Gaul at Trier. Then, having endured incredible calamities, he traversed a great part of the world; and often expelled from his church, he was often also restored to it, by the authority of Julius, Bishop of Rome, and by the decrees of the councils of Sardica and Jerusalem, while the Arians were ever hostile to him. Finally, delivered by divine providence from so many great perils, he died at Alexandria under Valens. His life and death were made illustrious by great miracles. He wrote much that was devout and splendid in defense of the Catholic faith, and governed the church of Alexandria most holily for forty-six years amid the greatest vicissitudes of the times.

Athanasius of Alexandria, the most ardent defender of the Catholic religion, was made a deacon by Alexander, Bishop of Alexandria, in whose place he afterward succeeded. He had also previously followed Alexander to the Council of Nicaea; where, having suppressed the impiety of Arius, he incurred such hatred from the Arians that from that time they never ceased to plot against him. For at a council assembled at Tyre, composed largely of Arian bishops, they suborned a woman to accuse Athanasius of having violently assaulted her during his stay as a guest. And so Athanasius was brought before them, and with him the priest Timothy; who, feigning to be Athanasius, said: Did I, woman, stay as a guest with you? Did I do you violence? To whom she pertly replied: You did violence to me; and confirming it with an oath, she appealed to the judgment of the judges to avenge so great an outrage. When this fraud was discovered, the woman's shamelessness was dismissed.

This was especially held as a solemn duty by those same predecessors of ours: to keep safe and intact, with all care, zeal, and effort, the doctrine of the Immaculate Conception of the Mother of God. For not only did they in no way permit the doctrine itself to be marked or reviled by anyone in any manner, but going much further, they repeatedly declared in clear pronouncements: That the doctrine by which we profess the Immaculate Conception of the Virgin is, and by its own merit is held to be, entirely consonant with ecclesiastical worship; and that it is ancient, and nearly universal, and of such a kind as the Roman Church has taken upon herself to cherish and defend, and wholly worthy to be used in the sacred liturgy itself and in more solemn prayers. And not content with these measures, in order that the doctrine itself of the Immaculate Conception of the Virgin might remain inviolate, they most severely forbade that the opinion adverse to this doctrine could be defended, whether publicly or privately, and willed that it be considered overthrown by multiple wounds, as it were.

But it is not that after the head is bowed that the spirit is breathed out, but that after the spirit is breathed out the head is bowed. Here, however, the reverse occurred: by which the Evangelist shows him to be the Lord of all. But the Jews, who strain out a gnat and swallow a camel, having dared to commit so great a crime, deliberate in broad daylight: Because it was the Preparation, lest the bodies should remain on the cross on the Sabbath, they asked Pilate that their legs should be broken. Do you see how great a thing truth is? Through what they do, the prophecy is fulfilled; for another was thereby made manifest. The soldiers came therefore and broke the legs of the others; not Christ's; but to curry favor with the Jews they opened his side with a lance, and continue to insult him even in death. O most wicked and criminal will!

But hearing that Archelaus reigned in Judea in place of Herod his father, he was afraid to go there. Many fall into error through ignorance of history, thinking this to be the same Herod by whom the Lord was mocked in his Passion and who is now reported to have died. Therefore, that Herod who afterward made friendship with Pilate is the son of this Herod, the brother of Archelaus.

Augustine, a monk at the Lateran monastery in Rome, was sent with some forty fellow monks to England by Gregory the Great in the year five hundred and ninety-seven. Invited by King Ethelbert to Canterbury, the metropolis of his kingdom, he built an oratory near the city with his companions. Through the preaching of heavenly doctrine he led many of the islanders and the king himself to the Christian faith, to the great joy of Bertha, the king's wife, who was a Christian. Ordained bishop at the command of Gregory, he established the See of Canterbury, and from the same Pontiff obtained the use of the pallium with authority to establish a hierarchy in England. At last, having endured the greatest labors for Christ, after setting Mellitus over the church of London and Justus over Rochester, and Laurence over his own, he departed to heaven on the seventh day before the Kalends of June, and was buried in the monastery of Saint Peter, which from then on was the burial place of the archbishops of Canterbury and of certain kings.

Augustine, born at Tagaste in Africa of honorable parents, quickly surpassed all his contemporaries in learning. As a youth, while at Carthage, he fell into the heresy of the Manicheans. Afterward going to Rome, thence sent to Milan to teach rhetoric, there, at the urging of Monica his most devout mother, being a frequent hearer of the bishop Ambrose, kindled by his influence with zeal for the Catholic faith, he was baptized by him at the age of thirty-three. Returning to Africa, joining holiness of life to religion, he was made a priest by Valerius, the bishop of Hippo renowned for his holiness. At that time he established a community of religious, with whom sharing common food and the same manner of life, he trained them most diligently in the discipline of the apostolic life and doctrine. Moved by this piety of Augustine, Valerius took him on as an assistant in the episcopal office. He wrote much with piety, subtlety, and copiousness, to overthrow heresies and to illuminate Christian doctrine. When the Vandals were ravaging Africa with war and Hippo had already been under siege for three months, he was seized with fever and departed to the Lord in the seventy-sixth year of his age. His body, first translated to Sardinia, then to Pavia, is there honored with veneration.

Augustine, a monk at the Lateran monastery in Rome, was sent to England by Gregory the Great with about forty fellow monks in the year five hundred and ninety-seven, to convert those peoples to Christ. At that time King Ethelbert was the most powerful king in Kent, who, having heard the purpose of Augustine's coming, invited him with his companions to Canterbury, the metropolis of his kingdom, and there liberally granted him the opportunity to reside and to preach Christ. Accordingly, the holy man built an oratory near Canterbury, where he himself remained for some time and emulated the apostolic way of life with his companions.

Augustine, born at Tagaste in Africa of honorable parents, and as a boy surpassing his companions by far in natural ability and docility, quickly excelled all in learning. As a youth, while at Carthage, he fell into the heresy of the Manicheans. Afterward going to Rome, thence sent to Milan to teach rhetoric, there being a frequent hearer of the bishop Ambrose, kindled by his influence with zeal for the Catholic faith, he was baptized by him at the age of thirty-three. Returning to Africa, joining holiness of life to religion, he was made a priest by Valerius the bishop of Hippo, renowned for his holiness. At that time he established a community of religious, with whom sharing common food and the same manner of life, he trained them most diligently in the discipline of the apostolic life and doctrine. But since the Manichean heresy was flourishing, he began to attack it more vehemently and refuted Fortunatus the heresiarch.

Hail, O richly fruitful and shady mountain of God, on which the rational Lamb was nurtured, who bore our sins and infirmities: the mountain from which that stone was rolled down, cut out by no hand, that shattered the altars of idols and became the head of the corner, wonderful in our eyes. Hail, holy throne of God, divine gift, house of glory, most beautiful ornament, chosen treasure, and propitiation for the whole world, and heaven telling forth the glory of God. Hail, vessel fashioned of pure gold, containing the most sweet delight of our souls, namely Christ who is the manna. O most pure Virgin, most worthy of all praise and service, a gift consecrated to God surpassing every rank of creatures, uncut earth, unplowed field, most flourishing vine, fountain pouring forth waters, virgin bearing, and mother ignorant of a man, hidden treasury of innocence and glory of holiness; by your most acceptable prayers, powerful with maternal authority, before the Lord and God the Maker of all things, your Son begotten of you without a father, bring it about that you guide the helm of the ecclesiastical order and lead it to a tranquil haven.

Barnabas the Levite, a Cypriot by birth, was ordained together with the Apostle Paul to preach the Gospel of Jesus Christ. Having sold the field he owned, he brought the money obtained from it to the Apostles. Sent to Antioch for the purpose of preaching, he there confirmed by his exhortations many who had been converted to the faith of Christ. Setting out from there with the same Paul, he traveled through many cities and regions with the greatest benefit to his hearers. Finally, parting from Paul, he sailed with John, who is surnamed Mark, to Cyprus, and there, in the seventh year of Nero, added the crown of martyrdom to the glory of his apostolic office.

Barnabas the Levite, a Cypriot by birth, who was also called Joseph, was ordained with Paul as an Apostle to the Gentiles to preach the Gospel of Jesus Christ. Having sold the field he owned, he brought the money obtained from it to the Apostles. Sent to Antioch for the purpose of preaching, when he found that many there had been converted to the faith of Christ the Lord, he rejoiced exceedingly and exhorted them to remain in the faith of Christ. By this exhortation he made much progress, because he was held by all to be a good man and full of the Holy Spirit.

Bartholomew the Apostle, a Galilean, when he had gone into nearer India, which had fallen to him by lot among the regions of the earth for preaching the Gospel of Jesus Christ, preached to those peoples the coming of the Lord Jesus according to the Gospel of Saint Matthew. But having converted very many in that province to Jesus Christ, and having endured many labors and hardships, he came to greater Armenia.

He also dedicated the basilica of the Apostle Paul on the Ostian Way, built most magnificently by the Emperor Constantine, which the Emperor enriched with many estates assigned to it and adorned with most ample gifts. Such was the ardor of religion in that Emperor that, demolishing temples of idols, he built churches in many places throughout the world, and especially at Rome, among which were the basilica of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem in the Sessorian estate, of Saint Lawrence outside the walls in the Verano estate, of Saints Peter and Marcellinus on the Lavican Way, and very many others.

He built two basilicas: one in the name of Saint Lawrence near the theater of Pompey, which he enriched with the greatest gifts and to which he assigned houses and estates; the other on the Ardeatine Way at the Catacombs. He also dedicated the Platonia, where the bodies of Saints Peter and Paul rested for a time, and adorned it with elegant verses. He also wrote in prose and verse on virginity and published many other works in verse.

Basil, a noble Cappadocian, having been marvelously educated at Athens together with his closest friend Gregory Nazianzen first in secular letters and then in a monastery in sacred matters, quickly ran his course to every excellence of doctrine and morals, so that he earned the surname Great. Called to Pontus to preach the Gospel of Jesus Christ, he brought that province back to the way of salvation; soon he was taken on as an assistant by Eusebius, bishop of Caesarea, to instruct that city, and afterward succeeded to his place. He was first in defending that the Son is consubstantial with the Father, and by miracles so softened the Emperor Valens, who was angry with him and threatening exile, that he forced him to depart from his purpose. He was admirable in abstinence and continence; constant in prayer, he often spent the entire night in it. Having built monasteries, he so regulated the institution of monks as to combine brilliantly the advantages of the solitary and the active life. He wrote much with learning; and no one, as Gregory Nazianzen testifies, explained the books of Sacred Scripture more truly or more abundantly. He died on the first of January.

Basil, a noble Cappadocian, having been marvelously educated at Athens together with his closest friend Gregory Nazianzen first in secular letters and then in a monastery in sacred matters, quickly ran his course to every excellence of doctrine and morals, so that he earned the surname Great. Called to Pontus to preach the Gospel of Jesus Christ, he brought that province, which had strayed from Christian practice, back to the way of salvation. Soon he was taken on as an assistant by Eusebius, bishop of Caesarea, to instruct that city, and afterward succeeded to his place. He was first in defending that the Son is consubstantial with the Father, and by miracles so softened the Emperor Valens, who was angry with him, that he forced him, when he was pressing to carry out his will to drive him into exile, to depart from his purpose.

Basilides, Cyrinus, Nabor, and Nazarius, Roman soldiers, noble by birth and illustrious in virtue, having embraced the Christian religion and proclaiming Christ the Son of God under the Emperor Diocletian, were seized by Aurelius the prefect of the City and, when they despised his orders to offer sacrifice to the gods, were sent to prison. While they were praying, a most brilliant light suddenly arose and illumined the prison before the eyes of all who were there; moved by that heavenly splendor, Marcellus, who was set over the guard, and many others believed in Christ the Lord. But afterward, released from prison, and when under the Emperor Maximian they continued, even in defiance of his command, to proclaim Christ alone as God and Lord, they were tortured with scorpions and cast again into chains: from which, led out on the seventh day and set before the feet of the emperor, they persisted in mocking the empty gods, confessing Jesus Christ as God with the utmost constancy. For this reason, condemned, they were struck with the axe. Their bodies, thrown to wild beasts, untouched by them, were honorably buried by Christians.

The regions of Bavaria, of which, as the Supreme Pontiff Pius VII himself testified, none in the world have been more flourishing in zeal for the Catholic religion, had distinguished themselves from ancient times by a singular devotion toward the most Blessed Virgin Mary. Testimonies of this are the very ancient church at Augsburg, the metropolitan church of Munich, the cathedral church of Speyer, and very many other Marian temples and shrines both in the ancient and in the more recent parts of Bavaria, conspicuous either for venerable antiquity or for the constant throng of pilgrims. The same is attested by confraternities or congregations established under the patronage of the same glorious Virgin, and by Marian statues and images placed for the devout veneration of the faithful everywhere on the fronts of houses, in streets and at crossroads, beside fields and farmland, amid the shadows of forests, and upon the summits of mountains.

Blessed Agnes, when she had appeared one night to her parents, who were keeping constant vigil at her tomb, accompanied by a choir of virgins, is said to have spoken to them thus: Do not mourn me as dead, my parents; for I live in heaven with him whom I loved with my whole heart on earth, together with these virgins. Some years later, when Constantia, the daughter of the Emperor Constantine, not yet a Christian, had come to the same tomb seeking a cure for an incurable ulcer, she fell asleep and seemed to hear the voice of Agnes saying: Be constant, Constantia; believe in Jesus Christ the Son of God, who will make you whole. And having been healed, she soon received baptism together with many of the emperor's household, and built there a church in the name of Blessed Agnes.

Blessed are you, O land of Bethlehem of Judah, who endured the cruelty of King Herod in the slaughter of the children: who merited under one time to offer to God a white-robed people of defenseless infancy. Yet we rightly celebrate their nativity, those whom the world of eternal life brought forth more blessedly than the birth of their mothers' wombs delivered. For indeed they attained the dignity of perpetual life before they received the enjoyment of the present one.

When Blessed Martin the First of that name was relegated to Cherson by the tyrannical sentence of the heretical emperor, at the urging of the exarch Theodore, Eugene, a Roman by birth, who had devoted himself to the sacred clerical order almost from the cradle, administered the functions of the absent Pontiff, lest the governance of the Roman Church should seem to have entirely ceased; but he appeared to use this authority in practice with modesty, since he knew well that, while Martin was still alive, he was not a legitimate Pontiff but only, as it were, acting in his place.

That the Blessed Archangel Michael has appeared to men many times is confirmed both by the authority of the sacred Books and by the ancient tradition of the Saints. For this reason the memory of these events is celebrated in many places. As of old the synagogue of the Jews, so now the Church venerates him as the guardian and patron of God. Now under Gelasius I, Supreme Pontiff, there was a celebrated apparition of the Archangel Michael in Apulia on the summit of Mount Gargano, at the foot of which the people of Siponto dwell.

After three days the Archangel Michael warned the bishop that that place was under his protection, and by this sign showed that he wished worship of God to be offered there in memory of himself and the Angels. Wherefore the bishop proceeded to go to that cave together with the citizens. And when they found it fashioned in the likeness of a certain temple, they began to celebrate divine services in that place, which was afterward made illustrious by many miracles. And not long after, Pope Boniface, at Rome in the great circus, dedicated a church of Saint Michael on the third day before the Kalends of October; on which day also the Church celebrates the memory of all the Angels. But this present day is consecrated by the apparition of the Archangel Michael.

Blessed Raymond of Barcelona, from the noble family of Penyafort, imbued from infancy with the rudiments of the Christian religion, appeared even as a little child to give promise of something great by his outstanding gifts of mind and body. For as a young man, after teaching the humanities in his native city, he went to Bologna, where applying himself diligently to the duties of piety and to pontifical and civil law, and having been honored with the degree of doctor, he there expounded the sacred canons with great admiration from all. As the fame of his virtues spread abroad, Berenger, Bishop of Barcelona, returning from Rome to his church, set out on a journey to Bologna for the purpose of meeting him, and at length by his most earnest entreaties obtained that he return with him to his native land. Soon adorned with the canonry and the provostship of the same church, he shone forth before the whole clergy and people in integrity, modesty, learning, and gentle manners, and always increased to the best of his ability the honor and worship of the Virgin Mother of God, whom he venerated with singular devotion.

Blessed is she who alone among human beings merited to hear before all others: You have found grace. How much? As much as he had said above: full. And truly full, since she would pour it out and pour it in upon all creation as in a great shower: for you have found grace with God. When he says this, even the Angel marvels that either a woman so great, or all human beings, have merited life through a woman; the Angel is astonished that the whole of God comes within the narrow confines of a virginal womb, for whom all creation is narrow at once. Hence it is that the Angel lingers, hence it is that he addresses the virgin according to her merit and greets her according to her grace, hardly discloses the purpose to her as she listens — surely to stir her understanding — and barely composes himself after long trembling.

Blessed finally are those who suffer persecution for the sake of justice, and by their unconquered patience obtain the eternal kingdom of Christ. To this kind of blessedness none are to be referred more fittingly than the protomartyr Stephen and the other most valiant soldiers and martyrs of Christ: for, led as sheep to the slaughter, they strove even to the shedding of blood for Christian justice, so that no force or barbarism of enemies, no bitterness of tribulation or temptation, could draw them away and separate them from the confession of the faith, the charity of Christ, the doctrine of the Church, and the path of justice. O happy those who could testify with a good conscience: Who shall separate us from the charity of Christ? Tribulation? or distress? or famine? or nakedness? or danger? or persecution? or the sword? In all these things we overcome because of him who loved us. We passed through fire and water, and you have brought us forth into refreshment.

Blessed therefore are those who suffer persecution for the sake of justice, because theirs is the Kingdom of Heaven. This eighth beatitude, which returns to the beginning and declares the perfect man, is perhaps signified also by the circumcision on the eighth day in the Old Testament; and by the Lord's resurrection after the Sabbath, which is at once the eighth and the first day; and by the celebration of the octaves which we observe in the regeneration of the new man; and by the number of Pentecost itself: for by the sevenfold multiplication of the number seven, which yields forty-nine, an eighth is added as it were, so that fifty is completed. And as if returning to the beginning, on that day on which the Holy Spirit was sent, we are led into the Kingdom of Heaven, and we receive the inheritance, and are comforted, and are fed, and obtain mercy, and are cleansed, and are made peaceable. And so, being made perfect, we all endure from without the troubles brought against us for the sake of truth and justice.

Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted. Mourning is grief over the loss of dear ones; but those who have been converted to God lose the things they used to hold dear in this world. For they do not rejoice in those things in which they formerly rejoiced; and until the love of eternal things is formed in them, they are wounded by a certain sadness. They shall be comforted, therefore, by the Holy Spirit, who is called Paraclete for this very reason — that is, Comforter — so that, losing temporal things, they may enjoy eternal joy.

Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for justice, for they shall be satisfied. He now speaks of lovers of the true and unshaken good. With that food therefore shall they be satisfied, of which the Lord himself says: My food is to do the will of my Father, which is justice; and with that water of which whoever shall drink, as he likewise says, there shall become in him a fountain of water leaping up to eternal life. Blessed are the merciful, for God will show them mercy. He says that those are blessed who come to the aid of the wretched: which is so repaid to them that they are freed from wretchedness.

Bede the priest was born at Jarrow on the borders of Britain and Scotland. Having become a monk, he so ordered his life that, while devoting himself entirely to the studies of the arts and sciences, he never relaxed anything of regular discipline. There was no branch of learning in which he was not most diligently versed; but his chief care was the meditation on the divine Scriptures, so that, upon being ordained to the priesthood, he set about expounding the sacred books; in this he adhered so closely to the teachings of the holy Fathers that he brought forth nothing except what was approved by their judgment, making use almost of their very words. Ever averse to idleness, he passed from reading to prayer and from prayer back to reading. He wrote several books for the correction of the faithful's morals, for the vindication and assertion of the faith, by which he gained such a reputation for himself among all that his writings were read publicly in the churches even during his lifetime. At last, broken by age and labors, he fell asleep devoutly in the Lord. Leo XIII declared him a Doctor of the universal Church.

Bede the Priest, born on the borders of Britain and Scotland at Jarrow, was entrusted at the age of seven to be educated by the holy Abbot Benedict Biscop of Wearmouth. Having then become a monk, he so ordered his life that, while devoting himself entirely to the study of the arts and sciences, he never in any way relaxed his regular discipline. There was no branch of learning in which he was not most diligently versed; but his chief concern was the meditation of the divine Scriptures, and, that he might more fully grasp their meaning, he acquired a knowledge of the Greek and Hebrew tongues. Ordained a priest at the age of thirty by the command of his abbot, he straightway, at the urging of Acca, Bishop of Hexham, undertook to expound the sacred books; in this he adhered so closely to the teachings of the holy Fathers that he put forward nothing that was not approved by their judgment, using even their very words for the most part. Ever averse to idleness, he would pass from reading to prayer and from prayer back to reading; in which pursuit he was so inflamed in soul that he was often bathed in tears while reading and teaching. And lest he be distracted by the cares of transitory things, he most steadfastly refused the office of abbot when it was offered to him.

Benedict the Second of that name, a Roman by birth, son of John, was raised to the Apostolic office after the death of Leo the Second, in the year of Christ six hundred and eighty-four, and held the supreme helm of the Christian commonwealth for about nine months — most worthy indeed to have held it longer, since from the earliest years of his boyhood he had devoted himself entirely to ecclesiastical ministries, and had applied himself diligently to the divine Scriptures and to sacred psalmody.

Benedict, of noble birth from Norcia, educated in the liberal disciplines at Rome, in order to give himself wholly to Jesus Christ, penetrated into a very deep cave in the place called Subiaco; in which he lay hidden for three years, so that only one Roman monk, Romanus, who served him in the necessities of life, knew of this. While therefore on a certain day burning temptations to lust were stirred up in him by the devil, he rolled himself for a long time in thorns, until, with his body lacerated, the sense of pleasure was overcome by pain. But when the fame of his holiness began to spread abroad from those hiding places, certain monks entrusted themselves to him to be formed by him; whose license of living, being unable to bear his reproofs, resolved to give him poison in his drink. But when they presented the cup to him, he shattered the vessel with the sign of the Cross, and, leaving the monastery, withdrew again into solitude.

But when the fame of his holiness began to spread abroad from those hiding places, certain monks entrusted themselves to him to be formed by him; whose license of living, being unable to bear his reproofs, resolved to give him poison in his drink. But when they presented the cup to him, he shattered the vessel with the sign of the Cross, and, leaving the monastery, withdrew again into solitude.
But when many disciples came to him daily, he built twelve monasteries and fortified them with most holy laws. Afterwards he migrated to Cassino, where he broke in pieces the image of Apollo which was still worshipped there, overturned the altar, and burned the groves; and there he built a chapel of Saint Martin and a small oratory of Saint John, and imbued the townspeople and inhabitants with Christian precepts. Thereupon Benedict was daily more and more increased by divine grace, so that he also foretold things to come by prophetic spirit. When Totila, king of the Goths, heard of this, wishing to test whether it were so, he sent his sword-bearer before him in royal dress and retinue, to pretend to be the king. But when Benedict saw him, he said: Put off, son, put off what you are wearing; for it is not yours. And to Totila himself he foretold his coming to Rome, his crossing of the sea, and his death after nine years.
Some months before he departed from this life, he forewarned his disciples on what day he would die; and he ordered that the sepulchre, in which he wished his body to be laid, should be opened six days before he was carried to it; and on the sixth day he wished to be brought into the church; where, having received the Eucharist, and raising his eyes to heaven in prayer, he breathed forth his soul in the hands of his disciples: two monks saw his soul going to heaven, adorned with a most precious pallium, surrounded by gleaming lamps, and heard a man of most bright and solemn appearance, standing above him, saying: This is the way by which Benedict, beloved of the Lord, ascended to heaven.

Benedict the Eleventh, from the honest family of the Boccasini of Treviso, embraced the Order of Preachers at the age of fourteen; in which he devoted himself intensely for fourteen years to human and divine studies, and taught privately and publicly for an equal number of years, to the highest praise of his learning. Conspicuous for his fame of holiness and prudence, he was advanced through the various ranks and dignities of his order to its supreme mastership; in which office, shining as an example to all the others, he wonderfully fostered discipline and in a brief time enlarged the order itself. Boniface the Eighth made happy use of his services in making peace between the kings of France and Britain; and while he was journeying through the provinces committed to him in France, he created him Cardinal Priest of the holy Roman Church, and, summoning him to Rome, designated him legate to Pannonia, where he composed with wonderful skill a dispute among three princes contending for the succession of that kingdom.

Blessed is the Lord God, who has visited his people through the ministry of so many Pontiffs; and now that they have been taken up into the holy city, by the remembrance of such great sweetness they do not cease to console our captivity. May their spirits exult in the Lord, for, lifted from the burden of bodily weight, they are no longer weighed down by any foul or earthly matter, and so with all swiftness and vitality, passing through all corporeal and incorporeal creation, they make their way wholly into God, and, cleaving to him, are one spirit with him for ever. Holiness befits this house, in which so great a memorial of sanctity is honored.

Benno, born in Hildesheim, a city of Saxony, of illustrious parents, was entrusted at the age of five to the holy Bernard, Bishop of Hildesheim, his kinsman, and to a provost of the monastery of Saint Michael to be formed in the fear of God and trained in the pursuit of learning. Grown to young manhood, by the counsel of the bishop he took the monastic habit in that same monastery and lived there so holily that upon the death of the abbot he was compelled to take up the burden of abbatial care; yet leave for its vacation, out of love for the contemplative life, he obtained after a space of about three months, with his eyes often in tears. When, however, he hoped to spend the rest of his life in private prayer, the Emperor Henry the Third of that name, desiring to establish in the church of Goslar, newly completed by himself, a congregation of Canons living according to rule, drawn from the most proven and learned men of Germany, obtained Benno by earnest petition from Pope Leo the Ninth and, by the Pope's authority transferred from the monastic to the canonical state, gave him as master to that new congregation, that he might be to it a leader in spiritual warfare and might form it by the training of ecclesiastical discipline.

Bernard, born in Fontaines in Burgundy of an honorable family, was as a young man most vehemently solicited by women on account of his outstanding beauty, yet could never be moved from his resolve to preserve chastity. To flee these temptations of the devil, at the age of twenty-two he resolved to enter the monastery of Cîteaux, where this order began and which was then flourishing in holiness. When Bernard's purpose became known, his brothers most earnestly endeavored to deter him from it; in which he himself proved more eloquent and successful. For he so brought them and many others to his own mind that thirty young men embraced the same religious life together with him. As a monk he was so given to fasting that whenever food was to be taken, he seemed to be undergoing a torment. He also exercised himself wonderfully in vigils and prayers; and, cherishing Christian poverty, he led as it were a heavenly life on earth, removed from all care for and desire of transitory things.

Bernard, born in Fontaines in Burgundy of an honorable family, cherished chastity most diligently from his boyhood. At the age of twenty-two, entering the monastery of Cîteaux, where the order of that name began, he brought also his brothers and many others to embrace the same religious life. He exercised himself wonderfully in vigils and prayers. In him there shone humility, mercy, kindness, prudence, and an unceasing zeal for meditating on heavenly things. Made Abbot of Clairvaux, he built monasteries in many places, where his distinguished rule and discipline long flourished. He also wrote many works, in which it is apparent that he was instructed by a doctrine divinely bestowed rather than acquired by labor. Entreated by great princes to settle their disputes and to order ecclesiastical affairs, he came several times to Italy. He aided Pope Innocent the Second in an outstanding way in refuting the schism of Peter of Leon. Having lived sixty-three years, and having merited greatly of the Church, he fell asleep in the Lord.

Bernardine Albizesca, born of a noble Sienese family, devoted his mind to works of piety amid his first studies of grammar, neglecting childish games, given in a special way to fasting, prayer, and the veneration of the Blessed Virgin. Conspicuous for mercy toward the poor, he consecrated himself to their service in Siena at the hospital of Blessed Mary of the Scala. Deliberating upon the way of religious life to embrace, by God's disposition he chose the Order of Blessed Francis above all others, in which he excelled in humility, patience, and the other virtues of a religious man. Having taken up the burden of preaching at the command of his superiors, when he recognized himself as less suited for it by reason of the smallness and hoarseness of his voice, he implored God's help and was miraculously freed from this impediment. Traveling through cities and towns, he extinguished civic discords everywhere in the name of Jesus, which he always carried in his mouth and in his heart, and restored in great measure by word and example the decayed piety and morals. He composed books piously and learnedly. Full of merits and renowned for miracles, at the age of sixty-six, he rested with a blessed end in the city of Aquila in the Vestini.

Bernardine Albizesca, born of a noble Sienese family, gave clear signs of holiness from the beginning of his youth; for, honestly educated by pious parents, neglecting childish games, amid his first studies of grammar he devoted his mind to works of piety, given especially to fasting, prayer, and the veneration of the most Blessed Virgin. Indeed, he was conspicuous for mercy toward the poor. And in order to cultivate all these things the better as time went on, he wished to be enrolled among those who serve God in Siena in the hospital of Blessed Mary of the Scala, from which many men renowned for holiness have come forth. There, by bodily mortification and the care of the sick, while a dreadful pestilence was raging, he exercised himself with incredible charity. Among his other virtues, he preserved chastity most holily, despite his distinguished appearance that resisted it, so that in his presence no one ever, not even the most shameless, dared to utter an immodest word.

Bibiana, a Roman Virgin, born of noble family, was made nobler still by the Christian faith. For her parents, Flavian and Dafrosa, suffered martyrdom under Julian the Apostate. Then Bibiana and her sister Demetria, stripped of all their goods and tempted by Apronianus, the prefect of the City, with blandishments and threats to turn from the right faith, most steadfastly abominated the impiety of the prefect. In this contest Demetria, suddenly falling before Bibiana's eyes, died in the Lord. Bibiana, however, was handed over to be seduced by the most cunning woman Rufina; but, having overcome her snares, she foiled the prefect's craftiness. Therefore by his order she was beaten with leaded rods until she breathed forth her soul. Her sacred body, left for two days to be thrown to dogs, was nonetheless miraculously preserved unharmed; the Priest John buried it by night near the tomb of her sister and mother at the Licinian Palace, where now stands the church dedicated to God under the name of holy Bibiana.

Bibiana, a Roman Virgin, born of noble family, was made nobler still by the Christian faith. For her father Flavian, a former prefect, was deported to the Taurine waters under the most impious tyrant Julian the Apostate, branded with the marks of slaves, and died as a martyr. Her mother Dafrosa and her daughters were first confined to their home to be worn down by hunger; then the mother was banished outside the City and beheaded. Their pious parents now dead, Bibiana and her sister Demetria were stripped of all their goods; Apronianus, prefect of the City, greedy for money, persecuted the sisters; and when he saw that they, utterly destitute of all human help yet miraculously fed by God who gives food to the hungry, had become more lively and vigorous, he was greatly astonished.

For two years before he departed from this life, when he was afflicted by long infirmities, amid the most bitter torments of the body, purified like gold in a furnace, he gave unceasing thanks to God. But when the sacred day of Pentecost came, having governed with the highest praise the church entrusted to him for many years, renowned for holy works and miracles, he rested in peace. Pope Celestine the Third enrolled him in the number of the Saints. His virtue shines forth especially in the driving out of unclean spirits. His body, incorrupt through so many centuries, is venerated with great devotion by the faithful in his homeland, which he has more than once delivered from pressing danger.

Bridget, born in Sweden of illustrious and pious parents, lived most holily. She was so affected by meditation on the Lord's Passion that she could never think of it without tears. Given in marriage to Ulf, prince of Nericia, she urged her husband himself toward the duties of piety, both by her excellent example and by her effective words. Most devout in the education of her children, she served the poor and the sick. When her husband had become a Cistercian monk and had shortly afterward died, Bridget undertook a stricter form of life. Then many hidden things were divinely revealed to her. She founded the monastery of Vadstena under the rule of the Holy Savior; she went to Jerusalem out of devotion. At last in Rome, afflicted by grave illnesses for a whole year, she departed to heaven. Pope Boniface the Ninth, when miracles had made her illustrious, enrolled her in the number of the Saints.

Bridget, born in Sweden of illustrious and pious parents, lived most holily. While she was yet being carried in the womb, her mother was rescued from a shipwreck on her account. At ten years of age, after hearing a sermon on the Lord's Passion, the following night she saw Jesus on the Cross, covered with fresh blood, and heard him speaking to her about that same Passion. From that time she was so affected by meditation on it that she could never afterward think of it without tears.

Blaise, while he was flourishing in the praise of his virtues in Sebaste in Armenia, was chosen bishop of that city. When Diocletian was exercising his insatiable cruelty against Christians, Blaise hid himself in a cave of Mount Argaeus; where he lay concealed until he was captured by soldiers of the governor Agricolaus who were hunting, and was brought before the governor, by whose order he was cast into chains. In that place he healed many sick persons who were brought to Blaise, drawn by the fame of his holiness. Among these was a boy who, with a bone lodged crosswise in his throat and his recovery despaired of by the physicians, was at the point of death. Brought before the governor, Blaise refused once and again to be induced either by blandishments or threats to sacrifice to the gods, and was first beaten with rods, then torn on the rack with iron combs; and finally, beheaded, he gave an illustrious testimony of faith to Christ the Lord on the third day before the Nones of February.

Bonaventure, born in Bagnoregio in Etruria, as a child escaped a deadly illness by the prayers of Blessed Francis, to whose religious order he had been vowed by his mother's vow if he should recover. And so as a young man he wished to embrace the order of the Friars Minor, in which he made such progress in learning under the master Alexander of Hales that seven years later at Paris, having attained the title of Master, he publicly expounded the books of the Sentences to the highest praise, which he afterward also illustrated with distinguished commentaries. Nor did he excel only in the erudition of learning, but also wonderfully in integrity of morals and innocence of life, in humility, meekness, contempt of earthly things, and desire for heavenly things; plainly worthy to be held as a model of perfection and to be called a saint by Blessed Thomas Aquinas, to whom he was joined in the highest charity. For when the latter had found him writing the life of Saint Francis, he said: Let us leave a Saint to labor for a Saint.

Bonaventure, born in Bagnoregio in Etruria, embraced as a young man the religious life of Saint Francis of Assisi; in which, devoted to the study of letters under the teacher Alexander of Hales, he made such progress that seven years later at Paris he publicly expounded the books of the Sentences to the highest praise. A man of the greatest meekness and humility, most devoutly disposed toward the Passion of Christ our Lord, at barely thirty-five years of age he was created minister general of the whole order. In wisely administering this office he gained distinguished praise not only for doctrine and holiness, but also for talent and skill. Drawn by this fame, Pope Gregory the Tenth created him Cardinal and Bishop of Albano. He wrote many works most learnedly, and especially the Commentaries on the Four Books of the Sentences. He died at Lyons during the council, in the fifty-third year of his age, and was enrolled among the Saints by Sixtus the Fourth. Sixtus the Fifth then honored him with the title of Seraphic Doctor.

Abandoning no part of the good shepherd's office, he strove especially that the youth called to the Lord's inheritance should be duly formed for sacred things, that pious associations should grow with new increases, that greater dignity and devotion should be added to the rites of divine worship. He never ceased to proclaim more urgently the precepts upon which the Christian city is grounded, and, himself living a life of poverty, he never neglected to bring relief to the poor. And so, with so many merits pleading for him, he was enrolled among the purple-clad Fathers and created Patriarch of Venice. Finally, after the death of Leo the Thirteenth, when the votes of the Cardinal Fathers converged upon him, and when he himself had striven in vain to avert so great an office from himself by supplications and tears, yielding at last to persuasion, he said, 'accepted upon the Cross,' and received the summit of the Supreme Pontificate as a cross offered to him by God, with a humble yet resolute spirit.

Boniface, formerly called Winfrid, was born among the English toward the end of the seventh century, and from his very infancy held the world in aversion and had the monastic life in his desires. When his father had tried in vain to change his purpose by the allurements of the world, he entered a monastery and was imbued under the discipline of the blessed Wolfhard with every kind of virtue and knowledge. In his thirtieth year he was distinguished with the priesthood, and as an assiduous preacher of the divine word he labored in this office with great fruit for souls. Yet, desiring to extend the kingdom of Christ, he continually wept over the vast multitude of barbarians, immersed in the darkness of ignorance, who served the demon. And when this zeal for souls increased daily with an inextinguishable ardor, having sought out the divine will through tears and prayers, he obtained from the superior of the monastery permission to set out for the German shores.

Boniface, formerly called Winfrid, was born among the English toward the end of the seventh century. Having entered a monastery and been elevated to the priesthood, he labored in the office of preacher with great fruit for souls. Inflamed by zeal for spreading the faith, he preached the Gospel among the Frisians. Returning to England, after he had most holily governed a monastery for two years and then resigned the superior's office, he betook himself to Rome, where he received the name Boniface from Gregory the Second and, sent to Germany, announced Christ to the peoples of Thuringia and Saxony. Returning to the Frisians, he preached the Gospel with great fruit together with the holy Willibrord. Presently summoned to Rome, he was distinguished with episcopal dignity, and going again to Germany, he thoroughly purged Hesse and Thuringia of the remnants of idolatry. Created legate of the Apostolic See and Archbishop of Mainz, he erected and governed, through himself or through his disciples, several churches. Finally, having undertaken again to preach the Gospel to the Frisians who had relapsed into idolatry, he was put to death with a bloody slaughter together with Eoban his co-bishop and many others near the river Borne, and thus received the palm of martyrdom. His body was laid to rest in the monastery of Fulda.

When Boniface the Fourth of that name had been taken from the living, and the Apostolic See had been vacant for five months and twelve days, the blessed Deusdedit, conspicuous for eminent virtues and outstanding holiness, a Roman by birth, son of Stephen, was created Roman Pontiff by the unanimous consent of all, from the rank of subdeacon. That a subdeacon should be created Pontiff then occurred for the first time, without the precedent of former ages; but that Deusdedit should be chosen in preference to others was due to the outstanding holiness of his life, by which he shone wonderfully illustrious amid so many shadows.

Boniface the Fourth of that name, son of John, born in Valeria of the Marsi, was raised to the pontificate from being a monk of Saint Sebastian outside the City, and a Cardinal Priest, under the Emperor Phocas; and was consecrated on a Sunday, the fifth day before the Kalends of September, in the year of the Lord six hundred and seven; and he sat six years, eight months, and thirteen days; having performed two ordinations in the month of December, in which he created twenty-five bishops and eight deacons.

Boniface, a Roman, son of the priest Jucundus, obtained the episcopate of the Roman Church after the death of the blessed Zosimus. This aged priest, most learned in the law and approved in good morals, was consecrated against his will and with his resistance, by the acclamation of all the people and the consent of the leading men, by seventy priests and nine bishops of various provinces, following the order of divine institution, in the basilica of Julius. At that time the archdeacon Eulalius, circumventing the deacons and with a very small number of the clergy and a turbulent crowd of the common people, rushed presumptuously into a place that was not his due and was ordained in the Constantinian basilica. In that schism the legitimate Pontiff Boniface was greatly oppressed, and was compelled to abandon the basilica of blessed Peter and withdraw with his followers to that of blessed Paul. The matter being then referred to a council of bishops, when the Fathers disagreed among themselves, the whole affair was reserved for a fuller synod, and in the meantime, by the action of the Emperor Honorius, both Boniface and Eulalius were ordered to depart from the City. The latter therefore made for Antium, the former for the basilica of holy Felicitas.

Boniface, a Roman citizen, having lived immorally with Aglae, a noble matron, was seized with such grief at her intemperance that he betook himself, out of penance, to seek out and bury the bodies of the Martyrs. And so, having left his traveling companions, when at Tarsus he had seen many persons tortured with various torments on account of their profession of the Christian faith, he kissed their bonds and earnestly exhorted them to bear their punishments steadfastly, since brief labor would be followed by everlasting rest. He was therefore seized and torn with iron claws; and sharp reeds were also thrust between his nails and his flesh, and molten lead was poured into his mouth. Amid these torments there was heard from Boniface no other word but: I give thanks to you, Lord Jesus Christ, Son of God. Presently he was cast into a kettle of boiling pitch with his head plunged in; and when he had come out unharmed, the judge, inflamed with anger, ordered him to be struck with the axe. At that time a great earthquake occurred, so that many unbelievers were converted to faith in Christ the Lord. His companions, seeking him the following day and learning that he had suffered martyrdom, redeemed his body for five hundred solidi, and having embalmed it and wrapped it in linen cloths, took care to carry it to Rome. When the matron Aglae, who had herself also repented and devoted herself to pious works, learned this through an Angel, she came out to meet the holy body and built a church in his name; in which the body was buried on the Nones of June, when his soul had departed to heaven the day before the Ides of May at Tarsus in Cilicia, under the Emperors Diocletian and Maximian.

He says: I have fought the good fight. I inquire by what virtue he fought: whether it was one that came from himself, or one given from above? But far be it that so great a teacher should be ignorant of the law of God, whose voice is in Deuteronomy: Do not say in your heart, My strength and the power of my hand have wrought for me this great virtue; but you shall remember the Lord your God, because he himself gives you strength to do virtue. But what does the good fight profit, unless victory follows? And who gives the victory, if not he of whom he himself says: Thanks be to God, who gives us the victory through our Lord Jesus Christ?

Returning therefore to Brescia, where she had taken a house near the temple of holy Afra, she established there a new society of virgins, as she had been commanded by a heavenly voice and vision, under a fixed discipline and holy rules of life, and adorned it with the patronage and name of holy Ursula, the unconquered leader of virgins; and, as she lay near death, she foretold that it would endure for ever. At last, near the age of seventy, rich in merits, she flew to heaven on the sixth day before the Kalends of February in the year one thousand five hundred and forty. Her body, left unburied for thirty days, remained flexible and most like the living. Then, having been laid to rest in the temple of holy Afra among the other relics of the Saints with which that place abounds, many miracles began at once to be wrought at her tomb; the fame of which spread far and wide, and she began to be called blessed by the common people not only in Brescia and Desenzano but also elsewhere, and her image was placed on altars: indeed, holy Charles Borromeo himself not many years later openly declared in Brescia that she was worthy to be enrolled by the Apostolic See in the register of holy Virgins. And the veneration long shown her by the people, approved both by the local Ordinaries and fortified by the indults of several Supreme Pontiffs, was ratified and confirmed by Pope Clement the Thirteenth by solemn decree. Her miracles having been duly attested and approved, Pope Pius the Seventh at last enrolled her in the catalog of holy Virgins, with a solemn canonization performed in the Vatican basilica on the twenty-fourth day of May in the year one thousand eight hundred and seven.
Breve Pii X diei 18 Sept. 1908

Pontius Meropius Anicius Paulinus, in the year of salvation three hundred and fifty-three, born at Bordeaux in Aquitaine from a most illustrious family of Roman citizens, was of keen mind and agreeable manners. Under the master Ausonius, he excelled in eloquence and poetry. Most noble and very wealthy, having entered upon the cursus honorum, he attained senatorial dignity in the flower of his age. Then he went to Italy as consul, and having obtained the province of Campania, he settled his seat at Nola. Here, touched by divine light, on account of the heavenly signs that illumined the tomb of Felix, priest and martyr, he began more earnestly to cleave to the true faith of Christ, which he was already pondering in his soul. He therefore laid down the fasces and the axe, unstained by any blood, and returning to Gaul, tossed about by various troubles and great labors by land and sea, he lost the sight of one eye; but restored to health by the blessed Martin, Bishop of Tours, he was washed in the saving waters of baptism by the blessed Delphin, bishop of Bordeaux.

His sleep was brief, and on the ground; his clothing was such as to ward off nakedness only, his food such as to ward off death alone. Virginal chastity, like a lily among thorns, he guarded by rough haircloth, scourging, and fasting. Moreover, for some thirty-five years before his death, he abstained perpetually from the eating of meat. At last, full of days as well as of merits, having long and diligently prepared himself for the death that he had foreseen was near, so that nothing might hold him any longer, he distributed everything that remained in his house entirely to the poor. Then, duly fortified by the Sacraments of the Church, already desiring to be dissolved and to be with Christ, he flew to heaven on the eve of His Nativity, renowned for miracles before and after death. After his death he was brought to the nearby church of the academy of holy Anne and honorably buried there. With the veneration and concourse of the people increasing daily, he is devoutly honored among the chief patrons of Poland and Lithuania. Resplendent with new miracles, he was enrolled in the register of the Saints with solemn rite by Pope Clement the Thirteenth, Supreme Pontiff, on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of August, in the year one thousand seven hundred and sixty-seven.

Bruno, founder of the Carthusian religious order, was born at Cologne. From boyhood he was distinguished by gravity of morals and desire for solitude. Sent by his parents to Paris, he there made such progress in the studies of philosophy and theology that he obtained the title of Doctor and Master in both faculties; and not long after, by reason of his outstanding virtues, he obtained a canonry of the church of Reims. Having founded the Order of Carthusians and lived the eremitical life in it for some years, he was summoned to Rome by Urban the Second, who had been his disciple. The Pope made use of his counsel and learning for some years amid so many calamities of that time; until the man of God, having refused the archbishopric of Reggio, obtained permission to depart and again sought out the desert, where, full of virtues and merits, he fell asleep in the Lord.
