Bruno, founder of the Carthusian religious order, was born at Cologne. From his very cradle he showed a foretaste of his future holiness; and, by the favor of divine grace declining the ways of childhood for that age of his, so excellent was he in gravity of morals that he was already recognized as a future father of monks and restorer of the anchoritic life. Sent by his parents, who were distinguished in birth and virtue, to Paris, he made such progress in the studies of philosophy and theology that he obtained the title of Doctor and Master in both faculties; and not long after, by reason of his outstanding virtues, he obtained a canonry of the church of Reims.

Cecilia, a Roman Virgin, born of noble family, vowed her virginity to God from her earliest youth. But when she was given against her will in marriage to Valerian, she persuaded him to leave her undefiled and to go to the blessed Pope Urban, so that, having received baptism, he might be worthy to see the Angel who was Cecilia's protector. When Valerian had obtained this, he converted his brother Tiburtius to Christ, so that both of them a little while later suffered martyrdom under the prefect Almachius. Cecilia, however, having been seized by the same Almachius for having distributed their goods among the poor, was ordered to be burned in a bath. But when the flame did not dare to touch her, she was struck three times in the same place with the axe and left half dead; and after three days she obtained the palm of virginity and martyrdom, and was buried in the cemetery of Callistus. Her body, and those of the Pontiffs Urban and Lucius, of Tiburtius, Valerian, and Maximus, translated to Rome by Pope Paschal the First, were laid to rest in the church consecrated in the name of holy Cecilia herself.

Cecilia, a Roman Virgin, born of noble family, formed from her earliest age in the precepts of the Christian faith, vowed her virginity to God. But when afterwards, against her own will, she was given in marriage to Valerian, on the first night of their nuptials she spoke these words to him: Valerian, I am under the protection of an Angel, who guards my virginity; therefore do not commit anything against me that might arouse the wrath of God upon you. Moved by these words, Valerian dared not touch her; indeed he also added that he would believe in Christ if he could see that Angel. When Cecilia told him that this could not happen without baptism, he, inflamed with desire to see the Angel, replied that he wished to be baptized. Therefore, at the Virgin's urging, he came to Pope Urban, who was hiding for fear of persecution in the tombs of the Martyrs on the Appian Way, and was baptized by him.
Then by heavenly counsel ...

Presiding by authority delegated by Celestine over the Council of Ephesus, in which the Nestorian heresy was utterly proscribed, Nestorius condemned and deposed from his See, and the Catholic dogma concerning the one, divine Person in Christ and the divine motherhood of the glorious Virgin Mary asserted; the whole people applauding, who, exulting with incredible joy, escorted the bishops home by torchlight. But on this account Cyril was attacked by very many calumnies, injuries, and persecutions from Nestorius and his supporters; which he bore with the greatest patience, so that, anxious only for the faith, he counted as nothing whatever the heretics said or plotted against him. At last, having fulfilled the greatest labors for the Church of God, and having published very many writings both to refute pagans and heretics and to expound the sacred Scriptures and the Catholic doctrines, he rested with a holy end in the year four hundred and forty-four, the thirty-second of his episcopate. Pope Leo the Thirteenth extended the Office and Mass of this most distinguished champion of the Catholic faith and light of the Eastern Church to the universal Church.
Celestine, a Roman, son of Priscus ...

The heavenly teaching, confirmed by the preaching of very many miracles and by the example of his life, so won over those island folk that he brought most of them to the Christian faith, and at last the king himself, whom together with his innumerable retinue he washed in the sacred font, to the great joy of Queen Bertha, who was already a Christian. Once on the feast of the Lord's Nativity, when he had conferred baptism on more than ten thousand persons in the channel of the river at York, it is recorded that all of those among them who were afflicted with any illness received, along with the salvation of their souls, the health of their bodies as well. By the command of Gregory, ordained bishop, he established his see at Canterbury in the church of the Savior that he himself had erected, in which he placed monks as helpers in his work; and he built the monastery of Saint Peter, which was afterward called by his own name as well, in the suburbs. Gregory likewise granted him the use of the pallium with the power to establish an ecclesiastical hierarchy in England, for which purpose he also sent a new band of workers, namely Mellitus, Justus, Paulinus, and Rufinian.

He was unwilling to receive the canons appended by the Greeks to the sixth synod, even though the emperor pressed and threatened dire consequences, but steadfastly rejected them as spurious, not without peril to his life. A great portion of the Lord's Cross, which he had found by divine revelation, he placed in the Constantinian basilica for the adoration of the people. The body of Saint Leo, laid in an obscure corner, he by the inspiration of God removed from there and displayed in a more honored place for the veneration of all. Finally he adorned the Vatican basilica with innumerable gifts, distinguished monuments indeed of his love toward the Prince of the Apostles.

He betook himself, therefore, to Pope Alexander the Third, by whom he was graciously received; and from there he set out, commended by the same Pope to the monks of the monastery of Pontigny, of the Cistercian order. When Henry learned this, sending threatening letters to the assembly of the Cistercian brothers, he attempted to drive Thomas out of the monastery of Pontigny. Wherefore the holy man, fearing lest his cause might bring some harm upon the Cistercian family, departed of his own accord and met Louis, king of France, at his invitation; where he remained until, through the action of the Supreme Pontiff and the king himself, he was recalled from exile, to the great rejoicing of the whole kingdom. While therefore he was carrying out securely the duty of the good shepherd, behold, calumniators reported to the king that he was plotting much against the kingdom and the public peace, so that the king more than once complained that he could not have peace in his kingdom with one priest.

Charity, therefore, is our fruit, which the Apostle defines as: from a pure heart, and a good conscience, and faith unfeigned. With this we love one another, with this we love God; for we would not truly love one another were we not loving God. For each one loves his neighbor as himself, if he loves God. For if he does not love God, he does not love himself; for on these two commandments of charity hang the whole law and the prophets. This is our fruit. And so, giving us his commandment concerning fruit, he says: This I command you, that you love one another. Hence also the Apostle Paul, when he wished to commend the fruit of the spirit against the works of the flesh, placed this at its head: The fruit, he says, of the spirit is charity; and then wove in the other things, as if sprung from this head and bound to it, which are joy, peace, long-suffering, kindness, goodness, faith, meekness, continence, chastity.

Charles, born in Milan of the noble Borromeo family, when he was in his twenty-third year, was enrolled by his uncle Pope Pius the Fourth in the sacred college of cardinals. Soon after, he was created Archbishop of Milan by the same Pope; and he applied the greatest effort to ordering the church entrusted to him in accordance with the most holy Council of Trent, which had already been brought to completion chiefly by his diligence. When plague was raging in Milan, he contributed his household furnishings to the feeding of the poor; and, visiting assiduously those laboring under that disease, he consoled them in a wonderful way, ministering the Sacraments of the Church with his own hands. He was a most ardent defender of ecclesiastical liberty, and wrote many things most useful especially for the instruction of bishops; by his labor also the catechism for parish priests was published. He died in Milan in the forty-seventh year of his age, on the third day before the Nones of November. Pope Paul the Fifth, when he was renowned for miracles, enrolled him in the number of the Saints.

Charles, born in Milan of the noble Borromeo family, the greatness of holiness that was to come was foretold by a divine light gleaming by night over the chamber of his mother in labor. Enrolled in the clerical ranks from boyhood, and afterward distinguished with an abbacy, he admonished his father not to convert the revenues to domestic use; and having himself obtained their administration, whatever remained he spent upon the poor. As a young man he devoted himself to the liberal disciplines at Pavia. He so cultivated chastity that immodest women, sent several times to undermine his purity, he put to flight with unconquered constancy. In his twenty-third year, enrolled by his uncle Pope Pius the Fourth in the sacred college of cardinals, he shone forth with distinguished splendor of piety and all virtues. Soon after, created Archbishop of Milan by the same Pope, he applied the greatest effort to ordering the church entrusted to him in accordance with the most holy Council of Trent, which had already been brought to completion chiefly by his diligence; and, that he might reform the depraved morals of his flock, besides the repeated celebration of synods, he presented himself as a model of outstanding holiness. He labored greatly in routing out the heretics from the regions of Rhaetia and Helvetia, very many of whom he converted to the Christian faith.

When he had sought out Caesarea of Cappadocia, led by the divine Spirit, he there saw Basil himself, the very mouth of the Church, and each made profitable use of the other's company. To refute the countless errors that were then spreading and afflicting the Church of God, and to diligently illuminate the mysteries of our Lord Jesus Christ, he published many learned works, composed in the Syriac tongue and translated into Greek for the most part; and, as Saint Jerome himself bears witness, he attained such renown that, after the reading of the Scriptures, his writings were read publicly in certain churches.

Cajetan, born of the noble Thiene family in Vicenza, was at once offered by his mother to the Virgin Mother of God. Having obtained his doctorate in both laws at Padua, he went to Rome, where he was placed among the prelates by Julius the Second and initiated into the priesthood. Having founded hospitals at his own expense, he served with his own hands even those laboring under the plague. He devoted himself assiduously to the salvation of his neighbors, and was therefore called the Hunter of Souls. Desiring to restore the collapsed discipline of ecclesiastics to the form of apostolic life, he founded the Order of Regular Clerics, who, having renounced all care of earthly things, should neither possess revenues nor seek from the faithful the means of subsistence, but should live by alms freely offered. And so, with the approval of Clement the Seventh, at the high altar of the Vatican basilica, together with John Peter Carafa, Bishop of Theate, who afterward was Pope Paul the Fourth, and two other men of outstanding piety, he made his solemn vows. He greatly promoted the love of divine worship, the dignity of the house of God, the observance of sacred rites, and the more frequent use of the most holy Eucharist. Full of merits, he departed to heaven at Naples, and his body is venerated there with great devotion in the church of Saint Paul.

Cajetan, born of the noble Thiene family in Vicenza, was at once offered by his mother to the Virgin Mother of God. From his tenderest years a wonderful innocence of morals shone forth in him, so that he was called Saint by all. Having obtained his doctorate in both laws at Padua, he went to Rome; where, having been placed among the prelates by Julius the Second and initiated into the priesthood, he was inflamed with such ardor of divine love that, leaving the court, he gave himself wholly to God. Having founded hospitals at his own expense, he served with his own hands even those laboring under the plague. He devoted himself with assiduous care to the salvation of his neighbors, and was therefore called the Hunter of Souls.

Caius, a Dalmatian, of the lineage of the Emperor Diocletian, ordained that advancement to the episcopate in the Church should proceed through these ranks and honors: Doorkeeper, Lector, Exorcist, Acolyte, Subdeacon, Deacon, Priest. Fleeing the cruelty of Diocletian against Christians, he hid for some time in a cave; but after eight years he obtained the crown of martyrdom together with his brother Gabinus, having sat twelve years, four months, and five days; having created in the month of December twenty-five priests, eight deacons, and five bishops. He was buried in the cemetery of Callistus on the tenth day before the Kalends of May. Pope Urban the Eighth renewed his memory in the City, restored his ruined church, and adorned it with his title, his stational Mass, and his relics.

Callistus, a Roman, ruled the Church under the Emperor Antoninus Heliogabalus. He established the four Ember Seasons of the year, in which the fast received from apostolic tradition should be observed by all. He built the basilica of Saint Mary beyond the Tiber, and enlarged the old cemetery on the Appian Way, in which many holy Priests and Martyrs were buried; hence it is called the cemetery of Callistus from him. He sat five years, one month, and twelve days. After long hunger and repeated blows, he was thrown headlong into a well and crowned with martyrdom under the Emperor Alexander, and was buried in the cemetery of Calepodiuus on the Aurelian Way, at the third milestone from the City, on the day before the Ides of October. His body, afterward brought to the basilica of Saint Mary beyond the Tiber, is venerated with great devotion beneath the high altar.

Camillus, born in the town of Bucchianico in the diocese of Chieti, of the noble Lelli family, followed the military profession as a young man and indulged for a time in the vices of the world. Yet, seized with grief at the offense against God, he ran to the Friars Minor, known as the Capuchins, and earnestly besought to be enrolled among their number. Having obtained his wish once and yet again, a foul ulcer which had at some time afflicted his leg breaking out again repeatedly, he humbly submitted himself to the pleasure of his superiors and twice put off the habit of that religious order which he had twice sought and received. Going to Rome and duly initiated into the priesthood, he laid the first foundations of the congregation of Regular Clerics ministering to the sick, whose members are bound by a fourth vow, the most arduous of all, of ministering to the sick, even those infected with plague. Worn down by repeated fasts and unceasing labors, and having bravely endured five grievous and long-lasting illnesses, which he called mercies of the Lord, he died in the Lord on the day before the Ides of July in the year one thousand six hundred and fourteen, at the age of sixty-five. Pope Leo the Thirteenth declared him the heavenly patron of all hospitals and the sick, and ordered his name to be invoked in the litanies of the dying.

Camillus, born in the town of Bucchianico in the diocese of Chieti, of the noble Lelli family, followed the military profession as a young man and indulged for a time in the vices of the world; until, at the age of twenty-five, being filled with a more abundant light and sweetness of heavenly grace, he firmly resolved to cleanse the stains of his past life and to put on the new man. Wherefore, running to the Friars Minor known as the Capuchins, he earnestly besought by his highest prayers to be enrolled among their number. He obtained his wish; but, by the design of divine providence disposing greater things for him, he put off the habit of that religious order which he had received, and going to Rome he was received into the hospital called of the incurables; whose administration also, committed to him on account of his outstanding virtues, he conducted with the greatest integrity and truly fatherly solicitude. Counting himself the servant of all the sick, and giving his attention especially to relieving souls in their final peril, he gave most distinguished examples of admirable patience and heroic charity. Later initiated into the priesthood, he laid the first foundations of the congregation of Regular Clerics ministering to the sick; and in promoting this most wholesome institution, marvelously strengthened by a heavenly voice issuing from a crucifix which also extended its hands in a wondrous prodigy drawn from the wood, he overcame all adverse difficulties with a steadfast soul.

Camillus, born in the town of Bucchianico in the diocese of Chieti, of the noble Lelli family, was born of a sixty-year-old mother, who in a dream while pregnant saw herself give birth to a boy bearing the sign of the Cross on his breast, and walking at the head of a company of boys bearing the same sign. Following the military profession as a young man, he indulged for a time in the vices of the world; until, at the age of twenty-five, he was seized by so great a light of heavenly grace and grief at the offense against God that he was at once bathed in an abundant flood of tears, and firmly resolved to cleanse without ceasing the stains of his past life and to put on the new man. Wherefore, on that very feast day of the Purification of the most Blessed Virgin on which this occurred, running to the Friars Minor known as the Capuchins, he earnestly besought by the highest prayers to be enrolled among their number. He obtained his wish once and yet again; but, a foul ulcer which had at some time afflicted his leg breaking out again repeatedly, he humbly submitted himself to the counsel of divine providence disposing greater things for him; and, master of himself, he twice put off the habit of that religious order which he had twice sought and received.

In the Canary Islands, where he had charge of the brothers of his order, having suffered much and burning with desire for martyrdom, he converted many unbelievers to the faith of Christ by word and example. Coming to Rome in the jubilee year, under Pope Nicholas the Fifth, he was assigned to the care of the sick in the convent of the Ara Coeli; and he discharged this office with such affection of charity that, even while the City was suffering from a shortage of provisions, nothing whatsoever of what was necessary was lacking to the sick, whose ulcers he would sometimes cleanse even by licking them. Remarkable faith and the grace of healing also shone forth in him, when, anointing the sick with the oil of the lamp that burned before the image of the most Blessed Mother of God, whom he venerated with the greatest devotion, and impressing the sign of the Cross, he wondrously healed the diseases of many.

Canute the Fourth, son of Sweyn Estridsen, King of the Danes, conspicuous for his faith, devotion, and uprightness of character, gave outstanding evidence of extraordinary holiness from his tender years. Having obtained his father's scepter amid the highest acclamation of all, he began to apply himself diligently to promoting religion, to increasing the revenues of the churches, and to adorning them with precious furnishings. Then, enkindled with zeal for the propagation of the faith, he attacked barbarian kingdoms in just warfare, and subjected the conquered and subdued nations to the Christian law. Renowned for very many victories and enriched with wealth, he cast his royal crown at the feet of Christ crucified, subjecting himself and his kingdom to him who is King of kings and Lord of lords. He chastised his body with fasts, hair-shirts, and scourgings. Assiduous in prayer and contemplation, always generous toward the poor, always beneficent toward all, he never turned aside from the path of justice and the divine law.

Since such is the case, let us not suppose that anything reaches those dead for whom we care unless it be that which we solemnly offer for them in the sacrifice of the altar, in prayers, or in almsdeeds: though not all such acts profit equally all those for whom they are performed, but only those for whom, while they yet live, provision is made that such acts may profit them. When, however, we know not who these are, it is fitting that we perform these things for all who have been reborn, so that none may be passed over among those to whom these benefits can and ought to reach. For it is better that these things abound for those whom they neither harm nor help, than that they should fail those whom they do help. Yet does each one perform these rites the more diligently for his own dear ones, that the like may be performed for him in turn by his own. Whatever, however, is bestowed upon the burial of the body is no safeguard of salvation, but an office of humanity, according to that affection by which no one ever hates his own flesh. It is therefore fitting that such care as is possible be taken for the flesh of a neighbor, from which he who cared for it has departed. And if those who do not believe in the resurrection of the flesh do these things, how much more ought those who believe to do them; so that the service rendered to a body that is dead, yet destined to rise again and to endure in eternity, may also be in some measure a testimony of that same faith!

But since the Apostle Paul clearly states that Christ is of the seed of David according to the flesh, we must not doubt that Mary herself also drew some kinship from the stock of David. And since the priestly lineage of this woman is not passed over in silence either — Luke indicating that she was a kinswoman of Elizabeth, whom he calls one of the daughters of Aaron — it is most firmly to be held that the flesh of Christ was propagated from both lineages, namely that of kings and that of priests; in the persons of which, among the Hebrew people, the mystical anointing was also prefigured, that is, the chrism, from which the name of Christ shines forth, foretold so long before by this most evident signification.

There is no doubt that the disposition of commemoration and prayer, which is offered to those dearest who have died in faith, profits those who, while they yet lived in the body, merited that such things should profit them after this life. But even if some necessity either forbids the burial of bodies, or permits no opportunity for burial in sacred places, the prayers to be offered for the spirits of the dead must not be neglected; prayers which the Church has undertaken to make for all who have died in Christian and Catholic fellowship, even without mention of their names, under a general commemoration: so that those who lack parents, or children, or any kindred or friends to offer these things for them may receive them from the one common devout mother. For if these prayers were lacking — prayers offered with upright faith and devotion for the dead — I think it would avail nothing for their spirits, however much their lifeless bodies might be placed in sacred sites.

She shone with singular charity toward her neighbor; for she often spent sleepless nights either attending to the ministries of the sisters or in service to the sick, some of whose sores she once healed by licking them. Weeping bitterly over the perdition of unbelievers and sinners, she offered herself ready to undergo any torments whatsoever for the sake of their salvation. For many years before her death, renouncing with heroic virtue all the delights of heaven with which she abounded, she had these words frequently on her lips: To suffer, not to die. At length, worn out by a long and most grievous infirmity, she passed to her Spouse on the twenty-fifth day of May, in the year sixteen hundred and seven, having completed the forty-first year of her age. Clement the Ninth enrolled her, renowned for many miracles both in life and after death, in the number of holy Virgins; and her body is preserved incorrupt to the present day.

Burning with charity toward God, often spending whole nights in pouring forth prayers and chastising his body, he allowed himself no relief except leaning upon a stone or lying on the bare ground. Having returned to his homeland, he first erected at Friesach, on his journey, a most spacious monastery of his order, then soon another at Kraków. Thence, having built four others through the other provinces of the Polish kingdom, it is incredible to say how greatly he profited all by the preaching of the word of God and the innocence of his life. He let no day pass in which he did not give remarkable evidence of faith, devotion, and innocence.

He burned with such charity toward the poor that he would give to the needy the wages he earned by his labors. Indeed, when he had once brought a great many poor people to the common midday meal with his fellow brothers, and found nothing left for himself after the meal had ended, save a portion of broth that had been set aside for him, that man of God, trusting with singular faith, distributed it in such a way that, miraculously multiplied, it sufficed to feed and satisfy all of them. Among other remarkable things was this: that during the summer heat, when his master was begging for a drink of water to quench his thirst in the field, and water was nowhere flowing, Isidore, striking the earth with the goad he was carrying, drew forth from it an abundant and perennial spring, which flows to this day.

The ardor of his charity toward God shone forth from his face while he was celebrating the sacred rites, and he could not speak of God's goodness without tears. Admitted by obedience into the college of canons of the basilica of Saint Mary in Cosmedin, he seemed to be rapt out of his senses while chanting the psalms. Most diligent in sacred ceremonies, he promoted the beauty of the house of God, and gladly spent his own resources for that purpose. He poured forth his love for the Mother of God upon others, fostered her cult in his own church, and added also the daily proclamation of her praises in psalmody. Earnestly desiring to be imbued with the spirit of Philip Neri, and devout toward all the saints, he took care to increase the veneration of the Princes of the Apostles. Assiduous in prayer and in every exercise of virtue, and endowed also with heavenly charisms, he was at last brought to the end of his life, worn out by his labors, in the hospice named after the Most Holy Trinity to which he had retired to live in community with other priests; and, refreshed with the Sacraments of the Church, commending to all works of charity and care for the poor, he departed in the kiss of the Lord, on the twenty-third day of May, in the year of Christ seventeen hundred and sixty-four, in the sixty-sixth year of his age. God was pleased to illustrate this outstanding example of priestly virtue with miracles, which being duly approved, the Supreme Pontiff Pius the Ninth enriched him with the honors of the blessed on the third day before the Ides of May in the year eighteen hundred and sixty; and Leo the Thirteenth, shining with new signs, enrolled him in the catalog of the saints on the sixth day before the Ides of December in the year eighteen hundred and eighty-one.

Wounded by the love of God, he languished continually, and so great a fervor burned in his heart that, since it could not be contained within its bounds, the Lord miraculously enlarged it by breaking and lifting two of his ribs. When celebrating Mass or praying with greater fervor, he was sometimes raised into the air and seen to shine with wondrous light on every side. He followed all the poor and needy with every service of charity: so worthy was he that he both gave alms to an Angel appearing in the guise of a poor man, and, when he was bearing bread to the needy by night and fell into a pit, was likewise rescued unharmed from it by an Angel. Given to humility, he always shrank from honors, and very steadfastly refused ecclesiastical dignities, even the highest, when offered to him more than once.

Casimir, born of Casimir and Elizabeth of Austria, the King and Queen of Poland, was trained from childhood under the best teachers in piety and the liberal arts; he tamed his youthful limbs with a rough hair-shirt and wore them down with constant fasting. Disdaining the softness of a royal bed, he lay on the hard ground, and by night, secretly and at an unseasonable hour, prone upon the earth before the doors of churches, he implored the divine clemency. Assiduous in contemplating the Passion of Christ, he was wont to attend the solemnities of Mass with so elevated a mind toward God that he seemed to be rapt out of himself.

Casimir, son of the King of Poland, trained from childhood in piety and the liberal arts, tamed his youthful limbs with a rough hair-shirt and wore them down with constant fasting. Assiduous in contemplating the Passion of Christ, he did not relax his spirit of prayer. He earnestly endeavored to advance the Catholic faith and to abolish the schism of the Ruthenians. Beneficent and merciful toward the poor and those oppressed by calamities, he obtained the name of father and defender of the needy. He kept his virginity inviolate to the very end of his life. Perfected in a brief time, full of virtues and merits, having foretold the day of his death, he rendered his spirit to God at the twenty-fifth year of his age. Leo the Tenth, renowned for miracles, enrolled him in the number of the Saints.

A most ardent champion of the Catholic faith, he endeavored by fatherly admonitions and letters to bring the iconoclast Emperor Leo the Isaurian back to sounder thinking. But when he made no headway, he convened a council of ninety-five bishops at Rome, confirmed the veneration of sacred images by an apostolic decree, and struck the Iconoclasts with a terrible anathema. When this came to the ears of Leo, he began to rage more fiercely, and sent against Gregory a most flourishing fleet with a most powerful army; but this, by the will and vengeance of God, was assailed by a fierce storm in the Adriatic and perished in a foul shipwreck.

Catherine, a noble virgin of Alexandria, combining the study of the liberal arts with fervor of faith, when she saw many Christians being dragged to execution by the order of Maximin, approached Maximin himself and vigorously affirmed to him that the faith of Christ was necessary for salvation. The tyrant, admiring her prudence, ordered her to be kept under detention; and, summoning the most learned men from all quarters, endeavored to persuade her to convert to the worship of idols. But the opposite occurred: for several of those men, overcome by the most wise arguments of Catherine, embraced the faith of Christ and did not hesitate to die for it. For this reason, Maximin first attempted with blandishments, then with torments, to draw Catherine away from her resolve; but when he made no headway, he ordered her to be struck with the ax.

Catherine, a virgin of Siena, born of devout parents, obtained the habit of Blessed Dominic, which the Sisters of Penance wear. Her abstinence was surpassing and the austerity of her life admirable. She was found to have prolonged her fast from Ash Wednesday until the Ascension of the Lord, sustained only by the Communion of the Eucharist. She wrestled most frequently with demons and was vexed by many of their molestations; she was racked by fevers and lacked not the torment of other diseases. The name of Catherine was great and holy, and the sick and those vexed by evil spirits were brought to her from all sides. She commanded illnesses and fevers in the name of Christ, and compelled demons to depart from the bodies they had possessed.

Catherine, a noble virgin of Alexandria, combining from her earliest age the study of the liberal arts with fervor of faith, soon attained such perfection of holiness and learning that, at the age of eighteen, she surpassed even the most learned. When she saw many who, by Maximin's command, were subjected to various torments for the profession of the Christian religion and dragged to execution, she unhesitatingly approached Maximin himself, and charging him with wicked cruelty, affirmed with most wise arguments that the faith of Christ was necessary for salvation.

Catherine, a virgin of Siena, born of devout parents, obtained the habit of Blessed Dominic, which the Sisters of Penance wear. Her abstinence was surpassing, and the austerity of her life admirable. While staying at Pisa, on a Sunday, having been refreshed with the heavenly food and caught up in ecstasy, she saw the Lord crucified approaching with great light, and from the scars of his wounds five rays descending to five places on her body. Perceiving the mystery, she prayed to the Lord that the scars might not appear; and immediately the rays, their blood-red color changed to brilliant white, came in the form of pure light to her hands, feet, and heart. So great, indeed, was the pain which she sensibly endured, though the bloody signs of the wounds did not appear, that she believed she would die in a short time, had not God lessened it. Her learning was infused, not acquired. Setting out for Avignon to Pope Gregory the Eleventh, she showed him that she had known by divine revelation his secret vow to go to Rome, known to God alone, and was the occasion of the Pontiff's going in person to the Roman See. In about the thirty-third year of her age she went to her Spouse. Pius the Second enrolled her in the number of holy Virgins.

He strove with the utmost zeal to advance the Catholic faith and to abolish the schism of the Ruthenians: wherefore he induced his father Casimir to enact a law forbidding schismatics to build new temples or to restore old ones that were falling into ruin. Beneficent and merciful toward the poor and those oppressed by calamities, he obtained the name of father and defender of the needy. The virginity which he had kept inviolate from his cradle, he strongly asserted at the very end of his life, when, pressed by grave infirmity, he steadfastly resolved rather to die than, on the advice of physicians, to incur the loss of chastity.

But the cause of our restoration is nothing other than the mercy of God: whom we would not love, had he not first loved us himself, and dispelled the darkness of our ignorance with the light of his truth. This the Lord declared through holy Isaiah, saying: I will lead the blind in a way that they do not know, and in paths that they have not known I will make them walk; I will turn the darkness before them into light, and the crooked places into straight. These things I will do for them, and I will not forsake them. And again he says: I was found by those who did not seek me, and I appeared openly to those who did not ask for me.

Let teachers and bishops therefore take heed, and let the Powerful understand that they must endure torments with strength; and that there is no remedy, but that the ruin of the greater leads to hell. You are the light of the world. A city set on a hill cannot be hidden; nor do men light a lamp and put it under a bushel, but on a lampstand, so that it gives light to all who are in the house. He teaches the confidence of preaching, lest the Apostles hide themselves out of fear and be like a lamp under a bushel; but rather that with all freedom they make themselves known, so that what they have heard in inner rooms they proclaim upon the housetops.

Certainly, when he set forth new commandments for those who would follow him, he said: Unless one renounces all that he possesses, he cannot be my disciple. As if to say openly: You who through the old life coveted the goods of others, through the pursuit of a new conversion also bestow your own. But let us hear what he says in this reading: Whoever wishes to come after me, let him deny himself. There it is said that we deny what is ours; here it is said that we deny ourselves. And perhaps it is not laborious for a man to leave his own possessions; but it is very laborious to leave himself. It is indeed less to deny what he has; but it is very great to deny what he is.
Certe et crux ...

While the other guards were given over to sleep, the doorkeeper alone kept watch, and beholding those who were praying and surrounded by light, and certain Angels descending from heaven as if sent by a King, distributing crowns to thirty-nine soldiers, he spoke to himself thus: There are forty of them — where is the crown of the fortieth? While he was pondering this, one from their number, whose spirit had failed him in enduring the cold, leaped down into the nearby heated bath, and brought deep sorrow upon those holy men. But God did not allow their prayers to be in vain: for the doorkeeper, struck with wonder at the outcome of the matter, quickly roused the sleeping guards, stripped off his own garments, and with a clear voice professed himself to be a Christian, and joined himself to the Martyrs. And when the president's satellites learned that the doorkeeper too was a Christian, they broke the legs of all of them by shattering them with clubs.

Moreover, beyond the admirable and mysterious spectacle of the glory of Christ, something else also took place, both useful and necessary, to confirm faith in himself, not for the disciples alone but also for us ourselves. For from on high there came the voice of God the Father, saying: This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased; hear him. And when the voice was made, the Evangelist says, Jesus was found alone. Behold, with Moses present, the Father commands the holy Apostles to hear him; for if he had wished them to follow the precepts of Moses, he would have said: Keep the law. But now God the Father says not even this. Moses had indeed departed, and Elijah was not present; Christ alone remained: he commanded therefore that he himself be heard. For he is the end of the law and the prophets.

Chosroes, King of the Persians, in the last days of the reign of Phocas, having seized Egypt and Africa, and having captured Jerusalem and slaughtered many thousands of Christians there, carried off into Persia the Cross of Christ the Lord, which Helen had placed on Mount Calvary. Accordingly Heraclius, who had succeeded Phocas, afflicted by many troubles and calamities of war, was seeking peace; which he could not obtain from Chosroes, insolent with his victories, not even on unjust terms. Therefore, placing himself in extreme peril, he exercised himself with unceasing fasts and prayers and implored God's help with great earnestness; and, warned by him, having assembled an army, he engaged the enemy, and overcame three generals of Chosroes with their three armies.

Kilian, a noble Scotsman, having won the highest renown for holiness in a monastery, summoned companions from there — Colman the priest and Totnan the deacon — and set out for Rome, where he received permission to preach; he then came to Gosbert, Duke of Franconia, at Würzburg. There, having converted many to the faith, he persuaded him to consider putting away Gail, the wife of his own brother, who had been joined to him in marriage. Whereupon she, inflamed with fury, began to lay snares for him; and he, learning of these, did not cease to give himself to prayers and fasting with his companions. And so, as they were joyfully awaiting the day of martyrdom, assassins appointed for this purpose burst in upon them while they were singing the divine praises, and slew them with a wicked sword; and their bodies were afterwards buried in the same place.

He then sent Kilian and his companions, who had suffered martyrdom, into Germany, and Willibrord and Swithbert with their companions into Frisia and the surrounding regions, in which they converted a very great multitude of pagans to the faith of Christ. He received Caedwalla, King of the Britons, when he came to Rome, and washed him in the sacred font of Baptism. He ordained Damian as bishop for Ravenna, Hubert for Liège, and Berctwald for Britain. He ordained that the pious verse should be added to the sacred Liturgy: Lamb of God, who takes away the sins of the world, have mercy on us. Finally, full of merits, after he had held the see for thirteen years and eight months, he rested in a holy death, and was buried in the Vatican.

Who shall recount the generation of Christ and the Assumption of Mary? For as much grace as she obtained on earth beyond all others, so great and singular glory does she hold in heaven as well.
But if eye has not seen nor ear heard, nor has it entered the heart of man, what God has prepared for those who love him, what appeared to her who bore him, and what is known with certainty to all who love him above all things — who can speak of it? Truly blessed is Mary, and in many ways blessed: whether when she receives the Savior, or when she is received with the Savior; in both cases a wondrous dignity, the virginity of a mother; in both worthy of embrace, the condescension of majesty.

Christ is called and is the power of God, who, coming upon the strong man armed who was accustomed to guard his courtyard in peace, overcame him with his own arm; and so powerfully snatched from him the vessels of captivity. The Angel, moreover, is called the strength of God, either because he merited this prerogative of office, by which he announced the coming of that same power; or because he was to strengthen the Virgin, who by nature was timid, simple, and modest, lest she be seized with fear at the newness of the miracle — which he also did, saying: Fear not, Mary, for you have found favor with God. It is fitting, therefore, that Gabriel was chosen for this work; or rather, since such a commission was laid upon him, he is rightly designated by such a name.

Christ therefore, the head of the Martyrs, suffered first for us, leaving you an example, that you should follow in his footsteps. Blessed Stephen, following in the footsteps of his Passion, was stoned by the Jews for confessing Christ and merited a crown as if placed there for him by his own name. For Stephen in Greek is called crown in Latin. He already bore the name of crown, and therefore by his name he carried in advance the palm of martyrdom.

Chrysogonus, during the reign of the Emperor Diocletian, was confined at Rome in prison, where he lived for two years supported by the resources of the holy Anastasia; he also consoled by mutual letters the same Anastasia, who was afflicted on account of Christ by her husband Publius, and who therefore begged his help through her prayers by letter. But when the Emperor wrote to Rome ordering that, after the remaining Christians in chains had been put to death, Chrysogonus should be sent to him at Aquileia, he was brought there. The Emperor said to him: I have summoned you, Chrysogonus, to honor you with honors, if only you will bring yourself to worship the gods. But he replied: I venerate with mind and prayer him who is truly God; but the gods, who are nothing but the images of demons, I hate and abhor. Enraged by this reply, the Emperor ordered him to be struck with the ax at Aquas Gratas on the eighth day before the Kalends of December. His body, thrown into the sea, was found a little while later on the shore, and the priest Zolus buried it in his own house.

Chrysanthus and Daria, husband and wife, born of noble lineage and made more illustrious still by faith — which Daria, through the influence of her husband, had received with Baptism — converted at Rome an innumerable multitude of people, she of women and he of men, to Christ. For this reason the prefect Celerinus arrested them and handed them over to the tribune Claudius, who ordered Chrysanthus to be bound and tortured by soldiers; but all his bonds were loosed, and then the fetters into which he had been cast were broken. Then, enclosed in an ox-hide, they placed him in the most burning sun. Then, with hands and feet bound in a chain, they thrust him into a dark prison; where, the chains being loosed, a most brilliant light illuminated the place. Daria, on the other hand, was forced into a brothel, but was defended by divine providence from dishonor through the guardianship of a lion while she was absorbed in prayer. Finally, both were led to a sand-quarry on the Via Salaria, and, the earth being dug away, they were buried under stones, attaining the equal crown of martyrdom.

Mary wished to be occupied with one thing alone. Already she was holding fast to it: But for me it is good to cling to God. She sat at the feet of our Head. The more humbly she sat, the more abundantly she received. For water flows down to the humility of a valley, not from the swellings of a hill. The Lord did not therefore rebuke the work, but distinguished the gift. You are busy about many things; yet one thing is necessary. This Mary has already chosen for herself.

And so, secretly departing from his home, he undertook a pilgrimage to the most distinguished churches of the world. Having spent seventeen years unknown in this manner, he was once at Edessa, a city of Syria, when his name was divulged there through an image of the Most Holy Virgin Mary; and in order to escape the vain glory of the world, he departed thence by ship: soon put ashore at the Port of Rome, and, by God's disposition, meeting his own father, he was received by him in his own house as an unknown poor man given hospitality.

Clare, a noble virgin, born at Assisi in Umbria, following in the steps of her fellow-townsman Saint Francis, distributed and converted all her goods into almsdeeds and support for the poor. Fleeing the tumult of the world, she withdrew to a country church, where, having received the tonsure from the same Blessed Francis, she firmly resisted her relatives who tried to bring her back. And at length she was led by him to the church of Saint Damian, where the Lord gathered many companions for her; and thus she herself founded the community of the sacred sisters, whose governance she accepted, having overcome the importunity of Saint Francis by her perseverance. She governed her monastery diligently and prudently for forty-two years with wonderful care, in the fear of the Lord and in full observance of the rule; for her life was an instruction and doctrine to the others, from whom the rest learned the rule of living.

When Saracens attempted to invade the monastery, she ordered the Most Holy Sacrament to be carried out, and praying most humbly put them utterly to flight. She flew to heaven on the day before the Ides of August, and was enrolled among the holy Virgins by Pope Alexander the Fourth.

Clement Mary Hofbauer, born at Tasovice in Moravia, was formed in the school of Christian perfection from his earliest age; his teacher above all being his most devout mother, who is said to have addressed the young boy after his father's death, showing him an image of Christ the Lord hanging from the cross, in these words: See, my son, who is henceforth to be your father; take care to walk in the way that pleases him. As a young man he learned the baker's trade; but sensing that he was called to greater things, he began, amid the labors of his craft, to apply himself to the study of letters. Twice he made a pilgrimage on foot to Rome to the thresholds of the Apostles; twice also he withdrew into solitude to give himself more freely to the contemplation of heavenly things. But God calling him to higher things, he resumed his interrupted studies at the University of Vienna, and prosecuted them diligently; until, in order to drink in the sacred disciplines from a purer source, he migrated to Rome for a third time. There, by a singular providence of God, he was admitted into the family of Saint Alphonsus, which that same holy Father had sensed with divine instinct and publicly foretold would be propagated to distant regions through his efforts.

Clement, a Roman, a disciple of blessed Peter, divided the seven regions of the City among seven notaries, assigning one to each, to commit to writing with the greatest diligence the passions of the Martyrs and their deeds. He himself also wrote many things accurately and beneficially, by which he illustrated the Christian religion. But when by his teaching and holiness of life he was converting many to the faith of Christ, he was exiled by the Emperor Trajan beyond the Black Sea, in the solitude of the city of Cherson, where he found two thousand Christians who had been condemned by the same Trajan. When he had there converted many unbelievers to the faith of Christ, he was, by the order of the same Emperor, thrown headlong into the sea with an anchor tied to his neck, and crowned with martyrdom. His body, translated to Rome by the first Pope Nicholas, was honorably laid in the church which had previously been dedicated in his name.

Clement, a Roman, son of Faustinus, from the region of the Caelian hill, a disciple of blessed Peter, whom Paul mentions when writing to the Philippians: I ask you also, my true companion, help those women who have labored with me in the Gospel, together with Clement and the rest of my fellow workers, whose names are in the book of life. He divided the seven regions of the City among seven notaries, assigning one to each, to commit to writing with the greatest diligence the passions of the Martyrs and their deeds. He himself also wrote many things accurately and beneficially, by which he illustrated the Christian religion.

But Clement the Eleventh, reflecting in his mind upon the notable victory likewise won in the year seventeen hundred and sixteen in the kingdom of Hungary by Charles the Sixth, elected Emperor of the Romans, over innumerable forces of the Turks, taking note that it had occurred on the day when the feast of the Dedication of Saint Mary of the Snows was being celebrated, and at almost the same time when the confraternity of the Most Holy Rosary, performing a public and solemn procession in the Eternal City with an enormous gathering of people and great devotion, was pouring forth fervent prayers to God for the defeat of the Turks and humbly imploring the powerful aid of the Virgin Mother of God in assistance of the Christians; — for this reason, he piously deemed that this victory, and also the liberation soon after of the island of Corfu from the siege of those same Turks, was to be attributed to the patronage of the same Blessed Virgin. Wherefore, in order that a perpetual memory and gratitude for this so remarkable a benefit might always endure, he extended the feast of the Most Holy Rosary, to be celebrated with the same rite, to the universal Church. All these things Blessed Benedict the Thirteenth commanded to be inserted in the Roman Breviary. But Leo the Thirteenth, in the most turbulent times of the Church and amid the fierce storm of long-pressing evils, stirred up all the faithful throughout the world, by repeated apostolic letters, with the greatest urgency toward the frequent recitation of the Marian Rosary, especially during the month of October, also having augmented the rite of the annual feast's solemnity, having added the invocation of the Queen of the Most Holy Rosary to the Litany of Loreto, and having granted to the whole Church a proper Office of the same solemnity. Let us therefore continually venerate the Most Holy Mother of God with this devotion most dear to her; so that she who so many times, prevailed upon by Rosary prayers, has granted Christ's faithful to rout and destroy earthly enemies, may likewise grant that they overcome those of hell as well.

Cletus, a Roman, governed the Church during the reigns of the Emperors Vespasian and Titus. At the command of the Prince of the Apostles he ordained twenty-five priests in the City. He was the first to use in his letters these words: Greeting and apostolic blessing. When the Church was well ordered, under the Emperor Domitian, in the second persecution after Nero, he was crowned with martyrdom, and was buried in the Vatican near the body of blessed Peter. Marcellinus, a Roman, presided over the Church during the immense persecution of the Emperor Diocletian. He endured many distresses on account of the undue severity of those who rebuked him for excessive indulgence toward those who had lapsed into idolatry, which gave occasion for him to be defamed by calumny, as if he had offered incense to the idols. But this blessed Pontiff, in confession of the faith, together with three other Christians, Claudius, Cyrinus, and Antoninus, was beheaded.

A council was assembled at Milan in the following year, to which Eusebius had been invited by Constantius and was earnestly desired and summoned by the legates of Liberius; yet so far was the malignant synagogue of the Arians, raging against the holy Athanasius, from drawing him to their side, that he himself straightway declared openly that certain among those present were known to him to be tainted with the heretical stain, and proposed that they should first subscribe to the Nicene faith before other matters were treated. When the Arians, bitterly angered, refused, he not only declined to subscribe against Athanasius himself, but most ingeniously set free the captivated simplicity of the holy martyr Dionysius, who had been deceived by them into subscribing. For which reason, those men, greatly indignant, after inflicting many injuries upon him, punished him with exile; but the holy man, shaking off the dust, fearing neither the threats of the emperor nor drawn swords, accepted exile as the duty of his ministry; and being sent to Scythopolis, enduring hunger, thirst, beatings, and various torments, he strenuously despised life for the faith, feared not death, and delivered his body to the executioners.

Desiring to restore the collapsed discipline of the clergy to the form of apostolic life, he established the order of Clerks Regular, who, having renounced all concern for earthly things, would neither possess revenues nor seek the necessities of life from the faithful, but live solely on alms freely offered. Accordingly, with the approval of Clement the Seventh, he made his solemn vows at the high altar of the Vatican basilica together with Giovanni Pietro Carafa, the Bishop of Chieti, who was afterwards Paul the Fourth, Supreme Pontiff, and two other men of outstanding piety. During the sack of the City, he was most cruelly harassed by soldiers to compel him to produce money, which the hands of the poor had long since carried off to the treasuries of heaven; he endured blows, torments, and imprisonment with invincible patience. He persevered most steadfastly in the way of life he had undertaken, clinging solely to divine providence, which certain miracles on occasion confirmed had never failed him.
Commemoration of Saints Proto and Hyacinth, Martyrs.

Protus and Hyacinth, brothers, eunuchs of the blessed virgin Eugenia, who were baptized together with her by the bishop Helenus and devoted to the study of the divine scriptures, lived for some time in Egypt among the ascetics with wondrous humility and holiness of life. But afterwards, having accompanied the holy Virgin Eugenia to Rome, during the reign of the Emperor Gallienus they were arrested in the City for professing the Christian faith. And when it was by no means possible to prevail upon them to abandon the Christian religion and worship the gods, they were beaten with cruel lashes and struck with the ax on the third day before the Ides of September.

Gorgonius, born at Nicomedia, a chamberlain of the Emperor Diocletian, with the help of his colleague Dorotheus, brought all the other servants of the chamber to the faith of Christ. Both of them, moreover, when they had seen a Martyr most cruelly tortured before Diocletian one day, were enkindled with love of martyrdom by his example. And so this utterance burst from both of them: What is this, O Emperor, that while the sentence passed against him is one we share, you punish him alone? His faith is also ours, and the same is our resolve. The Emperor therefore ordered them to be bound and lacerated with scourges, so that the skin was rent over their entire bodies, and vinegar mixed with salt to be poured into the wounds; then, having been bound again, he ordered a fire of glowing coals to be placed under a gridiron. Finally, after various tortures, they were put to death by hanging. And the body of Saint Gorgonius was once carried to Rome, buried between the two laurels on the Via Latina, and afterwards translated by Pope Gregory the Fourth into the basilica of the Prince of the Apostles.

But for the confirmation of the Apostles and for their advancement to all knowledge, another lesson was also added in that miracle. For Moses and Elijah — that is, the law and the prophets — appeared speaking with the Lord; so that, in the most true sense, the saying was fulfilled in the presence of those five men: In the mouth of two or three witnesses every word shall stand. What is more firm, what more sure, than the word whose proclamation the trumpet of the old and new Testament sounds in harmony, and where the instruments of ancient testimonies concur with the evangelical doctrine? For the pages of both Covenants give assent to each other; and him whom preceding signs had promised under the veil of mysteries, the splendor of the present glory showed manifest and clear.

Conrad, born in a rural estate near the town of Parzham in the Diocese of Passau, to devout and upright parents, showed from boyhood, by his modesty and love of solitude, what great holiness he was destined to attain. Even then, a wondrous ardor of devotion shone in him, especially when he prayed in church; to which he was accustomed to make his way, undeterred by the distance of the journey or by cold. Enkindled with the greatest love for the Blessed Virgin, he recited her Rosary daily and without ceasing, and on feast days often made his way to the more remote shrines of the same Mother of God: from these pilgrimages on foot, undertaken with unceasing prayer, he would return home toward evening almost always still fasting. Having spent his whole youth in the cultivation of the fields, he resolved to bid farewell to the world in order to serve God more freely; and for this reason, having renounced a very large inheritance, he obtained admission among the lay brothers of the Order of Friars Minor Capuchin.

Conrad, born in the village of Parzham in the Diocese of Passau, to devout and upright parents, showed from boyhood, by his modesty and love of solitude, what great holiness he was destined to attain. Having spent his whole youth in the cultivation of the fields, he resolved to bid farewell to the world in order to serve God more freely; and for this reason, having renounced a very large inheritance, he obtained admission among the lay brothers of the Order of Friars Minor Capuchin. From the moment of his profession, he was sent to the convent of Saint Anne in the city of Altötting, and was assigned the office of doorkeeper; this he exercised until his death for the very great benefit of his neighbors in all their needs, both of soul and of body. He burned with constant devotion toward the Eucharist, and he honored the Virgin Mother of God as a mother with daily services. He went to the Lord in the year eighteen hundred and ninety-four, having completed the seventy-fifth year of his age.

It must also be considered that when the bishop chosen to care for the people approaches, he comes, as it were, to a physician tending to a sick man. If, therefore, the passions still live in his own body, with what presumption does he hasten to heal the stricken, when he bears the wound on his own face? He, then, must in every way be drawn to the example of a good life who, dying already to all the passions of the flesh, now lives spiritually: who puts aside the prosperities of the world; who fears no adversities; who desires only interior things. One whose body, well attuned, does not resist at all through weakness, nor does the spirit resist greatly through stubbornness: who is not led to covet the things of others, but rather bestows his own.

He urged upon the most devout prince Constans Augustus, who was ruling in the West, to move his brother Constantius, the Arian sympathizer reigning in the East, by prayers and threats to recall Athanasius from exile. He rejected the deceitful formula of faith conceived by the Eusebians, the followers of Arius, at the second synod of Antioch, and convened the great Council of Serdica from the bishops of West and East, and, having sent his legates, settled many useful matters there for the restoration of the Catholic faith and ecclesiastical discipline.

He ordained that no man from overseas was to be received into clerical honor without the written endorsement of five bishops. He also decreed that whenever the holy Gospels were being recited, the priests should not sit, but stand bowed. He built in the City the basilica of Crescentiana in the second region, on the Via Mamertina. In two ordinations in the month of December, having ordained eight priests, five deacons, and ten bishops in various places, he rested in peace, and was buried in his own cemetery at Ursus Pileatus, under the Emperors Arcadius and Honorius: a man whom (as Saint Jerome writes) Rome did not long deserve to have, lest the head of the world should be beheaded under such a Bishop: rather he was taken away and translated for this reason, lest he should endeavor once more to bend by his prayers a sentence already passed; for not long after his death, Rome was captured and devastated by the Goths.

He also ordained, from apostolic tradition, that marriage should be celebrated publicly and that the blessing of a priest should be employed. In the exercise of these and other salutary and useful ordinances he passed the time of his pontificate; nor did he neglect to root out the cult of idols from the minds of men; and having labored strenuously in this matter, he was crowned with martyrdom and buried near the tomb of the Prince of the Apostles in the Vatican, on the seventh day before the Kalends of November.

He ordained that churches should be consecrated only by bishops; he forbade under severe penalties the rebaptism of those who had once been baptized. He built the basilica of Saint Agapetus. In the third year of his pontificate, the Apostle Saint Barnabas appeared to Anthemius, bishop of Salamis in Cyprus, together with the Gospel of Saint Matthew; and so, after a triple prior revelation, the body of Saint Barnabas was found together with the aforesaid Gospel. He held two ordinations in the month of December, in which he ordained twenty-nine priests, five deacons, and thirty bishops in various places at Rome. On the fifth day before the Kalends of March he departed from this world and flew to the heights.

He endeavored, both by letters sent to him by a legate, once and again, to induce Constantine Copronymus to embrace sounder doctrine; but the heretical and hardened prince refused to hear the voice of his solicitous pastor, and did not cease to persecute Catholics, and especially monks, with cruelty: very many of whom, in order to escape the tyrant, withdrew to Italy; Paul received them kindly and assigned them churches and monasteries, provided with appropriate revenues, in which they might celebrate the sacred rites in the Greek tongue and in their ancestral rite.

But from that time many calamities befell the Emperor Constans; by which, being made no better, he sent Theodore Calliopas to the City with orders to lay hands upon the Pontiff. Martin, seized by him through treachery and brought to Constantinople, was thereafter sent into exile in Cherson; where, worn down by hardships for the Catholic faith, he departed this life on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of October, renowned for miracles. His body, afterwards translated to Rome, was laid in the church which had been dedicated under the names of Saints Silvester and Martin. He governed the Church for six years, one month, and twenty-six days. He held two ordinations in the month of December, in which he ordained eleven priests, five deacons, and thirty-three bishops in various places.

He set out for Constantinople, with an altogether different purpose from the one to which men had destined him — namely, at divine instigation and direction: to depose and condemn Anthimus, the heretical patriarch of Constantinople, who had been intruded by the evil arts of the Empress Theodora, and to put Mennas in his place; likewise to restore the patriarchal sees of Alexandria and Antioch, expelling the heretics, to Catholic pastors. But at last, before two years of his pontificate had been completed, that most holy man — in whom the Catholics desired nothing but a longer life — died devoutly at Constantinople, in the year of Christ five hundred and thirty-six. His body, translated to Rome, was laid in the Vatican.

When Constantius died, and Julian the Apostate, who succeeded him in the empire, permitted the exiled bishops to return to their churches, Athanasius returned to Alexandria and was received with the greatest honor. But not long afterwards, goaded by the same Arians, he was driven out again by Julian, and forced to depart. And when he was being sought out to be put to death by Julian's satellites, the little boat in which he was fleeing was turned about toward the opposite bank of the river; and he himself deliberately encountered those who were pursuing him; and when they asked how far away Athanasius was, he replied that he was not far off. And so he escaped them as they held a contrary course, and returning to Alexandria, he lay hidden there until the death of Julian. A little later, as another storm arose at Alexandria, he lay concealed for four months in his father's tomb. And at last, divinely snatched from so many and such great dangers, he died at Alexandria in his own bed, under Valens: his life and death were made renowned by great miracles. He wrote many things devoutly and admirably for the elucidation of the Catholic faith, and governed the Church of Alexandria most holily for forty-six years amid the greatest vicissitudes of the times.

He says that the measure of Jewish impiety is complete, and their fury for cruelty spent. For what did the Jews leave untried, or what extreme cruelty did they not employ? What kind of torment or indignity did they pass over? Wherefore he rightly says, It is consummated: but now, the hour summoning him to preach to the spirits who were in the lower regions (for he came so that he might have dominion over the dead and the living), he took upon himself this very death for our sake, and endured in his flesh this suffering common to our nature.

Perfected in a short time, full of virtues and merits, having announced the day of his death beforehand, he gave up his spirit to God in the midst of choirs of priests and religious, in the twenty-fifth year of his age. His body, brought to Vilna, shines with many miracles. For beyond the fact that a dead girl was restored to life, the blind received sight, the lame the use of their limbs, and various sick persons recovered health at his tomb, he appeared in the air to the Lithuanians, few in number, who were trembling at the unexpected assault of a most powerful enemy, and granted them a notable victory. Moved by these things, Leo X enrolled him in the catalog of the Saints.

Straightway the Angel rejoices over the reward he had considered, who had been sent to perform an act of piety freely. Tobias, he says — or Tobit — why do you think so much and more than enough about my reward? Keep what the heavenly Father has given you. I am the minister of the healing; he is the author of the health. You do not know by the help of what servant you have merited to profit. You were not afraid to bury the dead of the captivity: Tobias, your works have ascended to the Lord, because, leaving your meal, you returned the dead man to burial. I offered rich sacrifices to the Lord for the venerable burial. I am sent as a worker of the heavenly forum. You buried the dead, and you did not fear the sting of death. He himself, buried for you, proclaimed it in silent voice. The blindness of your eyes had been for a test, so that your patience might more gloriously merit an adornment from heaven. I am Raphael, one of the seven Angels who stand before the splendor of God. I have no need of the fruit of human reward; converse with Majesty makes me rich. Rich is he who sent me: freely he commanded to be spent what he himself freely granted. Nor should you attribute the very honor of thanks to me, because you received nothing through my own powers. Bless God, and give thanks to him, and glorify him, because he has done good things with you.

Against these, therefore, watches this same word of Christ, so many times repeated, whom he laments as Apostles who seek their own things, not the things of Jesus Christ. For what else is it, if you love me, feed my sheep, than if it were said: if you love me, think not of feeding yourself? But feed my sheep, and feed them as mine, not as yours; seek my glory in them, not yours; my dominion, not yours; my gains, not yours; lest you be in the company of those who belong to perilous times, lovers of themselves, and the rest that is joined to this beginning of evils.

But feed my sheep, and feed them as mine, not as yours; seek my glory in them, not yours; my dominion, not yours; my gains, not yours; lest you be in the company of those who belong to perilous times, lovers of themselves, and the rest that is joined to this beginning of evils.

It was therefore fitting that he should also dispose all things sweetly — both heavenly and earthly — so that by casting down from that quarter the restless one he might establish the rest in peace; and that here, about to overthrow the envious one, he should first leave us a most necessary example of his humility and meekness: and so it should come about, by a wonderful moderation of wisdom, that he might appear gentle to his own and strong to his enemies.

Let us be converted, therefore, and let us beware lest there can be among us any contention leading to ruin over precedence. For if the Apostles contended, this is set forth not as an excuse but as a warning. If Peter was at some point converted, who had followed at the first word of the Lord, who can say that he was quickly converted? Beware, therefore, of boastfulness; beware of the world. For he is commanded to strengthen his brothers who said: We have left all things and followed you.

Cornelius, Roman, holding the pontificate under the emperors Gallus and Volusianus, boldly resisted the schism of Novatian, and wrote many things with great charity concerning the lapsed; eight letters of Saint Cyprian to him are extant. Worn out by hardships in exile at Centumcellae, he died a martyr. Cyprian of Africa first taught rhetoric with distinction; then, at the persuasion of the presbyter Caecilius from whom he also received his surname, becoming a Christian, he distributed all his substance to the poor, and after no long time, having been chosen as a presbyter, was also appointed Bishop of Carthage. He too, bearing much in the schism of Novatus, strove with all his power to repair the damage done to the Church. To enumerate the catalogue of his genius is superfluous, since his works are clearer than the sun. He suffered under the emperors Valerian and Gallienus, in the eighth persecution.

Cornelius, Roman, holding the pontificate under the emperors Gallus and Volusianus, together with Lucina, a most holy woman, transferred the bodies of the Apostles Peter and Paul from the catacombs to a more convenient place; and Lucina placed the body of Paul in her estate on the Via Ostia, near the place where he had been struck by the sword; Cornelius placed the body of the Prince of the Apostles not far from where he had been crucified. When this was reported to the emperors, and that many were becoming Christians through the authority of the Pontiff, he was sent into exile at Centumcellae; where Saint Cyprian, Bishop of Carthage, consoled him by letters.

His family will crown him with a crown of justice, and in this it is terrible; his Father crowns him with a crown of glory, and in this it is desirable. Let sinners therefore see him in the crown of misery — that is, the crown of thorns — and be compunctious: let the daughters of Sion, souls full of affection, see him in the crown of mercy, and imitate him. The impious will see him in the crown of justice, and will perish; the saints will see him in the crown of glory, and will rejoice forever. Others, his imitators, are indeed also crowned; but this is by effort aided through grace. He alone was crowned by his mother, because he alone, with rightly ordered affections, went forth from his mother's womb as a bridegroom from his bridal chamber.

Cosmas and Damian, Arab brothers, born in the city of Aegea, skilled physicians, under the emperors Diocletian and Maximian, healed even incurable diseases not so much by medical knowledge as by the power of Christ. But when he realized that he was proposing these things to them in vain: Bind, he said, the hands and feet of these men, and torture them with exquisite torments. While his servants carried out his orders, Cosmas and Damian nonetheless persisted in their resolve. Therefore, as they were bound, they were thrown into the deep sea. When they came out safe and freed, the prefect, attributing the deed to magic arts, handed them over to prison, and the next day had them brought out and ordered them thrown into a blazing pyre; where, when the flame shrank back from them, he had them variously and cruelly tortured and then struck with the axe. And so, confessing Jesus Christ, they received the palm of martyrdom.
