You believe in God, and believe in him for whom it is a matter of nature, not of robbery, to be equal to God; for he emptied himself — yet not losing the form of God, but taking on the form of a servant. You fear death for this form of a servant: let not your heart be troubled; the form of God will raise it up. But what is it that follows: In my Father's house there are many mansions, unless it is because they feared even for themselves? Wherefore they needed to hear: Let not your heart be troubled. For which of them would not have feared, when it was said to Peter, the bolder and readier: The cock will not crow until you deny me three times?

When, however, the Virgin replied that she had distributed all of their goods to the poor, he was inflamed with such fury that he had her brought back to his house and ordered her to be burned in a bath-house. In that place, when she had remained a day and a night without the flame so much as touching her, an executioner was sent in, who struck her three times with an axe; but, being unable to cut off her head, left her half dead. Three days later, on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of October, in the reign of the emperor Alexander, adorned with the double palm of virginity and martyrdom, she flew up to heaven. Her body was buried by Pope Urban himself in the cemetery of Callistus, and a church was consecrated in her honor in her house. Her body, together with those of the Pontiffs Urban and Lucius, Tiburtius, Valerian, and Maximus, was translated to the city by the first Pontiff Paschal, and laid to rest in that same church of Saint Cecilia.

We can understand from this what great merit belongs to the most blessed Peter and Paul, since, whereas the Lord illuminated the region of the East by his own Passion, he saw fit to illuminate the lands of the West, lest anything be lacking, with the blood of his Apostles in his stead. And although his Passion suffices for our salvation, yet the martyrdom of these men also afforded us an example. On this day, therefore, the blessed Apostles poured out their blood: but let us consider the reason why they suffered, namely that among their other wondrous deeds, they also brought down that magician Simon, by their prayers, with a headlong fall from the void of the air.

Maximinus, admiring her wisdom, ordered her to be detained, and summoned the most learned men from everywhere, with great rewards promised, to convince Catherine and lead her away from the Christian faith to the worship of idols. The opposite occurred. For several philosophers who had gathered to refute her, inflamed by the force and subtlety of her argumentation with so great a love of Jesus Christ, did not hesitate to die for him. Maximinus therefore set about to draw Catherine from her position by flatteries and promises; but, understanding this to be in vain, he kept her shut up for eleven days without food or drink, having been beaten with rods and battered with leaden whips.

The foremost promoters of this Marian devotion were the dukes and princes of Bavaria. Some, even from the Middle Ages, dedicated certain most celebrated monasteries under the invocation and name of the Blessed Virgin Mary and enriched them with truly royal generosity; others gave splendid examples to their subjects by devoutly venerating the Mother of Sorrows or the Virgin conceived without stain. They were accustomed especially to heap pious and precious gifts upon the royal chapel of Oettingen, in which a miraculous statue of the Mother of God has been venerated with great devotion from the most ancient times, and to pour out prayers from their hearts in that place. Indeed, even after death, they piously professed themselves to be united by the bonds of the greatest love with their most august Patroness, by having their hearts enclosed in silver urns and laid up in that very Marian shrine.

When he had been left half dead by the impious, his eyes gouged out and his body pierced with wounds, the next day he was found healed through a remarkable miracle, and obtained the life of the same parricides through his prayers. He bestowed the Roman Empire upon Charles the Great, king of the Franks; built a most spacious hospice for pilgrims; assigned his patrimony and other estates to the poor. He enriched the basilicas of the city, especially the Lateran (in whose patriarchate he founded a great triclinium above all others), and the sacred buildings with so many and such great riches that they seem to surpass all belief. He finally crowned a most devout life with a holy end, on the day before the Ides of June in the year of the Lord eight hundred and sixteen, and was buried in the Vatican.

When the Albigensian heresy was raging impiously through the region of Toulouse and striking its roots ever deeper from day to day, Saint Dominic, who had recently laid the foundations of the Order of Preachers, devoted himself wholly to uprooting it. That he might accomplish this more effectively, he implored with earnest prayers the assistance of the Blessed Virgin, whose dignity was being most shamefully assailed by those errors, and to whom it had been given to destroy all heresies throughout the whole world. When he had been advised by her (as has been handed down to memory) to preach the Rosary to the people as a singular defense against heresies and vices, it is wonderful with what fervor of mind and how happy a success he carried out the task enjoined upon him. Now, the Rosary is a certain fixed form of prayer in which we distinguish fifteen decades of angelic salutations, with the Lord's Prayer interposed, and with each of them we devoutly recollect in meditation an equal number of the mysteries of our redemption. From that time, therefore, this pious manner of prayer began to be proclaimed and increased wonderfully by Saint Dominic. That he was its founder and originator, the Supreme Pontiffs have repeatedly affirmed in apostolic letters.

When he had lived most holily in canonical congregation for seventeen years, and had enriched the monastery of Goslar by the attribution of many estates, houses, and revenues from his paternal inheritance, and at the persuasion of Blessed Anno, Archbishop of Cologne, had been placed over the vacant church of Meissen, he resisted the acceptance of the episcopate by every means in his power; but at length, compelled rather than persuaded by the sharp rebuke of Blessed Anno, he accepted it, not unaware, however — for the Holy Spirit revealed it to him — of how great a flood of tribulations he would be tossed about in the episcopate; as the event itself proved, when the emperor Henry IV, stirring up a war against the Saxons, attacked the holy bishop as he was discharging the duties of a good shepherd and suspecting no evil, seized him though innocent, plundered all the goods of his church, and condemned the captive to the harshest imprisonment and exile.

When Paul and Barnabas were serving the Lord at Antioch in the Church, with the other prophets and teachers, in fasting and prayer, the Holy Spirit said: Set apart for me Saul and Barnabas for the work to which I have called them. Then, fasting and praying and laying their hands upon them, they sent them forth. And so they came to Seleucia, and from there to Cyprus; and they traveled through many other cities and regions, preaching the Gospel to the very great benefit of those who heard them. Finally, Barnabas, parting from Paul, sailed with John who was surnamed Mark to Cyprus; and there, around the seventh year of Nero, on the third day before the Ides of June, he added the crown of martyrdom to the honor of the apostolic office. His body was found, under the emperor Zeno, on the island of Cyprus; on his breast was the Gospel of Matthew, written in Barnabas's own hand.

Although she was continually giving examples of virtue, she burned with so anxious a desire to mortify her body that, even though the illnesses by which she was afflicted urged otherwise, she frequently tormented her body with hair shirts, chains, bundles of nettles, and other most severe scourges, and sometimes would roll herself among thorns, being accustomed to address God thus: Lord, either to suffer or to die; always considering herself to be dying the most wretched death as long as she was far from the heavenly source of eternal life. She excelled in the gift of prophecy, and the Lord enriched her so liberally with divine charisms that she would cry out frequently, begging that a limit be placed upon the divine favors bestowed upon her, and that the memory of her sins not be blotted out so swiftly. And so, consumed by an intolerable fire of divine love rather than by the force of illness, as she lay at Alba on the day she had foretold for her death, fortified by the sacraments of the Church, having exhorted her children to peace, charity, and regular observance, she gave back her most pure soul to God in the likeness of a dove, at the age of sixty-seven, in the year one thousand five hundred and eighty-two, on the Ides of October, according to the amended Roman Calendar. As she was dying, Jesus Christ was seen to be present among throngs of Angels; and a dry tree near her cell immediately put forth blossom. Her body, uncorrupt to this day, bathed in fragrant liquid, is honored with devout veneration. She was renowned for miracles before and after her death, and Gregory XV enrolled her in the number of the Saints.

When he had converted many to the Christian faith by his doctrine and holiness of life, he was banished by the emperor Trajan across the Black Sea to the wilderness of the city of Cherson; in which place he found two thousand Christians who had been condemned by the same Trajan. When they were suffering from lack of water while digging and cutting marble, Clement, having prayed, ascended a nearby hill, on the summit of which he saw a Lamb touching with his right foot a spring of sweet water that welled up from that spot; where all quenched their thirst. By that miracle, many unbelievers, converted to the Christian faith, also began to venerate the holiness of Clement.

When those who had been sent by Gallienus to summon Zeno found him fishing and were given by him three choice fish that he had caught, not content with the number, they added a fourth stolen from him; this fish, thrown into boiling water together with the three received from the holy man, swam about playfully. Struck with wonder at this miracle, they returned to the holy man, confessed themselves guilty of the theft, and obtained pardon from him.

When he had heard that passage from the Gospel: Do not possess gold, nor silver, nor money in your belts, no bag on the road, nor two tunics, nor shoes, he resolved to keep that rule for himself. And so, putting aside his shoes and content with one tunic, when he had gathered twelve companions, he instituted the Order of Minors. Wherefore he came to Rome in the year of salvation twelve hundred and nine, that the rule of his order might be confirmed by the Apostolic See. When the Supreme Pontiff Innocent III had at first rejected him as he came, because he afterward saw in a dream that this very man whom he had rejected was holding up the collapsing Lateran basilica on his own shoulders, he had him sought out and summoned, and receiving him kindly, confirmed the whole constitution of his institutions. Francis, therefore, having sent his brothers into all parts of the world to preach the Gospel of Christ, and himself desiring that some occasion of martyrdom should be given to him, sailed to Syria; where, having been most liberally received by the sultan, but accomplishing nothing, he returned to Italy.

When the demon in the temple of Serapis refused to give responses while a disciple of the Apostle Peter was staying there, Apollinaris was long sought and at last found: he was again ordered to sail. Returning thus to Ravenna, accused by those same priests of idols, he was handed over to a centurion for custody; who, himself secretly venerating Christ, released Apollinaris by night. When this became known, soldiers pursued him, and having beaten him on the road, left him as they believed dead. When the Christians had taken him from there, on the seventh day he exhorted them to steadfastness in the faith, and, glorious in the grace of martyrdom, departed this life. His body was buried near the wall of the city.

When Nestorius, Bishop of Constantinople, was plotting to introduce a new error into the Church — preaching that Christ was born of Mary as merely a man and not also as God, and that divinity had been conferred upon him as a reward for his merits — Celestine vigorously opposed his impiety with his own authority. Wherefore he delegated his role to Saint Cyril, Bishop of Alexandria, to pronounce sentence against him unless Nestorius repented within an interval of ten days. But when Nestorius had refused this more stubbornly, and the dissensions and tumults had grown greater, a third ecumenical council was assembled at Ephesus, at which Celestine presided through his legates: to whom he prescribed in his instruction the limits within which they were to judge the opinions of the bishops, not to enter the contest themselves. And so in that council, Nestorius was condemned along with the heresy that bears his name, and with many Pelagians who were supporting a doctrine akin to his error.

When the most illustrious philosopher and Martyr of Christ Justin had a short time before written an apology for the Christian religion to the Emperor Antoninus Pius Augustus, he obtained that the persecution should abate. Hence, by a public edict of the prince, killing of Christians was restrained — though not entirely — for the most part. Yet the most holy pastor, by whose care the Lord's flock had been looked after, was not spared; for this man ended his most innocent life by a glorious martyrdom, lest he be unlike his predecessors, on the eleventh day of January, and was buried in the Vatican.

When one of the satraps who had spoken ill of the king revealed to him that Gregory was the son of Anak, the slayer of his father Khosrov, he ordered him to be brought in, bound hand and foot and neck, into the province of Ararat, and to be thrust into the top of the fortress of Artashat and cast down into the lowest pit, there to die. But God, who had delivered him alive from such torments, likewise preserved him unharmed in this, and after a long time led Tiridates himself — tried by temptation like another Nebuchadnezzar — to the light of faith; Gregory, having purified him through fasting, reconciled him to God through baptism. And so, having been given the freedom to preach the Gospel of Christ publicly, he instructed the nation of greater Armenia in the faith and washed them in the sacred font, erected churches everywhere, destroyed the images of superstition and overthrew their temples, was ordained Archbishop of his people at Caesarea, and instructed the Armenians more intensely in divine doctrine and confirmed them in the faith they had received. Finally, most desirous of quiet and divine repose, he withdrew into solitude, where, devoted to fasting and contemplation, laden with merits, he fell asleep in the Lord in a good old age, under the emperor Constantine the Great. Christians fleeing from Armenia brought his body to Italy; his head, along with the chains with which he had been bound, was placed in Naples, and his arm in the cathedral of Nerito.

When Callistus III, chiefly at his pleading, had decided to send crusaders, John hastened through Pannonia and other provinces, and by word and by letters so inflamed the spirits of princes for the war that seventy thousand Christian soldiers were soon enlisted. By his counsel and valor, the victory of Belgrade was chiefly won, with a hundred and twenty thousand Turks partly slain and partly put to flight. When news of this victory reached Rome on the eighth day before the Ides of August, the same Callistus consecrated in perpetual solemnity the feast of the Transfiguration of Christ the Lord as a memorial of that day. Sick with a fatal illness and brought to Villach, he was visited by several princes; exhorting them to defend the faith, he gave back his soul to God holily, in the year of salvation fourteen hundred and fifty-six. God confirmed his glory after death by many miracles: these having been duly examined, Alexander VIII in the year sixteen hundred and ninety enrolled John in the number of the Saints; and Leo XIII, a century after his canonization, extended his Office and Mass to the universal Church.

For when the same Simon claimed to be Christ, and asserting as a son to the Father that he could ascend by flying, and raised aloft by magic arts had begun to fly: then Peter, fixing his knees in prayer, prayed to the Lord, and by holy prayer conquered the magic levitation. For prayer ascended to the Lord before the flight, and the just petition arrived before the unjust presumption; Peter standing on earth obtained first what he asked before Simon arrived in the heavens toward which he was heading. Then therefore Peter, as it were binding him, brought him down from the high air, and dashing him with a certain headlong fall upon the rock, broke his legs: and this in reproach of his deed, so that he who a little before had attempted to fly could suddenly not walk, and he who had assumed wings lost the use of his feet.

Since it is necessary — both Evangelists narrating truly, both Matthew and Luke — that one of them followed the lineage of the father who begat, and the other of the father who adopted Joseph; which is it more probable to understand: that the one who adopted held the lineage, or the one who was unwilling to say that Joseph was begotten by him whose son he was narrating him to be? Matthew, however, saying, Abraham begat Isaac, Isaac begat Jacob, and so persevering in this word begat all the way until he says at the end: but Jacob begat Joseph, expressed sufficiently that he had carried the line of generation to the father by whom Joseph was not adopted but begotten. Although even if Luke had also said that Joseph was begotten of Heli, not even so should this word disturb us such that we believed otherwise than that one Evangelist commemorated the begetting father, the other the adopting father. Nor is it absurd for anyone to be said to have begotten in charity and not in flesh one whom he has adopted as his son. But indeed we too, to whom God has given the power to become his children, he has not begotten from his own nature and substance as the only-begotten Son, but has certainly adopted in love.

For when, wishing to build a church in a suitable place, he saw it was too narrow for what the situation required, being cramped on one side by the sea cliff and on the other by a nearby mountain, he came by night to the place and, kneeling down, reminded the Lord of his promise, that he would move the mountain further away according to the faith of him who asked. And when morning came and he returned, he found that the mountain had left the builders of the church as much space as they needed. This man, therefore, could — as could another man of equal merit, if the occasion had required — obtain from the Lord by the merit of faith that even a mountain might be removed and cast into the sea.

When, therefore, you hear, brethren, the Lord saying: Where I am, there also my servant will be, do not think only of good bishops and clergy: you also, according to your means, serve Christ by living well, by giving alms, by preaching his name and teaching as best you can to those you are able: so that each householder may recognize that by his parental affection he owes service to his household in this name. For Christ and for eternal life, let him admonish, teach, exhort, correct all his own, bestow kindness, exercise discipline: thus in his own house he will fulfill an ecclesial and, in a certain manner, episcopal office, serving Christ, that he may be with him forever.

When, therefore, we apply our exhortations to the ears of your holiness, believe that he himself, in whose place we serve, is speaking to you: for we admonish you with his own affection, and we preach to you nothing other than what he taught; beseeching you that, with the loins of your mind girded, you may lead a chaste and sober life in the fear of God. You are my crown, as the Apostle says, and my joy, if your faith, which from the beginning of the Gospel has been proclaimed throughout the whole world, shall endure in love and holiness. For although the whole Church, which is throughout the whole world, ought to flourish in all virtues, yet it especially befits you above other peoples to excel in the merits of piety, you who are founded on the very summit of the apostolic rock, and whom our Lord Jesus Christ has redeemed together with all, and the blessed Apostle Peter has instructed above all.

Having therefore persuaded many in Rome to renounce their false religion and embrace the true faith, he brought to Christ certain senators and Hermes, the prefect of the city, along with his wife, children, sister, and the whole of his household. On this account, accused of being a Christian, he was seized by command of the prince and cast into prison, where he was detained for a long time because he would not abandon his profession of the Christian faith. While he was held bound, he was led forth prodigiously in the silence of the deep night by the ministry of a boy carrying a burning torch from the prison to the house of Quirinus the tribune, where the blessed Hermes, prefect of the city, had shortly before been captured and was being kept in custody; first he healed his sick daughter Balbina, then, by the miracle, Quirinus himself was moved and led to Christ, and Alexander washed him and his daughter in the bath of baptism. From this it came about that Quirinus granted freedom to depart to all those, however many, whom he held bound for the faith of Christ. Among them were Eventius and Theodulus, who, joined to Saint Alexander, refused to leave the prison, but paying praises to God, steadfastly awaited the palm of martyrdom.

When, therefore, the Roman Pontiff had compared the Roman chain with the one that had been brought from Jerusalem, it came about that they joined together so that they seemed not two but one chain made by the same craftsman. By this miracle, such great honor began to be paid to those sacred chains that, for this reason, the church of Saint Peter ad Vincula, with the title of Eudoxia, was dedicated on the Esquiline Hill, and a feast day was established in its memory on the Kalends of August.

When it is now said: Who shall separate us from the charity of Christ? Tribulation, or distress, or persecution, or famine, or nakedness, or danger, or the sword? Seven things therefore are those that bring to perfection: for the eighth glorifies, and shows what is perfect, so that through these steps others may also be perfected, beginning again as it were from the head. It seems to me, therefore, that the sevenfold operation of the Holy Spirit, of which Isaiah speaks, also corresponds to these steps and sentences. But there is a difference of order: for there the enumeration began from the more excellent, but here from the less. For there it begins from the wisdom of God, and ends at the fear of God: but the beginning of wisdom is the fear of the Lord.

When his zeal could not be contained within the then-prescribed borders of the Church, he turned his mind to the conversion of unbelievers, and brought it about that the vast nation of the Bulgarians, together with their king, was converted to the Christian faith and joined to the Roman Church, even though the schismatic emperor gnashed his teeth. He also applied himself diligently to the private duties of piety. Hence he wished to have the names of all the needy written out for himself, that he might the more carefully assist each one. He also applied a generous hand to the restoration and adornment of the basilicas of the city, especially the Lateran patriarchate, and spared no expense. Finally, having completed ten years of his pontificate, he migrated to heaven, and was buried in the Vatican.

When the holy Gregory himself, as death drew near, had designated him as the most worthy to succeed him on the Apostolic See, Desiderius was elected Pontiff by common suffrage. But his humility shone most brightly at that moment, for he declined so great a dignity for nearly a whole year. Then, persuaded by the earnest entreaties of bishops, princes, and people, he received at the Synod of Capua the name of Victor and the insignia of the supreme pontificate. Brought to Rome, he was consecrated with solemn rite, with the pseudo-pontiff Guibert and the men of his faction driven away. He dispatched an army gathered from almost all of Italy under the banner of Saint Peter against the Saracens in Africa, where, battle being joined, it utterly routed their forces. Having convened a synod at Benevento, he struck the schismatics with anathema and absolutely proscribed investitures, which were suppressing the freedom of the Church in elections; and decreed many other things pertaining to ecclesiastical discipline. Having completed the synod, struck with a fatal illness, he wished to be carried to Monte Cassino escorted by Cardinals and Bishops, where, worn out by labors and hardships in the cause of reconciling the Church to peace, he gave back his soul to God, illustrious in holiness and miracles, in the year ten hundred and eighty-seven. He held office from the day of his consecration for four months and seven days; and his body is honored with the greatest veneration in the basilica of Monte Cassino.

While he was at Laon, asked by the bishop not to leave his diocese, he chose for himself a deserted place in it called Prémontré; and there, having gathered thirteen companions, he founded the Premonstratensian Order, having received its rule from Saint Augustine in a vision through divine inspiration. As his reputation for holiness grew greater from day to day and many disciples came to him daily, the same order was confirmed by Honorius II and other Supreme Pontiffs, and, with many monasteries built by him, was spread wonderfully.

When the martyrs themselves and the clergy of Lyon were especially concerned about the peace of the churches of Asia, which the faction of the Montanists had disturbed, they chose from among them all the one most to be regarded — Irenaeus, whose merits they proclaimed the highest — to send to Rome to the Pontiff Eleutherius with a request that, the new sectaries having been condemned by the authority of the Apostolic See, the cause of discord might be removed. Pothinus the bishop, a martyr, had already departed; when Irenaeus succeeded him, he so happily discharged the office of bishop that, by his wisdom, speech, and example, he saw not only all the citizens of Lyon, but many also of other cities of Gaul, who in a short time had cast aside their superstition and error and enrolled in the Christian ranks. Meanwhile, when a controversy had arisen about the day of celebrating Easter, and Victor, the Roman Pontiff, had either forbidden communion to the Asian bishops, who disagreed with nearly all their other colleagues, or had threatened to forbid it, Irenaeus, as a mediator of peace, admonished him fittingly, and using the examples of earlier Pontiffs, brought him not to allow so many churches to be torn from Catholic unity on account of a rite which they said they had received from their ancestors.

When the emperor Maximian, having led his army into Gaul, had taken his stand within the borders of the Seduni for the purpose of sacrifice, the Theban legion, lest it contaminate itself by sharing in impious rites, withdrew from the rest of the forces. Wherefore the emperor sent soldiers to them to announce in his name that, if they wished to be safe, they should return to camp for the sacrifices: they replied that they were hindered by the Christian religion. Bearing their reply with the greatest indignation, he was inflamed with greater fury than before. And so, sending part of the army against the Thebans, he first ordered that every tenth man among them be killed; which martyrdom they preferred to endure of their own free will, and most especially at the urging of Maurice, rather than carry out the commands of an impious emperor. And then he ordered all the rest, who were most steadfastly proclaiming Christ, to be slaughtered by the whole army on the tenth day before the Kalends of October.

While staying at Pisa on a Sunday, having been refreshed with the heavenly food and caught up in ecstasy, she saw the Lord crucified coming with a great light, and from the wounds of his five stigmata five rays descending to five places on her body; and perceiving the mystery, she prayed to the Lord that the marks not appear; immediately the rays changed from a blood-red color to a brilliant one, and in the form of pure light reached her hands, feet, and heart: and the pain which she sensibly endured was so great that, had God not lessened it, she believed she would soon die. This grace the most loving Lord accumulated with a new grace, that she should feel the pain of the inflowing force of the wounds yet the bloody marks not appear. When the servant of God had reported this to her confessor Raymond as it had taken place, so that it might also be represented to the eyes, the devout care of the faithful expressed in painted colors the rays reaching to the said five places in images of blessed Catherine.

When one day old oil was lacking in the monastery and the time for gathering olives was at hand, and only a few olives seemed to be on the trees of the monastery, he ordered them to be gathered, put in the press, and however little oil could be pressed out to be brought to him. This was done, and the oil collected in a small vessel was brought to Nonnosus. He placed it before the altar, and when all had gone out he prayed, and then, calling the brothers back, ordered them to take up this oil they had brought and divide it by pouring a small amount into all the vessels of the monastery. The next day, all the vessels were found open and full of oil. Nonnosus, finally made superior of that monastery, spent the remaining days of his life in holiness: his sacred body, transported to Freising by Bishop Nitger, after a great fire was replaced in the crypt of the cathedral church by Bishop Adalbert, in the presence of Blessed Eberhard, Archbishop of Salzburg, in the year eleven hundred and sixty-one; and finally, discovered again by John Francis on the twenty-seventh of January in the year seventeen hundred and eight, it was set forth in the same crypt for public veneration with the greatest solemnity on the second of September of the following year, where God through the intercession of this holy abbot lavishes many and nearly daily benefits on the faithful who flock there in great numbers.

When the favorable report of their achievements had announced the glory of their deeds to Rome, the holy Pope Nicholas I ordered the two excellent brothers to hasten to Rome. Setting out on the Roman journey, they brought with them the relics of Saint Clement, first Supreme Pontiff, which Cyril had found at Cherson. At this news, Hadrian II, who had been appointed to succeed the deceased Nicholas, with the clergy and people accompanying him, went out to meet them on the Bovian road with great honor. Then Cyril and Methodius reported to the Supreme Pontiff, in the presence of the assembled clergy, on the apostolic task in which they had been laboring holy and diligently. When they were accused on this account by envious persons for having used the Slavonic language in the performance of sacred duties, they made their case with arguments so certain and so clear that the Pontiff, the clergy, and all present praised and approved these men. Then both, having sworn to remain firm in the faith of blessed Peter and of the Roman Pontiffs, were consecrated bishops by Hadrian. But it was divinely foreseen that Cyril should end the course of his life in Rome, ripe more in virtue than in years. And so his body, carried forth in a public funeral, was laid in the very tomb which Hadrian had built for himself; then brought to Saint Clement's and placed near his ashes. As he was borne through the city amid the festive chanting of Psalms — a procession seeming more of triumph than of funeral — the Roman people seemed to have offered the libations of heavenly honors to the most holy man. Methodius, returning to Moravia, and there having become a pattern of the flock from the heart, set himself with ever greater zeal to serve the Catholic cause. Indeed, he confirmed the Pannonians, Bulgarians, Dalmatians in the faith of the Christian name; and in leading the Carinthians to the worship of the one true God he labored greatly.

When she had completed her seventh year, burning with desire for solitude, she chose the narrow cell of her own house, in which she shut herself as in a voluntary prison, and ardently devoting herself to prayer and bodily mortification, she besought the mercy of God for the tranquility of the holy Church, which was being most bitterly harassed by the impiety of the emperor Frederick II. Having fallen into a fatal illness from long austerity, she was restored by a visit from the Blessed Virgin and was ordered to put on the habit of the third order of Saint Francis. From the age of ten, inspired by God, she led back many heretics to the faith and obedience of the Roman Pontiff by pious exhortations and powerful arguments. On this account, having been expelled into exile together with all her kindred, she came to neighboring towns, where in prophetic spirit she foretold the death of Frederick and the peace of the Church. She illuminated a woman who had been blind from birth, and to confirm the truth of the faith, entering a burning pyre and remaining in it for three hours unharmed, she overcame the obstinacy of a certain heretical woman and converted her together with others to the faith.

On the holy day of Pentecost, as it is said, many men who had been treading in the footsteps of the holy prophets Elijah and Elisha embraced the evangelical faith; and in that place on Mount Carmel where Elijah had once seen the rising cloud, remarkable as a type of the Blessed Virgin Mary, they began to build a chapel to the same most pure Virgin; and they venerated her as the singular patroness of their order, from that time taking the name of the Brothers of Our Lady of Mount Carmel. The special protection of the most Blessed Virgin never failed them; she dissuaded Honorius III from suppressing the order through a dream, and bestowed upon the order the remarkable sign of the sacred scapular, by the wearing of which, with the keeping of a modest abstinence and recitation of certain prayers, those detained in the fire of purgatory are piously believed through her intercession to be brought as quickly as possible to the heavenly homeland. Enriched with so many and such great benefits, the order instituted the solemn annual Commemoration of the most Blessed Virgin.

On the holy day of Pentecost, when the Apostles, filled with the Spirit from on high, were speaking in various tongues, and by invoking the most august name of Jesus were working many wonders, many men (as it is said) who had been treading in the footsteps of the holy prophets Elijah and Elisha, and had been prepared for the coming of Christ by the proclamation of John the Baptist, having perceived and proved the truth of events, straightway embraced the evangelical faith, and with a singular affection began to venerate the most Blessed Virgin — with whose conversation and intimacy they had been happy to enjoy — so ardently that they were the first of all to build in that place on Mount Carmel, where Elijah had once seen the rising cloud, remarkable as a type of the Virgin, a chapel to the same most pure Virgin.

While the Church was enjoying the fullness of peace, he also converted many from among the nobility to the Christian faith in Rome. Having received from Lucius, king of the Britons, letters through ambassadors requesting ministers of the divine word, he sent to him the priests Fugatius and Damianus of the Roman Church, by whom the king himself with his whole household, and nearly all his subjects, were regenerated in the sacred font. Having at last completed these and other works in the service of the divine cult, he rested in a holy end, under the emperor Commodus, on the fifth day before the Kalends of June, and was buried in the Vatican.

When the body of the same Valentine had rested for nearly five hundred years in the church of Passau, renowned for many miracles, the whole diocese felt his patronage again and again, especially in the incursions of the Hungarians, not yet initiated into the Christian rites: in which the inhabitants experienced his most immediate assistance.

When she had spent her life most devoutly in these and many other holy works, the end of her pilgrimage at last arrived, which she had foretold to her household beforehand. And with her eyes fixed upon heaven, absorbed in divine contemplation, wondrously refreshed by God and strengthened by the sacraments, she fell asleep in the Lord. And immediately many miracles were worked at her tomb. These having been heard and duly approved, Gregory IX enrolled her in the number of the Saints.

When he had given himself wholly to God, he set out for Palestine, to visit the holy places and venerate them in person. On this journey, embarking on a ship under a serene sky and calm sea, he foretold a terrible storm to the sailors; and when it arose while all were in the greatest danger, by his prayers he miraculously stilled it. Thereupon, returning home and giving to all examples of singular holiness, at God's prompting he came to Myra, which was the metropolis of Lycia; at which time the bishop of that city had died, and the provincial bishops were deliberating about the choice of a successor. And so in that deliberation they were divinely instructed to choose the man who would first enter the church on the following morning, by the name of Nicholas. This rule having been applied, Nicholas was found at the door of the church, and with the unanimous consent of all he was made Bishop of Myra. In the episcopate he perpetually observed the chastity which he had always cultivated, dignity, assiduity of prayer, vigils, abstinence, generosity and hospitality, mildness in exhortation, severity in correction.

When he came to his cell, he found the lifeless body with knees drawn up, neck erect, and hands outstretched on high: wrapping it in a cloak and chanting hymns and psalms according to Christian tradition, and having no hoe with which to dig the earth, two lions came at a swift pace from the inner desert to the body of the blessed elder; so that it was easy to understand that they were giving vent to mourning as best they could: and competing with one another in digging up the earth with their feet, they made a grave large enough to hold a man comfortably. When they had departed, Anthony brought the holy body to that place, and covering it with earth, fashioned a mound after the Christian manner: but he carried away with him the tunic of Paul, which the latter had woven for himself in the manner of a basket from palm leaves, and wore that garment on the solemn days of Easter and Pentecost for as long as he lived.

When the next day the same venerable woman had withdrawn to her own cell, the man of God returned to the monastery. And behold, after three days, remaining in his cell, he lifted up his eyes to the air and saw the soul of his same sister departing from the body in the form of a dove, penetrating the secret recesses of heaven. Rejoicing at her so great glory, he returned thanks to almighty God in hymns and praises, and announced her death to the brothers. He also sent them immediately to bring her body to the monastery and to place it in the tomb which he himself had prepared. By which deed it came to pass that those whose mind had always been one in God, their bodies also should not be separated in burial.

As those times were overflowing with vices and crimes, and in Italy all things divine and human were confounded by bloody factions, Bernardino, hastening through cities and towns, in the name of Jesus which he always bore on his lips and in his heart, largely restored the collapsed piety and morals by word and example. By which means it came about that distinguished cities demanded him as their bishop from the Supreme Pontiff; which office he declined with unconquerable humility most steadfastly. Finally, the man of God, exhausted by immense labors, having brought forth many great miracles, and having also written books devoutly and learnedly, after having lived sixty-six years, rested in a blessed end in the city of Aquila in the Vestini. Nicholas V, Supreme Pontiff, enrolled him, shining daily with new signs, in the number of the Saints six years after his death.

Cunegund, daughter of Siegfried the Palatine, though united in marriage to Henry, Emperor of the Romans, yet with his consent consecrated the flower of her untouched virginity to the eternal King. But the devil, enemy of such great virtue, stirring up the accusations of envious persons, brought the Empress under the suspicion of having violated the marriage bed. She, however, walking barefoot over red-hot ploughshares unharmed, proved her integrity to all.

Cyprian, first a magician, then a Martyr, when he was attempting to lure Justina, a Christian Virgin whom a certain young man loved ardently, to consent to his lust by incantations and sorceries, consulted the demon as to by what means he could achieve this. The demon replied to him that no art of his could prevail against those who truly worshipped Christ. Moved by this reply, Cyprian began to grieve most vehemently over the way of life he had previously chosen. And so, abandoning the magical arts, he converted himself wholly to the faith of Christ the Lord.

Cyprian, first a magician, then a Martyr, when he was attempting to lure Justina, a Christian Virgin whom a certain young man loved ardently, to consent to his lust by incantations and sorceries, consulted the demon as to by what means he could achieve this. The demon replied to him that no art of his could prevail against those who truly worshipped Christ. Moved by this reply, Cyprian began to grieve most vehemently over the way of life he had previously chosen. And so, abandoning the magical arts, he converted himself wholly to the faith of Christ the Lord.
Wherefore he was seized together with the Virgin Justina, and both were struck with blows and lashed with scourges; then they were thrown into prison, in case they might change their minds. But, having afterward been released from there and found most constant in the Christian religion, they were cast into a pan full of boiling pitch, fat, and wax. Finally at Nicomedia they were struck with the axe. Their bodies, having lain unburied for six days, were by night secretly taken aboard a ship by certain sailors and brought to Rome. And first they were buried in the estate of Rufina, a noble woman; afterward, translated to the city, they were laid to rest in the Constantinian basilica near the baptistery.

Cyriacus the deacon, having been shut up for a long time in prison together with Sisinnius, Largus, and Smaragdus, worked many miracles, among which he freed Arthemia, the daughter of Diocletian, from a demon by his prayers; and sent to Sapor, king of the Persians, he also freed his daughter Jobia from an evil spirit. The king her father having been baptized together with four hundred and thirty others, he returned to Rome; where, seized by command of the emperor Maximian, he was bound in chains and dragged before his chariot; and after four days, brought out of prison, drenched with liquid pitch and stretched on the rack, he was finally struck with the axe along with Largus and Smaragdus and twenty others on the Via Salaria, near the gardens of Sallust. Their bodies, buried on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of April in the same road by the priest John, afterward on the sixth of the Ides of August by the Pontiff Marcellus and the noble woman Lucina were wrapped in linen cloths and embalmed with precious ointments, and were transferred to the estate of Lucina herself on the Via Ostia, at the seventh milestone from the city.

Cyril of Alexandria, whose praises have been confirmed not merely by the testimony of one or another, but have been celebrated in the acts of the ecumenical councils of Ephesus and Chalcedon, was born of illustrious parents, and being the nephew of Theophilus, Bishop of Alexandria, gave clear proofs of his outstanding genius even as a youth. Thoroughly trained in letters and the sciences, he betook himself to John, Bishop of Jerusalem, to be perfected in the Christian faith. Having returned to Alexandria thereafter, upon the death of Theophilus, he was raised to his see: in which office he so steadfastly displayed the form of the best shepherd as defined by the Apostle, that he deservedly attained the glory of a most holy bishop.

Cyril of Alexandria, the nephew of Theophilus, Bishop of Alexandria, gave proofs of outstanding genius even as a youth. Upon the death of Theophilus, raised to his see, and having become a pattern of the flock from the heart, he attained the glory of the best shepherd. His singular zeal for the preservation of the Catholic faith shone forth against Nestorius, Bishop of Constantinople, who was asserting that Jesus Christ was born of the Virgin Mary as merely a man and not as God, and that divinity had been conferred upon him for his merits; when he had vainly attempted his correction, he denounced him to the holy Pope Celestine. With the authority of this Pontiff delegated to him, he presided over several sessions of the Council of Ephesus, in which the Nestorian heresy was utterly proscribed, Nestorius condemned and deposed from his see, and the Catholic dogma concerning the one — and that divine — person in Christ, and the divine motherhood of the glorious Virgin Mary, was defined. Concerned solely for the faith, and having suffered greatly on this account, having discharged the greatest labors for the Church of God and published very many writings, he rested in a holy end in the year four hundred and forty-four, the thirty-second year of his episcopate.

Cyril and Methodius, brothers by blood, born of the most distinguished family in Thessalonica, sent by the emperor Michael III to Moravia, quickly brought that nation to the Christian faith. When the favorable report of their achievements had announced the glory of their deeds to Rome, the holy Pope Nicholas I, the Supreme Pontiff, ordered the two excellent brothers to hasten to Rome; where they were consecrated bishops by Hadrian, the successor of Nicholas. But when Cyril shortly died most devoutly in Rome, Methodius, returning to Moravia, set himself to serve the Catholic cause with ever greater zeal. Indeed, he also confirmed the Bohemians, Pannonians, Bulgarians, and Dalmatians in the Christian faith; and in leading the Carinthians to the worship of the one true God he labored greatly. Likewise he brought the light of the Gospel into Poland, and, as some writers record, having founded an episcopal see at Lviv, he departed under his own name into Muscovy and established the pontifical throne of Kiev. Finally, returning to Moravia, having exhorted the clergy and people with his last counsels to virtue, he died most peacefully. The feast of Cyril and Methodius, long celebrated among the peoples of Slavonia, was extended by Leo XIII to the universal Church.

Cyril of Jerusalem, from his tender years devoted supremely to the study of the divine scriptures, advanced so greatly in the knowledge of them that he became a strenuous defender of the orthodox faith. Imbued with monastic principles, he devoted himself to perpetual continence and every stricter rule of life. After being ordained presbyter by Saint Maximus, Bishop of Jerusalem, he fulfilled with the highest praise the task of preaching the divine word to the faithful and teaching the catechumens, and wrote those truly wonderful catecheses in which, having comprehended clearly and copiously the whole of ecclesiastical doctrine, he defended firmly the individual dogmas of religion against the enemies of the faith. He discussed these matters so precisely and distinctly that he overthrew not only the heresies that had already arisen, but also those yet to come, as it were in prophetic foresight, as he demonstrated in asserting the real presence of the Body and Blood of Christ in the wonderful Sacrament of the Eucharist. When the holy Maximus had died, he was appointed to his place by the bishops of the province.

Diego, a Spaniard, from the town of San Nicolás del Puerto in the diocese of Seville, served his novitiate in a holier way of life from his earliest years under the discipline of a devout priest. Submitting himself there with great alacrity to the yoke of humble obedience and regular observance, devoted especially to contemplation, he was bathed in a wondrous light from God, so much so that concerning heavenly matters, though ignorant of letters, he spoke in a wondrous manner and plainly as if by divine inspiration. Having suffered much in the Canary Islands, burning with the desire of martyrdom, he converted many unbelievers to the faith of Christ by word and example. Assigned at Rome in the convent of the Ara Coeli to the care of the sick, he fulfilled this office with a wondrous affection of charity. The grace of healings also shone forth in him. Finally he departed most devoutly from this life at Alcalá, in the year of the Lord one thousand four hundred and sixty-three. Sixtus V enrolled him, renowned for many miracles, in the number of the Saints.

For the Lord loves those who keep the commandments of the law, even the lesser ones: but nonetheless, what had been lacking in the law, he shows to those who desire to be perfect, because he came not to abolish the law or the Prophets, but to fulfill them. To this fulfillment belongs indeed what is added next in order: Go, sell whatever you have and give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven, and come, follow me. Whoever wishes to be perfect must sell what he has; and not sell only in part, as Ananias and Sapphira, but sell all: and when he has sold, give everything to the poor, and so prepare for himself a treasure in the Kingdom of Heaven. Damasus, a Spaniard, an excellent man and learned in the sacred Scriptures, having convened the first Council of Constantinople, extinguished the nefarious heresy of Eunomius and Macedonius. He condemned again the assembly of Ariminum, which had already been rejected by Liberius; in which, as Saint Jerome writes, chiefly through the treachery of Valens and Ursacius, the condemnation of the Nicene faith was proclaimed. He built two basilicas: one in the name of Saint Lawrence near the theater of Pompey, the other on the Via Ardeatina at the Catacombs. He decreed that, as was already the custom in several places, the Psalms should be chanted antiphonally in all churches day and night, and that at the end of each Psalm it should be said: Glory be to the Father, and to the Son, and to the Holy Spirit. At his command, Saint Jerome translated the New Testament according to the Greek original. He also discovered many bodies of the holy Martyrs and adorned their memorials with verses. Renowned for virtue, learning, and prudence, at nearly eighty years of age, under the elder emperor Theodosius, he fell asleep in the Lord.

From the Letter of Saint Cyprian, Bishop and Martyr, and of his colleagues, to Saint Lucius, Pope and Martyr. We congratulated you recently, most dear brother, when the divine favor, in its double honor, established you as Confessor and Priest alike in the governance of his Church. But now we congratulate you no less, you and your companions and the whole brotherhood, in that the benign and generous protection of the Lord has brought you back again to your own people with the same glory and the same praise, so that the pastor might be restored to his flock to feed it, the helmsman to his ship to steer it, and the ruler to his people to govern it; and that it might be made manifest that your exile was divinely ordained not so that a bishop, banished and expelled, should be absent from his churches, but that he might return to his church the greater. For in the three young men the dignity of martyrdom was no less because, death being frustrated, they came forth unharmed from the furnace of fire; nor was Daniel left unconsummated in his praises because, having been thrown to the lions as their prey, he was protected by the Lord and lived to his glory. In the Confessors of Christ, martyrdoms deferred do not diminish the merit of confession, but display the great works of divine protection.

Princes have persecuted me without cause, and my heart has trembled at your words. The Martyr rightly says this: that he endures the torments of persecution unjustly; for he has seized nothing, has violently oppressed no one, has shed no one's blood, has thought that any man's marriage bed was to be violated; he owes nothing under the laws, yet is compelled to suffer punishments harsher than those of robbers; he speaks justly and is not heard; he speaks what is full of salvation and is attacked, so that he can say: When I spoke to them, they attacked me without cause. His foundations are in the holy mountains; the Lord loves the gates of Zion. Why are the Apostles and Prophets foundations? Because their authority bears up our weakness. Why are they gates? Because through them we enter into the Kingdom of God. For they preach to us, and when we enter through them, we enter through Christ, for he himself is the door. And when twelve gates of Jerusalem are spoken of, and Christ is both the one gate and the twelve gates, this is because Christ is in the twelve gates; and hence the twelvefold number of the Apostles. Of this solicitude of the Church for the newly formed body of workers, the same Pontiff gave proof when, having seized the opportunity of a gathering of workers held at Rome on the first of May in the year nineteen hundred and fifty-five and addressing the vast multitude assembled in the square before the Basilica of Saint Peter, he warmly commended the instruction of workers. For in our times this claims a more prominent part: that workers, duly imbued with Christian doctrine, should shun the errors concerning the constitution of society and the economy that are spreading widely, and should come to know well the moral order established by God, which the Church sets forth and interprets, regarding the rights and duties of workers; and, having become sharers in the work to be done, they may labor effectively for its advancement. For Christ was the first in the world to proclaim and hand on to the Church those principles which remain unchangeable and most powerful for the resolution of these questions.

From this Heart, then, as from a furnace of divine ardor, the Blessed Virgin brought forth good words, that is, words of most fervent charity. For just as from a vessel full of the finest and most excellent wine nothing can come forth but the finest wine; or just as from a furnace of supreme heat nothing goes forth but burning fire; so from the Mother of Christ no word could come forth but one of the highest and most divine love and ardor. It belongs also to a wise mistress and matron to have few words, yet solid and weighty; and accordingly seven times — as it were, seven words of wonderful import and power — are read to have been spoken by the most blessed Mother of Christ, so that it might be shown mystically that she herself was full of grace in sevenfold form. She spoke with the Angel only twice. With Elizabeth, likewise twice. With her Son also twice: once in the Temple, the second time at the wedding. With the servants, once. And in all of these she always spoke very little, except that in praise of God and in giving thanks she spread herself more broadly, namely when she said: My soul magnifies the Lord. Where she spoke not with man, but with God. These seven words were uttered according to seven progressions and acts of love, in wondrous degrees and order; as though they were seven flames from the furnace of her Heart.

And as this ardent desire was more and more enkindled in him through the devout daily celebration of Mass, it came about by the wonderful providence of God that this valiant athlete of Christ was chosen to be the head of those missions which the Congregation for the Propagation of the Faith had at that time established for Rhaetia. Taking up this arduous office with a ready and joyful spirit, he discharged it with such fervor that, many heretics having been converted to the orthodox faith, no small hope shone forth of reconciling that entire people to the Church and to Christ. Endowed with the gift of prophecy, he frequently foretold the future calamities of Rhaetia and his own death at the hands of heretics. When, fully aware of the snares being laid for him, he had prepared himself for the impending struggle, on the twenty-fourth day of April in the year sixteen hundred and twenty-two, he made his way to the church of the place called Seewis; where, after the heretics — who the day before had feigned conversion and treacherously invited him to preach — had violently interrupted the sermon and cruelly inflicted upon him blows and wounds, he with great and joyful heart endured a glorious death, and consecrated with his own blood the first fruits of the Martyrs of that Congregation; thereafter illustrious by many signs and miracles, especially at Chur and Feldkirch, where his relics are preserved with the utmost veneration of the people.

The Virgin Mother of God, to whose service he had dedicated himself from his earliest years, he honored as a mother with daily acts of devotion and implored with filial confidence. Moreover, it is difficult to say with what ardent affection he was held toward the most holy Sacrament of the Eucharist; an affection which he seemed to retain even after death in his corpse, for as he lay on the bier, he twice opened and closed his eyes at the elevation of the sacred Host, to the great wonder of all who were present. Having publicly and openly professed the truth of this same Sacrament among heretics, he suffered much and greatly on that account; and frequently sought for death, yet was snatched from the hands of the impious by the singular providence of God. Often in prayer he was deprived of all his senses and languished in a sweet swoon of love; in which time he is believed to have drawn that heavenly knowledge by which, though an unlearned and illiterate man, he was able to answer concerning the most difficult mysteries of the faith, and even to write several books. Finally, full of merits, at the very hour he had foretold, he passed happily to the Lord in the year of salvation fifteen hundred and ninety-two, on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of June, on the same feast of Pentecost on which he had been born, being in his fifty-second year. Pope Paul V, acknowledging him distinguished by these and other virtues, and illustrious by miracles both in life and after death, declared him Blessed; Alexander VIII enrolled him in the catalogue of Saints; and finally Leo XIII declared and established him as the heavenly patron of Eucharistic gatherings and of all societies of the Most Holy Eucharist, whether existing or to come.

After the death of Lanfranc, archbishop of Canterbury, once his teacher, Anselmus — urged by William, king of England, and pressed by the clergy and people, though he himself resisted — was called to the governance of that same church. He immediately set about reforming the corrupt morals of the people, first by word and example, then by writings and councils held, and thus restored ancient piety and ecclesiastical discipline. But when the same King William soon attempted by force and threats to usurp the rights of the Church, he resisted with priestly constancy; and, having suffered the plundering of his goods and exile, he betook himself to Rome to Urban II, by whom he was honorably received and adorned with the highest praise, having in the Council of Bari defended with innumerable testimonies of Scripture and the holy Fathers the procession of the Holy Spirit from the Son as well, against the error of the Greeks. When William had died, he was recalled to England by King Henry his brother, and fell asleep in the Lord, having gained a reputation not only for miracles and holiness — especially on account of his outstanding devotion to the Passion of our Lord and to the Blessed Virgin his Mother — but also for learning, which it is clear from all his books he drew from heaven for the defense of the Christian religion, the advancement of souls, and the model of all theologians who have taught sacred Scripture by the scholastic method.

Such a birth befitted God: that he should be born of none but a Virgin. Such a birth also suited the Virgin: that she should give birth to none but God. Accordingly, the maker of mankind, that he might become man, being about to be born of a human being, was bound to choose for himself — or rather to fashion for himself — from among all women such a mother as he knew would befit him and would please him. He willed, therefore, that she should be a Virgin, from whom the stainless one would proceed unstained, who was to cleanse the stains of all. He willed also that she should be humble, from whom the meek and humble of heart would come forth, who was to show himself to all as the necessary and most salutary example of these virtues. He granted to the Virgin the gift of birth, having already inspired in her beforehand the vow of virginity and bestowed upon her in advance the merit of humility. In order, then, that she who was alike to conceive and to bring forth the Holy of holies should be holy in body, she received the gift of virginity; and that she might be holy in mind as well, she received the gift of humility.

On the tenth day of August in the year of the Lord twelve hundred and eighteen, King James resolved to carry out that institution, long conceived by those same holy men, with its members bound by a fourth vow to remain as pledges in the power of the pagans, if need be, for the liberation of Christians. The King himself granted them the right to bear his own royal arms on their breast, and he had Gregory IX confirm that institution of so surpassing a charity toward neighbor and that religious order. But God himself, through the Virgin Mother, gave increase to it, so that such an institution might spread more swiftly and happily throughout the whole world and might flourish among holy men distinguished by charity and piety, who would expend the alms gathered from the faithful of Christ as the ransom price for the liberation of their neighbors, and at times would give themselves as the ransom of many. And so that fitting thanks might be rendered to God and the Virgin Mother for so great a benefit and institution, the Apostolic See granted the celebration of this particular festival and the recitation of the Office, having also conferred at the same time almost innumerable other privileges upon the same order.

In the most difficult period of the Roman Church, he rendered wonderful assistance to the Supreme Pontiffs by his learning, his legations, and other labors he undertook. He fought strenuously to the death against the heresies of the Nicolaitans and simony. Having driven out these evils, he reconciled the Church of Milan to the Roman Church. He resolutely resisted Benedict and Cadalus, false pontiffs; he deterred Henry IV, King of Germany, from an unjust divorce of his wife; he restored the people of Ravenna, recalled to the obedience owed to the Roman Pontiff, to the sacred rites; he brought the canons of Velletri to the rule of a more holy life. In the province of Urbino especially, there was hardly a bishop's church of which Peter had not rendered great service: the church of Gubbio, which he once held in trust, he relieved of many difficulties; others elsewhere he tended in like manner, whenever the occasion arose, as though they had been committed to his guardianship. Having laid aside the cardinalate and episcopal dignity, he abated nothing of his former diligence in helping his neighbors. He propagated the fast on Fridays in honor of the holy Cross of Jesus Christ, the hourly prayers to the blessed Mother of God, and her veneration on Saturdays. He also advanced the practice of self-flagellation for the expiation of sins committed. Finally, illustrious in holiness, learning, miracles, and outstanding deeds, as he was returning from his legation to Ravenna, he went to Christ at Faenza on the eighth day before the Kalends of March. His sacred body, which rests there with the Cistercians and is famous for many miracles, is venerated with frequent popular devotion; and the people of Faenza have more than once chosen him as their intercessor before God in present dangers. Leo XII, Sovereign Pontiff, by the counsel of the Sacred Congregation of Rites and with the addition of the title of Doctor, extended to the universal Church the Office and Mass in his honor as a Confessor Bishop, which were already celebrated in certain dioceses and in the Camaldolese order.

Dionysius, a monk before becoming Bishop of the Roman Church, was appointed after the blessed Sixtus II. He wrote against the Sabellians, and published many volumes against those who asserted that the Son of God was a work or a creature. He examined the case of Dionysius, Bishop of Alexandria, who had been accused before him of saying that the Son of God was made and was not consubstantial with the Father, in a Roman Synod, and he wrote the opinion of that same Synod, which took the accusation ill, to Dionysius. But when the Bishop of Alexandria had over and again cleared and defended himself by writings sent to Rome, he was at length absolved after mature deliberation. Dionysius distributed churches among the presbyters throughout the city and divided the cemeteries, parishes, and dioceses. Finally, having borne many labors for the Church and being distinguished for proofs of faith, he went to the Lord under the Emperor Aurelian and was buried in the cemetery of Callistus on the Appian Way, on the sixth day before the Kalends of January. He held, in the month of December, two ordinations, in which he created twelve presbyters, six deacons, and seven bishops in various places. He held his see for eleven years, three months, and fourteen days.

Dionysius of Athens, one of the judges of the Areopagus, while he was still wandering in the error of paganism, is reported, on the day when Christ the Lord was nailed to the Cross, to have observed the sun eclipsed contrary to nature, and to have exclaimed: Either the God of nature is suffering, or the structure of the world is being dissolved. When the Apostle Paul had proclaimed Christ in the Areopagus, Dionysius embraced the Christian faith and was placed by the same Apostle at the head of the church of Athens. Afterward, as tradition has it, he came to Rome, and having been sent by Pope Clement into Gaul, he preached the Gospel as far as Lutetia of the Parisians, together with Rusticus the priest and Eleutherius the deacon. There, all of them were seized by the prefect Fescennius for preaching Christ, tormented by various sufferings, and at last beheaded on the seventh day before the Ides of October.

Dionysius of Athens, one of the judges of the Areopagus, was a man versed in every kind of learning. While he was still wandering in the error of paganism, on the day when Christ the Lord was nailed to the Cross, he is reported to have observed the sun eclipsed contrary to nature and to have exclaimed: Either the God of nature is suffering, or the structure of the world will be dissolved. But when Paul the Apostle came to Athens and was brought to the Areopagus and had given an account of the teaching he was preaching, affirming that Christ the Lord had risen and that all the dead would return to life — among many others, Dionysius himself believed in Christ.

Having set the affairs of his church in order, Augustine held a synod with the bishops and teachers of the ancient Britons, who had long since dissented from the Roman Church in the celebration of Easter and other rites. But when he could move them neither by the authority of the Apostolic See nor by miracles to cease their dissension, he foretold their destruction by prophetic spirit. At last, having endured very great labors for Christ and being illustrious for miracles, after he had placed Mellitus over the church of London and Justus over that of Rochester, he migrated to heaven and left Laurence over his own church, on the seventh day before the Kalends of June, in the reign of Ethelbert; and he was buried in the monastery of Saint Peter, which thereafter became the burial place of the Archbishops of Canterbury and of several kings. The English people pursued his veneration with fervent zeal, and Pope Leo XIII extended his Office and Mass to the universal Church.

For the authority we believe is divine; the teaching we follow is divine. He was in the beginning with God. All things were made through him, and without him nothing was made. And equally true is what the same herald added: The Word was made flesh and dwelt among us; and we saw his glory, the glory as of the Only Begotten of the Father.

Enkindled by the flame of divine love, he was moved by a singular affection of devotion toward the Passion of Christ the Lord, which he continually meditated upon, and toward the Virgin Mother of God, to whom he had wholly consecrated himself; this devotion he strove most eagerly to stir up in others also by word and example, and to increase by his written works. Hence that sweetness of character, that grace of speech, and that charity poured out upon all, by which he bound the hearts of individuals to himself most closely. For this reason, when he had barely reached his thirty-fifth year, he was elected at Rome, with the unanimous consent of all, as Minister General of his order; and he bore that office entrusted to him for eighteen years with admirable prudence and the praise of holiness. He established many things useful for regular discipline and for the enlargement of his order, which together with other mendicant orders he successfully defended against the slanders of detractors.

Scorning the riches with which he abounded, he sold his goods, distributed the proceeds to the poor, left his wife Therasia, changed his country, broke the bonds of the flesh, and withdrew to Spain, following the venerable poverty of Christ, more precious to him than all the world. At Barcelona, while he devoutly attended the sacred rites on the solemn day of the Lord's Nativity, he was seized by the sudden amazement of the people and, resisting in vain, was ordained a priest by Bishop Lampius. He then returned to Italy and at Nola, whither the devotion of Saint Felix had drawn him, he founded a monastery near that saint's tomb, and gathering companions, he entered upon the common life. This man, already distinguished by senatorial and consular dignity, embraced the folly of the Cross — to the wonder of nearly the whole world — and clothed in a poor tunic, amid vigils and fasts, he remained fixed day and night in constant contemplation of heavenly things. But as the fame of his holiness grew, he was raised to the bishopric of Nola, and in fulfilling that pastoral office he left behind wonderful examples of piety, wisdom, and especially of charity.

Ardently enkindled with the desire to spread divine charity and the Catholic faith, he was named General of his order, reluctantly and against his will, and sent brothers to preach the Gospel of Christ in Scythia; while he himself, traveling through many cities of Italy, composed the growing civil discords among them and recalled many to obedience to the Roman Pontiff; and omitting nothing that pertained to the salvation of others, he led the most abandoned men out of the mire of vices to penance and to the love of Jesus Christ. Devoted most earnestly to prayer, he was often seen to be rapt in ecstasy. He cultivated virginity to such a degree that he preserved it unimpaired by voluntary and most severe mortifications to the very last breath of his life.

She contemplated the divine mysteries, and above all the Passion of Christ the Lord, with such ardor of mind and such a flood of tears that she seemed nearly to be consumed by the greatness of her grief. Often also when she was praying, and especially after receiving the most holy Sacrament of the Eucharist, she was elevated in spirit to God and, rapt in the contemplation of heavenly things, remained motionless. For this reason the enemy of the human race strove to turn her from her purpose by various insults and blows; but she always eluded him undaunted, and especially with the aid of her Angel, through familiar intercourse with whom she won a glorious triumph over him. She was distinguished by the grace of healing and the gift of prophecy, by which she predicted the future and penetrated the secrets of hearts. Not once, but several times, water — whether flowing in a stream or falling from the sky — left her wholly unsoaked while she was occupied with God. Small fragments of bread, barely sufficient to refresh three sisters, the Lord so multiplied at her prayers that fifteen were satisfied from them, and so much remained that a basket was filled; and on another occasion the thirst of those same sisters, who were gathering wood outside the City in January, was wondrously quenched by grapes of fresh vine hanging from a tree. Finally, illustrious in merits and miracles, she migrated to the Lord in the fifty-sixth year of her age. Pope Paul V enrolled her in the number of the Saints.

He was most zealous for the worship of God, for the beauty of the house of God, for the observance of sacred rites, and for the more frequent use of the most holy Eucharist. More than once he uncovered and routed the monsters and lairs of heresies. He prolonged prayer throughout eight hours with unceasing tears: often rapt in ecstasy and illustrious with the gift of prophecy, in Rome, on the night of the Nativity, at the crib of the Infant Lord, he merited at the hands of the Mother of God to receive the child Jesus into his own arms. At times he afflicted his body with flagellations through entire nights; nor could he ever be induced to soften the austerity of his life, declaring that he wished to die in ashes. At last, taken ill from grief of soul at seeing the people stir up sedition against God, he was refreshed by a heavenly vision and migrated to heaven at Naples; and his body is venerated there in the church of Saint Paul with great devotion. Clement X, Sovereign Pontiff, who was illustrious by many miracles in life and after death, enrolled him in the number of the Saints.

Now the holy Martyr Sixtus, whose feast we celebrated five days ago, had said to him: Do not mourn, my son — for he was a bishop and this man a deacon — do not mourn, he said; you shall follow me after three days. He said three days, meaning the interval between the day of the passion of Saint Sixtus and this present day of the passion of Saint Lawrence: three days between them. What comfort! He did not say, Do not mourn, my son, for the persecution will end and you will be safe; but, Do not mourn: where I go before you, you shall follow; your following is not deferred. Three days will lie between, and you shall be with me. He received the oracle, overcame the devil, and attained the triumph.

He said to the man: Stretch out your hand; and he stretched it out, and his hand was restored. Stretch out your hand: it is loosed by the command by which it had been bound by command. Stretch out your hand: suffering acknowledged the Judge, the work acknowledged God, the pardon betrayed the Creator. Pray, brethren, that such a withering may afflict the synagogue alone, and that there be no one in the Church whose hand avarice may wither, covetousness contract, rapine weaken, or stinginess bind in sickness; but if this should happen, let him hear the Lord and quickly extend it in a work of piety, relax it, and stretch it out in mercy and almsgiving. He who does not know how to lend to the poor does not know how to be healed.

Her learning was infused, not acquired; she answered professors of sacred letters who put to her the most difficult questions about divinity. No one came to her who did not leave the better for it; she extinguished many hatreds and calmed deadly enmities. For the sake of peace for the Florentines, who were at odds with the Church and placed under ecclesiastical interdict, she journeyed to Avignon to Pope Gregory XI. To him she revealed that she knew by divine inspiration the vow he had made — known to God alone — of returning to the City; and the Pontiff resolved, on her urging as well, to go in person to his Roman see: which he did. She was most highly regarded by that same Gregory and by his successor Urban VI, so much so that she served as their envoy. Finally, after countless marks of virtue and being illustrious by the gift of prophecy and many miracles, she migrated to her Spouse in about the thirty-third year of her age. Pope Pius II enrolled her in the number of the holy Virgins.

Dominic, born at Caleruega in Spain from the noble family of the Guzmans, and educated at Palencia in the liberal arts and theology, became first a canon of the church of Osma, and afterward the founder of the Order of Preachers. His genius and virtue shone out most brilliantly in converting heretics who were endeavoring to pervert the people of Toulouse. Coming to Rome, he sought from Pope Innocent III the approbation and confirmation of his order, which he obtained from his successor Honorius III. And when through his labors countless men were establishing a religious and pious way of life, he fell asleep in the Lord at Bologna in the year twelve hundred and twenty-one, leaving to his disciples charity, humility, and poverty as their certain inheritance, with those words: Come to my aid, holy ones of God; hasten to meet me, O Angels. Pope Gregory IX enrolled him in the number of the Saints.
