Dominic, born at Caleruega in Spain from the noble family of the Guzmans, devoted himself at Palencia to the liberal arts and theology; and when he had made great progress in that study, he became first a canon regular of the church of Osma, and afterward the founder of the Order of Friars Preachers. His mother, while pregnant, dreamed that she bore in her womb a dog carrying a torch in its mouth, which, when brought forth into the light, set the whole world on fire. By this dream it was signified that he would set nations alight with the splendor of his holiness and learning to kindle Christian piety. The event confirmed the truth of it; for he achieved this himself, and afterwards through his companions in the order.

Let us therefore imitate the Lord also, and omit nothing for our brethren, not even those things which seem too lowly and base; but if even our service is needed, no matter how poor and abject the one to be served, no matter how arduous and full of toil the task may appear to us — may all these things, I pray, seem more bearable and easier for the sake of our brother's salvation: for God has shown the soul to be of so great worth that he spared not even his own Son.

But the Lord replied on Mary's behalf to Martha: he himself became her advocate, who had been appealed to as judge. Martha, he says, you are busy about many things, yet one thing is necessary. Mary has chosen the better part, which shall not be taken away from her. For we have heard both the petition of the one who made the appeal and the verdict of the judge. The verdict answered the petitioner and defended the course she had undertaken. For Mary was intent upon the sweetness of the word of the Lord. Martha was intent on how she might feed the Lord; Mary on how she might be fed by the Lord. Martha was preparing a banquet for the Lord, at whose banquet Mary was already taking her delight.

Donatus, his parents having been put to death for their faith in Jesus Christ, took flight with the monk Hilarinus to Arretium in Etruria, of which city he was also created bishop. There, when both were commanded by the prefect Quadratianus, during the persecution of Julian, to venerate idols, and they refused to commit so wicked a crime, Hilarinus was beaten with clubs before the eyes of Quadratianus until he breathed his last; Donatus, himself also harshly tortured, was struck with the sword. Their bodies were honorably buried by Christians near that city.

The virgin Dorothea, from Caesarea of Cappadocia, was apprehended by the prefect Apricius for her confession of Christ and handed over to the sisters Chrystae and Callistae, who had lapsed from the faith, in order to turn her from her purpose. But the opposite happened; for Dorothea brought them back to the practice of the Christian religion, for which they also suffered martyrdom. Wherefore the virgin, long stretched on the rack and beaten with palms, was at last condemned to beheading, and received the twofold palm of virginity and martyrdom.

There are two lives: consider them more fully among yourselves. What does this life hold — I do not say an evil life, an unjust, wicked, dissolute, or impious life, but a laborious one, full of hardships, disciplined by fears, troubled by temptations: this very innocent life I speak of, such as it was fitting for Martha to have. Contemplate it, then, as much as you are able, and think upon it, as I said, more fully than we are now speaking of it. But the unjust life was absent from that house; it was not with Martha, nor with Mary; and if it ever was there, when the Lord entered, it fled.

When Thomas saw, then, when he touched — why is it said to him: Because you have seen me, you have believed? But he saw one thing and believed another. For divinity could not be seen by a mortal man. He saw a man, therefore, and confessed God, saying: My Lord and my God. He believed by seeing, who, by contemplating the true man, cried out to this God whom he could not see. Most joyful is what follows: Blessed are those who have not seen and have believed. In that sentence we ourselves are surely specially marked out, who hold in mind him whom we have not seen in the flesh. We are specially marked out; but only if we follow up our faith with works. For he truly believes who enacts by his deeds what he believes.

While he was celebrating the solemnities of Mass, a dove was seen by devout men to descend from heaven and settle on his right shoulder, spreading its wings to cover his head — by which it was signified that he was guided in the governance of the Church by the breath of the Holy Spirit, not by the calculations of human prudence. When Rome was hard pressed by the army of the wicked Henry, he quenched with the sign of the Cross a fire stirred up by the enemy. He was at last rescued from Henry's hands by Robert Guiscard, the Norman duke, and withdrew to Cassino; and from there he made his way to Salerno for the dedication of the church of Saint Matthew the Apostle. Having once delivered a sermon to the people in that city, he fell worn down with hardships into an illness, from which he foreknew he would die. The last words of the dying Gregory were: I have loved justice and hated iniquity; therefore I die in exile. Countless are the things he either bravely endured or wisely decreed in many synods convened in the City; a truly holy man, a punisher of crimes, and a most zealous defender of the Church. Having thus spent twelve years in the pontificate, he migrated to heaven in the year of salvation ten hundred and eighty-five, illustrious for many miracles in life and after death; and his sacred body is honorably enshrined in the cathedral basilica of Salerno.

While he was delivering public sermons to the people, he was so vehement in speaking that at times his voice would fail him from excessive fervor — as happened in the sermon on the woman with a hemorrhage. Thereupon the people of Ravenna were so moved that they filled the place with so many tears, cries, and prayers, that he afterward gave thanks to God for having turned the loss of that sermon into a gain of love. When at last, after governing that church most holily for about eighteen years, he foreknew by divine intimation that the end of his labors was at hand, he betook himself to his homeland; and there, entering the church of Saint Cassian, he placed upon the high altar a great golden diadem set with most precious gems, and also a golden chalice and a silver paten — the water drawn from it having been proved time and again to heal both the bite of a mad dog and fevers. From that time he dismissed the people of Ravenna who had followed him, admonishing them to watch attentively in choosing the best pastor. He then humbly prayed to God and to Saint Cassian as his patron to receive his soul graciously, and on the fourth day before the Nones of December departed this life in peace, about the year of the Lord four hundred and fifty. His sacred body, buried with the universal weeping and devotion of the entire city near the body of that same Saint Cassian, is religiously venerated even in our own times; and his arm, adorned with gold and gems and brought to Ravenna, is venerated in the Ursian basilica.

While residing in Rome, three times a week he made his way on foot, barefoot, at night, praying and singing psalms, from the most holy Lateran church to the Vatican. He ceded by pontifical diploma to the Prince of the Apostles the tenth part of offerings which customarily fell to himself. He spent his own private patrimony on the building of a monastery, from which also money was sent each year for the expenses of the golden rose that the Roman Pontiffs bless by ancient and solemn rite. He exercised lavish generosity toward the poor and pilgrims. Under the form and habit of a leper he once received Christ in his own bed. Finally, having endured many labors for the Church, he died on the nineteenth day of April in the year one thousand and fifty-four, illustrious for many miracles before and after death, and was buried in the Vatican.

From such a harsh manner of living she fell into an illness of the stomach, which grew more serious as she entered her seventieth year of age, reducing her to the very last span of her life. She bore the inconveniences of her long illness with a serene countenance and steadfast spirit; she was heard to complain of only one thing: that, being unable in any way to take or retain food, she was kept from the Eucharistic table out of reverence for the Sacrament. But in this extremity she asked a priest to take the divine Bread that had been brought and, since she could not receive it by mouth, at least to apply it externally to her breast. The priest did as she asked; and — a marvel! — at that very moment the divine Bread disappeared, and Juliana breathed her last with a serene and smiling face. The matter was beyond belief for a long time, until the virginal body was cared for in the customary way; for there was found upon the left side of her breast, as if imprinted on her flesh like a seal, the form of a host depicting the figure of Christ crucified. The fame of this prodigy and of her other miracles won her the veneration not only of Florence but of the whole Christian world, and was so greatly increased over nearly four full centuries that at last Pope Benedict XIII ordered the proper Office to be recited at her feast by the entire order of the Servants of the Blessed Virgin Mary. Clement XII, most generous protector of the same order, enrolled her, shining with miracles new each day, in the catalogue of the holy Virgins.

On that same day he was put to death together with Felicissimus and Agapitus, deacons; Januarius, Magnus, Vincent, and Stephen, subdeacons; and was buried in the cemetery of Callistus on the eighth day before the Ides of August: the rest in the cemetery of Praetextatus. He held his see for eleven months and twelve days. During that time he held an ordination in the month of December, creating four presbyters, seven deacons, and two bishops.

That same night the most holy Virgin appeared to Blessed Raymond of Penyafort and to James, King of Aragon, admonishing them in the same terms about founding a religious institute, and urging them to render assistance for the construction of so great a work. Peter at once threw himself at the feet of Raymond, who was his confessor, and disclosed the whole matter to him; and he found Raymond also instructed from heaven, and submitted himself most humbly to his direction. Then King James arrived, and resolved to carry out the revelation which he himself had also received from the most blessed Virgin. Wherefore, having taken counsel together and with one accord of heart, they set about founding an order in honor of that same Virgin Mother, under the invocation of holy Mary of Mercy for the Redemption of Captives.

Behold, the Lord sends out his disciples two by two to preach: thereby hinting to us in silence that he who has no charity toward another must by no means undertake the office of preaching. Moreover, it is well said that he sent them before his face into every city and place where he himself was about to come. For the Lord follows his preachers, since preaching goes before, and it is then that the Lord comes to the dwelling of our mind when the words of exhortation have gone ahead; and so truth is received into the mind.

Behold, we have now accompanied you with such prayers as we could, and followed from afar, O blessed Virgin, as you ascend to your Son. May it be the part of your loving kindness to make known to the world that grace which you have found with God — obtaining pardon for sinners, healing for the sick, courage for the faint of heart, consolation for the afflicted, help for those in peril, and liberation by your holy prayers. And on this day of solemnity and gladness, may Jesus Christ, your Son, our Lord, who is above all things God blessed forever, through you, O gracious Queen, shower the gifts of his grace upon the servants who invoke the most sweet name of Mary with praise. Amen.

Behold, he says, your son; behold, your mother. Christ bore witness from the Cross, and between mother and disciple distributed the duties of devotion. The Lord was making not only a public but also a private testament: and John, a witness worthy of so great a testator, was setting his seal to this testament of his. A good testament — not of money, but of eternal life; written not with ink, but with the Spirit of the living God, who says: My tongue is the pen of a scribe writing swiftly.

Behold what is said: If anyone serves me, let him follow me. With what fruit? what reward? what prize? And where I am, he says, there also will my servant be. Let him be loved freely, so that the reward for the work of serving him may be to be with him. For where will it go well without him, or when can it go ill with him? Hear it more plainly: If anyone has served me, my Father will honor him. With what honor, if not to be with his Son? For what he said above — Where I am, there also will my servant be — he is understood to have explained when he says: My Father will honor him. For what greater honor can an adopted son receive than to be where the Only-begotten is — not made equal to the divinity, but associated with eternity?

Behold, your house shall be left to you desolate. This same thing he had already said before in the person of Jeremiah: I have forsaken my house, I have dismissed my inheritance; my inheritance has become to me like the den of a hyena. That the house of the Jews — that is, that temple which shone so magnificently — is desolate, our own eyes confirm; for it lost Christ its inhabitant, and in its eagerness to seize the inheritance, it slew the heir.

He adorned the Church with most holy institutions and laws. At a synod convened near Saint Peter's he established many things: among them, that in the Mass the Kyrie eleison should be repeated nine times; that outside the time contained between Septuagesima and Easter, the Alleluia should be said; and that there should be added in the Canon: Dispose our days in your peace. He augmented the Litanies, Stations, and the ecclesiastical Office. He wished the four Councils of Nicaea, Constantinople, Ephesus, and Chalcedon to be held in honor as the four Gospels. He granted that the bishops of Sicily, who according to the ancient custom of the churches gathered in Rome every three years, need come but once every five years. He composed many books; and while he was dictating them, Peter the deacon testified that he often saw the Holy Spirit in the form of a dove upon his head. What he said, did, wrote, and decreed is admirable, the more so since his health was always frail and infirm. He who at last, after many miracles performed, was called to heavenly blessedness in the thirteenth year, sixth month, and tenth day of his pontificate, on the fourth day before the Ides of March — a feast day celebrated with special honor even by the Greeks, on account of the outstanding wisdom and holiness of this Pontiff — whose body was buried in the basilica of Saint Peter, near the Secretarium.

We read that he distributed the titular churches of the City of Rome among the presbyters, so that each one might be distinguished by the boundaries and limits of his own parish; and that he commanded that altars, upon which the sacred rites are performed, if built of stone, should be blessed; and that seven deacons should stand guard over the bishop and attend him while he fulfilled the office and ministry of proclaiming the Gospel, as witnesses of the teaching handed down by him.

He was most tenacious of ecclesiastical discipline, having sent many weighty letters everywhere for its preservation or restoration. He decreed, in accordance with the approved custom of the Church, that if anyone from childhood had given his name to the ecclesiastical ministries, he should remain among the readers until his twentieth year of age, with continuous observance. But if one were already older, and advanced in age after baptism, he should be kept either among the readers or among the exorcists for five years, and thence as an acolyte or subdeacon for four years, and so proceed (if he were worthy) to the diaconate, in which order he ought to remain for five years, and then, with the support of the votes, could merit the priesthood.

He also decreed that deacons should cover their left arms with linen vestments; and he granted the power that the paschal candle might be blessed in parish churches. He further took care that no cleric should be offered a cup in public, except in the dwellings of the faithful and especially of clerics. Having governed the Church most holily for one year, four months, and seven days, he rested in peace; and was buried next to the body of Saint Lawrence the Martyr on the Tiburtine Way, on the seventh day before the Kalends of January, in the reign of Honorius and the younger Theodosius. At one ordination, in the month of December, he created ten presbyters, three deacons, and eight bishops in various places.

Having made the vow of virginity, he preserved his chastity spotlessly throughout his life. He shone wonderfully in patience, humility, abstinence, and the other virtues. Distinguished by the gift of prophecy, he foretold the future; among his predictions, the most celebrated is that King James would conquer Valencia, then occupied by the Moors, having first received from him an assurance of victory to be obtained. He was refreshed by the frequent apparition of the Guardian Angel and of the Virgin Mother of God. At last, worn out by old age, and made aware of his approaching death, he fell ill; and, refreshed by the holy sacraments and having exhorted his brethren to charity toward captives, he was devoutly reciting the Psalm, I will give praise to you, O Lord, with my whole heart, and at those words, The Lord has sent redemption to his people, he gave up his spirit to God at midnight on the Vigil of the Lord's Nativity, in the year twelve hundred and fifty-six. Pope Alexander VII extended his feast to the universal Church.

He also decreed that priests should not be rebuked by the people, out of regard for the dignity of so exalted an order. Hyginus of Athens, the son of a philosopher, having already been a priest of the Roman Church, was chosen as successor to Telesphorus by the votes of the clergy. He sat on the holy seat of Peter, in the reign of the Emperor Antoninus Pius Augustus, for three years, eleven months, and twenty-eight days. As soon as he was made Pontiff, he distinguished the orders of the clergy in their proper grades, and he decreed that in those churches called Titles there should be both principal ministers and others subordinate to them, who, when the occasion required, would administer the sacred rites to the faithful.

Edward, surnamed the Confessor, nephew of Saint Edward King and Martyr, the last of the Anglo-Saxon kings, was sought out for death by the Danes who were ravaging England while he was ten years old, and was compelled to live in exile with his uncle, the Duke of Normandy. There, his innocence of character was the admiration of all. When the tyrants who had robbed his brothers of life and kingdom were soon destroyed, he was recalled to his homeland. There he turned himself entirely to erasing the traces of hostile fury, beginning with the sacred churches. Distinguished by the gift of prophecy, he foresaw from heaven many things about the future state of England. He had a wonderful devotion to John the Evangelist. He died most devoutly on the very day foretold by the Evangelist, namely on the Nones of January, in the year of salvation ten hundred and sixty-six. Pope Alexander III enrolled him in the roll of the Saints.

Edward, surnamed the Confessor, nephew of Saint Edward King and Martyr, the last of the Anglo-Saxon kings — whom the Lord had shown to the most holy man Brithuald in a mental ecstasy as the future king — was sought out for death by the Danes who were ravaging England while he was ten years old, and was compelled to live in exile with his uncle, the Duke of Normandy. There, amid the allurements of vices, he showed himself of such integrity of life and innocence of character that he was the admiration of all. Even then his wonderful piety toward God and holy things shone forth in him, and his nature was most gentle and altogether free from any desire to dominate. This saying is recorded of him: that he would rather be without a kingdom that could not be obtained without slaughter and blood.

In him there bloomed continually a singular mercy toward the poor, but especially when at Camillano, a village in the territory of Siena, he gave to a naked leper who was begging alms his own garment in which he was clothed; and when the leper was covered with it, he was immediately cleansed of his leprosy. When the fame of this miracle had spread far and wide, some of the cardinals who had gathered at Viterbo after the death of Clement IV to choose a successor fixed their gaze on Philip, whose heavenly wisdom they also had come to know well. When the man of God became aware of this, lest he should be compelled to take up the burden of pastoral governance, he lay hidden near Mount Tuniato until Gregory X had been declared Sovereign Pontiff; where at the baths, still called the Baths of Saint Philip even today, he obtained by his prayers the power of healing illnesses. Finally, at Todi, in the year twelve hundred and eighty-five, in the embrace of Christ the Lord hanging on the Cross — whom he called his book — he departed most holily from this life. At his tomb the blind received sight, the lame recovered their gait, the dead recovered life. Clement X, Sovereign Pontiff, enrolled him, who shone with these and very many other signs, in the number of the Saints.

How, then, will each one receive according to his merits? When? Certainly, they say; but bodies will not rise. Do they not hear Paul saying: For this corruptible must put on incorruption? He was adorned with splendid titles of praise by the ancient Fathers, who called him herald of justice, trumpet of the Gospel, a catholic vessel, a man most celebrated for piety and miracles — by which God illustrated his heroic virtues and the holiness of his apostolic life. Several decretals of this most holy Prelate survive, in which the dogmas of the Catholic faith are kept safe and sound, the form and rule of ecclesiastical discipline is set forth, the integrity of the sacred canons and ancient traditions is safeguarded, and finally all the particular duties of pastoral solicitude are fulfilled.

Finally it was brought to Rome by the Emperor Otto III, and placed on the Tiber Island in the church dedicated to God under his name.

Through his care and zeal not only was the clergy greatly increased, but the universal Church also grew with great advances. Admirable indeed was his prudence in this matter, since at that time Anastasius, the heretic emperor, and Theodoric the Arian held sway over both empires. He also accomplished, established, and wrote very many other things pertaining to the dignity and discipline of the Church. He condemned the defenders of Acacius, especially Euphemius of Constantinople; and by most vigorous and learned letters written to various persons, he either held them to their duty or brought back those who had gone astray. He repressed the Pelagians, Manicheans, and other heretics, and had their books committed to public flames. Besides decretals and ecclesiastical hymns, he wrote excellent short works against Nestorius, Arius, Pelagius, and Eutyches. But what is above all to be remembered is that in a Roman synod of seventy bishops, he distinguished by a singular decree the canonical books from the others, and the approved from the apocryphal. After many labors at last endured in ruling the universal Church, that most holy and most learned Pontiff died devoutly in the Lord on the eleventh day before the Kalends of December, in the year of Christ four hundred and ninety-six, and was buried in the Vatican.

Of the same piety was the fact that he carefully arranged for the body of the blessed Callixtus, Priest and Martyr, which had been cast into the Tiber, to be sought out, and, having found it, buried it honorably. Having washed Palmatianus, distinguished by consular rank, Simplicianus, distinguished by senatorial dignity, and Felix and Blanda with the waters of baptism — all of whom afterward suffered martyrdom — he was cast into prison, where he wondrously restored to health Privatus the soldier, who was full of ulcers, and joined him to Christ; for which same soldier, being newly received in the faith, he was beaten to death with leaded whips.

Elizabeth, daughter of Andrew, King of Hungary, began to fear God from childhood; and as she grew in age, she also grew in devotion. Having been united in marriage to Ludwig, Landgrave of Hesse and Thuringia, she fulfilled with no less care what belonged to God than what belonged to her husband. Assiduously devoted to prayer and given to works of mercy, she served widows, orphans, the sick, and the needy with diligence, and for their relief she also built a notable hospice. After the death of her husband, in order to serve God more freely, she clothed herself in a poor tunic and, entering the Order of Penitents of Saint Francis, she shone forth especially in the virtue of patience and humility. For stripped of all her goods, driven from her own houses, and forsaken by all, she endured contumely, mockery, and detraction with an unconquered spirit — so much so that she greatly rejoiced in suffering such things for God. At last, having passed her life most devoutly in holy works, she fell asleep in the Lord. Gregory IX, who saw her illustrious in miracles, enrolled her in the number of the Saints.

Elizabeth was born of the kings of Aragon in the year of Christ twelve hundred and seventy-one. The joy of her birth turned the ruinous discord of her grandfather and father into concord, from which it was at once apparent how blessed a peacemaker of kings and kingdoms she would be. She was admirable in mortifying the body, in the assiduous recitation of prayers, and in the exercise of works of charity. Given in marriage to Dionysius, King of Portugal, she devoted herself no less to the cultivation of virtue than to the rearing of children, seeking to please her husband, but more to please God. She not only built monasteries, colleges, and churches, but endowed them magnificently as well. She was admirable in resolving the discords of kings, tireless and renowned for miracles in relieving the private and public calamities of mortals. After the death of King Dionysius, having put on the habit of the Seraphic Order, she offered whatever remained dear or precious to her to the shrine of Compostela for the king's soul, and converted it to sacred and pious uses. Finally, as she set out to make peace between two kings, her son and her son-in-law, having contracted an illness on the journey and having been visited by the Virgin Mother of God, she died most holily. Urban the Eighth, renowned for miracles, enrolled her among the Saints.

Elizabeth, born of the kings of Aragon in the year of Christ twelve hundred and seventy-one, was given, as a presage of her future holiness, the name at baptism, by her parents, setting aside, contrary to custom, the names of her mother and grandmother, from her great-aunt, the lady of Thuringia, Saint Elizabeth. When she was born, it was at once apparent how blessed a peacemaker of kings and kingdoms she would be; for the joy of her birth turned the ruinous discord of her grandfather and father into concord. Her father, marveling later at the disposition of his growing daughter, affirmed that this one Elizabeth would far surpass in virtue the other women born of the blood of the kings of Aragon. Thus, venerating her heavenly manner of life in despising bodily adornment, in fleeing pleasures, in frequenting fasts, in the assiduous recitation of divine prayers, in the exercise of works of charity, he attributed the happiness of his affairs and kingdom as gained through the merits of his one daughter. At length, known everywhere and desired by many princes, she was duly joined in marriage to Dionysius, King of Portugal, with Christian ceremonies.

After several years had passed, renouncing the world together with six other companions, he approached Saint Hugh, Bishop of Grenoble. Having learned the cause of their coming, and understanding them to be the same men whom he had seen the same night in a dream as seven stars falling at his feet, he granted them the most rugged mountains of his diocese, called the Chartreuse. Thither Bruno withdrew with his companions, Hugh himself accompanying them; and after he had lived the eremitic life for some years, he was summoned to Rome by Urban the Second, who had been a disciple of Bruno himself. Eleutherius, a Greek by nationality, born at Nicopolis, a town of Epirus, of a father named Abundius, was, after the death of Soter, unanimously acclaimed Roman Pontiff by the suffrage of the whole clergy, in the reign of the Emperor Marcus Aurelius Augustus, in the year of the Lord one hundred and seventy-nine. He discharged that office excellently, and with the highest praise, for fifteen years and twenty-three days, holding three ordinations in the month of December, and creating twelve priests, eight deacons, and fifteen bishops in various places.

Eleutherius, born at Nicopolis in Greece, deacon of Pope Anicetus, presided over the Church in the reign of the Emperor Commodus. To him, at the outset of his pontificate, a petition came from Lucius, King of the Britons, that he and his people might be received into the number of Christians. For this reason he sent Fugatius and Damianus, learned and pious men, into Britain, through whom the king and the rest received the faith. Under this Pontiff, Irenaeus, a disciple of Polycarp, came to Rome and was graciously received by him. At that time the Church of God enjoyed the highest peace and tranquility; and throughout the whole world, especially in Rome, the faith was propagated. Eleutherius lived in the pontificate fifteen years and twenty-three days. He held three ordinations in the month of December, in which he created twelve priests, eight deacons, and fifteen bishops in various places; and was buried in the Vatican near the body of Saint Peter.

Elizabeth, daughter of Andrew, King of Hungary, began to fear God from childhood; and, as she grew in age, she grew also in piety. Joined in marriage to Louis, Landgrave of Hesse and Thuringia, she attended with no less care to the things of God than to those of her husband. Rising in the night hours, she gave herself long to prayer; and, devoted to the various offices of mercy, she diligently served widows, orphans, the sick, and the needy, and when a grave famine pressed, she freely distributed the grain of her household. Receiving lepers into her home, she kissed their hands and feet. For the care and nourishment of the poor she built a notable hospice.

Humility, mercy, and kindness shone forth in him; and he was so given to contemplation that he scarcely used his senses except for the duties of piety, in which nonetheless he excelled in the praise of prudence. Occupied in this pursuit, he refused the bishoprics of Genoa, Milan, and others that were offered him, declaring himself unworthy of the charge of so great an office. Having become Abbot of Clairvaux, he built monasteries in many places, in which the noble rule and discipline of Bernard long flourished. At Rome, over the monastery of Saints Vincent and Anastasius, restored by Pope Innocent the Second, he set as abbot the man who afterward was Supreme Pontiff Eugene the Third, to whom he also sent his book On Consideration.

His most ardent charity shone forth especially in the sweetest ecstasies and wondrous raptures toward God, by which he was frequently seized. Remarkable it was that, when his mind was taken from his senses, obedience alone immediately recalled him from ecstasy. This virtue he pursued with exceptional zeal, being accustomed to say that he was led about by it as if blind, and that he would rather die than not obey. He so emulated the poverty of the Seraphic Patriarch that, when near death, he could truly affirm to his superior that he had nothing that he needed to resign in the manner of religious. And so, dead to the world and to himself, he manifested the life of Jesus in his flesh; which, whenever it perceived some shameful vileness in others, breathed forth from itself a wondrous fragrance, a sign of that most pure chastity which, while an unclean spirit long strove in vain to obscure it with the most violent temptations, he preserved unharmed — by strict custody of the senses, by continual mortification of the body, and finally by the special protection of the most pure Virgin Mary, whom he was accustomed to call his mother, and whom he venerated with the deepest affection of heart as a most sweet mother, and desired that she be venerated by others, so that, as he himself would say, all good things might be obtained through her patronage.

Emerentiana, a Roman virgin, foster-sister of the blessed Agnes, still a catechumen, burning with faith and charity, when she more vehemently accused the furious worshipers of idols who were raging against Christians, was overwhelmed with stones by the excited crowd. She, praying in her torments at the tomb of Saint Agnes, was baptized by her own blood, which she steadfastly shed for Christ, and gave up her soul to God.

Sent down from the castle through a window, he was brought back to Naples; thence led to Rome, and afterward to Paris, by Friar John the Teutonic, Master General of the Order of Preachers, he devoted himself to philosophy and theology under the teacher Albert the Great. At the age of twenty-five he was called a master, and publicly expounded philosophers and theologians with the highest praise. He never gave himself to reading or writing except after prayer. In the difficulties of passages of Sacred Scripture, he would add fasting to prayer. Indeed, he was accustomed to say to his companion, Friar Reginald, that whatever he knew he had acquired not so much by his own study and labor as by divine gift. When at Naples he was praying more fervently before an image of the Crucified, he heard this voice: You have written well of me, Thomas; what reward will you receive? To which he replied: None other, Lord, but yourself. He constantly read through the Conferences of the Fathers; and there was no kind of writing with which he was not most diligently acquainted. His writings excel so greatly in number, variety, and facility in explaining difficult matters that his most abundant and incorrupt doctrine, wonderfully consonant with revealed truths, is most apt for overcoming the errors of every age.

Men were held captive under the devil and served demons; but they were redeemed from captivity. For they were able to sell themselves, but they were not able to redeem themselves. The Redeemer came and paid the price; he shed his blood and bought the whole world. You ask what he bought? See what he gave, and you will find what he bought. The blood of Christ is the price. What is of such great worth? What, if not the whole world? What, if not all nations? They are greatly ungrateful for their price, or very proud, who say either that it was so small as to have bought only the Africans, or that they themselves are so great that it was given for them alone. Let them therefore not exult, let them not be proud. He gave as much as he gave for the whole.

It is wonderful how many evils, how many hardships and labors, how many adversaries that apostolic man endured in that ministry. But by the kindness of God breathing upon him, that land, formerly devoted to idols, soon under Patrick's preaching bore such fruit that it was henceforth called the Island of Saints. Very many peoples were regenerated by him in the sacred bath; very many bishops and clerics were ordained; virgins and widows were instructed in the rules of continence. He established the see of Armagh, by the authority of the Roman Pontiff, as the chief metropolis of the whole island, and adorned it with relics brought from the City. Endowed by God with heavenly visions, the gift of prophecy, and mighty signs and wonders, he shone so brightly that the fame of Patrick spread far and wide.

By this miracle and through their preaching, first the people of Marseille, then those of Aix and the neighboring peoples believed in Christ; and Lazarus was made bishop of Marseille and Maximinus of Aix. But Magdalene, accustomed to prayer and to the feet of the Lord, in order that she might enjoy the best part of contemplating heavenly beatitude, which she had chosen, withdrew into a vast cave of a most lofty mountain; where she lived for thirty years, separated from all human society, and daily during that time was lifted on high by Angels to hear the praises of heaven.

Ephrem, a Syrian by race, was born of a father from Nisibis. While still young he went to Saint Jacob the Bishop, by whom he was baptized, and made such swift progress in holiness and learning that he was appointed master in the flourishing school of Nisibis, a city of Mesopotamia. Ordained deacon of the church of Edessa, and refusing the priesthood out of humility, he shone with the splendor of every virtue and strove to acquire piety and religion by true profession of wisdom. All his works, filled with such splendid light of learning, brought it about that the same Saint was held in great honor even while still living, as a Doctor of the Church. He excelled above all in a wondrous and devout love for the Immaculate Virgin. Full of merits, he departed this life at Edessa in Mesopotamia, on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of July, in the reign of the Emperor Valens; and Pope Benedict the Fifteenth, by consultation with the Congregation of Sacred Rites, declared him a Doctor of the Universal Church.

Ephrem was a Syrian by race, born of a father from Nisibis. While still young he went to Saint Jacob the Bishop, by whom he was baptized, and made such swift progress in holiness and learning that he was appointed master in the flourishing school of Nisibis, a city of Mesopotamia. After the death of Bishop Jacob, Nisibis having been captured by the Persians, he set out for Edessa; where he first settled on a mountain among monks, and then, to avoid the great numbers of men who flocked to him, led the eremitic life. Ordained deacon of the church of Edessa, and refusing the priesthood out of humility, he shone with the splendor of every virtue and strove to acquire piety and religion by true profession of wisdom. Fixing all hope in God alone, despising all human and transitory things, he continually desired the divine and eternal.
Epist. 25 ad Ecclesiam Vercellensem, prope finem

Mary, the Mother of the Lord, stood before the Cross of her Son. No one taught me this except the holy John the Evangelist. Others wrote of the world shaken at the Lord's Passion, the sky covered with darkness, the sun fleeing; of the thief received into paradise, but after his pious confession. John taught what the others did not teach: how he, placed on the Cross, addressed his Mother. It is thought more significant that the victor over torments rendered to his Mother the offices of piety than that he bestowed on her the heavenly kingdom. For if it is a holy thing that pardon was given to the thief, how much richer in piety is it that the Mother is honored with such great love by the Son.
Now in that gathering… [the reading ends here].

In him there was a wondrous grace of speaking; he preserved perpetual virginity; he cultivated humility so greatly that he called himself the least of all, and wished his disciples to be called the Minims. Wearing rough garments, going barefoot, he slept on the ground. His abstinence from food was admirable: he refreshed himself once a day after sunset, and besides bread and water he scarcely allowed himself anything of such provisions as are permitted to be eaten in Lent; and he bound his brothers to observe this custom throughout the whole year by a fourth vow.

At that time the King of Poland was Bolesław, whom he gravely offended by publicly reproving his notorious licentiousness. Therefore, at a solemn assembly of the kingdom, he arranged for Stanislaus to be summoned to judgment before him on a false charge, as if he were occupying a village that he had purchased in the name of his church. When he could not prove this either by documents, and the witnesses feared to speak the truth, the Bishop pledged that he would bring before the court within three days Peter, the seller of the village, who had died three years before. The condition being accepted with mockery, the man of God spent the whole three days in fasting and prayer; on the very day of the pledge, after offering the Sacrifice of the Mass, he commanded Peter to rise from the tomb; who, immediately restored to life, followed the Bishop as he went to the royal tribunal, and there, with the king and the rest struck dumb with astonishment, bore witness concerning the field sold by him and the price duly paid to him by the bishop, and fell asleep in the Lord once more.

Come then, brethren, let us undertake the journey of life, let us return to the heavenly city in which we are enrolled and appointed as citizens. We are not strangers, but fellow citizens of the Saints and members of the household of God, and also his heirs, but heirs of Christ. The strength of this city will open its gates to us, and trust will afford us a broad entrance. Let us therefore contemplate the noble blessedness of that city, insofar as it is possible to contemplate it: for as it truly is, no speech will suffice to comprehend it.

And so the Magi offer gifts from their treasures. Do you wish to know how great a merit they have? The star is seen by them; where Herod is, it is not seen; where Christ is, it is seen again, and shows the way. Therefore this star is the way, and the way is Christ: because according to the mystery of the Incarnation, Christ is the star. For a star shall rise from Jacob, and a man shall arise from Israel. Indeed, where Christ is, there the star also is. For he himself is the bright morning star. He therefore marks himself with his own light.

Therefore, one life is good, but still wretched; the other is better, and blessed. The first was signified by the Apostle Peter, the second by John. The first is enacted entirely here until the end of this world, and there finds its end; the fulfillment of the second is deferred until after the end of this world, but in the age to come it has no end. Therefore to the first it is said: Follow me. But of the other: So I will that he remain until I come; what is that to you? You follow me. For what is this? As far as I understand, as far as I grasp, what is this? — unless: you follow me through the imitation of enduring temporal evils; let him remain, until I come to render eternal goods.

So then, when he learned from the mouth of the priest and martyr that he too was about to be taken away in every respect, he gathered the crowds of the poor and distributed the ecclesiastical treasury with a devout generosity. How deep was the counsel of that spiritual man, and how heavenly, both to provide for the needy, and, with the multitude consuming what he had given, that there might be nothing found for the persecutor to snatch — following indeed that saying: He has scattered abroad, he has given to the poor; his righteousness endures forever.

That the fire of the Savior is to be found in the Gospel we read, when the Lord himself says: Do you not know that I came to cast fire on the earth? And what do I desire but that it be kindled? Kindled by this fire, those two disciples said: Was not our heart burning within us while he spoke on the way and opened to us the Scriptures? Inflamed, therefore, by this fire, blessed Lawrence does not feel the burning of the flames; and while he burns with desire for Christ, he does not feel the torment of the persecutor.

Renunciation, then, as we have taught, is the loosing of the bonds of this earthly and temporal life, and liberation from human affairs, by which we are made more apt and ready to enter upon the way by which one arrives at God; and it is the ready means for the acquisition and use of those things that are far and away more precious than gold and precious stone. And in sum, it is the translation of the human heart to a heavenly manner of life, so that it is permitted to say: Our citizenship is in heaven; and (what is greatest) it is the beginning by which we come to the likeness of Christ, who, though he was rich, became poor for our sake.

And from the deportation to Babylon until Christ are fourteen generations. Count from Jechoniah to Joseph, and you will find thirteen generations. The fourteenth generation, therefore, shall be reckoned to Christ himself. Now the generation of Christ was thus. Let the diligent reader inquire and say: Since Joseph is not the father of the Lord Savior, what concern of the Lord is the line of descent traced down to Joseph? To which we shall reply, first, that it is not the custom of the Scriptures to weave a genealogical order of women. Then, that Joseph and Mary were from one tribe, from which he was compelled by law to take her as a kinswoman, and because they were both enrolled at Bethlehem, as if descended from one stock.

And he added: Can you drink the chalice that I am about to drink, and be baptized with the baptism with which I am baptized? Do you see how he at once removed them from that opinion, arguing contrary things to them? For, he says, you are treating with me about honors and crowns; but I speak of struggle and sweat. This is not the time for rewards, nor will that glory of mine appear now; but the present time is one of slaughter and dangers. Consider moreover how by the very manner of his question he both exhorts and entices them. For he did not say: Can you submit to slaughter, can you shed your blood? But: In what manner can you drink the chalice? Then, enticing them, he said: That I am about to drink; so that by that very sharing of labors with him they might be made more ready.

And, opening their treasures, they offered him gifts: gold, frankincense, and myrrh. Most beautifully does Juvencus the Priest comprehend the sacramental significance of the gifts in one verse: They bring gifts of frankincense, gold, and myrrh to him who is King, and man, and God. And having received a response in a dream not to return to Herod, they went back by another way to their own region. Those who had offered gifts to the Lord consequently received a response, not through an Angel, but through the Lord himself: so that the privilege of Joseph's merits might be shown. But they returned by another way: because they were not to be mingled with the faithlessness of the Jews.

And rightly so was the just man, who sought not his own glory but that of the people, himself desiring to be freed from the bonds of bodily frailty, yet waiting to see the promised One: for he knew that blessed were the eyes that would see him. And he himself received him into his arms, and blessed God, and said: Now dismiss your servant, Lord, according to your word in peace. See the just man, enclosed as in the prison of bodily burden, wishing to be dissolved, so that he might begin to be with Christ. For to be dissolved and to be with Christ is far better.

And he offered these with a loud cry — that is, with the most intense and efficacious intention of pious devotion, as when he prayed at greater length and even with tears; for in that prolonged prayer he is to be believed to have shed tears, since even drops of blood ran from his body in place of sweat; and he was heard, because what he had sought he received in the Resurrection. He was heard — that is, he was heard beyond the number of all others — because after the warfare of his labor he was exalted above every creature by the Father, and this for his own reverence — that is, according to the fact that he himself, as the Son of God, is worthy of reverence and veneration. Or for his own reverence toward God — that is, because he himself above all things revered and honored the Father. Or for his own reverence — that is, as his own holiness merited. The shedding of his blood also can be understood as the loud cry in which he was heard, for the reverence of that same Passion. It is reverence, because he suffered without sin, by charity alone.

And as he was going out onto the road, a certain man running up, kneeling before him, asked him: Good Master, what shall I do that I may receive eternal life? I believe this seeker of eternal life had heard from the Lord that only those who wished to be like little children are worthy of entry into the Kingdom of Heaven; and therefore, desiring a more certain treatment, he asks to have explained to him not through parables but openly by what merits of works eternal life can be attained. But Jesus said to him: You know the commandments. This is the chastity of childlike innocence, which is set before us to imitate if we wish to enter the Kingdom of God. But he answering said to him: Master, all these have I observed from my youth. This man is not to be thought to have questioned the Lord either out of the intention of one who tempts (as some have supposed), nor to have lied about his life when he said he had kept the commandments of the law; but, simply, to have confessed how he had lived. For if he had been guilty of the fault of lying or pretense, Jesus would never, looking upon the secrets of his heart, have been said to love him.

And since he was the physician of souls and bodies alike, he who had come to heal all the souls of those who would believe, from among those who lay ill he chose one to heal, so that he might signify unity. If we consider what he did with a mediocre and, as it were, merely human grasp and understanding — with respect to power, it was not a great thing he accomplished; and with respect to kindness, he did but little. So many were lying there, and one was healed, when he could have raised all with a single word.

And therefore, because judgment comes from every direction, there are twelve thrones; just as, because that city is entered from every direction, there are twelve gates. Therefore not only those twelve and the Apostle Paul, but all who are to judge, belong, for the significance of universality, to the twelve thrones; just as all who are to enter belong to the twelve gates. For there are four parts of the world: East, West, North, and South. These four parts are continually named in the Scriptures. From these four winds, as the Lord says in the Gospel, he will gather his elect from the four winds; from all these four winds, therefore, the Church is called. How is she called? She is called from every side in the Trinity. She is not called except through baptism in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit. Four multiplied by three therefore yields twelve.

And Peter's confession was altogether fittingly followed by its reward, because he had seen the Son of God in a man. Blessed is this man, who is praised for having looked and seen beyond human eyes: not beholding what was from flesh and blood, but by the revelation of the heavenly Father perceiving the Son of God; and judged worthy to be the first to acknowledge what in Christ belonged to God. O foundation of the Church, blessed in the naming of a new name, and a rock worthy of that building, which would dissolve the laws of the underworld and the gates of Tartarus and all the bars of death! O blessed keeper of heaven's gate, into whose discretion are entrusted the keys of the eternal entrance, whose earthly judgment shall be a predetermined authority in heaven!

And I, he says, say to you: that is, as my Father has manifested to you my divinity, so I also make known to you your excellence, because you are Peter — that is, though I am the inviolable rock, I the cornerstone, who make both one, I the foundation besides which no other can be laid: yet you also are a rock, because you are made firm by my strength, so that those things which are proper to me by power may be shared with me by participation with you. And upon this rock I will build my Church, and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it. Upon this strength, he says, I will raise an eternal temple: and the loftiness of my Church, which is to be set in heaven, will rise on the firmness of this faith.

And he was, it says, spending the night in prayer to God. A model is given to you, O Christian, a form is set before you which you ought to imitate. For what ought you to do for your own salvation, when Christ spends the night in prayer for you? What is fitting for you to do when you wish to undertake some work of piety, when Christ, about to send forth the Apostles, first prayed, and prayed alone? Nor, if I am not mistaken, is he found anywhere else to have prayed with the Apostles; everywhere he prays alone. For the counsel of God does not encompass human desires, nor can anyone be a sharer in the inner counsels of Christ.

And it came to pass, as he reclined at table in the house, behold, many tax collectors and sinners coming reclined at table with Jesus. They saw the tax collector, converted from sins to better things, to have found a place of repentance; and for that reason they too did not despair of salvation. Nor indeed do they come to Jesus while persisting in their former vices, as the Pharisees and scribes murmur, but doing penance, as the subsequent words of the Lord signify, saying: I desire mercy, and not sacrifice; for I came not to call the righteous, but sinners. But the Lord went to the banquets of sinners in order to have an occasion for teaching, and to offer his hosts spiritual food.

And therefore those who were fasting in spirit murmured, saying: Why does he eat and drink with tax collectors and sinners? This is the voice of the serpent. For indeed the serpent first uttered this voice, saying to Eve: Why has God said: Do not eat of every tree? Therefore they pour forth the poisons of their father, who say: Why does he eat and drink with tax collectors and sinners? Hence the Lord, by eating with sinners, does not forbid us even to enter into a meal with the Gentiles, saying: Those who are well do not need a physician, but those who are sick.

And the Angel entered to her. Learn the virgin in her ways, learn the virgin in her modesty, learn in the oracle, learn in the mystery. It is the way of virgins to tremble, and to be afraid at every entrance of a man, to be in awe of every address of a man. Let women learn to imitate the purpose of chastity. Alone in her innermost chambers, whom no man had seen, the Angel alone found her; alone without a companion, alone without a witness, lest she be corrupted by some base address, she is greeted by the Angel.

And it is an altogether just recompense that those who here for Christ's sake despised the glory of human loftiness should there sit glorified as judges with Christ, uniquely beside him, who could by no means be torn from following in his footsteps. But let no one suppose that only the twelve Apostles — since Matthias was elected in place of the traitor Judas — will then be judges; just as neither are only the twelve tribes of Israel to be judged: otherwise the tribe of Levi, which is the thirteenth, will depart unjudged.

And rightly so; for no one has approached God so close as you; no one has been enriched with the gifts of God as you; no one has been a sharer in the grace of God as you. You surpass all things that may be eminent among men; you exceed all gifts that have flowed out from the generosity of God to anyone whatsoever. For you are enriched above all by the possession of the indwelling God. No one could so embrace God in himself; no one could so enjoy the presence of God; no one has been deemed worthy to be so illumined through God: and therefore you have received not only God, the Creator and Lord of all things, into yourself, but you have him ineffably incarnate from you, borne in your womb, and afterward born, and redeeming all men from the condemnation of the Father, and bestowing upon them the salvation that shall have no end. And therefore I have cried out to you, and again I shall cry out with great fervor: Hail, full of grace; the Lord is with you: blessed are you among women.

And he did not say: Who does not obey, but, Who hates. For just as we cannot bear with equanimity even to hear the voice or see the face of those whom we hate, so also the soul ought vehemently to turn away from whatever commands us contrary to the will of God. For since he was about to speak to them of death — his own death, that is — and foresaw their sorrow and despondency, he spoke by excess, saying: What do I say, if you will not bear my death nobly? Unless you yourselves also die, no benefit will follow you.

And it is to be noted that our Redeemer, when he was now of perfect age, the Apostles proclaim him to the same Gentiles, while the star announces him as a little child, not yet speaking through the office of a human body, to the nations: because without doubt the order of reason required that the speaking Lord should become known to us through speaking preachers, and the not-yet-speaking one should be proclaimed by mute elements. But in all the signs that were shown either at the Lord's birth or at his death, we must consider how great was the hardness of heart in certain Jews, who acknowledged him neither through the gift of prophecy nor through miracles.

And will Paul, who is the thirteenth Apostle, be deprived of the lot of judging? when he himself says: Do you not know that we shall judge angels, how much more the things of this world? For it is to be known that all who, after the example of the Apostles, have left all things and followed Christ, will come as judges with him, just as also every mortal race is to be judged. For since the whole is often designated in the Scriptures by the number twelve, through the twelve thrones the totality of all who are to judge from among the Apostles is shown, and through the twelve tribes of Israel the totality of those who are to be judged.
We praise you, O God: * we acclaim you as the Lord.
All the earth * worships you, the eternal Father.

To you the Cherubim and Seraphim * with unceasing voice proclaim:
(A bow is made) Holy, Holy, Holy * Lord God of Sabaoth.

The glorious choir * of the Apostles,
The admirable company * of the Prophets,
The white-robed army * of Martyrs praises you.
Throughout the world * the holy Church confesses you,
Father * of immeasurable majesty;
Your true * and only Son, worthy of worship;
And the Holy * Paraclete Spirit.

You are the everlasting * Son of the Father.
(A bow is made) You, about to take upon yourself humanity for its liberation, * did not shrink from the Virgin's womb.
You, about to take upon yourself humanity for its liberation, * did not shrink from the Virgin's womb.
You, having overcome the sting of death, * opened the Kingdom of Heaven to those who believe.
You sit at the right hand of God, * in the glory of the Father.
You are believed * to be the Judge who is to come.

And as often as something of wondrous power is done, Michael is said to be sent; so that from the very deed and name it may be understood that no one can do what God alone has the power to do. Hence also that ancient enemy, who coveted through pride to be like God, saying: I will ascend into heaven, above the stars of heaven I will exalt my throne, I will be like the Most High — when at the end of the world he will be left to his own power to be destroyed with the final punishment, he is said to be about to do battle with Michael the Archangel, as John says: There was war with Michael the Archangel. To Mary also Gabriel is sent, who is named the Strength of God; for he came to announce him who in his humility was pleased to appear in order to overcome the powers of the air. Raphael also is interpreted, as we have said, as the Medicine of God; because, namely, when he touched the eyes of Tobit, as it were in the office of healing, he wiped away the darkness of his blindness.

And indeed the distinguished monuments of venerable antiquity of both the Eastern and Western Church most powerfully testify that this doctrine concerning the Immaculate Conception of the most Blessed Virgin has always existed in the Church itself as if received from our ancestors and marked with the character of revealed doctrine, daily more and more splendidly expounded, declared, confirmed, and propagated in wondrous fashion among all the peoples and nations of the Catholic world, through the most grave sense, the magisterium, the study, the knowledge, and the wisdom of the Church. Indeed the Fathers and writers of the Church, taught by heavenly utterances, held nothing more ancient than, in the books they labored over to expound the Scriptures, to vindicate dogmas, and to instruct the faithful, to proclaim and extol by striving emulously in many and wondrous ways the supreme holiness, dignity, and integrity from every stain of sin of the Virgin, and her glorious victory over the most abominable enemy of the human race.

And, having received a response in a dream not to return to Herod, they went back by another way to their own region. Consider now, I pray you, their faith — how they are not offended but are calm and obedient, and are not troubled, nor do they say such things to one another: Surely, if this child is great, and if he has some power, what need is there of flight and secret departure? And why does the Angel send us away from the city as fugitives — we who came publicly and with confidence to so great a people, and stood before a raging king? But they neither said nor thought anything of the kind. For this belongs above all to faith: that no reason for the commands be sought, but that only obedience be given to what is commanded.

And Samuel likewise…

And it was altogether fitting that the divine announcement of joy should take its beginning from words and speech that draw forth joy. For this reason too the Angel announces joy above all else, because he is not ignorant of the outcome of his glad embassy, and knows well that the conversation being held was manifestly to result in the joy of all the world. And indeed what joy, or what delight, can be found that the address made to that blessed Virgin, the mother of joy, does not far exceed? Rejoice, O mother of supracelestial joy. Rejoice, O nurse of the most sublime joy. Rejoice, O foremost seat of saving joy. Rejoice, O author of immortal joy. Rejoice, O mystical dwelling-place of ineffable joy. Rejoice, O most blessed fount of unfailing joy. Rejoice, O God-bearing treasure of eternal joy. Rejoice, O most verdant tree of life-giving joy. Rejoice, O virgin Mother of God. Rejoice, O Virgin most whole after childbirth. Rejoice, O spectacle supremely wonderful above all marvels.

And as Moses, he says, lifted up the serpent in the desert, so must the Son of Man be lifted up. What is the serpent lifted up? The death of the Lord on the Cross. For since death came from the serpent, death was figured by the image of a serpent. The bite of serpents is deadly; the death of the Lord is life-giving. The serpent is gazed upon, so that the serpent may have no power. What is this? Death is gazed upon, so that death may have no power. But whose death? The death of Life. Is not Christ Life? And yet Christ died.

And there are some who confess him to be both God and King, but deny that he took on mortal flesh. These indeed offer him gold and frankincense, but refuse to offer the myrrh of the mortality he assumed. Let us therefore, at the birth of the Lord, offer gold, that we may confess him to reign everywhere; let us offer frankincense, that we may believe that he who appeared in time existed as God before all time; let us offer myrrh, that we who believe him impassible in his divinity may also believe him to have been mortal in our flesh.

And you, child, shall be called the prophet of the Most High. Fittingly, while prophesying of the Lord, he turned his words to the prophet, so that he might designate this too as a benefit of the Lord: lest, while publicly enumerating his own gifts, he might seem, as if ungrateful, to have passed over in silence what he acknowledged in his son. But perhaps some may think it an irrational excess of mind that he addresses an infant of eight days. But if we hold fast to the truth, we shall surely understand that he who, before he was born, heard the greeting of Mary, could hear the voice of his father when born.

And how has this happened to me, that the Mother of my Lord should come to me? That is: How has so great a good come to me, that the Mother of my Lord should come to me? I perceive the miracle, I acknowledge the mystery: the Mother of the Lord, pregnant with the Word, is full of God. Now Mary stayed with her for three months, and returned to her own house. It is well said that the holy Mary both performed the office of kindness and observed the mystical number.

And his wife, he says, was of the daughters of Aaron. Therefore the noble birth of Saint John extends not only from his parents but also from his ancestors — illustrious not by secular power but venerable by succession in religion. For such ancestors ought the forerunner of Christ to have had; so that he might seem to preach the faith of the Lord's coming not as something suddenly conceived, but received from ancestors and instilled by the very law of nature. They were, he says, both just before God, walking in all the commandments and ordinances of the Lord without reproach. What do those reply who, preferring consolation for their sins, think a man cannot exist without frequent sins; and use the verse, because it is written in Job: No one is clean from defilement, not even if his life upon earth be but one day?

And he came to Nazareth, and was subject to them. For what else would the master of virtue do but fulfill the duty of piety? And do we marvel if he defers to the Father, who is subject to his mother? This subjection is not of weakness but of piety — though the serpent of treachery sent forth from its savage lair may raise its head and spew out its serpentine poisons from its breast. When the heretic says the Son was sent, let him call the Father greater, so as to declare the Son imperfect because he can have one greater than himself: so as to assert that he who is sent stands in need of external help. Did he then need human aid in order to serve his mother's authority?
