And see what he does, when he has discoursed about the kingdom and about hell. For in what he said — He who finds his soul will lose it; and whoever loses it for my sake will find it — and in what he says — He will render to each according to his works — he indicated both the kingdom and hell. When, therefore, he has discoursed about both, he grants that the kingdom is to be perceived by the eyes, but hell not at all; because that would have been necessary for the more unlearned and dull-witted, but since they were of good judgment and discernment, it was sufficient for them to be confirmed by the better things. This too was far more fitting for him. Yet he did not omit it altogether, but at times sets before the eyes, as it were, the dreadfulness of hell, as when he described the image of Lazarus, and when he recalled the man who demanded back the hundred denarii.

For it is not enough for the evangelical Doctor to shine before the people by word, and to provide the voice of one crying in the desert, and to give his tongue's labor to helping many in piety — lest otherwise, if he should omit the ministry of the word, he be called by the prophet a dumb dog not able to bark. But he must also burn, so that, equipped with work and charity, he may adorn his evangelical office. And let him follow Paul as his leader. For Paul, not content to charge the bishop of Ephesus: Command this and teach it; be diligent as a good soldier of Christ Jesus — continued steadfastly to evangelize before friends and enemies alike, and said before the bishops assembled at Ephesus with a good conscience: You know that I kept back nothing that was profitable, so as not to announce it to you and teach you publicly and from house to house, testifying to Jews and Gentiles of penance toward God and faith in our Lord Jesus Christ.

Eugene, the third of that name, formerly called Bernard, was a native of Pisa. Having completed his youth, he enrolled in the clerical life, and later initiated into the priesthood, he merited by his outstanding qualities of soul to be numbered among the canons of the metropolitan church of Pisa. Attracted by the example of Saint Bernard, who had then come to Pisa, he submitted himself to his guidance, and put on the monastic habit at Clairvaux. He made such progress under the discipline of so great a man that he was first placed by him as superior of the monastery of Farfa, and then elected by Pope Innocent the Second as abbot of the monastery of Saints Vincent and Anastasius at the Aquae Salviae. Having shone in that office with a wondrous splendor of holiness and prudence, he was created Supreme Pontiff by the cardinals with unanimous suffrage after the death of Lucius the Second. But scarcely had his pontificate begun when, the tumults of rebels striving to overturn the principate of the Roman Church, he was forced to depart from the City once and then again, and thereafter, the storm having been calmed, he returned to it with the highest honor and the rejoicing of the good.

Euphemia, Lucia, and Geminianus were crowned with martyrdom during the persecution of Diocletian, not in the same place but on the same day. Euphemia the Virgin, at Chalcedon, under the proconsul Priscus, bravely endured various kinds of torments — rods, the rack, wheels, fire — and at length, being thrown to the beasts, when one of them inflicted a bite upon her holy body while the rest licked her feet, she gave up her immaculate spirit to God. Lucia, a Roman widow, accused by her son Eutropius because she had worshiped Christ for many years, was thrown into a pot of boiling pitch and lead; escaping unharmed, and as she was being led through the City loaded with iron and lead, she converted Geminianus, a nobleman, to Christ by her constancy in faith and martyrdom. Him also, together with many others led to the faith, variously tormented, she had as a companion in glorious martyrdom, his head having been cut off. Their bodies were honorably buried by Maxima, a Christian woman.

Eusebius, a Greek by nationality, his father a physician, was appointed bishop of the Roman Church after Saint Marcellus. He found heretics in the City, whom, having repented, he reconciled to the Church by the imposition of hands alone. To him also came from Sardinia a noble woman, Restituta, who entrusted to him her son for instruction, whom he excellently imbued with the Christian faith, baptized, and marked with his own name, calling him Eusebius. A fitting offspring of so great a Pontiff, through whom the Catholic faith, nearly extinguished in the East under the later bishop of Vercelli, should revive with a more joyful growth.

Eusebius, a Sardinian by nationality, lector of the Roman Church, and afterward Bishop of Vercelli, fought so manfully against Arianism that his unconquered faith raised up Liberius, the Supreme Pontiff, as a consolation of life. For his confession of the same Catholic faith he was sent by the Emperor Constantius to Scythopolis, where he endured hunger, thirst, stripes, and various torments. Thence banished to Cappadocia, he bore the hardships of exile until the very death of Constantius, after which he was permitted to return to his church. Then Italy exchanged its garments of mourning; where, after he had published his revised commentaries on all the Psalms by Origen, and those of Eusebius of Caesarea, which he had translated from Greek into Latin, he departed to the Lord at Vercelli under Valentinian and Valens, to the unfading crown of glory merited by such great labors.

Eusebius, a Sardinian by nationality, lector of the Roman Church, and afterward Bishop of Vercelli, was deservedly believed to have been chosen by divine judgment to govern this church: for though those appointed as electors had never known him before, they at once, on seeing him, both approved him; and it mattered as much to approve him as to see him. He was the first in the regions of the West to establish in that same church those who were both monks and clerics, so that in those men there might be both a contempt of earthly things and the diligence of levites. When Arian impieties were being spread far and wide throughout the West in that age, he fought against them so manfully that his unconquered faith raised up Liberius, the Supreme Pontiff, as a consolation of life. Wherefore this one, knowing that the Spirit of God was burning in him, when Liberius signified to him that he should undertake the patronage of the faith before the Emperor together with his legates, he at once set out with them to Constantius; in whose presence, pressing earnestly, he obtained all that the embassy sought: namely, that a council of bishops should be held.

Eustachius, also called Placidus, distinguished among the Romans by birth, wealth, and military glory, merited the title of Master of the Soldiers under the Emperor Trajan. But when at one time he was engaged in hunting and was pursuing a fleeing stag of wondrous size, he suddenly saw between the antlers of the standing beast the lofty and shining image of Christ the Lord hanging on a Cross. Invited by his voice to the prey of immortal life, he gave his name to Christian service, together with his wife Theopista and his two young sons Agapitus and Theopistus.

Eutychianus, a Tuscan by nationality, a native of Luni, his father named Marinus, after the priesthood of the blessed Felix received the episcopate of the Roman Church. He decreed that grain, beans, and grapes should be blessed upon the altar; and likewise that no martyr should by any means be buried by the faithful without a dalmatic or a purple tunic. Having with his own hand buried three hundred and sixty-two martyrs in various places, he was himself joined to them and crowned with martyrdom under the Emperor Numerian on the sixth day before the Ides of December, and was buried in the cemetery of Callistus on the Appian Way. In five ordinations in the month of December he created fourteen priests, five deacons, and nine bishops in various places. He lived in the pontificate eight years, five months, and some days.

He applied himself tirelessly, even to advanced old age, to the evangelization of the poor, especially country people, and bound himself and the students of the congregation which he established under the name of the Secular Priests of the Mission — confirmed by the Holy See with a perpetual vow — specifically to that apostolic work. How greatly he labored for the increase of clerical discipline is attested by the major seminaries he erected, the frequent conferences on divine things among priests, and the spiritual exercises to be made before sacred ordination; to which, just as to the pious retreats of the laity, he willingly wished the houses of his congregation to be open. Moreover, for the spread of faith and piety, he sent evangelical workers not only into the provinces of France, but also into Italy, Poland, Scotland, Ireland, and to the Barbarians and the Indians. He himself, after the death of King Louis the Thirteenth, at whose deathbed he stood as an exhorter, was summoned by Queen Anne of Austria, mother of Louis the Fourteenth, into her more intimate council, and worked most zealously that only the more worthy should be placed over churches and monasteries; that civil discords, private duels, spreading errors, which he at once perceived and abhorred, should be cut away; and that due obedience to apostolic judgments should be rendered by all.

Evaristus, a Greek, of a Jewish father, held the pontificate in the reign of the Emperor Trajan. He distributed the titular churches of the city of Rome among the priests, and ordained that seven deacons should guard the bishop while he was performing the office of preaching the Gospel. He likewise decreed, from apostolic tradition, that marriage should be celebrated publicly and that the blessing of a priest be employed. He presided over the Church for nine years and three months, holding four ordinations in the month of December and creating seventeen priests, two deacons, and fifteen bishops in various places. Crowned with martyrdom, he was buried near the tomb of the Prince of the Apostles in the Vatican on the seventh day before the Kalends of November.

Evaristus, Greek by nationality, born of a Jewish father, most zealous for Christian piety, was raised to the Chair of Peter in the reign of the Emperor Trajan, and sat in it nine years and three months. He held four ordinations in the month of December and created seventeen priests, two deacons, and fifteen bishops in various places.

It came to pass, not without divine providence, that Otto arrived at the court of the Emperor, serving him in the ministry of a chaplain. It then happened that he became the imperial chancellor. Meanwhile, Bishop Rupert of the church of Bamberg having died, prayers were offered to the Emperor for the appointment of a pastor. But he wished to allow himself a period of six months for deliberation. In the meantime the clergy and people of the church of Bamberg, even instituting processions, were beseeching the Lord most ardently for a worthy bishop. After six months had elapsed, Otto was appointed by the Emperor as Bishop of Bamberg against his will. He, forced in this way to ascend the chair of the pontificate, consented with difficulty on account of that controversy which existed between the kingdom and the priesthood over the cause of investiture and the election of churches, which the imperial authority was endeavoring beyond all measure to nullify and claim for itself. But again he feared that it was not without the guidance of divinity that the episcopate was now offered to him a third time, and that if he rejected it, that sentence might justly apply to him: He refused the blessing and it shall be removed far from him. Standing therefore in these straits, Otto made a vow to the Lord, the one thing he judged salutary: that he would never remain in the episcopate unless, with the consent of his own church, he should merit to be consecrated and to receive investiture at the hand of the Supreme Pontiff himself.
Ex actis Ecclesiæ Passaviensis

It is established that from the later centuries of Christian antiquity there existed in Castra Batava a church dedicated to Saint Stephen the Protomartyr. Here in the middle of the fifth century Saint Bishop Valentine, as is handed down, exercised the office of pastor for a long time. Here Saint Severinus the abbot flourished in prayer and works of charity. The diocese of Passau, canonically erected by Saint Boniface, was raised to an episcopal see and at the same time to the mother church of this diocese. Both the church of Esztergom in Hungary and the cathedral church of Vienna in Austria received Saint Stephen the Protomartyr as patron from this holy mother church. The dukes of Bavaria of the house of the Agilolfings enriched her with great estates, and also donated the relics of Saint Valentine the bishop, brought from the town of Meissen. Pilgrim, the celebrated Bishop of Passau, restored the cathedral church in the Romanesque style, and transferred the bones of Saint Maximilian, bishop and martyr, from the collegiate church of Wörth. Twice in the seventeenth century, when a dreadful fire devastated the city, the cathedral church itself was reduced almost to its foundations. But with tireless spirit the bishops of that time restored to the episcopal church the form that all admire to this day. Finally, after the immense war again raging in the twentieth century, Simon Conrad of the Order of Saint Benedict, Bishop of Passau, had the high altar rebuilt in a more excellent manner.

From the Acts of Pope Pius XII

Since the Universal Church has manifested throughout the course of the centuries its faith in the bodily Assumption of the Blessed Virgin Mary, and the Bishops of the whole world have petitioned with nearly unanimous consent that this truth, which is grounded in Sacred Scripture, deeply implanted in the souls of Christ's faithful, and plainly consonant with all other revealed truths, should be defined as a dogma of divine and Catholic faith, Pope Pius XII, the Supreme Pontiff, acceding to the wishes of the whole Church, resolved to solemnly proclaim this privilege of the Blessed Virgin Mary. And so, on the first day of November of the great Jubilee year of nineteen hundred and fifty, at Rome, in the square open before the Basilica of Saint Peter, with a great assembly of the Cardinals and Bishops of the Holy Roman Church standing round, come even from distant regions, before a vast multitude of Christ's faithful, the whole Catholic world applauding, he proclaimed the bodily Assumption of the Blessed Virgin Mary into heaven by infallible oracle in these words: After we have again and again raised suppliant prayers to God and invoked the light of the Spirit of Truth, to the glory of Almighty God who has lavished his special benevolence upon the Virgin Mary, for the honor of his Son, the immortal King of the ages and the Victor over sin and death, for the increase of the glory of that same august Mother and for the joy and exultation of the whole Church, by the authority of our Lord Jesus Christ, of the Blessed Apostles Peter and Paul, and of our own, we pronounce, declare, and define it to be a divinely revealed dogma: that the Immaculate Mother of God, the ever-Virgin Mary, having completed the course of her earthly life, was assumed body and soul to heavenly glory.

From the Acts of Pope Pius IX

The victory of the Virgin Mother of God over the most abominable enemy of the human race in her Conception — which the divine oracles, venerable tradition, the perpetual sense of the Church, the singular agreement of bishops and faithful, and the illustrious acts and constitutions of the Supreme Pontiffs had already wondrously illuminated — Pope Pius IX, the Supreme Pontiff, acceding to the wishes of the whole Church, resolved to proclaim solemnly by his supreme and infallible oracle. And so, on the sixth day before the Ides of December of the year eighteen hundred and fifty-four, in the Vatican Basilica, with a great assembly of the fathers, cardinals, and bishops of the Holy Roman Church standing round, come even from distant regions, and the whole world applauding, he solemnly pronounced and defined: that the doctrine which holds that the most Blessed Virgin Mary was, in the first instant of her Conception, by a singular privilege of God, preserved immune from all stain of original fault, is revealed by God, and is therefore to be believed firmly and constantly by all the faithful.
Ex Actis Pii Papæ XII

The Church, the most provident Mother of all, bestows the greatest care on protecting and relieving workers, establishing and favoring their associations, which Pope Pius XII, the Supreme Pontiff, long ago wished to have been entrusted to the most powerful patronage of Saint Joseph. For Saint Joseph, since he was the reputed father of Christ, who was pleased to be called a craftsman and the son of a craftsman, through the closeness with which he was joined to Jesus, drew abundantly from that spirit by which labor is ennobled and elevated. In like manner, associations of workers of this kind must strive that Christ may always be present in their midst, in their members and in their families, and in every gathering of workers; since the chief end of these associations is to preserve and nourish Christian life in their members, to spread the Kingdom of God more widely, and especially among the fellow workers of the same workplace.

Setting sail from England with two companions, he came to Dorestad, a town of Frisia. But when a most grave war broke out between Radbod, King of the Frisians, and Charles Martel, he preached the Gospel without fruit. He therefore returned to England and went back to his monastery, over which he was placed as superior against his will. After the lapse of two years, with the consent of the Bishop of Winchester, he resigned the charge, and went to Rome, that he might be delegated by apostolic authority for the conversion of the Gentiles. When he had arrived in the City, he was graciously received by Gregory the Second, and was named Boniface by the Pontiff in place of Winfried. Directed into Germany, he preached Christ to the peoples of Thuringia and Saxony. In the meantime, Radbod, King of Frisia and most bitter enemy of the Christian name, having died, Boniface returned to the Frisians, where as a companion of Saint Willibrord he preached the Gospel for three years with such fruit that, with the idols destroyed, churches were raised up without number to the true God.

From the Dogmatic Bull of Pope Pius IX

All know with what zeal the doctrine of the Immaculate Conception of the Virgin Mother of God has been handed down, maintained, and defended by the most distinguished religious families, the more celebrated theological academies, and the most eminent doctors skilled in divine things. All likewise know how zealously the bishops were at pains, even in ecclesiastical assemblies, openly and publicly to profess that the most holy Virgin Mother of God, Mary, by virtue of the foreseen merits of Christ our Lord the Redeemer, was never infected with original sin, and was thus redeemed in a more sublime manner. To these testimonies there is added that most weighty and altogether supreme consideration, that the Tridentine Synod itself, when issuing its dogmatic decree on original sin, by which, in accordance with the testimonies of the sacred Scriptures, the holy Fathers, and the most approved councils, it established and defined that all men are born infected with original guilt, solemnly declared that it was not its intention to include in that decree, in its scope and breadth of definition, the blessed and immaculate Virgin Mary, Mother of God. For by this declaration the Fathers of Trent sufficiently indicated, in the circumstances of the time, that the most blessed Virgin was free from original stain, and thus clearly signified that nothing can rightly be adduced from divine letters, from tradition, or from the authority of the Fathers, to contradict in any way the prerogative of that great Virgin.

From the Dogmatic Bull of Pope Pius IX

From ancient times, bishops of holy things, ecclesiastical men, religious orders, and even emperors and kings urgently entreated this Apostolic See that the Immaculate Conception of the most holy Mother of God might be defined as a dogma of the Catholic faith. These petitions were repeated in our own age as well, and were presented most especially to our predecessor of happy memory, Gregory XVI, and to us ourselves, both by bishops and by the secular clergy, by religious families, by sovereign princes, and by the faithful peoples. And so, knowing and considering all these things with singular joy of soul, we had scarcely been raised, though unworthy, by the hidden counsel of divine providence to this sublime Chair of Peter, and had undertaken the governance of the whole Church, when we made nothing more our care than, by virtue of our supreme veneration, piety, and affection for the most holy Virgin Mary, Mother of God — cherished from our earliest years — to accomplish all that could still remain in the desires of the Church, so that the honor of the most blessed Virgin might be increased and her prerogatives might shine forth in a fuller light.

From the Dogmatic Bull of Pope Pius IX

The very words by which the divine Scriptures speak of uncreated Wisdom and represent her eternal origins, the Church has been accustomed to apply both in the ecclesiastical offices and in the sacred liturgy, and to transfer them to the beginnings of that Virgin who had been foreordained by one and the same decree together with the incarnation of divine Wisdom. Now, although all these things, received as they are almost universally among the faithful everywhere, demonstrate with what zeal even the Roman Church herself, mother and teacher of all churches, has pursued this doctrine of the Immaculate Conception of the Virgin, the illustrious deeds of this Church are plainly worthy of being recounted by name, since the dignity and authority of this same Church are so great as are altogether owed to her who is the center of Catholic truth and unity, in whom alone religion has been kept inviolate, and from whom all other churches must draw the root of faith.

From the Dogmatic Bull of Pope Pius IX

As the true High Priest he offered prayers: for in the Gospel he is frequently read to have prayed, and most especially in Luke, who described in him the person of a priest. Indeed, whatever he himself did in the flesh, his prayers and supplications were on behalf of men. Throughout his whole life he prayed to the Father for the resurrection of his flesh and for our salvation; and with the Passion now at hand he offered up supplications — that is, most humble and urgent prayers with the utmost devotion of heart and feeling — when, being in agony, he prayed at greater length and his sweat became as drops of blood running down to the ground. And these prayers and supplications he offered — that is, he brought them before the Father, who came to meet them in hearing. He offered them to him who could save him from death, that is, raise him up again; to him whom he knew to be sufficient to save him, that is, to make him immortal and impassible by snatching him from death; so that neither might his soul remain in hell, nor his flesh see corruption in the tomb.

Francis, the true and faithful servant and minister of Christ, two years before he returned his spirit to heaven, having begun in a lofty and secluded place called Mount La Verna a forty-day fast in honor of the Archangel Michael, was flooded more abundantly than usual with the sweetness of heavenly contemplation and enkindled by a more ardent flame of heavenly desires, and began to sense in richer measure the gifts of celestial infusions. While, therefore, he was being borne upward to God by seraphic ardors of desire, and his affection was being transformed by compassionate tenderness into him who was pleased to be crucified out of exceeding charity, one morning around the feast of the Exaltation of the Holy Cross, as he prayed on the side of the mountain, he saw descending from the height of the heavens what appeared to be one Seraph having six wings, as brilliant as they were fiery. When, arriving with swift flight at a place in the air close to the man of God, it appeared, not only winged but crucified as well, with hands and feet extended and fastened to a cross, and its wings so disposed in a wondrous manner on either side that two were raised above its head, two were extended for flight, and with the remaining two it enclosed and veiled the whole body. Beholding this, Francis was seized with a great astonishment, and into his mind there entered a joy mingled with sorrow: for in the gracious aspect of one appearing to him so wondrously and yet so familiarly, he conceived an excessive gladness; but the terrible sight of the cross to which it was fastened pierced his very soul with the sword of compassionate grief.

Yet by divine providence he was reserved for a higher state of the Church, and was placed, against his will, as bishop over the church of Augsburg. Wherefore, that he might offer his flock a living example of piety, he chastised his flesh with a woolen garment; he abstained entirely from the eating of meat (though otherwise most sparing in his intake of food); he slept little, and not upon feathers but on a harder bed, sometimes keeping vigil in prayer for nearly the whole night.

From among those members of the Society of Jesus who in the middle of the seventeenth century greatly advanced the beginnings of the Church in North America, God chose eight most pure victims, so that the seeds of the faith, watered by their blood, might thereafter spring up into more abundant harvests. All these Martyrs, born in France and, except for two laymen, ordained to the priesthood, were sent by their Superiors to the Canadian Mission, then called New France; and after innumerable apostolic journeys from the city of Quebec through those various vast regions, and most arduous labors, they were most cruelly put to death for one and the same cause of religion, though not at the same time or in the same place. Those rightly regarded as their leaders and masters are John de Brébeuf, of noble lineage from Condé in the diocese formerly of Bayeux now of Coutances, and Isaac Jogues of Orléans, vigorous men aflame with apostolic zeal, most given to mortification, most intimately united with God in prayer, at times also illumined by heavenly visions. Not unlike them were the four fellow priests: Anthony Daniel of Dieppe; Gabriel Lalemant and Charles Garnier, both of Paris; and Natalis Chabanel of Mende; all of whom faithfully performed their sacred duties in various villages, especially among the Hurons.

Since the Holy Year has not been lacking in opportunity for illustrating the Kingdom of Christ, we seem to be doing something especially consonant with our Apostolic office if, yielding to the petitions of very many Cardinals, Bishops, and faithful, brought to us either severally or in common, we close this same Year by introducing into the liturgy of the Church a special feast of Our Lord Jesus Christ the King. It has long been customary to call Christ a King in the transferred sense of the word, on account of the supreme degree of excellence by which he towers above and excels all created things. And so it comes about that he is said to reign «in the minds of men» — not so much on account of the keenness of his mind and the vastness of his knowledge, as because he himself is the Truth, and it is necessary that mortals draw from him and obediently receive the truth; to reign also «in the wills of men», because not only does the full integrity and obedience of the human will correspond perfectly to the sanctity of his divine will, but he also subjects our free will to himself by his impulse and inspiration, so that we may be enkindled to all that is most noble. Finally, Christ is acknowledged as «King of hearts» on account of his «charity which surpasses knowledge» and his gentleness and kindness which draw souls to him: for it has never befallen anyone, nor will it befall anyone in the future, to be loved so greatly by the whole of mankind as Christ Jesus has been and will be loved. But, to enter more closely into the matter, no one fails to see that the name and power of king ought in the proper sense of the word to be ascribed to Christ as man; for it cannot be said that he received «power, honor, and kingdom» from the Father except insofar as he is man; since the Word of God, who has the same substance as the Father, cannot but have all things in common with the Father, and therefore supreme and most absolute dominion over all created things.

Scholastica, the sister of the venerable father Benedict, had been consecrated to the almighty Lord from her infancy, and was accustomed to come to him once a year; to her the man of God would come down not far from the gate, at a property of the monastery. On a certain day she came, as was her custom, and her venerable brother came down to her with his disciples; and they spent the whole day in the praises of God and sacred conversation; and when the darkness of night was already gathering, they took food together. And while they were still sitting at table, and the hour prolonged itself amid holy discourse, that consecrated woman, his sister, begged him, saying: I pray you, do not leave me tonight, that until morning we may speak of the joys of the heavenly life. But he replied: What are you saying, sister? On no account can I remain outside my cell. The sky at that time was so serene that not a single cloud appeared in the air. But that consecrated woman, when she heard the refusing words of her brother, placed her head on her hands and bowed down to pray to the almighty Lord. And when she raised her head from the table, so great a flash of lightning and crack of thunder broke forth, and so great a flood of rain poured down, that neither the venerable Benedict nor the brethren who were with him could move a foot outside the threshold of the place where they were sitting.

The simplicity of the just man is mocked. The wisdom of this world is: to cover the heart with contrivances, to veil one's thought with words; to show what is false as true, and what is true as false. This prudence is learned in practice by the young; this is purchased by children at a price; those who know it puff themselves up in contempt of others; those who know it not, submissive and timid, marvel at it in others; because this same iniquity of duplicity is loved by them under a veiled name, while perversity of mind is called urbanity. This worldly wisdom prescribes to those who comply with it: to seek the heights of honors, to rejoice in the vanity of temporal glory once obtained, to repay evils inflicted by others many times over; to yield to no one when strength is available; and when the capacity for virtue is lacking, to simulate in peaceful goodness whatever they are unable to accomplish through malice.

But what worthy thing can we say of her, whose very name is not without its praise? Devotion beyond her age, virtue beyond her nature: so that it seems to me she bore not a human name, but an oracle of the Martyr, which declared what she was to be. Now our discourse is to virgins, for whom the higher their glory, the greater also is our concern. That is the flower of the ecclesiastical growth, the grace and ornament of spiritual grace, a joyful nature, an intact and uncorrupted work of praise and honor, the image of God corresponding to the holiness of the Lord, the more illustrious portion of the flock of Christ. The glorious fruitfulness of Mother Church rejoices through them and in them it flowers abundantly: and the more copious virginity adds to its number, the more the joy of the mother increases. To these we speak, these we exhort, with affection rather than authority: not because we claim anything to censure by license — for we are most conscious of being last and least and of our own lowliness — but because, being more cautious in our solicitude, we fear the more for the harassment of the devil.
From the Book of Saint Ambrose the Bishop on Virgins
Lib. 3 post initium.

Since the memory of blessed John the Baptist is not to be passed over briefly, it concerns us to note who he was, by whom, for what reason, in what manner, and at what time he was killed. By adulterers the just man is slain, and the penalty of capital crime is turned by the guilty against the judge. Next, the reward of a dancing girl is the death of the Prophet. Finally — a thing which even all barbarians have been accustomed to abhor — the decree for completing this cruelty is issued amid feasts and banquets; and from the banquet to the prison, from the prison to the banquet, the service of this murderous outrage is made to circulate. How many crimes are there in one deed!

Such was Mary, that her life alone is a discipline for all. If the author does not displease, let us approve the work; that whoever desires for herself her reward may imitate her example. At Tibilis, when Bishop Projectus was bringing the relics of the most glorious Martyr Stephen, a great crowd was coming and going to the shrine. There a blind woman, praying to be led to the bishop who was carrying the sacred pledge, gave him the flowers she was carrying; she received them back, applied them to her eyes, and immediately saw. While those who were present stood in amazement, she went before them rejoicing, making her way and no longer needing a guide on the road. The memorial of the aforementioned Martyr, which is situated in the village of Sinicum near the colony of Hippo, was being carried by Lucillus, the bishop of that place, with the people going before and following; a fistula, from the affliction of which he had long suffered, and for which he was awaiting the hand of his very familiar physician to cut it, was suddenly healed by the bearing of that holy burden.
From the Book of Saint Augustine the Bishop on the Care to be Taken for the Dead
Cap 2 et 3

The care of burial, the preparation of the tomb, the solemnity of the funeral rites are more a consolation for the living than an aid for the dead. Yet for all that, the bodies of the departed are not to be despised and cast aside, especially those of the just and faithful, whose bodies the spirit has used as organs and vessels for every good work. For if a father's garment and ring, and anything of that sort, is all the dearer to those who follow the greater the love they bore toward their parents, in no way ought the bodies themselves to be spurned, which we wear in a far more familiar and intimate union than any clothing whatsoever. For these belong not to adornment or assistance applied from without, but to the very nature of man. Hence also the funerals of the ancient just were attended with dutiful piety, their obsequies were celebrated, and provision was made for burial; and they themselves, while they lived, gave charge to their children concerning the burial or even the translation of their bodies.
Ex libro sancti Augustíni Epíscopi de grátia et líbero arbítrio
Cap. 6-7

The Apostle Paul, whom we certainly find to have received the grace of God without any good merits whatsoever, and indeed with many evil merits, God rendering good for evil — let us see what he says, as his own Passion draws near, writing to Timothy: For I am already being sacrificed, he says, and the time of my dissolution is at hand. I have fought the good fight, I have finished the course, I have kept the faith. These indeed are the good merits he now recalls; so that after good merits he may receive the crown, who after evil merits received grace. Then mark what follows: There remains for me, he says, the crown of justice, which the Lord, the just Judge, will render to me on that day. To whom would the just Judge render the crown, if the merciful Father had not first bestowed grace? And how would this crown be one of justice, if grace, which justifies the ungodly, had not gone before? How would that which is owed be rendered, unless what is freely given had first been granted?

We must consider, most beloved brethren, and reflect again and again, that we have renounced the world, and are dwelling here meanwhile as strangers and sojourners. Let us embrace the day that assigns each one to his own dwelling, that snatches us hence and looses us from the snares of the world and restores us to paradise and the heavenly kingdom. Who, settled in a foreign land, would not hasten to return to his homeland? Who, eager to sail homeward, would not more ardently long for a favoring wind, so as swiftly to embrace those dear to him?
Ex libro sancti Epiphanii Epíscopi adversus hæreses

The blessed Mother of God, Mary, is prefigured by Eve, who received in figure the title of Mother of the living. For she was called the mother of the living even after she heard: You are dust, and to dust you shall return, after the transgression. And it is wondrous that after the transgression she bore this great name. And as regards the visible order, from that Eve all the race of men upon earth is derived; but here truly from Mary this life is born into the world, that she might bring forth the Living One and become Mary, the mother of the living. In figure, therefore, Mary is called the mother of the living.
Ex libro sancti Hierónymi Presbýteri contra Iovinianum.
Liber 1, n. 26

John the Apostle, one of the disciples of the Lord, who is handed down as having been the youngest among the Apostles, and whom the faith of Christ had found a virgin, remained a virgin; and therefore is he loved more by the Lord, and reclines upon the breast of Jesus; and what Peter, who had a wife, does not dare to ask, he asks him to inquire; and after the Resurrection, when Mary Magdalene announced that the Lord had risen, both ran to the tomb, but he arrived first; and when they were in the boat and were fishing on the lake of Gennesareth, Jesus was standing on the shore, nor did the Apostles know whom they saw; the virgin alone recognizes the Virgin, and says to Peter: It is the Lord.

John the Apostle, one of the disciples of the Lord, who is handed down as having been the youngest among the Apostles, and whom the faith of Christ had found a virgin, remained a virgin; and therefore is he loved more by the Lord, and reclines upon the breast of Jesus; and what Peter, who had a wife, does not dare to ask, he asks him to inquire; and after the Resurrection, when Mary Magdalene announced that the Lord had risen, both ran to the tomb, but he arrived first; and when they were in the boat and were fishing on the lake of Gennesareth, Jesus was standing on the shore, nor did the Apostles know whom they saw; the virgin alone recognizes the Virgin, and says to Peter: It is the Lord. John the Apostle, whom Jesus loved most, the son of Zebedee, brother of James the Apostle whom Herod beheaded after the Passion of the Lord, wrote the Gospel last of all, having been urged by the bishops of Asia against Cerinthus and other heretics, and especially the then-rising doctrine of the Ebionites, who assert that Christ did not exist before Mary; wherefore he was also compelled to proclaim his divine nativity.
Cap. 67

Cyprian, an African, first taught rhetoric with distinction. Thereafter, at the persuasion of the presbyter Caecilius, from whom he also received his surname, he became a Christian and distributed all his substance to the poor. And after no great time, elected to the presbyterate, he was also appointed Bishop of Carthage. To give a list of the works of his genius is superfluous, since they are clearer than the sun. He suffered under the emperors Valerian and Gallienus, in the eighth persecution, on the same day as Cornelius at Rome, but not in the same year.
Cap. 16

Ignatius, third bishop of the Church of Antioch after the Apostle Peter, when Trajan stirred up a persecution, was condemned to the beasts and sent in chains to Rome. And when, sailing, he had come to Smyrna, where Polycarp, a hearer of John, was bishop, he wrote one letter to the Ephesians, another to the Magnesians, a third to the Trallians, a fourth to the Romans. And departing thence, he wrote to the Philadelphians, and to the Smyrnaeans, and a personal letter to Polycarp, commending to him the Church of Antioch; in which he also sets down testimony concerning the Gospel, which I have recently translated, regarding the person of Christ.
Cap. 17

Polycarp, a disciple of the Apostle John and ordained bishop of Smyrna by him, was the foremost man in all Asia, inasmuch as he had had as teachers some of the Apostles and of those who had seen the Lord, and had seen them himself. On account of certain disputes concerning the day of Easter, in the reign of the Emperor Antoninus Pius, when Anicetus was governing the Church in the City, he came to Rome; where he brought back to the faith very many of the faithful who had been deceived by the persuasion of Marcion and Valentinus. And when Marcion happened to meet him and said: Do you know us? he replied: I know the firstborn of the devil. Afterwards, under Marcus Antoninus and Lucius Aurelius Commodus, in the fourth persecution after Nero, at Smyrna, while the proconsul sat and the whole people in the amphitheatre cried out against him, he was delivered to the flames. He wrote to the Philippians a very useful letter, which is read to this day in the assemblies of Asia.
Ex libro sancti Hierónymi Presbýteri de Scriptóribus Ecclesiásticis
Cap. 7

Luke the physician, of Antioch, as his writings indicate, was not unskilled in the Greek tongue. He was a follower of the Apostle Paul and the companion of all his journeys. He wrote the Gospel, of which the same Paul says: We sent with him the brother whose praise is in the Gospel throughout all the churches. And to the Colossians: Luke, the most dear physician, greets you. And to Timothy: Luke alone is with me. He also published another outstanding volume, which is headed with the title: Acts of the Apostles; whose history extends to the two-year sojourn of Paul in Rome, that is, to the fourth year of Nero. From this we understand that the book was composed in that same city.
De viris illustribus, cap 8

Mark, the disciple and interpreter of Peter, according to what he had heard Peter recounting, wrote at the request of the brethren at Rome a brief Gospel. When Peter heard of it, he approved it and gave it to the Church to be read by his authority. Mark then, taking up the Gospel he had himself composed, went to Egypt, and preaching Christ first at Alexandria, established a Church of such doctrine and sobriety of life that he constrained all the followers of Christ to follow his example.
Ex libro sancti Ioánnis Damascéni de fide orthodóxa
Liber 4, Cap. 15

Joachim joined in marriage to himself that most excellent woman Anna, worthy of the highest praises. But, just as the ancient Anna, laboring under the disease of sterility, brought forth Samuel through prayer and promise; so also this woman likewise, through supplication and promise, received the Mother of God from God, that in this too she might yield to none of the illustrious matrons. And so Grace — for that is what the name Anna signifies — brings forth the Lady — for that is what the name Mary denotes. Truly indeed has she become Lady of all created things, since she became the Mother of the Creator. She was brought into the light in the house of the Probatic Pool belonging to Joachim, and was led to the Temple. And thereafter, planted in the house of God and fattened by the Spirit, like a fruitful olive tree, she became the dwelling place of all virtues; so that, having withdrawn her mind from every concupiscence of this life and of the flesh, and thus having preserved her soul a virgin together with her body, in the manner befitting her who was to receive God in her womb.

Among the sacred sites that have been held in veneration by Christians from the beginning, the Confession of Saint Peter in the Vatican, consecrated by the tomb of the Prince of the Apostles, has always been held in singular honor. Constantine the Great is reported to have gone thither, and, taking up mattock and spade, to have dug the earth and marked out the site of the basilica which he himself built at his own cost. Pope Saint Sylvester dedicated it on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of December, and from that time prescribed that altars should henceforth be made only of stone. That basilica, long since fallen into ruin with age, and raised more magnificently from the foundations through the piety of many Pontiffs, Urban VIII solemnly dedicated on the same day, in the year one thousand six hundred and twenty-six. Likewise the basilica of the Apostle Saint Paul on the Ostian Way, built most sumptuously by the same Emperor Constantine and consecrated by Pope Saint Sylvester, which was consumed by a dreadful fire and raised more splendidly than before by the unwearied care of four Pontiffs; Pius IX, having seized the most auspicious occasion of the definition of the dogma of the Immaculate Conception of the Blessed Virgin Mary, surrounded by a solemn assembly of bishops, consecrated it.

Among the sacred sites that from of old were held in veneration by Christians, the most celebrated and most frequented were those in which the bodies of the Saints were enshrined, or some trace or monument of the Martyrs preserved. Among the number of such holy places, that part of the Vatican which was called the Confession of Saint Peter has always been preeminently distinguished. For thither Christians from all parts of the world, gathering as to the rock of faith and the foundation of the Church, venerated with supreme religious devotion the place consecrated by the tomb of the Prince of the Apostles.

Ex orátione sancti Ephræm Syri Diáconi ad Deíparam
My Lady, most holy Mother of God and full of grace, inexhaustible sea of divine and hidden gifts and favors, the bestower of all good things, Lady of all after the Trinity, another Consoler after the Paraclete, and Mediatrix of the whole world after the Mediator — look upon my faith and my divinely given desire. Do not despise the unworthy, nor let the foulness of my deeds interrupt your immeasurable mercy, O Mother of God, name most dear to me; for there is no trophy more steadfast than your help. For you have wiped away all tears from the face of the earth; you have filled creation with every kind of benefit, you have brought joy to the heavenly ones, you have saved those upon earth. Through you we hold the most certain pledge of our resurrection; through you we hope to attain the heavenly kingdom; through you all glory, honor, and holiness has been derived, is derived, and shall be derived, from the first Adam even to the consummation of the age, to the Apostles, Prophets, the just, and the humble of heart — you alone immaculate; and in you, full of grace, rejoices all creation.
Ex Oratióne S. Gregórii Nysséni
Append. Gretseri, 237., sive tom. 3. Oper. S. Greg.

Break your bread for the hungry, and bring the homeless poor into your house. This season brings us an abundance of naked and wandering people. Strangers and exiles are not lacking; everywhere one may see hands stretched out imploring aid. For these, the open air serves as a roof. Porches, crossroads, and the more deserted parts of the marketplace are their lodging-places: like night-herons and owls they lurk in caverns. They are covered with threadbare, worn, and tattered garments. The kindness of pitying souls is the harvest of their fields; food is whatever they have managed to obtain from a passerby; their drink the same as that of brute animals, namely the fountains. They lead a wandering and rough life, driven by calamity and necessity. Supply these with what they need for sustenance, you who fast. Be kind to your afflicted brethren; what you take away from the belly, give to the hungry.
Ex publicis Monumentis

The Christian people has many times experienced in a wondrous manner the most powerful aid of the Mother of God in the vanquishing of the enemies of religion; from which it came about that the most holy Pontiff Pius V, after the signal victory won by Christians over the tyranny of the Turks at the Echinades Islands through the intercession of the most Blessed Virgin, established that she be called among her other praises Queen of Heaven, in the Loretan Litany, by the title Help of Christians. But that above all is memorable and to be held as an undoubted miracle: that when the Roman Pontiff Pius VII, expelled from the Apostolic See of Peter by the counsels and arms of the impious and held under close confinement, especially at Savona for more than five years, with all ways utterly shut off so that he could not govern the Church of God — without any precedent for such a persecution in the ancient records — it came to pass unexpectedly and beyond the expectation of all that he was restored with great acclaim, as if by the hands of the whole world, to the pontifical throne. This occurred a second time as well, when, amid renewed turmoil, departing from the City and accompanied by the sacred College of Cardinals, he set out for Liguria. But by the most present benefit of God, the storm that threatened grave ruin having subsided, he returned to Rome amid the rejoicing of the people with fresh-felt gladness. But first, fulfilling what he had long desired and had been unable to carry out during his captivity, he crowned with a golden crown the venerable image of the Mother of God, the Virgin Mary, under the title of Mother of Mercy at Savona, with solemn rite and with his own hands. This wondrous turn of events the same Supreme Pontiff Pius VII, who was intimately acquainted with the whole affair, rightly attributed to the intercession of the most holy Mother of God, whose powerful aid he himself had earnestly implored and had caused to be implored by all the faithful of Christ; and in honor of the same Virgin Mother, under the appellation of Help of Christians, he instituted a solemn feast to be perpetually celebrated on the twenty-fourth day of the month of May, the anniversary of his most joyful return to the City, a proper Office also being approved, that a distinct and enduring memorial of so great a benefit might remain, and that thanksgiving might be rendered.

Thereupon the impious king's satellites, hoping to do the king a pleasure by removing Thomas from the midst, gathered secretly and made their way to Canterbury, and attacked the bishop as he was engaged in evening prayer in the church. When his clerics attempted to bar the doors of the church, he ran forward and opened them, using these words to his own people: The Church of God is not to be guarded in the manner of a fortress; and I am ready willingly to die for the Church of God. Then to the soldiers: By God's command, take care not to harm any of my people. Thereupon, kneeling and commending the Church and himself to God, to blessed Mary, to Saint Dionysius, and to the other Saints who were patrons of his church, he offered his sacred head to be cut down by the impious sword, with the same steadfastness with which he had resisted the most unjust edicts of the king, on the fourth day before the Kalends of January, in the year of the Lord one thousand one hundred and seventy-one; and the whole pavement of the church was sprinkled with his brain. The same Pope Alexander, after many miracles had glorified him, enrolled him in the number of the Saints.

For from the time that Life itself and the Author of life was numbered among the dead, we call those who have closed their last day in the hope of the resurrection and of faith in him by no means dead. For who could it be that is able to work miracles through a dead body? Through them demons are expelled, diseases are driven out, the sick are healed, the blind see, lepers are cleansed, temptations and sorrows are dispersed, and finally every good gift from the Father of lights descends through their ministry to those who ask with unfeigned faith. What labor would you not undertake in order to obtain some patron who might present you to a mortal king and speak on your behalf before him? Are these not then to be honored, who proclaim themselves the patrons of the entire human race and make supplication to God on our behalf?

She gave glory to the heavens, God to the earth, faith to the nations, an end to vices, order to life, discipline to conduct. The grace which the Angel brought, the Virgin received, to restore salvation to the ages. Truly blessed is the Virgin, who possesses both the glory of virginity and the dignity of motherhood: truly blessed, who both merited the grace of heavenly conception and preserved the crown of integrity. Truly blessed, who both received the glory of the divine offspring and stood forth as queen of all chastity.

Otto, born in Swabia of his father Berthold the count and his mother Sophia, distinguished in nobility of birth rather than in abundance of wealth, was given over to learning from his earliest years. Having been left an orphan by his parents while already versed in the precepts of grammar and having memorized certain poets and philosophers, and lacking the means necessary for more advanced studies, as a modest young man he set out for Poland, where by teaching others and by pressing himself ever more eagerly toward advancement in learning he soon both increased his private means and was held in honor; he also learned the language of that region, and advancing gradually to higher things, he enhanced his learning by the practice of frugality, temperance, and self-discipline, and by this means, becoming dear to all, he contracted the friendship and intimacy of great and powerful men, to which his personal elegance contributed in no small measure. He was then taken into the court of the Duke of Poland, who sent him as envoy to the Emperor Henry IV.

Called from Thuringia to Heidenheim by her brother Willibald, she came to preside over a newly founded monastery of virgins. She presided over it so successfully that, upon the death of the holy Winebald, the monastery of men was also entrusted to her. While she discharged this office with the highest praise for integrity, prudence, and holiness, not without miracles, she passed to the joys of heaven, for which she burned with fervent desire, in the year of salvation seven hundred and seventy-nine, and was buried at Heidenheim, Bishop Willibald performing the last rites for his holy sister.
Ex Tractatu sancti Augustíni Epíscopi in Epístolam Ioánnis.
Tract. 5. in cap. 3.

Perfect charity is this, that one be ready to die for a brother. This the Lord himself showed in himself, dying for all, praying for those by whom he was crucified, and saying: Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do. But if he alone did this, he would not be a Teacher if he had no disciples. If anyone shall have had so great a charity that he is ready even to die for his brethren, charity is perfect in him. But is it immediately altogether perfect as soon as it is born? It is born so that it may be perfected; when it has been born it is nourished; when it has been nourished it is strengthened; when it has been strengthened it is perfected; when it has come to perfection, what does it say? For me to live is Christ, and to die is gain; I longed to depart and to be with Christ, for it is by far the better; but to remain in the flesh is more necessary for your sake. For their sake he was willing to live, for whom he was ready to die.
Ex Tractatu sancti Augustíni Epíscopi in Ioánnem
Tractatus 36

In the four Gospels, or rather in the four books of the one Gospel, the holy Apostle John, not without reason compared to the eagle in his spiritual understanding, raised his proclamation higher and far more sublimely than the other three; and in that elevation he willed that our hearts too should be lifted up. For the other three Evangelists, as it were, walk with the Lord upon earth as man, and spoke little of his divinity; but this one, as though it were wearisome to him to walk upon the earth, just as he thundered forth in the very beginning of his discourse, raised himself not only above the earth and above the whole compass of air and sky, but above every host of Angels and every ordering of the invisible Powers; and he came to him through whom all things were made, saying: In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.
Ex Tractatu sancti Augustíni Epíscopi in Ioánnem.
Tractatus 27. in fine.

We are certain, brethren, that all of us who are in the body of the Lord and abide in him, that he too may abide in us, must needs live in this age until the end among the wicked — not among those wicked, I say, who blaspheme Christ; for seldom now are found those who blaspheme with the tongue, but many who do so with their lives. Of necessity, therefore, we must live among them until the end. But what is it that he says: He who abides in me, and I in him? What else but what the Martyrs were hearing: He who perseveres to the end, he shall be saved?

Ex Tractatu sancti Cypriáni Epíscopi et Mártyris !De Oratióne Domínica
Nor in words only, but also in deeds, did the Lord teach us to pray, himself praying frequently and making supplication, and showing by the attestation of his own example what we ought to do, as it is written: But he himself withdrew into the wilderness and prayed. And again: He went out to the mountain to pray, and continued the whole night in prayer to God. But if he who was without sin prayed, how much more ought sinners to pray! And if he, watching and praying continually through the whole night with unceasing prayers, prayed; how much more ought we to be watchful in prayer through the night! Now the Lord prayed and made petition not for himself — for what would the innocent pray for himself? — but for our sins, as he himself makes clear when he says to Peter: Behold, Satan has sought to sift you as wheat; but I have prayed for you, that your faith may not fail. And afterwards he prays to the Father for all, saying: And I pray not for these alone, but for those also who are to believe in me through their word; that they all may be one, as you, Father, are in me, and I in you; that they also may be one in us.
Ex Tractatu sancti Ioánnis Damascéni de fide orthodoxa
Liber 4, Cap. 16

Christ the Lord has provided the relics of the Saints as most health-giving fountains, from which many benefits flow to us and a most sweet ointment streams forth. And let no one give less than full credence to this saying; for if water in the desert gushed forth from hard and solid rock, and from the jawbone of an ass to slake the thirst of Samson, according to God's will, shall there be reason for anyone to find it incredible that sweet ointment should spring from the relics of the Martyrs? By no means, indeed, for those to whom the power of God and the honor with which he regards his Saints is plain and evident. And that indeed was ordained under the old law, that whoever had touched a dead person should be accounted unclean; but these are not at all to be reckoned in the number of the dead.

This saying therefore spread abroad among the brethren, that that disciple would not die; and Jesus had not said to him that he would not die; but: If I wish him to remain until I come, what is that to you? Do not suppose, he says, that I have disposed of you in the same way. But he said this in order to take away inopportune affection and the longing of habit. For since they were about to take charge of the whole world, it was no longer fitting for them to be together; for it would have been a great loss to the world. For this reason he says: You have taken up a work; attend to it; complete it, labor, and expose yourself to the contests. What is it to you if I wish him to remain here? Attend to your own duty and carry it out.

The very nature of things shuddered at the wickedness of men; and the earth trembling bears witness that he whom rebellious creation does not acknowledge is Lord of the world, and the sun fleeing confesses him King of heaven. He is clothed in a scarlet robe, because the body of the Church is adorned with the blood of his Martyrs. A crown of thorns is placed upon his head, because the sting of our sins, by whose remission the glory of the Redeemer is built up, is likened to dry thorns. Let us strive now in turn that the life of the members may be the crown of the head. And as for his saying, when placed on the Cross, that he thirsts — he desires the faith of the unbelieving people; but in return they proffer the vinegar of malice, because they had corrupted by sin the wine of wisdom they had received from God. The veil of the Temple is rent, because the Synagogue is stripped of honor, the ancient observance is dissolved, the unity of the Church is foreshown. The tombs are opened, because the rights of death are rightly overcome.

Rejoice, Joachim, for from your daughter a Son is born to us; and his name is called the Angel of great counsel, that is, of the salvation of the whole world. Let Nestorius be put to shame and put his hand upon his mouth. This child is God. How then shall she not be the Mother of God who bore him? Whoever does not confess the holy Mother of God is estranged from the Godhead. These words are not mine, though in another sense they are mine; for I received this most divine inheritance from my theological father Gregory. O blessed pair, Joachim and Anna! By the fruit of your womb you are known to be immaculate, even as Christ said in a certain place: By their fruits you shall know them. As was pleasing and worthy in God's sight, in view of her who was born of you, you ordered the manner of your lives. For serving your function chastely and holily, you brought forth the treasure of virginity.

Let Sara exult, leaping for joy with an elder woman's gladness, prefiguring my conception from sterility. Let the barren and fruitless together sing of my visitation, wrought in wondrous fashion from on high. Let all mothers endowed with this fruitfulness say: Blessed is he who has granted to those who prayed what they desired, and has given fruitfulness to the barren, and has bestowed that most blessed offspring of the Virgin, who was the Mother of God according to the flesh, whose womb is heaven, in whom dwelt he who is contained by no place. Let us ourselves also, who was once called barren but who have now become mother of the virginal bridal chamber, offer in harmony with these words our praise. Let us say to her with Scripture: How blessed is the house of David, from which you came forth, and the womb in which God fashioned the ark of sanctification, that is, her from whom he was conceived without seed.

Matthew, therefore, sets forth the human generation of Christ, recounting the ancestors from Abraham, and leading them down to Joseph, the husband of Mary, of whom Jesus was born. Nor was it fitting that for this reason he should be thought to be separating him from the union with Mary, because not of her marriage-bed but as a virgin did she give birth to Christ. For by this example it is magnificently intimated to faithful married persons that even with like consent maintained in continence, it is possible for the marriage to remain and be called such, not through commingling of the flesh, but through the keeping of the affection of the mind: especially since it was possible for a son to be born to them without any carnal embrace, which is employed solely for the begetting of children.

There are extant many letters written by him to Pippin, King of the Franks, in which he gives thanks to that excellent prince, well deserving of the Roman Church, for his undertaking the defense of the Church against the incursions of the Lombards; and, heaping on him rare praises, he earnestly urges him never to desist from the work begun. Moreover, when cemeteries outside the walls had been destroyed by the Lombards, he brought many relics of the Saints into the City, lest they fall as plunder to the barbarians; a not inconsiderable part of which he placed in the church of the monastery he had built in his ancestral home and enriched with a generous endowment. For the rest, if any time was left to him by the care of ecclesiastical government, he spent it entirely in feeding the poor of Christ, comforting the sick, widows, and those held in prison, and in freeing those oppressed by debt. And at last, ripe for heaven, he died piously in the eleventh year of his pontificate then begun, and was buried in the Vatican.

There are extant very many letters written by him, in which he corrected the erring, cast down the proud, and refreshed the oppressed. He kept bishops, kings, and emperors in their duty: he broke the contumacy of John, Archbishop of Ravenna; he sharply rebuked Hincmar, Archbishop of Reims, for the unjust deposition of Rhotaldus, Bishop of Soissons, and annulled his sentence in that matter, as well as the judgment of the Synod of Senlis; then, while celebrating the solemnity of Mass at Saint Mary Major on the vigil of the Lord's Nativity, he restored the bishop himself to his former dignity, and shortly after fully to his own see. He brought King Lothair back to his senses, having been estranged from his lawful wife Theutberga and taken Waldrada as his concubine, by threatening anathema. He rejected the election of Photius, a layman, and restored the Patriarch Ignatius to his former see. Finally, he defended the rights of the Roman Church so well that each of his letters seems to be so many most powerful fortifications of the Apostolic See.

The tyrants who had robbed his brothers of their lives and their kingdom being at last destroyed, he is recalled to his homeland. There, amid the greatest desires and rejoicing of all, having come into possession of the kingdom, he turned himself entirely to blotting out the traces of hostile wrath, beginning with sacred things and the temples of the Saints, some of which he raised from their foundations, others he repaired and increased in revenues and privileges; being intent above all on this purpose, that the collapsed religion might revive. The historical writers consistently attest that he was compelled to marriage by the nobles of the court, yet preserved his virginity together with that of his virgin bride in the marriage itself. Such was his love and faith in Christ, that he merited at times to see him during the celebration of Mass, his countenance serene and radiant with divine light. On account of his overflowing charity, he was called everywhere the father of orphans and the needy; never more joyful than when he had emptied the royal treasury for the poor.

Make for yourselves purses that grow not old — namely, by performing works of almsgiving whose reward may endure forever. This commandment is not to be understood as meaning that the saints should keep no money, either for their own use or to supply the needs of the poor; since the Lord himself, for whom Angels ministered, is yet recorded, in order to form his Church, to have had a purse, preserving what was offered by the faithful and distributing it to the needs of his own and to others in want; but rather that God should not be served for the sake of these things, nor that justice should be abandoned out of fear of want.

Joseph is said to have been a carpenter, seeking his livelihood by craft and the work of his hands, and not eating his bread in idleness and luxury as the scribes and Pharisees did. Mary also sought her livelihood by the distaff and the work of her hands. And the sense is: This man is of despised and most humble birth; he cannot be Christ the Lord, whom God has anointed. And therefore he is not to be believed in, so rustic and so mean is he.

The Lord, however, was a craftsman; because the prophet said of him: You have made the dawn and the sun. A similar expression of contempt appears in the book of Kings, where, when Saul was promoted to his kingdom, they said: What has happened to the son of Kish? Is Saul also among the prophets? A small word, then, carries great contempt. The Lord, however, said: Amen, I say to you, no prophet is accepted in his own homeland. Now the Lord here calls himself a prophet. For he who by his divinity knows all things receives absolutely no revelation of inspiration. By his homeland here he strictly designates the place of his conception and upbringing. But among his fellow-villagers, who were stirred by envy against him, he was not accepted.

Fabian, a Roman, governing the Church from Maximinus until Decius, divided the regions among seven deacons to have care of the poor. He created an equal number of subdeacons to gather the acts of the Martyrs written by the seven notaries. He likewise decreed that each year on the Thursday of the Lord's Supper the Chrism should be renewed, the old being burned. Finally, on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of February he was crowned with martyrdom, and was buried in the cemetery of Callixtus on the Appian Way. Sebastian, dear to Diocletian for his noble birth and valor, a commander of the first cohort, aided Christians, whose faith he privately professed, with his efforts and resources, and strengthened them in the confession of Christ. When this was reported to Diocletian, he attempted by every artifice to turn Sebastian away from faith in Christ. But when neither promises nor threats availed anything, he ordered him bound to a post and pierced with arrows. But God's servant, judged dead by the opinion of all, when a short while later he appeared before Diocletian in good health and charged his impiety more freely, was by order of the tyrant beaten with rods until he gave up the spirit.

Fabian, a Roman, governing the Church from Maximinus until Decius, divided the regions among seven deacons to have care of the poor. He created an equal number of subdeacons to gather the acts of the Martyrs written by the seven notaries. He likewise decreed that each year on the Thursday of the Lord's Supper the Chrism should be renewed, the old being burned. Finally, on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of February, in the persecution of Decius, he was crowned with martyrdom and was buried in the cemetery of Callixtus on the Appian Way, having sat for fifteen years and four days. He held five ordinations in the month of December, in which he created twenty-two priests, seven deacons, eleven bishops in various places.

It came to pass that from the herds of a certain Garganus a bull strayed far away; and after a long search it was found halted at the entrance of a cave. When one of the men shot an arrow to strike the bull, the arrow turned back and fell upon the marksman himself. This event so struck with great fear those present, and thereafter all the others, that no one dared approach that cave any nearer. The men of Siponto therefore consulted their bishop, who, having imposed a three-day fast and prayer, declared that the matter ought to be inquired of God.

Faustinus and Jovita, brothers, nobles of Brescia, endured the most cruel tortures in many cities of Italy to which they were led in chains while Trajan's persecution raged, and held firm in their confession of the Christian faith. For at Brescia, long held in bonds, having also been thrown to wild beasts and cast into the fire, they were preserved unharmed and whole from both the beasts and the flames. From there, bound in the same chains, they came to Milan; where their faith, tested by the most exquisite torments as gold in fire, shone forth all the more in their sufferings. Afterwards sent to Rome, confirmed by the Pontiff Evaristus, they were cruelly tortured there as well. Finally brought to Naples, variously tormented in that city too, they were plunged into the sea with hands and feet bound; from whence they were miraculously rescued by Angels. Wherefore they converted many to the faith of Christ both by their constancy in torments and by the power of their miracles. At last, brought back to Brescia at the beginning of the reign of Hadrian, they were beheaded and received the illustrious crown of martyrdom.

Truly blessed the kisses imprinted upon the lips of one suckling, whom his mother applauded as a virgin in her lap. But shall we not judge yet more blessed those which, in the blessed greeting of this day, she received from the mouth of him who sits at the right hand of the Father, as he ascended to the throne of glory, singing the marriage-hymn and saying: Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth? Who shall declare the birth of Christ and the Assumption of Mary? For as great as was the grace she obtained on earth beyond all others, so great also is the singular glory she holds in heaven.

But Felicitas, as the day of the spectacle drew near, was already eight months with child, and was in great grief lest she be put off; for the law forbade that pregnant women should suffer punishment. But by the prayers of her fellow-martyrs her delivery was hastened, and she gave birth to a daughter. And when she was groaning in pain during the birth, one of the guards said to her: You who suffer so now, what will you do when thrown to the beasts? To which she replied: Now it is I who suffer; but there another will be in me who will suffer for me, because I also am to suffer for him.

Felix of Cantalice, born in the Sabine country to parents humble but devout, was from boyhood set to tending flocks, and then to working the fields; yet with far greater diligence he nourished his soul by meditation on heavenly things and disciplined his body by constant vigils and fasts, leading more of a hermit's life than a rustic's. Burning with a more fervent piety toward God, since he was unable to be present at the sacred mysteries daily as he wished, he was accustomed to drive his flock to solitary places and there pray long before a cross carved into the bark of trees, and to chastise himself severely; and at times he was seen to be turning the clods in the field and at the same time attending the sacred rites in the church. At other times, while plowing, when the untamed bullocks he had yoked ran furiously, he lay prostrate on the ground and, the plow being drawn over him and plainly about to cut him down, he rose unharmed with only his garment torn. Warned by this peril to obey God, who had long been calling him to the safer arena of regular discipline, he ordered his rustic equipment to be distributed among the poor, and hastened to join the Friars Minor, known as the Capuchins.

Blessed indeed the day that conveyed so precious a gift from the desert of this world and led her to the holy and eternal city, so that a joy common and beyond belief, no less than wonder, was created for all the heavenly ones. Blessed the day that satisfied the languishing Bride's desires — both so ardent and so long endured — so that she found what she had sought, received what she had asked, and securely possessed what she had awaited, resting in deepest peace in that perfect vision and fruition of the supreme and eternal Good. Blessed the day that advanced and exalted the most humble handmaid of the Lord to such heights that she became the most excellent Queen of heaven and Lady of the world, and could ascend no higher, since, raised to the throne of the Kingdom, she sits in glory after Christ. Blessed and truly venerable is this day, which established and confirmed for us in the Kingdom of God a Queen and Mother both powerful and clement, so that we might have her, who continually remains Mother of the Judge, as a mother of mercy favorable to us, interceding for us before Christ, and faithfully managing the business of our salvation.

Felix, under the emperors Diocletian and Maximian, was arrested on account of his profession of the Christian faith and brought to the temple of Serapis. When he was commanded to sacrifice, he spat upon the mouth of the idol. At this, the bronze statue immediately fell. When the same was done a second and a third time in the temple of Mercury and Diana, he was accused of impiety and the practice of magic, and was racked upon the equuleus. He was then led out to the second milestone from the City on the Ostian Way to be beheaded. On the way, a certain Christian who encountered them, recognizing Felix and seeing him led to martyrdom, cried out in a loud voice: I too live by the same law as this man, and I worship that same Jesus Christ. And so, having embraced Felix, he was beheaded together with him on the third day before the Kalends of September. Since his name was unknown to the Christians, he was honored by the name Adauctus, because he had been added to the crown of the holy Martyr Felix.

Felix, formerly called Hugh, born of the royal house of Valois in France, from his youth began, out of devotion to heavenly contemplation, to think of solitude. Having been ordained a priest, he withdrew into a hermitage, where he lived for some years with Saint John of Matha, until both, admonished by an Angel from God, set out for Rome, where from the Supreme Pontiff Innocent III, who had likewise been divinely admonished, they obtained the approval of a new Order for the redemption of captives; which the same Pontiff, from the white garments marked with a two-colored cross received from the Angel, adorned with the name of the most Holy Trinity. Soon in the diocese of Meaux, at a place called Cerfroid, they constructed the first monastery of the Order. There Felix received a distinguished favor from the Blessed Virgin Mary, when he found her in the midst of the choir, clothed in the habit marked with the cross of the Order. Perfected in age and merits, he died in the Lord in the year one thousand two hundred and twelve.
