Felix, formerly called Hugh, born of the royal family of Valois in France, gave from his earliest years no slight signs of future holiness, particularly in mercy toward the poor. For, while still an infant, he distributed coins to the needy with his own hand, as though he were older and endowed with mature judgment; when somewhat grown, he would send from the dishes set upon the table to the poor themselves, and would refresh impoverished children with whatever was most savory at the meal; as a youth, he more than once stripped himself of his clothing in order to cover the destitute. He obtained from his uncle Theobald, Count of Champagne and Blois, the life of a man condemned to death, foretelling that this notorious cutthroat would soon be adorned with the holiest manner of life: the event proved the prophecy true.

Happy Mary, in whom neither humility was wanting, nor virginity! A singular virginity indeed, which fruitfulness did not violate but rather honored. And likewise a special humility, which fecund virginity did not take away but rather exalted: and an altogether incomparable fruitfulness, which virginity and humility accompany together. Which of these is not admirable? Which is not incomparable? Which is not singular? It is truly wonderful, if you do not hesitate, when weighing these things, as to which you judge more worthy of admiration—whether, that is, fruitfulness in the Virgin is more to be marveled at, or integrity in the Mother; majesty in the offspring, or humility together with such majesty—unless it be that all of these together are undoubtedly to be preferred to each one singly, and it is incomparably more excellent and more blessed to have received all than any one. And why wonder, if God, who is seen and declared wonderful in his Saints, showed himself more wonderful in his Mother? Let married persons therefore reverence, in corruptible flesh, the integrity of the flesh; let you, consecrated virgins, reverence fruitfulness in the Virgin. Let all people imitate the humility of the Mother of God.

Felix, a priest of Nola, as he inveighed more vigorously against the idols, was variously harassed by unbelievers and cast into prison. Led out thence by an Angel in the night, he was commanded to seek Maximus, the Bishop of Nola; who, worn out by old age and despairing of being able to bear the torments of the persecutors, had hidden himself in a forest. When Felix, guided by God, had come to him, he beheld the holy Bishop lying on the ground, nearly dead; he revived him, lifted him upon his shoulders, and brought him to be cared for at the house of a faithful widow. But when the Bishop once again rebuked the worshipers of idols, an attack was made upon him; Felix fled and hid himself in the narrow space between two walls, which, when the entrance was suddenly seen to be covered over with spiders' webs, left no one with any suspicion of a recent hiding-place. Escaping thence, Felix lay hidden for three months in the dwelling of a devout woman. When the Church of God had begun to enjoy rest, he returned to Nola; and there, after converting many by the example of his life, the precepts of his teaching, and miracles to the faith of Christ, and having steadfastly refused the episcopate of that city, he fell asleep in the Lord, and was buried near Nola in the place they called in Pincis.

Felix, a Roman, son of Constantius, governed the Church under the Emperor Aurelian. He decreed that Mass should be celebrated over the tombs and memorials of the Martyrs. When in the month of December he had held two ordinations, and had created nine priests, five deacons, and five bishops for various places, he was crowned with martyrdom and was buried on the Aurelian Way in the basilica which he had built and dedicated. He served in the pontificate for two years, four months, and twenty-nine days.

Felix the Second, a Roman, son of Anastasius, was elected Pontiff from the archidiaconate of the Roman Church while Liberius was still living. When, however, a grave controversy arose in the time of Gregory XIII concerning the pontificate of Felix, and men of great weight held different views, it came to pass at that very time that in the diaconal church of the holy Martyrs Cosmas and Damian, in the Roman Forum, certain persons seeking a treasure came upon a marble chest, in which the body of Saint Felix was found, together with a small stone tablet placed inside, engraved with these words: The body of Saint Felix, Pope and Martyr, who condemned Constantius. This occurred on the day before that on which the feast of Felix was customarily observed in the Church, the fourth day before the Kalends of August, in the year of the Lord 1582. Wherefore, with Felix himself as it were bearing witness on his own behalf, the feast has been customarily celebrated each year with greater solemnity in that same diaconal church.

Felix the Third, a Roman by birth, born of the most noble house of Anicia, and the great-great-grandfather of the blessed Gregory the Great, was raised to the summit of the supreme pontificate after Simplicius. With admirable steadfastness of soul, even though Rome seemed almost held captive under the Arian Herulians, and other Patriarchs had approved the accommodation of the Emperor Zeno, he alone refused communion with him. He boldly resisted the audacity of the same emperor in promulgating an edict on the faith, deposed Peter the Fuller from the patriarchate of Antioch, compelled Acacius, Bishop of Constantinople, to come to Rome to answer the charges brought against him before the judgment of the Apostolic See, and visited upon him the sentence of excommunication.

Ferdinand the Third, King of Castile and León, to whom the title of Saint has been given by the consensus of churchmen and laymen for four centuries now, gave, while still a youth, so great a proof of prudence that his mother Berengaria, Queen of Castile, by whom he had been most devoutly educated, abdicated the kingdom in favor of her son. In him, joined with the cares of the kingdom, royal virtues shone forth: magnanimity, clemency, justice, and above all zeal for the Catholic faith and a burning devotion to protecting and propagating its religious worship. He excelled first in persecuting heretics, whom he permitted to live nowhere in his kingdoms, and himself carried with his own hands the wood to the pyre for those condemned to be burned. He excelled furthermore in erecting, endowing, and consecrating with Christian rite the churches of Córdoba, Jaén, Seville, and other cities recovered from the Moorish yoke, as well as in restoring the principal churches of Toledo, Burgos, and others, with pious and royal munificence.

Fidelis, born in the town of Sigmaringen in Swabia of the honorable Rey family, shone from his earliest years adorned with singular gifts of nature and grace. Endowed with a distinguished character and formed in the best discipline of morals, while earning his laureateship in philosophy and both branches of law at Freiburg, he also began in the school of Christ to strive diligently toward the summit of perfection by the exercise of the virtues. Taken as a companion of noblemen who were touring various provinces of Europe, he never ceased urging them to pursue Christian piety by both words and deeds. Indeed, on that same journey he labored by frequent austerities to mortify the desires of the flesh, and so governed himself that in the midst of so great a vicissitude of affairs he was never seen to be disturbed by any movement of anger. A vigorous champion moreover of law and justice, after his return to Germany he acquired a distinguished name in the office of advocate; yet, having experienced the perils of the court, he resolved to enter a safer path to eternal salvation, and, enlightened by a heavenly vocation, shortly thereafter sought to be enrolled among the Minor Brothers, called Capuchins.

Fidelis, born in the town of Sigmaringen in Swabia of the honorable Rey family, acquired a distinguished name in the office of advocate; yet, having experienced the perils of the court, he gave it up, and, enlightened by a heavenly vocation, sought to be enrolled among the Minor Brothers, called Capuchins. Having obtained his wish, he was a source of admiration and an example to all by his regular observance. A devoted client of the Virgin Mother of God and of the rosary, he asked of God that he might die a martyr for the Catholic faith, and this he obtained. For, chosen as president of the Missions which the Congregation for the Propagation of the Faith had at that time established for Rhaetia, sparing no labor and having converted several heretics to the faith of Christ, he incurred the envy of evildoers. And so, on the twenty-fourth day of April in the year 1622, at the church of the place called Seewis, beaten with blows and wounds by heretics who had deceitfully invited him by feigning conversion, he consecrated with his own blood the firstfruits of the Martyrs of the said Congregation.

Little children, this ladder of sinners, this is my greatest confidence, this is the whole ground of my hope. For what? Can the Son either reject or endure rejection? Can the Son fail to hear, or fail to be heard? Neither, clearly. She has found grace with God, said the Angel—happily. She will always find grace, and that grace alone is what we need: it is indeed the sole grace by which we are saved. What else do we desire, brethren? Let us seek grace, and let us seek it through Mary, for what she seeks she finds, and she cannot be frustrated. Let us seek grace, but grace with God: for with men grace is deceitful. Let others seek merit; let us strive to find grace. For what? Is it not of grace that we are here? Truly it is of the mercy of the Lord that we are not consumed.

Flavia Domitilla, a Roman virgin, niece of the emperors Titus and Domitian, having received the sacred veil of virginity from the blessed Pope Clement, was denounced by her betrothed Aurelianus, son of the consul Titus Aurelius, on the charge of being a Christian, and was deported by the Emperor Domitian to the island of Pontia, where she endured a long martyrdom in prison. At length, led to Terracina, and having confessed Christ again while appearing ever more steadfast, under the Emperor Trajan she completed the course of a glorious martyrdom, by order of the judge, when her chamber was set on fire, together with the virgins Theodora and Euphrosyna, her companions and foster-sisters, on the Nones of May. Their bodies, found intact, were buried by the deacon Caesarius. On this day, however, the bodies of the two brothers and of Domitilla, translated together from the diaconal church of Saint Hadrian, were restored to the basilica of those Martyrs themselves, of the title of Fasciola.

Florian, whom we invoke as patron against the ravages of fire, was sent to the life above by water. For while he was serving as military tribune in Noricum Ripense under the Emperor Diocletian, when an inquiry into the Christians was instituted, he voluntarily gave his own name.
Fragmentum serm. 10 pro Feria II post Pascha, in fine

He bears our miseries and thereby ennobles them, he sets misery before his own Heart, he shows his side. But we must love him in return, otherwise he who showed his wounds out of love will one day show them out of wrath and indignation. Grant, O good Jesus, that we may receive the peace you offer, and may behold your wounds, so that, since faith, hope, and charity abide, rooted in faith, rejoicing in hope and fervent in charity, we may await the blessed hope and your coming, in such a way that in that hour we may see you as the Lamb at the right hand and not the Lion at the left; and that in place of faith we may have vision, in place of hope possession, and in place of imperfect charity perfect charity, in which we shall rejoice for ever and ever. Amen.
Fragmentum sermo 16, in III Dominica post Pentecostem, initio

Our Lord, the great and most illustrious physician of all our infirmities, before he came into this world, had openly declared through his prophets: What is broken I will bind up, and what is sick I will strengthen. And thereafter he cried out with his own mouth, saying: Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you. Why is it surprising, then, if we behold him surrounded by the sick, by sinners and publicans? Is it not the glory of a physician to be sought out by the sick?

Frances, a noble Roman matron, at eleven years of age resolved to consecrate her virginity to God and to enter a monastery; but, obedient to her parents' will, she married Lorenzo de' Ponziani, a youth as wealthy as he was noble. In marriage she always preserved, as far as was permitted, the resolution of a more austere life, always admirable in her patience amid adversity. In order to draw the matrons of Rome back from the pomp of the world and the vanity of adornment, she established in the City the house of the Oblates, under the Rule of Saint Benedict of the Congregation of Mount Olivet; and, upon the death of her husband, flying to it, she humbly begged to be numbered among them. Having obtained her wish, although she was the mother of all, she gloried in the title of servant and most lowly handmaid. She always eluded the cunning of the ever-restless devil, and under the protection of her Angel carried off a glorious triumph over him. Distinguished by merits and miracles, she departed to the Lord in the forty-sixth year of her age: Pope Paul V enrolled her in the catalog of the Saints.

Frances Xavier, born in the town of Sant'Angelo in the diocese of Lodi, established a devout manner of life dedicated to God from her very childhood. At thirteen years of age, she vowed her virginity to the most Sacred Heart of Jesus. Yet, being in poor health, when she applied for admission to a religious institute, she suffered one rejection after another. The bishop assigned her to serve as a schoolteacher, and then set her over the management of an orphanage, while also encouraging her to found a new missionary religious congregation. Accordingly, at Codogno, at the chapel of the Blessed Virgin of Graces, when she herself was thirty years of age, she laid the foundations of the missionary sisters of the Sacred Heart of Jesus. When she remained undecided, she believed the command of Leo XIII to sail toward the western shores to be the will of God. Having crossed the ocean twenty-four times, she merited to be called the mother of the Italians in North America. Ever intent upon God and trusting in him, she saluted the Blessed Virgin Mary as the Mother of her Congregation. She propagated her institute wonderfully, personally establishing sixty-seven houses. At last, at Chicago, on the twenty-second day of December in the year 1917, she completed her course, and her remains were transferred to New York. Pope Pius XI numbered her among the Blessed, and Pope Pius XII among the holy Virgins.

Francis, born at Assisi in Umbria, following his father's example, practiced trade from his earliest years. Seized by a grave illness, when he had recovered, he began to cultivate the offices of charity more ardently, and, when his father took this amiss, he relinquished all his goods, adding that in the future he would have greater freedom to say: Our Father, who art in heaven. When he had heard from the Gospel the counsels of apostolic poverty, he removed his shoes and, content with a single tunic, gathered twelve companions to himself and founded the Order of Friars Minor; which, having been confirmed by the Supreme Pontiff Innocent III, himself moved from heaven, he propagated wonderfully. Shortly afterward he withdrew to the solitude of Mount La Verna, and there, on the feast of the Exaltation of the Holy Cross, as a Seraph bearing before him the image of the Crucified between its wings descended, he received the sacred stigmata; the marks of the nails and the lance appearing in his hands, feet, and side. Two years later, gravely ill, in the church of Saint Mary of the Angels, where he had received the spirit of grace from God, he exhorted the brothers to preserve poverty, patience, and fidelity to the holy Roman Church, and most devoutly breathed forth his soul on the fourth day before the Nones of October.

Francis, born at Assisi in Umbria, following his father's example, practiced trade from his earliest years. One day, when he had rebuffed a poor man begging money for the love of Christ, contrary to his custom, he was suddenly moved by the act, and lavished mercy upon him abundantly; and from that day he promised God that he would never refuse alms to anyone who asked. When thereafter he fell into a serious illness, and was at some point recovered from it, he began to cultivate the offices of charity more ardently; in which exercise he made such progress that, desiring evangelical perfection, he would distribute whatever he had to the poor. His father, taking this ill, brought him before the Bishop of Assisi, so that he might there renounce his paternal estate; and Francis, setting aside even his clothing, gave up everything to his father, adding that in the future he would have greater freedom to say: Our Father, who art in heaven.

Francis, formerly called Ascanius, born of the noble Caracciolo family in the town of Santa Maria di Villa in Abruzzo, shone from his earliest years in an eminent practice of piety. Falling gravely ill as a young man, he resolved to devote himself entirely to the service of God and of his neighbor. Setting out for Naples, ordained to the priesthood and enrolled in a sacred confraternity, he gave himself wholly to contemplation and to the winning of souls, and offered himself as an assiduous encourager to those condemned to capital punishment. It came to pass that a letter intended for another was delivered to him by mistake, in which he was summoned by the most devout men John Augustine Adorno and Fabricio Caracciolo to the founding of a new religious institute. Seized by the novelty of the matter and marveling at the counsels of the divine will, he joined himself to them with a ready heart. Having composed in the Camaldolese hermitage, to which they had withdrawn, the laws of the new order, they then set out together for Rome and obtained confirmation from Sixtus V, who wished these same clerics to be called Regular Minors, with a fourth vow added to the customary three, concerning the non-seeking of dignities.

Francis, formerly called Ascanius, born of the noble Caracciolo family in the town of Santa Maria di Villa in Abruzzo. Falling gravely ill as a young man, he resolved to devote himself entirely to the service of God and of his neighbor. Setting out for Naples and ordained to the priesthood, he gave himself wholly to contemplation and to the winning of souls, and offered himself as an assiduous encourager to those condemned to capital punishment. Joined by the wonderful disposition of God to John Augustine Adorno and Fabricio Caracciolo, he founded the Order of Regular Minor Clerics, with a fourth vow added to the customary three, concerning the non-seeking of dignities; which, after the death of Adorno, he governed most holily and propagated with the greatest zeal throughout Spain and Italy. He burned with such great affection toward the most holy Sacrament of the Eucharist that he would spend almost entire nights in adoration of it; which pious exercise he established as a perpetual distinguishing mark of his order to be observed therein. Enriched at last with the gift of prophecy and the discernment of hearts, in his forty-fourth year he was seized by a fatal fever in the town of Agnone in Abruzzo and fell asleep in the Lord on the day before the Nones of June in the year 1608. His sacred body, brought to Naples, was laid to rest in the church of his order.

Francis, the fourth Duke of Gandia, first distinguished himself by the integrity of his life at the court of the Emperor Charles V. When he had escorted the Empress Isabella to her tomb at Granada and, reading upon her disfigured face the transience of all mortal things, he bound himself by a vow to cast aside all else and serve the King of kings alone, upon the death of his wife Eleanor de Castro he entered the Society of Jesus. Appointed by Saint Ignatius as vicar general in Spain, he was shortly thereafter elected, though reluctant, as the third superior general by the whole Society. Assigned as a companion to Cardinal Alessandrino, sent as legate by the blessed Pope Pius V to unite the Christian princes against the Turks, he took up the arduous journey out of obedience, yet happily completed the course of his life at Rome, as he had wished, in the year of salvation 1572. He was enrolled among the Saints by Clement X.

Francis, born in the town of Sales, from which the family takes its name, to devout and noble parents, and educated in the liberal arts, applied himself to philosophy and theology at Paris and obtained his doctorate in both laws at Padua with the highest distinction. Ordained to the priesthood and appointed provost of the church of Geneva, he fulfilled the duties of that office so well that the Bishop Granier designated him as a herald of the divine word for the recovering of the Chablaisians from the Calvinian heresy. Taking up this expedition with a ready heart, and overcoming so many difficulties and dangers with God's help, he is said to have brought seventy-two thousand heretics back to the Catholic faith. On the death of Granier, he was consecrated bishop, founded a new order of nuns called after the Visitation of the Blessed Virgin, and illumined the Church with his writings full of heavenly teaching. Seized by a grave illness at Lyons, he departed to heaven in the year 1622, and by the Supreme Pontiff Pius IX, on the advice of the Congregation of Sacred Rites, was declared a Doctor of the universal Church.

Francis, born of noble parents at Xavier in the diocese of Pamplona, joined himself at Paris to Saint Ignatius as companion and disciple. Under that master he advanced so quickly that, absorbed in the contemplation of divine things, he was sometimes raised from the ground, which happened to him several times when he was offering the sacrifice in the presence of a multitude of people. He purchased these spiritual consolations at the cost of great bodily torments. For, having forbidden himself the use not only of meat and wine but also of wheaten bread, and accustomed to feed on coarse food, he would abstain from all nourishment whatsoever for two or three days at a stretch. He scourged himself so savagely with iron disciplines that he often flowed with copious blood; the briefest sleep he took lying on the ground.

Francis, born of noble parents at Xavier in the diocese of Pamplona, joined himself at Paris to Saint Ignatius as companion and disciple, and quickly became distinguished by a wonderful austerity of life and assiduous contemplation of divine things. Appointed by Paul III as apostolic nuncio for the Indies, he always traveled the countless provinces on foot, and often barefoot. He brought the faith to Japan and six other regions. He converted many hundreds of thousands of people to Christ in the Indies, and purified with the sacred font great princes and several kings. So great was his humility, however, that he wrote to Saint Ignatius, his superior, kneeling. The Lord confirmed his ardor for spreading the Gospel by the multitude and excellence of his miracles. At last, on the island of Sancian off the coast of China, he died on the second day of December, full of merits and worn out by his labors. Gregory XV enrolled him among the Saints, and Pius X appointed him heavenly patron of the Society and of the work of the Propagation of the Faith.

Francis of Paola was born in Calabria. As a young man, enkindled by divine ardor, he withdrew into the desert, where for six years he led a life austere in sustenance but sweet in heavenly contemplation. When the fame of his virtues spread far and wide, however, and many came flocking to him out of zeal for piety, he came forth from his solitude out of fraternal charity, built a church near Paola, and there laid the first foundations of his order. He observed perpetual virginity; he so cultivated humility as to call himself the least of all, and he wished his disciples to be called Minims. Going about in coarse garments and with bare feet, he slept on the ground. He was so devoted to charity that he appointed it as the badge of his Order. God confirmed the holiness of his servant by many miracles, among which that one is particularly celebrated whereby, having been turned away by sailors, he crossed the Strait of Sicily with a companion, having spread his cloak over the waves. He also foretold many things by the prophetic spirit. He departed to the Lord at Tours in the year of salvation 1507, in the ninety-first year of his age.

Francis of Paola was born of humble station in Paola, a town of Calabria; his parents, having long been without offspring, received him through a vow made by the intercessions of the blessed Francis. As a young man, enkindled by divine ardor, he withdrew into the desert, where for six years he led a life austere in sustenance but sweet in heavenly contemplations. But when the fame of his virtues spread further and many came flocking to him out of zeal for piety, he came forth from his solitude out of fraternal charity, built a church near Paola, and there laid the first foundations of his order.

Francis appeared adorned with a singular privilege not granted to any in former ages, when, decorated with the sacred Stigmata, he came down from the mountain bearing with him the image of the Crucified, not depicted by an artist's hand on tablets of stone or wood, but inscribed on his fleshy members by the finger of the living God. Since the seraphic man, knowing full well that it is good to keep the secret of a king, was aware of the royal mystery, he hid those sacred marks with all his strength. Yet, because it belongs to God to reveal greatly for his glory the great things he does, the Lord himself, who had secretly impressed those marks, openly manifested certain miracles through them; so that the hidden and wondrous power of the Stigmata might be made clear by the evidence of signs. Furthermore, this admirable and so abundantly attested thing, exalted with special praises and favors in pontifical documents, Pope Benedict XI wished to be celebrated with an annual solemnity; which afterward the Supreme Pontiff Paul V extended to the whole Church, so that the hearts of the faithful might be enkindled with love of the Crucified Christ.

Frances, a noble Roman matron, gave illustrious examples of virtue from her earliest years: for, spurning childish games and the allurements of the world, she took great delight in solitude and prayer. At eleven years of age she resolved to consecrate her virginity to God and to enter a monastery; yet, humbly obeying her parents' will, she married Lorenzo de' Ponziani, a young man as wealthy as he was noble. In marriage she always preserved, as far as was permitted, the resolution of a more austere life: shunning spectacles, banquets, and other diversions of this kind, wearing woolen and plain clothing, and devoting to prayer or to the service of her neighbors whatever time remained from her domestic duties; and for this she took the greatest care, that she might draw the matrons of Rome back from the pomp of the world and the vanity of adornment. Therefore, while still bound to her husband, she established in the City the house of the Oblates, under the Rule of Saint Benedict of the Congregation of Mount Olivet. Her husband's exile, the loss of their goods, and the grief of the whole household she bore not only with the utmost constancy, but, giving thanks with blessed Job, she frequently repeated those words: The Lord gave, the Lord has taken away: blessed be the name of the Lord.

Francis, the fourth Duke of Gandia, born of John Borgia and Joanna of Aragon, niece of Ferdinand the Catholic, after a childhood spent among his household servants in wonderful innocence and piety, was more admirable still for the examples of Christian virtue and austerity of life, first at the court of the Emperor Charles V and then in the governorship of Catalonia. When he had escorted the Empress Isabella to her tomb at Granada and, reading upon her disfigured face the transience of all mortal things, he bound himself by a vow to cast aside all things, as soon as the occasion arose, and to serve the King of kings alone. From that point he made such progress in virtue that, amid the turmoil of affairs, exhibiting the very image of religious perfection, he was called the wonder of princes.

Francis, born in the town of Sales, from which the family takes its name, to devout and noble parents, gave from his tender years signs of future holiness in the innocence and gravity of his manners. As a young man, educated in the liberal arts, he soon applied himself to philosophy and theology at Paris; and, that nothing might be lacking for the cultivation of his soul, he obtained the doctorate in both laws with the highest distinction at Padua. In the holy shrine of Loreto he renewed the vow of perpetual virginity by which he had earlier bound himself at Paris; from which resolution of virtue he could never be drawn away by any frauds of demons, by any allurements of the senses.

Frequent incursions by the neighboring Iroquois, who often ravaged the Huron mission, not seldom brought the lives of the Fathers into extreme peril. In the year 1642, Isaac Jogues, journeying with René Goupil, a temporal coadjutor of the Society of Jesus, from the city of Quebec to the Hurons, fell in with the Iroquois, who tortured him and his companion most cruelly and reduced them to servitude. In the same year, on the twenty-ninth day of September, René, ordered to be killed by an old savage out of hatred for the saving cross, breathed forth his most pure soul near Auriesville in the present State of New York. Isaac, the following year, having found an opportunity to escape, returned to France; but a year later he went back to America, and having ventured once and again to those same barbarians, his former torturers, with John de la Lande, also a coadjutor of the Society of Jesus, was struck with a hatchet on the eighteenth day of October in the year 1646, in the present diocese of Albany, and thus obtained the palm of martyrdom. The following day his companion John, crowned with the same crown, flew to heaven.

Now John was at once Apostle, Evangelist, and Prophet: Apostle, because he wrote to the churches as a teacher; Evangelist, because he composed the book of the Gospel, which the other eleven Apostles, with the exception of Matthew, did not do; Prophet, because on the island of Patmos, to which he had been exiled by the Emperor Domitian for bearing witness to the Lord, he saw the Apocalypse, containing the infinite mysteries of things to come. Tertullian moreover records that at Rome he was thrown into a cauldron of boiling oil, and came out purer and more vigorous than when he went in.

Gabriel, born at Assisi in Umbria, and called Francis in memory of that city's seraphic citizen, showed a distinguished character of soul. As a young man, when by the gift of a merciful God, who had long been calling him to a more perfect life, he fell ill, he began to be disgusted with the vanity of the world. Embracing the Institute of the Clerics of the Passion, he preferred to be called Gabriel of the Sorrowful Virgin, in order to keep perpetually fresh the memory of her joys and sorrows. He was accustomed to honor her with every kind of service, and especially to contemplate her worn down and afflicted by the torments of Jesus with such sorrow that he would pour forth floods of tears. He preserved the unsullied flower of his virginity, and using the austerities of his congregation, crucified utterly to the world, he lived solely for God. Thus completing the brief course of his life in the exercise of all the virtues, consumed more truly by the fire of charity than by the force of disease, and refreshed by the help of the divine Mother, he flew to the realms above in the year 1862. Pope Pius X then numbered him among the Blessed, Benedict XV among the Saints, and Pius XI was pleased to extend his Office and Mass to the whole Church.

Gabriel, born at Assisi in Umbria of an honorable family, and called Francis in memory of that city's seraphic citizen, showed a distinguished character of soul from boyhood. As a young man, when he was studying letters at Spoleto, he seemed to have been drawn somewhat by the empty appearance and pomp of the world. But by the gift of a merciful God, who had long been calling him to the perfection of the Christian life, when he fell ill, he began to be disgusted with the vanity of the world and to desire only immortal goods. In order that he might the sooner obey God who was calling him, it came about that, upon beholding the renowned icon of the most Blessed Virgin being carried in solemn procession outside the precincts of the church of Spoleto, he conceived a flame of divine love, and at the same time resolved to embrace the Institute of the Clerics of the Passion of Jesus. And so, having overcome no slight difficulties, in the retreat of Morrovalle he gladly put on the mourning habit, and preferred to be called Gabriel of the Sorrowful Virgin, in order to keep perpetually fresh the memory of her joys and sorrows.

Gallicanus, a man of consular rank, most illustrious for his triumphal honors, won the favor of the Emperor Constantine Augustus by his valor and military glory. Seeking rather the things of God, however, illumined by heavenly light through the holy John and Paul, and instructed in the teaching of the Gospel, he began to profess the faith of Jesus Christ alike in word and deed. For, withdrawing with the holy Hilarinus to Ostia Tiberina, he gave himself wholly to the care and service of pilgrims and the sick; and when the report of this spread throughout the whole world, many coming there from all sides would see a man who had been patrician and consul washing the feet of the poor, setting the table, pouring water over their hands, ministering attentively to the infirm; and finally showing even the most lowly services to the least of Christ, namely to beggars and pilgrims, as though to Christ himself.

Rejoice, Peter, to whom it was given to share in the wood of the cross of Christ. And indeed in likeness to your Master you wished to be crucified, yet not in the same upright position as Christ the Lord; but with your head turned to the ground, as one making his way from earth to heaven. George, that distinguished champion, renounced earthly service that he might become an excellent soldier of Christ; the goods he possessed he scattered among the poor, that he might possess enduring riches in heaven; his own soul too he hated in this world, that he might preserve it unto that eternal life. He had found the precious pearl hidden in the field, for which, having sold all he had, he purchased it. He had heard the Lord say: Unless a man renounce all that he possesses, he cannot be my disciple; he preferred discipleship to Christ over riches, honors, pleasures, his body, and temporal life; and therefore, fearless, armed and stripped bare, he followed Christ. He did not dread dungeons, swords, clubs, chains, the rack, torturers, fire, tyrants, nor death. Naked, he kept his gaze upon the naked Christ upon the stake, was enkindled by his example, and was strengthened by the sufferings of his Passion. O blessed soul of the martyr, which could be separated from Christ by neither tribulation nor anguish, neither stripes nor things present nor things to come!

Gelasius, African by race, son of Valerius, appointed in the place of Felix III, governed the pontificate for four years, eight months, and eighteen days. In two ordinations he created two deacons, thirty-two priests, sixty-seven bishops in various places. A man truly most ardent with a singular zeal for propagating and guarding the faith, most learned in every branch of letters, especially sacred letters, and armed with the strength of a fearless heart both to vindicate the rights of the Church and the Apostolic See and to repel the insolence of heretics and schismatics.

Gertrude, born at Eisleben in Saxony, at five years of age in the monastery of Rodarsdorf of the Order of Saint Benedict, offered her virginity and herself to Jesus Christ. She had Saint Mechtild as her teacher, and under her guidance attained to the highest gifts of contemplation. She burned with so great a charity toward the most holy Sacrament of the Eucharist and toward the Passion of the Lord that, when she called these to mind, she would be drenched with abundant tears. She wrote many things for the nourishing of piety. She also became distinguished for the gift of divine revelations and prophecy. At last, languishing more from the most ardent love of God than from illness, she departed this life, illustrious in miracles both in life and after death.

Gertrude, born at Eisleben in Saxony of noble family, at five years of age in the monastery of Rodarsdorf of the Order of Saint Benedict, offered her virginity and herself to Jesus Christ. From that time onward, wholly estranged from worldly things and diligently intent upon virtue, she established for herself a manner of heavenly life. To the knowledge of humane letters she added the knowledge of divine things; enkindled more ardently to virtue by their meditation, she soon attained Christian perfection. She would speak often about Christ and the mysteries of his life with devout feeling of soul, and, thinking only of the glory of God, she referred to it all her intentions and actions. Although she had been enriched by God with many distinguished gifts of nature and grace, she nonetheless held herself in such low esteem that among the chief marvels of divine goodness she would number this as well: that he bore with her most mercifully, utterly unworthy as she was.

Gervasius and Protasius, sons of Vitalis and Valeria, whose father suffered martyrdom for the faith of Christ the Lord at Ravenna, and whose mother did the same at Milan, distributed their patrimony to the poor and granted freedom to their household servants. For this the priests of the Gentiles conceived a monstrous hatred toward them. Wherefore, when the commander Astasius was about to go out to war, they thought they had found in this occasion an opportunity to destroy the devout brothers. Giles of Athens, of royal lineage, was so devoted from his earliest years to sacred letters and the offices of charity that he seemed to care for nothing else. And so, on the death of his parents, he distributed his entire patrimony to the poor; and going yet further, he stripped off his tunic to clothe a sick and destitute man, who, upon putting it on, immediately recovered. But thereafter made more illustrious by many miracles, fearing the celebrity of his name, he made his way to Blessed Caesarius at Arles. Departing from him after two years, he withdrew into the desert; where for a long time he lived a life of admirable holiness on roots of plants and the milk of a doe that would come to him at appointed hours. Godehard, born of honorable parentage at lower Altaich, was instructed there in the good arts while still a boy, and becoming older, professed the Rule of the holy father Benedict; he was afterward ordained priest by the holy Wolfgang, Bishop of Regensburg. When he had made wonderful progress in the pursuit of the virtues, he was created from Abbot of the monastery of Altaich as Bishop of Hildesheim, where he wrought many wonders beyond nature. Especially notable is what happened when, at the time of the sacrifice, he ordered some of his subjects who were excommunicated to leave the church, and they stubbornly refused: certain of the dead rose from their tombs in their excommunicated state and, more obedient than the living, left the church. When Godehard had pronounced absolution over them, they bowed their heads to the holy Bishop and returned to their graves; from which the living may learn to obey the commands of their bishop. At last, full of days, he rested in a blessed death in the year 1038. Illustrious by many miracles after his death, Innocent II enrolled him in the catalog of the Saints at the Council of Vienne.

She took upon herself, though herself destitute, the patronage of the sick in hospitals and of the poor with every zeal, and in order to bring relief to them, she not only labored with her own hands and deprived herself of her daily sustenance, content with morsels of bread, but also drew in nuns and matrons of the city, and wealthy men, to that work, and gathered support from every quarter she could; and moreover, to make permanent the solicitude for the poor and the infirm that she had shown, she took care to establish two confraternities charged with their care. She was most fervent in devotion to the most holy Sacrament of the Eucharist: and to promote the veneration of it in others as well, she applied all her effort to having it frequently exposed throughout the year for public veneration in solemn procession, which God showed to be pleasing to him by certain miracles. She venerated the Virgin Mother of God so devotedly that she was deemed worthy to be refreshed by her apparition. She flourished with the gifts of prophecy, contemplation, tears, and other charisms. At last, in the year 1640, at the beginning of the fifty-fifth year of her age, she was called to heaven; her body is venerated in the church of Saint Bernardino at Viterbo. Pope Benedict XIII enrolled her, glorious in merits and miracles, among the Blessed, and Pope Pius VII among the holy Virgins.

Grieving deeply that so very many peoples in remote regions were without the light of the Gospel, he was inflamed with the desire to go to those shores and pour forth the light of the true religion. But when he had learned from Saint Philip Neri, by whom he was called a true reformer, that he and his congregation were destined for the instruction of the peoples of Italy, he acquiesced in the divine will; yet he did not altogether refrain from attempting whether he might be able to bring some help to unbelievers. Hence, having taken counsel with the most devout bishop Vives, he established a group of priests whose purpose it would be to form suitable young men to be sent in turn to distant regions for the propagation of the faith. Wherefore he is rightly considered the founder of that most distinguished institute which, enlarged by the work of the Supreme Pontiffs, has served marvelously for the spreading of the Catholic faith throughout the entire world. He wrote several works on sacred and moral subjects, most suited to every condition of people. At last, never failing in his sacred ministry, he departed to the Lord in ashes and sackcloth at Rome, on the ninth day of October in the year 1609, in his sixty-sixth year of age. Pope Pius IX, Supreme Pontiff, enrolled him, illustrious in holiness and miracles, in the roll of the Blessed.

Designated Archbishop of Granada, he refused the distinguished office with wonderful humility and constancy. Yet not long afterward, compelled by the authority of his superiors, he undertook the governance of the church of Valencia; which he governed for almost eleven years in such a way as to fulfill the role of the holiest and most watchful pastor. Moreover, having changed his customary manner of living not at all, he gave himself far more freely to his insatiable charity, when he dispersed the ample revenues of the church among the needy, leaving himself not even a bed: for the one on which he lay when he was called to heaven he had obtained on loan from the same person to whom a little before he had given it as alms. He fell asleep in the Lord on the sixth day before the Ides of September, at sixty-eight years of age. God was pleased to bear witness to the holiness of his servant, both while he lived and thereafter after death, by miracles; especially when a granary, completely empty after grain had been distributed to the poor, was suddenly found to be full, and when a dead boy was restored to life at his tomb. Alexander VII, Supreme Pontiff, enrolled him, shining with these and not a few other signs, among the Saints.

When the Emperor Gratian had been slain, he went again as legate to Maximus his murderer; and when the latter refused to do penance, he withdrew from communion with him. He forbade the Emperor Theodosius to enter the church on account of the slaughter carried out at Thessalonica. When Theodosius pleaded that King David too had been both adulterer and murderer, Ambrose replied: You have followed him who sinned; follow him who repented. Wherefore Theodosius humbly performed the public penance imposed upon him by him. Thus, the holy bishop, having undergone the greatest labors and cares on behalf of the Church of God, and also having composed many books with distinction, before he fell ill he foretold the day of his death. Honoratus, Bishop of Vercelli, thrice summoned by the voice of God, hastened to him as he lay sick and offered him the holy Body of the Lord; which, having received, with his hands composed in the likeness of a cross, he gave back his soul to God in prayer on the day before the Nones of April, in the year 397 after the birth of Christ.

The grace of contemplation was admirable in him: refreshed by it continually in spirit, it sometimes happened that he abstained from all food and drink for several days. Frequently raised into the air, he was seen to shine with a wondrous radiance. He crossed rushing rivers with dry foot. He fed his brothers in extreme want with food brought down from heaven. A staff thrust by him into the ground soon grew into a green fig tree. When he was traveling by night, with heavy snow falling, he entered a roofless ruined house, and the snow hanging in the air served as a roof for him, lest he be suffocated by its weight. That he was imbued with the gift of prophecy and the discernment of spirits, holy Teresa bears witness. Finally, in his sixty-third year, at the hour he had foretold, he departed to the Lord, strengthened by a wonderful vision and by the presence of the Saints. That he was carried to heaven at that very moment the blessed Teresa, at a great distance, beheld; and afterward appearing to her, he said: O happy penance, which merited for me so great a glory! After death he became illustrious by very many miracles, and was enrolled in the catalog of the Saints by Clement IX.

Tried by serious illness, and having endured it most patiently for four months, he at last recovered and began to deliberate about taking up the religious life. To prepare the way, he rented a small dwelling on the outskirts of the city; and when he had shut himself away in it, he lived a most austere life in every respect, praying to God without ceasing that he might show him what he ought to follow. By divine providence it came about that he preferred above all others the Order of the blessed Francis, in which he excelled in humility, patience, and the other virtues of a religious. When the rector of the monastery observed this, and had already formed a clear judgment of his learning in doctrine and sacred letters, he imposed upon him the duty of preaching: which he undertook most humbly, and when he recognized himself to be insufficiently fitted for it on account of the weakness and hoarseness of his voice, he implored the help of God and was freed from this impediment, not without a miracle.

Afflicted by a grave illness, which he endured with the utmost patience for four months, he recovered at length and began to deliberate about embracing the religious life. To prepare the way for himself, he rented a small dwelling at the edge of the city; withdrawing into it, he led a life of the greatest austerity in every respect, praying to God without ceasing that he might be shown what course he ought to follow. By divine providence it came about that he chose above all others the Order of Blessed Francis, in which he excelled in humility, patience, and the other virtues of a man of religion. When the superior of the monastery took note of this, and had already come to know Bernardine's learning and mastery of the sacred Scriptures, he laid upon him the burden of preaching. Having accepted this office in all humility, yet recognizing himself to be less than adequate on account of the weakness and hoarseness of his voice, he implored the help of God, and was freed from that impediment not without a miracle.

Gregory, born of the royal line of Armenia — in which Saint Bartholomew the Apostle had first planted the faith of Christ — was called in his native tongue the Illuminator. As an infant he was secretly carried away to escape the death being sought against his family, and was devoutly reared at Caesarea in Cappadocia, where he learned the law of Christ and received Baptism. Tiridates, son of Chosroes the king of Armenia — who had been treacherously slain by Anach, the father of Gregory — had been deprived of his kingdom by the Persians and had taken refuge there. Gregory, fully aware of his father's crime, gave himself into Tiridates' service; and when Tiridates had recovered his kingdom from the Romans, Gregory returned with him to Armenia. There, repeatedly pressed by Tiridates to sacrifice to idols, he refused with the utmost constancy, and was forced to endure an almost countless and incredible variety of torments.

Gregory Barbarigo, born in Venice of a most ancient family, received his doctorate in both laws from the University of Padua with great distinction. When he was nineteen years of age and had gone to the Peace Congress of Münster, he resolved, at the urging of the pontifical legate Fabio Chigi, to devote himself to the service of the Church. Ordained to sacred orders, he was first appointed Bishop of Bergamo by the same Chigi, who had assumed the Pontificate under the name of Alexander VII; then, having been enrolled in the College of Cardinals, he was chosen for the see of Padua. In the discharge of his episcopal office, taking Saint Charles Borromeo as his model, he labored until his last breath — relying on the warnings and decrees of the Most Holy Council of Trent — to uproot vices and to foster virtue. In both dioceses he enlarged the Seminary; at Padua he enriched it especially with a library and a printing press, from which books could also be published for distribution among the peoples of the nearby East. He zealously promoted catechetical instruction, and traveled eagerly through every village of his diocese, teaching and exhorting. He shone in works of charity and holiness of life, so liberal toward the needy and poor that he spent even his household furnishings, clothing, and bed for their relief. At last, after a brief and fatal illness, he fell peacefully asleep in the Lord on the fourteenth of the Kalends of July, in the year one thousand six hundred and ninety-seven. Clement XIII enrolled him among the Blessed for his merits and virtues, and John XXIII numbered him among the Saints.

Gregory, then, having returned home for a time, was first appointed Bishop of Sasima, and afterwards administered the church of Nazianzus. Then, summoned to Constantinople to govern the church there, he brought back the city — purged of the errors of heresy — to the Catholic faith; this achievement, which should have won him the highest love of all, instead aroused the envy of many. And so, when a great schism had arisen among the bishops on that account, he willingly resigned the episcopate, applying to himself the prophetic saying: If it is on my account that this storm has arisen, cast me into the sea, that you may cease to be tossed about. Returning to Nazianzus, after he had seen to it that Eulalius was set over that church, he gave himself entirely to contemplation and to writing on divine things.

Gregory, the second of that name, a Roman by birth, son of Marcellus, was raised to the supreme pontificate of the Catholic Church in the year of Christ seven hundred and fourteen, by the wonderful unanimity of the entire clergy and people. From his boyhood he had been devoted to divine worship in the Lateran patriarchate, living under the oversight and discipline of blessed Sergius, first as a subdeacon, then serving as sacristan. The care of the library was next entrusted to him, and advancing at length to the diaconate, he set out for the imperial city together with the most holy Pope Constantine. There, questioned by the emperor on several points, he gave satisfaction to the prince with the best and most Catholic of answers, being most learned in sacred letters and a most steadfast defender of ecclesiastical affairs.
He repaired in part the walls of the city against the incursions of the Lombards. He restored several basilicas that had fallen into ruin through the ravages of time. He recalled to their former form and discipline the urban monasteries that had become nearly deserted, and the monks who inhabited them. Indeed, after the death of his mother Honesta, he converted his father's house into a church and monastery, which he left endowed with many estates. He sent Corbinian and Boniface, men filled with apostolic spirit, into Germany to preach the Gospel of Christ to the Gentiles, and adorned them with the sacred insignia of the episcopate, after receiving word that an innumerable multitude of pagans had been converted to the faith of Christ by them. That he might fulfill all the duties of a good shepherd, he ordered the discipline of the Church and the conduct of Christians with excellent laws. He held a double synod at Rome: one against unlawful marriages, another against the Iconoclasts.

Gregory the Third, a Syrian by birth, son of John, was chosen as successor to Gregory the Second upon the latter's death, by the unanimous consent of the clergy and people, and indeed by a certain divine impulse, he being the most worthy of all; this was in the year of Christ seven hundred and thirty-one. A man of singular learning and virtue, educated in both Latin and Greek, of wonderful eloquence, and gifted with so happy a memory that he could recite the whole Psalter by heart — he was at last judged by the wisest men to be the equal of his predecessor Gregory in learning and prudence.

Gregory the Great, a Roman, son of the senator Gordianus, devoted himself as a young man to philosophy; and having served in the praetorian office, after his father's death he built six monasteries in Sicily and a seventh in Rome under the name of Saint Andrew in his own home, near the basilica of Saints John and Paul on the Caelian Hill. There, under the masters Hilarion and Maximianus, he made profession of the monastic life and afterwards became abbot. Soon created cardinal deacon, he was sent as legate by Pope Pelagius to the Emperor Tiberius Constantine at Constantinople; where he also accomplished this notable deed: he so thoroughly refuted the Patriarch Eutychius, who had written against the true and tangible resurrection of bodies, that the emperor threw his book into the fire. Whereupon Eutychius, falling ill a little later and drawing near death, held the skin of his hand before many witnesses, saying: I confess that we shall all rise in this flesh.
Returning to Rome, after Pelagius had been taken away by plague, he was elected Pontiff by the highest common consent; but he refused this honor as long as he could, hiding in a cave in the garb of another. Discovered by the sign of a fiery column, he was consecrated at Saint Peter's. In his pontificate he left to his successors many examples of learning and holiness. He admitted pilgrims daily to his table; among them he received both an Angel and the Lord of Angels in the guise of a pilgrim. He graciously sustained the poor, both from the city and from without, whose number he kept on record. He restored the Catholic faith where it had been undermined in many places. For he repressed the Donatists in Africa and the Arians in Spain; he expelled the Agnoitae from Alexandria. He refused to give the pallium to Syagrius, Bishop of Autun, unless he expelled the neo-Arian heretics from Gaul. He compelled the Goths to abandon the Arian heresy. Sending to Britain the learned and holy men Augustine and other monks, he converted that island to the faith of Jesus Christ, being justly called by Bede the priest the Apostle of England. He broke the presumption of John, Patriarch of Constantinople, who arrogated to himself the name of Bishop of the Universal Church. He deterred the Emperor Mauritius from his decree forbidding soldiers to become monks.
He adorned the Church with most holy institutions and laws. Having convened a synod at Saint Peter's, he established many things: among them, that the Kyrie eleison should be repeated nine times in the Mass; that the Alleluia should be sung outside the season between Septuagesima and Easter; that the words, And dispose our days in your peace, should be added to the Canon. He augmented the Litanies, the Stations, and the Divine Office. He decreed that the four Councils — of Nicaea, Constantinople, Ephesus, and Chalcedon — should be honored like the four Gospels. He granted to the Bishops of Sicily, who by ancient custom came to Rome every three years, permission to come only once every five years. He composed many books; and when he was dictating them, Peter the deacon testified that he had often seen the Holy Spirit in the form of a dove on his head. Wonderful are the things he said, did, wrote, and decreed, especially given that his health was always frail and infirm. He was at last called to heavenly beatitude, having worked many miracles, in the thirteenth year, sixth month, and tenth day of his pontificate, on the fourth of the Ides of March — a feast day celebrated with special honor even by the Greeks on account of this Pontiff's outstanding wisdom and holiness. His body was buried in the basilica of Saint Peter, near the Sacristy.

Gregory of Nazianzus, a noble Cappadocian, who obtained the title of Theologian for his singular knowledge of the sacred Scriptures, was educated at Athens in every branch of learning together with Saint Basil, and then devoted himself to the study of sacred letters. He was first appointed Bishop of Sasima, and then administered the church of Nazianzus. Afterwards summoned to Constantinople to govern that church, he brought back the city — purged of the errors of heresies — to the Catholic faith; this achievement, which should have won him the love of all, aroused instead the envy of many. And so, when a great schism had arisen among the bishops on that account, he willingly resigned the episcopate, applying to himself the prophetic saying: If it is on my account that this storm has arisen, cast me into the sea, that you may cease to be tossed about. Returning to Nazianzus, after he had arranged for Eulalius to be set over that church, he gave himself entirely to prayer and the study of divine things. He wrote abundantly in both prose and verse, and was the most ardent champion of the consubstantiality of the Son. Under the Emperor Theodosius, worn out by old age, he passed to the heavenly life.

Gregory, Bishop of Neocaesarea in Pontus, illustrious for holiness and learning, but far more illustrious for signs and miracles — on account of the multitude and excellence of which he was called the Wonderworker, and was compared by the testimony of Saint Basil to Moses, the Prophets, and the Apostles — moved a mountain by prayer that was obstructing the building of a church. Likewise he dried up a swamp that had been a source of discord between brothers. The river Lycus, which was flooding the fields to their ruin, he checked by planting at the bank the staff on which he leaned, which immediately grew into a leafy tree, so that afterwards it never overflowed that boundary.

Very frequently he cast out demons from the images of idols and from the bodies of men, and accomplished many other wondrous deeds, by which he drew innumerable people to the faith of Jesus Christ, for he also predicted future events by the spirit of prophecy. As he was about to depart this life, he asked how many unbelievers still remained in the city of Neocaesarea; and when he was told that there were only seventeen, he gave thanks to God, saying: There were exactly that many faithful when I began my episcopate. He wrote many works, by which he further illuminated God's Church — not only by miracles.

Gregory, a noble Cappadocian, who obtained the title of Theologian for his singular knowledge of the sacred Scriptures, born at Nazianzus in Cappadocia, was educated at Athens in every branch of learning together with Saint Basil, and devoted himself to the study of sacred letters; in which studies they exercised themselves for some years in a monastery, interpreting the mind of the Scriptures not from their own ingenuity but from the reasoning and authority of the Fathers. As they flourished in learning and holiness of life, they were called to the office of preaching the evangelical truth and brought forth many children for Jesus Christ.

Pope Gregory VII, formerly Hildebrand, born at Soana in Tuscany, most distinguished for learning, holiness, and every kind of virtue, wonderfully illuminated the entire Church of God. As a young man he put on the religious habit in the monastery of Cluny, and served God with such ardor of devotion that he was chosen prior by the holy fathers of that same community. Afterwards appointed abbot of the monastery of Saint Paul Outside the Walls of the City, and then created a Cardinal of the Roman Church, he fulfilled the most important offices and legations under the Supreme Pontiffs Leo IX, Victor II, Stephen IX, Nicholas II, and Alexander II. Upon the death of Alexander II, he was unanimously elected Supreme Pontiff and proved to be the most ardent champion and defender of ecclesiastical liberty; on that account he suffered greatly and was compelled to leave Rome. His last words as he lay dying were: I have loved justice and hated iniquity; therefore I die in exile. He departed to heaven in the year of salvation one thousand and eighty-five, and his body was honorably laid to rest in the cathedral basilica of Salerno.

Pope Gregory VII, formerly Hildebrand, born at Soana in Tuscany, most distinguished for learning, holiness, and every kind of virtue, wonderfully illuminated the universal Church of God. When as a small child he played at the feet of a carpenter hewing wood, already ignorant of letters, he is said to have formed by chance from the discarded chips the characters of that Davidic oracle, He shall rule from sea to sea — the divine power guiding the boy's hand, to signify that his authority in the world would be most far-reaching. He then went to Rome and was educated under the protection of Saint Peter. As a young man, grieving deeply over the liberty of the Church oppressed by laymen and the corrupt morals of the clergy, he put on the monastic habit at Cluny — where under the rule of Saint Benedict the observance of a stricter life was then especially flourishing — and served the divine majesty with such fervor of devotion that he was chosen prior by the holy fathers of that same community. But divine providence, disposing greater things for him for the salvation of many, drew Hildebrand out from Cluny; he was elected first abbot of the monastery of Saint Paul Outside the Walls, and afterwards created a Cardinal of the Roman Church. Under the Supreme Pontiffs Leo IX, Victor II, Stephen IX, Nicholas II, and Alexander II he fulfilled the most important offices and legations; a man of most holy and pure counsel, as blessed Peter Damian called him. Sent by Pope Victor II as legate a latere into Gaul, he brought by a miracle the Bishop of Lyons — infected with the stain of simony — to confession of his crime. He compelled Berengarius at the Council of Tours to a renewed abjuration of his heresy. He also suppressed by his strength the schism of Cadalous.

William, born at Vercelli in Liguria of noble parents, had scarcely completed his fourteenth year when, burning with a wondrous ardor of devotion, he undertook a pilgrimage to Compostela to the most celebrated shrine of Saint James. This journey he pursued clothed only in a single tunic, girded with a double iron ring, and barefoot, enduring with the utmost peril of his life the most severe discomforts of cold and heat, hunger and thirst. Returning to Italy, he planned a new pilgrimage to the Holy Sepulchre of the Lord; but various and most serious obstacles intervened to prevent him from carrying out this plan, as divine providence drew the young man's religious inclination toward higher and holier things. He then lived for two years on a solitary mountain amid constant prayers, vigils, sleeping on the bare ground, and fasts; and, sustained by divine assistance, he restored sight to a blind man. When his fame from this miracle had spread abroad, William could no longer remain hidden; and so he again set his thoughts on Jerusalem, and eagerly committed himself to the journey.

William, born at Vercelli of noble parents, had scarcely completed his fourteenth year when he made a pilgrimage to Compostela with a wondrous spirit of penance and ardor of devotion. Then, a new pilgrimage to the Sepulchre of Christ the Lord having been fruitlessly attempted, he lived in hiding for two years on a solitary mountain amid constant prayers, vigils, and fasts. After he had restored sight to a blind man, he fled human esteem and built a monastery on Mount Virgilian — which thereafter was called the Virgin's — in a rough and inaccessible place; there he received companions and formed them, by word and the example of his most holy life, according to fixed rules drawn largely from the institutions of blessed Benedict. Then, as other monasteries were founded, William's growing holiness drew men to him from every side, drawn also by the fame of frequent miracles. Finally, having foretold the day of his death, he fell asleep in the Lord in the year of salvation one thousand one hundred and forty-two.

This solicitude of blessed Joseph flowed from his charity toward his neighbors; for he burned with such zeal for souls that he sought the salvation of all by every possible means with the utmost urgency. He likewise extended his charity to his neighbor, whether poor, sick, or afflicted by any other tribulation, and refreshed that person as much as was within his power. Nor were those who attacked him with reproaches, insults, and injuries of every kind estranged from his charity; for he received such treatment with the same patience, gentleness, and cheerfulness of countenance with which he shone amid so many and such great vicissitudes, while he was compelled by the order of his superiors or of the Holy Inquisition to wander and move from place to place. Yet although not only the people but also princes of rank admired his outstanding holiness and heavenly charisms, he was nonetheless so humble that, counting himself a great sinner, he earnestly besought God to withdraw his illustrious gifts from him; and he implored men to cast his dead body into a place where all memory of him would be utterly obliterated. But God, who raises the humble on high, who had adorned his servant during his life with heavenly wisdom, prophecy, the discernment of hearts, the grace of healing, and many other gifts in the most lavish measure, also made his death precious — in the place and at the time he had himself foretold — in the sixty-first year of his age, at Osimo in Picenum, and rendered his tomb glorious. Benedict XIV enrolled him among the Blessed; Clement XIII numbered him among the Saints on his rolls. And Clement XIV of the same order extended his Office and Mass to the universal Church.

The Saints, knowing this, maintained such a rule of life in their conduct. For what the Lord has now commanded, he also spoke in the Saints before his coming in the flesh; and this rule leads men to perfection. For what God has commanded must without fail be done. And therefore the Word himself, made man for our sake, did not think it unworthy — when he was sought — to hide himself as we do; and when he suffered persecution, to flee and to avoid ambushes. But when he himself had brought about the time appointed by himself, in which he willed to suffer in the body for all, he freely gave himself up to those who lay in wait for him.

This is the Lamp that is lit — namely, the power of our mind and understanding — so that the lost coin might be found again. Let no one therefore confine faith within the measure of the law; for the law is within measure, but grace is beyond measure; the law casts a shadow, grace gives light. And therefore let no one enclose his faith within the measure of the law, but let him bring it to the Church, in which the sevenfold grace of the Spirit shines, which the great High Priest illuminates with the splendor of the divine light above, lest the shadow of the law extinguish it. For that lamp which the high priest, by the ancient rite of the Jews, was accustomed to light at morning and evening hours — as it were set under the bushel of the law — has gone out; and that earthly Jerusalem, which killed the prophets, lies hidden as if placed in a valley of weeping. But that Jerusalem which is in heaven, in which our faith does battle, set upon that highest of all mountains, namely Christ, cannot be hidden in the darkness and ruin of this world; but shining with the brightness of the eternal Sun, it illumines us with the light of spiritual grace.

This is the perfection of charity — a greater cannot be found; but because it is not perfect in all, yet one in whom it is not perfect ought not to despair, provided that it has already been born and is capable of being perfected; and indeed, if it has been born, it must be nurtured, and brought by certain nourishments proper to it to its own perfection. We sought where the beginning of charity takes its start, and there we found it immediately: If anyone has the goods of this world, and sees his brother in need, and closes his heart against him, how does the love of the Father abide in him? Therefore, brethren, this charity begins here: that one gives from his surplus to the one who is in need and in some distress, freeing his brother from temporal tribulation with what he has in abundance according to the time — this is the beginning of charity. If you nourish this charity thus begun with the word of God and the hope of the life to come, you will arrive at that perfection whereby you will be ready to lay down your life for your brethren.

Among these things, filled with wisdom, he had published writings dealing with religion and faith; he had often also, indulging in well-turned verse, celebrated the deeds of the Saints in harmonious verse, having attained the highest fame as a Christian poet. However many men were most outstanding in holiness and learning at that time, so many did he bind to himself in friendship and admiration. Very many came to him from every direction, as to a master of Christian perfection. When Campania was laid waste by the Goths, he gave over all his wealth for the feeding of the poor and the ransoming of captives, leaving nothing for himself, not even the necessities of life. Afterwards, when the Vandals were ravaging those same regions, a widow begged him to ransom her son who had been taken captive by the enemy; and when all his goods had been spent in works of devotion, he gave himself as a slave in the son's place, and was cast in chains and carried off to Africa. At last, not without the manifest assistance of God, he was given his freedom and returned to Nola, where the good shepherd again visited his beloved flock; and there, in the seventy-eighth year of his age, he fell asleep in the Lord with a most peaceful end. His body, laid near the tomb of Saint Felix, was afterwards translated to Benevento in the time of the Lombards, and then, under the Emperor Otto III, to Rome at the basilica of Saint Bartholomew on the Tiber Island. But Pope Pius X ordered the sacred remains of Paulinus to be restored to Nola, and raised his feast to a double rite for the universal Church.

This lance, by opening his very side, opened for us the most sacred gates of the heavenly kingdom. This lance, by wounding him who was already dead, healed our wounds and restored life and salvation to us. This lance, by piercing him who was without sin, wiped away our faults with his Blood; and at last, irrigated by the most sacred streams of that same Blood, it took away the darkness of our blindness and cleansed us with the rivers of his divine mercy. Those sweet nails also, with which the Savior himself was affixed to the Cross — nails that were not only worthy to be sprinkled with his immaculate Blood and to bear the weight of so great a burden, but through whose saving wounds we also received such a sweetness of his divine charity that our hands were freed from the bonds of sin and our feet were liberated from the snares of death — are to be devoutly commemorated.

These things I have therefore often on my lips, as you know; these things always in my heart, as God knows; these things most familiar to my pen, as is apparent; these things are my higher philosophy for the present: to know Jesus, and him crucified. I do not seek, as the bride does, where he rests at midday — for I joyfully embrace him as he dwells among my breasts. I do not seek where he feeds at midday, for I behold the Savior on the Cross. That is more sublime, this is sweeter; that is bread, this is milk; this refreshes the inner parts of little ones; this fills the breasts of mothers; and therefore he shall dwell between my breasts. Do you also, most beloved, gather up this so beloved bundle for yourselves; insert it into the marrow of your hearts; with this guard the entrance of your breast, that he may also dwell between your breasts. For if you keep before your eyes him whom you carry, seeing for certain the sufferings of the Lord, you will bear your own more lightly — with the help of him who is the Spouse of the Church above all things, God blessed forever. Amen.

She is said to have endured a martyrdom of thirteen years. How much more detestable is the cruelty that spared not even her tender age; indeed, how great is the power of faith that found even from that age a witness! Was there room for a wound in that little body? And she who had nothing whereby to receive the sword had that whereby to conquer the sword. Fearless amid the bloody hands of executioners, unmoved by the heavy dragging of clanking chains, now offering her whole body to the raging sword of the soldier — not yet knowing how to die, yet ready — even if she were dragged unwilling to the altars, stretching out her hands to Christ through the flames and signing the trophy of the victorious Lord in those sacrilegious fires; now inserting neck and both hands into iron fetters. But no bond could enclose such slender members. A new kind of martyrdom! Not yet fit for punishment, yet already ripe for victory; hard to combat, easy to crown: she fulfilled the school of virtue, who bore with her the prejudice of her age.

Today that prophecy is fulfilled which says: Drop down dew, you heavens, from above, and let the clouds rain down the Just One; let the earth open and bring forth the Savior. Therefore, he who had made became himself, so that he who had been lost might be found. For in the Psalms man confesses: Before I was humbled, I sinned. Man sinned and became guilty; man and God was born so that the guilty one might be freed. Man therefore fell, but God descended. Man fell wretchedly, God descended mercifully; man fell through pride, God descended with grace.

Today the immaculate Virgin, who was defiled by no earthly affections but was formed in heavenly thoughts, has not returned to earth; but, since she was a living heaven, she is placed in the heavenly tabernacles. For from whom true life flowed to all — how could she taste death? But she submits to the law laid down by him whom she bore; and as a daughter of the old Adam, she underwent the ancient sentence (for her Son also, who is life itself, did not refuse it); yet as the Mother of the living God, she is worthily assumed to him.
