Helena, having found the saving Cross, built a most magnificent church there, in which she left a part of the Cross enclosed in silver reliquaries, and brought a part to her son Constantine; this was kept at Rome in the church of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem, built in the Sessorian palace. She also brought nails to her son — those with which the most holy body of Jesus Christ had been fixed to the Cross. From that time Constantine enacted a law that the cross should no longer be used as an instrument of punishment for anyone. Thus the object that had formerly been a reproach and mockery to men began to be held in veneration and glory.

Having assumed the habit of the Third Order of Saint Dominic, she doubled her former austerities of life: into a long and very rough hairshirt she wove tiny needles here and there; under her veil she wore day and night a crown armed within with dense points. Following hard in the footsteps of Saint Catherine of Siena, she girded her loins with a triple-linked iron chain. She fashioned her bed of knotted logs, filling the empty joints with fragments of pottery. She built herself a very narrow cell in the far corner of a garden, where, dedicated to heavenly contemplation, she exhausted her body with frequent disciplines, fasting, and vigils; yet invigorated in spirit, she trod down and overcame the assaults of demons in frequent combat, fearless and victorious.

Moved by this devotion of Augustine, Valerius engaged him as an assistant in the episcopal office. No one was more humble than he, no one more continent. His bed and clothing were moderate, his table plain — which he always seasoned with sacred reading or discussion. Such was his kindness to the poor that, when there was no other resource, he would break the sacred vessels to sustain their need. He avoided the company and familiarity of women — even his sister and his brother's daughter — saying that even if women relatives were not themselves suspect, those who came frequently to visit them could give rise to suspicion. He never ceased from preaching the word of God until he was laid low by serious illness. Persistently pursuing heretics both in person and in writing, and giving them no rest anywhere, he freed Africa in large part from the error of the Manicheans, Donatists, Pelagians, and other heretics besides.

Raised to this dignity, he yielded nothing of his former manner of life, and had at heart nothing but the divine worship and the salvation of the sheep entrusted to him. A strenuous champion of Catholic unity and truth, he labored with all his strength to bring back schismatics and heretics to communion with the See of blessed Peter. He never ceased to defend the Supreme Pontiff and the fullness of his power from the most shameless calumnies and errors of the impious, both by sermons and by writings full of piety and learning. He vindicated episcopal jurisdiction and the goods of the Church from usurpation by laymen. It is incredible how many heretics he recalled to the bosom of mother Church. Indeed, pontifical documents expressly testify that Josaphat was the most eminent promoter of the union of the Greek Church with the Latin. Beyond this, he willingly expended the revenues of his table on restoring the beauty of the house of God, on building houses for consecrated virgins, and on assisting other pious works. So open-handed toward the poor was he that once, when nothing was at hand to relieve a certain widow's need, he ordered his episcopal pallium, that is, his omophorion, to be pledged.

She is the mother of him who was begotten by the Father before all beginning, whom Angels and men acknowledge as the Lord of all things. Do you wish to know by how much this Virgin surpasses the heavenly powers? They stand before him with fear and trembling, veiling their faces; she offers to him the human race — the one whom she bore. Through her we also obtain the pardon of sins. Hail therefore, Mother, heaven, maiden, virgin, throne, glory and adornment and firm foundation of our Church — intercede for us unceasingly with Jesus your Son and our Lord, that through you we may find mercy on the day of judgment, and that we may obtain the good things laid up for those who love God, by the grace and goodness of our Lord Jesus Christ: to whom, together with the Father and the Holy Spirit, be glory, honor, and dominion now and for ever and ever. Amen.

By this manner of life and by his zeal for the reform of monastic discipline, he recalled not only his own monastery but also those of Hersfeld, Tegernsee, and Kremsmünster — the care of which rested upon him — to the perfect observance of the holy rule. His fame for holiness having spread far and wide, Godehard was called by the holy Emperor Henry to govern the church of Hildesheim. Long and much resistant, he at last obeyed the manifest call of God and was appointed Bishop of that church. How great his holiness then shone forth, the wonderful works which God deigned to accomplish through him sufficiently declare.
Hadrian III ...

Hadrian, who at the command of the Emperor Maximian was persecuting Christians at Nicomedia, having repeatedly marveled at their constancy in confessing the faith and enduring torments, was powerfully moved by this and converted himself to Christ. For this reason he was thrown into prison along with twenty-three other Christians; where his wife Natalia, who had herself already believed in Christ, came to visit him and enkindled him to martyrdom. And so, led out from custody, he was flogged until his bowels were laid open. Finally, with his legs broken and his hands and feet cut off, he brought the contest of martyrdom to a happy close together with many others.

The gates of hell shall not hold fast this confession, the bonds of death shall not bind it; for that voice is the voice of life. And just as it raises those who confess to the heavenly realms, so it plunges those who deny into the depths below. For this reason he says to the most blessed Peter: To you I will give the keys of the kingdom of heaven; and whatever you bind on earth shall be bound also in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth shall be loosed also in heaven. Indeed, the power of this authority passed also to the other Apostles, and the establishment of this decree spread to all rulers of the Church; but it is not without reason that it is entrusted to one man, even as it is made known to all. For it is entrusted to Peter individually because the form of Peter is set before all who govern the Church. Peter's privilege therefore endures wherever judgment is rendered according to his equity. Nor is there excess in either severity or leniency, where nothing shall be bound, nothing loosed, except what blessed Peter shall either loose or bind.

Hedwig, illustrious by royal birth, the aunt of Saint Elizabeth daughter of the King of Hungary, was given in marriage at twelve years of age to Henry, Duke of Poland, and reared the children born of that union in the fear of God. That she might be more free to devote herself to God, she persuaded her husband, by a mutual vow and unanimous consent, to separate from the marriage bed. After his death she herself received the Cistercian habit in the monastery of Trebnitz; and there, intent on contemplation, she took delight in attending the Divine Office and the solemn celebrations of Mass without fail. Flourishing in the most exalted virtues, most strict penance, gravity of counsel, and purity of soul, she became an outstanding example of religious devotion. It was habitual with her to subject herself freely to all, to undertake the most lowly tasks, to serve the poor on bended knee, to wash and kiss the feet of lepers. Her wonderful patience and constancy of soul shone out especially at the death of Henry, Duke of Silesia, her son slain in battle by the Tartars. Clement IV enrolled her among the Saints, renowned as she was for the glory of miracles, especially after her death.

Hedwig, illustrious by royal birth but far more illustrious by the innocence of her life, the aunt of Saint Elizabeth daughter of the King of Hungary, daughter of Berthold and Agnes the Margraves of Moravia, showed from her earliest years a moderation of soul. For even as a small child she abstained from childish things, and being given in marriage at twelve years of age by her parents to Henry Duke of Poland, having faithfully kept the fidelity of the marriage bed, she reared the children born of that union in the fear of God. That she might be more free to devote herself to God, she persuaded her husband, by a mutual vow and unanimous consent, to separate from the marriage bed. After his death, inspired by God whom she had sought in constant prayer, she devoutly received the Cistercian habit in the monastery of Trebnitz; and there, intent on contemplation, attending the Divine Office and the solemn celebrations of Mass assiduously from sunrise until midday, she bravely despised the ancient enemy of the human race.

The holy virgin had her dwelling and her tomb at Heidenheim until the time of Otkar the sixth Bishop of Eichstätt. By his authority and with the approval of the clergy, the relics of the most chaste virgin were translated to Eichstätt with a solemn procession attended by people of every rank, to the place that now bears the name of Saint Walburga; yet in such a way that part of the sacred relics should pass to the monastery of Monheim at the request of the abbess Lioba. At both places very many miracles soon began to be reported. Eichstätt has this special distinction: from the blessed bones of Walburga kept there flows a most limpid oil, health-giving for various infirmities.

Henry, surnamed the Pious, from Duke of Bavaria became King of Germany and afterwards Emperor of the Romans, and devoted himself zealously to the advancement of religion. He made the See of Bamberg, founded with his hereditary wealth, subject to blessed Peter and the Roman Pontiff; he received the fugitive Benedict VIII and restored him to his See; and, having undertaken a war for the protection of the Roman Church against the Greeks, he recovered Apulia, long held by them. Protected by divine assistance, he overcame barbarous nations more by prayers than by arms. He brought Pannonia, still unbelieving, to the faith by giving his sister in marriage to King Stephen and having him baptized. He joined virginity to marriage, and on his deathbed restored his holy wife Cunegund to her kinsmen undefiled. Finally, more illustrious for holiness than for his scepter, he was called to the rewards of the heavenly kingdom in the year one thousand and twenty-four, and was numbered among the Saints by Eugene III.

To Eve it was given to cover the sensible body on account of sensible nakedness; but to Mary it was given by God that she might bear for us the Lamb and the Sheep, and that from the glory of that Lamb and Sheep there might be made for us, as it were from fleece, through his power, in wisdom, the garment of incorruptibility. Eve also became the cause of death for men, for through her death entered into the world; but Mary is the cause of life, through whom life was born for us, and through her the Son of God came into the world. And where sin abounded, there grace also superabounded; and from where death was brought in, from there life also proceeded, that life might be made in place of death; and he who through a woman became life for us might exclude the death brought in through a woman. And since there Eve, while still a virgin, transgressed through disobedience; on the contrary, through a Virgin obedience unto grace was accomplished, when the coming in the flesh from heaven was announced, and eternal life.

For Eve mourned, but she rejoiced; Eve carried tears in her womb, Mary carried joy; because the one brought forth a sinner, the other brought forth the Innocent. The mother of our race brought punishment upon the world, the Mother of our Lord brought salvation upon the world. Eve was the author of sin, Mary the author of merit. Eve by killing did harm, Mary by giving life did good. The one struck, the other healed. For disobedience is exchanged for obedience, faithlessness is recompensed by faith.

Eve, who gave her assent to the suggestion of the serpent, is condemned to the pain of childbirth and the sentence of death, and is placed in the depths of the underworld. But this truly blessed woman, who gave ear to the word of God, was filled with the operation of the Holy Spirit, and conceived the Son of God at the spiritual greeting of the Archangel without pleasure and without union with a man, and bore him without any pain, and consecrated her whole self to God — how could death devour her? How could the underworld receive her? How could corruption invade that body in which Life was received? For her the way to heaven is made straight, level, and easy. For if, as the life and truth Christ says, Where I am, there also shall my servant be, how much more shall the mother be with him?

There is, however, this one and singular incident that has not been forgotten. For when a plague of elephantiasis had arisen from very violent earthquakes, while the most holy Pontiff was watching over the afflicted City and with rare example visiting the sick in person, he gently embraced and kissed one of them in whom he beheld Christ, and by divine miracle cleansed him from the leprosy, as the ancient monuments of the Church attest. A fragment of a letter written by him survives, containing a luminous decree on spiritual relationship. After sitting there for three years, he departed this life in the year of Christ six hundred and seventeen, and was buried in the Vatican.

Here the opinions of philosophy were to be trampled down, here the vanities of earthly wisdom were to be dissolved, here the worship of demons was to be refuted, here the impiety of all sacrileges was to be destroyed — a place where with the most diligent superstition there had been gathered together whatever had anywhere been established by vain errors. To this city, then, do you, most blessed Apostle Peter, come without fear; and, while your companion in glory, the Apostle Paul, is still occupied with establishing other churches, you enter — more steadfast than when you walked upon the sea — this forest of roaring beasts and this ocean of most turbulent depths.

This is he whom, by divine inspiration, Isaiah prophetically announces, saying: A voice of one crying in the desert, Prepare the way of the Lord. How fittingly, dearest brethren, was blessed John proclaimed a voice — he who was sent as both the herald and the witness of the heavenly Word. This is he whose birth, name, and merit are foretold through the Angel Gabriel. This is he who by heavenly judgment is preferred above all mortals, the Lord saying: There has not arisen among those born of women one greater than John the Baptist. How beautifully it is said that there is none greater among those born of women: for he was in every way greater than John who was born of a Virgin.

This salt, therefore, made for every use of the human race, bestows incorruptibility on the bodies upon which it is sprinkled, and is most suited to every taste of seasoned food. The Apostles, however, are the preachers of heavenly things and, as it were, sowers of eternity, conferring immortality on all bodies upon which their word has been sprinkled. Therefore they were fittingly called the salt of the earth — preserving bodies for eternity in the manner of salting through the power of their teaching.

He was blessed not by his name alone, but also by the grace of heavenly blessing and the example of his holy life: gentle, meek and humble, remarkable also for patience, and most loving of the poor, upon whom he poured out with a generous hand the revenues of the Church. He also applied mind and hand to restoring and adorning the basilica of the Prince of the Apostles and other churches of the City, on which he piously spent many thousands of gold pieces.

He, in gratitude and mindful of the great benefit received from the Prince of the Apostles through the conferral of holy orders, while still a priest, built and adorned in the Vatican a memorial or church dedicated to the Prince of the Apostles — fittingly called by the ancient Fathers the trophy of the Apostles — which was found never to have been overthrown by any tempest of raging persecution, but, what surpasses all admiration, to have grown day by day in greater glory: a noble beginning, to be sure, of the greater and more ample structure to follow in later times.

Hence it came about that he was imprisoned, beaten with rods and scorpions, burned with the flames of torches, torn, racked, and slain. In all these things, since he lived in Christ, he showed himself as one dead. Not a single word of complaint resounded in him, not a single impulse of resistance. Like a preeminent warrior he deemed it incongruous that, while the King was suffering and dying for the salvation of souls, he himself should live slothfully and perish without the exercise of combat. He often turned over in his mind that saying of the Gospel: Greater love than this no one has, that a man lay down his life for his friends. For this reason he chose to show by his deeds rather than his words the love he bore for the Lord. He was not ungrateful in imitating his Redeemer in death — of whom the Prophet says: As a sheep he was led to slaughter, and like a lamb before its shearer without a voice, so he did not open his mouth. This man fell utterly silent and opened his mouth only in prayer, so that he might become an acceptable sacrifice to God the Father, and that he might be found no less like him in long-suffering patience, who in the suffering of the punishment of the Cross uttered no word of contradiction. Hence it came to pass that, as he had been a companion of his Lord's suffering, so he was made a partaker of his glory, who triumphs in the heavenly kingdom with the Father and the Holy Spirit forever.

Hence Isaiah says to these same preachers: Prepare the way of the Lord, make straight the paths of our God. Hence the Psalmist says to the sons: Make way for him who ascends above the west. For the Lord ascended above the west: because from where he lay down in his Passion, from there he manifested his greater glory by rising. He ascended above the west, that is; because the death he endured, he trampled down by rising. For him therefore who ascends above the west we make way, when we proclaim his glory to your minds, that he himself may come afterwards and, by the presence of his love, illumine them.

We read that by new decrees he established many excellent ordinances concerning the morals of the faithful, the liberty of the clergy, and the sacred rites: namely, that he restored by a new edict the Lenten fast, long since handed down by the Apostles; and that he commanded the holy sacrifice of the Mass to be celebrated three times on Christmas — at midnight, at the dawning of the day, and at the third hour after sunrise; and that he decreed that the angelic hymn of the sacred Liturgy, Glory to God in the highest, should be added.

Hippolytus, baptized by Saint Lawrence, was apprehended in his home while receiving the Eucharist, and brought before the Emperor Valerian; questioned by him concerning the profession of his religion, he freely professed himself a Christian. For this he was beaten with clubs; and when his faith was found the more steadfast under this beating, he was tempted with gifts and promises of honors. When all of these were spoken to no avail, he was handed over to the prefect to be killed. The prefect, coming to Hippolytus' house to confiscate his goods, discovered that his entire household was Christian; and when these had been deterred from the Christian faith in vain, he first had Concordia, the nurse of Hippolytus who was strengthening the others, beaten to death with leaded whips, and then ordered the rest to be put to death outside the Tiburtine gate. Hippolytus, dragged by wild horses through places covered with thorns and thistles, with his body torn apart, gave up his spirit to God, and was buried together with the others by the priest Justin in the field of Verano. On the same day, at Forum Syllae, the martyr Cassian was put to death with most cruel torment; bound with his hands behind his back, he was handed over to be pierced and torn apart with iron styluses by the boys he was teaching. The weaker their strength, the more painful and prolonged was his martyrdom — and the more glorious his palm.

These things accomplished, the holy Pontiff turned to restoring and building churches. At his urging the devout woman Demetria built the church of Saint Stephen on her estate on the Via Latina, three miles from the City; he himself founded another on the Via Appia under the name of Saint Cornelius. He furthermore restored many other sacred buildings and their sacred vessels. In the three basilicas of Peter, Paul, and the Lateran he constructed vaulted chambers; he built a monastery adjacent to the basilica of Saint Peter; he appointed guardians for the tombs of the Apostles, whom he called cubicularii. He decreed that in the celebration of the mystery the words should be said: A holy sacrifice, an immaculate victim. He enacted that no consecrated virgin should receive the blessed veil for her head unless she had proved her virginity for forty years. These and other notable achievements accomplished, having written much that was holy and distinguished, he fell asleep in the Lord on the fourth of the Ides of November. He occupied the pontificate for twenty-one years, one month, and thirteen days.

Imbued with these and other virtues, the holy king was hastening toward the highest summit of perfection. But it came to pass that the kingdom of England was invaded by William, Duke of the Normans, with a formidable army. When the English implored the help of the Danes, and the king had resolved to go to their aid, he entrusted the conduct of the war to his brother Olaf. But Olaf, enticed by the desire of ruling, turned his arms against the king's destruction, stirring up soldiers and people against him. Nor were there lacking fuel for the rebellion. For when the king, by issuing laws, had decreed that tithes be paid to the churches, that the precepts of God and the Church be observed, and that transgressors be punished, many wicked and evil men were embittered and began first to make tumult, then to stir up the common people, and finally to plot the death of the most holy king.

Therefore the Apostle Peter, enkindled by these revelations of the mysteries, despising worldly things and scorning earthly things, was caught up by a certain ecstasy of mind into desire for eternal things; and, filled with the joy of the whole vision, he desired to dwell there with Jesus where he rejoiced in his manifest glory. Hence he said: Lord, it is good for us to be here; if you will, let us make three tabernacles here: one for you, one for Moses, and one for Elijah. But the Lord did not assent to this desire — signifying that what he desired was not wrong, but disordered; since the world could not be saved except by the death of Christ, and in the example of the Lord, the faith of believers was called to this: that though one ought not to doubt the promises of beatitude, we should nonetheless understand that among the temptations of this life, patience must first be sought from us before glory.

By these works of mercy which he showed to his brethren, he merited the mercy of the heavenly Father, and to be associated with Christ the Son of God in his Passion. For when the impious Apostate Julian had seized the empire, Gallicanus was driven from that seat of mercy and the hospice of the poor and pilgrims, and went to Alexandria; where the judge Raucianus commanded him to sacrifice to demons, that is, to the gods of the pagans. But the soldier of Christ, scorning the judge's threats and disregarding his enticements, teaching that honor is owed not to the idols of the Gentiles as to dead images but to the living God alone, showed himself ready for torments and death. And so, struck down by the sword, he crowned with glorious martyrdom a life made noble by the service of the poor.

Moved by this, Urban V sent Andrew as legate to Bologne to quell the disturbances there. In this mission he endured much, and with great prudence extinguished the hatreds of the citizens that had blazed up to the point of mutual slaughter; then, tranquillity being restored, he returned home. Not long afterwards, worn out by constant labors and voluntary mortification of the flesh, he departed for the heavenly kingdom on the day of his death foretold to him by the Blessed Virgin, in the year of the Lord one thousand three hundred and seventy-three, in the seventy-first year of his age. Urban VIII enrolled him among the Saints, illustrious for many and great miracles. His body rests in Florence in the church of his order, and is venerated with the greatest reverence by the citizens, to whom it was more than once a protection in present danger.

But when they frequently rendered this office of Christian charity to one another, the emperors took it in bad part, summoned Cornelius to Rome as one accused of lèse-majesté, had him beaten with leaded whips, and dragged him to the statue of Mars, ordering him to sacrifice to it. But this same thing also befalls those who say that he suffered only in appearance. For if he did not truly suffer, there is no grace in him, since there was no passion; and when we begin to suffer truly, he will seem to be a deceiver, exhorting us to be struck and to offer the other cheek, if he himself did not first do so in truth. And just as he deceived them, so that he appeared to them to be what he was not, so he deceives us, exhorting us to endure what he himself did not endure. But we shall be above the Master, when we suffer and sustain things which the Master neither suffered nor sustained. But since our Lord alone is truly the Master and truly the good Son of God; and the suffering Word of God the Father, made the son of man — for he struggled and conquered; for he was a man contending for the fathers, and through obedience discharging the debt of disobedience. For he bound the strong one, and freed the weak, and bestowed salvation on his creature, destroying sin. Therefore those who say that he appeared in appearance only, that he was not born in the flesh nor truly made man, are still under the ancient condemnation.

But this which I said last seems to have the more evangelical meaning; for it follows: And he who hates his soul in this world keeps it for eternal life. Therefore what was said above — He who loves — it is understood: in this world, keeps it himself for eternal life. A great and wonderful saying: how a man's love for his own soul is such that it perishes, and hatred of it that it does not perish. If you have loved badly, then you have hated; if you have hated well, then you have loved. Blessed are those who have hated by keeping, lest they lose by loving.

Yet what I said later seems more to have an evangelical sense; for it follows: And he who hates his soul in this world keeps it unto eternal life. Therefore, what was said above, He who loves, is to be understood as: he who loves in this world will in any case lose it; but he who hates in this world will in any case keep it unto eternal life. A great and wondrous saying, how for a man there can be love for his soul such that it perishes, and hatred such that it does not perish. If you have loved it badly, then you have hated it; if you have hated it well, then you have loved it. Blessed are they who have hated it by keeping it, lest they lose it by loving it.

Therefore let us hold to this commandment of the Lord, that we love one another, and whatever else he has commanded, we shall do; for whatever else there is, we have it here. This love is, to be sure, distinguished from that love by which people love one another; for in order to distinguish it, there was added: As I have loved you. For why does Christ love us, if not that we might reign with Christ? To this end, then, let us also love one another, so that we may distinguish our love from that of others, who do not love one another for this end, because they do not truly love. But those who love one another for the sake of possessing God — these truly love themselves. Therefore, in order to love themselves, they love God. This love is not in all people: few love themselves for this reason, that God may be all in all.

In this service he showed himself to be such a teacher of truth that he likewise offered himself as an example of virtue. Assiduous in prayer, vigils, and fasts, supremely beneficent and generous toward the poor. Devoted to divine worship, he partly built and partly restored sacred churches. Above all, he promoted the beauty of the Church, the Bride of Christ, by restoring the fallen discipline of the sacred order and by ensuring regular observance among monks. He founded two distinguished monasteries: one of Blessed Nicholas near Passau on the Inn, and one of Blessed Mary on Mount Göttweig on the Danube. He cooperated in the founding or restoration of other monasteries as well, so that through him a new splendor of religious life seemed to spread everywhere.

In this place, in order to deceive the world by a new strategy, he took up a hard struggle: amid the long laments of his wife and parents, amid the contempt of servants, for seventeen years he offered an example of admirable virtue and unconquered patience, known to God alone. After his death, identified by his own written testament — which contained his name, lineage, and the whole course of his life — he was brought with the highest honor, under Pope Innocent I, to the church of Saint Boniface, which is also called by the name of Saint Alexis, where to this day he is venerated with devout reverence by the faithful. The Roman Senate, desiring to show fitting piety toward so distinguished a fellow citizen, obtained from the Supreme Pontiff Clement XII that his feast day be celebrated with a more solemn rite in Rome and in its district.

God showed by a miracle how acceptable to him was this manner of life. For when shortly thereafter these seven men were going from door to door through the city of Florence begging alms, it came to pass that suddenly by the voice of infants — among whom was Saint Philip Benizi, who had scarcely entered the fifth month of his age — they were acclaimed Servants of Blessed Mary: by which name they were thereafter always called. Therefore, led by love of solitude and the desire to avoid the gatherings of the people, they all assembled in the secluded heights of Monte Senario, and there undertook a certain heavenly manner of life. They lived in caves, content with water alone and herbs; they wore down their bodies with vigils and other austerities, meditating continually on the Passion of Christ and the sorrows of his most sorrowful Mother. When they were once observing this more earnestly on the sacred day of Good Friday, the Blessed Virgin herself appeared to them again, showed them a mournful garment to wear, and signified that it would be most pleasing to her if they were to establish a new religious order in the Church that would perpetually recall and promote the memory of the sorrows she had endured beneath the Cross of the Lord. When Saint Peter, the illustrious Martyr of the Order of Preachers, had learned this from his familiar association with those holy men and also from a special vision of the Mother of God, he urged them to establish a religious order under the name of Servants of the Blessed Virgin: which was afterward approved by Pope Innocent IV.

They are certainly to be honored — and in such a way that we build temples to God in their name, offer gifts, keep their memory, and find spiritual joy in it; so that our rejoicing may be fitting to those by whom we are invited, lest, while we strive to honor and please them, we rather offend and provoke them. For the things by which God is worshipped are also those in which his servants delight; and the things by which God is offended are likewise those by which his soldiers are offended. Therefore let us honor the saints with psalms, and hymns, and spiritual canticles, with contrition, and with compassion for those who are in want — the very duties by which God is chiefly conciliated; let us erect statues and visible images to them; indeed, let us ourselves, by imitating their virtues, bring it about that we are their living statues and images.

Hormisdas, a Campanian by birth, whose father Justus was from Frosinone, was advanced to the holy See of Peter by unanimous consent seven days after the death of Symmachus, already being then a deacon of the holy Roman Church. In this office he so conducted himself and labored so diligently in feeding the Lord's flock that it became evident he had been chosen not without singular divine providence and divine counsel. For the Church at that time had need of such a man, who would both boldly undertake difficult tasks and vigorously bring them to their desired end.

The neighboring cities, each according to its zeal for adopting one of the martyrs as its own patron before God, took care of the burial of their bodies. The Neapolitans, guided by a divine admonition, took up the body of Januarius; which, translated first to Benevento, then to the monastery of Monte Vergine, and finally laid to rest in the chief church of Naples, was renowned for many miracles. But this above all is to be remembered: that it extinguished masses of flame once bursting forth from Mount Vesuvius, which were bringing fear of devastation not only to neighboring but also to distant regions. This too is remarkable: that his blood, which is preserved congealed in a glass vial, is seen to this day, when placed before the head of the same Martyr, to liquefy and bubble in a wondrous manner, just as if freshly shed.

By daily and nightly meditation on these words and deeds of the Lord, let us repel the troublesome assaults of vain and harmful thoughts; by frequent reflection on them let us take care to correct both ourselves and our neighbors from vain and slyly sweetened conversations of detraction, and to kindle ourselves to frequent divine praise.
(but on Monday these are said)

For if, dearest brethren, we desire to dwell in the blessedness of the age to come in the house of the Lord and to praise him forever, it is surely necessary that in this age too we earnestly practice what we seek in the age to come: namely, by frequenting the precincts of the Church, and not only singing there the praises of the Lord, but also in every place of his dominion showing forth by words and deeds alike those things that conduce to the praise and glory of our Creator.

He preached things congruent with this great sublimity of the beginning, and spoke of the divinity of the Lord as no one else has done: he poured out what he had drunk in. For not without reason is it related in this very Gospel about him, that at the supper he reclined upon the Lord's breast. From that breast he drank in secret, but what he drank in secret he poured out openly: so that to all nations there might come not only the Incarnation of the Son of God, his Passion, and Resurrection, but also what he was before the Incarnation — the Only-Begotten of the Father, the Word of the Father, coeternal with the one who begets him, equal to the one by whom he was sent.
To this reading indeed…

His genius and virtue shone forth most of all in overthrowing the heretics who were striving to corrupt the people of Toulouse with pernicious errors; in this endeavor he spent seven years. Afterward he came to Rome to the Lateran Council with the Bishop of Toulouse, in order that the order he had founded might be confirmed by Innocent III. While this matter was under deliberation, Dominic, at the Pope's urging, returned to his own people to choose a rule for himself. Returning to Rome, he obtained from Honorius III, who had succeeded Innocent, confirmation of the Order of Preachers. At Rome he established two monasteries, one for men and one for women. He also raised three dead persons to life, and performed many other miracles, by which the Order of Preachers began to spread marvelously.
Of this transformation…

His discourse ought to be pure, simple, open, full of gravity and honesty, full of sweetness and grace, treating of the mystery of the law, the doctrine of faith, the virtue of continence, the discipline of justice: admonishing each person with varied exhortation, according to his calling and the quality of his morals — namely, that he should know in advance what, to whom, when, or how he is to speak. His special duty above all others is to read the Scriptures, to study the Canons, to imitate the examples of the saints, to give himself to vigils, fasts, and prayers, to maintain peace with his brethren, and not to tear asunder any member of his body; to condemn no one unless proven guilty, to excommunicate no one unless examined. And he ought to preside with humility and authority alike, so that neither through excessive humility should he allow the vices of his subjects to grow strong, nor through immoderate severity should he exercise power, but be so much the more watchful over those entrusted to him as he fears more gravely to be searched out by Christ.

The charity of this man shone forth in particular when, having sold the principality of Oria, he distributed the entire sum — some forty thousand gold pieces — to the poor in a single day. With no less devotion he distributed twenty thousand which had been left to him as a bequest. He resigned the ecclesiastical revenues with which his uncle had abundantly endowed him, retaining some for his own needs and the necessities of the poor. When a plague was ravaging Milan, he gave away his household furnishings to feed the sick — save a single bed — and thereafter lay on a bare plank; he diligently visited those afflicted by the disease, refreshed them with fatherly affection, and wonderfully consoled them by administering the sacraments of the Church with his own hands. Meanwhile, approaching as a reconciler with the most humble prayers, having declared a public supplication, with a rope bound about his neck, his bare feet even wounded and bleeding on the rough ground, carrying a cross, offering himself as a victim for the sins of the people, he strove to avert divine wrath. He was the fiercest champion of ecclesiastical liberty. Solicitous for the restoration of discipline, while he was intent on prayer, a fuse on a war machine was lit by agitators and he was struck by a shot, yet was preserved unharmed by divine power.

He excelled so greatly in humility that, coming to Rome and received in a hospice for the poor, he associated himself with a leper, and steadfastly refused the ecclesiastical dignities offered him by Paul V. He preserved his virginity spotless all his life, and shameless women who plotted against his chastity he won for Christ. Burning with ardent love for the most holy mystery of the Eucharist, he spent almost entire nights sleeplessly in its adoration — which devout practice he established as a badge, as it were, of his order, to be perpetually observed therein. He earnestly fostered devotion to the Virgin Mother of God. He burned with exceptional charity toward his neighbor. He was enriched with the gift of prophecy and the scrutiny of hearts. When he was in his forty-fourth year, while persisting in prayer at the holy shrine of Loreto, he recognized that the end of his life was near. He immediately turned aside toward Abruzzo, and in the town of Agnone, while staying with the disciples of Saint Philip Neri, he was seized by a mortal fever; having received the sacraments of the Church with deepest devotion, on the eve of the feast of Corpus Christi, the day before the Nones of June in the year 1608, he fell peacefully asleep in the Lord. His sacred body, brought to Naples, was honorably laid to rest in the church of Saint Mary Major, where he had laid the first foundations of his order. Afterward, illustrious for miracles, Clement XIV solemnly enrolled him among the Blessed; and Pius VII, radiant with new signs, inscribed him in the roll of the Saints in the year 1807.

The Lord confirmed this zeal for spreading the Gospel by the multitude and excellence of miracles. He restored sight to a blind man. He converted by the sign of the cross as much sea water into fresh water as sufficed for a long time for five hundred travelers who were being driven to death by thirst; and when it was carried to various regions, very many sick persons were suddenly cured. He recalled several dead persons to life, among whom he raised up one who had been buried the day before, ordering him to be brought forth from the tomb, and restored two others alive to their parents from the bier, seizing them by the hand while they were being carried out. Inspired everywhere with the spirit of prophecy, he announced very many things most remote in place and time. Finally, at Sancian, an island of China, on the second day of December, he died, full of merits and worn out with labors. His corpse, buried twice under quicklime for many months yet wholly incorrupt, gave off fragrance and blood; and when it was brought to Malacca, it immediately extinguished a most severe plague. Finally, resplendent everywhere with new and great miracles, Gregory XV enrolled him among the Saints. And Pius X chose and appointed him as heavenly patron of the Society and of the work of Propagating the Faith.

Luke called this Joseph just, Matthew called him rich. And rightly is he called rich in this passage where he receives the body of Christ: for in receiving the Rich One, he did not experience the poverty of faith. Rich, therefore, is he who is just. The just man, then, wrapped him in a shroud; and the Israelite mingles various fragrant virtues and brings aloes of about a hundred pounds — that is, the measure of perfect faith. And they bound the body of Jesus according to the special custom of the Jews: not with the knots of perfidy, but with the bonds of faith; and they placed him in a garden, to which the Church is frequently compared, as she has the diverse fruits of merits and the flowers of virtues.

Hyacinth, a noble Roman virgin, daughter of Count Marco Antonio of Mariscotti Vignanello (the town in which she was born) and of Ottavia Orsini, began from an early age to experience signs of divine protection, when at the age of seven she was saved by a present benefit of God just as she was about to fall into a well. Sent to Viterbo to the nuns of Saint Bernardine to be educated by them, she received there in her youth the Third Order rule of Saint Francis — yet not in such a way as to put on religious habits together with the sacred habit; for she indulged for some time in pomp and pleasure, until, while she lay sick with fever, she was struck by the timely admonition of a confessor summoned to her, and bade farewell to all vanity. And so, having expiated the stains of her past life in the sacrament of penance, she cast herself humbly on her knees in the common refectory, bathing herself in tears, and chastising herself with a whip, she begged pardon of her sisters; then, scorning the world and herself, she renounced her annual income and her splendid and superfluous furnishings; and from that time forward, for the rest of her life, she went barefoot, or when illness compelled, with only a sole beneath her feet, content with a single tunic — rough, worn, and received as alms — and girded, as she continued until her death.

Hyacinth the Pole was born to noble and Christian parents in the village of Kamień in the diocese of Wrocław. Admitted among the canons of Kraków, he excelled the rest by the distinguished devoutness of his manner of life and by learning. Admitted at Rome into the Order of Preachers by its very founder Saint Dominic, he preserved most holily until the end of his life the perfect manner of living which he had learned from him, with perpetual virginity maintained. Sent back to his homeland, and having built six monasteries of his order, it is incredible to say how greatly he advanced in the eyes of all through the preaching of God's word and the innocence of his life, renowned for frequent miracles. Among these a notable one was that he crossed the river Vistula near Wyszogród, swollen with waters, using no boat, and carrying his companions across on a cloak spread out over the waves. Having led an admirable manner of life for nearly forty years after his profession, on the very feast of the Assumption of the Virgin, he gave back his spirit to God in the year of salvation 1257, and was enrolled among the Saints by Clement VIII.

Hyacinth the Pole was born to noble and Christian parents in the village of Kamień in the diocese of Wrocław. Instructed in letters from boyhood, after devoting himself to jurisprudence and sacred letters, he was admitted among the canons of Kraków, where he excelled the rest by the distinguished devoutness of his morals and supreme learning. Admitted at Rome into the Order of Preachers by its very founder Saint Dominic, he preserved most holily until the end of his life the perfect manner of living he had learned from him. He cultivated virginity perpetually; he cherished modesty, patience, humility, abstinence, and the other virtues as the sure patrimony of a religious life.

Hyginus of Athens, whose father was a philosopher, was elected by the suffrage of the clergy to succeed Telesphorus, already being then a priest of the Roman Church. He sat in the holy See of Peter under the Emperor Antoninus Pius Augustus for three years, eleven months, and twenty-eight days. As soon as he was appointed Pontiff, he distinguished the orders of the clergy according to their proper grades and arranged that in those churches called Titular churches there should be present both senior ministers and others subject to them, who would administer the sacred rites to the faithful when occasion required.

I am the younger, he says, and despised: I have not forgotten your justifications. Not as my enemies, who have forgotten your words. But it seems that the one younger in age who has not forgotten the justifications of God grieves for his enemies who are older in age and have forgotten them. For what else does I the younger have not forgotten mean, except that those elders have forgotten? But this younger one calls himself despised; and for that reason he has become greater: because God has chosen the ignoble and contemptible things of the world, and the things that are not, as though they were, that the things that are might be brought to nothing. And behold, the last are first who were first, and the first are last who were last.

Josaphat Kuntsevych was born to noble and Catholic parents at Vladimir in Volhynia; when as a small boy he heard his mother speaking of the Passion of Christ, a dart having been sent forth from the side of an image of the crucified Christ, he received a wound in his heart. At the age of twenty he made his monastic profession among the disciples of Saint Basil. Appointed shortly afterward as archimandrite of Vilnius and then as archbishop of Polotsk, he showed himself an example of all the virtues. He was a vigorous promoter of the union of the Greek Church with the Latin, and called back innumerable heretics into the bosom of mother Church. Having set out for Vitebsk on a pastoral visitation and sought out by schismatics for death, as they were already invading the archiepiscopal residence, he went out of his own accord to meet them, saying: Little children, if you have anything against me, behold I am here. Then, with a rush, they beat him with blows, pierced him with weapons, and, having slain him with an axe, cast him into the river. The blood of the Martyr benefited above all the murderers themselves, nearly all of whom, condemned to death, renounced the schism and confessed their crime. Pope Urban VIII honored him with the titles of the Blessed; and Pius IX enrolled this champion of ecclesiastical unity, the first from among the Orientals, in the order of the Saints.

Josaphat Kuntsevych was born to noble and Catholic parents at Vladimir in Volhynia; when as a small boy he heard his mother speaking of the Passion of Christ, a dart having been sent forth from the side of an image of Jesus crucified, he received a wound in his heart. Inflamed with love of God, he began to apply himself so ardently to prayer and other devout works that he was an example and wonder to those older than himself. At the age of twenty, having made his monastic profession among the disciples of Saint Basil, the advances he made in evangelical perfection were extraordinary. He went barefoot even in the bitterest winter cold of that region; he never ate meat, used wine only out of obedience, and afflicted his body with the harshest hairshirt until his death. He preserved inviolate the flower of chastity which from his youth he had vowed to the Virgin Mother of God. The fame of his virtue and learning spread so quickly that, although young, he was set over the monastery of Bytonia, then appointed archimandrite of Vilnius, and finally, though reluctant, was proclaimed archbishop of Polotsk, to the rejoicing of Catholics.

James the Brother of the Lord, surnamed the Just, from his earliest age drank neither wine nor strong drink, abstained from flesh, was never shorn, and used neither ointment nor bath. To him alone was it permitted to enter into the Holy of Holies. He also wore linen garments; and the constant practice of prayer had so hardened the skin on his knees that in hardness they resembled the hide of a camel. After the Ascension of Christ, the Apostles appointed him bishop of Jerusalem; to him also the Prince of the Apostles sent word to announce that he had been led out of prison by an Angel. And when at the council of Jerusalem a controversy arose concerning the law and circumcision, James, following the opinion of Peter, addressed an address to the brethren, in which he approved the call of the Gentiles and declared that absent brethren should be written to, that they should not impose on the Gentiles the yoke of the Mosaic law. Concerning him the Apostle also speaks to the Galatians: But of the other Apostles I saw none, except James the brother of the Lord.

James, son of Zebedee, blood brother of the Apostle John, a Galilean, was called among the first Apostles with his brother; leaving their father and their nets, they followed the Lord, and both were called by Jesus himself Boanerges, that is, sons of thunder. He was one of the three Apostles whom the Savior loved most dearly, and whom he wished to be witnesses of his Transfiguration, to be present at the miracle when he raised the daughter of the synagogue ruler from the dead, and to be with him when he withdrew to the Mount of Olives to pray to the Father before being seized by the Jews.

Jacob, however, begot Joseph. This passage was set against us by Julian Augustus as an instance of discordance among the Evangelists — why the Evangelist Matthew said Joseph was the son of Jacob while Luke called him the son of Heli — not understanding the custom of the Scriptures, that the one was his father according to nature, the other according to the law. For we know that this was prescribed through Moses at God's command: that if a brother or kinsman died without children, another should take his wife to raise up seed for the brother or kinsman. Joseph the husband of Mary. When you hear the word husband, let no suspicion of marriage enter your mind; but remember the custom of the Scriptures, that bridegrooms are called husbands and brides are called wives.

You had already taught the peoples who had believed from among the circumcised; you had already founded the Church of Antioch, where the dignity of the Christian name first arose; you had already filled Pontus, Galatia, Cappadocia, Asia, and Bithynia with the laws of evangelical preaching; and, not uncertain of the progress of your work, nor unaware of the extent of your age, you were bringing the trophy of the Cross of Christ to the Roman citadels, whither before you went the honor of authority and the glory of the Passion, both foreordained by divine providence.

Now concerning the fact that the same star which led the Magi to the place where the infant God was with his Virgin mother — which could certainly have led them directly to the city itself — withdrew itself and did not appear to them at all until the Jews were asked about the city in which Christ was to be born and named it according to the testimony of divine Scripture, saying: In Bethlehem of Judah. For thus it is written: And you, Bethlehem, land of Judah, are by no means the least among the rulers of Judah: for from you will come a Leader, who will rule my people Israel. What else did divine providence signify here except that only the divine Scriptures would remain with the Jews — by which the Gentiles would be instructed while they themselves would be blinded?

Now, so that they might understand that this is a new kind of warfare and an unaccustomed manner of fighting, when he sent them out naked, clothed only in a tunic, without sandals, without staff, without belt and wallet, and commanded them to be fed by those who received them — he did not end his discourse there, but displaying his inexplicable power, he said: Even so as you go, show the meekness of sheep, although you are going to wolves — and not simply to wolves, but even into the midst of wolves: (for he commands them to have not only the meekness of sheep but also the simplicity of the dove); for thus I shall display my power most fully, when wolves are overcome by sheep; and though they are in the midst of wolves, and are torn by countless cruelties, not only shall they not be consumed, but they shall even transform them to their own nature.

Januarius, bishop of Benevento, when Diocletian and Maximian were raging against the Christians, was vainly tried by fire and the rack by Timothy, governor of Campania, on account of his profession of the Christian faith. Bound and led with Festus his deacon and Desiderius his lector before the governor's carriage to Pozzuoli, and on the following day exposed with his companions — to whom were added Sosius a deacon of Misenum, Proculus a deacon of Pozzuoli, and Eutychetes and Acutius, laymen — to the wild beasts. But when these proved harmless to them, and nearly five thousand people had received the faith of Christ, the governor, driven to fury, ordered the holy Bishop and his companions to be put to the sword. The Christians took care to bury their bodies. The body of Januarius, first brought to Benevento, then to the monastery of Monte Vergine, and finally laid to rest in the chief church of Naples, became renowned for many miracles. His blood, which is preserved congealed in a glass vial, is to this day seen — when placed before the head of the same Martyr — to liquefy and bubble in a wondrous manner.

Januarius, bishop of Benevento, when Diocletian and Maximian were raging against the Christians, was brought to Nola to Timothy, governor of Campania, on account of his profession of the Christian faith. There, his constancy having been tried in various ways, he was cast into a burning furnace, from which he escaped so unharmed that the flame touched neither garment nor hair. Then the governor, inflamed with anger, ordered the body of the Martyr to be stretched until the joints of the sinews and limbs were undone. Meanwhile Festus his deacon and Desiderius his lector, seized and bound, were dragged along with the bishop before the governor's carriage to Pozzuoli, and thrust into the same prison where Sosius of Misenum and Proculus a deacon of Pozzuoli, and Eutychetes and Acutius, laymen, who had been condemned to the beasts, were being held.

12 Blessed is the man who suffers temptation. For when he has been proven, he shall receive the crown of life which God has promised to those who love him.
13 No one should say, when he is tempted, that he was tempted by God. For God does not entice toward evils, and he himself tempts no one.
14 Yet truly, each one is tempted by his own desires, having been enticed and drawn away.
15 Thereafter, when desire has conceived, it gives birth to sin. Yet truly sin, when it has been consummated, produces death.
16 And so, do not choose to go astray, my most beloved brothers.

6 But he should ask with faith, doubting nothing. For he who doubts is like a wave on the ocean, which is moved about by the wind and carried away;
7 then a man should not consider that he would receive anything from the Lord.
8 For a man who is of two minds is inconstant in all his ways.

Ignatius, a Spaniard by birth, born at Loyola in Cantabria, first followed the court of the Catholic king, then the military life. The austerity of his life was singular. Utterly unlettered, yet refreshed by clear illuminations from God, he composed that admirable book of the Exercises, approved by the judgment of the Apostolic See and by the benefit of all. At Paris, having associated with himself nine companions of various nations from that university, on Montmartre he laid the first foundations of the Society of Jesus, which he later perfected at Rome, adding a fourth vow concerning Missions to the three customary ones, to be fulfilled at the direction of the Apostolic See. The splendor of churches, the teaching of catechism, the frequenting of sermons and sacraments received increase from him. He was most zealous for the spreading of the Catholic religion everywhere, and exercised a wondrous authority over demons. At the age of sixty-five he passed to the embrace of his Lord, whose greater glory he had sought in all things. Pius XI appointed and declared him heavenly Patron of all Spiritual Exercises.

Thence, wearing sackcloth as he was, having first given his costly garments to a beggar, he withdrew to Manresa; where, living on begged bread and water, fasting except on Sundays, taming the flesh with a harsh chain and hairshirt, lying on the ground, and bloodying himself with iron whips, he remained for a year, so refreshed by clear illuminations from God that he was accustomed to say afterward: If the sacred Scriptures did not exist, he would nonetheless be prepared to die for the faith from those things alone which the Lord had revealed to him at Manresa. At that time, a man utterly unlettered, he composed that admirable book of the Exercises, approved by the judgment of the Apostolic See and by the benefit of all.

Victor, the third Pope of that name, previously called Desiderius, born of a princely family at Benevento, shone from his earliest years with exceptional piety and innocence of morals. Scarcely past adolescence, shunning the earthly marriage his parents had arranged, he secretly left his betrothed and sought the desert. When his mother and relatives bore this ill and endeavored to turn him from his holy purpose, he embraced the monastic life and changed his residence successively from place to place. He dwelt in the monastery of Monte Cassino, afterward withdrew to the monastery of the island of Tremiti, and for a time lived secretly among the hermits of Monte Maiella. Then, having recovered from a grave illness, he ascended Monte Cassino, where on account of his singular virtues he was designated abbot by the monks and confirmed by Pope Stephen IX. He formed the peoples of France in the preaching of the word of God with the most abundant fruit of souls, and won for himself no slight renown as a speaker.

He also showed remarkable generosity to the poor and to churches. For having truly shown himself the parent of all orphans and the sick, he erected basilicas to the holy Michael, to the princes of the Apostles, and to the Protomartyr Stephen, and endowed them with a very ample revenue; and he founded many monasteries for both sexes, enriching each one with various ornaments, estates, and furnishings in keeping with imperial magnificence. When Henry at last departed this life — for whose soul he arranged that solemn prayers and generous almsgiving be made everywhere — he put aside, as he had long desired, the cares of external affairs, laid down the purple, had his hair cut, and from the archbishop received the ring of faith still kept in the monastery and the veil of the sacred virgins.

He also decreed that temples or oratories should not be consecrated with the sacred rite without the celebration of Mass; that new ones should not be built, nor those already built demolished, without the knowledge of the bishop, and that materials gathered and set aside for that sacred use should not be converted to profane purposes. He further ordained that godfathers should attend baptism to raise the infants from the sacred font; that no bishop accused of a crime should be condemned unless his case had been thoroughly discussed by the bishops of the same province. All these things, enacted under his name and title, are still extant. He held three ordinations in the month of December, in which he created six bishops, fifteen priests, and five deacons.

Now when Justin, that most distinguished philosopher and Martyr of Christ, had presented his apology for the Christian religion before the Emperor Antoninus Pius Augustus, he obtained a mitigation of the persecution. From that point on, the slaughter of Christians was restrained — not entirely, yet greatly — by a public edict of the prince. The most holy shepherd, however, by whose care the flock of the Lord had been provided for, was not spared; for this man brought his most innocent life to an end by glorious martyrdom, so as not to be unlike his predecessors, on the eleventh of January, and was buried on the Vatican.

Moreover, they were greatly pleased to decree that the feast of the Conception should be held by the entire Church in the same rank and number as the feast of the Nativity, and that the same feast of the Conception with its octave should be celebrated by the universal Church, and kept holy by all among those feasts that are of precept, and that a pontifical chapel in our patriarchal Liberian basilica should be celebrated every year on the day of the Virgin's Conception. And desiring to foster day by day more and more in the hearts of the faithful this doctrine concerning the Immaculate Conception of the Mother of God, and to stir up their piety toward venerating and honoring the same Virgin conceived without original sin, they were most glad to grant the faculty that in the Loretan Litany, and in the Preface of the Mass itself, the Immaculate Conception of the same Virgin might be proclaimed, and that thereby the rule of believing might be established by the very rule of supplication.

Meanwhile the Church of Fiesole, widowed of her shepherd, chose him as bishop; judging himself unworthy of that office, he long remained in hiding, unknown, until he was revealed by the wondrous voice of a speaking child and found outside the city; and, lest he should resist the divine will, he accepted the episcopate. Honored with that dignity, he devoted himself more earnestly to the humility he had always cultivated; and to pastoral solicitude he joined mercy toward the poor, liberality, assiduous prayer, vigils, and other virtues, and was also renowned for the spirit of prophecy; so much so that his holiness was celebrated by all.

He understood indeed — taught inwardly by him who also appeared outwardly — that, although the weakness of the Passion in no way befitted the immortality of a seraphic spirit, yet this vision had been presented to his eyes for this reason: that the friend of Christ might know beforehand that he was to be transformed wholly into the express likeness of Christ Jesus crucified, not through the martyrdom of the flesh but through the enkindling of the mind. Therefore, when the vision disappeared, after a mysterious and intimate colloquy, it inflamed his mind inwardly with seraphic ardor; while outwardly it marked his flesh with an image conformed to the Crucified, as if a certain imprinting had followed upon the prior liquefying power of fire. For at once in his hands and feet there began to appear the marks of nails — their heads appearing on the lower part of the hands and the upper part of the feet, and their points projecting on the opposite side. His right side also, as if transfixed by a lance, was covered with a red scar, which often, pouring forth sacred blood, sprinkled his tunic and undergarment.

Understanding belongs to those who are pure of heart, as to a purified eye by which that may be seen which the eye of the body has not seen, nor the ear heard, nor has it risen into the heart of man; concerning whom it is said here: Blessed are the pure of heart, for they shall see God. Wisdom belongs to the peacemakers, in whom all things are now ordered, and no movement rebels against reason, but all things obey the spirit of man, since he himself also obeys God; concerning whom it is said here: Blessed are the peacemakers. But the one reward, which is the Kingdom of Heaven, is variously named for these different degrees.

Among other things …

Among the other tombs of the Martyrs that are wont to be found in the cemetery of Priscilla on the Via Salaria, there stood out that in which the body of holy Philomena had been laid, as could be read from the inscription on the tomb affixed on three tiles. And although a phial of blood had been found there, and other inscribed marks of martyrdom could be seen engraved, it is to be lamented that the deeds performed by her, and the acts and kind of martyrdom she underwent, remained obscure. But as soon as this sacred body — received as a gift of beneficence from Pius the Seventh at the beginning of his pontificate — was exposed for the veneration of the faithful people at Mugnano in the diocese of Nola, an immense celebrity and devotion toward the holy Martyr immediately spread abroad, especially on account of the signs reported from every side as having come to pass through her intercession. Hence it came about that Gregory the Sixteenth, Supreme Pontiff, moved by the petitions of several bishops and devotees of the Martyr, and having maturely weighed the whole matter, graciously permitted the feast of the same to be celebrated with Office and Mass in the aforementioned diocese of Nola and elsewhere.

Among the other virtues, he most especially cherished Christian humility and obedience: for, considering himself the least among all, he eagerly sought out for himself the most abject services of the house, and most diligently fulfilled not only the commands but even the wishes of his superiors. Likewise, having restrained his senses and practiced austerity of life, he preserved intact the flower of virginity, and, truly crucified to the world, lived solely for God, enjoying the intimate fellowship of his Lord. Thus bringing to a close the brief course of his life, adorned with so many virtues, at Isola in the Abruzzo — consumed more by the fire of charity than by the force of disease, and refreshed by the help of the divine Mother — he departed to the blessed above with a most peaceful end in the year one thousand eight hundred and sixty-two, in the twenty-fourth year of his age. Him, thereafter made illustrious by God with miracles, Pope Pius the Tenth numbered among the Blessed; and Benedict the Fifteenth, Supreme Pontiff, in the year one thousand nine hundred and twenty — the two hundredth anniversary of the founding of the Institute of the Passion — on the solemnity of the Ascension of the Lord, decreed the honors of the Saints for the blessed youth; and Pius the Eleventh extended his Office and Mass to the universal Church.

Looking upon the disfigured corpse of a handsome man, a nobleman and a relative of his, laid out in an open tomb, he said: I am what this man was; what this man now is, I shall be. And immediately, after the funeral, with that saying of the Lord coming to him — "If anyone wishes to come after me, let him deny himself, and take up his cross, and follow me" — he withdrew into solitude for the pursuit of greater perfection, and there, devoted to vigils, prayers, and fasts, he very often ate only raw herbs for food. And so that he might the more escape the notice of men, he changed his dwelling several times; and at length he arrived at Mount Fano, a place — though near Fabriano — at that time deserted, and there he erected a church in honor of the most holy Father Benedict and laid the foundations of the Silvestrine congregation, under the rule and habit shown to him in a vision by the same Saint.

Among these, through the kingdom of Castile and León, in which he had succeeded his father Alfonso, he gathered large armies and undertook annual expeditions against the Saracens, enemies of the Christian name. In these campaigns, that he might always be victorious, the chief forces were the prayers which the most devout king poured out to God, and the fact that before battle, to make God favorable to him, he would scourge himself with whips and fortify his body with a harsh hair-shirt; and so he won remarkable victories against vast Moorish armies, and restored several cities to Christian observance and dominion; and having seized the kingdoms of Jaén, Córdoba, and Murcia, and made Granada tributary, he transferred his victorious standards to the assault of Seville, the chief city of Baetica, urged on — as it is related — in a vision by the blessed Isidore, once bishop of that city. In that siege, as it is told, he had present divine assistance: for an iron chain stretched across the Guadalquivir as a barrier for the Mohammedans was broken by a stronger wind arising, by one of the royal ships carried there at the king's command with such force that, passing far beyond, it broke also the wooden bridge and at the same time shattered the hopes of the Moors and compelled them to surrender.

Meanwhile, with frequent prayer and assiduous meditation on heavenly things, often bathed in tears and sometimes drawn in spirit away from the senses, he was accustomed to unite himself to God. Held in great honor by leading men, by those most renowned for holiness, and by four Supreme Pontiffs, he thought so humbly of himself that he both called himself and considered himself the least of all. He refused the bishopric of Vienna once, a second time, and a third time. Most obedient to his superiors, he was ready at their slightest sign to leave or undertake anything, even at risk to his health and life. By voluntary self-mortification he perpetually guarded his chastity. At last at Freiburg in Switzerland, where he had labored most for the glory of God and the salvation of souls in the last years of his life, he departed to God on the twenty-first day of December in the year one thousand five hundred and ninety-seven, in the seventy-seventh year of his age. This strenuous champion of Catholic truth, Pope Pius the Ninth enriched with the honors of the Blessed in heaven; and Pope Pius the Eleventh, resplendent with new signs, enrolled him in the number of the Saints in the jubilee year, and at the same time declared him Doctor of the universal Church.

Among the most distinguished works of Justin, two apologies of the Christian faith stand out, which, having presented them before the senate, the emperors Antoninus Pius and his sons, and also Marcus Antoninus Verus and Lucius Aurelius Commodus, who were most savagely harassing the followers of Christ, and having vigorously defended that same faith in disputation, he obtained a public edict of the princes restraining the slaughter of Christians. Yet Justin himself was not spared. For, accused by the schemes of the Cynic Crescens, whose life and wicked ways he had exposed, he was seized by officers of the law. Brought before the prefect of Rome named Rusticus, when this prefect had asked him what were the teachings of the Christians, he made this good confession before many witnesses: The right teaching, which we Christian men observe with piety, is this: that we regard God as the one Maker and Creator of all things visible and those not seen by bodily eyes; and that we confess the Lord Jesus Christ, the Son of God, foretold by the prophets of old, who is also to come as Judge of the human race.

Mortifying his body amid royal delights with afflictions and vigils, he passed a great part of the night in devout prayers. Besides other fasts which he practiced from time to time, he was accustomed to fast for entire forty days before the Christmas feasts with such severity that he did not interrupt even in the most severe pains. Most devoted to divine worship, he built many churches and monasteries partly from the ground up, partly restored them, and enriched them with sacred furnishings and generous endowments. He brought the king her husband to a better way of life and to works like her own exercises by her most wholesome example, and raised all her children so holily and happily that very many of them, like their mother Agatha and their sister Christina, embraced a most holy manner of life. Finally, providing for the happiness of the whole kingdom, she cleansed the peoples from all vices that had crept in by stealth, and restored to them ways of life worthy of Christian piety.

Let the Savior therefore enter the house, and visit it often — that house which the penitent Lazarus purifies, which Martha adorns, and which Mary fills, given to interior contemplation. But perhaps some inquisitive person will ask why in the present Gospel reading there is no mention at all of Lazarus. I judge indeed that this too does not depart from the intended comparison. For the Spirit, wishing to signify a virginal house, fittingly kept silence about penance, which after all accompanies evil. Far be it from us to say that this house ever harbored any stain of its own, such that the broom of Lazarus would be sought in it.

Behold, O most cruel king, spectacles worthy of your banquet. Extend your right hand, lest anything be lacking to your savagery; that between your fingers the streams of sacred blood may flow. And since the hunger could not be satisfied with feasts, nor the thirst of unheard-of cruelty quenched with cups — drink the blood flowing from the severed head as it still gushes from the veins. Behold the eyes, witnesses of your crime even in death, averting their gaze from the sight of your revels. The lids close, not so much by the necessity of death as by horror at debauchery. That golden tongue, now bloodless, whose verdict you could not endure, falls silent — and is still feared.

He was very often invited by neighboring parish priests to provide for the salvation of souls in the manner of missionaries, both by preaching and by hearing confessions, and he was always available to each one. Inflamed by zeal for the glory of God, he brought it about that the pious exercises of Missions were established with a permanent endowment in more than a hundred parishes. Meanwhile, as God illustrated his servant with miracles and charismatic gifts, there arose that celebrated pilgrimage by which, for twenty years, nearly a hundred thousand people of every rank and age flocked each year to Ars — not only from the distant provinces of France and Europe, but also from America. Consumed more by labors than by old age, with the day of his death foretold, he rested in the kiss of the Lord on the fourth of August in the year one thousand eight hundred and fifty-nine, at the age of seventy-three. Him, illustrious for many miracles, Pius the Tenth enrolled among the Blessed, and Pius the Eleventh enrolled among the Saints in heaven in the holy year, extending his feast to the universal Church; and in the fiftieth year of his priesthood he appointed him the heavenly patron of all parish priests.

Jane Frances Frémiot de Chantal, born of most illustrious lineage at Dijon in Burgundy, was bereaved of her mother while still a girl and commended herself to the protection of the Virgin Mother of God. Given by her father in marriage to the Baron de Chantal, she was the perfect image of a strong woman and became all things to all people. When her husband was killed in a hunting accident, she bound herself by vow to continence, and, victorious over herself, did not hesitate to receive at the sacred font the son of the man who had killed him. Lest she should ever be turned aside from her resolve of preserving chastity, renewing her vow, she inscribed the most holy name of Jesus Christ with a burning iron upon her own breast. Taught by Saint Francis de Sales, whom she used as a guide of her spirit, regarding the divine will, she laid the foundations of the sacred Institute of the Visitation of Holy Mary, which she spread far and wide. When at last she had bound herself by vow always to do what she understood to be more perfect, laden with merits she departed to the Lord at Moulins on the thirteenth of December in the year one thousand six hundred and forty-one, and was added to the register of Saints by Clement the Thirteenth.

When John the Second of that name had been taken from among the living, Agapitus — a Roman by birth, son of Gordianus, archdeacon of the holy Roman Church — by reason of his singular erudition, in which he was well and thoroughly trained, and of the composed and most chaste habits of life in which he excelled above others, was promoted by the common votes of the whole clergy and with the rejoicing of all good men to the holy See of Peter; and he administered that lofty office just as if he had been chosen not by men but by God himself.

John of Sahagún, born of noble lineage in Sahagún in Spain, was obtained by his parents through pious works and prayers from God after they had long been without children. From his earliest years he gave signs of future holiness. Having been ordained a priest, in order to serve God more quietly he voluntarily relinquished all the ecclesiastical revenues with which he had been deservedly endowed. At Salamanca, when he had fallen into a very grave illness, he bound himself by a vow of stricter discipline; and to fulfil it he betook himself to the monastery of Saint Augustine, then especially flourishing in stricter discipline; admitted there, he advanced beyond all others in virtues. The citizens of Salamanca, torn apart by bloody factions, he recalled to tranquillity by sermons, private conversations, and the holiness of his life, more than once being miraculously delivered by God from imminent peril. To contemplate Christ the Lord present while he celebrated Mass, to see into hidden hearts, and to foretell the future were frequent experiences for him. Finally, the day of his death having been foretold, he departed this life most holily, glorious with many miracles both before and after his death. These being duly proved, Alexander the Eighth enrolled him in the number of the Saints.
