When John the Second of that name was taken from this life, Agapitus — a Roman by birth, son of Gordianus, archdeacon of the holy Roman Church — was raised to the holy See of Peter by the common suffrage of the entire clergy and the congratulation of all the faithful, on account of the singular learning with which he was thoroughly and admirably furnished, and the ordered ways of a most blameless life in which he surpassed all others; and he administered that exalted charge in such a manner as though he had been chosen not by men, but by God himself.

John, born of noble stock at Sahagún in Spain, was obtained from God by his parents through pious works and prayers after they had long been without offspring. From his earliest years he gave signs of future holiness. Ordained a priest, in order to serve God more tranquilly, he voluntarily relinquished all the ecclesiastical revenues with which he had deservedly been enriched. At Salamanca, having fallen into a very grave illness, he bound himself by a vow to a stricter discipline; to fulfil this vow, he betook himself to the monastery of Saint Augustine, which was then especially flourishing in the observance of severer discipline. There, once admitted, he surpassed all others more advanced in virtue. The citizens of Salamanca, torn by bloody factions, he led back to tranquility by his sermons and by private conversations and the holiness of his life, having been more than once delivered by divine power from imminent peril. It was frequent with him to behold Christ the Lord present at the celebration of Mass, to see into the hidden recesses of hearts, and to foretell things to come. Finally, having announced the day of his death beforehand, he passed from this life most holily, made glorious by many miracles both before and after his death. These being duly verified, Alexander VIII enrolled him in the number of the Saints.

John of Sahagún was born in Spain of noble lineage; his parents, having long been childless, obtained him from God through pious works and prayers. From his earliest years he gave an outstanding token of future holiness: for he would often speak from an elevated place to the other boys, exhorting them to virtue and the worship of God, and settling their quarrels. In his homeland he was entrusted to the monks of Saint Facundus of the Order of Saint Benedict for instruction in the first elements of learning. While he applied himself to these studies, his father arranged for him to administer a parish church; but this office the young man could be induced by no argument to retain. Admitted among the familiars of the Bishop of Burgos, he became the bishop's closest confidant on account of his well-attested integrity, and was ordained priest and canon by him, being enriched with many benefices. But leaving the bishop's household in order to serve God more quietly, he renounced all the revenues of the Church and devoted himself to a small chapel, where he celebrated Mass daily and frequently preached on divine matters to the great edification of his hearers.

John of the Cross, born of devout parents at Fontiveros in Spain, was known from his earliest years to be especially dear to the Virgin Mother of God; for at the age of five, having fallen into a well, he was lifted out by the hand of that same Mother of God and came to no harm. He burned with so great a desire to suffer that at the age of nine, scorning a softer bed, he made it his custom to sleep on brushwood. As a young man he devoted himself as a servant to the hospice of the sick poor at Medina del Campo, attending them with great ardor of charity and embracing the most lowly offices. The others, stirred by his example, fulfilled the same works of charity with greater fervor. Called to higher things, he embraced the Institute of the Blessed Virgin Mary of Mount Carmel; and there, made a priest out of obedience, most eager for stricter discipline and a more austere life, he professed the primitive rule of the Order with his superior's permission, so that, in perpetual remembrance of the Lord's Passion, having declared war on himself as on a most fierce enemy, he swiftly crucified the flesh with its vices and concupiscences by vigils, fasts, iron disciplines, and every kind of penance — truly worthy to be reckoned by Saint Teresa among the purer and holier souls then adorning the Church of God.

John of the Cross, born of devout parents at Fontiveros in Spain, was known from his earliest years to be especially dear to the Virgin Mother of God; for at the age of five, having fallen into a well, he was lifted out by her hand and came to no harm. As a young man he most lovingly devoted himself as a servant to the hospice of the sick poor at Medina del Campo; then, having embraced the Institute of the Blessed Virgin Mary of Mount Carmel and been made a priest out of obedience, he professed the primitive rule. Inflamed with zeal for promoting stricter discipline, he was given by God as a companion to Saint Teresa — who counted him among the purer and more excellent souls then adorning the Church of God — for the work of restoring among the friars the ancient observance of the Carmelite Order. Having labored strenuously in this work and suffered greatly, when asked by Christ what reward he sought for so many labors, he answered: Lord, to suffer and be despised for you. He composed books on mystical theology, filled with heavenly wisdom. Finally at Úbeda, having borne a dreadful illness with great patience, he fell asleep in the Lord in the year fifteen hundred and ninety-one, in the forty-ninth year of his age. Pope Pius XI, by decree of the Sacred Congregation of Rites, declared him a Doctor of the Universal Church.

John of God, born of Catholic and devout parents in the town of Montemor-o-Novo in the Kingdom of Portugal, was chosen for the Lord's portion. Called back from a more dissolute way of life by divine aid, he gave proof of great holiness. He built two large hospitals in the city of Granada from the alms of the devout, and founded the Order of Brothers Hospitallers for the care of the sick. He was renowned for his mercy toward the poor and his self-contempt. He excelled wonderfully in devotion to the Blessed Virgin, and was distinguished by the gift of tears. Seized by a grave illness, and pressing Christ the Lord hanging on the Cross with his hand and heart, he died in the Lord on the eighth of the Ides of March, in the year fifteen hundred and fifty. Pope Alexander VIII enrolled him in the number of the Saints; and Pope Leo XIII declared him the heavenly Patron of all hospitals and of the sick everywhere, and ordered his name to be invoked in the Litany for the Dying.

John, called Damascene from his native city, was born of noble lineage and trained in both human and divine letters by the monk Cosmas at Constantinople. When the Emperor Leo the Isaurian was waging his impious war against the veneration of sacred images, John, at the urging of Pope Gregory III, defended the holiness of that veneration zealously both in speech and in writing. By this act he aroused so great a hatred against himself in Leo that the emperor, by means of forged letters, accused him as a traitor before the Caliph of Damascus, who employed John as his counselor and administrator. The prince, credulous of the fraud, ordered John's right hand to be cut off, though John swore in vain that the accusation was false. But the most holy Virgin, defender of the innocent, came to the aid of her client, whose help he had earnestly implored in prayer, and by her benefit the severed hand was restored and rejoined to the arm as though it had never been severed. Moved above all by this miracle, John resolved to carry out what he had long conceived in his heart. Having with difficulty obtained his withdrawal from the Caliph, he distributed all his possessions to the poor and freed his servants; then, as a pilgrim, he visited the holy places of Palestine, and at last withdrew with his teacher Cosmas to the laura of Saint Sabbas near Jerusalem, where he was ordained a priest.

John was born in the year sixteen hundred and one in the village known as Ri, in the diocese of Séez, of devout and upright parents. Still a boy, already refreshed with the Bread of Angels, he joyfully vowed perpetual chastity. In the schools, where he completed his studies with distinction, he shone with remarkable piety. He loved the Blessed Virgin most ardently and burned with an extraordinary charity toward his neighbor. He joined the Congregation of the Berullian Oratory and was ordained a priest at Paris. Having been made Rector of the Oratorian house at Caen, he left it, though with difficulty, in order to form young men suited for the ministry of the Church. Accordingly, having gathered five companions, he founded a Congregation of Priests to which he gave the most holy names of Jesus and Mary, and he opened the first seminary at Caen, which was followed by many others. To call sinful women back to the Christian life, he founded the Institute of Our Lady of Charity, of which a branch is the Congregation of Angers of the Good Shepherd; he also added the Society of the Admirable Heart of the Mother of God and other works of charity. Burning with singular love for the most holy Hearts of Jesus and Mary, he was the first to think — not without some divine inspiration — of rendering them liturgical honor. As an Apostolic Missionary he preached the Gospel to many villages and cities. Broken by so many labors and near death, he peacefully expired on the nineteenth of August in the year sixteen hundred and eighty. Pope Pius X enrolled him, renowned for miracles, among the Blessed; Pope Pius XI, on the feast of Pentecost in the Holy Year, enrolled him among the Saints, extended his Office and Mass to the Universal Church.

John of Antioch, surnamed Chrysostom on account of the golden stream of his eloquence, turned from forensic and secular studies to divine letters with the highest distinction of talent and industry. And so, having been consecrated and made a priest of the Church of Antioch, upon the death of Nectarius he was placed, against his will, over the Church of Constantinople through the agency of the Emperor Arcadius. Taking up this pastoral office, he began to rebuke more vigorously the corrupt morals and the licentiousness of the life of the nobility; and on account of this freedom he incurred the great hostility of many. He also gravely offended the Empress Eudoxia, because he had reproved her concerning the money of the widow Callitropha and the farm of another widow.

John of Antioch, surnamed Chrysostom on account of the golden stream of his eloquence, having been made a priest of the Church of Antioch, upon the death of Nectarius was placed, against his will, over the Church of Constantinople through the agency of the Emperor Arcadius. In that office, as he rebuked more vigorously the corrupt morals and the licentiousness of the life of the nobles, he incurred the great hostility of many. He also gravely offended the Empress Eudoxia, because he had reproved her concerning the money of the widow Callitropha and the farm of another widow. He was therefore driven into exile, all the widows and the needy lamenting the expulsion of their common father. It is incredible to tell how many evils he endured in exile, and how many he converted to the faith of Jesus Christ. All admire the multitude, the piety, and the splendor of his sermons and of his other writings. He gave back his soul to God on the eighteenth day before the Kalends of October, and his body was laid in the Vatican Basilica. Pope Pius X declared this illustrious Doctor of the whole Church the heavenly Patron of preachers.

John Baptist de la Salle, born of illustrious family at Rheims, studied letters and philosophy as a young man at the Rheims Academy. Enrolled in the clerical state, he was admitted among the canons of Rheims at the sixteenth year of his age, and was afterwards received at Paris into the Sulpician seminary. Ordained to the priesthood, he took up the governance of the Sisters of the Infant Jesus, who devote themselves to the education of girls, whom he guided and defended with great prudence. For the religious and moral formation of children of the people, after very many difficulties, he founded a brotherhood which he named the Brothers of the Christian Schools, later confirmed by Pope Benedict XIII. Having renounced his canonry, distributed his goods to the poor, and humbly resigned the governance of the Institute he had founded, laden with virtues and merits, he fell asleep in the Lord at the age of sixty-eight. Pope Leo XIII first enrolled him in the catalogue of the Blessed, and then transferred him to the register of the Saints. Pope Pius XII declared him the chief heavenly Patron before God of all teachers engaged in the instruction of boys and young men.

John Baptist de Rossi, born of honorable family at Voltri in Liguria, was, while still a boy, an object of admiration to all for the gentleness of his character and his zeal for piety. At the age of thirteen he seemed sent by God's design to Rome to fulfill the role of an apostle there. Admitted among the students of the Roman College of the Society of Jesus, he excelled in talent and virtue. He took great care that they frequented the Marian sodality, ministered to the sick in hospitals, and were drawn back from harmful things by wholesome recreation of their souls; meanwhile, treating heavenly things in his discourses, he roused the more sluggish, and thus earned the title of Apostle. Having been seized by a grave illness on account of the harsh mortification of his body, he was compelled to relax somewhat from his accustomed severity of study: which, he used to say, had been brought about by God's will, lest, puffed up by knowledge, he seek what was his own rather than the things of Jesus Christ. Enrolled in the clerical state, he applied himself to sacred studies in the college of Saint Thomas, and growing in virtue, he was then ordained to the priesthood with great joy of soul. He so established the Lord as his inheritance that he bound himself by a singular vow never to accept any ecclesiastical benefice, even if offered, unless compelled by obedience.

John baptizes, and Jesus comes — sanctifying indeed the one who baptizes, but above all in order to bury the old Adam in the waters, and before all else, in order that the waters of the Jordan might be sanctified through this act: so that, as there had been spirit and flesh, so also for those who were to be baptized, succession in spirit and in the water of sanctification might be handed on. The Baptist refuses; Jesus insists. I, he says, have need to be baptized by you. The lamp speaks to the Sun, and the voice speaks to the Word.

John Baptist de la Salle, born of illustrious family at Rheims, showed even as a boy, by his conduct and deeds, signs that he was to be called to the Lord's portion and to be honored with the glory of holiness. As a young man he studied letters and philosophical disciplines at the Rheims Academy: at which time, although on account of his virtues of soul, his lively intellect, and his amiable manner he was dear to all, he nevertheless shrank from the company of his peers, so that, devoted to solitude, he might more freely attend to God. Long before enrolled in the clerical state, he was admitted among the canons of Rheims at the age of sixteen, and hastened to Paris to pursue theology at the Sorbonne, where he was received into the Sulpician seminary. But soon bereaved of his parents, he was compelled to return home and undertook to educate his brothers; which task, without meanwhile interrupting his studies of the sacred sciences, he carried out with the best fruit, as the outcome confirmed.

John Bosco, born of humble stock, after an arduous and most innocent childhood, devoted himself to studies at Chieri, where he distinguished himself by excellence of talent and virtue. Ordained a priest, he went to Turin, where he became all things to all; but above all he devoted his care to assisting adolescent boys, especially the poor and abandoned. He strove with every means to keep youthful years away from the poisonous food of errors and vices through the liberal arts, schools for artisans, and assemblies on feast days: for this purpose he raised up in the Church two religious families, of men and of virgins. He himself published very many books filled with Christian wisdom. He also rendered the greatest service for the eternal salvation of unbelievers through the sacred missions of his religious companions. With his mind constantly raised to God, this most holy man was seen to be terrified by no threats, wearied by no labors, oppressed by no cares, and disturbed by no adversities. He died in the year of salvation eighteen hundred and eighty-eight, in the seventy-third year of his age. He was enrolled in the number of the Saints by Pope Pius XI.

John Bosco, born in humble circumstances at Castelnuovo in the Astigiano, and trained with the greatest holiness under his mother's discipline after the loss of his father, gave remarkable portents of himself even from his earliest years. Gentle by nature and inclined to piety, he bore himself with singular authority among his peers, whose quarrels he soon began to settle, petty brawls to compose, base words and wanton jests to suppress. Then he strove to call them to himself with pleasant words, to weave prayers into games, to retell with wonderful abundance and sweetness of speech what sacred sayings he had heard in church, and to lead the boys as soon as possible, and as frequently as possible, to receive the Sacraments of Penance and the Eucharist worthily. The modest grace of his countenance, the pleasantness of his character, and the brightness of his most innocent life drew all hearts to him. And although pressed by straitened family circumstances he spent an adolescence full of labors and hardships, he pressed on cheerfully and trusting in God toward the one goal: to be raised to the priesthood.

John of God, born of Catholic and devout parents in the town of Montemor-o-Novo in the Kingdom of Portugal, was shown by an unwonted splendor shining over his house and by the spontaneous pealing of a bell from the very time of his birth to have been chosen for the Lord's portion in a most sublime manner. Called back from a more dissolute way of life by the power of God at work within him, he began to give proof of great holiness, and, having heard the preaching of the word of God, felt himself so stirred to better things that he seemed from the very first rudiments of a holier life to have touched something consummated and perfect. Having distributed all his goods to the poor confined in prison, and having become a spectacle to all the people of remarkable penance and contempt for himself, he was grievously afflicted by many who thought him mad and was cast into a prison appointed for the insane. But John, more and more inflamed with heavenly charity, built two large hospitals in the city of Granada from the alms of the devout, and laying the foundation of a new Order, enriched the Church with new offspring — the Brothers Hospitallers, who serve the sick with notable benefit to souls and bodies, and who have spread far and wide throughout the world.

John of Matha, born of devout and noble parents at Faucon in Provence, when he first offered the Holy Sacrifice to God, understood through a vision that he was destined for the redemption of captives from the infidels. Accordingly, moved by divine inspiration, he withdrew into a desert, where he found Felix of Valois, who had already been dwelling there for many years. While they were more fervently devoted to prayer in that place, warned three times in sleep, they set out for Rome and obtained from Pope Innocent III the approval of a new Order of the Most Holy Trinity for the redemption of captives. They then built their first monastery in the diocese of Meaux, and Felix remained to govern it. John returned to Rome with several companions, where Innocent gave them the house, church, and hospital of Saint Thomas in Formis on the Caelian Hill. Letters also having been sent to the Miramolin king of Morocco, the work of redemption was happily begun. John then set out for Spain, oppressed in great part under the yoke of the Saracens; having moved all hearts to compassion for the captives, he erected hospitals and redeemed many captives. Finally returning to Rome, broken by continual labors and worn out by illness, he died in the Lord on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of January, in the year twelve hundred and thirteen.

John of Matha, founder of the Order of the Most Holy Trinity for the Redemption of Captives, was born at Faucon in Provence of parents distinguished for piety and nobility. Having gone for his studies first to Aix and then to Paris, and having completed the course of theology and obtained the degree of master, he excelled by the splendor of his learning and virtues. Moved by these, the Bishop of Paris promoted him, though he resisted out of humility, to the sacred Order of the Priesthood, with the intention that, residing in that city, he might give light to studious youth by his wisdom and conduct. When he was celebrating his first Mass in the bishop's chapel, with the bishop himself and others standing by, he merited to be refreshed by heavenly favor. For an Angel appeared, clothed in a white and shining garment, with a cross of red and blue sewn upon his breast, his arms crossed and extended over two captives placed at his sides — one a Christian, the other a Moor. Caught up into ecstasy by this vision, the man of God understood at once that he was destined for the redemption of captives from the infidels.

His name is John, he says — meaning: it is not we who give him his name, for he has already received his name from God. He has his own designation, which we have acknowledged, not chosen. It is the privilege of the Saints to receive their name from God. Thus Jacob is called Israel, because he saw God. Thus our Lord Jesus was named before he was born; to whom not an Angel but the Father gave the name. You see that Angels announce what they have heard, not what they have presumed. Nor should you wonder that a woman affirmed a name which she had not heard; for the Holy Spirit, who had given the charge to the Angel, revealed it to her.

John and Paul, Roman brothers, when they were distributing among the poor of Christ the possessions left to them by Constantia, daughter of Constantine, whom they had served devoutly and faithfully, were invited by Julian the Apostate into the number of his household; but they freely refused to remain with one who had apostatized from Jesus Christ. A period of ten days was therefore set for them, to bring them to sacrifice to Jupiter; but when they most steadfastly refused to commit that crime, they merited the palm of martyrdom by being beheaded in their own home by the judge Terentianus. Their glorious death was made widely known by the unclean spirits who tormented the bodies of many; among these was the son of Terentianus himself, oppressed by a demon, who was freed at the tomb of the Martyrs. By this miracle both he and his father Terentianus believed in Christ; by whom the life of these blessed Martyrs is also said to have been written.

John and Paul, Roman brothers, when, with the possessions left to them by Constantia the daughter of Constantine whom they had served devoutly and faithfully, they were supporting the poor of Christ, were invited by Julian the Apostate into the number of his household; but they freely refused to remain with one who had apostatized from Jesus Christ. He set them ten days for deliberation, so that they might know for certain that they must die unless by that day they resolved to adhere to him and sacrifice to Jupiter.

John Gualbert, born of noble family at Florence, was following the military profession in obedience to his father when Ugo, his only brother, was slain by a kinsman. When John, accompanied by weapons and soldiers, encountered this man alone and unarmed on Good Friday, and neither was able to avoid the other, out of reverence for the holy Cross, which the homicide — a suppliant, about to die at once — was making with his arms, John mercifully granted him his life and received him as a brother. He then entered the church of Saint Miniato, where he beheld the image of the Crucifix which he had adored bow its head toward him. Moved by this, he left the military life and put on the monastic habit, at the persuasion of Saint Romuald, inhabitant of the Camaldolese hermitage. Afterwards he founded a monastic Order under the Rule of Saint Benedict at Vallombrosa, which he used above all to root out the stain of simony and to propagate the apostolic faith. Full of virtues and merits and gifted with the familiar company of Angels, in the seventy-eighth year of his age, at Passignano he passed to the Lord on the fourth of the Ides of July, in the year ten hundred and seventy-three.

John Gualbert, born of noble family at Florence, was following the military profession in obedience to his father when Ugo, his only brother, was slain by a kinsman. When John, accompanied by weapons and soldiers, encountered this man alone and unarmed on Good Friday, and neither was able to avoid the other, out of reverence for the holy Cross, which the homicide — a suppliant, about to die at once — was making with his arms, John mercifully granted him his life. Having received his enemy as a brother, he entered the nearby church of Saint Miniato to pray, and there he beheld the image of the Crucifix which he had adored bow its head toward him. Moved by this marvelous act, John resolved thenceforth to serve God even against his father's will, and with his own hands sheared his hair on the spot and put on the monastic habit: and so quickly did he shine in devout and religious virtues that he offered himself to many as a model and norm of perfection; so that, when the abbot of that place died, he was chosen superior by the common vote of all. But the servant of God, desiring to be subject rather than to rule, was preserved by divine will for greater things, and made his way to Romuald, the inhabitant of the Camaldolese hermitage, from whom he received a heavenly prophecy concerning the institute he was to found; then he established his Order under the Rule of Saint Benedict at Vallombrosa.

John, born in the town of Kęty in the diocese of Kraków — from which he took the surname Cantius — of devout and upright parents Stanislaus and Anna, gave from his very infancy the promise of the greatest virtue by the gentleness of his character, innocence, and gravity. At the University of Kraków he was first a student of philosophy and theology, then, having ascended through all the academic grades, a professor and doctor; the sacred teaching which he imparted for many years not only enlightened the minds of his hearers but inflamed them to all piety, as he both taught and practiced. Once ordained a priest, not relaxing his literary labors at all, he increased his pursuit of Christian perfection. And as he grieved above all things to see God offended everywhere, so he strove to propitiate him for himself and the people by offering daily the unbloody Sacrifice with many tears. He administered the parish of Ilkuś admirably for some years; but moved by concern for the danger of souls, he afterwards resigned it and, at the academy's request, returned to his former office of teaching.

John, born in the town of Kęty in the diocese of Kraków — from which he took the surname Cantius — of devout and upright parents Stanislaus and Anna, gave from his very infancy the promise of the greatest virtue by the gentleness of his character and his innocence. Once ordained a priest, he increased his pursuit of Christian perfection. He administered the parish of Ilkuś admirably for some years. Whatever time remained from study he devoted partly to the care of the salvation of his neighbor, especially through sacred preaching, and partly to prayer. Four times he came on foot to the threshold of the Apostles, bearing his traveling pack, both to honor the Apostolic See and, as he would say, to redeem on those days of indulgence for sinners daily offered there the pains of his own purgatory. He guarded his virginal chastity most vigilantly, and refrained from eating meat for some thirty-five years before his death. He flew to heaven on the eve of the Nativity of Christ. Enrolled in the register of the Saints by Pope Clement XIII, he is venerated among the principal patrons of Poland and Lithuania.

John Leonardi, born not far from the city of Lucca, showed from his earliest age a certain gravity and maturity. Called by God at the age of twenty-six to enroll in the ranks of the Church's service, he was first instructed among boys in the rudiments of the Latin tongue, and then made such progress in letters and in philosophical and theological disciplines that in barely four years he was promoted to the priesthood out of obedience. He founded a Congregation of Regular Clerks of the Mother of God, by whose care and zeal a great transformation of souls was accomplished in the republic of Lucca. He thereby fell into the most bitter persecutions of wicked men, but bearing all things willingly with an even mind, he obtained from Pope Gregory XIII the confirmation of his Congregation. Grieving deeply that very many nations in remote regions lacked the light of the Gospel, he formed plans with the most devout Bishop Vives and established a body of priests whose purpose it was to train suitable young men to be sent at intervals to distant regions for the propagation of the faith. Never failing in his sacred ministry, he passed to the Lord at Rome in sackcloth and ashes on the ninth of October in the year sixteen hundred and nine, and was enrolled in the register of the Saints by Pope Pius XI.

John Leonardi, born of devout and upright parents in the town of Decimo not far from the city of Lucca, showed from his earliest years, through his love of solitude and prayer, a certain gravity and maturity. Called by God at the age of twenty-six to enroll in the ranks of the Church's service, he at once sent worldly cares their dismissal. He was first instructed among boys in the rudiments of the Latin tongue, and then made such progress in letters and in philosophical and theological disciplines that in barely four years he was promoted to the priesthood out of obedience. Soon having gathered some well-disposed young nobles and having diligently trained them in the perfection of virtue, in the following year he founded a Congregation of Regular Clerks which he named after the Mother of God, out of the ardent affection of his devotion to her. Through their care and zeal, such a transformation of souls was accomplished that, where in the republic of Lucca — especially through the perfidious arts of heretics — the hatreds of citizens were ablaze and morals were debased, in a short time the ancient piety of Christians seemed to have revived there.

John Mary Vianney, born of devout country folk at Dardilly in the diocese of Lyons, gave many signs of holiness. When he was eight years old and tending sheep, he was accustomed to teach the Rosary by word and example to little boys kneeling before an image of the Mother of God; and, devoted to the tilling of fields, he meditated on heavenly things. He had the greatest love for the poor and delighted to assist them in every way. Being of slower intellect, he implored divine aid, and having laboriously completed his course of theology, was deemed worthy to be initiated into holy orders. Appointed a pastor, he most splendidly renewed the face of a wholly wretched and forsaken parish. Assiduous daily in judging and directing consciences, he patiently endured the most atrocious vexations of Satan. He established devout mission exercises in more than a hundred parishes. But as he thought most humbly of himself, he endeavored to withdraw from the holy desire of the faithful who came even from distant provinces to visit him in his parish. Worn out more by labors than by old age, with the day of his death foretold, he rested in the Lord on the fourth of August in the year eighteen hundred and fifty-nine, in the seventy-third year of his age. Renowned for so many miracles, Pope Pius X enrolled him among the Blessed, Pope Pius XI enrolled him among the Saints in the Holy Year, and in the fiftieth year of his priesthood appointed him the heavenly Patron of all parish priests.

John Mary Vianney, born of devout country folk at Dardilly in the diocese of Lyons, gave many signs of holiness from infancy. When he was eight years old and tending sheep, he was accustomed at one time to teach little boys kneeling before an image of the Mother of God the Rosary by word and example, and at another time, entrusting the flock to his sister or to someone else, to seek a more secluded spot where, freer to stand before the image of the Virgin, he might attend to prayer. He had the greatest love for the poor, and delighted to bring them in groups to his father's house and assist them in every way. He was placed with the pastor of Écully to be instructed in letters; but as he was of slower intellect, he encountered almost insurmountable difficulties in his studies. He implored divine aid by fasting and prayer, and visited the tomb of Saint Francis Regis seeking alms and petitioning for ease in learning. Having laboriously completed the course of theology, he was found sufficiently qualified to be initiated into holy orders.

John of Nepomuk, born in a Bohemian town from which he took the surname Nepomucen, was born of parents of advanced age — not without a presage of future holiness, marvelous flames shining over the house where he was born. When he fell as an infant into a grave illness, he escaped unharmed from danger of life through the aid of the Blessed Virgin, to whom his parents commended their child as a gift received. With excellent natural ability and devout upbringing following the heavenly signs, he spent his boyhood among holy and devout exercises: for he delighted often to go to church and to minister to priests serving at the altar. Educated in polite letters at Žatec for a humanistic formation, and then trained in more serious disciplines at Prague, he gained the mastery and laureate in philosophy, theology, and the sacred canons. Ordained to the priesthood, and duly equipped by the knowledge of the saints for the winning of souls, he devoted himself entirely to the ministry of the Word of God. Bearing such free fruit by his eloquence and piety in the rooting out of vices and in recalling the straying to the way of salvation, he was co-opted among the canons of the metropolitan church of Prague, and soon took up the office entrusted to him of preaching the Gospel before King Wenceslaus IV, with such success that, at John's urging, the king accomplished many things and held his virtues in great honor. Nevertheless the servant of God most steadfastly refused the notable dignities which the king offered him, lest he be called away from the proclamation of the divine word.

Jane Frances Frémiot de Chantal, born at Dijon in Burgundy of the most illustrious stock, from her earliest years gave clear signs of extraordinary holiness. For it is reported that she was barely five years old when she withstood a certain Calvinist nobleman with arguments of a solidity beyond her years, and immediately cast into the flames the small gift offered by him, saying: See in this manner heretics will burn in hell who deny their faith to Christ who is speaking. Bereaved of her mother, she commended herself to the protection of the Virgin Mother of God, and dismissed the servant who was drawing her to love of the world. Expressing nothing childish in her conduct, shrinking from the pleasures of the world, and longing for martyrdom, she applied herself earnestly to religion and piety. Given in marriage to the Baron de Chantal by her father, she devoted herself to the cultivation of all virtues, striving to imbue her children, servants, and all those subject to her with the doctrine of the faith and good morals. With lavish generosity she relieved the need of the poor, the food being often multiplied by God's gift: by reason of which it came about that she pledged herself never to refuse alms to anyone who asked her in the name of Christ.

John was born in the year sixteen hundred and one in the village known as Ri, in the diocese of Séez, of devout and upright parents. Still a boy, refreshed by the Bread of Angels, he joyfully vowed perpetual chastity. Received into the college at Caen directed by the Fathers of the Society of Jesus, he shone with singular piety; and committing himself to the protection of the Virgin Mary, he sealed with his own blood as a young man the special covenant he had entered into with her. Having completed the course of letters and philosophy with great distinction, and having rejected a proposed marriage, he joined the Congregation of the Berullian Oratory and was ordained a priest at Paris. He burned with wonderful charity toward his neighbor: for in many places he devoted diligent care to the cure both of bodies stricken by the Asian plague and of souls. Made rector of the Oratorian house at Caen, having long pondered how to form young men suitable for the ministry of the Church, he departed with strong spirit from the companions with whom he had lived for twenty years, having implored divine aid, though with great difficulty.

John Baptist de Rossi, born of honorable family at Voltri in Liguria, was, while still a boy, an object of admiration to all for the gentleness of his character and his zeal for piety. At the age of thirteen he seemed sent by God's design to Rome to fulfill the role of an apostle there. Admitted among the students of the Roman College of the Society of Jesus, he excelled in talent and virtue. He took great care that they frequented the Marian sodality, ministered to the sick in hospitals, and were drawn back from harmful things by wholesome recreation of their souls; meanwhile, treating heavenly things in his discourses, he roused the more sluggish, and thus earned the title of Apostle. Having been seized by a grave illness on account of the harsh mortification of his body, he was compelled to relax somewhat from his accustomed severity of study: which, he used to say, had been brought about by God's will, lest, puffed up by knowledge, he seek what was his own rather than the things of Jesus Christ. Enrolled in the clerical state, he applied himself to sacred studies in the college of Saint Thomas, and growing in virtue, he was then ordained to the priesthood with great joy of soul. He so established the Lord as his inheritance that he bound himself by a singular vow never to accept any ecclesiastical benefice, even if offered, unless compelled by obedience.

John, born at Capistrano in the Peligni country, was sent to Perugia for his studies, and made such progress in Christian and liberal disciplines that, on account of his outstanding knowledge of law, he was appointed by Ladislaus, king of Naples, as governor of several cities. But while he was most rightly administering the affairs of these cities and striving to restore tranquility to their troubled affairs, he was himself seized and thrown into prison; from which being miraculously freed, he professed the rule of Francis of Assisi among the Friars Minor. Advancing in the study of divine letters, he found in Saint Bernardine of Siena his teacher, whose examples of virtue also he eminently imitated, especially in promoting devotion to the most holy name of Jesus and to the Mother of God. He refused the bishopric of Aquila, and distinguished himself above all by stricter discipline and by the many writings he published for the reform of morals.

John, a Tuscan, governed the Church during the reign of the elder Emperor Justin: he traveled to Constantinople for help, because the heretical King Theodoric was oppressing Italy. And God also illumined his journey with miracles. For when a nobleman had lent him at Corinth a horse — gentle, on which his wife was accustomed to ride — for the journey, it came about that, when later returned to its owner, the horse became so fierce that it always thereafter expelled the mistress by its neighing and agitation of its whole body: as if it were indignant to receive a woman, since the Vicar of Jesus Christ had sat upon it. For this reason they donated the horse to the Pontiff. But that miracle was greater which he wrought at Constantinople, at the entrance of the Golden Gate, before a very large crowd of people who had come out together with the emperor to honor the Pontiff: he restored sight to a blind man. And even the emperor, prostrating himself at his feet, venerated him.

Having settled affairs with the emperor, he returned to Italy, and at once wrote a letter to all the bishops of Italy, commanding them to consecrate to the Catholic rite the churches of the Arians, adding this: Because also we, when we were at Constantinople both for the Catholic religion and for the cause of King Theodoric, consecrated as Catholic whatever churches of theirs in those parts we were able to find.

Theodoric, bearing this most unjustly, treacherously summoned the Pontiff and threw him into prison at Ravenna; where, afflicted with squalor and hunger, he departed this life in a few days, having sat for two years, nine months, and fourteen days, having ordained fifteen bishops during that time. Shortly after, Theodoric died: whom a certain hermit, as Saint Gregory writes, saw being plunged into the fires of Lipari between Pope John and the patrician Symmachus, whom he had likewise slain; so that those to whom he had brought death might, as it were, be the judges of his destruction. The body of John was brought from Ravenna to Rome and buried in the Basilica of Saint Peter.

John, born in the town of Nepomuk in Bohemia, from which he took the surname Nepomucen, having received the degrees in philosophy, theology, and the sacred canons and been ordained a priest, was co-opted among the canons of the metropolitan church of Prague and was entrusted with the office of preaching the Gospel before King Wenceslaus IV. Appointed by the king to oversee the distribution of royal alms to the poor, he was chosen by Queen Joanna as the director of her conscience. When Wenceslaus was headlong in vices and bore impatiently the entreaties of his devout wife, he dared to demand that the secrets entrusted by the queen to a priest in the sacramental tribunal be revealed to him by John. But the minister of God, tried by blandishments, tortures, and the squalor of prison, resisted firmly the king's wicked desire; and when Wenceslaus threatened imminent drowning in the water if he continued to resist, John with invincible constancy refused and repelled his terrors and threats. And so, cast by the king's command by night into the Moldau river flowing through Prague, he attained the glorious palm of martyrdom. Pope Benedict XIII enrolled him first in the catalogue of the holy Martyrs as the first asserter of the sacramental seal, sealing his fidelity to the secret with his blood.

Joseph of Cupertino, born of devout parents, was notable as a young man for chaste conduct, and was enrolled among the Conventual Friars Minor at the monastery of Grotella — first among the lay brothers, on account of his lack of learning, and then by divine disposition among the clerics. Ordained to the priesthood, he afflicted his body with hair-shirts, disciplines, and every kind of austerity; but he nourished his spirit with the constant food of holy prayer, by which it came about that he was called by God to the highest degree of contemplation. Distinguished in obedience and poverty, he cultivated chastity supremely, and preserved it unharmed after overcoming great temptations. He followed the Virgin Mary with wondrous love and shone with great charity toward the poor. Such was his humility that, accounting himself a great sinner, he earnestly besought God to take away from him his illustrious gifts. Traveling through many regions by the command of his superiors or of the Holy Inquisition, he finally flew to heaven at Osimo in Piceno in the sixty-first year of his age.

Joseph Calasanz, born at Peralta in Aragon, even as a small child would call his companions together and instruct them in the mysteries of the faith and in sacred prayers. Having been made a priest by vow, afflicting his body with the utmost severity of life, vigils, and fasts, he passed days and nights in prayer and the contemplation of heavenly things. Having received by divine inspiration that he was destined above all to form young men — especially the poor — in the spirit of understanding and piety, he founded the Order of Regular Clerics Poor of the Mother of God of the Pious Schools, who by their own institute professed a special care for the education of children. Having borne innumerable labors and hardships with unconquered spirit on this account, he died in the Lord in the ninety-second year of his age, on the eighth of the Kalends of September in the year sixteen hundred and forty-eight.

Now Joseph her husband, being a just man and not wishing to expose her, intended to put her away secretly. If anyone joins himself to a harlot, he becomes one body with her; and in the law it is commanded that not only those guilty of crimes but also those complicit in them are liable to sin: how then is Joseph called just when he conceals his wife's crime? But this is a testimony to Mary: that Joseph, knowing her chastity and marveling at what had come to pass, conceals in silence that whose mystery he did not know.

Joseph, son of David, do not be afraid to take Mary as your wife. We have already said above that betrothed women are called wives: which the book against Helvidius explains more fully. And the Angel speaks soothingly, to confirm the justice of his silence. And at the same time it should be noted that Joseph is said to be the son of David, so that Mary might also be shown to be of the stock of David.
And you shall call his name Jesus. For he will save his people from their sins. Jesus in the Hebrew tongue means Savior: therefore the Evangelist marked the etymology of his name, saying: You shall call his name Jesus, because he will save his people.

Joseph of Cupertino, born in the year sixteen hundred and three in a town in the Salentine country of the diocese of Nardò of devout parents there, and forestalled by the love of God, spent his boyhood and youth in the greatest simplicity of conduct and innocence of life and, after patiently bearing a troublesome illness, was freed through the aid of the Virgin Mother of God, and gave himself entirely to works of piety and the cultivation of virtues; and in order to unite himself more intimately with God who was calling him to higher things, he resolved to join the Seraphic Order. After various events, finally attaining the goal of his desire, he was enrolled among the Conventual Friars Minor at the monastery of Grotella — first among the lay brothers on account of his lack of learning, and then by divine disposition among the clerics. Initiated into the priesthood after solemn vows, he proposed to himself a more perfect rule of life. To this end, at once renouncing whatever worldly affections and earthly things almost necessary for life, he afflicted his body with hair-shirts, disciplines, chains, and every kind of austerity and penance; but he sweetly nourished his spirit with the constant practice of holy prayer and of the highest contemplation. From this it came about that the charity of God, which had already been poured out in his heart from his earliest years, shone forth day by day in a wondrous and altogether singular manner.

Joseph Calasanz of the Mother of God, born of noble family at Peralta in Aragon, gave signs from his tender years of his future charity toward children and of their instruction. For even as a small child he would call them together and instruct them in the mysteries of the faith and in sacred prayers. Having been excellently educated in human and divine letters, and while pursuing theological studies at Valencia, he triumphantly overcame the seductions of a noble and powerful woman and preserved with a notable victory the virginity he had vowed to God. Having been made a priest by vow, he was summoned by several bishops as a helper in the kingdoms of New Castile, Aragon, and Catalonia, and surpassed the expectations of all by correcting corrupt morals everywhere, restoring ecclesiastical discipline, and wonderfully extinguishing enmities and bloody factions. But admonished frequently by a heavenly vision and the voice of God, he set out for Rome.

The Saints themselves — understand this, brethren — the good ones who belong to the dove, who belong to the lot of that city of Jerusalem; these good ones in the Church, of whom the Apostle says: The Lord knows those who are his; they are of varied graces, and not all have equal merits. Some are holier than others, some are better than others. Why, then, if one is baptized by one man — say by that just and holy one — and another by another of lesser merit before God, of lesser standing, of lesser continence, of lesser life — that which they have received is nonetheless one and equal and the same, except that he is the one who baptizes?

Irenaeus, born not far from the city of Smyrna in proconsular Asia, had from his boyhood delivered himself to Polycarp — disciple of John the Evangelist and likewise bishop of the Smyrnaeans — for instruction. Under this most excellent teacher he made outstanding progress in the learning and precepts of the Christian religion. After Polycarp had been raised to heaven in the glory of martyrdom, although Irenaeus was excellently versed in the sacred letters, yet, because he burned with incredible zeal to learn what doctrines others who had been trained by the Apostles had received to be kept as a deposit, he met as many of these as he could, and what he had heard from them he held in a retentive mind, to bring it forth at the appropriate time against the heresies — which, when he saw them spreading ever more widely to the great harm of the Christian people, he had determined to refute diligently and at length. Proceeding then to Gaul, he was appointed a priest of the Church of Lyons by Bishop Pothinus. This office he discharged by laboring in word and teaching in such a manner that, as the holy Martyrs who had strenuously contended for true piety under the Emperor Marcus Aurelius bear witness, he showed himself an emulator of the testament of Christ.

Irenaeus, born not far from the city of Smyrna, had from his boyhood delivered himself to Polycarp — disciple of John the Evangelist and likewise bishop of the Smyrnaeans — for instruction. After Polycarp had been raised to heaven in the glory of martyrdom, burning with incredible zeal to learn what doctrines others who had been trained by the Apostles had received to be kept as a deposit, he met as many of these as he could, and what he had heard from them he held in a retentive mind, to bring it forth at the appropriate time against the heresies. Having gone to Gaul, he was appointed a priest of the Church of Lyons by Bishop Photinus; and having succeeded him, he so happily fulfilled the office of bishop that, by his wisdom, prayer, and example, he saw not only all the citizens of Lyons but also many inhabitants of other cities of Gaul swiftly lay aside their superstition and error and give their names to Christian service. He wrote much, a great part of which was lost through the injury of time. There survive five books of his against the heresies, in the third of which he bore a most weighty and illustrious testimony above all concerning the Roman Church and the succession of her bishops, the faithful, perpetual, and most certain guardian of divine tradition. And to this Church, he said, on account of its more powerful preeminence it is necessary that every Church — that is, the faithful who are everywhere — should come together. Crowned with martyrdom, he passed to heaven in the year of salvation two hundred and two.

Irmengard, born of noble parents, King Louis the German and Emma, gave from her tender years a sign of future holiness. Scarcely past infancy, she so preferred the company of Virgins dedicated to the Spouse over parents, sisters, and friends that, bidding farewell to the pleasures of the world and the pomp of the royal court, with her parents' consent she devoted herself entirely to the service of God. The monastery of Buchau, which she first obtained from her royal father, she consecrated for many years with holy conduct, as an ancient tradition relates. Finally she happily restored the abbey of Chiemsee — of nuns living under the Rule of Saint Benedict, which she received from her father in a nearly ruinous state.

1 Who is this, who arrives from Edom with dyed garments from Bozrah? This is the Handsome One in his robe, advancing by the fullness of his strength. It is I, the Speaker of Justice, and I am the Fighter for Salvation.
2 So then, why is your garment red, and why are your vestments like the ones of those who tread the winepress?
3 I have trod the winepress alone. And among the nations, there is no man beside me. I have trampled on them in my fury, and I have tread them down in my wrath. And so, their blood has been sprinkled on my vestments, and I have stained all my garments.
4 For the day of vengeance is in my heart. The year of my redemption has arrived.
5 I gazed around, and there was no one to assist. I sought, and there was no one who would help. And so, my own arm has saved for me, and my own wrath itself has assisted me.

Warned through a vision by the Blessed Apostle Peter, who appeared to him together with Saint Apollinaris, the first Bishop of the Church of Ravenna — his disciple — whom he was to ordain as Pontiff of that same Church, he appointed over them as bishop, contrary to the will of the Ravennans, Peter the deacon of the Church of Fornocornelius, whom an admirable holiness of conduct and distinguished learning commended wonderfully, surnamed Chrysologus. But when Sixtus refused to allow Church property to be alienated and strove to relieve those who were oppressed, he drew upon himself the hatred of the ex-consul Anicius Bassus and the patrician Marinianus, by whom he was harassed with a shameful calumny; he willingly chose to have his case judged in synod. Accordingly, in the Helenian Basilica, called the Sessorianum Atrium, with a council of fifty-six bishops convened and the Emperor Valentinian present, together with all the clergy and senate, Sixtus was declared innocent, while Bassus and Marinianus were condemned as calumniators and proscribed, with the goods of Bassus moreover adjudicated to the Church: and Bassus having died by divine vengeance within three months, Sixtus, returning good for evil, laid out and buried him with his own hands handling the linens and spices, in the tomb of his ancestors near the Blessed Apostle Peter.

He hid for some time with certain Christians, and from there set out into Aemilia, where he raised to life the dead daughter of the patrician Rufinus; so that the whole family of Rufinus believed in Jesus Christ on that account. The prefect, greatly enraged, summoned Apollinaris and dealt with him more harshly, demanding that he put an end to spreading the faith of Christ in the city. When Apollinaris disregarded his commands, he was tortured on the rack; boiling water was poured into his wounds, and his mouth was struck with a stone: then, bound with iron chains, he was shut up in prison. On the fourth day he was put on a ship and sent into exile; and having suffered shipwreck he came to Moesia, thence to the bank of the Danube, and afterwards to Thrace.

1 And a rod will go forth from the root of Jesse, and a flower will ascend from his root.
2 And the Spirit of the Lord will rest upon him: the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and fortitude, the spirit of knowledge and piety.
3 And he will be filled with the spirit of the fear of the Lord. He will not judge according to the sight of the eyes, nor reprove according to the hearing of the ears.
4 Instead, he will judge the poor with justice, and he will reprove the meek of the earth with fairness. And he will strike the earth with the rod of his mouth, and he will slay the impious with the spirit of his lips.
5 And justice will be the belt around his waist. And faith will be the warrior's belt at his side.

1 The desolate and impassable land will rejoice, and the place of solitude will exult, and it will flourish like the lily.
2 It will spring up and blossom, and it will exult with rejoicing and praising. The glory of Lebanon has been given to it, with the beauty of Carmel and Sharon. These will see the glory of the Lord and the beauty of our God.
3 Strengthen the lax hands, and confirm the weak knees!
4 Say to the fainthearted: "Take courage and fear not! Behold, your God will bring the vindication of retribution. God himself will arrive to save you."
5 Then the eyes of the blind will be opened, and the ears of the deaf will be cleared.
6 Then the disabled will leap like a buck, and the tongue of the mute will be untied. For the waters have burst forth in the desert, and torrents in solitary places.
7 And the land that was dry will have a pond, and the thirsty land will have fountains of water. In the hollows where the serpents lived before, there will rise up the greenery of reed and bulrush.

1 "Be consoled, be consoled, O my people!" says your God.
2 Speak to the heart of Jerusalem, and call out to her! For her malice has reached its end. Her iniquity has been forgiven. She has received double for all her sins from the hand of the Lord.
3 The voice of one crying out in the desert: "Prepare the way of the Lord! Make straight the paths of our God, in a solitary place.
4 Every valley will be exalted, and every mountain and hill will be brought low. And the crooked will be straightened, and the uneven will become level ways.
5 And the glory of the Lord will be revealed. And all flesh together will see that the mouth of the Lord has spoken.

7 The grass has dried up, and the flower has fallen. For the Spirit of the Lord has blown over it. Truly, the people are like grass.
8 The grass has dried up, and the flower has fallen. But the Word of our Lord remains for eternity.

6 Lift up your eyes to heaven, and look down to the earth below. For the heavens will vanish like smoke, and the earth will be worn away like a garment, and its inhabitants will pass away in like manner. But my salvation will be forever, and my justice will not fail.

3 For thus says the Lord: You were sold for nothing, and you will be redeemed without money.

1 In the earlier time, the land of Zebulun and the land of Naphtali were lifted up. But in the later time, the way of the sea beyond the Jordan, the Galilee of the Gentiles, was weighed down.

Isidore the Farmer, near the city of Madrid in Spain, where he had been born, was hired to till the fields; and in that occupation he quickly prepared for himself a most abundant harvest of great virtues. For, being an admirable imitator of Christ and the Saints, he never set out to work in the morning without first diligently seeking the Kingdom of God and visiting the churches dedicated in honor of God and the Mother of God. On this account, when his master was greatly troubled by his delays, and on a certain day had taken up a position on higher ground to rebuke him more freely while waiting for him, he caught sight of two Angels clad in white garments plowing with a double yoke of oxen, with Isidore in the midst of them. When this miracle became widely known, he began thereafter to be held in great honor, both by his master and by all other men.

Isidore, born at Madrid, tilled the fields for wages; but, a truly blessed farmer who was not ignorant of his own goods, he knew also how to enrich the field of his soul with the fruits of virtue. For he sought first the Kingdom of God, visiting the churches, especially those of Our Lady, early in the morning, before going to work. When his master was greatly troubled by these delays, and on a certain morning had taken up a position on higher ground, intending to rebuke him, he beheld Isidore between two Angels who were driving a double yoke of oxen plowing in his stead. Serving God in his brethren, he gave his wages to the poor. Once, having set aside for himself a portion of his soup, he satisfied with it the poor whom he had invited to a meal. On another occasion, in the heat of summer, from the ground struck with the ox-goad, he drew forth a spring and quenched the thirst of his master. When he was old, he fell asleep in the Lord, and his body, still incorrupt, was translated from the cemetery of Saint Andrew into the church, where, placed in an elevated position, it became renowned for miracles. Four hundred years later he was enrolled in the calendar of the Saints by Gregory XV; and thereafter Pius XII declared and constituted him Patron of rural workers in the Federated States of Northern America.

Isidore, a Spaniard by birth, born at Cartagena of his father Severianus, governor of the province, was devoutly and liberally educated by the holy bishops Leander of Seville and Fulgentius of Cartagena, his brothers, and excelled in every kind of learning and Christian virtue. When Leander died, he was appointed to the See of Seville and was constituted the Vicar of the Apostolic See throughout all of Spain. In his episcopate he showed himself a pattern of every good work, and was most earnestly devoted to the restoration of ecclesiastical discipline. Having convened a council at Seville, he broke and crushed by vigorous and eloquent disputation the heresy of the Acephali, which was already threatening Spain. He acquired such a reputation for holiness and learning among all men that, scarcely sixteen years after his death, he merited to be called the distinguished Doctor. He wrote books of great usefulness and full of erudition. He presided over the Fourth Council of Toledo, the most celebrated of all the councils of Spain. Finally, after having governed his church for about forty years, he departed from Seville to heaven, in the year six hundred and thirty-six.

Isidore, a distinguished Doctor, a Spaniard by birth, born at Cartagena of his father Severianus, governor of the province, was devoutly and liberally educated by the holy bishops Leander of Seville and Fulgentius of Cartagena, his brothers, and instructed in Latin, Greek, and Hebrew letters, as well as in divine and human law; he excelled in every kind of learning and Christian virtue. While still a youth, he publicly opposed the Arian heresy, which had long held sway over the Visigothic nation that ruled over vast stretches of Spain, with such constancy that he came near to being killed by the heretics. When Leander died, he was appointed, though unwillingly, to the See of Seville, urged especially by King Recared and by the great consensus of clergy and people; it is held that the holy Gregory the Great not only confirmed his election by apostolic authority, but also honored the elect by sending him the pallium according to custom, and furthermore constituted him his own Vicar and that of the Apostolic See throughout all Spain.

Now, this younger man did not forget that he did not wish to possess his own righteousness, but God's; concerning which he now says: Your righteousness is righteousness forever. Therefore the younger man suffered persecution from the elder, so that the younger might say what follows: Tribulation and distress have found me; but your commandments are my meditation. Let them rage, let them persecute; so long as God's commandments are not abandoned, and even those who rage are loved out of those very commandments. Give me understanding, that I may live. The younger asks for understanding, which if he did not have, he would not understand beyond his elders. But he asks for it in tribulation and distress, so that he may understand how little worth is what the persecuting enemies can take from him — by whom he says he is despised.

These are your fathers and true pastors, who planted you for the heavenly kingdoms far better and far more happily than those through whose efforts the first foundations of your walls were laid — of whom he who gave you your name defiled you with a brother's murder. These are they who raised you to this glory, that as a holy nation, a chosen people, a priestly and royal city, you were made the head of the world through the sacred See of blessed Peter, and might rule more widely through divine religion than through earthly dominion. For although, enriched by many victories, you extended the right of your empire over land and sea, yet what military labor subjected to you is less than what Christian peace has brought into submission.

Thus did God's handmaid Irmengardis fulfill many ages in a few years of life. Wherefore, full of merits, and hearing a certain hidden voice of the Bridegroom saying 'Come, O bride,' she flew away to the heavenly nuptials of the divine Lamb, on the sixteenth day of July in the year eight hundred and sixty-six, in the thirty-fourth year of her age. Her body was honorably laid to rest in the church of the abbey of Chiemsee. The faithful people soon began to invoke and venerate the Handmaid of God, and through her intercession obtained not a few heavenly favors. In the year one thousand and four, and again in the sixteenth century, her mortal remains were elevated and honorably enshrined with great concourse of people. And the cult of the Blessed Abbess, exhibited for eleven centuries and more, was ratified and confirmed by Pope Pius XI by a decree of the Sacred Congregation of Rites, at the petition of all the bishops of Germany and the faithful people of Bavaria.

Therefore, under the authority of Sylvester, the pious Emperor confirmed by his own example the faculty of publicly building churches for the faithful in Christ, which he had granted to them. For he erected many basilicas: namely, the Lateran to Christ the Savior, the Vatican to Saint Peter, the Ostian to Saint Paul, one to Saint Lawrence in the Ager Veranus, the Holy Cross in the Sessorian Atrium, one to Saints Peter and Marcellinus and to Saint Agnes on the Lavican and Nomentan Ways, and others; which he splendidly adorned with sacred images and richly endowed with gifts and estates. Under this Pontiff the first Council of Nicaea was held, at which, with his legates presiding and Constantine present along with three hundred and eighteen bishops, the holy and catholic faith was expounded, and Arius and his followers condemned; which Council he also confirmed in a synod held at Rome, where Arius was again condemned. He likewise made many decrees useful to the Church of God, which are recorded under his name: namely, that chrism should be consecrated by a bishop alone; that a priest should anoint with chrism the crown of the head of one baptized; that deacons should use dalmatics in church, and a linen cloth on the left side; and that the sacrifice of the altar should be performed only on a linen cloth.

He was therefore honorably conducted to Bamberg and received by the clergy and the people in procession with great pomp and rejoicing. He sent letters to the Supreme Pontiff Paschal, by whom he had been summoned by letter; and he set out for Rome, where he laid the staff and ring he had received from the Emperor at the feet of the Pontiff, begging pardon. And when, after full deliberation, he had resolved to renounce everything and live in private retirement, he bade farewell to the court; but, after traveling one day's journey, he was recalled by the Pontiff's command, and, having invoked the Holy Spirit and received investiture from him, he was consecrated bishop on that most sacred day of Pentecost during the solemnity of Mass, to the great rejoicing of the whole court. In his episcopate he left to his successors many examples of wondrous holiness, incredible frugality and thriftiness. When at last he had become so renowned for his munificence in building, adorning, endowing, founding, and restoring very many churches and monasteries that it is rightly to be wondered how so much could have been contributed by one bishop to so many places, and had converted to the faith of Christ an almost innumerable multitude of Pomeranians, he rested at a blessed end and was buried in the church of Saint Michael, in the year of salvation one thousand one hundred and thirty-nine, on the third day before the Nones of July, in the thirty-seventh year of his episcopate. His body was translated in the year one thousand one hundred and eighty-nine, on the day before the Kalends of October, on which day his feast is for the most part also celebrated.

He therefore withdrew into the vast solitude of Egypt, where, advancing daily toward Christian perfection, he so despised the demons — whose attacks were all the fiercer the more stoutly Anthony proved himself in resistance — that he would upbraid them for their weakness; and frequently rousing his disciples to fight against the devil, and teaching them by what weapons he might be conquered, he would say: Believe me, brothers, Satan is afraid of the vigils, prayers, fasts, voluntary poverty, mercy, and humility of the devout, but above all of a burning love for Christ our Lord, by the one most holy sign of whose Cross he is weakened and flees. He was so terrible to the demons that many throughout Egypt who were tormented by them were set free by the invocation of the name of Anthony; and such was his fame for holiness that Constantine the Great and his sons commended themselves to his prayers by letter. At length, when he was in his one hundred and fifth year, having countless imitators of his way of life, he called together the monks and instructed them in the perfect rule of Christian life; and, renowned for holiness and miracles, he departed to heaven on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of February.

Juliana, of the noble Falconieri family, was heard from her very cradle to bring forth of her own accord, from babbling lips, the most sweet names of Jesus and Mary. Before she had yet completed her fifteenth year, having set aside both her considerable worldly fortune and an earthly marriage, she solemnly vowed her virginity to God into the hands of the holy Philip Benizi, and was the very first of all to receive from him the religious habit of those who are called Mantellate. And when many women of the more noble families followed her example, and her own mother gave herself to be formed in the religious life by her daughter, Juliana established the Order of the Mantellate. She excelled in wondrous humility, in constant devotion to prayer, and in singular abstinence. Since by reason of her poor health she was in no way able to take and retain food, and was therefore kept from the Eucharistic table, she begged a priest to apply to her breast at least externally the divine Bread he had brought, which she could not receive by mouth. When the priest had done this, the divine Bread at once disappeared, and Juliana breathed her last with a joyful countenance.

Many women of the more noble families followed Juliana's example, and her own mother gave herself to be formed in the religious life by her daughter, so that, with the number gradually increasing, she established the Order of the Mantellate, and with the greatest prudence and holiness handed down to it the laws of a devout life. Since Saint Benizi had the most thorough knowledge of her virtues, when he was near death he wished to entrust no one more than Juliana not only with the women but with the entire Order of the Servants, of which he had been the propagator and director. Yet she herself always thought humbly of herself; and, though she was the teacher of the others, she served her sisters in every domestic task, however lowly. By her assiduousness in prayer she would spend entire days most often rapt in ecstasy; and if any time remained, she devoted it to calming civil disputes, drawing sinners back from the way of iniquity, and serving the sick; and at times, licking with her mouth the pus flowing from their sores, she would restore them to health. She was accustomed to mortify her body with scourges, knotted cords, iron girdles, vigils, and lying naked on the ground. She sustained herself on very sparse and coarse food for four days of the week, and on the remaining two was content with the Bread of Angels alone, except on Saturday, when she was nourished by bread and water only.

Lucy, a virgin of Syracuse, noble both in lineage and in Christian faith, at the tomb of the blessed Agatha in Catania, obtained healing for her mother Eutychia, who was suffering from a flow of blood. She then obtained her mother's permission to distribute to the poor all the goods she was about to receive as a dowry. Therefore, having been accused before the prefect Paschasius for being a Christian, she could be induced by neither flatteries nor threats to offer sacrifice to idols. Then Paschasius, inflamed with anger, ordered Lucy to be dragged to a place where her virginity might be violated; but it was brought about by divine power that the steadfast Virgin stood so firm that no force could move her from the spot. For this reason the prefect commanded a fire to be kindled around her; but since even the flame did her no harm, her throat was pierced with a sword amid many torments. Receiving that wound, Lucy foretold the peace of the Church that was to come after the deaths of Diocletian and Maximian, and on the Ides of December gave back her spirit to God. Her body, buried at Syracuse, was thereafter translated to Constantinople, and finally to Venice.

A Homily of Saint Cyril, Bishop of Alexandria

A Homily of Saint Augustine, Bishop.

This whole span of time, in which the present age flies past, is brief. Hence the same Evangelist says in his Letter: It is the final hour. For this reason he added: Because I go to the Father — which must be referred to the former statement, where he says: A little while, and you will not see me; not to the latter, where he says: And again a little while, and you will see me. For by going to the Father, he was about to bring it about that they should not see him. And therefore this was not said because he was going to die, and, until he rose again, would withdraw from their sight; but because he was going to go to the Father, which he did after he rose from the dead and, having conversed with them for forty days, ascended into heaven.

At that time: Jesus said to his disciples: Amen, amen, I say to you, unless a grain of wheat falls into the ground and dies, it remains alone. And so forth.

The present life is pleasant and full of many delights — yet not for all, but only for those who are attached to it. But if anyone looks up toward heaven and contemplates the glorious things that are there, he will immediately despise this life and count it as nothing. For even the beauty of bodies is admired as long as something more beautiful is not discovered; but once a more excellent thing appears, the former is looked down upon. But if we too should desire to behold that beauty and contemplate the splendor of the heavenly Kingdom, we shall at once loose ourselves from the chains of this age.

For who would not most gladly have dwelt with that Mother who carried the incarnate Word in her womb for nine months, and dwelt with him most devoutly and sweetly for a full thirty years? Who would not envy the beloved of the Lord, who, in the absence of the Son of God, obtained the presence of the Mother of God? But, unless I am mistaken, we too can obtain by our prayers, through the goodness of our Word who took flesh for our sake and was crucified out of exceeding love for us, that he may say to us as well: Behold your Mother; and may say to his Mother concerning us: Behold your son.

He continues and says: Seeing his signs which he performed. And what does he say of Nicodemus? He was a leader of the Jews, named Nicodemus. He came to him at night and said to him: Rabbi, we know that you have come as a teacher from God. He too, therefore, had believed in his name. And on what basis had he believed? It follows: For no one can perform these signs that you do, unless God is with him.
If, therefore, Nicodemus was among those many who had believed in his name, let us now consider, in this Nicodemus, why Jesus did not trust himself to them.

The Evangelist used a watchful word, so as not to say: He struck his side, or wounded it, or anything else, but Opened it; so that there, in a manner of speaking, the door of life might be thrown open, from which the sacraments of the Church flowed forth, without which one does not enter into life, which is true life. That blood which was shed was shed for the forgiveness of sins. That water tempers the saving cup; it also furnishes both a washing and a drink. This was foreshadowed when Noah was commanded to make a door in the side of the ark, through which the animals that were not to perish in the flood might enter — by which the Church was prefigured. For this reason the first woman was made from the side of the sleeping man, and was called life and mother of the living. For she signified a great good, before the great evil of the transgression. This second Adam, bowing his head, slept upon the Cross, so that from there a spouse might be formed for him, which flowed from the side of the sleeper. O death, by which the dead return to life! What is purer than that blood? What more wholesome than that wound?

What great thing was it for the King of the ages to become King of men? For Christ is not King of Israel in order to exact tribute or to arm an army with the sword and visibly vanquish enemies; but King of Israel in this: that he governs minds, that he counsels for eternity, that he leads those who believe, hope, and love into the Kingdom of Heaven. The Son of God, therefore, equal to the Father, the Word through whom all things were made, wished to be King of Israel — this is condescension, not promotion; it is a sign of mercy, not an increase of power. For he who was called on earth King of the Jews is in heaven the Lord of Angels. But is Christ King of the Jews alone, or also of the nations? Indeed, also of the nations. For when it was said in prophecy: But I have been established as King by him upon Zion his holy mountain, proclaiming the commandment of the Lord — lest anyone, on account of Mount Zion, should say he had been established king for the Jews alone — he immediately added: The Lord said to me, You are my Son; today I have begotten you; ask of me, and I will give you the nations as your inheritance, and the ends of the earth as your possession.

This I say to Christians, who claim to believe the Scriptures.

At that time: Thomas, one of the twelve, who is called Didymus, was not with them when Jesus came. And so forth.
