What, dearest brothers, what do you observe in all this? Do you think it happened by chance that that chosen disciple was absent at the time, and then coming afterward he heard, hearing he doubted, doubting he touched, touching he believed? This did not happen by chance, but by divine dispensation. For the supreme clemency acted in a wondrous way, so that the doubting disciple, while touching the wounds of the flesh in his Master, might heal the wounds of unbelief in us. Thomas's unbelief was more profitable to our faith than the faith of the believing disciples; because, as he is brought back to faith through touching, our mind is strengthened in faith, with all doubt set aside.

At that time: Jesus said to Nicodemus: No one ascends into heaven except he who descended from heaven, the Son of Man, who is in heaven. And so forth.

A Homily of Saint Augustine, Bishop

No one ascends into heaven except he who descended from heaven. For he descended, and died, and by that very death freed us from death. Slain by death, he slew death. And you know, brothers, that this death entered the world through the envy of the devil. God did not make death, as Scripture declares: He does not rejoice, it says, in the destruction of the living; for he created all things that they might exist. But what does it say there? Through the envy of the devil, death entered the world. Man, driven on, would not come to the death administered by the devil: for the devil had not the power to compel, but the craft to persuade. If you had not consented, the devil would have brought in nothing; your consent, O man, led you to death. Born mortal from a mortal, and made mortal from immortal beings. From Adam all men are mortal; but Jesus, the Son of God, the Word of God, through whom all things were made, the only-begotten, equal to the Father, was made mortal, because the Word was made flesh and dwelt among us. If, therefore, he took on death, and suspended death upon the Cross, mortals are freed from that very death. What was done in figure among the ancients, the Lord recalled.
Ioan 16:

At that time: Jesus said to his disciples: Amen, amen, I say to you, that you shall mourn and weep, but the world will rejoice. And so forth.

From a Homily of Saint John Chrysostom
Homil. 78 in Ioann.

A great thing, most beloved, a great thing, I say, is the governance of the Church — one that requires much wisdom and fortitude, of the kind Christ set forth: that we lay down our life for the sheep, and never abandon them; that we resist the wolf with courage. For this is the difference between a shepherd and a hireling: the one, disregarding the sheep, cares only for himself; the other, disregarding himself, always watches over the safety of the sheep. Therefore, having set forth the example of the shepherd, he mentions two deceivers: the thief who slaughters and plunders the sheep, and the hireling who permits the wolf and does not defend those entrusted to him.

We must, brothers, lift up our minds to God with greater attention, so that we may be able in some way to grasp in our minds the words of the holy Gospel that have just resounded in our ears. For the Lord Jesus says: Let not your heart be troubled. You believe in God; believe also in me. Lest they should fear death as men, and be troubled on that account, he consoles them, bearing witness that he himself is also God. You believe, he says, in God; believe also in me. For it follows that if you believe in God, you ought also to believe in me — which would not follow unless Christ were God.

When Christ is exalted, dearest ones, through the Cross, let not only that sight present itself to the eye of the mind which was before the eyes of the ungodly, to whom it was said by Moses: And your life shall hang before your eyes, and you shall fear night and day, and shall not trust in your life. For these could think of nothing in the crucified Lord but their own crime, having a fear not of the kind by which true faith is justified, but by which an iniquitous conscience is tormented. But our understanding, illumined by the Spirit of truth, let it receive with a pure and free heart the glory of the Cross, shining out over heaven and earth; and let it see with the interior gaze what sort of thing it is that the Lord, when he spoke of the imminence of his Passion, said: Now is the judgment of the world; now will the prince of this world be cast out. And I, if I am lifted up from the earth, will draw all things to myself.

At that time: Jesus said to his disciples: Amen, amen, I say to you, unless a grain of wheat falls into the ground and dies, it remains alone. And so forth.

From a Homily of Saint Augustine, Bishop.

When, therefore, the critical moment arrives, and this condition is set before us — either to act against the commandment of God, or to depart from this life — if a man is compelled to choose between the two, when the persecutor threatens death, let him choose to die as one beloved of God rather than to live as one who has offended him. There let him hate his soul in this world, so as to keep it unto eternal life. If anyone serves me, let him follow me. What is Follow me, if not, Imitate me? For Christ suffered for us, says the Apostle Peter, leaving us an example, that we should follow his footsteps.

Tract. 1 in Ioann., circa médium

Lest you think something base, of the kind you were accustomed to imagine when you had been used to hearing human words, hear what you are to think: God was the Word. Let some faithless Arian now come forward and say that the Word of God was made. How can it be that the Word of God was made, when God made all things through the Word? If the Word of God was itself also made: through what other word was it made? If you say that this is the word of the Word, through which that Word was made, then I say that this other word is the only-begotten Son of God. But if you do not say the word of the Word, then grant that that through which all things were made was not itself made. For that through which all things were made could not itself have been made through itself. Believe the Evangelist, therefore.

How often must I, brethren, after your tearful complaints, implore the Mother of mercy that she would suggest to her most gracious Son that you have no wine? And she herself, I tell you, dearest ones, if she is devoutly entreated by us, will not fail our need, for she is merciful and the Mother of mercy; for if she had compassion on the embarrassment of those who had invited her, how much more will she have compassion on us if she is devoutly invoked.

Quadragesimale de christiana Religione, Sermo 51 de Passione Domini, parte 2, art. 1, cap. 3

The minds of all who read or hear are struck with wonder — namely, by what movement, by what feeling, by what possibility, by what true authority these things are said: that the disciple passes over into becoming a son of the Virgin, and that the Virgin has as her own son a mere man whom she did not bear; just as it also cannot be that one who was born of corrupt parents from seed should be a son of the Virgin. These things indeed seem impossible, but nothing is impossible with God. Piety and prayer are indeed needed in order to enter into such a mystery. For the blessed Virgin is called by Christ 'Woman' — she whom he never addressed by the word 'mother.' Woman, yet not woman: but one surpassing angels and men and women. She received from the Son whom she possessed together with the eternal Father as an only Son, a son apart from the womb — the One whom she had previously borne in the flesh as, in a sense, her own grandson.

Holy Scripture teaches us that, in those who are praiseworthy, not only their character but also their parents ought to be praised; so that, as it were, an inheritance of unsullied purity may be preeminent in those whom we wish to commend. For what other intention does the holy Evangelist have in this passage, if not to ennoble Saint John the Baptist by his parents, his miracles, his character, his office, and his Passion? Thus also the mother of holy Samuel, Hannah, is praised; thus Isaac received from his parents a nobility of piety which he bequeathed to his posterity. Therefore Zechariah is a priest, and not merely a priest, but also of the section of Abijah — that is, of noble rank among the higher priestly families.

For this reason it is put: From God. Or it is said From God, lest anyone should think that God revealed his counsel to any of the blessed spirits before he revealed it to the Virgin — with the sole exception of the Archangel Gabriel; who could certainly have been found to be of such preeminent rank among his companions that he was judged worthy both of such a name and of such a message.

The Church celebrates the sacred feasts of the Mother of God as frequently as reverently, knowing with certainty that it is both pleasing to God and worthy of the faithful of Christ — this duty by which the most blessed Mother of our Lord and God, among all the blessed of either sex, is celebrated at certain times of the year and with public ceremonies. Among these feasts, which have been religiously observed for so many centuries, the feast of the Assumption is reckoned the greatest and holds the preeminent place. Nor did any day turn out more joyful or more blessed for Mary, if we rightly contemplate the new happiness of soul and body bestowed upon her on that day: and therefore if ever at any time, then especially and above all did her spirit and soul and body marvel and exult in the living God, and she herself could most rightly say: He has looked upon the humility of his handmaid: For behold, from this time all generations shall call me blessed, because he who is mighty has done great things for me.

And what he says — Not my will, but yours, be done — he referred his own will to his humanity, and the Father's to the divinity. For the will of man is temporal; the will of the divinity, eternal. The will of the Father is not other than the will of the Son. For there is one will where there is one divinity. Learn, therefore, to be subject to God, so that you do not choose what you yourself wish, but what you know will be pleasing to God.

Consider more deeply, therefore, with what affection of devotion he wished her to be honored by us — he who placed the fullness of all good in Mary — so that we should know that, if there is any hope in us, if any grace, if any salvation, all of it overflows from her who ascended abounding with delights. A Homily of Saint Sophronius, Bishop
Homilia in Deiparæ Annunt.

What does the blessed Angel, sent to the most pure Virgin, say? Or how does he bring this most auspicious message to her? Hail, full of grace, the Lord is with you. He who is the herald of joy begins to address her with joy. For he knew and clearly understood that his message would bring joy to all men and equally to all creatures, and would drive away all sorrows of every kind; he knew that, from the divine knowledge of this mystery, the world would be illuminated with light; he knew that the darkness of error would be dispersed; he knew that the sting of death would be blunted; he knew that the power of corruption would be broken; he knew that the victory would be wrested from hell; he knew that salvation would shine forth for fallen man, who had long been crushed under the yoke of these evils, ever since he had been expelled from the delights of paradise and cast out from that blessed dwelling. For this reason he takes his start as an ambassador from joy; for this reason he prefaces his words with voices of gladness; for this reason joy goes before these auspicious tidings — inasmuch as they were destined to be a cause of joy to all who believe.

At that time: The Angel Gabriel was sent from God to a city of Galilee named Nazareth, to a virgin betrothed to a man whose name was Joseph, of the house of David; and the name of the virgin was Mary. Et réliqua.

A Homily of Saint Bernard, Abbot
Ex Homilía 2 super Missus

Rejoice, father Adam, but more so you, O mother Eve, take exultation — you who were parents of all, yet also destroyers of all; and what is more unhappy, destroyers before you were parents. Both of you, I say, take comfort in your daughter, and in such a daughter — but she the more from whom the evil first arose, whose reproach has passed upon all women. For the time is at hand when at last the reproach shall be taken away, nor shall man have cause to accuse woman: he who, while rashly trying to excuse himself, did not hesitate cruelly to accuse her, saying: The woman whom you gave me, she gave me of the tree, and I ate. Therefore run, Eve, to Mary; run, mother, to your daughter; let the daughter answer for the mother; let her take away the mother's reproach; let her make satisfaction to the Father on the mother's behalf: for behold, if man fell through a woman, he is lifted up again only through a woman.

At that time: Jesus entered into a certain town, and a certain woman named Martha received him into her home. Et réliqua.

A Homily of Saint Augustine, Bishop
Serm. 27 de Verb. Dom. t. 10

As the holy Gospel was read, you heard it with the greatest attention; and the event narrated was set before the eyes of your heart. You saw — not with the flesh, but with the mind — the Lord Jesus Christ reclining at table in the house of the Pharisee, and not disdaining the invitation extended to him. You also saw a woman well-known in the city — well-known, to be sure, for a bad reputation — a sinner, who had not been invited, burst in upon the banquet where her physician reclined, and who sought healing through pious boldness; breaking in, as it were an intruder upon the banquet, yet timely for the benefit. For she knew how great a disease afflicted her; and she knew that he to whom she had come was capable of healing her.

At that time: Jesus entered into a certain town, and a certain woman named Martha received him into her home. Et réliqua.

A Homily of Saint Bernard, Abbot
Serm. 2. de Assumpt. B. M. V.

What do we mean in saying that he entered into a town? He entered even into the most narrow lodging of the virginal womb. Then also a certain woman received him into her home. Happy woman, in whose home, upon receiving the Savior, it was found to be clean indeed, but plainly not empty. For who would call her empty whom the Angel greets as full of grace? Nor only this, but he also asserts that the Holy Spirit would still come upon her. For what purpose, do you think, if not to fill her even to overflowing? For what purpose, if not that, when the Spirit had already come and she was full, by his further coming upon her she might be made overflowing and superabundant for us as well?

At that time: Jesus went out to a mountain to pray, and he was in the prayer of God throughout the night. And when day came, he called his disciples. Et réliqua.

A Homily of Saint Ambrose, Bishop
Lib. 5 Comment. in Luc. cap. 6, post initium

All the great, all the sublime, ascend the mountain. For the prophet does not say to just anyone: Ascend the high mountain, you who bring good tidings to Sion; lift up your voice with strength, you who bring good tidings to Jerusalem. Ascend this mountain not with bodily footsteps but with more exalted deeds, and follow Christ, so that you yourself may be able to be a mountain: For mountains are round about him. And therefore in the Gospel you will find that only the disciples ascended the mountain with the Lord. The Lord prays, then, not that he may intercede for himself, but that he may obtain for me. For even though the Father has placed all things in the power of the Son, the Son nevertheless, in order to fulfill the form of man, considers that the Father is to be entreated on our behalf — for he is our Advocate.

At that time: The Angel Gabriel was sent from God to a city of Galilee named Nazareth, to a virgin betrothed to a man whose name was Joseph, of the house of David; and the name of the virgin was Mary. Et réliqua.

A Homily of Saint Ambrose, Bishop
Liber 2 in Lucam

The divine mysteries are hidden, and not easily — according to the prophetic saying — can any man know the counsel of God. Yet from the other deeds and precepts of the Lord our Savior we can understand that it was the design of a more deliberate counsel that she was chosen above all others to bear the Lord who was betrothed to a man. But why was she not filled with the Spirit before she was betrothed? Perhaps so that it might not be said that she had conceived as a result of adultery.

At that time: A certain Pharisee asked Jesus to dine with him. And entering the house of the Pharisee, he reclined at table. Et réliqua.

A Homily of Saint Augustine, Bishop
Liber 50 Homilía 23, tom. 10

As the Gospel was read, you heard it with the closest attention; and the event narrated was turned over and set before the eyes of your heart. You saw — not with the flesh, but with the mind — the Lord Jesus Christ reclining at table in the house of the Pharisee, not disdaining the invitation of one who had invited him. You also saw in the city a notorious woman — notorious, that is, for a bad reputation — a sinner, who had not been invited, yet burst in upon the banquet where her physician reclined, and sought healing through pious boldness; breaking in as if an unwelcome intruder upon the banquet, yet timely for the benefit. For she knew how great a disease she suffered; and she knew that he to whom she had come was fit to heal her.

At that time: The Angel Gabriel was sent from God to a city of Galilee named Nazareth, to a virgin betrothed to a man whose name was Joseph, of the house of David; and the name of the virgin was Mary. Et réliqua.

A Homily of Saint Tarasius, Bishop
De Præsentatióne Deiparæ

With what praises shall we heap you, Mary? O immaculate girl; O undefiled virgin; ornament of women, brilliance of daughters! O holy Virgin Mother, you are blessed among women; you are celebrated for your innocence; you are sealed with virginity. You are the expiation of the cursed Adam; you are the payment of Eve's debt. You are the most pure oblation of Abel; the choice of the firstborn; the immaculate sacrifice. You are Enos's hope in God, unashamed; you are Enoch's attained grace, and migration to a secure life. You are Noah's ark, and the conciliation of the second regeneration with God. You are the most illustrious splendor of the kingdom and priesthood of Melchizedek; you are Abraham's firm trust and the submissive faith of the promised future posterity. You are Isaac's new sacrifice and rational holocaust; you are Jacob's cause of ascent on the ladder, and the most noble expression of the enduring fruitfulness in the twelve tribes. You appeared as a daughter according to the stock of Judah; you are the chastity of Joseph and the overthrow of ancient Egypt — that is, of the synagogue of the Jews — O Immaculate! You are the book of Moses himself, the same legislator, divinely composed, in which the mystery of regeneration is written, and the law inscribed by divine fingers in the tablets as though on Mount Sinai, where the new Israel will be delivered from the servitude of the spiritual Egyptians, even as the ancient people in the wilderness were satisfied with manna and water from the rock — and the rock was Christ, who would come forth from your womb as a bridegroom from his chamber. You are Aaron's rod flowering; you are the daughter of David, clothed about with fringes of gold, shining with varied adornment.

At that time: The Angel Gabriel was sent from God to a city of Galilee named Nazareth, to a virgin betrothed to a man whose name was Joseph, of the house of David; and the name of the virgin was Mary. Et réliqua.

A Homily of Saint Epiphanius, Bishop
Oratio de laudibus S. Maríæ Deiparæ

What shall I say, or what shall I speak, of the glorious and holy Virgin? For she surpasses all things, God alone excepted: by nature she is more beautiful than the Cherubim and Seraphim themselves, and than all the host of Angels; to proclaim her praises, the tongue of heaven and earth wholly fails, and indeed even that of Angels. O blessed Virgin, pure dove and heavenly spouse, Mary, heaven, temple, and throne of the divinity, who have Christ, the sun blazing in heaven and on earth! A bright cloud, who brought down Christ, the most brilliant lightning from heaven, to enlighten the world. Hail, full of grace, gate of the heavens, of whom the prophet in the Canticle speaks plainly and openly in the course of his prayer, crying out: A garden enclosed is my sister, my spouse, a garden enclosed, a fountain sealed.
Luc 15:

At that time: Tax collectors and sinners were drawing near to Jesus to hear him. And so forth.

A Homily of Saint Gregory the Pope
Hom. 34 in Evang.
You have heard in the reading ...

Now the time for Elizabeth to give birth arrived, and she brought forth a son. And her neighbors and relatives heard that the Lord had magnified his mercy with her, and so they congratulated her. And so forth.

From a Homily of Saint Ambrose the Bishop
Lib. 2 in Luc. cap. 1 in fine

And his father Zechariah was filled with the Holy Spirit, and he prophesied. See how good God is, and how ready to pardon sins; he not only restores what was taken away, but also grants what was not hoped for. He who was mute not long ago now prophesies; for this is the great grace of God, that he whom had denied, he now confesses. Let no one therefore despair, let no one who is aware of past offenses lose hope of divine reward. The Lord knows how to change his sentence, if you know how to amend your fault.

At that time: Jesus said to the crowds: If anyone comes to me, and does not hate his father, and mother, and wife, and children, and brothers, and sisters, and yes, even his own life, he is not able to be my disciple. And so forth.

A Homily of Saint Gregory the Pope.
Homil. 37. in Evangelia.

If we consider, dearest brethren, what and how great are the things promised to us in heaven, all things held on earth grow cheap in our estimation. For earthly substance, compared to heavenly felicity, is a burden, not a support. Temporal life, compared to eternal life, is to be called death rather than life; for what else is the daily wasting of decay, if not a certain prolonged death? Yet what tongue can speak, or what understanding grasp, how great are the joys of that heavenly city: to be present in the choirs of Angels, to stand with the most blessed spirits in the presence of the glory of the Creator, to behold the face of God present, to see the uncircumscribed light, to be touched by no fear of death, to rejoice in the gift of everlasting incorruption? But upon hearing these things the soul is set ablaze, and already longs to be present there, where it hopes to rejoice without end. Yet to great rewards one cannot arrive save through great labors. Hence also Paul, that excellent preacher, says: He shall not be crowned, unless he strives lawfully.

At that time: As Jesus came down from the mountain, he stood in a level place with a crowd of his disciples, and a copious multitude of people from all of Judea and Jerusalem, and the seacoast, and Tyre and Sidon. And so forth.

A Homily of Saint Peter Canisius the Priest
Notæ in evangelicas lectiones: in die festo Omnium Sanctorum, post initium

I will note that Christ teaches and proclaims blessedness in a manner far different from this world. For it is the world's own nature to tell lies about human happiness through perishable and fleeting things, which are to be left behind here, as if to say: Blessed is the people to whom these things belong. Indeed, those whom Christ here declares blessed, the foolish world regards only as wretched and unhappy, and after its fashion despises and shuns them; so that Christ himself even testifies to the Apostles: Amen, amen, I say to you, that you shall weep and mourn, but the world shall rejoice, and you shall be sorrowful. And rightly did Solomon say: One who walks in the right way and fears God is despised by one who treads the path of infamy.

At that time: The Angel Gabriel was sent from God into a city of Galilee named Nazareth, to a Virgin betrothed to a man whose name was Joseph, of the house of David; and the name of the Virgin was Mary. And so forth.

A Homily of Saint Bernard the Abbot
Sermo de S. Maria

To commend his grace and to confound human wisdom, God was pleased to take flesh from a woman, yet a virgin, that he might render like to like, cure contrary by contrary, pluck out the pestilent thorn, and most mightily blot out the handwriting of sin. Eve was a thorn; Mary appeared as a rose. Eve a thorn, by wounding; Mary a rose, by soothing the hearts of all. Eve a thorn, piercing death into all; Mary a rose, restoring to all a saving lot. Mary was a rose, white through virginity, red through charity; white in flesh, red in mind; white by following virtue, red by trampling down vice; white by purifying affection, red by mortifying the flesh; white by loving God, red by compassion toward neighbor.

At that time: Taking up the word, Jesus said: A certain man descended from Jerusalem to Jericho, and he happened upon robbers, who plundered him as well, and departing after inflicting wounds, left him half dead. And so forth.

A Homily of Saint Gregory of Nazianzus
Ex Orat. 16. Tom. 1.

Let us therefore be purified through works of mercy, let us wipe away the stains and filth of the soul, and let us be made white — some as wool, some as snow — in proportion, that is, to the mercy shown: and to say something yet more formidable, if you have no contrition, no bruise, no swelling wound, no leprosy of the soul, no touch of meaning, no whiteness — such as were healed but imperfectly by the law, yet require the healing hand of Christ — then at least venerate him who for the sake of our salvation was afflicted with wounds and sickness. You will venerate him if you show yourself kindly and humane toward a member of Christ. But if perhaps the plunderer and tyrant of our souls, encountering you either as you descend from Jerusalem to Jericho, or anywhere else unarmed and unprepared, has wounded you so deeply that you do not even seek a remedy — ah, that is truly the gravest of wounds, and a calamity spreading most deeply!

At that time: It happened also on another Sabbath that Jesus entered into the synagogue and taught; and there was a man there whose right hand was withered. And so forth.

A Homily of Saint Peter Chrysologus
Sermo 32

In this man the image of all men is figured; in him the care of all is carried on; in him the long-awaited healing of all is restored. For the hand of man had withered more from numbness of faith than from dryness of sinew, and more from the fault of conscience than from bodily weakness. That sickness was exceedingly ancient, having befallen at the very beginning of the world; nor could it be healed by any human skill or benefit, since it had been contracted by the indignation of God. He had touched what was forbidden, had presumed what was not granted, when he stretched out his hand to the tree of the knowledge of good and evil: he needed not one who would apply a poultice, but one who could relax the sentence that had been imposed, and resolve by pardoning what he had bound up by his indignation.

At that time: Jesus said to his disciples: Do not be afraid, little flock, for it has pleased your Father to give you the kingdom. And so forth.

A Homily of Saint Paulinus the Bishop
Sermo, alias Epistola 34 de Gazophylacio

The almighty Lord could have made all equally rich, most beloved, so that no one would be in need of another; but by the counsel of his infinite goodness, the merciful and compassionate Lord so arranged things as to put your heart to the test in them. He made one poor, that another might know mercy; he made one destitute, that he might exercise the wealthy. The material of your riches is the poverty of your brother, if you understand what it is to look with care upon the needy and the poor, and do not keep for yourself alone what you have received; for God has assigned even a share of that person's goods to you in this age, so that whatever you might offer to the needy out of his gifts by your own free choice, he would owe to you; and in turn he would enrich you on the eternal day from that person's portion. For through these poor ones Christ now receives, and then for their sake he will repay.

At that time: The Lord designated another seventy-two, and sent them in pairs before his face into every city and place where he was to come. And so forth.

A Homily of Saint Gregory the Pope.
Homilia 17. in Evang.

Our Lord and Savior, dearest brethren, sometimes admonishes us by words, and sometimes by deeds. For his very actions are precepts: for by doing something in silence, he makes known what we ought to do. Behold, he sends his disciples out in pairs to preach; for the commandments of charity are two — namely, love of God and love of neighbor — and charity cannot exist where there is fewer than two. For no one is properly said to have charity toward himself alone: but love reaches out toward another, so that it may be charity.

At that time: A contention arose among the disciples, as to which of them appeared to be the greater. And so forth.

A Homily of Saint Ambrose the Bishop.
Liber 10 in Lucæ, cap. 22, post initium.

The Kingdom of God is not of this world. It is not, therefore, an equality of man with God, but a striving after likeness. For Christ alone is the full image of God, by reason of the unity of the Father's splendor expressed in himself. Yet the just man is in the image of God, if, for the sake of imitating the likeness of the divine life, he despises this world by the knowledge of God, and scorns earthly pleasures by receiving the Word by which we are nourished unto life: and hence we eat the Body of Christ, that we may be able to be sharers of eternal life.
Luc 2:21

At that time: After eight days were completed for the circumcision of the Child, his name was called Jesus. And so forth.

A Homily of Saint Ambrose the Bishop
Liber 2 in cap. 2 Lucæ, circa medium

The Child is therefore circumcised. Who is this child, if not he of whom it was said: A child is born to us, a Son is given to us? For he was made under the law, that he might gain those who were under the law. That they might present him to the Lord. What it means to be presented to the Lord in Jerusalem, I would explain, had I not already done so in my commentary on Isaiah. For one who is circumcised from vices is judged worthy of the Lord's gaze; for, The eyes of the Lord are upon the just. You see that the whole series of the old law was a type of what was to come: for circumcision too signifies the purification of offenses.
Ex Serm. 27 de Verbis Dom., paulo ante medium

Martha well served — what shall I say — the need, or the will, of the Lord in bodily matters; she ministered to mortal flesh. But who was it in mortal flesh? In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. Behold what Mary was hearing. The Word was made flesh and dwelt among us. Behold the one to whom Martha was ministering. Therefore Mary has chosen the better part, which shall not be taken away from her. For she chose what will always remain, and therefore it shall not be taken away from her.

At that time: Now it came to pass that, as all the people were being baptized, Jesus also was baptized; and as he was praying, heaven was opened. And so forth.

A Homily of Saint Augustine the Bishop.
Liber 2. de Consensu Evang.

It is clear that he who said, As was supposed, the son of Joseph, said it on account of those who believed that he was born of Joseph as other men are born. But those who are troubled by the fact that Matthew enumerates different ancestors, descending from David to Joseph, while Luke enumerates others, ascending from Joseph to David — they may easily perceive that Joseph could have had two fathers: one by whom he was begotten, another by whom he was adopted. For the custom of adoption was ancient even in that people of God, so that men made sons for themselves of those whom they themselves had not begotten. Hence it is understood that Luke received into his Gospel the father of Joseph not from whom he was begotten, but by whom he had been adopted, whose ancestors he recounts in ascending order, until he reaches David.

Now the time for Elizabeth to give birth arrived, and she brought forth a son. And her neighbors and relatives heard that the Lord had magnified his mercy with her, and so they congratulated her. And so forth.

From a Homily of Saint Ambrose the Bishop.
Lib. 2. in Lucam.

His name is John, she said. Elizabeth could not be ignorant of the herald of the Lord, she who had prophesied Christ. And it is well added: Because no one in his kindred was called by this name — so that you may understand that the name belongs not to a lineage but to a prophet. Zechariah is questioned by a sign; but because unbelief had taken from him both speech and hearing, what he could not say by voice, he expressed by hand and in writing.

At that time: The Angel Gabriel was sent from God into a city of Galilee named Nazareth, to a Virgin betrothed to a man. And so forth.

A Homily of Saint Bernard the Abbot
Homil. 2 super Missus est

No one doubts that the Queen of virgins herself — indeed, the first among the rest — will be among those who shall sing that new canticle in the Kingdom of God that is to be sung by virgins alone. Moreover, I believe that she, beyond what is proper to virgins alone, will, together with all virgins as their equal, as I said, gladden the city of God with some sweeter and more graceful melody. Yet to bring forth or to express the sweet-sounding notes of that song, not one even of the virgins themselves will be found worthy, for by right it will be kept for her alone to sing, who alone glories in a childbirth — and a divine childbirth. She glories, I said, in the birth, not in herself, but in him whom she bore. For God — since God is he whom she bore — desiring to endow his Mother with singular glory in the heavens, took care to precede her with singular grace on earth: namely, that she might conceive ineffably and untouched, and bring forth uncorrupted.

At that time: Jesus said to his disciples: When you shall hear of wars and seditions, do not be terrified; these things must first come to pass, but the end is not yet. Then he said to them: Nation will rise against nation, and kingdom against kingdom. And there will be great earthquakes in various places. And so forth.

A Homily of Saint Gregory the Pope
Hom. 1 in Evang.
Our Lord and Redeemer, desiring to find us prepared, ...

At that time: Jesus was going to a city called Nain; and his disciples and a great crowd went with him. And so forth.

A Homily of Saint Augustine the Bishop
Sermo 44 de Verbis Dómini, circa initium

At the resurrection of that young man, his widowed mother rejoiced; at the daily raising up of souls in the spirit, Mother Church rejoices. He was dead in body; those others are dead in mind. His visible death was visibly mourned; their invisible death was neither sought out nor seen. He sought them out who knew the dead. He alone knew the dead who was able to make them alive. For if he had not come to raise up the dead, the Apostle would not say: Arise, you who sleep, and rise from the dead, and Christ will enlighten you.

At that time: Jesus saw a tax collector named Levi sitting at the customs office, and he said to him: Follow me. And so forth.

A Homily of Saint Ambrose the Bishop.
Liber 5 Comment. in Lucæ Cap. 5 post initium

What follows: this calling of the tax collector is mystical — he commands him to follow, not by the step of the body, but by the affection of the mind. And so he, who formerly converted greedy gains from wages, harsh profits from the labors and dangers of sailors, being called by a word, abandons his own possessions, he who used to seize those of others; and, leaving behind that base seat, walks after the Lord with the full step of his mind. He also makes ready the appearance of a great banquet; for whoever receives Christ into his inner dwelling is nourished with the greatest delights of overflowing pleasures.

At that time: The Angel Gabriel was sent from God into a city of Galilee named Nazareth, to a Virgin betrothed to a man whose name was Joseph, of the house of David; and the name of the Virgin was Mary. And so forth.

A Homily of Saint Bonaventure the Bishop
Sermo de regia dignitate Beatæ Mariæ Virginis

The Blessed Virgin Mary is the mother of the Most High King through a noble conception, according to what is said in the word spoken to her by the Angel: Behold, he says, you shall conceive and bear a son; and then: The Lord God will give him the throne of David his father, and he will reign in the house of Jacob for ever, and of his kingdom there will be no end. As if to say plainly: You shall conceive and bear a Son who is King, reigning eternally on a royal throne, and therefore as the Mother of the King you shall reign, and as Queen you shall sit upon the royal throne. For if it is fitting that a son give honor to his mother, it is fitting that he share with her the royal throne; hence the Virgin Mary, because she conceived him who has written on his thigh: King of kings and Lord of lords, from the very moment she conceived the Son of God, was Queen not only of earth but also of heaven, as is signified in the Apocalypse where it is said: A great sign appeared in heaven: a woman clothed with the sun, and the moon beneath her feet, and on her head a crown of twelve stars.

At that time: The Angel Gabriel was sent from God into a city of Galilee named Nazareth, to a Virgin betrothed to a man whose name was Joseph, of the house of David; and the name of the Virgin was Mary. And so forth.

A Homily of Saint Bernard the Abbot
Ex Homilía 1 super Missus

Who is this Virgin so venerable as to be greeted by an Angel, yet so humble as to be betrothed to a carpenter? A beautiful mingling of virginity and humility; nor does that soul displease God in a middling way, in whom humility commends virginity, and virginity adorns humility. But how great, think you, is the veneration she deserves, in whom fruitfulness exalts humility, and childbirth consecrates virginity? You hear of a virgin, you hear of one who is humble. Virginity is a praiseworthy virtue, but humility is more necessary: the one is counseled, the other commanded.

At that time: Jesus entered into a certain village; and a certain woman named Martha received him into her home. And so forth.

A Homily of Saint Augustine the Bishop
Sermo 20 de Verbis Domini

The words of our Lord Jesus Christ, which have just been read from the Gospel, admonish us that there is one thing toward which we must tend, even as we labor amid the multitude of this age. We tend, however, still as pilgrims, not yet as those who abide; still on the way, not yet in our homeland; still in longing, not yet in enjoyment. Yet let us tend, and without sluggishness and without ceasing let us tend, that we may at some point be able to arrive. Martha and Mary were two sisters, both kindred not only in flesh but also in devotion; both clung to the Lord; both served the Lord present in the flesh with one accord.

At that time: As Jesus was speaking to the crowds, a certain woman from the crowd lifted up her voice and said to him: Blessed is the womb that bore you. And so forth.

A Homily of Saint John Chrysostom
In Ioann. c. 2 Homilia 20, circa finem

When you hear that woman saying: Blessed is the womb that bore you and the breasts that nursed you; and then the Lord responding: Yes, but moreover: blessed are those who hear the word of God and keep it — understand that this was said not because he was neglecting his Mother, but to show that the name of mother would bring her no profit unless she excelled in goodness and faith. For if to Mary, without virtue, maternal love was to profit nothing; far less will the goodness of a father, brother, mother, or son profit us, unless we bring something of our own.

At that time: A decree went out from Caesar Augustus, that the whole world should be enrolled. And so forth.

A Homily of Saint Gregory the Pope
Homilia 8 in Evangelia

Since, by the Lord's bounty, we are this day to celebrate the solemn rites of Mass three times, we cannot speak at length of the Gospel reading; yet the very Nativity of our Redeemer compels us to say something, if briefly. For what does it mean that the world is enrolled at the birth of the Lord, if not that it is plainly shown that he who would inscribe his chosen ones in eternity was appearing in the flesh? Against this, it is said of the reprobate through the prophet: Let them be blotted out of the book of the living, and not be written with the just. He is fittingly born also in Bethlehem; for Bethlehem means house of bread. He himself is the one who said: I am the living bread who came down from heaven. The place, therefore, where the Lord is born was called house of bread before his coming, because it was surely to be that he who would refresh the minds of the chosen with inward satisfaction would appear there in the matter of flesh. He is born not in his parents' home, but on the road, to show plainly that through his humanity, which he had assumed, he was, as it were, born in a stranger's dwelling.

In that time: Jesus said to his disciples: Nothing is covered that will not be revealed; nor hidden that will not be known. Et cetera.

A Homily of Saint John Chrysostom.
Homilia in cap. x Matth. v. 26. et seq.

Nothing is covered that will not be revealed, nor hidden that will not be known. What he says amounts to this: It is sufficient consolation for you, if I, your Master and Lord, am a sharer in reproaches. But if you still grieve upon hearing this, consider also that you will not long afterward be freed from this suspicion. For why do you take it so hard? Because they call you impostors and deceivers? Wait but a little, and all men will proclaim you saviors and benefactors of the world. Time will indeed bring all obscure things to light, will expose their slanders, and will make your virtue conspicuous. For when by the very facts you are proved to be saviors and benefactors, conspicuous in every virtue, men will give no heed to their words but to the truth of the matter; and those accusers will be found to be sycophants, liars, and slanderers, while you will be found more radiant than the very sun. For a long stretch of time will make you known, will proclaim you, and will send forth a voice clearer than a trumpet, and will present all men as witnesses of your virtue. Let not, therefore, the things now spoken cast you down, but let the hope of future blessings lift you up. For the things that concern you cannot be hidden.

In that time: Mary arose and went with haste into the hill country, to a city of Judah; and she entered the house of Zechariah and greeted Elizabeth. Et cetera.
A Homily of Saint John Chrysostom.
Apud Metaphr. mense Iulio

When the Redeemer of our race had come to us, he went at once to his friend John, while John was still in the womb of his mother. When John beheld him from womb to womb, breaking the bounds of nature, he cried out: I see the Lord, who has set bounds to nature, and I will not await the time of birth. The nine months' span is not necessary for me here; for within me is he who is eternal. I will go forth from this dark tabernacle and proclaim in brief the knowledge of wondrous things. I am a sign: I will signify the coming of Christ. I am a trumpet: I will set forth the dispensation of the Son of God in the flesh. I will sound as a trumpet; by that very act I will bless my father's tongue and draw it to speak. I will sound as a trumpet, and I will quicken the womb of my mother.

When Jesus was twelve years old, as they went up to Jerusalem according to the custom of the feast, and the days were fulfilled, when they returned, the boy Jesus remained in Jerusalem. Et cetera.

A Homily of Saint Ambrose the Bishop.
Lib. 2. in cap. 2. Lucæ, in fine

From the twelfth year, as we read, the beginning of the Lord's teaching is taken. For to this number was owed the preaching of the faith by those who evangelize. Nor is it idly that, unmindful of his parents according to the flesh — he who was indeed filled with the wisdom and grace of God according to the flesh — he is found in the temple after three days; to be a sign that after the three days of that triumphant Passion, he who was believed dead would present himself risen to our faith in the heavenly dwelling and in divine honor.

In that time: Jesus spoke to his disciples this parable: A certain nobleman went into a far country to receive for himself a kingdom and to return. Et cetera.

A Homily of Saint Ambrose the Bishop.
Lib. 8. in Lucam.

A fitting order it was, that he who was about to call the Gentiles, and to command that the Jews who had not wished Christ to reign over them be put to death, should first set forth this comparison, lest it be said: He had given nothing to the Jewish people by which they could have become better; why is that demanded of one who has received nothing? This mina is not a small one — the one which the Gospel woman, because she did not find it, lit a lamp to seek by its light, and rejoiced when it was found.

In that time: When they returned, the boy Jesus remained in Jerusalem, and his parents did not know it. Et cetera.

A Homily of Saint Bernard the Abbot.
Hom. 1 de Laud. Virg. Matris

Mary calls God and the Lord of Angels her Son, saying: Son, why have you done this to us? Which of the Angels would dare this? It suffices them, and they count it a great thing, that whereas they are spirits by nature, they have been made and called Angels by grace, as David attests: Who makes his angels spirits. But Mary, recognizing herself as his mother, names with confidence as her Son that Majesty whom they serve with reverence; nor does God disdain to be called what he deigned to be. For shortly afterward the Evangelist adds: And he was subject to them. Who? To whom? God to human beings? God, I say, to whom the Angels are subject, whom Principalities and Powers obey — was subject to Mary.

In that time: Jesus said to his disciples: Fear not, little flock, for it has pleased your Father to give you the kingdom. Et cetera.

A Homily of Saint Bede the Venerable, Priest.
Lib. 4, Cap. 54, in Luc. 12

He calls the flock of the chosen a little flock, either in comparison with the greater number of the reprobate, or rather on account of the devotion of humility: because he clearly wills that his Church, however greatly it may have already expanded in multitude, should nevertheless continue to grow in humility until the end of the world, and by humility to attain the promised kingdom. And so, having gently consoled its labors, he promises with gracious and pleasing kindness the same kingdom to be given by the Father to those whom he commands to seek only the Kingdom of God.

In that time: Mary arose and went with haste into the hill country, to a city of Judah; and she entered the house of Zechariah and greeted Elizabeth. Et cetera.

A Homily of Saint Ambrose the Bishop.
Liber 2 Comment. in Lucæ. cap. 1, post initium

We must observe that the greater comes to the lesser, so that the lesser may be helped: Mary to Elizabeth, Christ to John. Indeed, afterward as well, the Lord came to baptism in order to sanctify the baptism of John. Swiftly too are the benefits of Mary's coming and of the divine presence made manifest. Mark the distinction and the propriety of each word. Elizabeth heard the voice first, but John felt the grace first. She heard in the order of nature; he exulted by the reason of mystery. She perceived the coming of Mary; he the coming of the Lord. These mothers speak of grace; those within work it inwardly; and they venerate the mystery of devotion through the maternal advances, and by a twofold miracle the mothers prophesy by the spirit of their little ones. The infant exulted; the mother was filled. Not the mother first, then the son; but when the son was filled with the Holy Spirit, he filled the mother as well.

In that time: Jesus entered Jericho and was passing through it. And behold, a man named Zacchaeus; he was a chief tax collector and he was rich. Et cetera.

A Homily of Saint Gregory the Pope.
Lib. 27. Moralium, cap. 27. post medium.

If we desire truly to be wise and to contemplate wisdom itself, let us humbly acknowledge ourselves to be fools. Let us abandon harmful wisdom; let us learn praiseworthy folly. For it is written: God chose the foolish things of the world to confound the wise. And again it is said: If anyone among you seems to be wise in this age, let him become a fool that he may be wise. The words of the Gospel story also testify: that Zacchaeus, when he could see nothing for the crowd, climbed a sycamore tree to behold the Lord as he passed. For the sycamore tree is indeed called the foolish fig.

In that time: Jesus said to the crowds: If anyone comes to me and does not hate his father and mother and wife and children and brothers and sisters, and even his own soul, he cannot be my disciple. Et cetera.

A Homily of Saint Basil the Bishop.
Lib. Regul. fusius explic. ad interrog. 8

Perfect renunciation consists in this: that we attain to the point of not being inclined even to attachment to life itself, and of having the sentence of death, so as not to trust in ourselves. Such renunciation, however, takes its beginning from detachment from external things, such as possessions, vain glory, habitual ways of living, and love of useless things; as the holy disciples of our Lord also showed us by their own example — James and John, who left behind their father Zebedee and the very boat on which their entire livelihood depended; and Matthew, who rose from the tax collector's table and followed the Lord.

In that time: The Angel Gabriel was sent from God to a city of Galilee, named Nazareth, to a Virgin betrothed to a man whose name was Joseph, of the house of David; and the Virgin's name was Mary. Et cetera.

A Homily of Saint Germanus the Bishop.
In Præsentatione Deiparæ

Hail, Mary, full of grace, holier than the Saints, higher than the heavens, more glorious than the Cherubim, more honorable than the Seraphim, and more venerable than every creature. Hail, dove, who brings us both the fruit of the olive and announces the Savior from the spiritual flood, and the harbor of salvation; whose wings are as silver, and the hinder part of her back as the pale gold of the most holy and illuminating Spirit's brightness. Hail, most pleasant and rational paradise of God, planted today toward the East by the same God's most benevolent and almighty right hand, and putting forth for him a sweet-smelling lily and an unfading rose as a remedy for those who had drunk at the West the pestilential and soul-destroying bitterness of death; a paradise in which the life-giving tree blossoms to the knowledge of truth, and those who have tasted of it attain immortality. Hail, holy dwelling, built sacred, immaculate, and most pure palace of the most high King God, adorned on all sides with the magnificence of the same God the King, receiving all as guests and refreshing them with mystical delights; in which is placed the bridal chamber, not made by hands, radiant with varied beauty, of the spiritual Bridegroom; in which the Word, wishing to call back the straying human race, espoused flesh to himself, that he might reconcile to the Father those who had made themselves exiles by their own will.

In that time: The Mother of Jesus said to him: Son, why have you done this to us? Behold, your father and I have been searching for you in sorrow. Et cetera.

From a Homily of the Venerable Bede, Priest.
In Homilía Hiem. de Témpore, Domin. I. post Epiph.

His mother, says the Evangelist, kept all these words in her heart. All that the Virgin Mother had learned of what was said or done concerning the Lord or by the Lord, she kept more carefully in her heart, and earnestly committed everything to memory, so that when at last the time should come to preach or write of his Incarnation, she could sufficiently set forth all things as they had occurred to those who inquired. Let us also imitate, my brothers, the devout Mother of the Lord, by likewise keeping all the words and deeds of the Lord and Savior fixed in our hearts.

In that time: The Angel Gabriel was sent from God to a city of Galilee, named Nazareth, to a Virgin betrothed to a man whose name was Joseph, of the house of David; and the Virgin's name was Mary. Et cetera.

A Homily of Saint Tarasius the Bishop.
De Præsentatione Deiparæ.

For Elizabeth, the time of her delivery was fulfilled, and she bore a son. And her neighbors and kinsfolk heard that the Lord had shown great mercy to her, and they rejoiced with her. Et cetera.

A Homily of Saint Ambrose the Bishop.
Liber 2 Comm. in Lucæ cap. 1, ante finem

Elizabeth bore a son, and the neighbors rejoiced with her. The birth of the Saints brings gladness to many, because goodness is a common good; for justice is a virtue that belongs to all. And therefore at the birth of the just man a sign of the life to come is set before us, and the grace of the virtue that is to follow is marked by the exultation of the neighbors as a prefiguring. It is well also that the time the Prophet spent in the womb is described, lest the presence of Mary be passed over in silence; but the time of his infancy is left unrecorded, because he did not know the hindrances of infancy. And therefore in the Gospel we read nothing of him except his birth, the oracle spoken at it, his exultation in the womb, and his voice in the desert.

In that time: Jesus entered a certain village; and a woman named Martha received him into her house. Et cetera.

From a Homily of Saint Augustine the Bishop.
Ex Serm. 27. de Verbis Dom.

The toil of the multitude passes away, and the charity of unity remains. Therefore what Mary has chosen will not be taken from her: but from you, Martha, what you have chosen will — at least this follows, at least this is implied — from you what you have chosen will be taken: but it will be taken for your own good, that what is better may be given. For your toil will be taken from you, that rest may be given. You are sailing; she is already in port.

In that time: Jesus called together the twelve Apostles and gave them power and authority over all demons, and to cure diseases. Et cetera.

A Homily of Saint Bonaventure the Bishop.
Expositio in cap. 9 Lucæ

The Apostles were so named that their authority might be commended. For Apostle is interpreted as one sent: and they were sent to preach, according to that saying: Christ did not send me to baptize, but to evangelize. They were sent to preach, not a small thing, but a great one — namely, the Kingdom of God — by which may be understood the teaching of truth, according to that saying: The Kingdom of God will be taken from you and given to a nation that yields its fruits. It may also be said to be the grace of the Holy Spirit, according to that saying: The Kingdom of God is not food and drink, but justice and peace and joy in the Holy Spirit; and below: Behold, the Kingdom of God is within you. It may also be said to be eternal glory, according to that saying: Amen I say to you, unless one is reborn of water and the Holy Spirit, he cannot enter into the Kingdom of God.

In that time: The Angel Gabriel was sent from God to a city of Galilee, named Nazareth, to a Virgin betrothed to a man whose name was Joseph, of the house of David; and the Virgin's name was Mary. Et cetera.

A Homily of Saint Peter Chrysologus.
Sermo 142 de Annuntiatione

Today, most beloved brethren, you have heard an Angel treating with a woman of the restoration of man. You have heard it being arranged that man should return to life by the same courses by which he had slipped down to death. The Angel deals, the Angel deals with Mary concerning salvation, because an angel had dealt with Eve concerning ruin. You have heard the Angel constructing from the clay of our flesh a temple of divine majesty by an ineffable art. You have heard God being placed on earth and man in heaven by an incomprehensible mystery. You have heard God and man being mingled in one body by a plan unheard of. You have heard the fragile nature of our flesh being strengthened by angelic exhortation to bear the whole glory of the Godhead.

In that time: The Angel Gabriel was sent from God to a city of Galilee, named Nazareth, to a Virgin betrothed to a man whose name was Joseph, of the house of David; and the Virgin's name was Mary. Et cetera.

A Homily of Saint Sophronius the Bishop.

Truly blessed are you among women, for you have changed the curse of Eve into a blessing; for Adam, who formerly lay struck down by the curse, you have brought about to be blessed through you. Truly blessed are you among women, for the blessing of the Father has shone forth upon men through you, and has freed them from the ancient curse. Truly blessed are you among women, for through you your forebears find salvation; for you are about to bear the Savior, who will procure divine salvation for them. Truly blessed are you among women, for without seed you have brought forth that Fruit which lavishes blessing upon the world, and redeems it from the curse that causes thorns to spring forth. Truly blessed are you among women, for although you are a woman by natural condition, you will in very truth become the Mother of God. For if he who is to be born of you is, according to truth, God incarnate, you yourself are rightly and justly called Mother of God, seeing that you truly bear God.
A Reading from the holy Gospel according to Mark.

In that time: Jesus said to his disciples: Go into all the world and preach the Gospel to every creature. Et cetera.

A Homily of Saint Gregory the Pope.
Homilia 29 in Evangelia, post initium

By every creature may be understood every nation of the Gentiles. For it had previously been said: Do not go into the way of the Gentiles; but now it is said: Preach to every creature — so that the preaching rejected with pride by Judea might first, to its testimony of condemnation, become a help to us when she had proudly rejected it. But when the Truth sends his disciples to preach, what else does he do in the world but scatter grains of seed? And he sends a few grains in the sowing, that he may receive the harvests of many crops from our faith.

By every creature may be understood every nation of the Gentiles. For it had previously been said: Do not go into the way of the Gentiles; but now it is said: Preach to every creature — so that the preaching rejected with pride by Judea might first, to its testimony of condemnation, become a help to us when she had proudly rejected it. But when the Truth sends his disciples to preach, what else does he do in the world but scatter grains of seed? And he sends a few grains in the sowing, that he may receive the harvests of many crops from our faith.

In that time: Jesus said to his disciples: Whoever does not receive the Kingdom of God as a little child will not enter into it. Et cetera.

A Homily of Saint Augustine the Bishop.
Sermo 47 de diversis

It seems hard and burdensome what the Lord commanded — that whoever wishes to follow him should deny himself; but it is not hard or burdensome what he commands, since he helps bring about what he commands. For that is true which is said to him in the Psalm: Because of the words of your lips I have kept to hard ways. For whatever is hard in the commandments, charity makes gentle. We know how much love itself accomplishes. But what is it: Let him deny himself? Let him not presume of himself; let him acknowledge himself to be a human being, and heed the prophetic saying: Cursed is everyone who places his hope in a human being. Let him withdraw from himself — but not downward; let him withdraw from himself so as to cleave to God.

In that time: They were bringing little children to Jesus, that he might touch them; but the disciples rebuked those who brought them. Et cetera.

A Homily of Saint Bede the Venerable, Priest.
Commentárium in Marcum 10:13-21

Jesus says to his disciples: Suffer the little children to come to me, and do not forbid them; for of such is the Kingdom of God. He said significantly: Of such; not: Of these; to show that it is not age that reigns, but conduct; and that the reward is promised to those who have like innocence and simplicity — the Apostle also agreeing in the same sense: Brethren, do not be children in understanding; but in malice be as little children, yet in understanding be mature. Amen, I say to you: whoever does not receive the Kingdom of God as a little child will not enter into it. As a child does not persist in anger, does not remember being hurt, is not delighted when he sees a beautiful woman, does not think one thing and say another; so you also, unless you have such innocence and purity of soul, will not be able to enter the Kingdom of Heaven. In another sense, we are commanded to receive the Kingdom of God — that is, the teaching of the Gospel — as little children; because just as a little child in learning does not contradict the teachers, nor compose arguments and words against them in resistance, but faithfully receives what is taught and with reverence obeys and is still; so also we ought to do in obeying the words of the Lord simply and without any wavering. And he embraced them and laid his hands upon them and blessed them. He embraces and blesses the little ones, to signify that the humble in spirit are worthy of his blessing, his grace, and his love.

In that time: Herod sent and seized John and bound him in prison for the sake of Herodias, the wife of his brother Philip, whom he had married. Et cetera.

A Homily of Saint Augustine the Bishop.
Sermo 10 in novis. Serm.

When the holy Gospel was being read, a cruel spectacle was set before our eyes: the head of Saint John on a platter, a deadly dispatch of cruelty on account of hatred of truth. A girl dances, and her mother rages; and amid the wantonness and pleasures of the banqueters, a rash oath is sworn, and what is sworn is impiously fulfilled. What John himself had foretold came to pass for him; for he had said of the Lord Jesus Christ: He must increase, but I must decrease. He was diminished in his head; he grew on the Cross. Truth begot hatred. What the holy man of God admonished could not be endured with equanimity; he who was surely seeking the salvation of those he thus admonished. They returned evil for good.

In that time: Jesus answered his disciples and said to them: Have faith in God. Amen I say to you, that whoever shall say to this mountain: Take up and cast yourself into the sea, and shall not waver in his heart, but shall believe that whatever he says will come to pass, it will be done for him. Et cetera.

A Homily of Saint Bede the Venerable, Priest.
Liber 3 Comment. in Marc. cap. 11

The Gentiles who have written slanders against the Church are accustomed to reproach our people for not having had perfect faith in God, since they have never been able to move mountains. To whom it must be answered that the things done in the Church have not been written down, just as Scripture also testifies concerning the deeds of Christ and our Lord himself. Hence it could also have come to pass that a mountain be removed from the earth and cast into the sea, if necessity had demanded that this be done — as we read was brought about by the prayers of the blessed Father Gregory, bishop of Neocaesarea in Pontus, a man outstanding in merits and virtues, so that a mountain yielded its place on the earth by just as much as the inhabitants of the city had need.
A reading from the holy Gospel according to Mark.

At that time: And when evening had now arrived (because it was the Preparation Day, which is before the Sabbath), there arrived Joseph of Arimathea, a noble council member, who himself was also awaiting the kingdom of God. And so forth.

A Homily of the Venerable Bede, Priest
In Fer. III. Palmarum

Parasceve in Greek means preparation in Latin, by which name the Jews who dwelt among the Greeks called the sixth day of the Sabbath, because on that day they were accustomed to prepare what was needful for the Sabbath's rest; in accordance with what was once commanded concerning the manna: But on the sixth day you shall gather a double portion. For since man was made on the sixth day, and the whole creation of the world was completed, while on the seventh the Creator rested from his work—for which reason he also wished it to be called the Sabbath, that is, rest—the Savior was rightly crucified on that same sixth day, fulfilling the mystery of humanity's restoration; and so, when he had received the vinegar, he said: It is consummated; that is, the work of the sixth day, which I undertook for the world's renewal, is now fully accomplished. But resting in the tomb on the Sabbath, he awaited the event of the Resurrection, which was to come on the eighth day.

At that time: And Jesus, walking near the Sea of Galilee, saw two brothers, Simon who is called Peter, and his brother Andrew, casting a net into the sea. And so forth.

A Homily of Saint Gregory the Pope
Homilia 5 in Evangelia

You have heard, dearest brethren, how Peter and Andrew, at the sound of a single command, left their nets and followed the Redeemer. They had not yet seen him work any miracle; they had not yet heard anything from him about the reward of eternal recompense: and yet, at one command of the Lord, they forgot what they seemed to possess. How great are the miracles we behold, by how many scourges we are afflicted, by how many harshnesses of threats we are deterred, and yet we disdain to follow him when he calls.

At that time: Jesus said to his disciples: Behold, I am sending you like sheep in the midst of wolves. And so forth.

A Homily of Saint John Chrysostom.
Homilia 34 in Matthæum, post initium

When the Lord had cast out all anxiety from the hearts of the disciples, and had armed them with the display of signs, and had made them, as it were, iron and adamantine—detached from all worldly affairs and freed from every care for temporal things—he then at length foretold the adversities that would befall them. For from this foretelling of future events many benefits followed. First, that they might learn the power of his foreknowledge. Next, that no one might suspect that such grave evils descended from the weakness of their Master. Furthermore, lest those who were to suffer them be thrown into confusion by a sudden and unforeseen turn of events. Finally, lest, when they heard these things just before the time of his own Passion, they be too greatly disturbed.
Matt 1:1-16

The book of the lineage of Jesus Christ, the son of David, the son of Abraham. Abraham conceived Isaac. And Isaac conceived Jacob. And so forth.

A Homily of Saint John Damascene
Lib. 4 de Fide orthodoxa, cap. 15 de Domini genealogia et sanctae Dei Genetricis

That Joseph drew his origin from the tribe of David, the most holy Evangelists Matthew and Luke have shown plainly. There is, however, this difference between them: Matthew traces Joseph's lineage from David through Solomon; Luke, however, through Nathan. But the holy Virgin's birth both of them passed over in silence. Therefore it is worth knowing that it was not the custom among the Hebrews, nor in Sacred Scripture, to enumerate the lineage of women. But this much was provided by law: that no tribe should take wives from another tribe. And accordingly Joseph, who was of the tribe of David and who cultivated justice (for this praise the divine Gospel bestows on him), could not have espoused the holy Virgin contrary to the prescription of the law, unless she had drawn her lineage from the same stock. And for this reason the Evangelist was satisfied to have shown from what origin Joseph drew his birth.
Matt 17:1-9

At that time: Jesus took Peter and James and his brother John, and he led them onto a lofty mountain separately, and he was transfigured before them. And so forth.

A Homily of Saint Ambrose, Bishop
Lib. 7. in Luc., cap. 9.

This is my beloved Son: that is, not the son of Elijah, not the son of Moses, but this is the Son, whom you alone behold; for those others had withdrawn when the Lord began to be designated. You see that this perfect faith—not only of the foolish, but even of the perfect, yea even of the heavenly—is to know the Son of God. But since we have already said these things above, recognize that this cloud is not one gathered from the misty vapor of smoking mountains nor black with the darkness of compressed air, which had overspread the sky with the horror of shadows; but a shining cloud, which does not drench us with rain-water and the flooding of a soaking shower, but from which, when the voice of God Almighty went forth, the dew of faith refreshed the minds of men.
Mt 19:

At that time: Little children were brought to Jesus, that he might lay his hands upon them. And so forth.

A Homily of Saint Augustine, Bishop
In Psalm 118.

What is a little child, if not one who is humble? These are the wondrous testimonies of yours, O Lord, which the soul of this little child has searched out: and therefore he found them, because he was humbled and made a little child. For who fulfills your commandments as they ought to be fulfilled—that is, from the faith which works through the love of God—unless that very love be poured into his heart through the Holy Spirit? This also the little child confesses: My mouth, he says, I opened and drew in spirit, because I yearned for your commandments. What did he yearn for, if not to fulfill the divine commandments? But there was no means by which the weak could do what is strong, and the little child what is great. He opened his mouth, confessing that he could not do it of himself, and drew in that by which he might do it.

At that time: Jesus said to his disciples this parable: The kingdom of heaven shall be like ten virgins, who, taking their lamps, went out to meet the groom and the bride. And so forth.

A Homily of Saint John Chrysostom
Homilia 79 in Matth., post initium

Why does he set forth this parable in the person of virgins, and not subject some indiscriminate person without distinction? He had spoken of virginity at great length, saying: There are eunuchs who have made themselves eunuchs for the kingdom of heaven; and, He who is able to receive it, let him receive it. Nor was he unaware that virginity is held in great esteem by the common people, since it is by nature a sublime thing: which is evident from the fact that it was not practiced by those early holy men of the Old Testament, and in the New it is enjoined by no necessity of law. For he did not command it, but left it to the free will of the faithful. Hence Paul also says: Now concerning virgins, I have no commandment of the Lord; and I praise him indeed who follows this way of life, but I do not compel one who is unwilling, nor do I make it a commandment.
Matt 5:1-12

At that time: Seeing the crowds, Jesus ascended the mountain, and when he had sat down, his disciples drew near to him. And so forth.

From the Homily of Saint Augustine, Bishop.
Ex Lib. 1. de Serm. Domini in monte. Cap. 2.et 3.

Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God. How foolish, then, are those who seek God with these outward eyes, since he is seen with the heart, as it is written elsewhere: Seek him in simplicity of heart. For a pure heart is a simple heart; and just as this visible light cannot be seen except with pure eyes, so neither can God be seen except with the heart that is pure. Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called sons of God. In peace there is perfection, where nothing is in conflict; and therefore the peaceful are sons of God, because nothing in them resists God, and indeed sons ought to bear the likeness of their father.

At that time: Jesus, coming into his own country, taught them in their synagogues, so much so that they wondered and said: "From where has this one such wisdom and power? Is this not the son of a workman?" And so forth.

A Homily of Saint Albert the Great, Bishop
In Evangelium Lucæ, cap. 4

On the Sabbath he entered the synagogue, where all were gathered with the intention of listening. And the eyes of all in the synagogue were fixed upon him. Yet some did this out of devotion, some out of curiosity, and some watched him in order to catch him in his speech. And the scribes and Pharisees said to the people, who had already conceived faith and devotion: "Is this not the son of Joseph?" The pointing out of someone whom they did not see fit to name is a mark of contempt. The son of Joseph: here the Evangelist says less than what he knew had been put more fully by both Matthew and Mark: "Is this not the son of a workman? Is this not the workman, the son of Mary?" All these things were said contemptuously.

At that time: Jesus answered and said: I acknowledge you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth, because you have hidden these things from the wise and the prudent, and have revealed them to little ones. And so forth.

A Homily of Saint Augustine, Bishop
Sermo 10 de verbis Domini

Come to me, all you who labor. For why do we all labor, unless it be that we are mortal men, fragile, infirm, carrying earthen vessels that press upon one another? But if the vessels of flesh are pressed, let the spaces of charity be enlarged. What then does he say—Come to me, all you who labor—if not that you may no longer labor? Moreover his promise is at hand; for since he has called those who labor, they will perhaps ask with what reward they are called. And I, he says, will refresh you. Take my yoke upon you and learn from me—not to fashion the world, not to create all things visible and invisible, not to work wonders in the world itself and raise the dead; but, Because I am meek and humble of heart.

At that time: Jesus said to his disciples: You are the salt of the earth. But if the salt loses its savor, with what shall it be salted? It is good for nothing further, except to be cast out and trodden upon by men. And so forth.

A Homily of Saint Isidore, Bishop.
Ex libro 2. Officiorum ad S. Fulgentium cap. 5.

Whoever is set over people to instruct and form them in virtue must of necessity be holy in all things and held blameless in nothing. For he who rebukes another for sins must himself be free from sin. For with what face will he be able to reprove his subjects, when the one corrected can straightway retort: First teach yourself what is right? He who strives to admonish others to live well must first correct himself; so that in all things he may offer himself as a model of life, and provoke all to good work both by teaching and by example. For him, too, a knowledge of the Scriptures is necessary: because if a bishop's life alone be holy, he profits only himself by so living. But if he be also learned in doctrine and speech, he can instruct others as well, teach his own people, and repel adversaries, who, unless they are refuted and confounded, can easily pervert the hearts of the simple.

At that time: Jesus answering said to the Sadducees: You have gone astray by knowing neither the Scriptures, nor the power of God. For in the resurrection they shall neither marry, nor be given in marriage: but they shall be like the Angels of God in heaven. And so forth.

A Homily of Saint John Chrysostom
Liber de Virginitate

Virginity is good: I too acknowledge this. But marriage also is better—and this I likewise grant you; and if you wish, I will add that it surpasses marriage by as much as heaven surpasses earth, as much as angels excel men; and if something further must be added, even more. For if the angels neither marry nor are given in marriage, they are not also compacted of flesh and blood; they dwell not upon earth; they are not subject to the disturbances of desires and passions; they have no need of food or drink; they are not of such a nature that sweet sound, or soft song, or a fair form could attract them; nor are they caught by any allurement of that kind.

The Lord shows that those are to be judged foolish who, either pursuing an abundance of temporal goods or fearing their lack, lose what is eternal—which can neither be given by men nor taken away. And so, if the salt loses its savor, with what shall it be salted? That is, if you, through whom peoples are as it were to be seasoned, out of fear of temporal persecutions have forfeited the kingdoms of heaven, who will be the men through whom your error may be taken away from you, since God has chosen you to take away the error of the rest?
Therefore the salt that has lost its savor is good for nothing, except to be cast out and trodden upon by men. He, then, is not trodden upon by men who suffers persecution; but he who, fearing persecution, loses his savor. For only what is lower can be trodden upon; but he is not lower who, though he endures much in body upon earth, is yet fixed in heart in heaven.

At that time: Jesus said to his disciples: You have heard that it was said: You shall love your neighbor, and you shall have hatred for your enemy. And so forth.

A Homily of Saint Jerome, Priest
Liber 1 Comment. in cap. 5 Matth.

But I say to you: Love your enemies; do good to those who hate you. Many people, measuring God's commandments by their own weakness rather than by the strength of the saints, think that what is commanded is impossible, and say that it suffices for virtue not to hate one's enemies; but to love them is more than human nature can bear. It must be understood, therefore, that Christ does not command what is impossible, but what is perfect. What David did toward Saul and toward Absalom; what Stephen the Martyr also prayed for those who were stoning him; and what Paul desired to be anathema for his own persecutors. And Jesus both taught and did these things, saying: Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do.

At that time: Seeing the crowds, Jesus ascended the mountain, and when he had sat down, his disciples drew near to him. And so forth.

From the Homily of Saint Augustine, Bishop
Liber 1 de Sermone Domini in monte, cap. 3 et 4

And so in this third degree, in which is knowledge, one mourns the loss of the highest good, because one cleaves to what is lowest. But in the fourth degree there is toil: where one labors strenuously to tear the soul away from the things to which it has been bound by their pernicious sweetness. Here, therefore, one hungers and thirsts for justice, and fortitude is greatly needed: because what is retained with delight is not relinquished without pain. But to those who persevere in toil in the fifth degree there is given the counsel of escape: because, unless one is helped by a superior, one is in no way sufficient of oneself to disentangle oneself from such snares of misery. Moreover, it is just counsel that he who wishes to be helped by one more powerful should also help one who is weaker, in whom he himself is the more powerful. And therefore, Blessed are the merciful, for God will have mercy on them.

At that time: An Angel of the Lord appeared in sleep to Joseph, saying: Rise up, and take the boy and his mother, and flee into Egypt, and remain there until I tell you. And so forth.

A Homily of Saint John Chrysostom
Ex Hom. 8 in Matth., ante med.

When Joseph heard these things, he was in no way scandalized, nor did he say: This matter is uncertain and utterly ambiguous.
