You said a little while ago that he would save his people, and now he cannot free himself from dangers: rather, we must flee, go into exile, and make a long journey. The things done are altogether contrary to the promises. Yet none of this did he set against the angel; for he was a faithful man; nor did he curiously inquire about the time of return, which had not been precisely expressed by the angel; but, Remain there, said the angel, until I tell you.
Matt 1:1-17

The book of the lineage of Jesus Christ, the son of David, the son of Abraham. Abraham conceived Isaac. And Isaac conceived Jacob. And so forth.

A Homily of Saint John Chrysostom.
Homil. 2. in Matth., post init.

It is wondrous to hear that the ineffable God, who can be explained by no words and comprehended by no thoughts, who is in all things equal to the Father, came to us through the womb of a Virgin, and deigned to be born of a woman, and to have David and Abraham as his forebears: and why do I say David and Abraham? Even those women—which is more astonishing—whom I mentioned a little above. Hearing this, therefore, rise up in mind, and think nothing of it as lowly, but rather on this account especially wonder: that, being the true and beloved Son of the eternal God, he deigned also to be the son of David, in this way to make you a son of God; he deigned to have a servant as father, in order that for you the servant he might make God himself your Father.

At that time: Jesus said to his disciples: If anyone is willing to come after me, let him deny himself, and take up his cross, and follow me. And so forth.

A Homily of Saint Bernard, Abbot
In Vigilia, et in die S. Andreæ Apostoli
Rightly do they venerate the lover of the Cross, ...

At that time: Jesus said to his disciples: You are the salt of the earth. But if the salt loses its savor, with what shall it be salted? And so forth.

A Homily of the Venerable Bede, Priest
In Evang. Vos estis sal terra

By earth is signified human nature; by salt, the wisdom of words. For the nature of salt makes the earth unfruitful; hence we read of certain cities, in the fury of their conquerors, sown with salt. And this is fitting to apostolic teaching, that by the salt of wisdom it may check the luxuriance of worldly life or the foulness of vices springing up in the earth of human flesh. But if the salt loses its savor, with what shall it be salted? That is, if you, through whom peoples are to be seasoned, out of fear of persecutions or terror have forfeited the kingdoms of heaven, set outside the Church, you will undoubtedly endure the reproaches of your enemies. You are the light of the world: that is, you, because you have been illumined by the true Light, ought to be a light to those who are in the world. A city set on a hill cannot be hidden: that is, the apostolic teaching founded upon Christ, or the Church built upon Christ from many nations by the unity of faith and cemented together by the mortar of charity; which is secure to those entering and arduous to those approaching, guards its inhabitants and keeps out all enemies.

Lesson vii. Ch. 1. The book of the lineage of Jesus Christ, the son of David, the son of Abraham. Abraham conceived Isaac. And Isaac conceived Jacob. And so forth.

From the Homily of Saint Jerome, Priest.
Lib. 1. Comm. in Matth.

And Jacob conceived Joseph. This passage Julian the Emperor raised against us, regarding the discrepancy of the Evangelists: why Evangelist Matthew said Joseph was the son of Jacob, and Luke called him the son of Heli—not understanding the custom of the Scriptures, that one is his father according to nature, the other according to law. For we know this was prescribed through Moses, at God's command: that if a brother or kinsman died without children, another should take his wife to raise up seed for his brother or kinsman. The husband of Mary. When you hear husband, let no suspicion of marriage enter your mind: but recall the custom of the Scriptures, that betrothed men are called husbands, and betrothed women wives.
Matt 18:1-4

At that time: The disciples drew near to Jesus, saying: Whom do you consider to be greater in the kingdom of heaven? And so forth.

A Homily of Saint Leo the Pope
Sermo 37, in Epiph. solemn. 7, cap. 3-4

The whole discipline of Christian wisdom, dearly beloved, consists not in abundance of words, not in shrewdness of disputation, nor in the pursuit of praise and glory, but in true and voluntary humility, which the Lord Jesus Christ, from the womb of his Mother to the torment of the Cross, chose and taught as his every strength. For when his disciples were inquiring among themselves, as the Evangelist says, which of them was greater in the kingdom of heaven, he called to himself a little child, and set him in their midst, and said: Amen, I say to you, unless you change and become like little children, you shall not enter into the kingdom of heaven. Whoever, therefore, shall humble himself like this little child, such a one shall be greater in the kingdom of heaven. Christ loves childhood, which he first embraced both in soul and in body. Christ loves childhood, the teacher of humility, the rule of innocence, the model of meekness. Christ loves childhood, to which he directs the ways of grown men, to which he recalls the aged; and he bends to his own example those whom he raises to his eternal kingdom.

At that time: Seeing the crowds, Jesus ascended the mountain, and when he had sat down, his disciples drew near to him. And so forth.

A Homily of Saint Augustine, Bishop
Lib. 1 de Sermone Domini in monte, sub initium

If it is asked what the mountain signifies, it is well understood to signify the greater precepts of justice, because those given to the Jews were lesser. Yet one God, through his holy prophets and servants, according to the most orderly distribution of times, gave lesser precepts to the people who still needed to be bound by fear; and through his Son, greater precepts to the people who were now to be set free by charity. But when lesser things are given to lesser ones, and greater things to greater ones, they are given by him who alone knows how to offer to the human race the fitting remedy for their times.
Matt 2:1-12

When Jesus had been born in Bethlehem of Judah, in the days of King Herod, behold, Magi from the east arrived in Jerusalem, saying: Where is he who has been born King of the Jews? And so forth.

From a Homily of Saint John Chrysostom
Homilia 8, in Matth. n. 1

The Magi, entering the house, saw the child with Mary, his mother. And falling down, they adored him; and, opening their treasures, they offered him gifts: gold, frankincense, and myrrh. But what moved them to adore the child? For the Virgin had nothing remarkable about her appearance, the house was not magnificent, nor was there anything else present that could strike or attract them. Yet they not only adore, but, opening their treasures, they offer gifts — gifts, I say, not as to a man, but as to God. For frankincense and myrrh were above all the symbol of deity. What, then, persuaded them to this? The very same thing that had stirred them to leave their home and undertake so long a journey: namely, the star and the illumination of mind implanted in them by God himself, which gradually led them to a more perfect knowledge.

At that time: Jesus said to his disciples: Do not be afraid of those who kill the body, but are not able to kill the soul; but rather fear him who is able to destroy both soul and body in Hell. And so forth.

From a Homily of Saint Irenaeus, Bishop and Martyr
Lib. 3 advérsus Hæreses cap. 18, alias 20, num. 5-6

The Lord knew those who were to suffer persecution; he knew also those who were to be scourged and killed for his sake. His word, therefore, was one of encouragement even for them: Do not be afraid of those who kill the body, but are not able to kill the soul. But fear rather him who has power to cast both body and soul into Hell, and to preserve those confessions made to him. For he himself promised to acknowledge before his Father those who would confess his name before men; but to deny those who denied him, and to put to shame those who were ashamed before the confession of him. And, things being so, certain ones have gone to such recklessness that they even despise the Martyrs, and reproach those who are killed for confessing the Lord, and who endure all the things foretold by the Lord, and who in this way strive to follow in the footsteps of the Lord's Passion, having been made Martyrs who suffer with him — whom we also concede to the Martyrs themselves. For when their blood shall be sought and they shall receive glory, then all those who dishonored their martyrdom shall be put to shame by Christ.

At that time: Jesus compelled his disciples to climb into the boat, and to precede him in crossing the sea, while he dismissed the crowds. And so forth.

From a Homily of Saint Jerome, Priest
Liber 2 Comment. in cap. 14 Matth.

The Lord commanded the disciples to cross the sea, and compelled them to board the boat. By this word it is shown that they departed from the Lord against their will, since out of love for their Teacher they wished not to be separated from him even for a moment. And, having dismissed the crowd, he ascended alone onto the mountain to pray. If the disciples Peter and James and John, who had seen the glory of the Transfiguration, had been with him, they might perhaps have ascended the mountain with him; but the crowd cannot follow to the heights, unless he has taught them beside the sea on the shore and fed them in the desert.

At that time: The disciples drew near to Jesus, saying: Who, do you think, is greater in the kingdom of heaven? And so forth.

From a Homily of Saint Jerome, Priest
Lib. 3 Comm. in cap. 18 Matth.

After the finding of the stater, after the payment of the tribute, what is the meaning of the Apostles' sudden question: Who, do you think, is greater in the kingdom of heaven? Because they had seen the same tribute paid for Peter and the Lord, they concluded from the equality of the price that Peter was set above all the Apostles, since in the payment of the tribute he had been compared to the Lord; and so they ask who is greater in the kingdom of heaven. And Jesus, seeing their thoughts and understanding the causes of their error, desires to heal the appetite for glory by the practice of humility.

At that time: Jesus came into the parts of Caesarea Philippi, and questioned his disciples, saying: Who do men say the Son of Man is? And so forth.

From a Homily of Saint Jerome, Priest
Lib. 3 Comment. in Matth. cap. 16

He asks beautifully: Who do men say the Son of Man is? — for those who speak of the Son of Man are men; but those who understand his divinity are called not men, but gods. And they said: Some say John the Baptist, and others Elijah. I am surprised that certain interpreters seek to inquire into the reasons for each one's error and weave a very lengthy disputation about why some took our Lord Jesus Christ for John, others for Elijah, others for Jeremiah or one of the prophets; when they could have erred about Elijah and Jeremiah in the same way that Herod erred about John, saying: John, whom I beheaded, has himself risen from the dead, and miracles are worked through him.

At that time: As Jesus sat upon the Mount of Olives, the disciples drew near to him privately, saying: Tell us, when will these things be? And so forth.

From a Homily of Saint Hilary, Bishop
Comment. in Matth. cap. 25

The disciples ask the Lord when these things would take place, and what sign they might know of his coming and of the consummation of the age. And, because these three things were asked together as one, they are separated by distinct significations both of time and of understanding. Answer is therefore given first concerning the fall of the city, and they are confirmed by the truth of the teaching, lest anyone deceitful might creep in upon the ignorant; for there were to come, even in their own time, those who would announce themselves as Christ. So that faith might not be undermined by pestilential falsehood, this warning was given in advance.

At that time: Jesus said to his disciples: You are the salt of the earth. But if salt loses its saltiness, with what will it be salted? And so forth.

From a Homily of Saint Ephrem the Syrian, Deacon
Sermo de vita et exercitatione monastica

It is a noble thing to begin and to complete what is good, and to be pleasing to God and useful to one's neighbor, and to be acceptable to our supreme and most sweet ruler, Christ Jesus, who says: You are the salt of the earth and the pillar of the heavens. The labor of your affliction, most beloved, is like a sleep; but the rest from that labor is unspeakable and beyond all reckoning. Take care, therefore, attentively for yourself, lest you lose both together by fully pursuing neither: that is to say, both present and eternal joy. Strive rather to attain perfect virtue, adorned and distinguished with all that God loves. If you attain this, you will never provoke God, nor will you wrong your neighbor.

When Jesus had been born in Bethlehem of Judah, in the days of King Herod, behold, Magi from the east arrived in Jerusalem, saying: Where is he who has been born King of the Jews? And so forth.

From a Homily of Saint Gregory the Pope
Ex Homilía 10 in Evangelia

The Magi bring gold, frankincense, and myrrh. For gold is fitting for a king; frankincense is placed in the sacrifice of God; and myrrh is used to embalm the bodies of the dead. Therefore the Magi also proclaim by their mystical gifts the one they adore: gold for a king, frankincense for God, myrrh for one who is mortal. There are indeed certain heretics who believe that he is God, but by no means believe that he reigns everywhere. These assuredly offer him frankincense, but refuse to offer gold as well. And there are some who consider him a king, but deny that he is God. These indeed offer him gold, but refuse to offer frankincense.

At that time: Jesus said to his disciples: When they persecute you in one city, flee into another. And so forth.

From a Homily of Saint Athanasius, Bishop
In Apologia de fuga sua, ante med.

In the law it was commanded that cities of refuge be established, so that those who in any way were sought for death might be preserved. Then, at the end of the ages, when that very Word of the Father had come — who had previously spoken to Moses — he gave this commandment again: When they persecute you in one city, he said, flee to another. And a little after he adds: When you see the abomination of desolation which was spoken of by Daniel the prophet standing in the holy place — let the reader understand — then let those who are in Judea flee to the mountains, and let him who is on the housetop not come down to take anything from his house; and let him who is in the field not turn back to take his cloak.

At that time: Peter said to Jesus: Behold, we have left all things, and followed you; what then shall there be for us? And so forth.

From a Homily of Saint Bede the Venerable, Priest
Homilia in Natali S. Benedicti Ep.

He is perfect who, going away, sells all that he has and gives it to the poor, and, coming, follows Christ; for he shall have a treasure that does not fail in the heavens. Hence it is that, when Peter asked, Jesus fittingly said to such men: Amen I say to you, that you who have followed me, in the regeneration, when the Son of Man sits on the throne of his majesty, you also shall sit upon twelve seats, judging the twelve tribes of Israel. In this present life, toiling for his name, he taught them to hope for a reward in another — that is, in the regeneration; namely, when we shall have been regenerated unto immortal life through the resurrection, we who were mortally born unto a passing life.
Liber 1. de Sermone Domini in monte, Cap. 4.

Therefore, if we count these as ascending steps, the first is the fear of God, the second is piety, the third is knowledge, the fourth is fortitude, the fifth is counsel, the sixth is understanding, the seventh is wisdom. The fear of God belongs to the humble, of whom it is here said: Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven — that is, those who are not puffed up, not proud, of whom the Apostle says: Do not be high-minded, but fear; that is, do not be lifted up. Piety belongs to the meek. For he who seeks with piety honors Holy Scripture, and does not criticize what he does not yet understand, and therefore does not resist — which is to be meek. Hence it is here said: Blessed are the meek, for they shall inherit the earth.

At that time: Jesus took Peter and James and John his brother, and led them up a high mountain apart, and was transfigured before them. And so forth.

From a Homily of Saint John Chrysostom
Homilia 57 in Matth., in init.

Since the Lord had spoken much of dangers, much of his own Passion, much of the death and slaughter of the disciples, and had enjoined upon them many things that were harsh and arduous — things which in the present life were already imminent — while the good things were still in hope and expectation; such as, that they would save their soul if they lost it, that he would come in the glory of his Father and would render rewards: in order that he might make them more certain even by sight, and show them what that glory is in which he is to come — as much as they were capable of receiving in this present life — he showed it to them and unveiled it, lest they should grieve either at their own death or at the Lord's, and especially Peter.

At that time: Jesus said to his disciples: You are the salt of the earth. But if salt loses its saltiness, with what will it be salted? And so forth.

From a Homily of Saint Peter Canisius, Priest
Notæ In Evangelia In festo S. Martini Ep, post initium

I shall love and honor the Apostles sent by Christ and their successors — diligent and untiring fellow-workers in the sowing of the seed of the Gospel and in the propagation of the Word — who can rightly testify: Let a man so regard us as ministers of Christ and stewards of the mysteries of God. For Christ willed, as a most watchful and faithful father of the household, that through such ministers and legates the evangelical lamp, lit by fire sent down from heaven, should be kindled and, once kindled, not be placed under a bushel, but set upon a candlestick, so that its splendor might spread far and wide, and scatter all the darkness and errors flourishing among both Jews and Gentiles.

At that time: Jesus said to his disciples: You are the salt of the earth. But if salt loses its saltiness, with what will it be salted? And so forth.

From a Homily of Saint John Chrysostom
Homilia 15 in Matthæum, sub medium

Consider what he said: You are the salt of the earth — by which he shows how necessary are these precepts that he enjoins. For it is not only of your own life, he says, but of the whole world, that you must render an account. For I send you not to two cities, or ten, or twenty, nor to a single nation, as I sent the prophets: but to every land and sea, to the entire world, and this world oppressed by manifold sins.

At that time, Jesus answered and said: I acknowledge you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth, because you have hidden these things from the wise and the prudent, and have revealed them to little ones. And so forth.

From a Homily of Saint Francis de Sales, Bishop
Sermo 23 in die Pentecostes alter, circa medium

There is no true knowledge other than that which is given by the Holy Spirit, but this is granted only to the humble. Have we not seen great theologians who spoke wonderful things about the virtues, yet did not practice them? On the other hand, we have seen many women who could not speak learnedly about the virtues, yet knew how to fulfill the works of the virtues worthily. For the Holy Spirit made them wise, because they possessed the fear of the Lord, and piety, and humility.

At that time: Jesus said to his disciples: You are the salt of the earth. But if salt loses its saltiness, with what will it be salted? And so forth.

From a Homily of Saint Robert Bellarmine, Bishop
Concio 9, de probitate Doctórum Ecclésiæ; ab initio

Just as in God — whom we venerate as one in Trinity and threefold in unity — three things eminently stand out: power, wisdom, and goodness; so also, hearers, God willed that his special friends and sons, our Fathers and Doctors, in order to render them as like to himself as possible and worthy of reverence and admiration among all peoples, should be most powerful, most wise, most good, and most holy. First he armed them with that power by which they might do many things plainly admirable and singular in elements, in trees, in brute animals, and in men themselves, beyond the ordinary course and order of nature. Then he so furnished their minds with wisdom that they not only perceived things present and past, but also foresaw and foretold future things long in advance. Finally, he enlarged their hearts with the highest and most ardent charity, both that they themselves might undertake the work with great courage, and that those who were to be converted through them might be moved not only by words and miracles, but also by example and uprightness of life.

At that time: Jesus said to his disciples: Behold, I send you as sheep in the midst of wolves. And so forth.

From a Homily of Saint John Chrysostom
Homilia 34 in Matth., longe post initium

But he seems to say: Do not be troubled if, when I send you among wolves, I command you to be as sheep and doves. For, even though I could also bring about the contrary, and not permit you to suffer anything grievous, nor to be subjected to wolves as sheep, but to make you more terrible than lions — yet it is thus expedient for things to be done; this also will make you more illustrious and will manifest my power. For he later said to Paul: My grace is sufficient for you, for my power is made perfect in weakness. It is I, then, who have made you to be such as you are.

When Jesus had been born in Bethlehem of Judah, in the days of King Herod, behold, Magi from the east arrived in Jerusalem, saying: Where is he who has been born King of the Jews? And so forth.

From a Homily of Saint Gregory the Pope
Homilia 10 in Evangelia

When the birth of our King was made known, Herod turned to crafty devices; and, lest he should be deprived of his earthly kingdom, he requested that it be reported to him where the child might be found. He pretended that he wished to adore him, so that, if the child could be found, he might destroy him. But how great is human malice against the counsel of divinity? For it is written: There is no wisdom, no prudence, no counsel against the Lord. For the star that had appeared leads the Magi; they find the newborn King, they offer gifts; and, so that they need not return to Herod, they are warned in their sleep. And so it comes about that Herod cannot find Jesus, whom he seeks. Whose person do those signify but hypocrites, who, because they seek with pretense, never merit to find the Lord?
Matt 18:1-5

At that time: The disciples drew near to Jesus, saying: Who, do you think, is greater in the kingdom of heaven? And so forth.

From a Homily of Saint John Chrysostom
Homilia 60 in Matth. cap. 18

See in how many ways the Lord moves us to care even for the lesser brethren. Therefore do not say: He is a coppersmith, or a cobbler, or a farmer, or an unlettered man, and so despise him. Lest you fall into that evil, consider in how many ways he moves you to conduct yourself with modesty and to take care of them. He placed a little child in the midst and said: Become as little children; and: Whoever receives such a little child receives me; and: Whoever leads one astray shall suffer the worst. If, then, God so rejoices over a little one who is found, why do you despise those of whom God takes such solicitous care — when you ought even to lay down your very soul for one of these little ones? For so great is God's care for the soul that he has not even spared his own Son. Therefore, I beseech you, from the first light of day, when we leave home, let us have this one aim and this surpassing concern: to rescue those who are in peril. I do not speak here of peril to the body, for that is no peril at all; but of peril to the soul, which the devil prepares for men.
Liber 1 de Sermone Domini in monte, cap. 5

Blessed shall you be, he says, when they revile you, and persecute you, and speak all manner of evil against you falsely, for my sake: rejoice and be glad, for your reward is great in heaven. Let whoever seeks the pleasures of this age and abundance of temporal goods in the Christian name take note that our beatitude is interior, as is said of the soul of the Church in the prophetic voice: All the glory of the king's daughter is from within. For outwardly curses and persecutions and slanders are promised — on account of which, however, there is a great reward in heaven — a reward felt in the heart of those who endure, of those who can already say: We glory in tribulations: knowing that tribulation works patience, and patience trial, and trial hope; and hope does not confound, because the charity of God has been poured forth in our hearts through the Holy Spirit, who has been given to us.
Sermo 3 in annivers. assumpt. suæ, post initium

The Lord asks the Apostles what men think of him; and the discourse of those who answer remains general for as long as the ambiguity of human understanding is being unraveled. But when an account is required of what the disciples themselves think, he who is first in apostolic dignity is first in the confession of the Lord. And when he had said: You are the Christ, the Son of the living God, Jesus answered him: Blessed are you, Simon Bar-Jonah, for flesh and blood has not revealed this to you, but my Father who is in heaven. That is to say: You are blessed for this reason — because my Father has taught you; earthly opinion has not deceived you, but heavenly inspiration has instructed you; and not flesh and blood, but he whose only-begotten Son I am, has made me known to you.

The book of the lineage of Jesus Christ, the son of David, the son of Abraham. Abraham conceived Isaac. And Isaac conceived Jacob. And so forth.

From a Homily of Saint Jerome, Priest
Liber 1 Comment. in Matth., in initium

In Isaiah we read: Who shall declare his generation? We should not, therefore, think that the Evangelist contradicts the Prophet, as though he sets out to narrate what the Prophet declared impossible to express: for there the reference is to the generation of the Divinity, while here it concerns the Incarnation. He began from fleshly things, so that through the man we might begin to learn of God. The son of David, the son of Abraham. The order is inverted, but necessarily so. For if he had placed Abraham first and David afterward, he would have had to return to Abraham again, in order that the sequence of the genealogy might be woven together.

The book of the lineage of Jesus Christ, the son of David, the son of Abraham. Abraham conceived Isaac. And Isaac conceived Jacob. And so forth.

From a Homily of Saint Jerome, Priest

And after the deportation to Babylon, Jechoniah conceived Salathiel. If we wish to place the first Jechoniah at the end of the first group of fourteen, there will not be fourteen in the following group, but thirteen. Let us therefore know that the first Jechoniah is the same one who is also called Joakim, while the second is the son, not the father. It is the former who is described; the confusion of one with the other, among Greek and Latin writers, has arisen through scribal error and the lapse of time.

At that time: Peter said to Jesus: Behold, we have left all things, and followed you; what then shall there be for us? And so forth.

From a Homily of the Venerable Bede, Priest
In Natali S. Benedicti

There are two orders of the elect at the future judgment: one of those who judge with the Lord — of whom he makes mention in this place, who have left all things and followed him; another of those to be judged by the Lord, who did not indeed equally leave all their possessions, but who were careful to give daily alms from what they had to the poor of Christ; and these shall hear at the judgment: Come, you blessed of my Father, take possession of the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world. For I was hungry, and you gave me to eat; I was thirsty, and you gave me to drink.

When his mother Mary had been betrothed to Joseph, before they lived together, she was found to have conceived in her womb by the Holy Spirit. And so forth.

From a Homily of Saint Jerome, Priest
Lib. 1 Comment. in c. 1 Matth.

Why is he conceived not of a simple virgin, but of one who was betrothed? First, that through the lineage of Joseph, the origin of Mary might be shown; second, lest she be stoned by the Jews as an adulteress; third, that she might have a companion when she fled into Egypt. The Martyr Ignatius added also a fourth reason why he was conceived of one betrothed: so that his birth, he says, might be hidden from the devil, who would think him to be the son not of a virgin, but of a wife.
The Reading of the Holy Gospel according to Matthew

Why is he conceived not of a simple virgin, but of one who was betrothed? First, that through the lineage of Joseph, the origin of Mary might be shown; second, lest she be stoned by the Jews as an adulteress; third, that she might have a companion when she fled into Egypt. The Martyr Ignatius added also a fourth reason why he was conceived of one betrothed: so that his birth, he says, might be hidden from the devil, who would think him to be the son not of a virgin, but of a wife.~
Before they lived together, she was found to have conceived in her womb by the Holy Spirit. She was found not by another, but by Joseph, who knew almost by the right of a husband all the affairs of his future wife. Moreover, where it says Before they lived together, it does not follow that they lived together afterward; but Scripture shows what did not happen.

At that time: Little children were brought to Jesus, so that he would place his hands upon them and pray. And so forth.

From a Homily of Saint John Chrysostom

At that time: Little children were presented to Jesus, that he might lay hands upon them and pray. And so forth.

A Homily of Saint John Chrysostom
Homilia 62 in Matthæum

Why did the disciples drive the children away? Out of regard for his dignity. What then did he do? To teach them to think humbly and to trample upon worldly pride, he received them and embraced them in his arms, and promised them the Kingdom of Heaven — which he had also said above. Let us therefore, if we wish to be heirs of heaven, pursue this virtue with great diligence. For this is the summit of wisdom: to be simple together with prudence; this is the angelic life. For the soul of a child is free from all the diseases of the soul; it retains no memory of injuries, but goes to those who have wronged it as to friends, as if nothing had happened. And although it may be beaten with blows by its mother, it always seeks her out and prefers her above all others.

The book of the lineage of Jesus Christ, the son of David, the son of Abraham. Abraham begot Isaac. And Isaac begot Jacob. And so forth.

A Homily of Saint Hilary, Bishop.
Comment. in Matth. can. 1.

The step which Matthew set forth in the order of royal succession, and which Luke enumerates through the priestly order, each signifies in the Lord the kinship of both tribes, and establishes the degree of rightful descent: for the union of the priestly and royal tribes, entered into through marriage by David, is already confirmed from Salathiel in Zerubbabel by lineage. And so, while Matthew reviews the paternal origin which descended from Judah, and Luke sets forth the lineage received through Nathan from the tribe of Levi, each of them proved in his own part the glory of both lineages for our Lord Jesus Christ, who is the eternal King and Priest, even in his bodily birth.

Truly the Magi signify something great to us, in that they return to their own country by another way. For in what they do at the prompting of the angel, they surely intimate to us what we ought to do. For our country is paradise: to which, once we have come to know Jesus, we are forbidden to return by the way we came. Indeed, we departed from our country through pride, disobedience, pursuit of visible things, and by tasting the forbidden food: but it is necessary that we return to it by weeping, by obedience, by despising visible things, and by restraining the appetite of the flesh.

At that time: After Herod had passed away, behold, an Angel of the Lord appeared in sleep to Joseph in Egypt, saying: Rise up, and take the boy and his mother, and go into the land of Israel. And so forth.

A Homily of Saint Jerome, Priest.
Liber 1 in Comment. in cap. 2 Matthæi

From this passage we understand that not only Herod, but also the priests and scribes had been plotting the death of the Lord at that same time. He who rose up took the boy and his mother. He did not say: He took his son and his wife, but the boy and his mother; as one who was a foster-father, not a husband.

At that time: The mother of the sons of Zebedee approached Jesus, with her sons, adoring him, and petitioning something from him. And so forth.

A Homily of Saint Jerome, Priest.
Liber 3 Comm. in Matth. c. 20.

Whence does the mother of the sons of Zebedee have the notion of a kingdom, so that when the Lord had said: The Son of Man shall be delivered to the chief priests and scribes, and they shall condemn him to death, and shall deliver him to the Gentiles to be mocked and scourged and crucified — and while this announcement of the ignominy of the Passion filled the disciples with fear — she should petition for the glory of his triumph? For this reason, as I think: because after all these things the Lord had said, And on the third day he shall rise again; the woman supposed that he would reign immediately after the Resurrection, and that what is promised at the second coming would be fulfilled at the first; and, with feminine eagerness she desires present things, unmindful of the future.

At that time: Jesus said to the scribes and Pharisees: Behold, I send to you prophets and wisemen and scribes; and some of these you will put to death and crucify. And so forth.

A Homily of Saint Jerome, Priest.
Liber 4 Comment. in cap. 23 Matthæi

What we said before — Fill up the measure of your fathers — can be referred, insofar as it pertains to the person of the Lord, to the fact that he was to be slain by them; but it can also be referred to his disciples, of whom he now says: Behold, I send to you prophets and wisemen and scribes. And at the same time observe, as the Apostle writes to the Corinthians, that the gifts of the disciples of Christ are various: some are prophets, who foretell things to come; others are wisemen, who know when they ought to bring forth a word; others are scribes most learned in the law — from among whom Stephen was stoned, Paul slain, Peter crucified, and the disciples in the Acts of the Apostles scourged.

At that time: The disciples came to Jesus, saying: Who, do you think, is the greater in the Kingdom of Heaven? And so forth.

A Homily of Saint Hilary, Bishop.
Comment. in Matth. can. 18, post initium

The Lord teaches that only those who have returned to the nature of children enter the Kingdom of Heaven: that is, that the vices of our bodies and soul are to be recalled through childlike simplicity. Now he called all believers children by reason of the faith of obedience. For they follow the father, love the mother, know not how to wish evil to a neighbor, are negligent of the care of riches; they are not haughty, they do not hate, they do not lie, they believe what is said, and hold what they hear to be true. We must therefore return to the simplicity of infancy; for, established in it, we shall bear about the likeness of the Lord's humility.

At that time: The mother of the sons of Zebedee approached Jesus, with her sons, adoring him, and petitioning something from him. And so forth.

A Homily of Saint John Chrysostom.
Homilia 66 in Matthæum

Let no one be troubled if we say that the Apostles were so imperfect; for the mystery of the Cross had not yet been accomplished, nor had the grace of the Spirit yet been poured into their hearts. But if you wish to learn of their virtue — what they were like after the grace of the Spirit had been given — consider it, and you will see that every perverse affection had been overcome in them. For this reason their imperfection is now revealed, so that you may clearly perceive what kind of men they suddenly became through grace. That they were asking for nothing spiritual and thinking of nothing concerning the heavenly Kingdom is evident. But let us also consider how they approach and what they say. We wish, they say, that whatever we shall ask, you do for us. To which Christ replied, What do you wish? — not because he was ignorant, certainly, but so as to compel them to answer and to lay bare the wound, and thus to apply the remedy.

At that time: While Jesus was still speaking to the crowds, behold, his mother and his brothers were standing outside, seeking to speak with him. And so forth.

A Homily of Saint Gregory, Pope.
Homilia 3 in Evangelia

Dearest brethren, the reading of the holy Gospel that has been recited is brief, but it is laden with the great weight of mysteries. For Jesus, our Creator and Redeemer, makes as though he does not know his Mother, and designates who is his mother and who are his kindred, not by the bond of flesh but by the union of spirit, saying: Who is my mother, and who are my brothers? For whoever does the will of my Father, who is in heaven, he is my brother and sister and mother. By which words he signifies to us nothing other than that by following his commands he gathers many from among the Gentiles; and the people of Judah, from whose flesh he was born, he does not acknowledge.

At that time: Jesus came into the district of Caesarea Philippi, and he questioned his disciples, saying: Who do men say the Son of Man is? And so forth.

A Homily of Saint Leo, Pope.
Sermo 2 in anniversari assumptionis suæ ante medium

When, as has been disclosed by the Gospel reading, the Lord had questioned his disciples as to whom they believed him to be, while many held differing opinions, and blessed Peter had replied saying: You are the Christ, the Son of the living God; the Lord said: Blessed are you, Simon Bar-Jona, for flesh and blood has not revealed this to you, but my Father who is in heaven: and I say to you, that you are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church, and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it. And I will give you the keys of the Kingdom of Heaven: and whatever you shall bind upon earth shall be bound also in heaven: and whatever you shall loose upon earth shall be loosed also in heaven. The order of truth therefore endures, and blessed Peter, persevering in the strength of the rock he has received, has not relinquished the governance of the Church committed to him.

At that time: Jesus spoke to the chief priests and the Pharisees in parables, saying: The Kingdom of Heaven is like a man who was king, who celebrated a wedding for his son. And so forth.

A Homily of Saint Gregory, Pope.
Liber 2 Homiliar. Hom. 38, circa medium

Since you have now entered the house of the wedding feast — that is, the holy Church — by the gift of the Lord, look carefully, brethren, lest the king upon entering should find anything to reproach in the disposition of your mind. For what is immediately added must be weighed with great fear of heart: But the king entered to see the guests, and he saw there a man who was not clothed in a wedding garment. What, dearest brethren, do we take to be signified by the wedding garment? If we call the wedding garment baptism or faith, who has entered this wedding feast without baptism and faith? For he who has not yet believed is thereby excluded. What then ought we to understand by the wedding garment, if not charity? For he who stands in the holy Church, having faith but not having charity, enters the wedding feast but does not enter with the wedding garment. For charity is rightly called the wedding garment, because our Creator had this within himself when he came to the wedding feast to unite the Church to himself.

At that time: Jesus came into the district of Caesarea Philippi, and he questioned his disciples, saying: Who do men say the Son of Man is? And so forth.

A Homily of Saint Augustine, Bishop.
Ex serm. 29 de Sanctis, in medio

Peter alone among the Apostles merited to hear: Amen I say to you, you are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church — worthy indeed to be a stone for the foundation, a column for the support, a key for the Kingdom, in building the peoples in the house of God. Of him the divine word says: And they laid their sick, so that at least the shadow of Peter passing by might overshadow them. If then the shadow of his body could then bring help, how much more now the fullness of his virtue? If then a kind of breath of one passing by profited those who made supplication, how much more now the grace of one who remains? With good reason throughout all the churches of Christ that iron of his penal chains is held more precious than gold.

At that time: Seeing the crowds, Jesus went up the mountain, and when he had sat down, his disciples came to him. And so forth.

From a Homily of Saint Augustine, Bishop.
Ex Lib. 1. de Serm. Domini in monte. Cap. 1. et 2.

Blessedness could nowhere begin more fittingly than with poverty of spirit, since it is directed toward the highest wisdom. For the beginning of wisdom is the fear of the Lord: since, contrariwise, it is written that pride is the beginning of all sin. But the proud seek and love the kingdoms of the earth. Blessed are the meek: for they shall possess the earth by inheritance — that earth, I believe, of which it is said in the Psalm: You are my hope, my portion in the land of the living. For it signifies a certain solidity and stability of perpetual inheritance, where the soul rests through a good affection, as in its own place, just as the body rests in the earth: and from there it is nourished by its food, as the body is nourished from the earth: this is the rest and life of the Saints. But the meek are those who yield to wickedness, and do not resist evil, but overcome evil with good.

Why was he conceived not of a simple virgin, but of one betrothed? First, that through the lineage of Joseph the origin of Mary might be shown; second, lest she be stoned by the Jews as an adulteress; third, that in her flight into Egypt she might have a companion and consolation. The martyr Ignatius also added a fourth reason why he was conceived of a betrothed woman: So that, he says, his birth might be hidden from the devil, who would suppose him to have been born not of a virgin but of a wife.

At that time: Seeing the crowds, Jesus went up the mountain, and when he had sat down, his disciples came to him. And so forth.

A Homily of Saint Augustine, Bishop.
Liber 1 de sermone Dómini in monte, cap. 2. et 3.

Blessed are the pure of heart: for they shall see God. How foolish, therefore, are those who seek God with these outward eyes, since he is seen with the heart, as it is written elsewhere: Seek him in simplicity of heart. For a pure heart is a simple heart. And just as this light cannot be seen except by pure eyes, so neither is God seen unless that by which he can be seen is pure. Blessed are the peacemakers: for they shall be called sons of God. In peace there is perfection, where nothing is in conflict; and therefore the peacemakers are sons of God, because nothing in them resists God, and surely sons ought to bear the likeness of their father.

At that time: Jesus said to his disciples: No one is able to serve two masters. And so forth.

A Homily of Saint Augustine, Bishop.
Liber 2 de Sermóne Dómini in monte, cap. 14

No one is able to serve two masters. This passage is to be referred to the very same intention which he goes on to expound, saying: For either he will have hatred for the one and love the other, or he will persevere with the one and despise the other. These words are to be considered carefully: for who the two masters are he shows immediately afterward, when he says: You cannot serve God and wealth. Among the Hebrews, wealth is said to be called mammon. The Punic name agrees with this; for in Punic, profit is called mammon. But whoever serves mammon serves, by the rightful punishment of his perversity, him who is set over earthly things and is called by the Lord the ruler of this age. For either a man will have hatred for the one and love the other, that is, God; or he will persevere with the one and despise the other. For whoever serves mammon will endure a hard and ruinous master; for, entangled by his own cupidity, he is subject to the devil, and does not love him. For who is there who loves the devil? Yet nonetheless he endures him.
Lib. 4. Comment. in cap. 23. Matth.

Jerusalem, Jerusalem, you who kill the prophets. By Jerusalem he calls not the stones and buildings of the city, but its inhabitants: over whom he weeps with a father's affection, just as we read in another place that, when he saw her, he wept. And when he says: How often I have wanted to gather your children together, he bears witness that all the prophets of old were sent by him. We also read in the canticle of Deuteronomy the image of a hen gathering her chicks under her wings: As an eagle protects its nest, and has longed over its young: spreading its wings, it took them up, and bore them upon its feathers.

At that time: When Jesus had been born in Bethlehem of Judah in the days of king Herod, behold, Magi from the east arrived in Jerusalem, saying: Where is he who has been born King of the Jews? And so forth.

A Homily of Saint Ambrose, Bishop.
Liber 2 in Lucam cap. 2, post init.

What are these gifts of true faith? Gold for the King, incense for God, myrrh for the dead. For one thing is the mark of kingship, another the sacrament of divine power, another the honor of burial — which does not corrupt the body of the dead, but preserves it. We too, who hear and read these things, let us bring forward from our treasures such gifts, brethren. For we have a treasure in earthen vessels. If therefore in your own self — what you are — you ought not to esteem from yourself, but from Christ: how much more in Christ ought you not to esteem what is yours, but what is Christ's?

At that time: An Angel of the Lord appeared in sleep to Joseph, saying: Rise up, and take the Child and his Mother, and flee into Egypt, and remain there until I tell you. And so forth.

A Homily of Saint Jerome, Priest.
Lib. 1 Comm. in c. 2 Matth. et apud Gloss. ord.

When he took the Child and his Mother to pass over into Egypt, he took them by night and in darkness: because he left the night of ignorance to the unbelievers from whom he departed. But when he returns to Judea, neither night nor darkness is mentioned in the Gospel: because at the end of the world the Jews, receiving the faith as they welcome Christ returning from Egypt, will be enlightened.

The book of the lineage of Jesus Christ, the son of David, the son of Abraham. Abraham begot Isaac. And Isaac begot Jacob. And so forth.

A Homily of Saint Augustine, Bishop.
Lib. 2. de consensu Evangelist. Cap. 1.

The Evangelist Matthew began thus: The book of the lineage of Jesus Christ, the son of David, the son of Abraham. By this opening he shows sufficiently that he undertook to narrate the generation of Christ according to the flesh. For according to this, Christ is the Son of Man: which he himself also very frequently calls himself, commending to us what in his mercy he deigned to be for us. For that heavenly and eternal generation, according to which the Son of God is only-begotten before all creation, since all things were made through him, is so ineffable that the saying of the prophet is understood to refer to it: Who shall declare his generation?

At that time: Peter said to Jesus: Behold, we have left all things and followed you; what then shall be for us? And so forth.

A Homily of Saint Bernard, Abbot.
In op. Gaufridi Abb.: Deolamationes de Colloquio Simonis cum Iesu. I.

I judge the words of this reading to be those about which the Church cries out to the immortal Bridegroom from the ends of the earth: Because of the words of your lips I have kept hard ways. For these are the words which have persuaded men to contempt of the world throughout the world, and to voluntary poverty. These are the words that fill monasteries with monks, and deserts with hermits. These, I say, are the words that despoil Egypt and carry off the best of its vessels. This is the living and effective word, converting souls through the happy zeal of holiness and the faithful promise of truth.
Liber 1 de Sermone Domini in monte, cap. 4

In the first rank, as was fitting, the Kingdom of Heaven is placed, which is the perfect and supreme wisdom of the rational soul. Thus it was said: Blessed are the poor in spirit: for theirs is the Kingdom of Heaven — as if it were said: The beginning of wisdom is the fear of the Lord. To the meek an inheritance was given, as a testament of the father to those who seek him with devotion. Blessed are the meek: for they shall possess the earth by inheritance. To those who mourn, consolation — as to those who know what they have lost and into what they are plunged. Blessed are those who mourn now: for they shall be comforted. To those who hunger and thirst, fullness — as refreshment to those who labor and strive mightily for salvation. Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for justice: for they shall be satisfied.

At that time: When Jesus had been born in Bethlehem of Judah in the days of king Herod, behold, Magi from the east arrived in Jerusalem, saying: Where is he who has been born King of the Jews? And so forth.

A Homily of Saint Jerome, Priest.
Liber 1 Comment. in cap. 2. Matth.

For we have seen his star in the east. To the confusion of the Jews, that they might learn of the birth of Christ from the Gentiles, a star rises in the east — which Balaam, whose successors these Magi were, had foretold by prophecy. Read the book of Numbers. The Magi are then led by the guidance of the star into Judea, so that the priests, questioned by the Magi as to where Christ was to be born, would be left without excuse regarding his coming.

The book of the lineage of Jesus Christ, the son of David, the son of Abraham. Abraham begot Isaac. And Isaac begot Jacob. And so forth.

From a Homily of Saint Hilary, Bishop.
Comment. in Matthaei, cap. 1.

It does not matter who is placed in the number and order of the lineage, provided that the family of all is understood to have begun from one. And so, since Joseph and Mary are of the same tribe, while Joseph is shown to have descended from the lineage of Abraham, Mary also is taught to have descended from the same. For this rule was observed in the law: that if the head of a family had died without children, a later brother of the same kinship would take the wife of the deceased, and the children born would be registered in the family of the one who had died; and thus the order of succession would be maintained in the firstborn, while those who had been born after them would be counted by name or by lineage as their fathers.

At that time: The disciples came to Jesus, saying: Who, do you think, is the greater in the Kingdom of Heaven? And so forth.

A Homily of Saint John Chrysostom.
In cap. 18. Matth. Hom. 60.

See that you do not despise one of these little ones, for their Angels always behold the face of my Father, and because I have come for their sake, and this is the will of my Father. He makes us more diligent in protecting and preserving the humble. You see what great walls he has erected for the defense of the weak, and what care and diligence he has that they should not be lost — both because he has appointed the severest punishments for those who despise them, and because he promises the highest reward to those who take care of them; and he confirms this both by his own example and by that of the Father.
Matth 1:

When his mother Mary had been betrothed to Joseph, before they lived together, she was found to have conceived in her womb by the Holy Spirit. And so forth.

Homilia 32 in Evangelia

Because our Lord and Redeemer, the new man, came into the world, he gave new commandments to the world. For he opposed the newness of his ways to our old life, which had been nurtured in vices. For what did the old man, what did the carnal man know, except to keep what was his own, to seize what was another's if he could; to covet it if he could not? But the heavenly physician applies remedies contrary to each particular vice. For just as in the art of medicine hot things are cured by cold and cold things by hot; so our Lord opposed contrary remedies to sins: prescribing continence for the wanton, generosity for the miserly, meekness for the wrathful, and humility for the proud.

At that time: When Jesus had been born in Bethlehem of Judah in the days of king Herod, behold, Magi from the east arrived in Jerusalem, saying: Where is he who has been born King of the Jews? And so forth.

A Homily of Saint Gregory, Pope.
Homilia 10 in Evang.

As you have heard, dearest brethren, in the reading of the Gospel, when the King of heaven was born, the king of the earth was troubled; for earthly exaltation is confounded when heavenly greatness is revealed. But we must ask ourselves what it means that, when the Redeemer was born, an Angel appeared to the shepherds in Judea, while the Magi were led from the East to adore him not by an Angel but by a star. For to the Jews, as those who make use of reason, it was fitting that a rational creature, that is, an Angel, should preach; but the Gentiles, since they did not know how to make use of reason, were led to the knowledge of the Lord not by a voice but by signs. Hence it is said through Paul: Prophecies are given to the faithful, not to unbelievers; but signs are given to unbelievers, not to the faithful. For prophecies were given to the former as faithful, not as unbelievers; and signs were given to the latter as unbelievers, not as faithful.

At that time: Jesus said to his disciples: When they shall persecute you in this city, flee into another. And so forth.

A Homily of Saint Athanasius the Bishop.
In Apologia de fuga sua, ante medium

In the Law it was commanded that cities of refuge should be established, so that those who were in any way sought for death might be preserved. Then, in the fullness of the ages, when the very Word of the Father, who had spoken to Moses beforehand, came, he again gave this commandment, saying: When they persecute you in this city, flee into another. And a little later he adds: When you shall see the abomination of desolation, which was spoken of by Daniel the prophet, standing in the holy place (let him who reads understand), then let those who are in Judea flee to the mountains; and let him who is on the housetop not come down to take anything from his house; and let him who is in the field not turn back to take his tunic.

At that time: Jesus came into the parts of Caesarea Philippi, and he asked his disciples, saying: Whom do men say that the Son of man is? And so forth.

A Homily of Saint Hilary the Bishop
Comment. in Matth. can. 16, post initium

The Lord asked his disciples whom men said he was; and he added, the Son of man. For the rule of confession must be held firm: that as we remember him to be the Son of God, so we also remember him to be the Son of man; because one without the other offers no hope of salvation. Having set forth the various opinions men held about him, he asked what they themselves thought of him. Peter answered: You are the Christ, the Son of the living God. But Peter had weighed the terms of the question. For the Lord had said: Whom do men say that I am, the Son of man? And certainly the contemplation of the body suggested the Son of man. But by adding, Whom do they say that I am, he indicated that, beyond what was seen in him, something else was to be understood; for he was indeed the Son of man. What judgment of opinion about himself, then, did he desire? We do not think it was that which he himself confessed; but it was the hidden reality about which inquiry was made, toward which the faith of believers was to be extended.

At that time: Jesus responded and said: I acknowledge you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth, because you have hidden these things from the wise and the prudent, and have revealed them to little ones. And so forth.

A Homily of Saint John Chrysostom
Homilia 38 alias 39 in Matth., n. 1-3

I acknowledge you: this signifies, I give you thanks. I give thanks, he says, because you have hidden these things from the wise and the prudent. Now by wise he means the scribes and the Pharisees. He says this in order to make his disciples more eager, and to show how great are the things that fishermen attained, from which those others have entirely fallen away. But when he calls those men wise, he is not speaking of true and praiseworthy wisdom, but of that which they seemed to have acquired by their gravity. Therefore he did not say, You have revealed them to the foolish; but, To little ones, that is, to the sincere and the simple. And he shows that those others were not only unworthy, but that it was with justice that they did not receive these things; and he teaches us in all things to flee from pride and to pursue simplicity. Then, after he had by these words kindled desire in them and had demonstrated his own ineffable power, he called them, saying: Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you.

At that time: The disciples came to Jesus, saying: Who, do you think, is the greatest in the kingdom of heaven? And so forth.

A Homily of Saint Hilary the Bishop
Comment in Matth. can. 18

The Lord teaches that only those who have returned to the nature of children shall enter the kingdom of heaven: that is, the vices of our bodies and souls are to be recalled through childlike simplicity. Now he called children all those who believe through the faith of hearing. For they follow their father, love their mother, know not how to wish evil to their neighbor, take no care for riches; they do not grow insolent, they do not hate, they do not lie, they believe what they are told, and they hold to be true what they hear. We must therefore return to the simplicity of children; for, established in it, we shall carry about the image of the Lord's humility.

At that time: Jesus responded and said: I acknowledge you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth, because you have hidden these things from the wise and the prudent, and have revealed them to little ones. And so forth.

A Homily of Saint Augustine the Bishop
Serm. 9 de verbo Domini n. 70

Love makes all that is harsh and terrible altogether easy and as nothing. How much more certainly and readily does charity lead to true blessedness what concupiscence, to the extent it was able, brought about for misery! How easily is any temporal adversity endured, that eternal punishment may be avoided and eternal rest obtained! Not without reason did that chosen vessel say with great joy: The sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the glory that is to come, which shall be revealed in us. Behold, this is why that yoke is sweet and that burden light; and though it is narrow for the few who choose it, it is nonetheless easy for all who love it. The Psalmist said: Because of the words of your lips, I have kept hard ways.
Matt 9:9-13

At that time: Jesus saw a man sitting at the tax office, named Matthew, and he said to him: Follow me. And so forth.

A Homily of Saint Jerome the Priest
Liber 1 Comment. in Matth. cap. 9

The other Evangelists, out of reverence and honor for Matthew, were unwilling to call him by his common name, and instead said Levi; for he had a double name. But Matthew himself — in accordance with what Solomon says: A just man is his own accuser at the beginning of his speech; and in another place: Declare your sins, that you may be justified — calls himself Matthew and a tax collector, to show readers that no one ought to despair of salvation, if he has turned to better things, since he himself was suddenly changed from a tax collector into an Apostle.

At that time: Jesus said to his disciples: You are the salt of the earth. But if the salt should lose its savor, wherewith shall it be salted? And so forth.

A Homily of Saint Jerome the Priest

The Apostles and Doctors are called salt, because through them the whole human race is seasoned. But if the salt should lose its savor, wherewith shall it be salted? If a doctor should go astray, by what other doctor shall he be corrected? It is good for nothing any more, but to be cast out and trodden underfoot by men. The example is taken from agriculture. For salt, just as it is necessary for the seasoning of food and for the drying of meats, has no other use. Indeed we read in the Scriptures that certain cities, through the wrath of the conquerors, were sown with salt, so that no seed should spring up in them.

At that time: Jesus said to his disciples: You are the salt of the earth. But if the salt should lose its savor, wherewith shall it be salted? And so forth.

A Homily of Saint Hilary the Bishop
Comm. in Matthæum, cap. 4, n. 10

You are the salt of the earth: But if the salt should become foolish, that which is to be salted is worth nothing. The salt of the earth, in my judgment, has none of its own. How then did he call the Apostles the salt of the earth? But the proper meaning of these words must be sought, which the office of the Apostles and the nature of salt itself will make clear. Salt contains in itself the two elements of water and fire combined into one, and this one thing is made of two.

At that time: The Pharisees came to Jesus, and one of them, a doctor of the law, asked him, tempting him: Master, which is the great commandment in the law? And so forth.

A Homily of Saint John Chrysostom
Homilia 72 in Matthæum

After the Sadducees had been confounded, the Pharisees came again to attack; and though they should have been at peace, they wished to contend; and they sent forward one who professed knowledge of the law, desiring not to learn but to test him; and so they ask: Which is the first commandment in the law? For since the first is, You shall love the Lord your God, thinking that he would bring forward reasons to amend this commandment by making some addition, since he was making himself God, they ask in this way. What then does Christ do? To show that the reason they had come to this was that there was no charity in them, but that they were consumed with the poison of envy, he says: You shall love the Lord your God: this is the first and great commandment. And the second is like to it: You shall love your neighbor as yourself.

See that you despise not one of these little ones, for their Angels always behold the face of my Father, and because I have come for their sake, and this is the will of my Father. He makes us more diligent in protecting and preserving the humble. You perceive what mighty walls he has raised for the protection of the lowly, and how great is his care and concern lest they be lost; both because he has decreed the severest punishments upon those who despise them, and because he promises the greatest reward to those who take care of them, confirming this both by his own example and by that of the Father.

The lamps in this place he calls the very dwelling of virginity and the purity of holiness; but the oil is benevolence, almsgiving, the help given to the needy. But while the bridegroom delayed, they all slumbered and slept. He shows again a rather long interval of time intervening, so as to lead the disciples away from the opinion that his kingdom was imminent; for this is what they hoped: and therefore he frequently recalls them from such hope. In addition, he also indicates that sleep is a kind of death. They slept, he says; but at midnight there was a cry: either to remain consistent with the same parable, or again to show that the Resurrection will take place at night. Paul also mentions the cry, saying: In command, in the voice of the Archangel, with the last trumpet he shall descend from heaven.

Distinguished by the gift of tears, he daily offered to almighty God a sacrifice of propitiation. Once, while performing this on the night of the Lord's Nativity, he was found worthy to behold Christ Jesus in the likeness of a most beautiful infant; and so great was his protection over the flock entrusted to him, that it was received from heaven that, on one occasion, the commonwealth stood firm through the intercession and merits of its pontiff. Filled with the spirit of prophecy, he foretold many things altogether beyond human knowledge; by his prayers he frequently drove away diseases and demons; and, though nearly unlettered in grammar, he also wrote books breathing heavenly doctrine and piety. At last, having fallen into a mortal illness, and when those about him were preparing a more comfortable bed for the aged and infirm man, he recoiled from such comforts as departing far too greatly from the most austere cross of his dying Lord, and ordered himself laid upon his accustomed straw mat; and, foreknowing that the end of his life was drawing near, with eyes lifted up to heaven, he said: I come to you, O good Jesus; and on the eighth of January he fell asleep in the Lord. His precious death was attested by angelic harmonies, heard by certain Carthusian monks, and by his sacred body, left unburied for more than two months, fragrant with sweet odor, with face fresh and blooming, intact and incorrupt, and by miracles newly wrought after his death: moved by these, Pope Alexander VIII enrolled him in the number of the saints. Pope Innocent XII assigned the fifth of September, the day on which the holy man had first been raised to the pontifical throne, for the celebration of his feast.

Let us rejoice that our Pontiffs have ascended to their fellow citizens, serving as legates on behalf of the children of captivity, winning our hearts for the blessed and making known to them the desires of the wretched. Let us rejoice, I say, and exult, because that heavenly court has from among us those who care for us, who protect us by their merits, who formed us by their example, who confirmed us by miracles — those holy Pontiffs who, in the spirit of humility, had frequently offered peaceful sacrifices to heaven, and who through themselves have entered into the altar of God, themselves being both victims and priests.

Lawrence, born in Brindisi in Apulia, entered the Order of Friars Minor Capuchin as a young man, and thoroughly mastered philosophy and theology, while gaining proficiency in several ancient and modern languages. Ordained a priest, he undertook the office of preaching, which he carried out with tireless zeal throughout nearly all of Italy and other regions of Europe. Endowed with singular prudence and the gift of counsel, he was placed in charge of governing the entire Order, and was frequently employed by the Supreme Pontiffs for the undertaking of most grave legations. It was chiefly through his efforts that Christian princes united their forces against the threatening hordes of the Turks: with whom the Christian army engaged in Hungary, Lawrence going before with the Cross, urging on soldiers and commanders, and won a most celebrated victory. Amid so many and such great affairs, he cultivated the virtues of a religious man in a heroic manner. Whatever time remained, he devoted to prayer, and marvelously joined the interior life with external activity. At last, in Lisbon, to which he had been sent as ambassador by the Neapolitan people to the King of Spain, a strenuous defender of Christian liberty and justice, he fell as if in battle, in the year one thousand six hundred and nineteen. He left behind many writings for the defense of the Catholic faith against heresies and for the explanation of Sacred Scripture. Pope Leo XIII enrolled him in the number of the Saints, and Pope John XXIII declared him a Doctor of the universal Church.

Lawrence, born at Venice from the illustrious family of the Justiniani, was distinguished from his youth by a wondrous zeal for the affliction of his body; and, spurning the allurements of the world and the marriage arranged by his mother, he was received into the congregation of canons of Saint George in Alga. Appointed bishop of his homeland by Eugene IV, with no great change in his customary manner of living, he never ceased to relieve the needs of the poor — even burdening himself with debt — trusting in divine providence, which always assisted him with unexpected resources. He founded several monasteries of virgins, or reformed them according to the norms of a more perfect life. A distinguished example of Christian humility, he devoted himself most earnestly to the reform of ecclesiastical discipline and morals, worthy to be called the glory of bishops by the Supreme Pontiffs, and to be named the first Patriarch of Venice, the title having been transferred from the city of Grado. Distinguished by the gifts of tears, prophecy, and healing, and though nearly unlettered in grammar, he also wrote books conspicuous for heavenly doctrine and piety. He fell asleep in the Lord on the eighth of January. His feast, however, is observed on this day, on which the man of God was raised to the episcopal throne.

Lawrence, born at Venice from the illustrious family of the Justiniani, displayed from childhood a remarkable gravity of character. His adolescence having been spent in the exercises of piety, invited by divine wisdom to the chaste union of the word and the soul, he began to deliberate about embracing the religious life. And so, secretly rehearsing his new warfare, and beyond other bodily mortifications sleeping upon bare planks, and sitting as though an arbiter between the attractions of the world on the one side, and on the other the austerities of the cloister, with his eyes fixed on the Cross of the suffering Christ, he said: You, O Lord, are my hope; there you have placed your most sure refuge; and he flew to the congregation of canons of Saint George in Alga; where, devising new torments, he waged ever fiercer war upon himself as upon the bitterest of enemies, indulging himself in no pleasure whatsoever, so that he never again entered even the domestic garden, nor indeed his father's house — save once, when with dry eyes he paid the last offices of piety to his dying mother. Equal was his zeal for obedience, gentleness, and above all humility, since he would voluntarily take upon himself the most lowly duties of the monastery, would beg in the most frequented places of the city not so much for food as for contempt, and would bear immovably and in silence the insults and slanders heaped upon him; sustained especially by assiduous prayer, by which he was frequently rapt into God through an elevation of mind; and so ardent was the burning of his heart that he would inflame even wavering companions to perseverance and to the love of Jesus Christ.

Lawrence, born at Brindisi of pious and honorable parents, gave from his childhood the most certain proofs of apostolic zeal, when he often spoke words of salvation to the surrounding multitude. Having entered the Seraphic Order of the Capuchins, he surpassed all in humility and obedience. His novitiate completed and devoted to sacred letters, he mastered not only philosophical and theological disciplines, but also the Greek, Hebrew, Chaldean, German, French, and Spanish languages, so that he was able to preach in these tongues. Ordained a priest, he devoted himself entirely to procuring the salvation of souls. He traveled through nearly all of Europe. He embraced every class of men, becoming all things to all, that he might gain all for Christ. He was a devoted cultivator of the Passion of Christ our Lord and of the Virgin Mary, Mother of God, to whom he attributed that singular gift of tongues. He penetrated the secrets of hearts, foresaw things absent and future, and shone forth with miracles and prodigies. At last, worn out by labors, he departed this life at Lisbon, having received all the sacraments with the greatest devotion, on the twenty-second of July, in the year one thousand six hundred and nineteen; and, renowned for miracles, he was solemnly enrolled in the catalogue of the Saints by Leo XIII on the eighth of December of the year eighteen hundred and eighty-one.

He strove by various letters to turn Leo the Isaurian, the destroyer of sacred images, away from that heresy, and to win him over by every kind of service; yet when the latter, to crown his wickedness, had sought six times by the sword and once by gold and gifts — though in vain — to deliver the most excellent Pontiff to death. When Liutprand, marching with the Exarch to the destruction of the City, the most holy Pontiff, trusting in the protection of God, went out to meet him at the Neronian meadows, and by his pious admonitions so softened the king's spirit that, no longer as an enemy but as a devoted worshiper, he offered his sword and crown to the Prince of the Apostles. But when the emperor contrived the city's ruin, he struck him with a dire anathema and, having entered into an alliance with the Franks, deterred him from his impious design. Having at last accomplished these most distinguished deeds, by which he is ranked equal to the greatest of his predecessors, he died piously in the Lord in the sixth year of his pontificate, and was buried in the Vatican Basilica.

Leo, received at Rome with singular rejoicing by all, a little later persuaded Genseric, who was invading the City, by the same power of eloquence and the fame of his sanctity, to refrain from fire, outrage, and massacre. But when he saw the Church assailed by many heresies, and especially agitated by the Nestorians and Eutychians, he summoned the Council of Chalcedon to purge it and confirm it in the Catholic faith, where, with six hundred and thirty bishops assembled, Eutyches and Dioscorus, and again Nestorius, were condemned; and he confirmed the decrees of this same council with his authority.

Leo the Ninth of this name, sprung from a noble Frankish family, Count of Dagsburg and Bishop of Toul, formerly called Bruno, was raised to the most holy See of Peter by the votes of all the Cardinals and the common rejoicing of the faithful, and occupied it for five years, two months, and eight days. A man distinguished by every kind of virtue and sacred learning, in order to fulfill this apostolic office he spared no labors, no expenses, no hardships.
He visited Germany and Italy several times, and Gaul once. He held nine councils, at Reims, Mainz, Vercelli, Pavia, and Rome, for the restoration of Christian morals. He wrote many letters to emperors, kings, patriarchs, and bishops, burning with zeal and devotion. He sent legates to the Emperor at Constantinople, once and again, for the reunion of the Greeks; he condemned the heretic Berengar once and again, and struck Michael Cerularius the patriarch, a notorious schismatic, with anathema.
While residing in Rome, three times a week he went from the most holy Lateran church to the Vatican, on foot, barefoot, at night, praying and singing psalms. He ceded by pontifical diploma to the Prince of the Apostles the tenth part of the offerings that customarily fell to him. He spent his own personal patrimony on the erection of a monastery, from which money was also sent yearly for the expenses of the Golden Rose, which the Roman Pontiffs bless by ancient and solemn rite. He exercised a lavish generosity toward the poor and pilgrims. Under the form and habit of a leper, he once received Christ in his own bed. Finally, after exhausting many labors for the Church, he died on the nineteenth of April, in the year one thousand and fifty-four, renowned for many miracles before and after death, and was buried in the Vatican.

Leo the Third of this name, a Roman, son of a father named Astippius, educated from childhood in the wardrobe of the Lateran patriarchate in every ecclesiastical and divine discipline, rising from monk of Saint Benedict to cardinal priest and finally to Supreme Pontiff, was created with incredible unanimity on the very day of Adrian's death, in the year seven hundred and ninety-five, and occupied the holy See of Peter for twenty years, five months, and seventeen days.

Leo the First, an Etruscan, presided over the Church at the time when Attila, King of the Huns, surnamed the Scourge of God, invading Italy, after capturing and burning Aquileia, had prepared his forces to march upon Rome. Leo went out to meet him and persuaded him by divine eloquence to withdraw. Then, received at Rome with singular rejoicing by all, a little later persuaded Genseric, who was invading the City, by the same power of eloquence to refrain from fires, outrages, and massacres. And when he saw the Church agitated by many heresies, most of all by the Nestorians and Eutychians, he summoned the Council of Chalcedon; where, with six hundred and thirty bishops assembled, Eutyches and Dioscorus, and again Nestorius, were condemned; and he confirmed the decrees of this Council by his authority. He erected many sacred buildings and built a monastery near the Basilica of Saint Peter. Having thus accomplished these and other distinguished deeds, and having written much that was holy and eloquent, he fell asleep in the Lord on the fourth before the Ides of November, in the twenty-first year of his pontificate.
