Leo the First, an Etruscan, presided over the Church at the time when Attila, King of the Huns, surnamed the Scourge of God, invading Italy, after besieging Aquileia for three years captured, plundered, and burned it. Thence, being carried away with burning fury toward Rome, and now preparing to cross his forces where the Mincio flows into the Po, Leo went out to meet him, moved by compassion for the evils threatening Italy; and by his divine eloquence Attila was persuaded to withdraw. When asked by his men why, contrary to his custom, he so humbly complied with the commands of the Roman Pontiff, he replied that, while Leo was speaking, he had seen standing at his side another figure in priestly attire, who threatened him with a drawn sword and death if he did not obey Leo. Wherefore he returned to Pannonia.

Leo the Second, Supreme Pontiff, a Sicilian, learned in human and divine letters in both Greek and Latin, was also skilled in music; for he himself brought the sacred Hymns and Psalms in the Church to a more harmonious arrangement. He approved the acts of the Sixth Synod, celebrated at Constantinople, with the legates of the Apostolic See presiding, in the presence also of the Emperor Constantine and two patriarchs, of Constantinople and Antioch, together with one hundred and seventy bishops; and he also translated it into Latin.

Leo the Second, a Sicilian, learned in human and divine letters in both Greek and Latin, was also skilled in music; for he himself brought the sacred Hymns and Psalms in the Church to a more harmonious arrangement. He approved the acts of the Sixth Synod, celebrated at Constantinople, with the legates of the Apostolic See presiding; and he also translated it into Latin. In that Council, Cyrus, Sergius, and Pyrrhus were condemned, for proclaiming only one will and operation in Christ. He was truly a father of the poor; for he relieved the poverty and desolation of the needy widows and orphans not only with money, but also with his own work, labor, and counsel. He fell asleep in the Lord in the eleventh month of his pontificate, on the fifth before the Nones of July, in the year six hundred and eighty-three, and was buried in the Basilica of Saint Peter.

He accomplished, established, and wrote very many other things pertaining to the dignity and discipline of the Church. He condemned the defenders of Acacius, and especially Euphemius the Patriarch of Constantinople; and by his most vigorous and learned letters addressed to various parties, he either held them to their duty or recalled those who had gone astray. He restrained the Pelagians, Manicheans, and other heretics, and took care that their books were handed over to public burning. Besides decretals and ecclesiastical hymns, he wrote distinguished short works against Nestorius, Arius, Pelagius, and Eutyches. But most worthy of remembrance above all others is the fact that, by a singular decree of a Roman synod of seventy bishops, he distinguished the canonical books from others, and the approved from the apocryphal. After at last exhausting many labors in governing the universal Church, this most holy and most learned Pontiff died piously in the Lord on the eleventh before the Kalends of December, in the year of Christ four hundred and ninety-six, and was buried in the Vatican.

When the treasures of the Church were demanded of him, he promised to show them. On the following day he brought forward the poor. Asked where were the treasures he had promised, he pointed to the poor, saying: These are the treasures of the Church. And truly treasures, in whom Christ is, in whom the faith of Christ is. For the Apostle says: We have this treasure in earthen vessels. What better treasures does Christ have than those in whom he said himself to be? For so it is written: I was hungry, and you gave me to eat; I was thirsty, and you gave me to drink; I was a stranger, and you took me in. And below: For what you have done to one of these least ones, you have done to me. These are the treasures that Lawrence displayed, and he prevailed, for not even his persecutor was able to take them away.

In the time of Pope Liberius, John, a Roman patrician, and his wife, of equal nobility, having had no children, vowed their inheritance to the most holy Virgin, Mother of God. The Blessed Virgin, graciously hearing their prayers and vows, confirmed them by a miracle. Therefore on the Nones of August, a time when the greatest heat is customary in the City, snow covered a part of the Esquiline Hill by night. That night the Mother of God separately warned John and his wife in their sleep to build a church on that spot. John reported this to Pope Liberius, who affirmed that the same thing had happened to him in a dream. Wherefore he came to the hill covered with snow, and marked out on it the site of the church, which was built at the expense of John and his wife, and afterwards restored by Sixtus III. Called by various names, so that by the very distinction of the title its excellence might be signified, it was named the Church of Saint Mary Major.

In the time of Pope Liberius, John, a Roman patrician, and his wife, of equal nobility, having had no children to whom they might leave their goods as heirs, vowed their inheritance to the most holy Virgin, Mother of God, beseeching her continually and earnestly to indicate in some way in what pious work she wished that money to be spent above all. The Blessed Virgin Mary, graciously hearing their prayers and vows, made in all sincerity, confirmed them by a miracle.

In the time of the Emperor Licinius and the governor Agricolaus, at Sebaste, a city of Armenia, the faith of forty soldiers in Jesus Christ, and their fortitude in enduring torments, shone forth. Cast more than once into a horrible prison, bound in chains, and with their faces beaten with stones, they were commanded in the bitterest winter to spend the night naked in the open air upon a frozen pond, so that, frozen with cold, they might be killed. But the prayer of all was one: Forty we entered the arena, grant us, O Lord, a crown of forty, let not even one be wanting to this number. This number is honored, which you adorned with forty days of fasting, through which the divine law entered into the world. Elijah, seeking God with forty days of fasting, obtained his vision. And such indeed was their prayer.

Pope Linus, born at Volterra in Etruria, governed the Church first after Peter. So great was his faith and holiness that he not only cast out demons but also recalled the dead to life. He wrote the acts of the blessed Peter, and especially those things performed by him against Simon Magus. He decreed that no woman should enter the church with her head uncovered. This Pontiff was beheaded for the constancy of his faith, by order of Saturninus, an impious and most ungrateful proconsul, whose daughter he had freed from affliction by demons. He was buried in the Vatican near the tomb of the Prince of the Apostles, on the ninth before the Kalends of October. He occupied his see for eleven years, two months, and twenty-three days, having ordained, in two ordinations in the month of December, fifteen bishops and eighteen priests.

Cyril and Methodius, brothers by blood, born at Thessalonica of a most distinguished family, betook themselves early to Constantinople, to learn the liberal arts in that chief city of the East. Both made great progress in a short time; but most of all Cyril, who attained such renown in the sciences that, as a singular mark of honor, he was called the Philosopher. Then Methodius began to live as a monk; Cyril, however, was deemed worthy of receiving from the Empress Theodora, on the advice of Patriarch Ignatius, the charge of instructing in the Christian faith the Khazars who dwelt beyond the Chersonese; these, taught by his precepts and moved by divine grace, having abandoned their manifold superstitions, he joined to Jesus Christ. Having excellently established this new Christian community, he returned joyfully to Constantinople, and Cyril himself withdrew to the monastery of Polychronios, to which Methodius had already retired. Meanwhile, when news of the successful deeds beyond the Chersonese had reached Rastislav, Prince of Moravia, he treated with the Emperor Michael III about summoning certain missionaries from Constantinople. Therefore Cyril and Methodius were assigned to that mission, and received in Moravia with great rejoicing, they set to work to cultivate the minds of its people with Christian teaching with such force and diligent industry that in no long time that nation most willingly gave its name to Jesus Christ. For this purpose, no little use was made of their knowledge of the Slavonic tongue, which Cyril had previously acquired, and great effect was had from the sacred letters of both Testaments, which he had rendered in the vernacular of the people; for Cyril and Methodius were found to be the originators of the very characters by which the Slavonic language itself is written and expressed, and for this reason they are rightly regarded as the authors of that same language.

Luke had learned the Gospel not only from the Apostle Paul, who had not been with the Lord in the flesh, but also from the other Apostles; as he himself makes clear at the beginning of his volume, saying: As those who from the beginning were themselves eyewitnesses and ministers of the word have delivered them to us. Therefore he wrote the Gospel as he had heard it; but the Acts of the Apostles he composed as he himself had witnessed them. He lived eighty-four years and had no wife. He was buried at Constantinople, to which city, in the twentieth year of Constantine, his bones were translated together with the relics of the Apostle Andrew from Achaia.

Lucius, a Roman, son of Porphyrius, after the consummation of Saint Cornelius, held the episcopate of the Roman Church. Full of the Spirit of God, as Saint Cyprian wrote, he indicated by his letters that two priests and three deacons should never leave the bishop's side, for the sake of ecclesiastical witness; and that peace must be given to the lapsed, and that after penance had been done, the fruit of communion must not be denied. Sent into exile for the faith of Christ, and afterward permitted to return safely to his Church, he finally, having first handed over all the property of the Church to his archdeacon Stephen, was beheaded on the fourth before the Nones of March, in the reign of Gallus and Volusianus. He held two ordinations in the month of December, in which he created four priests and seven bishops for various places. His body, first buried on the Appian Way near Saint Sixtus in the cemetery of Callistus, was thence translated by Pope Paschal to the title church of Saint Cecilia, together with the bodies of that same virgin and her companions, and was placed there beneath the holy altar.

Louis the Ninth, King of France, raised in the most holy discipline of his mother Blanche, crossing the sea with a great army to recover possession of Jerusalem, put the Saracens to flight in the first battle. But when a great multitude of soldiers had perished from plague, he was himself defeated and taken captive. With matters settled, he was released. He redeemed very many Christians in the East from the slavery of the barbarians, and converted many unbelievers to the faith of Christ. Returning to France, he built many monasteries and homes for the poor; he relieved the needy by his beneficence, frequently visited the sick and ministered to them; he wore common clothing, continually afflicted his body with hair shirt and fasting. When he crossed again, intending to make war on the Saracens, and had already pitched his camp in sight of them, he died of plague while in that prayer: I will enter into your house, I will worship toward your holy temple, and I will give praise to your name.

Louis the Ninth, King of France, twelve years old at the death of his father, and raised in the most holy discipline of his mother Blanche, when he had already been reigning twenty years, fell ill; at which time he began to think about recovering possession of Jerusalem. Wherefore, when he had recovered, he received the standard from the Bishop of Paris; then, crossing the sea with a great army, he put the Saracens to flight in the first battle. But when a great multitude of soldiers had perished from plague, he was himself defeated and taken captive.

Monica, the most devout mother of Saint Augustine, the model of wives and widows, having followed her son, a Manichean, to Milan, after winning him for Christ by her unceasing prayers, tears, and fasts, with the help of Bishop Ambrose, was returning with him to Africa when she fell into a fever at Ostia on the Tiber, and on the ninth day died most peacefully. Her son, mourning her death, writes in reflection: We did not think it fitting to celebrate that funeral with tearful laments and groans, because she neither died miserably, nor died at all; of this we were assured by the testimonies of her character, by her faith unfeigned, and by certain reasons. And so by degrees I recovered my former feeling about your handmaid, her way of life so devout toward you, so gentle and forbearing toward us, from which I was suddenly bereft; and I was glad to weep for her and for her sake. And if anyone finds sin in this, that I wept for my mother, dead for a time to my eyes, who had wept for me many years, that I might live to her eyes, let him not laugh me to scorn; but rather, if he is a man of great charity, let him weep for my sins before you, Father of all the brethren of your Christ. Her body, first buried in the church of Saint Aurea, was afterward, under Pope Martin V, translated to Rome, and honorably laid in the church of Saint Augustine.

Rightly is it said to Peter: Do you love me? and he answers, I love you, and it is said back to him, Feed my lambs — and this a second time, a third time. Here it is also shown that love and dilection are one and the same thing; for the Lord also in the end does not say, Do you love me, but, Do you love me. Therefore let us love not ourselves but him, and in feeding his sheep let us seek those things which are his, not those which are our own. For by some inexplicable manner, whoever loves himself and not God does not love himself; and whoever loves God and not himself, he himself loves himself. For whoever cannot live of himself certainly dies by loving himself; and so he does not love himself who loves himself that he may not live.

At Mexico, on the hill of Tepeyac, in the year fifteen hundred and thirty-one, the Virgin Mary, Mother of God, as is piously handed down, showed herself to Juan Diego, a neophyte, and gave him a message for Bishop Juan de Zumárraga about building a church for her there, which she urgently repeated. The Bishop, however, sought a sign. Shortly thereafter, when the neophyte was seeking the sacraments for his dying uncle at a distance from the place of the apparition, the gracious Mother deigned to appear to him a third time, reassured him of his uncle's health, and ordered him to carry to the Bishop roses which had blossomed out of season, arranged in his cloak. In the Bishop's presence, when the roses fell out, the image of Mary, impressed upon that same cloak, as is handed down, appeared miraculously to those present. Preserved first in the episcopal chapel, then translated to the church built on the hill of Tepeyac, it was finally received into a magnificent temple, to which the peoples of Mexico began to flock ever more in crowds, moved by devotion and by the frequency of miracles. And so, as a most present help, the Mexican bishops, with the applause of all the people, chose the Blessed Virgin Mary of Guadalupe as the principal Patron of the Mexican nation, which Benedict XIV duly confirmed by apostolic authority. Leo XIII adorned the sacred image with a golden crown, on the anniversary of Columbus, in the year eighteen hundred and ninety-five, through the Archbishop of Mexico. And Saint Pius X declared the Blessed Virgin of Guadalupe the Patron of all Latin America.

He thereafter administered the Church of Poitiers with great tranquility, and led all of Gaul to condemn the impiety of the Arians. He wrote many books of wondrous learning; all of which Saint Jerome, in his letter to Laeta, testifies may be read without any suspicion of error, in these words: Let him run through Hilary's books with unfaltering step. He departed to heaven on the Ides of January, in the reign of the Emperors Valentinian and Valens, in the year three hundred and sixty-nine after the birth of Christ.
Proclaimed an eminent Doctor of the Church by many Fathers and councils, and venerated as such in several dioceses, he was at last, at the instance of the Synod of Bordeaux, declared and confirmed as Doctor of the universal Church by Pope Pius IX, following the advice of the Congregation of Sacred Rites, who also ordered his Mass and Office to be recited by all on his feast day as for Doctors.

He shone with great splendor of virtues in the religious life: he kept his body and soul from all impurity in such a way that he never felt himself defiled by the stain of any mortal sin. He mortified his flesh with fasting and vigils; he exercised his mind in divine contemplations. He was continually occupied in procuring the salvation of souls; endowed with a special gift of grace, he vigorously refuted heretics. He had such power in preaching that an innumerable multitude of people flocked to hear him, and many were converted to penance.

A great miracle indeed, most beloved brethren, was the Blessed Mary, ever Virgin. For what greater or more illustrious thing has ever been found in any age, or will ever be able to be found? She alone surpassed heaven and earth in greatness. What is holier than she? Not the Prophets, not the Apostles, not the Martyrs, not the Patriarchs, not the Angels, not the Thrones, not the Dominations, not the Seraphim, not the Cherubim, nor indeed anything else among created things visible or invisible, can be found greater or more excellent than she. She is both the handmaid of God and his mother; at once a virgin and a mother.

A great mystery: he lay in a manger, yet led the Magi from the East. He was hidden in a stable, yet was acknowledged in heaven: so that he who was acknowledged in heaven might be made manifest in the stable, and this day be called Epiphany, which in Latin can mean manifestation — commending at once both his exaltedness and his lowliness, so that he who was proclaimed great in the open heaven by the signs of stars, when sought in a narrow lodging might be found helpless, born with infant limbs and swathed in infant cloths, adored by Magi, and feared by the wicked.

Great Athanasius clearly said that Mary is rightly and truly to be called not only Mother of God, but also Queen and Lady, since Christ born of her, his Virgin Mother, remains God and Lord and likewise King. Concerning this Queen, therefore, he interprets those words of the Psalmist: The Queen stood at your right hand in golden raiment. Mary is therefore rightly called not only Queen of heaven, but Queen of the heavens, as mother of the King of Angels and King of the heavens, and as his friend and spouse. But from you, most august Queen, and most faithful Mother Mary, whom no one implores devoutly without fruit, and to whom all mortals are bound by the everlasting memory of benefits received, I pray and beseech you again and again with reverence, that you would be pleased to hold this whatever-it-is testimony of my devotion toward you as ratified and welcome, and that you would measure the smallness of the gift offered by the earnest will of the one who offers it and confirm it before your all-powerful Son.

Do you wish to be great? Begin from the least. Are you thinking of building the great structure of loftiness? Think first of the foundation of humility. And however great a mass of building each one wishes and plans to pile upon it, the greater the building is to be, the deeper he digs the foundation. And indeed a building in the course of construction rises upward; but the one digging the foundation is pressed down to the depths. Therefore a building is humbled before its loftiness, and the height is raised up after the humiliation.

Great therefore is John, to whose greatness the Savior himself bears witness, saying: Among those born of women there has not risen one greater than John the Baptist. He excels the rest, he stands out above all: he surpasses the Prophets, he transcends the Patriarchs: and whoever is born of woman is inferior to John. Perhaps someone will say: If among those born of women John is the greatest, is he greater than the Savior? God forbid. For John was born of a woman, but Christ was born of a Virgin. John came forth from the womb of corruption, but Christ was brought forth from the flower of an undefiled Virgin.

It is certainly a greater and more admirable thing to change the minds of adversaries and turn their hearts in a different direction than to kill them; especially since there were only twelve of them, and the whole world was full of wolves. Let us therefore be ashamed, we who, doing things far different, rush upon adversaries like wolves. For as long as we are sheep, we prevail; for then the help of the shepherd departs from us, he who feeds not wolves but sheep.

He also refuted the Manicheans, and burned their codices by fire before the doors of the Constantinian basilica. He wrote many letters to various persons throughout the entire Christian world, in which his most ardent zeal for the spread of religion — by which he was inflamed to the marrow — his knowledge of sacred letters, joined with a most limpid and pleasing style in which he greatly excelled, his singular skill in conducting affairs, especially with kings and nobles, in which he surpassed all others, and his other heroic qualities of soul, shine forth in a wondrous manner. His pious liberality was lavished upon the poor and upon sacred buildings. At length, having attained the fulfilment of his desires, weighed down by years and merits, and most celebrated before God and men for the glory of his deeds, after nine years of pontificate he departed to his heavenly homeland, in the year of Christ five hundred and twenty-three, leaving the remains of his lifeless body to the Vatican Basilica.

Maria Crescentia Höss, born of devout parents who earned their living by weaving at Kaufbeuren in Swabia, showed signs of future holiness from her earliest years. She learned so early to lift up her hands in supplication to heaven, and to turn attentive ears to her father as he narrated the Gospel stories, and to shed tears over the suffering Christ, that she seemed to have attained knowledge of divine things before she had learned to speak. She passed through her youth innocently amid the dangers of the Lutheran sect, under the protection of the Mother of God, to whom she vowed the flower of her virginity; she so composed her step and her ways with such modesty, and distributed with such charity the bread taken from herself to the poor, that she drew the admiration even of the supporters of error.

Mary Magdalene, born at Florence of the illustrious family of the Pazzi, took to the path of perfection almost from the cradle. At the age of ten she vowed perpetual virginity, and upon receiving the habit in the monastery of the sisters of Carmel, she showed herself a model of every virtue. She was so chaste that she had no knowledge whatsoever of anything that could harm purity. She burned with so great a fire of divine love that, unable to bear it, she was compelled to cool her breast with water poured over it. She excelled in charity toward her neighbor; for she often spent nights without sleep, occupied either in attending to her sisters' needs or in caring for the sick, some of whose ulcers she healed at times by licking them. She often had these words on her lips: To suffer, not to die. At last, exhausted by a long and grave illness, she passed to her Spouse in the year sixteen hundred and seven, in the forty-first year of her age. Clement IX enrolled her in the number of holy Virgins.

Mary is Queen and dispenser of grace, which was prefigured in the book of Esther, where it is said: A small spring that grew into a river, and was turned into light and sun. The Virgin Mary is compared under the figure of Esther to the outpouring of a spring and of light, on account of the diffusion of grace with respect to its twofold use — of action, that is, and of contemplation. For the grace of God, which is the medicine of the human race, descends to us through her as through an aqueduct, because it belongs to the Virgin herself to dispense grace, not as its principle, but by way of merit. Rightly, therefore, is the Virgin Mary the most excellent Queen in relation to the people, since she obtains pardon, overcomes the battle, distributes grace, and consequently leads to glory.

Mary is Queen most illustrious with regard to glory, which the Prophet well designates in the psalm that is specifically about Christ and the Virgin Mary, where it is first said of Christ: Your throne, O God, is for ever and ever, and shortly after of the Virgin: The Queen stood at your right hand, that is, in the highest goods, which is said with respect to the glory of the soul. Then follows: In golden raiment, in which is expressed the garment of glorious immortality, which it was fitting for the Virgin to have at her Assumption. For far be it that the garment with which Christ was clothed, which was also perfectly sanctified on earth through the incarnate Word, should become food for worms. Just as it was fitting for Christ to give his Mother the fullest grace at her Conception, so it was fitting to grant her the fullest glory at his Mother's Assumption. And therefore it is to be held that the Virgin, glorious in soul and body, is seated beside her Son.

Marcellus, a Roman, held the pontificate from Constantius and Galerius down to Maxentius. At his urging, Lucina, a Roman matron, made the Church of God heir to all her goods. The number of the faithful in the City having increased, he established new Titles and distributed them like separate dioceses. Whereupon Maxentius, in anger, threatened grave punishments unless the pontiff, laying aside his pontificate, should sacrifice to idols. The pontiff resisted steadfastly, and was therefore sent to a cattle-pen, to take charge of the beasts kept there at public expense. He spent nine months there, visiting by letters the parishes he could not visit in person. Rescued from there by the clergy, he was received in the home of blessed Lucina, in whose house he dedicated a church where he preached to the faithful. Then Maxentius ordered the beasts from the pen to be transferred to that church and kept by Marcellus; and he, afflicted by the squalor of the place and its hardships, fell asleep in the Lord. His body was buried by blessed Lucina in the cemetery of Priscilla on the Via Salaria on the sixteenth of January.

Marcellinus, a Roman, presided over the Church from the year two hundred and ninety-six to the year three hundred and four, during the fierce persecution of the Emperor Diocletian. He suffered many tribulations on account of the excessive severity of those who reproached him for undue indulgence toward those who had lapsed into idolatry, which was the cause why he was falsely slandered, as if he had offered incense to the idols. But this blessed Pontiff, together with three other Christians — Claudius, Cyrinus, and Antoninus — was beheaded in the confession of the faith. Their bodies, having been deprived of burial for thirty-six days by the Emperor's command, were at last honorably buried by blessed Marcellus, warned in sleep by Saint Peter, together with priests and deacons, with hymns and lights, in the cemetery of Priscilla on the Via Salaria. He governed the Church for seven years, eleven months, and twenty-three days; during which time he held two ordinations in the month of December, creating four priests and five bishops for various places.

Marcellus, a Roman, held the pontificate from Constantius and Galerius down to Maxentius. At his urging, Lucina, a Roman matron, made the Church of God heir to all her goods. The number of the faithful in the City having increased, he established new Titles for their benefit — for the conferral of baptism and penance on those who would embrace the Christian religion, and for the burial of martyrs — and distributed them like separate dioceses. Inflamed with anger at these measures, Maxentius threatened Marcellus with grave punishments unless, laying aside his pontificate, he should sacrifice to idols.

Marcus and Marcellianus, Roman brothers, were seized by the commander Fabianus on account of the Christian faith, bound to a post, with nails driven through their feet. When the judge addressed them thus: Take pity on yourselves, wretches, and deliver yourselves from these torments, they replied: We have never feasted so joyfully as we now willingly endure this for the sake of Jesus Christ, in whose love we have begun to be fixed; would that he might allow us to suffer this as long as we are clothed in this corruptible body. Spending a day and a night in torments, singing the praises of God, they were at last pierced with weapons and attained the glory of martyrdom. Their bodies were buried on the Via Ardeatina.

Marcus, a Roman, as Pontiff under the Emperor Constantine the Great, decreed that the Bishop of Ostia, by whom the Roman Pontiff is consecrated, should use the pallium. He built two basilicas in Rome — one within the City, the other on the Via Ardeatina — which Constantine, having enlarged them, adorned with great gifts. He lived in the pontificate for eight months and was buried in the cemetery of Balbina.

Margaret, called after the place of her death at Cortona, was born at Laviano in Tuscany. In the first years of her youth she was captivated by the pleasures of the world, and in the city of Montepulciano she led a vain and dissolute life; but when the bravery of a dog led her to discover her lover, foully murdered by enemies and buried in a pit under a pile of wood, at once the hand of the Lord came upon her; and struck with great grief for her sins, she went out and wept with love. Returning therefore to Laviano, with her hair cut off, her head bare, and clothed in a dark garment, she sent away the sins of her past and the allurements of the world; and prostrating herself on the ground in houses of God with a rope tied around her neck, she begged pardon of all whom she had openly offended by her former conduct. Soon departing for Cortona, she strove in ashes and haircloth to appease the majesty of God she had offended, until, after three years of proving herself in the virtues, she obtained from the Friars Minor — her guides in the spiritual life — the habit of the Third Order. From that time copious tears became her companions, and deep sighs drawn with such contrition of soul that she would remain speechless for a long time. Her bed was bare earth, a stone or a piece of wood her pillow; and thus she was accustomed to pass sleepless nights in the meditation of heavenly things, no longer suffering any evil desire, while her prompt spirit lifted her weak flesh to undertake labors.

Margaret, born of the royal stock of the English kings in Hungary, after spending her childhood with the highest piety, came to England and then to Scotland together with her father, who was called by his uncle Saint Edward, King of the English, to the height of his paternal kingdom. There, having at her mother's command married Malcolm III, King of the Scots, she benefited the entire kingdom for thirty years by works of holiness and piety. She was marked by the greatest austerity of life and by the most fervent zeal for charity toward her neighbors, especially the poor; for the feeding of whom she more than once emptied the treasury. At length, after patiently bearing sharp pains and a long illness, she gave her soul to God on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of December. At that very moment her face, disfigured by emaciation and pallor, blossomed again with an unwonted beauty. Accepted as patroness of Scotland by the authority of Clement X, she is devoutly venerated everywhere on earth.

Margaret Mary Alacoque, born of honorable family in a village of the diocese of Autun, showed signs of future holiness from her earliest years. Burning with love for the Virgin Mother of God and for the august Sacrament of the Eucharist, she vowed her virginity to God as a young woman; and upon entering the Order of the Visitation, she immediately began to shine with the splendor of religious life. She was adorned by God with the gift of a higher form of prayer, and with other gifts of grace and frequent visions. The most celebrated of these was when, while she was praying before the Eucharist, Jesus offered himself to her sight and showed her his divine Heart burning with flames and encircled with thorns in his open breast, and commanded her to take care that public veneration be established for his Heart — with great promises of heavenly treasure as a reward — to atone for such charity and for the injuries of ungrateful men. Flourishing in the glory of religious perfection and joined each day more closely to her heavenly Spouse through the contemplation of eternal things, she flew to him in the forty-third year of her age, in the year of restored salvation sixteen hundred and ninety. Benedict XV, distinguished by miracles, enrolled her among the Saints; and Pius XI extended her office to the universal Church.

Margaret Mary Alacoque, born of honorable family in a village of the diocese of Autun, showed signs of future holiness from her earliest years. Burning with love for the Virgin Mother of God and for the august Sacrament of the Eucharist, she vowed her virginity to God as a young woman, desiring this alone — that she might order her life according to the Christian virtues. She delighted in lengthy prayers and contemplation of heavenly things, in contempt of herself, patience in adversity, affliction of the body, charity toward her neighbors, especially the poor; and with the greatest zeal she strove to reflect as much as possible the most holy examples of the divine Redeemer.

Margaret, Queen of the Scots, most illustrious by her father's blood of the kings of England and by her mother's blood of the emperors, was still more illustrious by her Christian virtue. Born in Hungary, where her father was then living in exile, after spending her childhood with the highest piety, she came to England together with her father, who was called by his uncle Saint Edward, King of the English, to the height of his paternal kingdom. Then, as her parents' fortune changed, setting sail from the shores of England and driven by a storm — or rather, led by the counsel of divine providence — she was brought to the seacoast of Scotland. There, having at her mother's command married Malcolm III, King of the Scots, who was captivated by her outstanding gifts, she marvelously benefited the entire kingdom for the thirty years of her reign by works of holiness and piety.

Mary Magdalene, born at Florence of the more distinguished family of the Pazzi, took to the path of perfection almost from the cradle. At the age of ten she vowed perpetual virginity, and upon receiving the habit in the monastery of Saint Mary of the Angels, of the Order of Carmel, she showed herself a model of every virtue. She was so chaste that she had no knowledge whatsoever of anything that could harm purity. For five years, at God's command, she lived on bread and water alone, except on Sundays, when she ate Lenten fare. She afflicted her body with haircloth, whips, cold, fasting, vigils, nakedness, and every kind of punishment.

Marius the Persian, born of noble birth, came to Rome under the Emperor Claudius, together with his wife Martha of equal nobility and their two sons Audifax and Abachum, in order to venerate the tombs of the Martyrs. There they sustained Christians who had been cast into chains, supporting them with their work and their resources, and burying the bodies of the Saints. For this reason they were all arrested and, being moved neither by the threats nor the terror of the impious to sacrifice to the gods, they were first weakened with clubs, then dragged with ropes, then burned with red-hot plates applied to their bodies, and lacerated with iron hooks. Finally, their hands cut off and tied around their necks, they were led through the middle of the city on the Via Cornelia to the thirteenth milestone from the City, to a place called Nymphe, and put to death: first Martha, who had vehemently urged her husband and sons to endure their sufferings steadfastly for the faith of Jesus Christ; then the necks of the rest were cut in the same sandpit, and their bodies thrown into the fire. These half-burned remains were gathered by Felicitas, a noble Roman matron, who saw to their burial on her estate.

Martina, a Roman Virgin, born of illustrious family, orphaned of her parents while still young, lavishly distributed her great wealth among the poor. Under the prince Alexander, commanded to sacrifice to the empty gods, she abhorred the monstrous crime. Therefore, tortured with various kinds of torments, she was at last condemned in the amphitheater to the beasts; escaping them unharmed by divine power, she was cast into a burning pyre and was similarly preserved unscathed. Some of her torturers, seized by the novelty of the miracle and embracing the faith of Christ, attained the palm of martyrdom. By the prayers of Martina, God wrought many wonders, by which the judge was keenly moved and, marveling at the Virgin's constancy, ordered her head to be struck off, during the pontificate of Saint Urban I. The body of Martina was found, under Pontiff Urban VIII, in her ancient church at the Mamertine Prison, together with the bodies of the holy Martyrs Concordius, Epiphanius, and their Companions; and it was solemnly reinterred in the same place, now more fittingly adorned, to the joy of the whole City.

Martin, born at Sabaria in Pannonia, when he had reached his tenth year, fled to the church against his parents' wishes and asked to be enrolled among the catechumens. At the age of fifteen he entered military service and served first in the army of Constantius, then of Julian. Having nothing but his weapons and the garment he wore, he gave half his cloak to a poor and naked man at Amiens who begged him to bestow alms on him for the name of Christ. On the following night Christ appeared to him clothed in that half-cloak, saying these words: Martin the catechumen has clothed me with this garment.

Martin, born at Sabaria in Pannonia, when he had reached his tenth year, fled to the church against his parents' wishes and asked to be enrolled among the catechumens. As a youth of fifteen years he entered military service and served first in the army of Constantius, then of Julian. At the age of eighteen, having given half his cloak to a certain poor man at Amiens, he was refreshed by a wondrous apparition of Jesus Christ and with eager spirit received baptism; then, leaving military life, he was received by Hilary, Bishop of Poitiers, into the number of the acolytes. Afterwards made Bishop of Tours, he built a monastery, where he lived most holily for a time with eighty monks. When at the village of Candes in his diocese he had fallen into a grave fever, pitying his disciples, he prayed to God thus: Lord, if I am still necessary to your people, I do not refuse the labor. Then, as death drew near, seeing the enemy of the human race, he said: Why do you stand here, bloodthirsty beast? You will find nothing deadly in me. With these words, at the age of eighty-one, glorious with many miracles, he gave his soul to God.

Martin, born at Todi in Umbria, at the beginning of his pontificate devoted his efforts, both by letters and by embassies, to recalling to Catholic truth Paul the Patriarch of Constantinople, a heretic, who, relying on the heretical Emperor Constans, had even banished the very legates of the Apostolic See to various islands. Moved by this crime, the Pontiff, having convened a council of a hundred and five bishops at Rome, condemned him. While the council was still in session, the Emperor sent to Italy the Exarch Olympius to expel the Supreme Pontiff. But when Olympius was unable to do Martin any harm and soon died most miserably, Theodore Calliopas, by the Emperor's command, occupied the Lateran Basilica and the nearby pontifical buildings, seized Martin by force, and first exiled him to the island of Naxos, then brought him to Constantinople. There the holy Pontiff was cast into chains and subjected to ridicule and insults, until he was expelled to Cherson, where, worn down by hardships and want for the sake of the Catholic faith, he departed this life in the eighth year of his pontificate. His body, afterwards translated to Rome, was enshrined in the church dedicated in the names of Saints Sylvester and Martin.

Martha, however, admirable in the holiness and charity of her life, having drawn the hearts of all the people of Marseilles to love and admire her, withdrew to a place remote from men with a few most honorable women; where she lived long with the highest praise of piety and prudence, and at last, having long before foretold her own death, glorious with miracles she departed to the Lord on the fourth day before the Kalends of August. Her body is held in great veneration at Tarascon.

Martha, born of noble and wealthy parents but more illustrious as the host of Christ the Lord, is said, after his Ascension into heaven, to have been seized by the Jews together with her brother, sister, and many other Christians, placed on a ship without sail or oar, and to have put in at Marseilles. By this miracle and by the preaching of these persons, the people of Marseilles and the neighboring nations believed in Christ. Martha, however, admirable in the holiness and charity of her life, having drawn the hearts of all the people of Marseilles to love and admire her, withdrew to a place remote from men with a few most honorable women; where she lived long with the highest praise of piety and prudence, and at last, having long before foretold her own death, glorious with miracles she departed to the Lord.

Martha, born of noble and wealthy parents but more illustrious as the host of Christ the Lord, after his Ascension into heaven was seized by the Jews together with her brother, her sister, and Marcella her handmaid, and Maximinus, one of the seventy-two disciples of Christ the Lord, who had baptized that entire household, and many other Christians, placed on a ship without sail or oar, and committed to the vast sea for certain shipwreck. But the ship, steered by God, put in at Marseilles with all safe.

Martina, a Roman Virgin, born of consular rank, of illustrious family, orphaned of her parents while still in tender years, inflamed with the ardor of Christian piety, distributed with wondrous generosity to the poor the wealth with which she abounded. Under the prince Alexander, when she was commanded to worship the empty gods, she abhorred the monstrous crime with the utmost freedom. Wherefore, afflicted again and again with blows, with hooks, with iron claws, lacerated with fragments of pottery, cut limb from limb with very sharp swords, anointed with boiling fat, she was at last condemned in the amphitheater to the beasts; escaping them unharmed by divine power, she was cast into a burning pyre and was preserved unscathed by an equal benefit.

Martin, born at Todi in Umbria, at the beginning of his pontificate devoted his efforts, both by letters and by embassies, to recalling Paul, the Patriarch of Constantinople, from his wicked heresy to the truth of the Catholic faith. He, relying on the heretical Emperor Constans, had advanced so far in his madness as to banish the legates of the Apostolic See in various ways to islands. Moved by his crime, the Pontiff, having convened a council of a hundred and five bishops at Rome, condemned him.

The Mother makes the request, and the Lord speaks to the disciples, understanding that her petition springs from the desire of her sons. Can you drink the chalice that I am about to drink? In the divine Scriptures we understand by the chalice the Passion, according to that word: Father, if it is possible, let this chalice pass from me; and in the Psalm: What shall I return to the Lord for all that he has given to me? I will take the chalice of salvation and call upon the name of the Lord. And he at once makes known what this chalice is: Precious in the sight of the Lord is the death of his Saints.

Matthew, who is also Levi, Apostle and Evangelist, was sitting at the tax collector's booth in Capernaum when, called by Christ, he at once followed him; and he also received him and the rest of the disciples at a banquet. After the Resurrection of Christ, before departing for the province that had fallen to him for preaching, he was the first, in Judea, to write the Gospel of Jesus Christ in Hebrew for the sake of those who had believed from the circumcision. Soon departing for Ethiopia, he preached the Gospel and confirmed his preaching with many miracles.

Maurus, a noble Roman, offered as a boy by his father Eutychius to God under the discipline of Saint Benedict, made such swift progress through divine grace that he was a wonder even to his master; who often used to hold him up as a model of regular observance and all the virtues for the other disciples to imitate.
The following admirable example of his obedience while still an adolescent is recounted by Saint Gregory the Pope. For when the monk Placid had fallen into a lake and was being swept away by the force of the waters, Maurus came running at the command of the holy Father and, walking on the water, seized the companion by the hair and drew him to land.
Sent into Gaul by Saint Benedict himself, and having built a celebrated monastery over which he presided for forty years, he propagated monastic discipline in a wondrous manner. At last, glorious in holiness and miracles, past the age of seventy he departed to heaven in the year of salvation five hundred and sixty-five.

Mennas the Egyptian, a Christian soldier, having withdrawn to the desert for reasons of penance during the persecution of the Emperors Diocletian and Maximian, rushed into the theatre on the birthday festival of the emperors, while the people were occupied with a celebrated spectacle, and with a free voice attacked the superstition of the pagans. For this reason he was arrested and, bound before the governor Pyrrhus in the metropolis of Phrygia Cotiaeum, was cruelly beaten with straps. Then, racked on the rack and with burning torches applied to his body and his wounds rubbed with haircloth, he was next dragged through thorns and iron spikes with his hands and feet bound, and beaten with lead-tipped scourges; finally he was slain with the sword and cast into the fire. His body, rescued from there by Christians, was buried and afterwards translated to Constantinople.

At Mexico, on the hill of Tepeyac, in the year fifteen hundred and thirty-one, the Virgin Mary, Mother of God, as is piously handed down, appeared to the neophyte Juan Diego and gave him a message for Bishop Juan de Zumarraga, which she also urgently repeated, concerning a church to be built there for her. The Bishop, however, asked for a sign. Soon the gracious Mother, appearing a third time to the neophyte who was seeking the sacraments farther from the place of the apparition for his uncle who was dying, reassured him about his uncle's health, and ordered that roses which had sprung up out of season, gathered in his cloak, be brought to the Bishop. In his presence, when the roses were poured out, the image of Mary, imprinted on the very cloak, appeared in a wondrous manner to those present, as is handed down. It was first kept in the episcopal chapel, then translated to the church built on the hill of Tepeyac, and finally received in a magnificent temple, to which the Mexican people began to come in ever greater crowds, out of veneration and on account of the frequency of miracles. And so the Bishops of Mexico, with the applause of all the people, as if for their most present protection, chose the Blessed Virgin Mary of Guadalupe as the principal Patroness of the Mexican nation, which Benedict XIV duly confirmed by apostolic authority. Leo XIII adorned the sacred image with a golden crown through the Archbishop of Mexico on the feast of Columbus, in the year eighteen hundred and ninety-five. Saint Pius X declared the Blessed Virgin of Guadalupe Patroness of all Latin America.

Admire whichever you will, and choose what you admire the more — whether the most gracious condescension of the Son, or the most excellent dignity of the Mother. In both there is wonder, in both there is miracle. And that God should obey a woman is a humility without example; and that a woman should rule over God is an exaltedness without equal. In praise of virgins it is sung in a singular way that they follow the Lamb wherever he goes. With what praises, then, do you judge her worthy who even goes before him? Learn, O man, to obey; learn, O earth, to be subject; learn, O dust, to comply. When speaking of your Creator, the Evangelist says: And he was subject to them. Be ashamed, O proud one who is but ashes! God humbles himself, and you exalt yourself? God submits himself to men, and you, eagerly desiring to rule over men, set yourself above your Creator?
Happy Mary, in whom neither humility was lacking, nor virginity! And indeed a singular virginity, which fruitfulness did not violate but honored. And nonetheless a special humility, which fruitful virginity did not take away but exalted; and an utterly incomparable fruitfulness, which virginity and humility together accompany. Which of these is not admirable? which not incomparable? which not singular? It is truly amazing if, in weighing these things, you do not hesitate which you judge most worthy of your admiration — whether the fruitfulness in a Virgin is the more astonishing, or the integrity in a Mother; the exaltedness in the offspring, or the humility along with such exaltedness — unless undoubtedly all these individually are to be ranked lower than all of them together, and it is incomparably more excellent and more blessed to have received all than any one of them. And what wonder, if God, who is seen and read as wonderful in his Saints, has shown himself more wonderful still in his Mother? Let married persons therefore venerate in corruptible flesh the integrity of the flesh; let you, consecrated virgins, venerate in the Virgin her fruitfulness. Let all people imitate the humility of the Mother of God.

Indeed, whenever he prayed at the altar or offered the Holy Sacrifice — which he never omitted — he would, by the force of his love, either melt with seraphic ardors, or be shaken by extraordinary movements, or be drawn away from his senses. He joined a wondrous innocence of life, which no mortal sin ever defiled, with equal penance, chastising his body with fasting, iron chains, hairshirts, and bloody scourging. Amid all this, he became renowned for the gifts of prophecy, the reading of hearts, bilocation, and miracles.

Do not think, therefore, he says, that you are to be led to trivial contests, or that you must give account of small matters. You are the salt of the earth. What then? Did they treat what was already putrefied? By no means; for it is not possible that what is already corrupted should be restored by the application of salt. Therefore they did not do this, but those who had first been renewed and delivered to them, and already freed from that putrefaction, they sprinkled with salt and preserved in that newness which they had received from the Lord. For to free from the corruption of sins belongs to the power of Christ; but that they should not return again to those sins is the care and labor of the Apostles.

Fear not, Mary, for you have found with God a grace that knows no perishing; you have found with God a grace surpassing all others; you have found with God a grace to be desired by all desires; you have found with God a grace most splendid of all graces; you have found with God a grace that shall never fade; you have found with God a grace that preserves you in salvation; you have found with God a grace that is shaken by no assault; you have found with God a grace fully unconquered; you have found with God a grace that shall endure for ever. Many others, and they very many, flourished before you in eminent holiness. But to no one, as to you, was grace given in its fullness: no one was raised to such great majesty as you; no one was preceded by purifying grace as you were; no one shone with heavenly light as you; no one was exalted above every height as you.

Nor was the most gracious Virgin wanting to his prayers. For from her he learned that it would be most pleasing to her if he were to enter the religious order recently founded at her suggestion under the title of Our Lady of Mercy, or of the Ransom of Captives. Having received this admonition, he immediately set out for Barcelona and embraced that institution of most excellent charity toward neighbor. Enrolled therefore in the regular militia, he faithfully preserved the virginity he had long since consecrated to the Blessed Virgin, and excelled in other virtues, especially in charity toward Christians who were leading a wretched life in captivity under the power of pagans. Sent to Africa to ransom them, after he had already freed many from servitude, lest, with his money spent, he should fail to help others who were in imminent danger of renouncing the faith, he gave himself as a pledge; but since, inflamed with the most ardent desire for the salvation of souls, he was converting many Mohammedans to Christ by his preaching, he was thrown into close confinement by the barbarians and tormented with various tortures, his lips being pierced and sealed with an iron lock, and he long endured a cruel martyrdom.

Nor does the name disagree with the messenger. For who was more fittingly to announce Christ as the power of God than he whom a similar name honors? For what else is fortitude but power? Nor should it seem unbecoming or incongruous that the Lord and the messenger should be regarded under a common name; for though there is a likeness in the title of both, the reason for the title is not the same in each. For Christ is called the strength or power of God in one way, and the Angel in another; the Angel is so called only by attribution, but Christ both by attribution and by substance.

Nor is it strange that greater commandments are given for the sake of the Kingdom of Heaven, and lesser ones were given for the sake of the earthly kingdom, by the same one God who made heaven and earth. Concerning this justice, which is greater, it is said by the prophet: Your justice is like the mountains of God — and this is well signified by the fact that such great matters are taught on a mountain by the one Master, the only one suited to teach such things. He sits while he teaches, which pertains to the dignity of the office of a teacher. And his disciples draw near to him, that those who would draw close to his commandments in spirit might also be bodily closer to hearing his words. And opening his mouth, he taught them, saying. This circumlocution, in which it is written, And opening his mouth, perhaps commends by its deliberateness that the discourse is to be somewhat long. Unless perhaps it is not without significance that it is now said that he opened his mouth, whereas in the old law he was accustomed to open the mouths of the prophets.

We must, however, brethren, acknowledge by what weapons Stephen, girded for the fray, was able to overcome the cruelty of the Jews, and thus merited to triumph in blessed victory. Stephen, therefore, in order to merit receiving the crown his name foretold, had charity as his weapons, and by it he conquered everywhere. By charity toward God he did not yield to the raging Jews; by charity toward neighbor he interceded for those who were stoning him. By charity he rebuked those who erred, that they might be corrected; by charity he prayed for those who were stoning him, that they might not be punished. Supported by the power of charity, he conquered Saul who cruelly raged; and he who had him as a persecutor on earth, he merited to have as a companion in heaven.

Nor do they light a lamp and place it under a bushel, but upon a lampstand. Under a bushel, therefore, places the lamp whoever obscures and hides the light of teaching for the sake of temporal advantages; but upon the lampstand, whoever so submits himself to the ministry of God that the teaching of truth stands higher than the service of the body. In another sense, the Savior lights the lamp, who filled the vessel of human nature with the flame of his divinity; and placed it upon the lampstand — that is, upon the Church — because he fixed the faith of his Incarnation in our foreheads. This lamp could not be placed under a bushel, that is, enclosed within the measure of the law; nor did it shine in Judea alone, but in the entire world.

For our predecessors themselves deemed it their duty to defend and champion with all diligence the feast of the Conception of the Blessed Virgin and the Conception in its first instant as the true object of devotion. Hence the decisive words by which our predecessor Alexander the Seventh declared the sincere mind of the Church, saying: The piety of the faithful toward his most blessed Mother, the Virgin Mary, is ancient, in that they hold that her soul, at the first instant of its creation and infusion into the body, was, by a special grace and privilege of God, in view of the merits of Jesus Christ her Son, the Redeemer of the human race, preserved immune from all stain of original sin; and in this sense they solemnly observe and celebrate the feast of her Conception.

Nor do they light a lamp and place it under a measure. Are we to think that what is said under a measure means only the concealment of the lamp? As if he were saying: No one lights a lamp and hides it. Or does the measure signify something further? So that to place the lamp under a measure means to put the advantages of the body above the preaching of truth — so that one does not preach the truth for fear of suffering something troublesome in bodily matters. And the measure is fittingly so called, whether on account of the retribution of the measure by which each one shall receive what he has done in the body — as the Apostle says: Each one shall receive what he has done in the body — and as they say elsewhere of this measure of the body: With what measure you measure, it shall be measured back to you. Or because temporal goods, which are accomplished through the body, begin and pass away within a fixed measure of days.

Nereus and Achilleus, brothers and eunuchs of Flavia Domitilla, having been baptized by the blessed Peter together with her and her mother Plautilla, having persuaded Domitilla to consecrate her virginity to God, were accused as Christians by her betrothed Aurelianus and, on account of their glorious confession of the faith, were exiled to the island of Pontia. There, called again to interrogation and beaten with stripes, they were soon brought to Terracina and, having been tortured with the rack and with flames by Minucius Rufus, and having steadfastly refused — though baptized by the holy Apostle Peter — to be compelled by any torments to sacrifice to idols, they were put to death with the sword. Their bodies were brought to Rome by Auspicium, their disciple and the guardian of Domitilla, and were honorably buried on the Ardeatine Way.

Nicholas, born of illustrious parents at Patara in Lycia, was obtained from God by their prayers. How great the holiness of this man would be was already apparent from his cradle. For as an infant, while on other days he frequently took the milk of his nurse, on the fourth and sixth day of the week he sucked only once, and that in the evening — a custom of fasting which he always maintained throughout the rest of his life. As a young man, bereaved of his parents, he distributed his wealth to the poor. Notable is that example of Christian generosity by which, when a fellow citizen in need was unable to provide dowries for his three marriageable daughters and was thinking of prostituting their virtue, Nicholas, learning of it, by night cast through a window into his house a sum of money sufficient for the dowry of one of the virgins; and having done this a second and a third time, all three virgins were given in marriage to honorable men.

Nicholas, first of that name, a Roman by birth, son of Theodore the regionary, when Benedict the Third had been taken from among the living, was chosen by the clergy with the wondrous agreement of all, in the year of Christ eight hundred and fifty-eight; and having been brought by force out of the basilica of the Prince of the Apostles, where he had been hiding, and led to the Lateran patriarchate, was proclaimed Roman Pontiff. From his earliest youth he cultivated piety and every virtue, and made such progress in sacred letters that Sergius the Second enrolled him in that same patriarchate as subdeacon of the Roman Church, Leo the Fourth made him deacon, and finally Benedict the Third administered the entire Church by his counsel and direction.

Nicholas, born of illustrious parents at Patara in Lycia, fasted from infancy on the fourth and sixth day of the week; and indeed this custom he always maintained throughout the rest of his life. As a young man, bereaved of his parents, he distributed his wealth to the poor. Notable is that example of charity by which he came to the aid of three girls in danger, having set aside a suitable sum of money for their dowry. Having made a pilgrimage to Palestine, he came by the prompting of God to Myra, the metropolis of Lycia; where, after the Bishop of Myra had died, he was unexpectedly appointed by the provincial bishops with wondrous consent. In that office he offered himself as a model of all virtues. When he was preaching the truth of the Christian faith contrary to the edicts of Diocletian and Maximian, he was cast into prison, where he remained until the Emperor Constantine. He was present at the Council of Nicaea, in which the Arian heresy was condemned. Returning to his own people, he died most holily at Myra. His body, translated to Bari in Apulia, is venerated there with the greatest solemnity.

Nicholas, called of Tolentino from his long residence in that city, was born at the town of Sant'Angelo in Piceno to devout parents, who obtained him from God by a vow through the intercession of Saint Nicholas. As a boy he gave proof of many virtues, above all of abstinence. Having then been enrolled in the clerical militia and made a canon, when one day he heard a preacher of the Order of the Hermits of Saint Augustine speaking of contempt for the world, inflamed by that sermon, he immediately entered that same Order; in which he observed so exact a rule of religious life that he subdued his body by fasting, rough garments, stripes, and a harsh chain, and excelled in all other virtues. He did not interrupt his assiduous practice of prayer, although variously vexed by the snares of Satan and sometimes beaten with stripes. For six months before his death, he heard angelic music each night, and at last, having foretold the day of his death, he fell asleep in the Lord. Renowned for miracles in life and after death, he was enrolled in the number of the Saints by Eugene the Fourth.

Nicholas, called of Tolentino from his long residence in that city, was born at the town of Sant'Angelo in Piceno to devout parents; who, desiring children, set out on a votive journey to Bari and there received from Saint Nicholas a promise of future offspring; and the son they received they named after him. From infancy he gave proof of many virtues, but especially of abstinence. For in barely his seventh year, imitating the blessed Nicholas himself, he began to fast for several days of the week; and this custom he afterward retained, content with bread and water alone.

Nicomedes the priest, when the Emperor Domitian was persecuting Christians, was ordered to be arrested because he had buried the body of the Virgin Felicola, who had been put to death by the count Flaccus for her confession of the Christian faith; and having been brought before the statues of the gods, when he steadfastly refused to sacrifice to them — as he was commanded to do — on the ground that sacrifice was owed to the one true God who reigns in heaven, he was beaten with leaded scourges and in that martyrdom yielded up his soul to God. When the same count ordered his body to be cast into the flowing Tiber, Justus, a cleric of Nicomedes, having diligently sought it out, honorably laid it in a tomb at the walls of the City on the Nomentan Way.

Rufina making no progress — who, besides her deceitful words, afflicted her daily with blows to move her from her holy purpose — the praetor, frustrated in his hope and burning with anger at having spent his efforts in vain on Bibiana, ordered his lictors to strip her, bind her hands to a column, and beat her with leaded scourges until she breathed her last. Her sacred body lay for two days exposed to dogs in the forum of Taurus, unharmed, however, and preserved by divine providence; it was then buried by night by the priest John near the tomb of her sister and mother at the Licinian palace, where to this day there stands the church dedicated to God under the name of holy Bibiana, which Urban the Eighth restored after the bodies of the holy Bibiana, Demetria, and Dafrosa had been found in it and placed beneath the high altar.

You gain nothing, you profit nothing, savage cruelty. The mortal material is taken from your torments, and while Lawrence departs to the heavens, you fail before your own flames. The charity of Christ could not be overcome by flame; and the fire that burned without was weaker than that which blazed within. You raged, persecutor, against the Martyr; you raged, and you increased his palm while you heaped up his punishment. For what did your ingenuity not devise for the glory of the victor, when even the instruments of execution passed over into the trophies of triumph? Let us therefore rejoice, dearly beloved, with a spiritual joy, and let us glory in the Lord for the most blessed end of this illustrious man, who is wonderful in his Saints, in whom he has established for us both a protection and an example; and so glorifies his glory throughout the entire world that, from the rising of the sun even to its setting, by the shining splendor of the Levitical lights, as Jerusalem was glorified by Stephen, so glorious did Rome become by Lawrence.

For nothing is so easy to a good will as itself, and this suffices for God. However much, therefore, this world may rage, the Angels most truly proclaimed at the birth of the Lord in the flesh: Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to men of good will. For his yoke is sweet and his burden light, he who was born. There was therefore nothing more continent than he, nothing more watchful. In patience, meekness, mercy, humility, labor, and the study of the divine Scriptures he surpassed all. He so recoiled from meeting or conversing with heretics and schismatics, above all with Arians, that he said one should not even draw near to them. He lay on the ground when necessary sleep overtook him. He observed fasting so strictly that he used only salt on his bread and quenched his thirst with water; nor did he refresh himself with food or drink before sunset, and often abstained from food for two days; very often he spent the night in prayer. When such and so great a soldier of God as Anthony had thus emerged, the enemy of the human race assailed that most holy young man with various temptations, which he overcame by fasting and prayer. Nor did frequent triumph over Satan make Anthony careless, for he knew the innumerable arts by which the devil does harm.

Nothing was found wanting in him that belonged to the perfect solicitude of Apostolic governance; he kept intact the discipline of the Western Church, which flourished above all under him; the Eastern Church, vexed by the iconoclast emperor and patriarch, he revived by letters and legation; and to Greeks taking refuge in Rome, he graciously granted the monastery of Saint Praxedes, which he had endowed with most ample revenues. He also brought into the City many bodies of the saints from the cemeteries — following the example of Paul the First, and especially that of holy Cecilia, who herself pointed out and revealed the place — and wondrously adorned old churches. He restored xenodochia and monasteries of sacred virgins with new endowments. Finally, made most famous by the miracle of an extinguished fire, he passed to the Lord in the eighth year of his pontificate and was buried in the Vatican basilica.

For nothing is so precious as the soul: what does it profit a man if he gains the whole world, but suffers the loss of his own soul? But the love of money perverts and overturns everything and shakes off the fear of God, seizing souls like a tyrant seizing a citadel. Hence we neglect both the salvation of our children and our own. Hence great foolishness; hence children become cheaper than servants. But why speak of servants? If a man has a mule, he takes great care to provide the best groom for it, one who is not wicked, not thieving, not drunken, not unskilled in his art. Yet if a tutor must be provided for a son, we take the first man who happens along, chosen at random and without discernment; yet no art is greater than this. What is equal to that art which is charged with guiding the mind and character of a young man? Whoever is endowed with such a skill ought to show more diligence than any painter or sculptor.

Yet nothing was equally marvelous in her as her most ardent charity toward her neighbors, especially the poor, for whose numerous throngs she was accustomed not only to supply alms in abundance, but also to set before three hundred each day, with motherly kindness, a daily meal; to serve them kneeling in the manner of a handmaid; to wash their feet with her royal hands; and even to tend their sores with loving kisses. In these and other pious expenditures she sold not only her royal garments and precious jewels, but more than once emptied even the royal treasury itself. Having finally endured most bitter sufferings to a miracle of patience, she restored her soul, purified by six months of bodily illness, to its Creator on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of December. At that moment of time her face, disfigured by the wasting pallor of long illness, bloomed again with a certain extraordinary beauty. Renowned also for wondrous signs after death, and accepted as patroness of Scotland by the authority of Clement the Tenth, she is most devoutly venerated everywhere in the world.

Yet do not be troubled, my dearest; for what they did with evil intent was in accord with the truth. The prophecy was thereby fulfilled which says: They shall look upon him whom they have pierced. And not only this, but for those who would not believe it was an argument of faith, as it was for Thomas and those who were with him. Those who have been initiated know this: for through water they were regenerated, and by blood and flesh they are nourished. From these the mysteries take their origin, so that whenever you approach the wondrous chalice, you approach it as one drawing from that very side.

Do not therefore reckon within yourselves what you possess, but what you are. Behold, the world that is loved is fleeing. These holy ones, at whose tomb we stand, trampled with contempt of mind upon a world that was flourishing. Then life was long, health continuous, wealth in abundance, fruitfulness in offspring, tranquility in lasting peace — and yet, while the world was flourishing in itself, it had already withered in their hearts. Behold, the world has now withered in itself, and yet still it blooms in our hearts. Everywhere is death, everywhere mourning, everywhere desolation; from every side we are struck, from every side filled with bitterness — and yet with blinded mind of carnal concupiscence we love even its very bitternesses, we follow what flees, we cling to what is falling.

With what terror the executioner acted to make himself feared, with what blandishments to persuade, with what entreaties from many to induce her to come to the marriage — but she said: This too is an injury to my Spouse, to wait to please him. He who first chose me for himself shall receive me; why do you delay, executioner? Let this body perish that can be loved by eyes I do not wish to please. She stood, she prayed, she bowed her neck. You might have seen the executioner tremble as though he himself had been condemned, the hand of the striker shaking, the face pale, fearful before another's peril, while the girl felt no fear for her own. Nonnosus lived under a most harsh father of his monastery, which was situated on Mount Soracte, but always bore his ways with wondrous equanimity; and he presided over the brethren with such meekness that he frequently calmed his father's anger by that very humility. Now since that monastery had been built on the very summit of the mountain, there was no level ground available for the brethren to cultivate even the smallest garden. But one very small place had appeared on the side of the mountain, which a mass of enormous rock projecting naturally occupied. Since this could not be moved from there by human labor, Nonnosus turned to divine consolation and gave himself to prayer there in the silence of the night. When morning came and the brethren came to the same place, they found that the stone of such great size had receded farther from its place, and by its withdrawal had given the brethren a spacious area for cultivating the garden.

Was it ever said to the holy Lawrence: You ought not to have distributed the treasures of the Church, you ought not to have sold the sacred vessels? It is necessary that one fulfill this office with sincere faith and discerning providence. Certainly if a man diverts them to his own gain, it is a crime; but if he distributes them to the poor, ransoms the captive, it is mercy. For no one can say: Why does the poor man live? No one can complain that captives have been ransomed. No one can accuse, because the temple of God has been built. No one can be indignant that space has been made for the human remains of the faithful. No one can grieve that there is rest for the departed in the tombs of Christians. In these three kinds it is permitted to break, melt down, and sell even the consecrated vessels of the Church.
