Intent on gathering up orphans, he set out for Milan and Pavia; and in both places, having collected companies of boys, he wisely provided them with shelter, food, clothing, and teachers, with the support of noble benefactors. Returning thence to Somasca, becoming all things to all men, he shrank from no task that he foresaw would redound to the good of his neighbor. Mingling with farm laborers scattered through the fields, while offering himself as a helper in gathering the harvests, he explained the mysteries of the faith; washing the heads of boys fouled with mange, and patiently treating them, he would heal them; he tended the festering wounds of rustics with such success that he was reckoned to have been given the grace of healing. On the mountain that overlooks Somasca, he found a cave and withdrew into it; there, scourging himself with disciplines, spending entire days in fasting, prolonging prayer far into the night, snatching brief sleep on bare rock, he made satisfaction for his own sins and those of others. In the inner recess of this cave, water flows from dry flint — obtained, as constant tradition holds, through the prayers of God's servant — which to this day flows without ceasing and, carried to various regions, most often restores health to the sick. Finally, from a contagion that was spreading through the whole valley, while he was serving the sick and carrying the dead upon his own shoulders to burial, he contracted the disease, and at fifty-six years of age underwent the precious death he had shortly before foretold, in the year fifteen hundred and thirty-seven. Benedict XIV enrolled him among the Blessed, and Clement XIII solemnly numbered him among the Saints.

He established the penalty of retaliation upon those who had accused another of a false crime. He decreed that, as was already the custom in several places, the Psalms should be sung antiphonally by alternating choirs in all churches by day and night; and that at the end of each Psalm the words should be said: Glory be to the Father, and to the Son, and to the Holy Spirit. By his command, Saint Jerome rendered the New Testament back into conformity with the Greek. When he had governed the Church for seventeen years, two months, and twenty-six days, and had held five ordinations in the month of December, at which he created thirty-one priests, eleven deacons, and sixty-two bishops in various places — illustrious for virtue, learning, and prudence — he fell asleep in the Lord at nearly eighty years of age during the reign of the elder Theodosius, and was buried on the Ardeatine Way together with his mother and sister in the basilica that he himself had built. His relics were afterward translated to the church of Saint Lawrence, which was called after his name the Damasian.

Those who are at peace within themselves are those who, ordering and subjecting all the movements of their soul to reason — that is, to the mind and spirit — and having the lusts of the flesh brought into subjection, become the kingdom of God. In that kingdom all things are so ordered that what is preeminent and excellent in man governs the rest without resistance — those faculties that we share with the beasts — and that which excels in man, namely the mind and reason, is itself subjected to what is greater, which is Truth itself, the Only Begotten Son of God. For the lower cannot be governed unless it subjects itself to what is higher. And this is the peace that is given on earth to men of good will; this is the life of the consummated and perfect sage.

Having pacified Hungary, he returned to Rome, and when Boniface was besieged at Anagni amid the threats and assaults of enemies, he stood by him boldly and clung to him inseparably, while nearly all the others fled from him. When that same Pontiff was shortly afterward taken from this world, he was appointed to the See of Peter by the wondrous agreement of the Fathers. At that height of dignity, utterly free from all ostentation, he so cultivated humility that he sent away his mother, still living and brought to him somewhat more splendidly adorned than seemed fitting, as though she were not his; but soon afterward, embracing her most lovingly when she was clothed in her native and more humble attire, he treated her with honor. Those who had violated the pontifical dignity in his predecessor he punished with anathema; but those who had been treated more harshly by that predecessor he restored to their former honors and received into pardon and grace. To bring peace to the provinces of Italy, wretchedly torn apart by the factions of the Guelfs and Ghibellines, the Whites and the Blacks, he created Cardinal Nicholas of Prato of the Order of Preachers as legate a latere, and bade him go to England, Scotland, and Ireland to reconcile the kings and princes.

A most zealous devotee of peace, he actively promoted it — both in Germany, to which he gave assistance when it was afflicted by internal discord, and in Sicily, which he restored to communion by lifting its interdict. He also happily restored the agreement between the Kingdom of France and the Apostolic See, which had been gravely damaged shortly before. He extended the pastoral concern of his apostolic heart to the East and to the other provinces of schismatics, and earnestly commended to Archbishop Martin of Antivar the restoration of ecclesiastical discipline. He stirred up Orosh, king of Serbia, with most affectionate letters to renounce the schism. Finally, while intent on recovering Syria and Palestine, and planning and working toward other advances for religion, he was forestalled by common necessity. He died at Perugia in the year twelve hundred and four, with the ninth month of his pontificate not yet complete, and was buried, in a humble place as he himself had commanded, among his Dominicans, immediately renowned for miracles after his death. Clement XII approved the devotion paid to him from time immemorial, and granted that his feast be celebrated with Office and Mass under a double rite in the entire Order of Preachers, and by the clergy of Treviso and Perugia.
Eugene, the third of that name — previously called Bernard — was a native of Pisa. Having completed his youth, he entered the clerical state, and after being ordained a priest, he merited to be received among the canons of the metropolitan church of Pisa by reason of his eminent gifts of soul. Attracted by the example of Saint Bernard, who had then come to Pisa, he gave himself to him to be formed, and put on the monastic habit at Clairvaux. He advanced so greatly under the direction of that great man that he was first appointed by him as prior of the monastery of Farfa, and then elected abbot of the monastery of Saints Vincent and Anastasius at the Acqua Salvia by Innocent II, Supreme Pontiff. When in the exercise of that office he had become renowned for a wondrous splendor of holiness and prudence, he was created Supreme Pontiff by the unanimous vote of the cardinals after the death of Lucius II. But scarcely had he begun his pontificate when, with factions of rebels striving to overthrow the primacy of the Roman Church, he was forced to leave the City once and again; and then, when the storm had been calmed, he returned to it again with the greatest honor and the congratulations of the good.

Pancras, born of a noble family in Phrygia, came to Rome as a boy of fourteen years under the emperors Diocletian and Maximian. There, baptized by the Roman Pontiff and instructed in the Christian faith, he was shortly afterward arrested on account of that same faith; and when he had steadfastly refused to sacrifice to the gods, he received the glorious crown of martyrdom by bowing his neck with manly fortitude. The matron Octavilla took up his body by night, and having anointed it with spices, buried it on the Aurelian Way.

Pantaleon of Nicomedia, a noble physician, was instructed in the faith of Jesus Christ by the presbyter Hermolaus and baptized. He at once persuaded his father Eustorgius to become a Christian. Wherefore, when he afterward freely preached the faith of Christ the Lord at Nicomedia and urged all men toward his teaching, he was put to the rack under the emperor Diocletian, and tortured with red-hot plates applied to his body. Bearing this torment with an equable and steadfast spirit, he was finally struck with a sword and obtained the crown of martyrdom.

With equal constancy he labored for the freedom of the Church against the impious audacities of Henry IV. For this reason, assailed by persecutions and compelled to resign his bishopric, driven into exile, he first withdrew to his homeland, then came to Rome, where he was most graciously received by Saint Gregory the Pontiff. And when shortly afterward his reinstatement was under discussion in the assembly of the cardinals, by the marvelous apparition of a dove hovering over his head he was seen to be divinely commended anew to the Fathers. Accordingly he was sent back by the Pope to his diocese, and confirmed in the office of legate of the Apostolic See. But being driven out of Passau again by the unjust faction of his adversaries, he governed the clergy and people most holily in that part of the diocese that was under the authority of Leopold of Austria and Ottokar of Styria. There at last, after twenty-six years spent in the episcopate, he was called from labor and strife to rest and reward on the sixth day before the Ides of August, in the year of salvation ten hundred and ninety-one. His sacred body, translated to Göttweig by Archbishop Thiemo of Salzburg — himself afterward a glorious Martyr of Christ — was honorably interred there and is venerated with the devoted reverence of the faithful even now. God notably commended the holiness of the man by many miracles, as memory has handed down.

Paschal Baylon, born of poor and devout parents in the town of Torre Hermosa in Aragon, spent his childhood and youth in the care of flocks. Afterward embracing an institute of stricter life and being enrolled in the Order of Friars Minor, he continually pondered by what means he might conform himself ever more fully to Christ crucified. The Virgin Mother of God, to whose patronage he had dedicated himself from his earliest years, he honored as a mother with filial and daily devotion. He burned with a tender and constant affection of devotion toward the Eucharist — a devotion he seemed to retain even after death, for as he lay upon his bier he twice opened and closed his eyes at the elevation of the sacred Host, to the great admiration of all who were present. Full of merits he departed to the Lord in the year fifteen hundred and ninety-two. Leo XIII declared and constituted him the special heavenly patron of Eucharistic congresses and of all associations of the Most Holy Eucharist.

Paschal, first of that name, scarcely two days after the death of Stephen V, was elevated by the common suffrage of the clergy, though unwilling and greatly reluctant, to the supreme height of the Apostolic See, in the year of our Lord Jesus Christ eight hundred and seventeen. A man indeed most fully instructed in all learning and especially in sacred letters, distinguished for holiness of life, most eminent in eloquence, and finally singular in piety toward God and charity toward his neighbor, he distributed outward goods to the poor ever with a joyful spirit, while, devoting himself to vigils, prayers, and fasts, he accumulated the riches of the inner soul.

Paschal Baylon, born of poor and devout parents in the town of Torre Hermosa in the diocese of Sigüenza in Aragon, gave many signs of future holiness from his tenderest years. Blessed with a good soul and supremely devoted to heavenly things, he spent his childhood and youth in the care of flocks — a way of life he loved especially because he judged it most useful and fitting for fostering humility and preserving innocence. He was moderate in food, assiduous in prayer, and so flourished in authority and grace among those of his own age and his companions that, settling their disputes, correcting their errors, instructing their ignorance, and stirring up their sloth, he was cultivated and loved with the greatest devotion as a kind of parent and teacher of them all, and was even then called blessed by many.

We reckon paradise as our homeland; we have already begun to count the Patriarchs as our parents: why do we not hasten and run, that we may see our homeland, that we may greet our parents? A great number of our beloved ones awaits us there; a thronging and abundant multitude of parents, brothers, and children desires us — already secure in their own immortality, yet still anxious for our salvation. To come into their sight and embrace — how great a joy for them and for us alike! What pleasures in that heavenly kingdom, without fear of dying and with eternity of life! What supreme and unending happiness!

Patrick, called the Apostle of Ireland, was born in greater Britain of his father Calphurnius and his mother Conchessa, who is said to have been a kinswoman of Saint Martin, Bishop of Tours. As a boy he repeatedly fell into the captivity of barbarians. In that condition, set over the tending of flocks, he even then gave proof of his future holiness: for, filled with the spirit of faith, the fear of God, and love of God, he rose diligently before daylight, through snow, frost, and rain, to pour out prayers to God; accustomed to pray to God a hundred times during the day and a hundred times during the night. Having been freed from slavery for the third time, and enrolled among the clerics, he exercised himself for a long time in divine studies. After traversing Gaul, Italy, and the islands of the Tyrrhenian Sea with great labor, he was at last summoned by a divine prompting to the salvation of the Irish; and having been given by the blessed Pope Celestine the power to preach the Gospel, and having been consecrated a bishop, he set out for Ireland.

He restrained Patroclus, Bishop of Arles, who was usurping the rights of a foreign metropolis; and having sent letters to Hilary, Bishop of Narbonne, he commanded him, by right of metropolitan and by the authority of the Apostolic See, to go to the usurped see, to examine what ought to be done, and to report all matters to the Apostolic See. He decreed that no soldier or consecrated nun should touch or wash the sacred vestments; and that no one should place incense in the church unless he were a minister. He forbade a slave, or one bound to the imperial treasury or to any other obligation, to be made a cleric. He built an oratory in the cemetery of the holy Martyr Felicitas, next to her body, and likewise adorned the tomb of Saint Silvanus, offering many gifts. Finally, most celebrated by fame and full of the grace of God, he attained his glory during the reign of the emperors Honorius and Theodosius, and was buried in the cemetery of Saint Felicitas on the Salarian Way, on the eighth day before the Kalends of November. In one ordination in December he created thirteen priests, three deacons, and thirty-six bishops in various places. He held the pontificate for five years, less two months and three days.
Paucis ante illíus …

Paulinus, born in the year of our salvation three hundred and fifty-three from a most illustrious family of Roman citizens at Bordeaux, attained to senatorial dignity. Having been appointed consul of Nola, he was touched by the divine light, resigned the consulship, and returning to Bordeaux, was baptized by the blessed Delphin. Then, distributing to the poor the price of the goods he possessed in abundance, he withdrew to Spain, where he was ordained a priest. When he had returned to Nola, near the tomb of Saint Felix he founded a monastery and, having gathered companions, undertook the cenobitic life in its most austere form. As the fame of his holiness spread more widely, he was raised to the bishopric of Nola, in which office he left admirable examples of piety, patience, and above all charity. He wrote many things pertaining to sacred learning, and moreover excelled in the praise of eloquence and poetry. When Campania was laid waste by the Goths, he devoted all his means to feeding the poor and ransoming captives. But afterward, when the Vandals were ravaging those same regions, having nothing more to give away, he gave himself into slavery for the sake of a certain widow's son, and was carried off to Africa. Finally, freed by the help of God, he fell asleep in the Lord at Nola in a most peaceful end.

Paulinus, Bishop of Nola, learned in the studies of the humanities and also versed in divine letters, wrote many things elegantly and ornately both in verse and in prose. This man's charity is especially celebrated, because, when Campania was laid waste by the Goths, he devoted all his means to feeding the poor and ransoming captives — not even keeping for himself what was necessary for life. At that time, as Saint Augustine writes, being of his own will most poor from the most opulent wealthy man, and most abundantly holy, when taken captive by the barbarians he prayed to God thus: Lord, let me not be tormented on account of gold and silver: for where all my goods are, you know. But afterward, when the Vandals were ravaging those same regions, and a widow came begging him to ransom her son, having consumed all his resources in works of devotion, he gave himself in place of the young man into slavery.

A little later he was led to an estate called Columna, and having been beheaded, he was thrown into a well; from which he was afterward raised up and carried to the basilica of the saints of Agaunum, where he was buried with fitting honor. Furthermore, Sigismund, who had striven throughout his life to blot out the crime of parricide by a continuous flood of tears, began after death to be reckoned worthy of the fellowship of the saints, as the frequent miracles performed at his tomb most clearly testify. For those who suffer from fever, if they faithfully offer the saving sacrifice, are freed from the ailment of their infirmity. His relics, renowned for many wonders, were translated to Prague by the Emperor Charles IV.

Paul of the Cross, born at Ovada in Liguria, burned from the first use of reason with love of Jesus Christ crucified. Inflamed with desire for martyrdom, he joined the army that was being assembled at Venice to wage war against the Turks. But when he had come to know the will of God, rejecting a most honorable marriage and the inheritance of his uncle offered to him, he was clothed in a rough tunic by his bishop and, not yet a cleric, cultivated the field of the Lord by preaching the divine word. At Rome, raised to the priesthood out of obedience by the Supreme Pontiff Benedict XIII, he withdrew into the solitude of Mount Argentario, whither the Blessed Virgin had long before invited him, showing him at the same time a garment of dark color adorned with the insignia of the Passion of her Son; and there he laid the foundations of a new congregation, whose members were to be bound by vow to promote the remembrance of the Lord's Passion. He also established consecrated Virgins to meditate devoutly on the Lord's Passion. Renowned for preaching, virtues, and divine charisms, he fell asleep in the Lord at Rome in the year seventeen hundred and seventy-five. Pope Pius IX enrolled him first among the Blessed and then among the Saints.

Paul of the Cross, born at Ovada in Liguria but of noble stock from Castellazzo near Alessandria Statiellorum, gave notice of the holiness for which he was to be renowned by the marvelous radiance that filled by night the chamber of his laboring mother, and by the signal favor of the august Queen of Heaven, who snatched the boy unharmed from certain drowning when he had fallen into a river. Burning from the first use of reason with love of Jesus Christ crucified, he began to give himself more at length to contemplation of him, and to afflict his most innocent flesh with vigils, disciplines, fasts, drinking on Fridays from vinegar mixed with gall, and every kind of harsh self-punishment. Inflamed with desire for martyrdom, he joined the army that was being assembled at Venice to wage war against the Turks; but when he had come to know the will of God through prayer, he returned his arms of his own accord, to devote himself to a more excellent warfare that would strive with all its strength to be a defense for the Church and to procure the eternal salvation of men. Returning to his homeland, rejecting a most honorable marriage and the inheritance of his uncle offered to him, he wished to enter upon a more austere path of the Cross and to be clothed in a rough tunic by his bishop. Then by his command, on account of his eminent holiness of life and knowledge of divine things, not yet a cleric, he cultivated the Lord's field with the greatest fruit for souls by preaching the divine word.

Paul, the founder and master of hermits, born in lower Thebaid, when the persecution of Decius and Valerian was raging, withdrew into a cave in the desert; where, a palm tree providing him with food and clothing, he lived most holily until his one hundred and thirteenth year, at which time he was visited by the ninety-year-old Anthony. Paul received him most graciously, and after carrying on holy conversation far into the night, he warned him of his death, which was close at hand, and urged him at the same time to bring the cloak that he had received from Athanasius to wrap about his body. While Anthony was doing this, on his return journey he saw Paul's soul ascending into heaven; and he found the body in his cell, bearing the likeness of one in prayer. Having wrapped it in the cloak with great grief, singing hymns as was customary, and having nothing with which to dig the earth, two lions came from the inner desert and dug a place capable of holding one man. Then Anthony buried the body, arranged the tomb, and departed, taking with him Paul's tunic woven from palm leaves — a garment he wore on the more solemn days of Easter and Pentecost as long as he lived.

Paul, the founder and master of hermits, born in lower Thebaid, was fifteen years of age when he was bereft of his parents. He afterward withdrew into a cave in the desert to avoid the persecution of Decius and Valerian, and to serve God more freely: where, a palm tree providing him with food and clothing, he lived until his one hundred and thirteenth year, at which time he was visited by the ninety-year-old Anthony at God's prompting. When these two greeted one another by their own names — not having known each other before — and were talking at length of the Kingdom of God, a raven that had always before brought Paul a half loaf of bread brought a whole one.

Paul, first of that name, a Roman by birth, son of Constantine, was appointed — by a new precedent — to succeed his brother Stephen III after his death, in the year of Christ seven hundred and fifty-seven. But this was owed to his own eminent virtue. For since he had been admirably formed from his early years by Gregory II in the Lateran patriarchium, together with his brother, in Christian morals and every branch of ecclesiastical learning, the clergy had no worthier person to choose as a devout successor to his troubled brother in those most turbulent times.

He never failed to provide the poor sick — whom he sometimes carried home on his own shoulders — with anything that might profit the health of soul and body. Extending his charity also outside the hospital to needy widows and especially to maidens in danger, he secretly furnished them with food, and applied unceasing care to root out from his neighbors the concupiscence of the flesh by which they were defiled in that vice. When a great fire broke out in the royal hospital of Granada, John leaped fearlessly into the flames, rushing here and there until he had saved both the sick carried out on his shoulders and the beds thrown from the windows from the fire; and having remained for half an hour among the flames, which were by then grown immense, he emerged thence by divine protection unharmed, to the wonder of all the citizens — teaching in the school of charity that the fire which burned without had been less ardent than that which burned within.

We return, therefore, to our homeland by another way: since we who departed from the joys of paradise through pleasures are recalled to them through lamentations. Hence it is necessary, most dear brethren, that we be always fearful and always suspicious, setting before the eyes of our heart on one side the faults of our deeds, and on the other the judgment of the final strictness. Let us consider how strict a judge is coming, who threatens judgment yet hides himself; who holds out terrors to sinners, yet still endures them; and who therefore delays his coming that he may find less to condemn.

In those days the blessed Cajetan and Pietro Carafa (afterward Paul IV) had arrived at Venice; and approving the spirit of Jerome and the new institute for gathering orphans, they brought him into the hospital of the Incurables, where he might at once educate orphans and serve the sick with equal charity. Soon at the urging of the same men he set out to the nearby mainland and erected orphanages first at Brescia, then at Bergamo and Como: at Bergamo especially, where beside two others — one for boys and one for girls — he opened, as a new example in those regions, a house to receive women converted from a disreputable life to penance. At Somasca, a humble village in the territory of Bergamo on the borders of Venetian dominion, he established a residence for himself and his companions, and introduced a form of a congregation, which for that reason received its name from Somasca; which congregation was afterward enlarged and propagated, and devoted not only to the governing of orphans and the service of churches, but to the greater benefit of Christian society, to the education of youth in letters and good morals in colleges, academies, and seminaries — and Saint Pius V enrolled it among the religious orders, while other Pontiffs adorned it with privileges.

Through him divine power, in confirmation of his life and preaching, wrought many signs and miracles. For he very frequently laid hands on the sick, and they recovered their health; he expelled unclean spirits from bodies; he restored hearing to the deaf, speech to the mute, and sight to the blind; he cleansed lepers and raised the dead. At last, worn out by old age and illness, this tireless herald of the Gospel, having traversed many provinces of Europe with immense fruit for souls, happily completed the course of his preaching and life at Vannes in lesser Brittany, in the year of salvation fourteen hundred and nineteen: and Callistus III enrolled him in the number of the saints.

By his letters Celestine rebuked the presumption of those priests who, having laid aside the old habit, ministered in the church wearing a pallium and with their loins girt. He moreover decreed that no one should be denied penance at the point of death; that no layman or criminal should be advanced to the episcopate; likewise that no Metropolitan should presume anything in another province, and that in the creation of bishops, outsiders should not be preferred to the clergy who had already served in their own church. He instituted that from all one hundred and fifty Psalms an antiphonal psalmody should be sung before the sacrifice. He dedicated the Julian basilica, adorned his own cemetery with paintings, and offered various gifts for the adornment of the church. When in three ordinations in December he had created thirty-two priests, twelve deacons, and forty-six bishops in various places, he fell asleep in the Lord on the eighth day before the Ides of April, and was buried in the cemetery of Priscilla on the Salarian Way during the reign of the emperors Theodosius and Valentinian. He held the see for eight years, five months, and three days.

Through you the Trinity is sanctified: through you the precious Cross is proclaimed and adored throughout the whole world. Through you heaven exults, Angels and Archangels rejoice, demons are put to flight, and man himself is recalled to heaven. All creation, held fast in the error of idols, has been converted to knowledge of the truth, and the faithful have come to holy baptism, and throughout the whole world churches have been built.
Through you the Trinity is sanctified: through you the precious Cross is celebrated and adored throughout the whole world. Through you heaven exults, Angels and Archangels rejoice, demons are put to flight, and man himself is recalled to heaven. Through you all creation, held fast in the error of idols, has been converted to acknowledgment of the truth, and the faithful have come to holy baptism, and throughout the whole world churches have been built.

As the fame of the favors received, so it was said, by the faithful in the holy grotto grew ever more widely known, the number of people flocking there, drawn by the sacred character of the place, increased day by day. And so the Bishop of Tarbes, moved by the fame of the wonders and by the purity of the maiden, four years after the events narrated, having conducted a juridical investigation of the facts, affirmed by his sentence that the signs of the apparition were supernatural, and permitted the veneration of the Immaculate Virgin in that same grotto. A chapel was soon built: from that day nearly countless throngs of the faithful come there each year for the purpose of vow and supplication from France, Belgium, Italy, Spain, and the other provinces of Europe, as well as from the distant regions of America, and the name of Our Lady of Lourdes becomes renowned throughout the whole world. The water of the spring, carried to all parts of the globe, most often restores health to the sick. The Catholic world, mindful of such great benefits, has erected sacred buildings there with marvelous workmanship. Countless banners, sent there from cities and nations as memorials of received benefits, adorn the sanctuary of the Virgin with wonderful decoration. In this her seat, as it were, the Immaculate Virgin is continually venerated — during the day indeed by prayers, religious song, and other solemn ceremonies; and by night by those sacred processions in which nearly infinite throngs of pilgrims proceed with lighted candles and torches and sing the praises of the Blessed Virgin.

It is known to all that pilgrimages of this kind have aroused faith in an age grown cold, have added determination to profess the Christian law, and have increased the veneration of the Immaculate Virgin in a wondrous manner. In this marvelous profession of faith, the Christian people have priests as their leaders, who bring their flocks thither. The bishops themselves also frequently visit the holy place, preside over the pilgrimages, and attend the more solemn feasts. Nor is it so rare to behold the very cardinals of the Roman Church approaching in the humble manner of pilgrims. The Roman Pontiffs themselves also, out of their piety toward Our Lady of Lourdes, have laden the sacred basilica with most noble gifts. Pius IX distinguished it with sacred indulgences, the privilege of an archconfraternity, and the title of a minor basilica; and by his apostolic legate in France he had the image of the Mother of God venerated there solemnly crowned in a formal rite. Leo XIII likewise conferred innumerable benefits, granted indulgences in the manner of a jubilee on the occasion of the twenty-fifth anniversary of the Apparition, advanced the pilgrimages by his authority and word, and had the solemn dedication of the Church under the title of the Rosary carried out in his name. He crowned the breadth of these benefits when, at the request of many bishops, he graciously granted that a solemn feast under the title of the Apparition of the Blessed Virgin Mary Immaculate should be celebrated with its proper Office and proper Mass. Finally, Pope Pius X, in his piety toward the Mother of God and complying with the wishes of many bishops, extended the same feast to the universal Church.

For a more perfect life, he entered the monastery of Avellana in the diocese of Gubbio, founded for the order of monks of the Holy Cross of Fonte Avellana by the blessed Ludolph, a disciple of Saint Romuald. Not long afterward, sent by his abbot first to the monastery of Pomposa, then to the monastery of Saint Vincent at Pietra Pertusa, he cultivated both communities with the sacred word, excellent institutions, and good morals. Recalled to his own community, after the death of its prior he was set over the family of Avellana, which, by erecting new dwellings in various places and most holy institutes, he so enlarged that he was rightly regarded as a second parent and the chief ornament of his order. Other monasteries of different institutes, assemblies of canons, and peoples also experienced the saving solicitude of Peter. He benefited the diocese of Urbino in more than one way: he assisted Bishop Theuzzone in a most serious matter, and aided him by counsel and action in the right administration of the episcopate. He excelled in contemplation of divine things, in bodily mortifications, and in other examples of proven holiness. Moved by these things, Pope Stephen IX, though he was unwilling and reluctant, created him Cardinal of the Holy Roman Church and Bishop of Ostia. Peter fulfilled these dignities with the most splendid virtues and with works consonant with the episcopal ministry.

Perpetua and Felicitas, in the persecution of the Emperor Severus, were arrested in Africa together with Revocatus, Saturninus, and Secundulus, and thrown into a dark prison, to whom Satyrus was afterward added. There, while they were still catechumens, they were baptized. Then they were condemned to the beasts; and when one of the guards asked Felicitas, who was suffering the pains of childbirth, what she would do in the amphitheater, she answered: Now it is I who suffer; but there another will be in me who will suffer for me, because I also am about to suffer for him. And so they were led into the amphitheater before the gaze of the whole people; first they were scourged; then they were tossed about for some time by a most savage cow, cut with blows, and hurled to the ground; and finally, with their companions who had been tormented by various beasts, on the seventh day of March they were finished off with the blows of swords.

Consider in all this who gave such a price on our behalf, and what interest he will exact from us. On this day, therefore, the faith of the prophetic proclamation has been fulfilled, which says: I gave my body to those who strike, and my cheeks to those who pull; I have not turned my face from the foulness of spitting. He took upon himself our evils that he might bestow upon us his goods. Hence let us understand how much he deigned to love man before his fault, who loves him thus after his ruin. Know yourself, O man, what you are worth and what you owe: and while you perceive the great dignity of your redemption, let shame of sinning speak to you. Behold — for the impious, piety is scourged; for the fool, wisdom is mocked; for the liar, truth is put to death; for the wicked, justice is condemned; for the cruel, mercy is afflicted; for the wretched, sincerity is filled with vinegar; sweetness is drunk with gall; innocence is surrendered for the guilty; life dies for the dead.

Perpetua and Felicitas, in the persecution of the Emperor Severus, were arrested in Africa together with Revocatus, Saturninus, and Secundulus, and thrown into a dark prison; to whom Satyrus was afterward added. They were still catechumens, but were shortly afterward baptized. A few days later, brought out from prison to the forum with their companions, after their glorious confession, they were condemned to the beasts by the procurator Hilarianus. Thence they descended joyfully to the prison, where they were refreshed by various visions and inflamed toward the palm of martyrdom. Perpetua could never be turned from the faith of Christ — neither by the repeated pleas and tears of her aged father, nor by a mother's love for the infant child hanging at her breast, nor by the atrocity of the punishment.

Petronilla, understanding that snares were being laid against her virginity, which she had consecrated to Jesus Christ, by the most bitter enemy of the human race, took for herself a space of three days for deliberation; she spent all that time in fasting and prayer, earnestly beseeching her heavenly Spouse not to suffer violence to be done to her holy purpose. And so God came to the aid of his virgin on the third day: for he called her, burning with love for her divine Spouse, as soon as she had received the Eucharist, to the heavenly nuptials. Her body, buried on the Ardeatine Way, was afterward translated by Pope Paul I into the basilica of the Prince of the Apostles.

Petronilla, daughter of Saint Peter, was a virgin of outstanding bodily beauty, but far more surpassing in the beauty of her soul. When she was sick, it was asked of the blessed Peter why he who healed strangers did not restore health to his own daughter; he answered: Because it is expedient for her so. Nevertheless, lest he leave anyone in doubt of his power, he bade her rise from her bed and serve at table. But a short time later she relapsed into the same illness; and when she had at some point recovered from it, Count Flaccus, moved by her fame, though he had never seen her, fell in love with her and eagerly pressed to have her given to him in marriage.

The Lord therefore named Peter the foundation of the Church: and for that reason the Church fittingly venerates this foundation upon which the height of the ecclesiastical edifice rises. Hence the psalm that was read aptly says: Let them exalt him in the assembly of the people, and let them praise him in the seat of the elders. Blessed is God, who commanded the blessed Apostle Peter to be exalted in the Church: for it is fitting that this foundation be honored in the Church, through which the ascent to heaven is made.

Peter, who was called Celestine as Pontiff from the name by which he was designated, was born of honest and Catholic parents at Isernia in Samnium; having scarcely entered youth, in order to keep his soul from the allurements of the world, he withdrew into solitude. There, nourishing his mind with contemplation and reducing his body to servitude, he wore an iron chain upon his bare flesh. He founded the congregation that was afterward called the Celestines, under the Rule of Saint Benedict. From that point, as a lamp set upon a lampstand that could not be hidden — while the Roman Church had long been widowed of a shepherd — he was chosen for the Chair of Peter while absent and unknown, and moved everyone with a great sense of wonder at the novelty no less than with sudden joy. But when, placed at the height of the pontificate and distracted by various cares, he recognized that he could scarcely devote himself to his accustomed meditations, he voluntarily gave up the burden and the honor alike. Thence returning to his former manner of life, he fell asleep in the Lord, and a shining cross in the air before the door of his cell rendered the precious death more glorious still. He was renowned for many miracles both living and after his death; and these having been duly examined, Clement V enrolled him in the number of the Saints in the eleventh year after his passing.

Peter of Alcantara, born of noble parents at Alcantara in Spain, was received into the Order of Friars Minor in his sixteenth year of age; he set himself forth as an example of all virtues, especially of poverty and chastity, and drew innumerable souls from vices to penance by preaching the word of God. Eager to restore the primitive institute of Saint Francis, in a most narrow and most poor monastery built near Pedroso, he happily began a most austere manner of life, which was afterward propagated in a marvelous way. He was a helper to Saint Teresa — whose spirit he had approved and who while he was alive customarily called him a saint — in promoting the reform of the Carmelites. The same Saint Teresa testifies that he was distinguished by the grace of contemplation and of miracles, and that he was endowed with the gift of prophecy and discernment of spirits. Finally, when he was in his sixty-third year, he departed to heaven. Blessed Teresa saw him in a vision shining with marvelous glory.

Peter, born of noble parents at Alcantara in Spain, gave signs of his future holiness from his tenderest years. At the age of sixteen he entered the Order of Friars Minor and set himself forth as an example of all virtues. Then exercising out of obedience the office of preacher, he drew innumerable souls from vices to true penance. Desiring to restore the primitive institute of Saint Francis with the utmost exactness, relying on divine aid and fortified by apostolic authority, he founded a most narrow and most poor monastery near Pedroso; which most austere manner of life, happily begun there, was propagated in a marvelous way through the various provinces of Spain and even as far as the Indies. He was a helper to Saint Teresa — whose spirit he had approved — in promoting the reform of the Carmelites. And she herself, taught by God that nothing petitioned in Peter's name was not immediately granted, was accustomed to commend herself to his prayers and to call him a saint while he was still living.

Peter Canisius, born at Nijmegen in Guelderland, as soon as he had enrolled in the Society of Jesus, undertook to defend the Catholic faith against the snares of innovators by missions, sermons, and written books. Intent solely on the amplification of God's glory, it is scarcely possible to say how many labors and hardships he endured over more than forty years. He attended the Council of Trent once and again; he traveled through very many regions of Germany; he cultivated every class of men with most wholesome instruction in public and in private; and he defended a number of cities and provinces against the contagion of heresy, or restored those infected with heresy to the Catholic faith. Appointed by Saint Ignatius as prefect of the province of Upper Germany, he founded houses and colleges in many places. Against the Centuriators of Magdeburg he composed two outstanding volumes, and he published for the people the Summary of Christian Doctrine — judged most excellent by theologians and approved by long use among the peoples — and many other works; deserving therefore to be called the Hammer of heretics and the second Apostle of Germany. At last, at Fribourg in Switzerland, having reached his seventy-seventh year, he rested in the Lord on the twenty-first day of December in the year fifteen hundred and ninety-seven. Pope Pius XI added him to the roll of the Saints and at the same time declared him a Doctor of the universal Church.

Peter Canisius was born at Nijmegen in Guelderland in the very year in which Luther openly rebelled against the Church in Germany, and in which Ignatius de Loyola, in Spain, renouncing earthly warfare, turned himself to fighting the battles of the Lord — God thereby foretelling what adversaries the one would have, and what leader of holy warfare. At Cologne, whither he had gone for the sake of studies, he bound himself to God by a perpetual vow of chastity, and shortly afterward enrolled in the Society of Jesus. Having been raised to the priesthood, he at once undertook to defend the Catholic faith against the snares of innovators by missions, sermons, and written books. Sought out most earnestly because of his outstanding wisdom and proven practical experience by the Cardinal of Augsburg and by pontifical legates, he attended the Council of Trent once and again; and also at the authority of Pope Pius IV he took care to have its decrees duly promulgated throughout Germany and introduced into practice. Sent by Paul IV to the assembly of Piotrków, and employed by Gregory XIII in other missions to be undertaken, always with an alert spirit never broken by difficulties, he dealt with the most serious affairs of religion, and brought them even amid present dangers to life to a successful conclusion.

Peter Claver, a Spaniard born at Verdú, enrolled in the Society of Jesus as a young man of most innocent character. At the Balearic Islands, he was taught by Saint Alfonso Rodriguez — who had received many divine revelations about his future apostolate — what labors had been prepared for him. Ordained a priest at Cartagena in South America, he devoted his whole life, pledging it by a sacred oath, to the African slaves brought thither in a base trade. In caring for, nourishing, nursing, instructing in Christian doctrine, and baptizing them, it is scarcely possible to say with what patience and charity he labored for more than forty years. He restored to sudden health very many whom doctors had given up; he gave sight back to many who had lost the use of their eyes; he raised three from the dead. By these outstanding merits and heroic virtues he had completed seventy-four years when, on the birthday of the Mother of God whom he had venerated with most tender affection, he departed to the Saints of heaven. Leo XIII enrolled him in the roll of the Saints of the blessed and constituted him the special heavenly patron of the sacred missions to the Africans.

Peter, casting his thought upon the Lord and projecting his whole anxiety upon him, certain that the Lord would have care of him, left all things and followed the Lord, not even asking about the reward — until from the peril of the rich, which the Savior was pressing upon, he took occasion to ask: What then shall be for us? Jesus said to him: Amen, I say to you. The word of confirmation is put first: know that what follows is great. In the regeneration you also shall sit. You shall attain, he says, the one whom you follow, so that when he himself is seated, you too may sit together. O seating! Who will grant me to express in worthy words what I conceive with the affection of the heart concerning this seating? Indeed, who will grant me to enjoy the undisturbed rest of this seating, which I desire, which I long for, which I seek?

Peter, Bishop of Alexandria, after the most holy Theonas, illumined not only Egypt but shone for the whole Church of God by the splendor of his holiness and learning. In the persecution of Maximian Galerius he bore the harshness of those times in such a way that many, beholding his admirable patience, profited greatly in Christian virtue. He was the first to separate Arius, deacon of Alexandria, from communion with the faithful, on account of the Meletian schism which he favored. When, condemned to death by that same Maximian, the presbyters Achillas and Alexander came to him in prison as intercessors for Arius, he answered that Jesus had appeared to him by night with his garment rent, and when asked the reason of it had said: Arius has torn asunder my garment, which is the Church. Also predicting to them that they would succeed him in the episcopate, he commanded them never to receive Arius back into communion, knowing him to be dead before God. And that this divine foreknowledge was true, the outcome of events proved not long afterward. Finally, in the twelfth year of his episcopate, on the sixth day before the Kalends of December, having been beheaded, he flew to the crown of martyrdom.

Peter the Exorcist, under the Emperor Diocletian, was sent to prison at Rome by the judge Serenus for confessing the Christian faith; there he freed Paulina, daughter of Artemius who had charge of the prison, from a demon that tormented her. By this deed he brought both the girl's parents with their whole household and the neighbors who had come together at the novelty of the event to Jesus Christ, and led them to the presbyter Marcellinus, by whom they were all baptized. When Serenus learned of this, he summoned Peter and Marcellinus and rebuked them harshly, adding threats and terrors to his sharp words, unless they renounced Christ. When Marcellinus answered him with Christian freedom, he had him beaten with fists, separated from Peter, and shut naked in a prison strewn with fragments of glass, without food and without light. He also ordered Peter to be bound with the tightest chains. But when the faith and spirit of both grew stronger from the torments, by their steadfast confession and by beheading, they gave a glorious testimony to Jesus Christ. Bishop Erasmus, under the emperors Diocletian and Maximian, was beaten with leaded flails and cudgels in Campania, and also drenched with pitch, sulfur, molten lead, and boiling pitch, wax, and oil, yet escaped from it unharmed and inviolate. By this miracle many were converted to the faith of Christ. But he, thrown into prison again and bound with heavy iron chains, was there miraculously delivered by an Angel. Then at Formia, afflicted by Maximian with various torments and clad in a burning copper tunic, he overcame even those torments by divine power. Finally, having confirmed many in the faith and converted many to the faith, he obtained the outstanding palm of martyrdom.

Peter, therefore, though unwilling, was consecrated as archbishop and brought to Ravenna; where he was received with the greatest joy by the Emperor Valentinian, by Galla Placidia his mother, and by the whole people. And he said to them that the one thing he asked of them was that, since he had not refused to take upon himself so great a burden for their salvation, they should strive to obey his admonitions and not resist the divine precepts. He buried with the finest ointments the bodies of two Saints who had died there — namely, Barbatian the presbyter, and Germanus the Bishop of Auxerre — whose cowl and hair-shirt he also claimed for himself as an inheritance. He ordained Projectus and Marcellinus as bishops. At Classis he erected a font of truly admirable size, and built some magnificent temples — both to the blessed Apostle Andrew and to other Saints. He restrained with a most forceful sermon the games customarily performed by masked men with various dances on the Kalends of January; where among other things he said excellently: He who wishes to jest with the devil will not be able to rejoice with Christ. By the command of Saint Pope Leo I he afterward wrote to the Council of Chalcedon against the heresy of Eutyches. He also replied to Eutyches himself in another letter, which was prefaced to that council in new editions and included in the ecclesiastical annals.

Peter Nolasco, born of a noble family at Recaud near Carcassonne in France, orphaned as a young man, abhorring the heresy of the Albigensians, sold his patrimony and withdrew to Spain, where the Blessed Virgin appeared to him as he prayed by night and suggested that it would be most acceptable to her Son and to herself if a religious Order were founded to free captives from the tyranny of the infidels. Therefore, together with Saint Raymond of Peñafort and King James I of Aragon — both also forewarned by the Mother of God on the same night about the same matter — he founded the Order of Blessed Mary of Mercy for the redemption of captives, whose members were bound by a fourth vow to remain as a pledge under the power of the pagans if necessary for the liberation of Christians. Frequently refreshed by apparitions of his Guardian Angel and of the Virgin Mother of God, when he had reached a good old age he died most devoutly at midnight on the Vigil of the Nativity of the Lord, in the year twelve hundred and fifty-six.

Peter Nolasco, born of a noble family at Recaud near Carcassonne in France, excelled in singular charity toward his neighbor. A presage of this virtue was the fact that while he was still an infant wailing in the cradle, a swarm of bees flew to him and built a honeycomb of wax in his right hand. Orphaned as a young man and abhorring the Albigensian heresy that was then spreading in France, he sold his patrimony and withdrew to Spain; and at the shrine of the Blessed Virgin of Montserrat he fulfilled the vow by which he had previously bound himself. Then, going to Barcelona, when he had spent all his money in redeeming faithful Christians from the bondage of enemies, he kept saying that he wished to sell himself for their liberation, or to be substituted in their chains.

Peter, who received the surname Chrysologus on account of his golden eloquence, born of honest parents at Imola in Emilia, from his earliest age directing his mind to religion, gave himself to Cornelius of Rome, at that time Bishop of the same city of Imola; by whom also, when he had shortly advanced in knowledge and holiness of life, he was ordained a deacon. Afterward it came about that the people of Ravenna, on the death of their archbishop, sent to Rome another man chosen by them (as was the custom) together with their own delegates and with the aforesaid Cornelius, who brought this same levite with him. In the meantime, Saint Peter the Apostle and the Martyr Apollinaris appeared to the Supreme Pontiff in sleep, standing on either side of this young man, and commanded him to create that man, and no other, as Archbishop of Ravenna. Hence the Pontiff, as soon as he saw Peter, recognized that he had been foreordained by the Lord for that place; and therefore, rejecting the man they themselves were offering, he appointed this one alone to that metropolitan church, in the year of Christ four hundred and thirty-three. When the delegates of Ravenna bore this ill, having heard of the vision they willingly acquiesced in the divine will and received the new archbishop with the greatest reverence.

Peter, who received the surname Chrysologus on account of his golden eloquence, born of honest parents at Imola in Emilia, from his earliest age directing his mind to religion, gave himself to Cornelius of Rome, then Bishop of the same city of Imola; by whom he was deservedly ordained a deacon. He was appointed Archbishop of Ravenna by Saint Pope Sixtus III, though unwilling, and was received by the Ravennans with the greatest reverence. Outstanding in his pastoral office, in order to restrain the games customarily performed by masked men, he said excellently in a sermon: He who wishes to jest with the devil will not be able to rejoice with Christ. Foreknowing by divine inspiration the end of his life, he withdrew to his homeland; and having entered the church of Saint Cassian, after offering precious gifts, he humbly prayed to God and to that same patron to graciously receive his soul. He departed this life on the fourth day before the Nones of December, in the eighteenth year of his episcopate. His sacred body was honorably interred near the body of Saint Cassian.

Peter, born at Ravenna and bereft of both parents, was educated through the care of his brother Damian in letters and sciences with such success that he taught them with distinction to others. For a more perfect life, in the monastery of Avellana, founded for the order of monks of the Holy Cross of Fonte Avellana by the blessed Ludolph, a disciple of Saint Romuald, he entered religion; which house he afterward governed and enlarged in such a way that he was rightly regarded as a second parent and the chief ornament of his order. Stephen IX created him, though unwilling and reluctant, Cardinal of the Roman Church and Bishop of Ostia. In a most difficult time, he gave marvelous assistance to the Supreme Pontiffs by learning, by missions, and by undertaking many labors. He deterred Henry IV, King of Germany, from the unjust divorce of his wife. Finally, renowned for holy deeds, while returning from the legation to Ravenna, he departed to the Lord at Faenza.

Peter, born at Ravenna of honest parents, was still nursing when he was abandoned by his mother, wearied of her numerous offspring; but through the help of a household woman he was received half-alive and revived, and returned to his mother when she had been recalled to a sense of humanity. Bereft of both parents, he endured hard servitude as a kind of vile chattel under the harsh guardianship of a brother. He then gave a remarkable example of religion toward God and piety toward his father: for a coin that he had chanced to find, he did not spend to relieve his own hunger, but gave it to a priest to offer the divine sacrifice for his expiation. Kindly received by his brother Damian — from whom, as tradition has it, he received his surname — he was educated through his care in letters, in which he made such rapid progress that he was a marvel to his teachers. And when he flourished in the liberal sciences and in reputation, he taught them with distinction. Meanwhile, to keep his body subject to reason, he wore a hair-shirt beneath soft clothing; diligently persisting in fasts, vigils, and prayers. While in the heat of youth he was sharply goaded by the impulses of the flesh, he plunged into the freezing waters of a river by night to quench the fires of besetting lust; then he was accustomed to visit all the venerable shrines and to recite the entire Psalter. By assiduous help he relieved the poor, whom he frequently invited to table and served with his own hands.

Peter, born at Verona of parents infected with the Manichaean heresy, fought against heresies from almost his very infancy, never moved from steadfast faith by any blandishments of his father or uncle. As a young man he came to Bologna for the sake of studies, and there embraced the institute of the Order of Preachers; in which he excelled both in great splendor of virtues — especially in purity of body and soul, never defiled by any mortal sin — and in wondrous zeal for penance and contemplation. He labored with the greatest fruit for the salvation of souls, inflamed with such ardor of faith that he prayed to God for the grace of dying for it; which he also obtained. For when, exercising the office of the holy Inquisition, he was returning from Como to Milan, he was wounded on the head with a sword by an impious assassin; and being already nearly dead, pronouncing the creed of the faith which he had defended with manly courage from his infancy in that very last breath, he flew to the palm of martyrdom in the year of salvation twelve hundred and fifty-two. Innocent IV enrolled him in the number of the holy Martyrs the following year.

Peter, born at Verona of parents infected with the Manichaean heresy, fought against heresies from almost his very infancy. When he was a boy of seven years, attending school, he was once asked by his heretical uncle what he had learned there; he answered that he had learned the creed of the Christian faith; nor could he ever be moved from steadfast faith by any blandishments or threats of his father or uncle. As a young man he came to Bologna for the sake of studies; where, called by the Holy Spirit to a form of higher life, he embraced the institute of the Order of Preachers.

Philip, born at Bethsaida, one of the twelve Apostles, who were the first called by Christ the Lord: by him, when Nathanael had been told that the Messiah promised in the Law had come, he was brought to the Lord. How familiarly Christ made use of him is easily shown by the fact that the Gentiles who desired to see the Savior came to Philip; and the Lord, when he wished to feed a multitude of men in a desert place, addressed Philip thus: Where shall we buy bread for these to eat? Having received the Holy Spirit, when Scythia had fallen to him for the preaching of the Gospel, he converted nearly the whole of that people to the Christian faith. Finally, when he had come to Hierapolis in Phrygia, he was fastened to a cross and overwhelmed with stones for the name of Christ, on the Kalends of May. His body was buried there by Christians, and was afterward brought to Rome and interred in the basilica of the twelve Apostles together with the body of the blessed Apostle James.

Philip, born of the noble Benizi family at Florence, was called by a singular vision by the most Blessed Virgin into the family of her Servants, recently founded. He first withdrew into a cave of Mount Senario, where he led a life austere indeed through continual bodily mortification, but made sweet by meditation on the sufferings of Christ the Lord; thence he founded brotherhoods of the Seven Sorrows of the Mother of God through nearly all of Europe and a great part of Asia. Appointed General of his Order though unwilling, deeply inflamed with the ardor of divine charity, he passed through very many cities of Italy, settling the growing civic discords among them, recalling many to obedience to the Roman Pontiff, and leading the most abandoned men to penance. Finally at Todi, in the year twelve hundred and eighty-five, in the embrace of Christ the Lord hanging upon the Cross — which he called his book — he departed most holily from this life. Clement X, Supreme Pontiff, enrolled him in the number of the Saints.

Philip Neri, born of pious and honest parents at Florence, having refused the ample inheritance of his uncle, betook himself to Rome; where, educated in philosophy and sacred letters, he dedicated himself wholly to Christ. Made a priest out of obedience, he was entirely devoted to the procuring of the salvation of souls, and persevering in hearing confessions to the very last day, he begot for Christ almost innumerable spiritual children; desiring that they be nourished by the daily food of the word of God, the frequent reception of the sacraments, assiduous prayer, and other devout exercises, he founded the Congregation of the Oratory. His heart, wounded by the charity of God, burned with so great an ardor that, when it could not be contained within its bounds, the Lord marvelously enlarged its cavity, with two ribs broken and lifted up. He was illustrious by the gift of prophecy, and shone wonderfully in penetrating the sentiments of souls. He preserved his virginity perpetually undefiled; and this he attained: that those who cultivated chastity he could discern by a fragrance, and those who did otherwise by a foulness. In the year of salvation fifteen hundred and ninety-five, at the age of eighty, he fell asleep in the Lord.

Philip, born of the noble Benizi family at Florence, gave signs of his future holiness even from the cradle. For scarcely had he entered the fifth month of his age when he loosed his tongue into speech in a wondrous manner and urged his mother to give alms to the Servants of the Mother of God. As a young man, while at Paris he joined the ardor of piety to his literary studies, he inflamed very many with a longing for the heavenly homeland. Having returned to his homeland, and called by a singular vision by the most Blessed Virgin into the family of her Servants recently founded, he withdrew into a cave of Mount Senario, where he led a life austere indeed through continual bodily mortification, but made sweet by meditation on the sufferings of Christ the Lord: and thence through nearly all of Europe and a great part of Asia, which he traversed with evangelical preaching, he founded brotherhoods of the Seven Sorrows of the Mother of God, and propagated his Order by outstanding example of virtues.

Philip Neri, born of pious and honest parents at Florence, gave from his very earliest age clear signs of his future holiness. As a young man, having refused the ample inheritance of his uncle, he betook himself to Rome; where, educated in philosophy and sacred letters, he dedicated himself wholly to Christ. Such was his abstinence that he sometimes remained fasting for three days. Intent on vigils and prayers, frequently visiting the seven churches of the City, he was accustomed to spend the night near the cemetery of Callistus in the contemplation of heavenly things. Made a priest out of obedience, he was entirely devoted to the procuring of the salvation of souls; and persevering in hearing confessions to the very last day, he begot for Christ almost innumerable spiritual children; desiring that they be nourished by the daily food of the word of God, the frequent reception of the sacraments, assiduous prayer, and other devout exercises, he founded the Congregation of the Oratory.

Having obtained the fulfillment of his pious petitions, a signal contemner of the world and of himself, from the very first days of his novitiate, and yet more when with the joy of the spirit he had made his solemn profession of vows to the Lord, he was an object of admiration and example to all in regular observance. Above all devoted to prayer and sacred letters, and excelling with singular grace also in the ministry of the word, he drew not only Catholics to a better life, but also those of other confessions to knowledge of the truth. Appointed prior of a monastery in several places, he exercised the charge entrusted to him with prudence, justice, meekness, discretion, and the praise of humility. An outstanding zealot of most strict poverty, he completely eliminated from the monastery whatever seemed even slightly unnecessary. Between austere fasts, vigils, and disciplines, pursuing himself with a saving hatred, he showed toward others the love a mother shows her children. When a pestilential fever was grievously afflicting the Austrian military forces, he devoted himself with his whole spirit to the assiduous works of charity for the most extreme needs of the sick. And in composing the discords of souls and in alleviating other necessities of his neighbor by counsel and deed, he conducted himself so outstandingly that he merited to be called the father of his country.

Pius, born at Bosco in Lombardy, entered the Order of Preachers at the age of fourteen. Raised to the priesthood, he preached to the people in several places with the greatest fruit for souls. He long and bravely and laudably sustained the office of inquisitor, and having been promoted by Paul IV to the bishopric of Nepi and Sutri, after two years he was enrolled among the cardinal fathers. Transferred by Pius IV to the church of Mondovì in Piedmont, he visited his diocese and suppressed abuses; and returning to Rome, he was occupied in expediting the most serious affairs. Upon the death of Pius IV, he was elected Pontiff contrary to all expectation, and changed nothing in his manner of life except his external habit. Against Selim, tyrant of the Turks, having assembled a great fleet, he conquered him at the Echinades Islands not so much by arms as by prayers poured out. While he was preparing a new expedition against the same Turks, he died most devoutly in the Lord in the year fifteen hundred and seventy-two, in the sixty-eighth year of his age. His body is venerated with the greatest devotion of the faithful in the basilica of Saint Mary Major. Pope Clement XI enrolled him in the catalog of the Saints.

Pius, first of that name, a native of Aquileia, son of Rufinus, was created Supreme Pontiff of the Holy Roman Church from the presbyterate, under the august emperors Antoninus Pius and Marcus Aurelius. In five ordinations, in the month of December, he created twelve bishops and eighteen priests.

Pius, first of that name, a native of Aquileia, son of Rufinus, was created Supreme Pontiff of the Holy Roman Church from the presbyterate, under the august emperors Antoninus Pius and Marcus Aurelius. In five ordinations, in the month of December, he created twelve bishops and eighteen priests. There remain some things admirably instituted by him, especially that the Resurrection of the Lord should be celebrated only on the Lord's day. He converted the house of Pudens into a church, and on account of its pre-eminence above all other titles — as the residence of the Roman Pontiff — he dedicated it to the title of the Good Shepherd; and in it he often celebrated the sacred rites, and baptized many who had been converted to the faith and enrolled them in the number of the faithful. While he was exercising the office of the good shepherd, he was crowned with martyrdom by shedding his blood for his sheep and for the supreme Shepherd Christ, on the fifth day before the Ides of July, and buried in the Vatican.

Pius of Aquileia, created Pontiff under the Emperor Marcus Antoninus Verus, established a penalty upon any priest through whose negligence anything of the Lord's Blood should drip. For, he said, let them do penance forty days if anything falls on the ground; three days if it falls on the altar; four days if it flows onto the upper linen cloth; nine days if it flows down to the lower; twenty days if it falls to the fourth cloth: wherever it may fall, if it can be recovered, let it be licked up; if not, let it be washed or scraped off; whatever has been washed or scraped off shall be burned, and the ashes placed in the sacrarium. Appointed by many other useful decrees, he was crowned with martyrdom and buried in the Vatican on the fifth day before the Ides of July; having sat for eleven years, two months, and twenty-one days, and having in five ordinations in December created ten bishops, nine priests, and twenty-one deacons.

Pius, first of that name, a native of Aquileia, son of Rufinus, was created Supreme Pontiff of the Holy Roman Church from the presbyterate, under the august emperors Antoninus Pius and Marcus Aurelius. In five ordinations, in the month of December, he created twelve bishops and eighteen priests. There remain some things admirably instituted by him, especially that the Resurrection of the Lord should be celebrated only on the Lord's day — which was afterward confirmed by his successors the Roman Pontiffs, whose chief concern it was that all the bishops of the whole Church should be in agreement in the paschal celebration.

Pius, born in the town of Lombardy called Bosco, but of Bolognese origin from the noble family of Ghislieri, entered the Order of Preachers at the age of fourteen. In him there was an admirable patience, a profound humility, a supreme austerity of life, a continual devotion to prayer, and a most ardent zeal for regular observance and the honor of God. Devoting himself to philosophy and theology, he excelled in them so greatly that he exercised the office of teaching them with great distinction for many years. He preached to the people in several places with the greatest fruit for his hearers. He sustained with inviolable fortitude of soul the office of inquisitor for a long time; and he kept many cities safe from the heresy then spreading, not without danger to his own life.

Pope Pius X, whose name before had been Joseph Sarto, was born in the Venetian village called Riese, of humble parents indeed, but conspicuous for uprightness and piety. Enrolled among the pupils of the Paduan Seminary, he advanced so greatly in piety and learning that he was an example to his fellow students and a source of wonder to his superiors. Ordained a priest, he labored for several years in the town of Tombolo first as curate and then at Salzano as pastor; and in the exercise of these offices he so excelled in such outpouring of charity, such priestly zeal, and such holiness of life, that the Bishop of Treviso enrolled him among the canons of the cathedral church, and appointed him chancellor of the episcopal curia and at the same time spiritual director of the diocesan seminary. Having fulfilled these offices so outstandingly, he was appointed by Leo XIII — to whom he was most highly regarded — as Prelate of the church of Mantua.

Pope Pius the Tenth, whose name had previously been Joseph Sarto, was born in a village of the Veneto called Riese. Enrolled among the students of the Paduan Seminary and advanced to the priesthood, he labored first in the town of Tombolo as assistant curate, then at Salzano as parish priest, and at Treviso as canon and chancellor of the episcopal curia, excelling so greatly that Leo the Thirteenth appointed him head of the Church of Mantua. Neglecting no part of the good shepherd's duty, he labored especially to give proper formation to the young called to the Lord's portion; he promoted the beauty of divine worship and the growth of pious associations; and with lavish charity he provided for the needs of the poor. With so many merits recommending him, he was numbered among the cardinals and created Patriarch of Venice. After the death of Leo the Thirteenth, when the votes of the cardinal fathers converged upon him, he accepted the Supreme Pontificate, resisting in vain, as a cross. Placed upon the chair of Peter, he yielded nothing of his former manner of life. He shone especially in humility, simplicity, and poverty. He governed the Church firmly and adorned her with most distinguished ordinances. A most vigilant guardian of the faith, he condemned and crushed Modernism, the sum of all heresies; a most zealous defender of ecclesiastical liberty, he boldly resisted those who sought to undermine it; he provided for the solid formation of the clergy; he reduced the laws of the Church into one body; and he most earnestly promoted devotion to the Eucharist and its more frequent reception. Broken by labors and worn down by grief over the European war then breaking out, he took flight to his heavenly homeland on the twentieth day of August in the year one thousand nine hundred and fourteen. Pope Pius the Twelfth enrolled him in the number of the Saints.

Placid, born in Rome of Tertullus, a man of the highest nobility, was offered to God as a child and entrusted to Saint Benedict; by his teaching and the rule of the monastic life, Placid made such progress as to be numbered among his foremost disciples. Sent by him to Sicily, he built a monastery and a church in honor of Saint John the Baptist near the port of Messina, where he lived with his monks in admirable holiness. When Eutychius and Victorinus, his brothers, and Flavia, his virgin sister, had come there to visit him, at that same time a certain savage pirate named Manucha sailed in; and, having seized the monastery, when he could by no means prevail upon Placid and the others to deny Christ, he ordered Placid, his brothers, and his sister to be cruelly slain. Together with them, Donatus, Firmatus the deacon, Faustus, and some thirty other monks also happily completed the contest of martyrdom on the fifth day of October in the year of salvation five hundred and thirty-nine.

He spread the Order of Clerks Regular in several places and established their residences in Milan and Piacenza. Saint Charles Borromeo and Paul of Arezzo, a Clerk Regular, both cardinals, to whom he was most dear, employed his assistance in the cares of their pastoral office. He cherished the Virgin Mother of God with singular love and devotion. He merited to enjoy the conversation of Angels, whom, while he was reciting the divine praises, he testified to have heard singing responsively on the other side. Finally, after heroic examples of virtue, distinguished also with the gift of prophecy, by which he foresaw the secrets of hearts, things absent, and things to come, broken by years and labors, as he was about to celebrate at the altar in those words repeated a third time, "I will go to the altar of God," he was suddenly struck by apoplexy; soon fortified with the sacraments in due form, he breathed forth his soul most peacefully among his own. His body is venerated in Naples in the church of Saint Paul to this day, with that most frequent concourse of the people with which it was borne out. Pope Clement the Eleventh, in solemn rite, enrolled him, illustrious by distinguished miracles in life and after death, in the catalogue of the Saints.

Let Mary now rejoice with instruments, and let the tambourines of the mother newly delivered sound among swift-moving fingers. Let rejoicing choirs sing together, and let sweet-sounding songs be mingled with alternating melodies. Hear, therefore, how our timbrel-player has sung; for she says: "My soul magnifies the Lord, and my spirit has rejoiced in God my Savior, because he has looked upon the humility of his handmaid: for behold, from henceforth all generations shall call me blessed. Because he who is mighty has done great things for me." The miracle of a new birth, therefore, overcame the cause of the prevailing error; and the song of Mary drove out the lamentation of Eve.

Pontianus, a Roman, governed the Church under the Emperor Alexander; who banished the holy Pontiff to the island of Sardinia together with the priest Hippolytus on account of his confession of the Christian faith. There, afflicted by many calamities for the faith of Christ, he departed this life on the third day before the Kalends of November. His body was brought to Rome by Pope Fabian together with the clergy and was buried in the cemetery of Callixtus on the Appian Way. He held the see for four years, four months, and twenty-five days. He held two ordinations in the month of December, in which he created six priests, five deacons, and six bishops for various places.

Furthermore, Heli, who was of the tribe of Nathan, having begotten no children, departed this life; and for this reason Jacob, his brother, who had descended from the tribe of Solomon, took his wife and raised up seed for his brother and begot Joseph. Joseph, therefore, was by nature the son of Jacob, descended from Solomon; but according to the law he had as his father Heli, descended from Nathan. Such being the case, Joachim took that most excellent and praiseworthy woman Anna to wife. But just as that ancient Anna, when she suffered from the disease of barrenness, brought forth Samuel through prayer and promise, so also this woman in like manner received the Mother of God from God through supplication and promise, so that here too she should yield to none among the illustrious matrons. Thus "Grace" — for that is what the name Anna means — gives birth to "the Lady" — for that is what the name Mary signifies. For she was truly made the Lady of all created things, when she became the Mother of the Creator.
