Furthermore, when those holy men had joined to themselves more companions, they began to travel through the cities and towns of Italy, especially of Etruria, preaching Christ crucified everywhere, restraining civil discords, and calling back almost countless straying souls to the path of virtue. Nor did they cultivate Italy alone, but also Gaul, Germany, and Poland with their evangelical labors. Finally, when they had spread the good fragrance of Christ far and wide, distinguished also by the glory of miracles, they passed to the Lord. But those whom one love of true brotherhood and religion had united in life, a single tomb covered alike after death, and the veneration of the people followed them together. Wherefore Popes Clement the Eleventh and Benedict the Thirteenth confirmed the undivided cult rendered to them by many generations; and Leo the Thirteenth, after previously approving their miracles, and after the veneration granted for miracles wrought by God in response to their collective invocation, crowned them with the honors of the Saints in the fiftieth year of his priesthood, and ordained that their memory be commemorated each year throughout the whole Church with Office and Mass.

Furthermore, she shone before the sisters consecrated to God as a true example of submission and all the virtues. She never took more rest, yet no less labor than the others. She extended her vigils, prayers, and reading of sacred things far into the night, and rested only upon a bed of haircloth. Therefore, after fifteen years spent in those labors and the exercise of the virtues, she was called by the Lord to eternal rest; and he illustrated the holiness of her life with frequent miracles. For while alive she extinguished a fire in the convent by the sign of the cross, and after death she cured very many who were afflicted with various diseases and came piously to her tomb. Her sacred body is kept reverently enshrined in the basilica of Saints Peter and Paul at Bamberg.

Furthermore, the Vatican basilica, long since falling into ruin with age and therefore rebuilt from its foundations more broadly and magnificently through the piety of many Pontiffs, was consecrated by Urban the Eighth in solemn rite on this same recurring day in the year one thousand six hundred and twenty-six. But the basilica of Ostia, after a terrible force of fire had utterly consumed it in the year one thousand eight hundred and twenty-three, was rebuilt more splendidly than before through the tireless care of four Pontiffs, and as it were snatched back from destruction; and Pius the Ninth, having obtained the most auspicious occasion when the dogma of the Immaculate Conception of the Blessed Virgin Mary, recently proclaimed by him, had drawn to Rome a great number of cardinals and bishops from even the most distant regions of the Catholic world, solemnly dedicated it on the tenth day of December in the year one thousand eight hundred and fifty-four, surrounded by so great a company of cardinalatial fathers and prelates, and decreed that the memory of its dedication be commemorated on this day.

Furthermore, this virtue is called singular and of a single kind, possessing within itself the beauty of the various virtues. A royal diadem cannot be woven and fashioned without precious stones and gleaming pearls; so too this singular virtue cannot stand without the radiance of the various virtues. For it is indeed most like a royal diadem. For as with a diadem, if one stone or pearl is missing, it cannot shine fully upon the royal head; so too this singular virtue, unless it is adorned with the honor of the other virtues, is not called a perfect virtue. It is likewise similar to the most precious foods, prepared with the most exquisite seasonings, but lacking salt. For just as those precious foods cannot be eaten without salt; so too this uniform virtue, even if it is adorned with the glory and honor of the various virtues, yet if the love of God and neighbor be absent, is utterly base and contemptible.

After the raven's departure, Paul said: "Come, the Lord has sent us our meal — truly he is holy, truly merciful. Sixty years have already passed since I receive each day half a loaf of bread; now for your coming Christ has doubled the ration for his soldiers." Therefore, giving thanks, they took their food at the fountain; and when they had refreshed themselves for a little while, and had given thanks to God in the customary manner, they spent the night in the divine praises. At dawn, Paul warned Anthony of the death that was now at hand for him, and urged him to bring the cloak which he had received from Athanasius, to wrap his body in. As Anthony was returning from this journey, he saw the soul of Paul ascending to heaven amid the choirs of Angels, amid the companies of Prophets and Apostles.

After a praiseworthy youth well spent, he began from his study of heavenly contemplation to think about the solitary life; yet he first wished to be initiated into Holy Orders, in order to cut off from himself all hope of the kingdom, from whose succession by the right of the Salic law he was not far removed. Having become a priest and celebrated his first Mass most devoutly, he withdrew before long into the desert, where, living on the strictest abstinence, he was nourished by an abundance of heavenly gifts. There he lived most holily for some years with Saint John of Matha, a Parisian doctor, who had sought and found him by divine inspiration; until both, warned by an Angel from God, made their way to Rome to obtain from the Supreme Pontiff a special rule of life. When therefore a revelation was made to Pope Innocent the Third during the solemnity of Mass concerning the religious life and the institution for the redemption of captives, the Pontiff himself clothed him, together with his companion, in white garments marked with a two-colored cross, after the form in which the Angel had appeared clothed. And moreover the Pontiff wished that the new religious order, according to the triple color of which the habit is composed, should be honored with the title of the Most Holy Trinity.

After the Ascension of Jesus Christ into heaven, he preached his divinity in Judea and Samaria and led very many to the Christian faith. Setting out then for Spain, he there converted some to Christ; from their number seven were afterwards ordained bishops by Blessed Peter and sent as the first to Spain. Returning then to Jerusalem, after he had imbued among others Hermogenes the magician with the truth of the faith, Herod Agrippa, exalted to the kingdom under the Emperor Claudius in order to gain favor from the Jews, condemned James, who freely confessed Jesus Christ as God, to death. When the man who had led him to the tribunal saw him boldly undergoing martyrdom, he immediately professed himself also to be a Christian.

After the great victory which the Emperor Constantine, having received by divine gift the sign of the Lord's Cross, gained over Maxentius, Helena, Constantine's mother, admonished in a dream, came to Jerusalem with zeal to search for the Cross; where she caused to be overturned a marble statue of Venus, placed by the Gentiles in the site of the Cross to destroy the memory of Christ the Lord's Passion, after about one hundred and eighty years. She did the same at the manger of the Savior and at the place of the Resurrection, removing from the one the image of Adonis and from the other that of Jupiter.

After three days, the Archangel Michael admonished the bishop that that place was under his protection, and by that sign had shown that he wished divine worship to be offered there in memory of him and of the Angels. Wherefore the bishop, together with the citizens, set out to go to that cave. And when they had seen it fashioned after the likeness of a temple, they began to celebrate divine offices in that place, which was afterwards made illustrious by many miracles. And not long after, Pope Boniface dedicated a church of Saint Michael in the great circus at Rome on the third day before the Kalends of October; on which day also the Church celebrates the memory of all the Angels. But the present day is consecrated by the apparition of the Archangel Michael.

Going afterwards to Salamanca for the sake of studies, enrolled in the celebrated college of Saint Bartholomew, he so exercised the priestly office as to pursue his desired studies at the same time and also to be constantly engaged in sacred preaching. When he had fallen into a most grave illness, he bound himself by a vow of stricter discipline; and to fulfill it, having first given to a certain poor man who was nearly naked the better of only two garments he possessed, he betook himself to the monastery of Saint Augustine, then flourishing especially in severe discipline: admitted there, he surpassed his elders in obedience, humility of soul, vigils, and prayer. When the care of the refectory was entrusted to him, a small cask of wine, at his touch, sufficed abundantly for all the monks throughout a year. After the year of novitiate, at the superior's command he undertook the office of preaching. At Salamanca at that time, all things divine and human were so confounded by bloody factions that murders took place at nearly every hour, and not only the streets and squares but even the churches overflowed with the blood of men of every rank, and especially of the nobility.

On the following day all were cast to the wild beasts in the amphitheater; but they, forgetting their natural ferocity, prostrated themselves at the feet of Januarius. Timothy, attributing this to magic incantations, when he had pronounced the sentence of death upon Christ's Martyrs, was suddenly struck blind; but soon, at the prayer of blessed Januarius, he received his sight again; by which miracle about five thousand men embraced the faith of Christ. Yet the ungrateful judge, made no more placated by this benefit, but driven into a rage by the conversion of so great a multitude, and fearing above all the decrees of the rulers, ordered the holy Bishop and his companions to be slain by the sword.

When therefore the new man Francis became renowned by a new and astonishing miracle, adorned with a singular privilege not granted to ages past, namely, adorned with the sacred Stigmata, he descended from the mountain carrying with him the image of the Crucified, not drawn by the hand of an artist on tablets of stone or wood, but inscribed by the finger of the living God upon his members of flesh. Since the seraphic man, knowing well that it is good to conceal the secret of a king, and conscious of the royal secret, hid those sacred marks with all his strength. Yet, because it belongs to God to reveal for his own glory the great things he does, the Lord himself, who had secretly impressed those marks, openly showed certain miracles through them; so that their hidden and wondrous power might be manifest in the brightness of signs. — Furthermore, the admirable event, so widely attested and exalted with highest praises and favors in pontifical documents, Pope Benedict the Eleventh wished to be celebrated with an annual solemnity; which Pope Paul the Fifth, Supreme Pontiff, afterwards extended to the whole Church, that the hearts of the faithful might be enkindled in love of Christ crucified.

On the day following, which was the fifteenth day before the Kalends of August, the seven brothers were individually bound to a stake and killed in various ways. Crescentius had his throat pierced with iron; Julian had his chest stabbed; Nemesius had his heart run through; Primitivus was pierced through the navel; Justinus was cut limb from limb; Stacteus was pierced with arrows; Eugenius was split from the chest into two parts. Thus eight most acceptable victims were sacrificed to God. Their bodies were thrown into a very deep pit on the Tiburtine Way, nine miles from the city; and these were afterwards translated to Rome and placed in the church of Saint Michael in the fish market.

A boy of brilliant character, Godehardus, born in Bavaria near the monastery of Altaich of Christian parents, was handed over to the same monastery to be educated in literary studies. There he made such progress in sacred studies and in piety alike, and showed himself to be such a man, that he merited to be not only initiated into Holy Orders, but also to be elected, by the common consent of the brethren, as pastor and abbot of that same monastery. So faithfully did he preside over the monastery, serving God in holiness and righteousness, that he expressed in himself the most exact rule of religious living, and was an object of admiration to all by the frequency and assiduity of his vigils, prayers, and fasts, and by the great austerity of his life.

Thomas, the most blessed man, the splendor of the Christian world and the light of the Church, born of noble parents, Landulf count of Aquino and Theodora of Naples, showed even as an infant his future devotion to the Mother of God. For a little parchment which he found, on which the Angelic Salutation was written, he firmly held clenched in his hand despite the nurse's vain effort to take it, sought back with weeping and gesture when violently snatched away by his mother, and swallowed it as soon as it was returned. At the age of five he was entrusted to the Benedictine monks of Montecassino to be kept. Sent then to Naples for the sake of studies, he as a young man embraced the Order of Friars Preachers. But when his mother and brothers took this badly, he was sent to Paris. His brothers seized him on the journey by force and brought him to the fortress of the castle of San Giovanni; where, harassed in various ways to make him change his holy resolve, he put to flight with a firebrand even a woman who had been introduced to undermine his constancy. Soon the blessed young man, kneeling in prayer before the sign of the Cross and there overtaken by sleep, seemed in his rest to feel his loins girded by Angels; and from that time he was ever after free from every movement of lust. His sisters, who had come to the castle to dissuade him from his holy purpose, he persuaded to put aside worldly cares and devote themselves to the practice of heavenly life.

Diligently devoting himself to the preaching of the word of God, he traversed almost all of Italy; in which ministry he led back to the path of salvation by the power of his words and the frequency of miracles almost countless souls. Martin the Fifth appointed him inquisitor to suppress the sect of the Fraticelli. Appointed by Nicholas the Fifth as general inquisitor against Jews and Saracens in Italy, he converted very many to the faith of Christ. In the East he ordered many things excellently, and at the Council of Florence, where he shone as a kind of sun, he restored the Armenians to the Catholic Church. The same Pontiff, at the request of the Emperor Frederick the Third, sent him as legate of the Apostolic See to Germany, to call heretics back to the Catholic faith and the minds of princes to concord. In Germany and other provinces he wondrously increased the glory of God through six years of ministry, bringing innumerable Hussites, Adamites, Taborites, and Hebrews to the bosom of the Church by the truth of doctrine and the light of miracles.

The preachers of our law, therefore — both those who first brought faith and the Gospel to us, and those whom God afterwards raised up in each succeeding age to confirm or spread that same faith — the whole world knows what manner of men they were, how holy, how just, how religious. Behold first the Apostles. What is more sublime or more excellent than the apostolic character? Behold next those holy men whom we call the Fathers and Doctors — those most brilliant lights which God willed to shine in the firmament of the Church, that all the darkness of heretics might be scattered by them: men such as Irenaeus, Cyprian, Hilary, Athanasius, Basil, the two Gregories, Ambrose, Jerome, Augustine, Chrysostom, Cyril. Do not their lives and characters shine forth as in certain mirrors in those monuments which they have left to us? For out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks.

Besides these, he built two basilicas in the City, adorned with sacred paintings: one near the Roman Forum, the other on the Flaminian Way. He built three cemeteries: one on the same Flaminian Way, another on the Aurelian Way, a third on the Portensian Way. He decreed that a priest should plead his cause nowhere but before an ecclesiastical judge, and ordered that all instruments pertaining to ecclesiastical matters be drawn up by the protonotary. In three ordinations in the month of December he created three deacons, eighteen priests, and nine bishops. After governing God's Church most holily for fifteen years, five months, and seventeen days, he happily passed to the Lord on the day before the Ides of April, and was buried in the cemetery of Calepodius. From there his relics were translated to the church of Saint Mary across the Tiber, which he himself had enlarged, and were honorably laid to rest beneath the high altar.

Beyond the daily care of the churches, he never relaxed his spirit unconquered in prayer. For they say that he was accustomed to recite the entire Psalter daily, together with the Canticles and Hymns and two hundred prayers, to adore God three hundred times each day on bended knees, and to fortify himself with the sign of the cross a hundred times at every canonical hour of the day. Dividing the night into three periods, he spent the first in going through a hundred Psalms and genuflecting two hundred times, the second in completing the remaining fifty Psalms, immersed in icy waters and with heart, eyes, and hands lifted up to heaven; and the third he gave over to scanty rest, stretched out upon a bare stone. An outstanding cultivator of humility, after the apostolic manner he did not abstain from the labor of his own hands. At last, consumed by unceasing cares for the Church, distinguished in word and deed, refreshed by the divine mysteries in extreme old age, he fell asleep in the Lord and was buried at Down in Ulster in the fifth century of the Christian era.

Beyond the rough garment, broken by the hairshirt, vigils, and labors, and worn down by continual fasts, she also lacerated her body with frequent stripes and bundles of thorns, sometimes borrowing the arm of another nun to inflict greater affliction upon her own body; and to wear it down more and more, she used a cot of planks furnished with only a cheap mat, and employed a stone for a pillow — which at the direction of obedience she exchanged for straw — on which, with one foot or the other chained to the Cross placed before her, she took the briefest sleep. Beyond this, she did not refuse to chew wormwood and the most bitter herbs, to kiss the ulcers of the nuns and rags soaked in pus; she was at times accustomed to climb the stairs of the monastery on her knees, burdened with a great cross; she also used nettles, melted wax, at times snow and ice, at times troughs of freezing water for her mortification. During Holy Week and each Friday she was accustomed to imitate, with a series of the most atrocious punishments aptly devised by herself, the Passion of Christ the Lord, which she venerated above all things. Patience in enduring injuries, Christian humility, virginal modesty, and the greatest diligence in leading the novices over whom she presided toward perfection shone wondrously in her. Enkindled also by zeal for souls, she ended many enmities; she placed imperiled young women in safety, bringing very many back to a better way of life; and she applied herself unceasingly with every effort — by prayers as well as by voluntary bodily torments — to procuring the salvation of her neighbors.

Furthermore, blessed are all who, ascending this ladder of Jacob, distinguished in its upper steps by eight rungs, from this day forward take the ascent, having laid aside all impediments, so that they overcome daily the capital enemies — the world, the flesh, and Satan — and make progress in the study of the virtues toward blessed immortality. Yet far more blessed are those who have brought their fighting and overcoming to an end and, the labor of the ascent itself completed, have reached the crown of the contest and now, as soldiers discharged and emerited, possess the highest rest and dwell in the heavenly tabernacle, laden with the most ample reward. Nor is there any doubt that the holy Martyrs and the holy Doctors flourish above the other elect throughout perpetual ages, for on account of their heroic virtues they will receive by a special privilege the aureole, as the Theologians call it — the excellent and pre-eminent laurel crown.

Praxedes, a Roman virgin, sister of the virgin Pudentiana, while the Emperor Marcus Antoninus was persecuting the Christians, ministered to them with her resources, labor, consolation, and every office of charity. For she hid some in her home; she exhorted others to constancy in the faith; she buried the bodies of others; and she was lacking in nothing to those who were shut up in prison and those who toiled in the workhouses. When she could no longer bear such a slaughter of Christians, she prayed to God that, if it were expedient for her to die, he would rescue her from such great evils. And so on the twelfth day before the Kalends of August she was called to heaven to receive the rewards of her piety. Her body was brought by the priest Pastor to the tomb of her father and her sister Pudentiana, which was in the cemetery of Priscilla on the Salarian Way.

The first flower of sanctity in South America, the virgin Rose, born of Christian parents at Lima, gave evidence from the very cradle of her future holiness; for the face of the infant, transformed miraculously into the likeness of a rose, gave occasion for this name. Lest she be forced by her parents into marriage, she secretly cut off her own most beautiful hair. The austerity of her life was singular. Taking upon herself the habit of the Third Order of Saint Dominic, she pressed hard upon the arduous footsteps of Saint Catherine of Siena. For fifteen years, pining most miserably for several hours each day in desolation of spirit and aridity, she bravely bore struggles more bitter than any death. Made wonderfully familiar, amid frequent apparitions, with her guardian Angel, with Saint Catherine of Siena, and with the Virgin Mother of God, she merited to hear from Christ these words: "Rose of my heart, be my spouse." Illustrious by many miracles both before and after death, Pope Clement the Tenth enrolled her in the catalogue of the holy Virgins.

The first flower of sanctity in South America, the virgin Rose, born of Christian parents at Lima, gave evidence from the very cradle of her future holiness. For the face of the infant, transformed miraculously into the likeness of a rose, gave occasion for this name; to which the Virgin Mother of God afterwards added a surname, commanding her henceforth to be called Rose of Saint Mary. At the age of five she made a vow of perpetual virginity. When she was older, lest she be forced by her parents into marriage, she secretly cut off her own most beautiful head of hair. Dedicated to fasts beyond human measure, she passed entire Lents abstaining from bread, and living daily on only five kernels of citron.

The brothers Primus and Felicianus, accused of the Christian religion in the persecution of Diocletian and Maximian, were cast into chains; but being freed from them, they were snatched away from there by an Angel. Soon brought before the praetor, as they were defending the Christian faith most strenuously, they were separated from each other; and first the constancy of Felicianus was tested in various ways. But when those who urged impiety despaired of being able to achieve anything by words, they nailed his hands and feet to a stake and left him hanging there for three days without food or drink. On the following day the praetor summoned Primus to him and addressed him thus: "Do you see how much more prudent your brother is than you? He has obeyed the emperors and is honored by them. If you too are willing to imitate him, you shall be a sharer in his honor and favor." To this Primus replied: "What happened to my brother I have learned from an Angel. Would that, as I am most closely united to him in will, I may not be separated from him even in martyrdom." At these words the praetor was inflamed with rage and, in addition to the other tortures he had inflicted on Primus, ordered, with Felicianus now present, molten lead to be poured into his mouth. Soon he ordered both to be led into the theater, and two lions to be set upon them; but the lions, prostrating themselves at their knees, fawned upon them with head and tail. When more than twelve thousand men had assembled for this spectacle, five hundred together with their families embraced the Christian religion. Moved by these things, the praetor ordered them to be slain with the axe.

The first of his order, on account of the excellence of his learning, he lectured on sacred scripture at Bologna and elsewhere, and presided over the studies of his brethren. After traveling through many provinces, he came in the year before his death to Padua, where he left illustrious monuments of his holiness. Finally, having performed great labors for the glory of God, renowned for his merits and miracles, he fell asleep in the Lord on the Ides of June in the year of salvation one thousand two hundred and thirty-one. Gregory the Ninth, Supreme Pontiff, enrolled him in the number of the holy Confessors; and Pius the Twelfth, by decree of the Sacred Congregation of Rites, declared him Doctor of the universal Church.

Declining with the greatest humility from the beginning the homage of those who consulted him as an oracle, he refused to be confessor to the Emperor Charles the Fifth. A most rigorous guardian of poverty, he was content with a single tunic, the worst of any there was. He cultivated purity to such a degree that he would not allow himself to be even slightly touched by the brother who was serving him in his last illness. He reduced his body to servitude by perpetual vigils, fasts, scourgings, cold, nakedness, and every kind of austerity; with his body he had entered into a pact that he would give it no rest in this world. The charity of God and neighbor, poured forth in his heart, at times kindled so great a fire that he was compelled to leap out from the narrowness of his cell into the open field, and to temper the ardor he had conceived by the refreshment of the air.

Prisca, a noble Roman virgin, thirteen years old, accused of the Christian faith under the Emperor Claudius, was led by his command to the temple of Apollo to offer sacrifice to the idols; when she abhorred the deed, she was struck with slaps and handed over to prison. Released from there, when she persevered in the constancy of her faith, she was afflicted with stripes and smeared with boiling fat, and was shut up again in prison. After three days she was brought into the amphitheater and thrown to a lion; who, forgetting his ferocity, humbly cast himself at her feet. She was afterwards afflicted in the workhouse with three days of starvation, suspended on the rack, and her flesh torn by iron hooks, then thrown onto a pyre, from which too she miraculously escaped unharmed. Finally, beheaded outside the City, she crowned the palm of her virginity with the crown of martyrdom. Her body was buried by the Christians on the Ostian Way, ten miles from the City, on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of February.

Therefore, let us consider those very merits of the Apostle Paul, by reason of which he said that the just judge would render him the crown; and let us see whether his merits as his own — that is, acquired by him from himself — or whether they are gifts of God. "I have fought the good fight," he says, "I have finished the course, I have kept the faith." First, these good works, had they not been preceded by good thoughts, would not exist at all. Attend therefore to what he says about those very thoughts; for in writing to the Corinthians he says: "Not that we are sufficient to think anything of ourselves as from ourselves, but our sufficiency is from God." Let us then examine each point.

Setting out from there to Tarsus to look for Paul, he came with him to Antioch. Having stayed for a year in the church of that city, they gave to those people the precepts of the Christian faith and life; where also those who worshiped Jesus Christ were first called Christians. Moreover, the disciples of Paul and Barnabas supported the Christians who were in Judea from their own means, sending money there through Paul and Barnabas. These, having discharged that office of charity, returned to Antioch, taking with them John, whose surname was Mark.

It is truly beyond doubt that Christ did not in heaven deny — but rather fulfilled and perfected — the intimacy, reverence, and most sublime dignity which he showed him while he lived among men, as a son to his own father. Hence it is fittingly added by the Lord in the text before us: "Enter into the joy of your Lord." Hence, although the joy of eternal beatitude enters into the heart of man, the Lord nevertheless preferred to say to him, "Enter into the joy," so that it might be mystically suggested that that joy is not only within him, but encompasses him on all sides, absorbing him, and as an infinite abyss submerging him entirely. Be mindful of us, therefore, blessed Joseph, and by the aid of your prayer intercede with your reputed Son; but also make the most Blessed Virgin your spouse favorable to us — she who is the Mother of him who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns for endless ages of ages. Amen.

He was distinguished by the gift of prophecy, and shone wondrously in penetrating the innermost thoughts of souls. He preserved his virginity perpetually undefiled; and he attained this gift: that he could distinguish those who cultivated purity by their fragrance, and those who did otherwise by their stench. At times he appeared to those who were absent and brought them help when they were in danger. He restored very many sick and those near death to health. He also called the dead back to life. He was often deemed worthy of the apparition of heavenly spirits and of the Virgin Mother of God herself, and he saw the souls of very many ascending to heaven surrounded by splendor. Finally, in the year of salvation one thousand five hundred and ninety-five, on the eighth day before the Kalends of June, on which day the feast of Corpus Christi fell, having completed Mass with the greatest exultation of spirit and having discharged all other duties, in the hour which he had foretold after midnight, he fell asleep in the Lord at the age of eighty. Gregory the Fifteenth, illustrious in miracles, enrolled him in the number of the Saints.

Distinguished by the gift of prophecy, he foresaw by divine illumination many things about England's future state; and this above all is memorable: that he understood by divine inspiration, at the very moment it happened, the death of Swein, king of the Danes, drowned in the sea while boarding his fleet with the intention of invading England. He honored John the Evangelist wondrously, being accustomed to refuse nothing to anyone asked in his name. Once, when the saint begged alms from him in tattered garb in his own name and he had no coin, the king drew a ring from his finger and gave it to him; which the saint not long after sent back to Edward, together with a message foretelling his approaching death. Wherefore the king, having appointed prayers for himself, died most piously on the very day foretold by the Evangelist, namely the Nones of January in the year of salvation one thousand and sixty-six. Alexander the Third, Pope, in the following century enrolled him, illustrious in miracles, in the lists of the Saints. And Innocent the Eleventh commanded that his memory be celebrated by public Office throughout the whole Church on that day on which his body, translated thirty-six years after his death, was found incorrupt and breathing a sweet fragrance.

For this reason he addressed the people of the Jews, saying: "If you had believed Moses, you would believe me also; for he wrote of me." But since they persevered in contemning the commandment given through the most wise Moses, and in counting as nothing what was spoken through the holy prophets, they have been rightly estranged and cast out from the good things that were promised to their fathers. For obedience is better than sacrifice, and hearkening better than the fat of rams, as it is written; and so indeed it is with the King of the Jews. But for us, who have acknowledged his coming, all good things whatsoever will be present through him and in Christ himself. Through whom, and together with whom, be glory and power to God and the Father, with the Holy Spirit, for ages of ages. Amen.

For this reason the first woman was made from the side of the sleeping man, and was called life and the mother of the living. She signified a great good, before the great evil of transgression. This second Adam, bowing his head, slept upon the Cross, that from there his bride might be formed, she who flowed from the side of the sleeping one. O death, from which the dead revive! What is more pure than that blood? What is more salutary than that wound?
For these things were done, says the scripture, that the Scripture might be fulfilled: "You shall not break a bone of him." And again another Scripture says: "They shall look upon him whom they have pierced."

A son of David entirely, I say — not in flesh alone, but in faith, in holiness, in devotion: whom the Lord found as another David according to his own heart, to whom he could safely entrust the most secret and most sacred mystery of his heart; to whom as to another David he revealed the uncertain and hidden things of his wisdom; and gave it to him not to be ignorant of the mystery which none of the rulers of this age knew; to whom, finally, was given that which many kings and prophets, though they longed to see it, did not see; to hear and did not hear; not only to see and to hear, but also to carry, to lead, to embrace, to kiss, and to nourish and to guard.

Pudentiana, a virgin, daughter of Pudens the Roman, bereft of her parents, while she cultivated the Christian religion with admirable piety, distributed together with her sister Praxedes the money raised from the sale of their inheritance to the poor, and gave herself to fasts and prayers. By her agency also, her entire household — in which there were ninety-six persons — was baptized by Pope Pius. And because it had been decreed by the Emperor Antoninus that Christians should not offer sacrifice publicly, Pope Pius celebrated the sacred mysteries with the Christians in the lodgings of Pudentiana. She kindly received them and provided what was necessary for life. So she departed this life in these duties of Christian piety, and was buried in her father's tomb at the cemetery of Priscilla on the Salarian Way, on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of June.

This child, who is now called King of the Jews by the Magi, is himself the Creator and Lord of the Angels. Therefore, the omnipotence of the one you fear as judge you ought to fear far more than the infancy of the one who is born. Fear him not as the successor to your kingdom, but fear him as the most just condemner of your infidelity. "Go," he says, "and bring me word, so that I too may come and adore him." O feigned cunning, O impious unbelief, O fraudulent wickedness! The blood of the Innocents, which you cruelly poured out, bears witness to what you wished of this child.

Let us punish our sins with weeping and, with the voice of the Psalmist, let us come before his face with confession. Let therefore no deception of pleasures lead us astray, no empty joy seduce us. For the judge is near at hand, who said: "Woe to you who laugh now, for you shall mourn and weep." Hence Solomon says: "Laughter shall be mingled with grief," and, "Mourning takes hold of the extremity of joy." Hence he again says: "I counted laughter an error, and to joy I said: Why do you deceive in vain?" And again he says: "The heart of the wise is where there is sorrow, and the heart of fools where there is joy."

The little Zacchaeus, therefore, climbed the sycamore and saw the Lord: because those who humbly choose the foolishness of the world themselves contemplate God's wisdom with subtlety. For our littleness is impeded from seeing the Lord by the crowd: because the tumult of worldly cares presses down the weakness of the human mind, preventing it from directing its gaze toward the light of truth. But we climb the sycamore wisely if we hold in our minds with foresight that foolishness which is divinely commanded. For what in this world is more foolish than not to seek what has been lost, to let go to those who seize it what we possess, to render no injury in return for injuries received — and even, when others are added on top, to exhibit patience?

This was the reason why Constans sent to Italy the exarch Olympius, to arrange for Pope Martin to be slain or brought to him. Therefore Olympius, coming to Rome, ordered his bodyguard to kill the Pontiff while he was celebrating the solemnity of Mass in the basilica of Saint Mary at the Manger. But when the bodyguard made his attempt, he was suddenly struck blind.

Since therefore it was also a great matter, and the esteem for it was great among many, lest anyone, having achieved it, should think he had achieved everything and neglect the rest, he set down this parable — to show that virginity, though it possess all else, if it lacks the good of mercy, is cast out with fornicators. And rightly indeed does he rank the unmerciful and merciless woman with them; for the fornicator is conquered by lust for bodies, while these women are conquered by lust for money. The lust for bodies and the lust for money are not equal; that for bodies is far more violent and vehement. Inasmuch, therefore, as they struggle against a weaker foe, they are the less worthy of pardon if they are overcome. For this reason also he called them foolish — because, having overcome the greater contest, they lost everything in the easier one.

Since Justin had explained in his first Apology how Christians assembled to celebrate the Sacred Mysteries, and what were the mysteries of this sacred assembly, in order to refute the calumnies of the pagans; the governor examined him as to the place where he and the other Christians of this City assembled. Justin, however, keeping silent about the places of assembly so as not to betray the holy things and the brethren to dogs, indicated only his own dwelling, where he was accustomed to stay and to instruct his disciples, near the celebrated station of the Pastor in the house of Pudes. Finally, the governor gave him the option either to sacrifice to the gods or to endure being flogged throughout his whole body. When the unconquered defender of the faith declared that he had always had it in his desires to suffer torments for the Lord Jesus Christ, from whom he expected a great reward in heaven, the governor pronounced capital sentence against him. And so the admirable philosopher, praising God, after stripes, was crowned with glorious martyrdom by the shedding of his blood for Christ. Certain faithful secretly removed his body and buried it in a suitable place. Pope Leo the Thirteenth commanded that his Office and Mass be celebrated by the whole Church.

"For he shall be called a Nazarene." Had he set down a fixed example from the Scriptures, he would never have said: "What was spoken by the prophets," but simply: "What was spoken by the prophet." But now by using the plural "prophets," he shows that he did not take the very words from the Scriptures, but the sense. Nazarene is interpreted as "holy"; and the whole of Scripture records that the Lord was to be holy.

We inquire who this Zechariah, son of Barachiah, might be, since we read of many men named Zechariah. And lest a free capacity for error be granted us, it was added: "Whom you killed between the temple and the altar." In different sources we read different things, and I must set forth the opinions of each. Some say he is Zechariah the son of Barachiah, who is the eleventh of the twelve prophets, and in his case the father's name agrees; but the Scripture does not say where he was killed between the temple and the altar — especially since in his time the ruins of the temple had hardly yet come to be. Others wish Zechariah the father of John to be understood, confirming it by certain fancies from apocryphal books, that he was killed for this reason: that he had preached the coming of the Savior.

It is asked how the sons of Zebedee — namely, James and John — drank the chalice of martyrdom, since Scripture relates that only James the Apostle was beheaded by Herod, while John ended his life by a natural death. But if we read the ecclesiastical histories, in which it is recorded that he too was cast into a vessel of boiling oil on account of martyrdom, and proceeded thence as an athlete of Christ to receive the crown, and was immediately exiled to the island of Patmos; we shall see that the spirit for martyrdom was not lacking, and that John drank the chalice of confession — which the three young men also drank in the fiery furnace — even though the persecutor did not shed his blood.

When Paschasius questioned her, "Is the Holy Spirit in you?" she answered: "Those who live chastely and piously are temples of the Holy Spirit." At which he said: "I will order you to be taken to a brothel, that the Holy Spirit may leave you." The virgin replied: "If you order me to be violated against my will, my chastity will be doubled to me as a crown." Wherefore Paschasius, inflamed with rage, ordered Lucy to be dragged to the place where her virginity might be violated; but by divine power it came about that the steadfast virgin stood so fixed that she could be moved from the spot by no force. For this reason the prefect ordered fire to be kindled around her, drenched with pitch, resin, and boiling oil; but when not even the flame could harm her, after many torments her throat was pierced with a sword. Having received that wound, Lucy, foretelling the tranquility of the Church that was to come with the deaths of Diocletian and Maximian, gave back her spirit to God on the Ides of December. Her body was buried at Syracuse, then translated to Constantinople, and finally to Venice.

The obedience she had vowed to God she cultivated through the guides of her conscience with a truly admirable perfection. She endured very long fasts at the command of obedience; nor did she breathe her last after a long struggle with death until she had been commanded to die — for she knew well that no sacrifice was more pleasing to her Spouse than obedience. For thirty-three years, during which she was constrained to discharge the duties of superior, she led the sisters entrusted to her care toward all holiness, chiefly by her own example. To satisfy her desire for suffering, to the apoplexy by which she was seized there were added almost all the diseases reckoned the most grievous. She bore everything with steadfast soul for thirty-three days, until she took flight into the embrace of Jesus her Spouse on the ninth day of July in the year of salvation one thousand seven hundred and twenty-seven, in the fiftieth year of her religious life. Finally, distinguished by a full measure of heroic virtues and by miracles, Pope Pius the Seventh named her Blessed, and Pope Gregory the Sixteenth in solemn rite on the Sunday of the Most Holy Trinity in the other year of one thousand eight hundred and thirty-nine enrolled her in the company of the holy Virgins.

And what other woman was Solomon seeking, when he said: "Who shall find a strong woman?" For the wise man knew the weakness of this sex, the fragile body, the slippery mind. Yet, since he had read that God had promised it, and saw that it was fitting thus — that he who had conquered through a woman should be conquered through that same woman — marveling greatly he said: "Who shall find a strong woman?" Which is to say: if our salvation and everyone's restoration of innocence and victory over the enemy depends thus on the hand of a woman, it is altogether necessary that a strong one be provided, who may be equal to so great a work.

In gold, frankincense, and myrrh, however, other things also can be understood. For by gold, wisdom is signified — as Solomon attests, who says: "A desirable treasure rests in the mouth of the wise." Although he presided over the whole order and applied all his strength to the salvation of souls, he never stopped teaching boys — especially the poorest ones — whose schools he was accustomed to sweep and whom he was accustomed to accompany home. In this ministry of the highest patience and humility, even with failing health, he persevered for fifty-two years; worthy therefore that God should illustrate him with frequent miracles before his disciples, and that the most Blessed Virgin should appear with the child Jesus, blessing them while they prayed. In the meantime, having refused the most illustrious dignities, distinguished by prophecy, by the gifts of knowing the hidden secrets of hearts and of things absent, and by miracles — deemed worthy of the frequent apparition of the Virgin Mother of God, whom he himself also honored from infancy with singular piety and commended above all to others, and of the apparition of other heavenly beings — after he had foretold the day of his death and the restoration and growth of the order then nearly overthrown, at the age of ninety-two he fell asleep in the Lord at Rome on the eighth day before the Kalends of September in the year one thousand six hundred and forty-eight. His heart and tongue were found intact and incorrupt after a century. He himself was first honored with the cult of the Blessed by Benedict the Fourteenth, and then was solemnly enrolled among the Saints by Clement the Thirteenth.

How great, I ask, is the humility that appears in the books of the Holy Fathers joined with the highest learning? How great the sobriety? Nothing obscene there, nothing base, nothing crafty, nothing arrogant, nothing inflated. In how many ways does the Holy Spirit, who dwelt in their hearts, reveal himself in their pages? Who can read Cyprian attentively without being immediately enkindled with love of martyrdom? Who has applied himself diligently to Augustine without having learned the most profound humility? Who has often opened Jerome without beginning to love virginity and fasting? The writings of the Saints breathe forth religion, chastity, integrity, charity. These, therefore, are the bishops and pastors — to use the words of Saint Augustine — learned, grave, holy, most keen defenders of truth, who sucked the Catholic faith as milk, took it as food, and ministered its milk and food to the little and the great. By such men after the Apostles the holy Church grew — by planters, waterers, builders, shepherds, and nurses.

How great the cruelty of the Arians was toward him at that time, and how brazen and shameless their insolence, is shown by the weighty letters full of strength, piety, and religion which he wrote from Scythopolis to the clergy and people of Vercelli, and to other neighboring communities; from which it is also well established that neither by their threats and inhuman savagery could he ever be deterred, nor by their serpentine soft cunning be brought into their society. From there, deported to Cappadocia, and finally to the upper Thebaid of Egypt for his constancy, he bore the hardships of exile until the death of Constantius; after which, permitted to return to his flock, he was not willing to return before betaking himself to the synod of Alexandria to repair the losses suffered by the faith, and, traversing the provinces of the East after the manner of a most eminent physician, restoring to full health those who were weak in the faith by instructing them in the Church's doctrine. From there, departing with equal salutary effect into Illyricum, and finally carried into Italy, at his return Italy put off her mourning garments; where, after he had published his corrected commentaries of Origen on all the Psalms, which he had rendered from Greek into Latin, along with those of Eusebius of Caesarea, he finally passed to the unfading crown of glory so greatly merited by such great labors, under Valentinian and Valens at Vercelli.

For one who, being wise according to the flesh, is not heeded when he instills evil things in us, is as it were loved through hatred. Now, so that the Lord might show that this hatred toward neighbors does not proceed from affection but from charity, he added immediately, that we must also hate our own soul. It is established, therefore, that one who thus hates his neighbor as he hates himself is loving him even in hating him. For we truly hate our own soul when we do not consent to its carnal desires, when we break its appetite, when we resist its pleasures. What is therefore disdained and led toward better things is, as it were, loved through hatred. So indeed we must show this discrimination of hatred toward our neighbors, that in them we both love what they are, and hold in hatred what obstructs us on God's path.

For the Lord bids us, as it were, to climb the sycamore tree, when he says: From one who takes away what is yours, do not ask it back. And again: If anyone strikes you on the right cheek, offer him the other also. The Lord is seen passing by the sycamore tree; for through this wise foolishness, the wisdom of God, even if not yet seen solidly as it is, is nonetheless glimpsed as in passing through the light of contemplation—something those who seem wise in their own eyes cannot see, because, caught up in the lofty crowd of their own thoughts, they have not yet found the sycamore tree.

Just as one who sees letters in a most beautifully written codex, and does not know how to read, praises indeed the hand of the copyist, admiring the beauty of the characters; but what those characters mean, what they indicate, he does not know, and he is a praiser with his eyes but not an understander with his mind. Another, however, both praises the craftsmanship and grasps the meaning: namely, the one who can not only see what is common to all, but also read—which one who has not learned cannot do. So those who saw Christ's miracles, and did not understand what they meant and what they were somehow signaling to those with understanding, marveled only that they were done; but others both marveled at the deeds and attained their understanding. Such must we be in the school of Christ.

Whom the venerable Xystus, Bishop of the city of Rome, while he was overcoming through torments the impiety of a raging world and was already near the heavenly realms, and when he saw Lawrence most sorrowful over his fatherly death, is said to have thus addressed him by the spirit of foreknowledge: Do not be sad, my son: you will follow me after three days. From this it appears, dearly beloved, that blessed Lawrence was not sorrowful over his priest's victory, but was grieved because even he himself was not conquering the world together with his priest. Do not be sad, my son: you will follow me after three days. That is to say: Do not be sad, as though left behind in the world; for neither your faith nor your life will deprive you of such a death.

He who in persecution will give the purple crown for the Passion will himself in peace give also the white one to those who conquer through the merits of justice. For neither Abraham, nor Isaac, nor Jacob was killed; and yet, honored for their merits of faith and justice, they merited to be first among the patriarchs: to whose banquet is gathered whoever is found faithful, and just, and praiseworthy. We must be mindful that we ought to do not our own will, but God's; for he who does his will remains forever, just as he also remains forever.

When he disregarded the man's mad cries, he had him sent to the stables, to take care of the beasts that were kept there at public expense; where Marcellus spent nine months in life of continual fasting and prayer, visiting by letter the parishes he was unable to visit in person. When he was being stoned, he not only did not expect to exact vengeance from his persecutors, but rather begged God's pardon for them. The Lord God bids us wait, that in the day of future retribution we may be vindicated together with the holy Martyrs.

Some months before he departed this life, he forewarned his disciples on what day he was to die; and he ordered his tomb, in which he wished his body to be placed, to be opened six days before he was to be laid in it. On the sixth day he wished to be brought to the church, where, having received the Eucharist and lifting his eyes to heaven in prayer, amid the hands of his disciples he breathed forth his soul. Two monks saw it going to heaven, adorned with a most precious mantle; and with gleaming lamps all around it, they heard a man of most luminous and grave countenance, standing above his head, saying: This is the way by which the beloved of the Lord, Benedict, ascends to heaven.

He who, in the world—that is, in a dry and waterless land—had flourished so happily, a flower of the valleys planted in the house of the Lord, spread everywhere the wondrous fragrance of holiness. And so Paschal, having embraced the way of a stricter life and been admitted into the Order of Friars Minor of the stricter observance of the Discalced, exulted like a giant to run his course; and giving himself wholly to the Lord to be cultivated, he pondered day and night in what way he might more and more conform himself to him. Thus it quickly came about that even those more advanced in the spiritual life proposed him as a model of seraphic perfection to be imitated. Placed in the humble rank of the servants, regarding himself as the offscouring of all, he embraced with the greatest cheerfulness every arduous and lowly service of the house, as though owed to him by some special right, and exercised them with equal humility and patience. He afflicted with constant mortification the flesh that at times strove to resist the spirit, and reduced it to subjection; while the spirit, through continual self-denial, he stretched forward more fervently day by day toward what lies ahead.

Because the Pharisees were driven to act from nothing other than malice and arrogance, he everywhere commands his disciples to be simple, and by instructing these he indirectly rebukes those. For nothing breeds pride so much as positions of leadership and the first places at table. Therefore, since his disciples were about to receive great honor throughout the whole world, he forestalled their minds and did not permit them to suffer anything merely human, nor to seek honor from the crowd, nor to exalt themselves above others. For even if these things seem to be small, they provide the cause for great evils. For in this way the Pharisees, cultivated thus, ascended to the summit of evils, seeking salutations, first places and middle places; and from there they fell into a burning desire for glory, and then into impiety.

By these and other documents it clearly appears that the Bavarian regions justly deserve the distinguished title of the Marian Kingdom. This was openly signified by Maximilian, the first Elector, who dedicated a Marian statue inscribed with the title 'Patroness of Bavaria' on the facade of his new palace, and afterward, when by the intercession of the same heavenly Patroness he had won a celebrated victory, caused with grateful memory a second statue to be erected in the public square in honor of the Blessed Virgin Mary, whom he greeted in words and writings as the Lady of Bavaria. From that time the title of the Blessed Virgin Mary, Patroness of Bavaria, gained such authority that it began to be frequently inscribed on coins and public monuments. Pope Benedict XV, graciously granting the most devoted petitions of King Louis III—who, even before he came to the throne, had not hesitated openly to make a solemn profession of Catholic faith and piety toward the most Blessed Virgin at Oettingen—while a terrible war was raging throughout Europe, appointed the same Virgin Mary by his supreme authority as the principal Patroness before God of all Bavaria, and granted that her solemnity under the same title should be celebrated in all the dioceses of Bavaria with proper Office and Mass, under the rite of double first class.

When these things were heard, the Bishop of Jerusalem, calling together the bishops and priests of the neighboring cities, went to the place and found caskets that had been dug out, from which a most sweet odor was exhaled. The sacred body of Saint Stephen, which was then brought into the holy church of Sion with the greatest solemnity, was later translated under Theodosius the Younger to Constantinople, and thence to Rome under the supreme Pontiff Pelagius I, and was laid in the tomb of the martyr Saint Lawrence in the Ager Veranus.

When Maxentius learned of these things, he ordered the beasts of the menagerie to be transferred to that church, to be kept by Marcellus; and there, afflicted by the foulness of the place and many hardships, he fell asleep in the Lord. His body was buried in the cemetery of Priscilla on the Via Salaria by blessed Lucina, on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of February. He held his see for five years, one month, and twenty-five days. He wrote an epistle to the bishops of the province of Antioch concerning the primacy of the Roman Church, which he demonstrates must be called the head of the churches; in which it is also written that no council may lawfully be celebrated except by the authority of the Roman Pontiff. In the month of December he ordained in Rome twenty-five priests, two deacons, and twenty-one bishops for various places.

Having observed these things, pay heed, most beloved, to what great reverence, what great devotion we owe to him: he who, that he might be honorable, was prophesied by the Holy Spirit, promised by an Angel, praised by the Lord, and consecrated by the everlasting glory of a holy death. For it was fitting that a wondrous life should follow his mystical birth, and that a death devoted to God should crown his holy and perfect life. For this reason, brethren, the Church of Christ throughout the whole world today most rightly celebrates with the most joyful solemnity the beginnings of his birth—he who, as the most faithful witness, revealed to a wondering world the eternal joys given to mortal men.

Those who object must first define what it means for a man to be without sin: whether it is never to have sinned at all, or to have ceased from sinning. For if they think that being without sin means never having sinned at all, I myself agree. For all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God. But if they deny that one who has corrected his former error and transformed himself to such a quality of life that he abstains from sin is abstaining from offenses, I cannot agree with their opinion, since we read: So the Lord loved the Church that he might present her to himself glorious, not having spot or wrinkle or anything of the kind, but that she might be holy and without blemish.

What were you saying, O Adam? The woman whom you gave me gave me of the tree, and I ate. These are words of malice, by which you augment rather than efface the fault. Yet Wisdom conquered malice, when it found in the treasury of its unfailing loving kindness the occasion for pardon that God tried, through questioning, to draw from you but could not. For a woman is restored in place of a woman—a prudent one for a foolish one, a humble one for a proud one—who might offer you the taste of life in place of the tree of death, and bring forth from that poisonous and bitter food the sweetness of eternal fruit. Therefore change the word of your wicked excuse into a voice of thanksgiving, and say: Lord, the woman whom you gave me gave me of the tree of life, and I ate; and it was made sweeter than honey to my mouth, for in it you gave me life. For behold, it was for this that the Angel was sent to the Virgin. O most admirable and most worthy of all honor, Virgin; O woman singularly to be venerated, admirable above all women, the restorer of parents and the vivifier of posterity.

For what would it have profited for the devil to be conquered by God, if we remained proud? Mary was therefore of necessity betrothed to Joseph, since by this the holy one is hidden from the dogs, the virginity is confirmed by the spouse, and care is taken both for the modesty and the reputation of the Virgin. What could be wiser? What more worthy of divine providence? By one such counsel, a witness is admitted to heavenly secrets and an enemy excluded, and the good name of the Virgin Mother is kept intact.

For what is holier than such a wound and such stripes? What is more salutary than these, from which our salvation proceeded, and in which the souls of the devout can continually be healed? Although, therefore, the aforesaid lance and nails and the other saving instruments of his Passion are to be venerated everywhere by all the faithful of Christ, and solemn Offices are celebrated annually in the same Church concerning the Passion itself; yet we judge it worthy and fitting that a solemn and special feast should be celebrated especially in those places where the instruments themselves are said to be held, and that we should particularly foster those faithful of Christ who rejoice that they possess some of those instruments, in their devotion by divine Offices and gifts.

What then does he say? Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven. We read it written concerning the appetite for temporal things: All is vanity and presumption of spirit. Now presumption of spirit signifies boldness and pride. In common speech, moreover, the proud are said to have a great spirit, and rightly so, since spirit is also called wind. Hence it is written: Fire, hail, snow, ice, the spirit of storms. Who does not know that the proud are said to be puffed up, as though swollen by wind? Hence also that saying of the Apostle: Knowledge puffs up, but charity builds up. Wherefore those who are poor in spirit are rightly understood here as the humble and those who fear God, that is, those who do not have a spirit that puffs them up.

What then? Is he always a ravening wolf? By no means; but he who in the morning seizes prey, in the evening distributes food. This was fulfilled in the Apostle Paul, because what had been said was also said of him. Now, if it please you, let us hear him seizing in the morning, distributing food in the evening. What then did he learn through the dove, lest he afterward be found a liar (which God forbid us to suppose), unless that a certain property would be found in Christ of such a kind, that however many ministers were to baptize, whether just or unjust, the sanctity of baptism would not be attributed except to him upon whom the dove descended, of whom it was said: This is he who baptizes in the Holy Spirit? Let Peter baptize—this is he who baptizes; let Paul baptize—this is he who baptizes; let Judas baptize—this is he who baptizes. For if holy baptism is holy according to the diversity of merits, because the merits are different, the baptisms will be different; and each person is thought to receive something better the more the one from whom he appears to have received it is better.

What then is stellar in the birth of Mary? Clearly this: that she sprang from kings, that she came from the seed of Abraham, that she was of noble stock from the line of David. If that seems too little, add that to her birth is known to have been granted by divine gift a singular privilege of holiness, that it was promised from heaven to those same patriarchs long beforehand, that it was prefigured by mystical miracles, that it was foretold by prophetic oracles. For this was what the priestly rod prefigured when it flowered without root; this was what the fleece of Gideon prefigured when it was wet in the middle of a dry threshing floor; this was what the Eastern gate in Ezekiel's vision, which was never open to anyone, prefigured.

Why then should I recount the frugality of his diet and the abundance of his duties: the one exceeding nature's demands, the other falling almost short of nature's needs? There, no hours were left without occupation; here, days were doubled by fasting. And whenever the desire for refreshment prevailed, the food at hand was mostly such as would keep death at bay, not minister to pleasure. There was no wish to sleep before necessity compelled it; and yet, when the body rested, the mind was awake, which frequently in dreams either reviews what has been read, or continues what sleep has interrupted, or carries out what has been planned, or foretells what is to be done.

Why did you seek me? There are two births in Christ: one is paternal, the other maternal. The paternal is more divine; the maternal, however, descends to our labor and use. And therefore the things that happen above nature, above age, above custom, are not to be attributed to human powers, but are to be referred to divine authority. Elsewhere his mother urges him to service; here the mother is rebuked, because she still asks for what is merely human. But since here he is described as twelve years old, while there he is said to have disciples, you see that the mother learned from her son not to demand service from him who was more powerful, she who was astonished at the miracle in the younger.

Some also report that there lamps were seen burning at night, and from this it came about that his body, as that of a Martyr, ought rightly to be venerated by all the faithful. His treacherous and parricide father, moved by penitence, grieved that he had done this, yet did not repent to the point of obtaining salvation. For he acknowledged that the Catholic faith was true, but, seized with fear of his people, he did not merit to attain it. He fell ill, was brought to his end, and took care to commend his son, King Reccared—whom he was leaving in his heresy—to Bishop Leander, whom he had previously grievously afflicted, that he might do for him likewise what he had done for his brother through his exhortations. When this commendation was completed, he died. After his death, King Reccared, following not his treacherous father but his martyr brother, was converted from the wickedness of the Arian heresy and led the whole Visigothic people to the true faith, in such a way that he permitted no one to bear arms in his kingdom who was not afraid of being the enemy of God's kingdom through heretical wickedness. Nor is it surprising that he became a preacher of the true faith, who is the brother of the Martyr: whose merits also assist him, that he may bring back so many to the bosom of almighty God.

Whatever of these things I contemplate, I contemplate God; and through all things he is my God. This I said it was wisdom to meditate upon, and I judged it prudence to bring forth the memory of sweetness; for in these kernels the priestly rod abundantly brought forth, which Mary, drawing from on high, has poured out more abundantly to us. Truly from on high and beyond the Angels, she who received the Word from the very heart of the Father.

Therefore, joining five priests to himself, in the year sixteen hundred and forty-three, on the feast of the Annunciation of the Blessed Virgin Mary, he established a congregation of priests, to which he gave the most holy names of Jesus and Mary, and at Caen he opened the first seminary, which was followed in Normandy and Brittany by several more, founded by the same author. For sinful women, to be recalled to the Christian life, he founded the Order of Our Lady of Charity; of which most noble tree a branch is the Congregation of Angers of the Good Shepherd. He also founded the Society of the Admirable Heart of the Mother of God and other works of charity. He published many distinguished writings, and as an Apostolic missionary evangelized so many villages, towns, and cities, and even the royal court, to the very end of his life.

For who rejoices well, who does not love the good from which he rejoices? Who can have true peace except with one whom he truly loves? Who is patient in persevering steadfastly in good work, unless he burns with love? Who is kind, unless he loves the one he helps? Who is good, unless made so by loving? Who is wholesomely faithful, unless by faith that works through love? Who is usefully gentle, unless love moderates him? Who abstains from that by which he is dishonored, unless he loves that by which he is made honorable? Rightly, therefore, does the good Master so often commend love, as though it alone were to be commanded, without which other goods cannot profit, and which cannot be had without the other goods by which a man is made good.

Who is this King of the Jews? Poor and rich, humble and sublime. Who is this King of the Jews, who is carried as an infant, yet adored as God? Small in the manger, immense in heaven; vile in swaddling clothes, precious in the stars. Why are you so troubled, Herod? This King who is born has not come to overcome kings by fighting, but wondrously to subdue them by dying. Nor was he born to succeed you, but that the world might faithfully believe in him. He has come, therefore, not to fight while alive, but to triumph when slain.

Who would not wish to be burned for a moment in the fire of Lawrence, so as not to suffer the eternal fire of Gehenna? We are therefore stirred by the example of blessed Lawrence to martyrdom, and set on fire toward faith, and grow warm in devotion; and if the flame of a persecutor is lacking to us, nonetheless the flame of faith is not lacking. We do not indeed burn in body for Christ, but we burn in affection; no persecutor puts fire under me, but the desire of the Savior suggests fire to me.

Who, when he saw men running from the banquet to the prison, would not have thought that the Prophet had been ordered to be released? Who, I say, when he had heard that it was Herod's birthday, a solemn banquet, with the option given to a girl to choose what she wished, would not have thought that John had been sent for in order to be set free? What has cruelty to do with delights? What has pleasure to do with funerals? The Prophet is snatched away to punishment at the time of the feast, by a feast-day command, by which he would not even want to be released; he is killed by the sword, and his head is brought on a platter. This dish was owed to cruelty, that ferocity unsated by the feast might feed upon it.

Who could speak of your splendor? Who would dare to tell in words the wonder that you yourself are? Who could be confident of expressing your magnificence? You have adorned the nature of human beings; you have surpassed the orders of the Angels; you have outshone the brilliance of the Archangels; you have shown the lofty seats of the Thrones to be beneath you; you have humbled the height of the Dominations; you have run before the leaderships of the Principalities; you have enfeebled the strength of the Powers; you came forth a virtue more powerful than the Virtues themselves; you surpassed with earthly eyes the most clear-sighted gaze of the Cherubim; you flew beyond the flight of the six-winged Seraphim on the wings of your soul divinely stirred; you have finally far surpassed all creatures, since you shone above every creature in purity, and you received in yourself the Creator of all creatures; and you carried him even in your bosom, and gave birth to him; and alone among all creatures you became the Mother of God.

Now, as to the foundation upon which this dignity and power of our Lord rests, Cyril of Alexandria aptly observes: "He holds dominion, to say it in a word, over all creatures, not by force extorted, nor brought in from elsewhere, but by his own essence and nature"; that is, his sovereignty is based upon that wonderful union which is called hypostatic. From this it follows not only that Christ is to be adored by Angels and men as God, but also that the Angels and men are to obey and be subject to his rule as Man: namely, that by the very name of the hypostatic union alone Christ obtains power over all creatures. Now, to declare briefly the force and nature of this sovereignty, it scarcely needs to be said that it is contained in a threefold power, without which sovereignty can hardly be understood. The testimonies drawn and adduced from sacred Scripture concerning the universal sovereignty of our Redeemer more than sufficiently signify this, and it is to be believed with Catholic faith that Christ Jesus was given to human beings as their Redeemer in whom they are to trust, and at the same time as their Lawgiver whom they are to obey. The Gospels, moreover, do not so much narrate that he established laws as introduce him in the act of establishing them: those who keep these precepts are said by the divine Master, in various words at various times, to be those who will prove their love for him and who will abide in his love. The judicial power attributed to himself by the Father, Jesus himself declares to the Jews, who accused him of violating the Sabbath rest through the wondrous healing of a disabled man: "For neither does the Father judge anyone, but all judgment he has given to the Son." In this is also comprehended (since the matter cannot be separated from judgment) that he bestows by his own right rewards and punishments upon men still living. Moreover, that power which they call executive is to be attributed to Christ, since it is necessary for all to obey his command, and this indeed is made known to the obstinate through the infliction of punishments which no one can escape.

So that the dignity of human labor and the principles that give it its worth might be more deeply implanted in minds, Pope Pius XII instituted the feast of Saint Joseph the Worker, who might be a model and protector for every working community. For from his example those who exercise laborious crafts must learn in what manner and with what spirit they should fulfill their duties, so that, equally obedient to God's first precept, they may both subdue the earth and care for economic prosperity, and at the same time obtain the rewards of eternal life. Nor will the watchful guardian of the Nazareth Family fail to protect with his care those who share his craft and labor, and to bless their homes from heaven. The Supreme Pontiff most fittingly ordered this feast to be celebrated on the first of May, the day which workers' assemblies have claimed for themselves; for from this shines forth the hope that this day, dedicated to Saint Joseph the Worker, may henceforth not sharpen hatreds and kindle quarrels, but, returning each year, may invite all to perfect more and more what still remains wanting for civic peace, and indeed may also stimulate those who govern the state to diligently complete what the right order of human society demands.

From that time onward, the honor which on that day used to be paid to the profane celebrations of the Gentiles began to be paid to the chains of Peter, which by their touch healed the sick and cast out demons. Of this kind it happened, in the year of human salvation nine hundred and sixty-nine, that a certain count, a familiar of the Emperor Otto, being seized by an unclean spirit, was tearing himself with his own teeth. Therefore he was brought by the Emperor's command to Pope John, who, when the sacred chain touched the count's neck, the wicked spirit broke forth and left the man free; and from that time forward the devotion to the holy chains was propagated in the City.

In order to please the Most High the more, when she had read in Sacred Scripture that admonition: If any one is a little one, let him come to me, she wished to be little in spirit, and from there with filial trust she surrendered herself perpetually to God as to a most loving Father. This way of spiritual childhood, according to the teaching of the Gospel, she taught to others, especially to the novices whom out of obedience she undertook to form in the practice of the religious virtues, and thus, filled with apostolic zeal, she opened to the world—puffed up with pride and devoted to vanities—the way of evangelical simplicity. Her Spouse Jesus inflamed her with a desire for suffering, both in soul and in body. Moreover, observing that love for God was being neglected on every side, and affected with the greatest sorrow, two years before her death she offered herself as a victim to the love of God's mercy. Then, as she herself relates, she was wounded by the flame of heavenly fire; and consumed by charity, rapt in ecstasy, most fervently repeating: My God, I love you, she flew to her Spouse at twenty-four years of age, on the thirtieth day of September, in the year eighteen hundred and ninety-seven. And what she had promised as she was dying—that she would send down a perennial rain of roses upon the earth—this she has in truth fulfilled and continues to fulfill day by day through countless miracles, having been received into heaven. Pope Pius XI, Sovereign Pontiff, enrolled her among the Blessed Virgins and, two years later, with the great Jubilee returning, numbered her among the Saints, and appointed and declared her the special Patroness of all the Missions.
