Where must the Lord be followed? Where he went, we know; for he rose again and ascended into heaven: he must be followed there. Certainly there is no cause for despair, because he himself has promised, not because man can do anything. And why should we despair, if we are members of that Head? It is good to follow him there; but we must see how. For the Lord Jesus was not saying these words at the time when he had already risen from the dead; he had not yet suffered; he was going to the Cross, going to dishonor, to insults, to scourging, to thorns, to wounds, to mockery, to reproaches, to death. The way has become, as it were, rough: you make yourself sluggish, you do not wish to follow. Follow. For who would not wish to go to exaltation? Heights delight everyone, but humility is the step.

At that time, the whole city trembled with a great earthquake, and two collapsing walls crushed Silvinus and Falconius, intimate familiars of the prefect. Therefore, when the city was greatly disturbed, Quinctianus, fearing a tumult of the people, secretly ordered Agatha, half-dead, to be brought back to prison. She thus prayed to God: Lord, who have guarded me from my infancy, who have taken from me the love of the world, who have given me victory over the torments of my torturers, receive my soul. In this prayer she departed to heaven on the Nones of February; and her body was buried by the Christians.

At that time, when countless faithful were unhappily held under the terrible servitude of the Saracens, with the danger of losing eternal salvation, the Blessed Virgin Mary appeared by night to Saint Peter Nolasco, to Blessed Raymond of Peñafort, and to James, King of Aragon, and said that it would be most pleasing to herself and to her Only Begotten Son if a religious order were established in her honor, upon whom should fall the care of freeing captives from the tyranny of the Turks. Therefore, having conferred their counsels together and being of one mind, they set themselves to establish an order in honor of the same Virgin Mother, under the invocation of Holy Mary of Mercy for the redemption of captives, with the members bound by a fourth vow of remaining as a pledge under the power of the pagans, if it should be necessary for the liberation of Christians. The king himself granted them the right to bear his royal arms upon their breast, and had the institution of such surpassing charity confirmed by Gregory IX. And so that thanks for so great a benefit and establishment might be duly rendered to God and the Virgin Mother, the Apostolic See granted the celebration of this special feast.

At that time the greater and more prosperous part of the Spains was oppressed under the dreadful yoke of the Saracens, and countless faithful were unhappily held in the most grievous servitude, with the greatest danger of renouncing the Christian faith and losing eternal salvation; when the most blessed Queen of heaven, graciously coming to meet so many and such great evils, showed her exceeding charity in redeeming them. For to Saint Peter Nolasco, who was flourishing in piety and resources, and who, devoting himself to holy meditations, was perpetually revolving in his mind by what means the sufferings of so many Christians dwelling in Moorish captivity might be relieved, the most blessed Virgin herself appeared with serene countenance and said that it would be most pleasing to herself and to her Only Begotten Son if a religious order were established in her honor, upon whom should fall the care of freeing captives from the tyranny of the Turks. Renewed by this heavenly vision, it is wonderful with what ardor of charity the man of God began to burn, keeping this one thing in his heart: that he and the religious order to be established by him should diligently practice that supreme charity, that each might lay down his soul for his friends and neighbors.

At that time the wife of Maximin and Porphyrius the military commander, having entered the prison to see the Virgin, and being converted by her preaching to faith in Jesus Christ, were afterward crowned with martyrdom. Meanwhile Catherine is led out of custody, and a wheel is prepared, fitted with many sharp swords, so that the body of the Virgin might be most cruelly torn. This device was shattered by a brief prayer of Catherine, and by that miracle many received the faith of Christ. Maximin himself, more obstinate in impiety and cruelty, ordered Catherine to be struck with an axe. She, boldly giving her head, flew to the doubled reward of virginity and martyrdom on the seventh day before the Kalends of December; her body was wonderfully placed by the Angels on Sinai, the mountain of Arabia.

At that time Peter and Paul were held under the custody of the Mamertine prison on the Tarpeian Hill. Two guards, Processus and Martinianus, together with forty others, moved by the preaching and miracles of the Apostles, were converted to faith in Jesus Christ; and when suddenly a spring arose from the rock, they were baptized. They permitted the Apostles to leave if they wished. But Paulinus, the commander of the soldiers, when the matter became known, attempted to recall Processus and Martinianus from the course they had undertaken. When he wasted time in vain, he ordered their mouths to be beaten with a stone and their teeth broken. Shortly afterward, brought to the statue of Jupiter and with the same constancy refusing to adore the idols, he ordered them to be racked on the strappado, with glowing iron plates applied to their bodies, and to be beaten with clubs; in which torments this one voice alone was heard from them: Blessed be the name of the Lord. Finally cast into prison, a little later they were struck with the axe outside the City on the Via Aurelia. Their bodies were buried by Lucina on her estate, on the sixth day before the Nones of July; which bodies were later translated to the City and laid in the basilica of the Prince of the Apostles.

At that time Tryphonia, the former wife of Decius, moved by the hidden grace of the Holy Spirit and wondrously enlightened by the light of truth, went to Justin with her daughter Cyrilla, and by him was converted to the Christian faith and cleansed in the heavenly font. By her example, forty-six soldiers were moved and came to blessed Justin with their wives and children, and prostrating themselves at his feet gave their names to Christ. When these things were heard, Prince Claudius ordered Cyrilla and the soldiers to be arrested and condemned to the final punishment.

Arriving there with a favorable journey, he applied himself with incredible ardor to the salvation of souls and the reform of morals, chiefly of the clergy; whom not long afterward Saint Boniface himself ordained to the priesthood, and in the year of the Lord seven hundred and forty-five consecrated as Bishop of Eichstätt, when Willibald was in the forty-first year of his age. Having administered that bishopric most holily for thirty-six years, he exchanged this mortal life for immortal life, weighty with merits and glorious with a remarkable working of miracles, in the year of Christ seven hundred and eighty-one, in the seventy-seventh year of his age: whose memory, especially among the people of Eichstätt, will never die.

In order to proceed more maturely in a matter of such great importance, he withdrew into solitude, and there by divine guidance it came about that he found Felix of Valois, who had already been living as a hermit for many years; with whom he formed a fellowship and for three years exercised himself in prayer, contemplation, and the pursuit of all the virtues. It happened that, while they were conversing near a spring about divine things, a stag approached them bearing a cross between its antlers, of red and blue color. And when Felix marveled at the novelty of the thing, John told him of the vision he had had at his first Mass; and from then on, applying themselves more fervently to prayer, admonished three times in sleep, they resolved to go to Rome, to obtain from the Supreme Pontiff the establishment of a new order for the redemption of captives. At that time Innocent III had been elected; who, having received them kindly and deliberating within himself about the proposed matter, on the feast of the second Agnes, at the Lateran, at the Elevation of the sacred Host during the solemnity of Mass, an Angel appeared to him in white garments, with a two-colored cross, in the form of one redeeming captives. Seeing this, the Pontiff approved the institution, and ordered the new order to be called the Most Holy Trinity for the Redemption of Captives, and gave its members white garments with a cross of red and blue.

But as for his ascending alone to pray, do not refer this to him who satisfied five thousand men from five loaves, not counting children and women; but to him who, having heard of the death of John, withdrew into solitude—not that we divide the one Lord into two persons, but because his works are divided between God and man. Now the boat was being tossed in the middle of the sea by the waves. Rightly had the Apostles, as if unwilling and reluctant, withdrawn from the Lord, lest, in his absence, they should suffer shipwreck.

That John, placed in prison, sends his disciples to Christ, means that the law transmits them to the Gospel. For the law, according to the type of John, as though shut in the prison of ignorance, lay in obscurity and hiddenness, and its sense was enclosed within the letter by Jewish blindness. Of him the blessed Evangelist says: He was a burning lamp, that is, kindled by the fire of the Holy Spirit, to show the light of salvation to a world possessed by the night of ignorance, and, as it were, among the densest darkness of sins to point out with the ray of his light the most brilliant sun of justice, saying of himself: I am the voice of one crying in the desert.

That he prophesied before his birth from the secret of his mother's womb, and, though not yet having experienced the light, is already a witness of the truth—this is to be understood as meaning that, lying hidden under the veil and flesh of the letter, he proclaimed the Redeemer to the world in spirit, and proclaimed our Lord to us from a certain womb of the law. Therefore, because the Jews went astray from the womb—that is, from the law which was pregnant with Christ—they went astray from the womb and spoke falsehoods; and for this reason he came to bear witness, that he might give testimony to the light.

When this was announced to the prefect, he immediately ordered Venantius to be thrown to the lions, who, setting aside their natural ferocity, cast themselves at his feet. Meanwhile he was teaching the people the faith of Christ. Therefore he was removed from there and cast into prison again. And when the next day Porphyrius reported to the prefect that he had seen in a vision during the night the people whom Venantius was baptizing shining with the clearest light, while the prefect himself was covered with the deepest darkness; the prefect, inflamed with anger, immediately ordered him to be beheaded, and then Venantius to be dragged through places covered with brambles and thistles until evening. He, left half dead, presented himself again to the prefect the next morning; by whose command he was at once thrown headlong from a cliff. But even from there he was rescued by divine intervention, and was again dragged for a thousand paces through rough country; where, when the soldiers were suffering from thirst in the heat, Venantius made the sign of the cross on a nearby rock—on which even now the impression of his knees can be seen, as is visible in his church today—and water flowed out. By that miracle many were moved to believe in Christ, and the prefect ordered all of them to be beheaded in that place together with Venantius. Lightning and earthquakes at that time were so great that the prefect fled; yet within a few days, unable to escape the divine justice, he met a most shameful death. In the meantime, the Christians buried the bodies of Venantius and the others with honor: which bodies are still laid at Camerino in the church dedicated to Venantius.

What is the summit of the building we are endeavoring to construct? To what height will the pinnacle of the edifice reach? I will say it quickly: to the sight of God. You see how lofty it is, what a great thing it is to behold God. He who desires it understands both what I say and what he hears. To us is promised the sight of God, of the true God, of the supreme God. For this is the good: for the one who sees, to see. For those who worship false gods can easily see them; but they see those who have eyes and do not see. But to us is promised the vision of the living and seeing God.

This deed was commended by an illustrious miracle. For Heraclius, adorned as he was with gold and jewels, was compelled to halt at the gate that leads toward the hill of Calvary. For the more he tried to advance, the more he seemed to be held back. While both Heraclius himself and all the others were astonished at this, Zacharias, Bishop of Jerusalem, said: Beware, O Emperor, lest in that triumphal adornment you imitate too little the poverty and humility of Jesus Christ in carrying the Cross. Then Heraclius, having thrown aside his magnificent garments, removed his shoes, and clothed himself in a plain garment, easily completed the rest of the way and set the Cross in that same place on Calvary from which it had been carried off by the Persians. And so the solemnity of the Exaltation of the Holy Cross, which was celebrated annually on this day, began to be held with greater distinction, on account of the memory of the fact that it was there restored by Heraclius where it had first been raised up for the Savior.

That the birthday of the Chair is therefore celebrated today, the priestly office is honored. These things the Church and the priesthood mutually confer upon each other, for the Church necessarily has as much greater dignity as the priestly office has greater honor. Since religious observance has rightly introduced this solemnity to the Churches, I wonder why among certain unbelievers today so pernicious an error has grown, that they place food and wine upon the tombs of the dead, as though souls that have departed from their bodies were in need of bodily food.

How this has been fulfilled, the Apostle John teaches, saying: We know that the Son of God has come and has given us understanding, that we may know the truth, and that we may be in his true Son. And again: Therefore let us love God, because he first loved us. And so God, by loving us, restores us to his image; and that he may find in us the form of his goodness, he gives the means by which we ourselves may also work what he works, kindling, that is, the lamps of our minds and inflaming us with the fire of his charity, so that we may love not only him but also all that he loves.
Moreover, if among men that friendship is at last firm which is bound together by likeness of character, though agreement of wills often tends toward reprobate affections: how much must we desire and strive that we may in nothing differ from those things which are pleasing to God? If, however, blessed Silvester afterward decreed in the consecration of the altar of the Prince of the Apostles that henceforth altars should be built only of stone, nonetheless the altar of the Lateran basilica was erected of wood. This is not surprising; for since from Saint Peter until Silvester, on account of the persecutions, the Pontiffs were unable to remain in a fixed place, wherever necessity had driven them, whether into crypts or cemeteries or the houses of the pious, they offered the sacred rites upon that wooden altar, hollow in the likeness of an ark. Saint Silvester, when peace was restored to the Church, placed that altar in honor of the Prince of the Apostles—who is said to have offered sacrifice upon it—and of the other Pontiffs who up to that time had used it for the celebration of the mysteries, in the Lateran as the first church, and decreed that henceforth no one but the Roman Pontiff should celebrate Mass upon it.
That same church, shattered and overturned by fires, ravagings, and earthquakes, and restored by the assiduous care of the Supreme Pontiffs, and then rebuilt with new construction, was solemnly consecrated by Pope Benedict XIII, of the Order of Preachers, on the twenty-eighth day of April of the year seventeen hundred and twenty-six, who appointed the celebration of its anniversary to be observed on this day. And as for what Pius IX had judged should be completed, Pope Leo XIII had the great nave, crumbling with age, extended and enlarged by a great reconstruction; had the old mosaic, already in many parts previously restored, restored to its ancient model and transferred to the new apse, adorned with magnificent workmanship and elegance; had the transept hall, with its coffered ceiling and floor renewed, polished; the sacristy, the canons' residence, and the permanent portico to the Constantinian Baptistery were added, in the year eighteen hundred and eighty-four.

But if you desire to see by actual events that this is so done, read the book of the Acts of the Apostles; you will see clearly that, when the people of the Jews often rose up against the Apostles and gnashed their teeth, those men, by imitating the simplicity of the dove and by responding with befitting modesty, overcame their anger, extinguished their fury, and slowed their assault. For when they said: Did we not strictly command you not to teach in this name? although they could have displayed countless miracles, they nevertheless said and did nothing harsh; but answering with the greatest gentleness they said: Whether it is right before God to obey you rather than God, judge for yourselves. You have seen the simplicity of the dove; now see the prudence of the serpent: For we cannot, they say, but speak the things which we have seen and heard.

But if you find them, as they truly are, still more full of piety and grace, full of gentleness and mercy—all the things that pertain to her—give thanks to him who, with most gracious compassion, provided such a mediatrix, in whom there can be nothing suspect. For in the end she became all things to all, and made herself a debtor to the wise and to the unwise with the most abundant charity. She opens the bosom of her mercy to all, so that from her fullness all may receive: the captive redemption, the sick healing, the sorrowful consolation, the sinner pardon, the just grace, the angel joy. She does not scrutinize past merits; but shows herself approachable to all, most merciful to all, and in the end compassionates the needs of all with a most ample affection. She is that woman once promised by God, who was to crush the head of the ancient serpent with the foot of her virtue; whose heel he has lain in ambush for in many cunning ways, but in vain. For she alone has crushed the entire wickedness of heresy. Those who lay in ambush are crushed, those who tried to trip her up are trampled down, those who detracted are refuted, and all generations call her blessed. Now if the Church seems to be understood by the name of the moon, you have the mediatrix plainly expressed: A woman clothed with the sun, it says, and the moon under her feet. Let us embrace the footsteps of Mary and with most devout supplication cast ourselves down before her blessed feet. Let us hold her and not let her go, until she has blessed us: for she is powerful.

This is what Ezekiel in former times rebuked with these words: Woe to the shepherds of Israel: were they not feeding themselves? Are not flocks fed by shepherds? But they were doing the contrary, which is a form of the greatest wickedness and the cause of very many evils. For this reason he says: Neither did they bring back what was cast away, nor did they seek what was lost, nor did they bind up what was broken, nor did they strengthen what was sick: for they fed themselves, not the flock. Paul also says the same thing in other words: All seek what is their own, not what is of Jesus Christ.

When the one to whom her parents had betrothed her against the Virgin's will learned of this, he accused Lucy before the prefect Paschasius on the ground that she was a Christian. Since he could draw her neither by entreaties nor by threats to the worship of idols, and saw her all the more inflamed to proclaim the praises of the Christian faith the more he tried to turn her from her resolve, he said: Words will cease when it comes to blows. To whom the Virgin replied: Servants of God cannot lack for words, since the Lord Christ said to them: When you shall stand before kings and governors, do not think about how or what you are to say; for it shall be given you in that hour what you are to say; for it is not you who speak, but the Holy Spirit, who speaks in you.

That Joseph's birth rather than Mary's is recorded makes no difference: for the whole tribe is the same, and the kinship is one. Moreover, Matthew and Luke gave an example by calling one another's forebears fathers, not so much by blood as by people: for what began from one tribe is contained under the family of one succession and origin. For since he was to be shown as the son of David and of Abraham, Matthew began thus: The book of the generation of Jesus Christ, the Son of David, the Son of Abraham.

How did blessed Lawrence, whose feast day we celebrate today, remain in him? He remained to temptation; he remained to the tyrant's questioning; he remained to the most bitter threatening; he remained to death. That is too little to say: he remained even to atrocious torture. For he was not killed quickly, but was tormented in fire. He was permitted to live long—rather, he was not permitted to live long, but was compelled to die slowly. In that long death, in those torments, because he had eaten well and drunk well, as though fattened by that food and made drunk by that chalice, he did not feel the torments.

Adding to his daily endurance of his brother's torments frequent fasts, scourgings, and other afflictions of his innocent little body, he fell into a deadly illness. When it grew worse, and he had put to flight three times with the sign of the Cross a demon leaping upon him in the form of a dreadful dog, he received the sacred Viaticum—which, lying sick in a heretical household, he had sought in vain from men—from the Angels. Soon, graciously admitted by the most Blessed Mother to the embrace of the boy Jesus and bidden to give his name to the Society, he suddenly recovered his health. But since fear of his father closed the way to it in Germany, he took to flight alone, on foot, as a beggar in pilgrim's garb, resolved not to stop until he had attained his desire. The journey was made prosperous by more than one benefit from God. For among other things, the horses of Paul, his brother already overtaking the fugitive, were halted by a divinely sent torpor; and Stanislaus, refreshed again by the bread of Angels through angelic ministry, at last, after twelve hundred miles of travel, at Rome merited to be admitted into the Society of Jesus by Saint Francis Borgia, the Superior General.

Each day he devoted whatever time remained from study partly to the salvation of his neighbors, especially through sacred preaching, and partly to prayer, in which he is said to have been at times favored with heavenly visions and conversations. He was so moved by the Passion of Christ that he sometimes spent entire sleepless nights in contemplating it, and for the sake of recalling it more deeply he made a pilgrimage to Jerusalem; where, burning also with the desire for martyrdom, he did not hesitate to preach Christ crucified to the Turks themselves. He also came to Rome four times to the threshold of the Apostles, on foot and laden with a traveler's pack, both to honor the Apostolic See, to which he was most devoted, and to redeem (as he used to say) the punishments of his purgatory by means of the daily pardon of sins granted there. On one such journey, having been robbed by bandits and then asked whether he had anything more, after denying it he suddenly remembered some gold coins sewn into his cloak, and called after the fleeing bandits to offer these as well; they, astonished at the holy man's candor and generosity, willingly returned even what they had taken. Lest anyone detract from another's reputation, following the example of blessed Augustine he had verses inscribed on the wall, wishing himself and others to be perpetually reminded. He fed the hungry from his own portion; and he clothed the naked not only with garments purchased but also with those stripped from himself, letting his own cloak hang down to the ground so that he might not appear to be returning home barefoot.

Feed the hungry soul, and you shall not fear on the evil day from the wrath that is to come. For blessed, he says, is he who understands the poor and the needy; on the evil day the Lord will deliver him. Therefore labor and cultivate this region of your land, brother, that it may bring forth for you a fertile harvest, full of the richness of wheat, bearing a hundredfold fruit of multiplied seed with great increase. For the pursuit and devotion of this possession or this commerce is a holy and salutary greed; for such a desire, which merits the Kingdom of Heaven and longs for an everlasting good, is the root of all good things. Covet such riches, therefore, and possess such a patrimony, that your creditor may reckon for you a return of a hundredfold, so that you may also enrich your heirs together with you with everlasting goods. For this possession is truly great and precious, which does not weigh down its possessor with a worldly burden, but enriches him with an eternal return.

Having been appointed by Queen Joanna as administrator of royal almsgiving to the poor, John was taken by her as the director of her conscience. But when Wenceslaus had departed from his office and way of life, and was being hurried headlong into vices, and bore the remonstrances and counsel of his devout wife with ill grace, he dared to demand that in sacramental judgment the secrets confided by the priest to the queen should be revealed to him by John. But God's minister, tried first by blandishments, then by torments and the squalor of prison, resolutely opposed the king's wicked craving. When, however, neither human nor divine law could deter the raging soul of Wenceslaus from his execrable purpose, the athlete of Christ, who knew his final agony was near, after warning the people in a sermon about the calamities impending over the kingdom, gave clear forewarning of it. He then set out for Boleslav, to implore heavenly aid for fighting the good fight with outpoured prayers before an ancient and venerated image of the Blessed Virgin. On his return in the evening, on the eve of the Lord's Ascension, the king caught sight of him from a window and summoned him; and as he pressed him more violently and threatened him with imminent drowning in the waters if he persisted in resisting, John with unconquered constancy repelled the king's threats and terrors. Thus, by the king's command, he was cast by night into the Moldau river flowing through Prague, and won the glorious crown of martyrdom.

Raymond of Barcelona, from the noble family of Peñafort, diligently applied himself at Bologna to pious duties and to pontifical and civil law, and having been distinguished with the doctor's laurel, there expounded the sacred canons with great renown. Soon adorned by Bishop Berengar with a canonry and the prepositorship of the church of Barcelona, he shone by his virtue, learning, and gentleness of character, and promoted with all his strength the veneration of the Mother of God. Having entered the Order of Preachers in his forty-fifth year, he was the one who brought Saint Peter Nolasco—whose confessions he himself heard—together with James I, King of Aragon, to found the Order of Blessed Mary of Mercy for the redemption of captives, for which Raymond himself drew up the most approved rules of life. By command of Gregory IX he compiled at Rome the decrees of the Supreme Pontiffs into a single volume of the Decretals. Having most steadfastly declined the archbishopric of Tarragona and resigned the mastership general of the Order of Preachers, which he had administered most holily for two years, he fell asleep in the Lord at nearly a hundred years of age, in the year of salvation one thousand two hundred and seventy-five. Clement VIII enrolled him in the number of the Saints.

Raymond, surnamed Nonnatus, because beyond the common law of nature he was brought into the light by a cut in the side of his dead mother, despising childish games and the allurements of the world, so devoted himself to piety that all marveled at the mature virtue they saw in the boy. He most earnestly loved the Mother of God, whom he devoutly implored. Having entered the Order under the title of Our Lady of Mercy for the redemption of captives, he perpetually cultivated the virginity he had long since consecrated to the Blessed Virgin, and shone with every other virtue, above all with charity toward Christians who were living a wretched life under the power of pagans. Gregory IX enrolled him among the cardinal fathers; but the man of God, abhorring all pomp in that dignity, was always most tenacious of religious humility. Worn out by a grave illness at Cardona, and strengthened by the sacraments of the Church, he passed to the Lord on the last Sunday of August in the year one thousand two hundred and forty.

Raymond, surnamed Nonnatus, because beyond the common law of nature he was brought into the light by a cut in the side of his dead mother, was born at Portell in Catalonia of pious and noble parents, and from his very infancy gave signs of future holiness. For despising childish amusements and the allurements of the world, he so devoted himself to piety that all marveled at the mature virtue in the boy. As he grew in age he applied himself to literary studies; but soon, living in the country at his father's command, he frequently visited the chapel of Saint Nicholas situated in the region of Portell, in order to venerate the sacred image of the Mother of God that is there honored to this day with the highest veneration of the faithful. There, poured out in prayer, he earnestly besought the Mother of God herself to be pleased to adopt him as her son and to teach him the way of salvation and the knowledge of holy things.

After settling matters with the emperor, he returned to Italy and at once wrote a letter to all the bishops of Italy, commanding them to consecrate the churches of the Arians to the Catholic rite, adding these words: Because when we ourselves were at Constantinople, both for the sake of the Catholic religion and for the cause of King Theodoric, we consecrated to the Catholic use whatever churches of theirs we were able to find in those regions. Theodoric, taking this very ill, summoned the Pontiff by treachery to Ravenna and cast him into prison; where, worn out by squalor and want of food, he died within a few days, having sat two years, nine months, and fourteen days, and having ordained fifteen bishops in that time. Shortly afterward Theodoric also died; a certain hermit, as Saint Gregory writes, saw him being plunged, between Pope John and the patrician Symmachus whom he had likewise put to death, into the fire of Lipari — so that those to whom he had brought death might be, as it were, the judges of his own destruction. The body of John was carried from Ravenna to Rome and buried in the basilica of Saint Peter.

After matters had been settled with the Saracens, the king and his army were set free. Having remained five years in the East, he redeemed very many Christians from the servitude of the barbarians, and converted many unbelievers as well to the faith of Christ; moreover, he rebuilt several Christian cities at his own expense. Meanwhile his mother passed from this life, wherefore he was compelled to return home, where he devoted himself entirely to the duties of piety.

As he refused and resisted their entreaties, the ardent desire of the people was brought before the Emperor Valentinian, who was greatly pleased that judges chosen by himself were being sought for the priesthood. This was also pleasing to the prefect Probus, who, as if divining the future, had said to Ambrose as he set out: Go, act not as a judge but as a bishop. And so, when the will of the emperor was added to the wish of the people, Ambrose was baptized — for he was a catechumen — was initiated into the sacred mysteries, and, all the degrees of orders being observed according to the institution of the Church, on the eighth day, which was the seventh of the Ides of December, he undertook the episcopal burden. Having become bishop, he defended the Catholic faith and ecclesiastical discipline with the greatest zeal, and converted many Arians and other heretics to the truth of the faith, among whom he brought to Jesus Christ, as the most brilliant light of the Church, Saint Augustine.

Having declined the highest dignity in the Senate of Savoy, he enlisted in clerical service. Then, having been ordained a priest and obtained the prepositorship of the church of Geneva, he fulfilled the duties of that office so perfectly that Bishop Granery appointed him as a preacher of the divine word to recover for Catholicism the people of Chablais and other regions bordering on Geneva, who had lapsed into Calvinist heresy. Undertaking this expedition with a willing spirit, he endured all manner of hardships, often sought out by heretics bent on killing him, and harassed by various slanders and plots. But amid so many dangers and contests his unconquerable constancy always shone forth; and, protected by God's help, he is said to have brought seventy-two thousand heretics back to the Catholic faith, among whom many distinguished by nobility and learning are numbered.

Having received his own rule, confirmed by the authority of the Supreme Pontiff Innocent, he enlarged in the diocese of Meaux at the place called Cervus Frigidus the first monastery of the order, which shortly before he and a companion had built, where he wondrously cultivated religious observance and the institute of redemption, and from there diligently propagated it through his disciples to other provinces. Here he received a remarkable favor from the Blessed Virgin Mother; for while all the brethren were sleeping and, by God's dispensation, failing to rise for the morning prayers to be recited at midnight on the vigil of the Nativity of the Mother of God, Felix, who as was his custom was keeping vigil and anticipating the hours, entered the choir and found the Blessed Virgin in the midst of the choir, clothed in the habit adorned with the cross of the order, and attended by heavenly beings similarly clothed. Having joined himself among them, with the Mother of God leading, Felix sang the divine praises and duly completed them. And, as though already being called from an earthly to a heavenly choir, notified by an Angel of his imminent death, he exhorted his sons to charity toward the poor and captives, and rendered his soul to God, complete in age and merits, in the year after Christ's birth one thousand two hundred and twelve, under the same Pontiff Innocent III.

Having made his religious profession, he excelled in all the virtues and adornments of a religious man, most conspicuous above all for humility, patience, continence, and most ardent charity; and amid varied and constant labors, he was always intent with unconquered spirit upon prayer and meditation on divine things. Being ordered to undertake the burden of preaching — since he was outstanding in holiness and learning — with the inspiration of heavenly grace he led innumerable men out of the mire of vices onto the way of salvation. Then, appointed to govern the brethren, he united prudence, equity, and gentleness with equal diligence and firmness; so that in many places he either strengthened or restored the ancient discipline of his order.

The zeal for protecting and spreading the faith, which he declared to be absolutely his greatest concern, was admirably assisted by the great Emperor Theodosius, who, having removed the idols of the pagans and forbidden or demolished their temples and ordered all worship of idols to be abolished, caused the Christian religion to spread wondrously while the Pontiff was in his see. Having performed illustrious labors for the Church and issued most holy laws, he fell asleep in the Lord at more than seventy years of age, in the year of salvation three hundred and ninety-eight. He held the pontificate for about fourteen years. His body was translated from the cemetery of Priscilla on the Via Salaria to the title church of Saint Praxedes by Paschal I. His name, moreover, was ordered to be entered in the tables of the Roman Martyrology by Pope Benedict XIV, after his innocence had been fully vindicated against the charges brought against him.

Gelasius, African by birth, his father Valerius, appointed in the place of Felix III, held the pontificate four years, eight months, and eighteen days. In two ordinations he created two deacons, thirty-two priests, and sixty-seven bishops in various places. A man burning with singular zeal for propagating and preserving the faith, most fully versed in every learning and especially in sacred letters, and armed with the strength of an intrepid heart, both to vindicate the rights of the Church and the Apostolic See, and to blunt the insolence of heretics and schismatics.

Remigius, bishop of Rheims, flourished in the reign of Clovis, king of the Franks; he also baptized him, and was the first of all to bring the Franks to faith in Christ the Lord by his teaching and miracles. By his prayer, a dead girl was restored to life. He interpreted many books of divine Scripture. He governed the church of Rheims for more than seventy years with the highest renown. The holiness of his life and death was confirmed by many miracles that followed.

We see represented in you what the brave and illustrious boys declared before the king: that they were indeed prepared to burn in the flames rather than serve his gods or adore the image he had made; yet that the God whom they worshiped, and whom we also worship, was able to deliver them from the fiery furnace and to free them from the king's hands and from present punishments — which we find now accomplished in the faith of your confession and in the Lord's protection of you: so that, though you were prepared and ready to undergo every punishment, the Lord withdrew you from the penalty and reserved you for the Church. As you return, the dignity of your bishop's confession has not been diminished, but rather his priestly authority has grown, so that the high priest stands at the altar of God who, when the time comes to take up the arms of confession and to achieve martyrdom, may encourage the people not by words but by deeds, and when Antichrist approaches, may prepare his soldiers for battle not only by the rousing of speech and voice, but by the example of faith and virtue.

The deeds he accomplished, which we may infer from many proofs to have been wonderful, remained obscure and buried in the common shipwreck of the ancient writers. He wisely established many things pertaining to religion and discipline, and above all that a bishop should not be consecrated by fewer than three bishops; that clerics should be publicly ordained in sacred orders by their own bishop; and that at Mass, after the consecration was complete, all should receive communion. He died at last crowned with martyrdom, on the third of the Ides of July, and was buried beside the body of blessed Peter.

And Jesus, answering, said to him: Blessed are you, Simon Bar-Jona. In return for the Apostle's testimony about himself, he renders a testimony. Peter had said: You are the Christ, the Son of the living God; true confession received its reward: Blessed are you, Simon Bar-Jona. Why? Because flesh and blood has not revealed this to you, but the Father has revealed it. What flesh and blood could not reveal, has been revealed by the grace of the Holy Spirit. Therefore, from the confession which has its revelation from the Holy Spirit, he receives a title, of whose Son he is also to be named. For indeed Bar-Jona in our language means Son of the dove.

Recalled then from exile and permitted to return to his own church, he was soon compelled to go into exile again as another storm arose against him, namely a dreadful schism breaking out between the Roman Pontiff Gregory VII and the emperor himself, in which he was forced either to incur the anger of Henry or to become a transgressor of the commands of God and the Pontiff. Choosing rather to incur the displeasure of men than to despise the divine command, and having overcome the ambushes laid for him on the way, he went to Rome and adhered to the Pontiff, fighting most vigorously for his authority and also for ecclesiastical liberty against the emperor himself, and was almost the only one from all Germany to attend and subscribe at the Roman council celebrated for the same cause against the emperor. When at last the emperor was broken in strength, he returned freely to his own church and, while diligently expending his efforts in restoring that church and reforming its morals, while entirely devoted to purging the Slavs from the error of idolatry by preaching and miracles, and sensing that the hour of his departure was approaching, he assembled the brethren, earnestly exhorted them to mutual charity, foretold the peace of the Church which was to come, and fell asleep in the Lord on the sixteenth of the Kalends of July; he was enrolled in the number of the Saints by Hadrian VI.

The rites that the Roman Church observes in the consecration of churches and altars were first instituted by blessed Pope Sylvester. For although from the time of the Apostles there had already been places dedicated to God, which some called oratories and others churches, where assemblies were held on the first day of the week, and the Christian people were accustomed to pray, to hear the word of God, and to receive the Eucharist; these were not yet consecrated with so solemn a rite, nor had there yet been erected within them an altar raised as a title, which, anointed with chrism, would express the figure of our Lord Jesus Christ, who is our altar, our Victim, and our Priest.

Robert of Bellarmine, from the patrician family of the Bellarmines, had as his most devout mother Cynthia Cervini, sister of Pope Marcellus II. Adorned with exceptional piety and most pure morals, as a young man of eighteen he entered the Society of Jesus in Rome, and in it was until death an example in all the virtues of religious life. After completing his course in philosophy, he was sent first to Florence, then to Montereaale, to Padua, and to Louvain, where he wondrously fulfilled the office of teacher and preacher, though not yet a priest. Moreover, at Louvain, having been ordained a priest, he taught theology in such a way that he was already reckoned the most distinguished theologian in Europe. Recalled to Rome, he taught the theological discipline of controversies in the Roman College, where, also appointed as master of the spiritual life, he guided the angelic young man Aloysius along the paths of holiness. Enrolled against his earnest resistance in the number of the Cardinal Fathers by Pope Clement VIII, and shortly afterward consecrated a Bishop, he governed the Archdiocese of Capua most holily for three years; having laid down that office, he lived in Rome as the most upright and faithful counselor of the Supreme Pontiff until, at nearly eighty years of age, on the seventeenth of September in the year one thousand six hundred and twenty-one, he rested piously in the Lord. Besides the volumes of the Controversies he wrote many other notable works, among which an admirable golden catechism stands out. Pope Pius XI enrolled this most valiant champion of Catholic truth in the number of the Saints and declared him a Doctor of the universal Church.

Robert of Bellarmine, from the patrician family of the Bellarmines, had as his most devout mother Cynthia Cervini, sister of Pope Marcellus II. He shone from his earliest years with exceptional piety and most pure morals, desiring only to please God alone and to win souls for Christ. He frequented the family college of the Society of Jesus with the highest distinction of talent and modesty; and having entered that same Society at Rome at eighteen years of age, he was an example to all in the virtues of religious life. Having completed the course of philosophy at the Roman College, he was sent first to Florence, then to Montereale; thereafter to Padua to study sacred theology, and afterward to Louvain, where he wondrously fulfilled the office of preacher, though not yet a priest. Moreover, at Louvain, having been ordained a priest, he taught theology in such a way that he brought very many heretics back to the unity of the Church, and was reckoned the most distinguished theologian in Europe, so that Saint Charles, bishop of Milan, and others urgently desired him for themselves.

Roch, born at Montpellier, showed above all how greatly he burned with charity toward his neighbor when, as a most dreadful plague was raging far and wide throughout Italy, he left his homeland, undertook a journey through Italy, and going about its cities and towns, did not hesitate to spend himself in service to the sick and to lay down his life for his brethren. How pleasing to God was the zeal of this blessed man was made known by wondrous healings. For he rescued several who were infected with the plague from the peril of death and restored them to complete health by the sign of the Cross. Returning to his homeland, rich in virtues and merits, he died most holily, and veneration by the faithful immediately followed his death; this veneration is said to have received great increase at the Council of Constance, when the image of Roch was carried in solemn procession through that city, with all the people attending and the bishops approving, to drive away the threatening pestilence. And so his cult was wondrously spread throughout the entire world, which with religious devotion adopted him as patron before God against contagious pestilence. Having carefully weighed all these things, Pope Urban VIII granted that his feast day be celebrated with the ecclesiastical Office in those places where churches were dedicated to God in the name of Saint Roch.

10 For with the heart, we believe unto justice; but with the mouth, confession is unto salvation.
11 For Scripture says: "All those who believe in him shall not be confounded."
12 For there is no distinction between Jew and Greek. For the same Lord is over all, richly in all who call upon him.
13 For all those who have called upon the name of the Lord shall be saved.
14 Then in what way will those who have not believed in him call upon him? Or in what way will those who have not heard of him believe in him? And in what way will they hear of him without preaching?
15 And truly, in what way will they preach, unless they have been sent, just as it has been written: "How beautiful are the feet of those who evangelize peace, of those who evangelize what is good!"

16 But not all are obedient to the Gospel. For Isaiah says: "Lord, who has believed our report?"
17 Therefore, faith is from hearing, and hearing is through the Word of Christ.
18 But I say: Have they not heard? For certainly: "Their sound has gone forth throughout all the earth, and their words unto the limits of the whole world."
19 But I say: Has Israel not known? First, Moses says: "I will lead you into a rivalry with those who are not a nation; in the midst of a foolish nation, I will send you into wrath."
20 And Isaiah dares to say: "I was discovered by those who were not seeking me. I appeared openly to those who were not asking about me."
21 Then to Israel he says: "All day long I have stretched out my hands to a people who do not believe and who contradict me."

17 But if we are sons, then we are also heirs: certainly heirs of God, but also co-heirs with Christ, yet in such a way that, if we suffer with him, we shall also be glorified with him.
18 For I consider that the sufferings of this time are not worthy to be compared with that future glory which shall be revealed in us.
19 For the anticipation of the creature anticipates the revelation of the sons of God.
20 For the creature was made subject to emptiness, not willingly, but for the sake of the One who made it subject, unto hope.

21 For the creature itself shall also be delivered from the servitude of corruption, into the liberty of the glory of the sons of God.
22 For we know that every creature groans inwardly, as if giving birth, even until now;
23 and not only these, but also ourselves, since we hold the first-fruits of the Spirit. For we also groan within ourselves, anticipating our adoption as the sons of God, and the redemption of our body.
24 For we have been saved by hope. But a hope which is seen is not hope. For when a man sees something, why would he hope?
25 But since we hope for what we do not see, we wait with patience.

In Rome he either restored or enriched all the sacred places. He renewed the images of the saints worn out by age, and restored almost from new the Lateran patriarchium, which he had found in great ruin, and distributed the many relics found there among various churches. He assigned revenues for feeding the poor. He built the library of Saint Peter; founded the basilica of Saint George in Velabro; and constructed an oratory of Saint Cecilia on the Via Tiburtina. He greatly loved the clergy and distributed a donation to each of the priests and deacons. He translated the books of the Dialogues of Saint Gregory into Greek, and having accomplished various matters for the benefit of the Church no less devoutly than successfully, he was crowned with the glory of holiness.

He devoutly visited and venerated first the threshold of the Apostles in Rome, then other places made glorious by the blood and miracles of the martyrs, always intent on fasting and the other austerities of life. And, that God might thoroughly test his servant, he permitted him to fall into a burning and long-lasting fever; recovering from this, he left his brother in Rome and crossed to Palestine, and reverently went round almost all its cities and villages where anything memorable from the miracles of Christ or the Saints was to be seen. This pilgrimage lasted seven years, in which time he also visited Constantinople for religious purposes; returning from there to Italy, he spent ten years in divine service on Monte Cassino; and when these were completed he came to Rome and was sent by Pope Gregory III to Saint Boniface in Germany.

Recalled to Rome at the desire of Pope Gregory XIII, he taught the theological discipline of controversies in the Roman College; and there, appointed as master of the spiritual life, he guided the angelic young man Aloysius along the paths of holiness. He himself governed the Roman College and then the Neapolitan Province of the Society of Jesus according to the mind of Saint Ignatius. Summoned again to Rome, he was engaged by Clement VIII for the highest affairs of the Church with the greatest benefit to the Christian cause; then, resisting in vain and against his will, he was enrolled in the number of the Cardinals, because, as the Pontiff himself openly declared, the Church of God at that time had no one his equal in learning. Consecrated a Bishop by the same Pontiff, he governed the Archdiocese of Capua most holily for three years; having laid down that office, he lived in Rome until his death as the most upright and faithful counselor of the Supreme Pontiff. He wrote many notable works, earning above all the distinction that, following Saint Thomas as his guide and master and wisely aware of the needs of his own times, he with invincible doctrinal strength and a most ample collection of testimonies aptly drawn from the Holy Scriptures and the most rich font of the holy Fathers, defeated new errors, a strenuous advocate above all of the Catholic tradition and the rights of the Roman Pontificate. He is also remarkable for several booklets for fostering piety, and especially for his golden catechism, which, though occupied with other very weighty affairs, he did not omit to teach to boys and the uneducated both at Capua and at Rome. A contemporary Cardinal judged Robert to have been sent by God to instruct Catholics, to cultivate the pious, and to overthrow heretics; Saint Francis de Sales considered him a fountain of learning; Pope Benedict XIV called him the hammer of heretics; and Benedict XV pointed him out as a model for those who propagate and defend the Catholic religion.

Having gone to Rome, he was received into the hospital called that of the Incurables; the administration of which, being entrusted to him on account of his manifest virtues, he carried out with the greatest integrity and with truly fatherly solicitude. Counting himself the servant of all the sick, it was his custom to make their beds, wipe away their filth, tend their wounds, and help them with pious prayers and exhortations in their final agony; in these offices he gave outstanding examples of admirable patience, unconquered fortitude, and heroic charity. But, realizing that the study of letters was of the greatest help in bringing relief to souls in extreme peril — the only thing he aimed at — at thirty-two years of age he was not ashamed to undertake a second novitiate among boys in the very first elements of grammar. Afterward duly ordained a priest, having joined some companions to himself, he laid the first foundations of the congregation of Clerics Regular ministering to the sick, despite the vain opposition of the enemy of the human race. For Camillus, wondrously confirmed by a heavenly voice sent from a crucifix whose hands were lifted in a remarkable prodigy even from the wood, obtained the approval of his order by the Apostolic See, with his companions bound by a fourth and especially arduous vow of ministering to the sick even those infected by the plague. How acceptable to God and how profitable to the salvation of souls this institute was, Saint Philip Neri, who was Camillus's confessor, confirmed when he frequently testified that he had seen Angels suggesting words to the disciples of Camillus as they ministered to the dying.

Having gone to Rome and duly grounded in theological disciplines, he was ordained a priest by the Supreme Pontiff Benedict XIII out of obedience. Having been granted by the same the power to gather companions, he withdrew into solitude on Monte Argentario, whither the Blessed Virgin had already been inviting him, having also shown him a garment of dark color adorned with the insignia of the Passion of her Son, and there laid the foundations of a new congregation. This congregation, after many labors endured by him, quickly grew, enriched with illustrious men and with God's blessing; confirmed more than once by the Apostolic See, along with the rules which he himself had received from God in prayer, and with a fourth vow added of promoting the grateful memory of the Lord's Passion. He also founded sacred virgins to meditate assiduously on the surpassing charity of the divine Spouse. Amid all this, never failing in the preaching of the Gospel with inexhaustible hunger for souls, he led almost countless men, even the most abandoned or those fallen into heresy, onto the path of salvation. He was especially powerful in narrating the Passion of Christ, by which, dissolving in tears together with his hearers, he broke even the most hardened hearts to repentance.

Returning to Rome, when Pelagius had been taken away by pestilence, he was elected Pontiff with the full agreement of all: an honor he refused to accept as long as he could, for he hid in disguise in a cave; where, discovered by the sign of a fiery column, he was consecrated at Saint Peter's. In the pontificate he left many examples of learning and holiness to his successors. He received pilgrims daily at his table, among whom he received both an Angel and the Lord of Angels in the guise of a pilgrim. He generously sustained the poor of the city and of foreign lands, a list of whom he kept. He restored the Catholic faith in many places where it had been shaken. For he suppressed the Donatists in Africa, the Arians in Spain, and expelled the Agnoites from Alexandria. He refused to give the pallium to Syagrius, bishop of Autun, unless he expelled the newly baptized heretics from Gaul. He compelled the Goths to abandon the Arian heresy. Having sent to Britain the learned and holy monks Augustine and others, he converted the island to faith in Jesus Christ, being justly called by the priest Bede the Apostle of England. He broke the audacity of John, patriarch of Constantinople, who was arrogating to himself the title of bishop of the universal Church. He dissuaded the Emperor Maurice from his decree forbidding those who had been soldiers from becoming monks.

Romuald, born at Ravenna of the noble family of his father Sergius, withdrew as a young man to the nearby monastery of Classe for the sake of penance; where, inflamed more ardently to the pursuit of piety by the words of a religious man, and having seen blessed Apollinaris in the church once and again by night, which a servant of God had promised him would happen, he became a monk. He soon betook himself to Marinus, celebrated at that time in the region of the Veneti for holiness of life and the strictness of his discipline, in order to follow him as teacher and guide on the narrow and sublime way of perfection.

Romuald, born at Ravenna of the noble family of his father Sergius, withdrew as a young man to the nearby monastery of Classe for the sake of penance; where, inflamed more ardently to the pursuit of piety and refreshed by an apparition of blessed Apollinaris, he became a monk. He exercised himself assiduously in fasting and prayer, yet his countenance was so cheerful that he gladdened those who looked upon him. Burning with the desire for martyrdom, while setting out for Pannonia he was seized by illness and compelled to turn back. He was the founder of the institution of the Camaldolese monks, whom he saw in a vision ascending like angels a ladder reaching to heaven. Finally, when he was one hundred and twenty years old and had served God for a hundred of them in the greatest austerity of life, he passed to him in the year of salvation one thousand and twenty-seven, and was honorably buried at Fabriano in the church of his order.

Rose of Viterbo, born to pious parents, shone from infancy in every virtue, becoming a teacher of perfection almost before she had learned to speak. Loathing the vanities of the world, afflicting her little body with rough clothing, bare feet, a hair-shirt, fastings, and other austerities, she was continually free for divine contemplation. This remarkable holiness God was pleased to confirm with a notable miracle; for while still a girl she recalled her deceased aunt from death to life. To virginity, which she preserved perpetually, she stirred the hearts of those who beheld her by her mere appearance. Most devoted to charity toward the poor, when once in winter she was secretly carrying to them bread taken from her own portion, her father commanded her to reveal what she was hiding in her lap, and the bread was changed into roses.

Rufina and Secunda, sisters, Roman virgins, having rejected marriage with Armentarius and Verinus to whom they had been betrothed by their parents, because they had vowed their virginity to Jesus Christ, were arrested under the emperors Valerian and Gallienus. When the prefect Junius could move them neither by promises nor by threats from their purpose, he ordered Rufina first to be beaten with rods; during her scourging Secunda addressed the judge thus: What is this? You honor my sister while you afflict me with disgrace? Command both of us to be beaten together, for we confess Christ God together. Inflamed by these words, the judge ordered both to be cast into a dark and fetid prison. When that place was at once filled with a most brilliant light and a most sweet fragrance, they were shut into a burning bath. And when they emerged from that also unharmed, they were at once cast with a stone tied to the neck into the Tiber; rescued from there by an Angel, they were beheaded outside the City on the Via Aurelia at the tenth milestone. Their bodies, buried by the matron Plautilla on her estate and afterward brought to Rome, were interred in the Constantinian basilica near the baptistery.

Rupert, bishop of the church of Worms (formerly Vangionensis), who lived in the reign of Childebert II, king of the Franks, was so richly endowed with humility, gentleness, chastity, prudence, and every other virtue, that he brought honor to his lineage, which traced its descent from the kings of the Franks, by his exceptional faith and piety toward God. Filled with the Holy Spirit and exhibiting to his own flock the best form of living, he confirmed by his life and deeds whatever he taught in words, wondrously strengthening religion by the assiduity of prayer, prudence in giving counsel, justice in pronouncing judgments, and abstinence in mortifying the body with perpetual fasting; and he was so generous and kind toward the poor that he counted as his own only what he had bestowed upon the wretched and the needy.

Rupert, having established his episcopal see at Lake Wallersee and having been the first to erect at the river Salzach in the place called Salzburg a church in honor of blessed Peter, the prince of the Apostles, furnished with the ministries of clerics and other necessary things, immediately turned his mind to imbuing the rest of the people of Bavaria with the holy religion of Christ; and having joined to himself twelve companions in labor and toil, brought them, with God at last blessing his pious endeavors, to the Catholic faith. For this reason it came about that he merited to be called the Apostle of the Bavarians. When at last, having laid the foundations of many churches in various places, he had governed the episcopate for many years with the highest renown, having completed the most holy sacrifice of the Mass on the very Sunday of the Resurrection and having strengthened the souls of his disciples with fatherly exhortation, he departed to the Lord, there to enjoy eternal life for ever.

When the honor of the heavenly mystery was suddenly made known, Tobis and Tobias, astonished at the voice of the Archangel Raphael, fell prostrate on the ground and completely hid their trembling voice, because they had heard an unaccustomed voice. Why were you afraid, father Tobis and son Tobias? Did you think you had hired a heavenly being and, as it were, engaged an angel as an earthly laborer? The Angel concealed his name from you: I am Azarias, he said, the son of the great Ananias; he did not say: I am the Angel Raphael. He concealed the dignity of his name at first, lest he cause terror to the one who had hired him. For if he had said: I am an Angel, he could not have been Tobias's hired man. The dignity of the name was kept back, so that the greatness of the dignity might become clear in the end. See, beloved, how great is the merit of almsgiving: it merited having an Angel as a hired man. See how profitable it is to bury the dead, so that his offering might ascend through the Angel Raphael to the heavenly majesty. See, because almsgiving delivers from death and itself cleanses sins, makes a cleansing of the eyes, delivers from the darkness of sins. Tobis is led on his way; Sara, saddened by so many husbands, is united in marriage through the Angel.

But worldly affairs, unless they touched on divine things or the salvation of souls, he could not bear to hear or to speak of. His prudence in action so excelled that there was neither excess in measure nor error in order, gentle and meek toward his neighbor in all other things. Moreover, he won a great triumph over himself through fastings and vigils and the roughness of his garments, harshly mortifying the flesh; thence flowering in the higher Christian virtues, in the gravity of his counsels, and in the candor and peace of his soul, he became an outstanding example of religious piety. To submit to all willingly and to undertake freely the more menial tasks in preference to the other nuns, to minister even to the poor kneeling down, to wash and kiss the feet of lepers, was his habitual practice; and he did not, overcoming himself, recoil from their wounds dripping with corruption.

In the thirteenth century, when the more cultivated peoples of Italy were being torn apart by the dreadful schism of Frederick II and by bloody factions, the provident mercy of God raised up, besides others illustrious for holiness, seven men from the Florentine nobility who, united in charity, might offer a splendid example of fraternal love. These, namely Bonfilius Monaldus, Bonagiunta Manettus, Manettus Antellensis, Amadeus de Amideis, Uguccio degli Uguccioni, Sosteneius de Sosteniis, and Alexis Falconieri, were each visited by an apparition of the Mother of God and admonished to embrace a holier and more perfect manner of life, while they were praying more fervently at a certain assembly of devout men called the Laudesi, on the feast day sacred to the Virgin assumed into heaven, in the thirty-third year of that century. And so, having first conferred with the bishop of Florence, these seven men, putting aside the nobility of their birth and their wealth, clothed in a coarse and worn haircloth garment, withdrew on the eighth of September to a certain rustic chapel, that on that day they might begin the first steps of a holier life, the very day on which the Mother of God herself, born of mortal parents, had begun her most holy life.

In the thirteenth century, seven men from the Florentine nobility, namely Bonfilius Monaldus, Bonagiunta Manettus, Manettus Antellensis, Amadeus de Amideis, Uguccio degli Uguccioni, Sosteneius de Sosteniis, and Alexis Falconieri, withdrew to a certain rustic chapel, assiduously meditating on the Passion of Christ and the sorrows of his most afflicted Mother. To them the Blessed Virgin, appearing on the sacred day of Good Friday, showed them the mournful garment they were to wear, and signified that it would be most pleasing to her if they would establish a new religious order that would perpetually recall and promote the memory of the sorrows she had endured beneath the Cross of the Lord. Then those holy men, with the help of blessed Peter, Martyr of the Order of Preachers, founded the Order of the Servants of the Blessed Virgin, and with their companions began to go about cities and towns, everywhere preaching Christ crucified by word and example. Those whom one true love of brotherhood had united in life, one tomb in death likewise covered, and one veneration of the people followed. Wherefore Clement XI and Benedict XIII confirmed the indivisible cult offered to them; and Leo XIII enrolled them in the register of the Saints.

He very frequently cast out demons from the images of idols and from the bodies of men, and worked many other wonders, by which he drew innumerable men to faith in Jesus Christ, even predicting future events by a prophetic spirit. When he was about to depart from this life, having asked how many unbelievers remained in the city of Neocaesarea, and having been told there were only seventeen, he gave thanks to God, saying: There were as many believers when I began the episcopate. He wrote many things by which he brought renown to the Church of God, not only through miracles.

For that Joseph, sold through his brothers' envy and led into Egypt, prefigured the betrayal of Christ; this Joseph, fleeing the envy of Herod, carried Christ into Egypt. That one, keeping faith with his master, refused to lie with his mistress; this one, recognizing his Mistress, the mother of his Lord, as a virgin, and being himself continent, faithfully guarded her. To that one was given understanding of the mysteries of dreams; to this one it was given to become a conscious sharer in the heavenly sacraments.

For that Joseph, sold through his brothers' envy and led into Egypt, prefigured the betrayal of Christ; this Joseph, fleeing the envy of Herod, carried Christ into Egypt. That one, keeping faith with his master, refused to lie with his mistress; this one, recognizing his Mistress, the mother of his Lord, as a virgin, and being himself continent, faithfully guarded her. To that one was given understanding of the mysteries of dreams; to this one it was given to become a conscious sharer in the heavenly sacraments.
That one kept grain not for himself but for all the people; this one received the living Bread from heaven to keep, not only for himself but for the whole world. There is no doubt that this Joseph was a good and faithful man, to whom the Mother of the Savior was espoused. Faithful, I say, and wise, the servant whom the Lord appointed as the comfort of his Mother, the nurturer of his flesh, and the one sole most faithful cooperator on earth in the great counsel.
This is heightened by what is said, that he was of the house of David. For truly of the house of David, truly of royal stock is descended this man Joseph of noble birth, and nobler in mind: plainly a son of David, not degenerating from his father David.

Sergius, of Antiochene descent, his father Tiberius, born at Palermo in Sicily, when Conon had passed from life, in the year of Christ six hundred and eighty-seven, with the assent of God and the votes of all, was taken up in the sacred Lateran palace, and extinguished at its very outset the most abominable schism which the greed of the imperial exarch and the ambition of the archdeacon Paschal had stirred up. Coming to Rome when Adeodatus was Pontiff, he was admitted into the clergy of the Roman Church by him, and ordained by Leo II, the second of that name, as priest of the title of Saint Susanna, and he discharged his office with diligence.

During the persecution of Diocletian raging against Christians, Bishop Narcissus came as a fugitive to Augsburg, and not knowing where to turn, chanced to enter with his deacon Felix the house of Afra, a pagan woman; who, conscious of the public shame of her unchastity, and at first supposing they had come there out of a liking for debauchery, prepared a sumptuous banquet in her usual manner. But when the bishop came to take food and first composed himself entirely in body, face, and eyes for prayer, she, to whom every custom of praying was not only unknown but had never even been seen, was astonished at the unusual piety and asked who he was; and having learned that he was a bishop of Christians, and having observed him and his deacon spending the whole night in hymns and praises of God, and the dwelling illuminated by a most brilliant light sent down from heaven, and also the man's admirable gentleness and holiness — she was at once suffused with salutary shame and seized with fear equally, threw herself at his feet, and of her own accord confessed the stain of her unchastity.

Sabina, a Roman woman, wife of the distinguished man Valentinus, instructed in the teachings of the Christian faith by the virgin Seraphia, after the martyrdom of that holy Virgin, gathered her relics and buried them with pious funeral rites. Because of this, shortly afterward, under the Emperor Hadrian, she was arrested and brought before the judge Elpidius. Who said to her: Are you not that Sabina most noble both by birth and by marriage? And she replied: I am; but I give thanks to my Lord Jesus Christ, who has freed me from the power of demons through the intercession of his servant Seraphia. When, after many attempts to make her change her purpose, he could not move her from the constancy of her faith, the prefect pronounced sentence that she had despised the gods and condemned her to death. Her body was laid by Christians in the same tomb in which she herself had placed Seraphia, the teacher of her faith.

Clothe priests most splendidly with justice and with the exultation of a proven, immaculate, and sincere faith. To Orthodox rulers who, in preference to all the splendor of purple or gold, to pearls and precious stones, have gained you as their diadem and garment and most firm adornment of their kingdom, direct their scepters in tranquil and prosperous state. Cast down at their feet and subdue the faithless nations that blaspheme you and the God begotten of you; and confirm the subjected people to persevere in the sweet obedience of God's commandment. Crown this your city, which has you as its tower and foundation, with the triumphs of victory, and girding it with your strength guard it as the dwelling of God; ever preserve the beauty of the temple; deliver those who praise you from every peril and anguish of soul. Grant redemption to captives; show yourself a comfort to pilgrims destitute of shelter and of every protection. Stretch out your helping hand to the whole world, that we may bring these your solemn feasts together with the present festival we celebrate to a most splendid close in joy and exultation, in Christ Jesus the King of all and our true God, to whom be glory and might together with the holy Father who is the principle of life, and the coeternal and consubstantial and co-reigning Spirit, now and always and for ever and ever. Amen.

Having at last been ordained a priest, the faith and fervor of spirit with which he first offered Mass, with the same he continued to celebrate the sacred rites for his entire life. Meanwhile, burning with zeal for the salvation of souls, he devoted himself entirely to their benefit. He undertook the governance of the Sisters of the Infant Jesus, established for the education of girls; and he not only directed them most prudently but also defended them from destruction. He then turned his attention to instructing the boys of the common people in religion and good morals. And indeed for this purpose God had raised him up: namely, that by founding a new family of religious men in his Church, he might provide a permanent and effective means for the schools of boys, especially the poor. The office entrusted to him by God's providence, through very many contradictions and great hardships, he fulfilled successfully, having founded the brotherhood which he named after the Christian Schools.

The sacrilegious deed committed in secret and the Martyr's glory were made known by a remarkable prodigy sent by God. For when the lifeless body had begun to be carried downstream on the current, burning torches appeared floating and moving about on the waters. Wherefore the body was lifted from the bank the following morning, and the canons, fearing the king's anger not at all, then carried it in solemn procession into the metropolitan church and committed it to burial. But as the memory of the unconquered priest grew day by day, confirmed by miracles and by the great veneration of the faithful, especially of those in danger of losing their reputation, after more than three hundred years at last, in the judicial recognition of the body that had lain so long under the earth, his tongue was found incorrupt and vivid; and exhibited six years later to judges delegated by the Apostolic See, it swelled up at once in a fresh prodigy and changed from a dark red to a deep purple. These and other signs having been duly verified, Pope Benedict XIII on the nineteenth of March in the year of salvation one thousand seven hundred and twenty-nine enrolled this first defender of the seal of the sacrament, who sealed the secrecy of the confessional with his blood, in the catalogue of the holy Martyrs.

Burning with zeal for the salvation of souls, he directed all his efforts to preserving the flock entrusted to him in the integrity of faith and morals and defending it from the poisoned pastures of unbelievers and heretics. Hence he endeavored both to expel the followers of Novatus from the city and to have the Jews punished according to the laws, who in their fury had conspired for the slaughter of Christians. The singular zeal of Cyril for the preservation of the Catholic faith shone forth especially against Nestorius, bishop of Constantinople, who claimed that Jesus Christ had been born of the Virgin Mary as man only and not as God, and that divinity had been conferred on him as a reward for his merits; and when he had tried in vain to correct him, he denounced him to the holy Supreme Pontiff Celestine.

He decreed that deacons should cover their left arms with linen vestments, and granted that the paschal candle be blessed in the parishes. He also provided that no cleric should be offered a drink in public except in the dwellings of the faithful and especially of clerics. Having most holily governed the Church for one year, four months, and seven days, he rested in peace; and was buried beside the body of Saint Lawrence the martyr on the Via Tiburtina, on the seventh of the Kalends of January, under the rule of Honorius and the younger Theodosius. In a single ordination in the month of December he created ten priests, three deacons, and eight bishops in various places.

The bodies of the Saints Stephen the Protomartyr, Gamaliel, Nicodemus, and Abibo, giving forth a most sweet fragrance, were found by John, bishop of Jerusalem, near Jerusalem. When news of this spread, a great multitude of people gathered there, and many who were ill and weak from various diseases returned home sound and whole. The sacred body of Saint Stephen, which was then received with the greatest solemnity in the holy church of Sion, was subsequently translated under the younger Theodosius to Constantinople, and from there to Rome under the Supreme Pontiff Pelagius I, and was placed in the tomb of Saint Lawrence the Martyr in the Ager Veranus.
