The bodies of the Saints Stephen the Protomartyr, Gamaliel, Nicodemus, and Abibo, which had long lain in an obscure and squalid place, were found near Jerusalem in the reign of the Emperor Honorius, after the priest Lucian had been divinely warned. For when Gamaliel had appeared to him in sleep in the grave and venerable form of an elder, he pointed out the place where the bodies were lying, commanding him to go to John, bishop of Jerusalem, and deal with him to have those bodies buried in a more fitting manner.

God illustrated the zeal of this most holy man for the salvation of his neighbors with the greatest miracles. Among these was the remarkable one by which he crossed the river Vandal near Vizovgrad, which was overflowing with waters, using no boat, and drew his companions across also on his cloak spread over the waves. Having led an admirable manner of life for about forty years after his profession, and having foretold to his brethren the day of his death, on the very feast of the Assumption of the Virgin, after completing the canonical Hours and receiving the sacraments of the Church with the highest veneration, with the words: Into your hands, O Lord, he rendered his spirit to God in the year of salvation one thousand two hundred and fifty-seven. Pope Clement VIII enrolled him, made illustrious even after death by miracles, in the number of the Saints.

The Holy Cross of the Lord, placed by Helena on Mount Calvary and from there carried off by Chosroes, king of the Persians, was recovered by the Emperor Heraclius after a threefold victory over the Persians, and borne on his own shoulders to the mountain to which the Savior had carried it. This deed was commended by a notable miracle. For Heraclius, adorned as he was with gold and gems, was forced to halt at the gate that leads to Mount Calvary. For the more he tried to advance, the more he seemed to be held back. And while Heraclius himself and all the others were astonished by this, Zacharias, bishop of Jerusalem, said: See, Emperor, lest in carrying the Cross in this triumphal adornment you imitate too little the poverty and humility of Jesus Christ. Then Heraclius, casting aside his magnificent garments, removing his shoes, and clothing himself in a common garment, easily completed the rest of the way. And so the solemnity of the Exaltation of the Holy Cross, which was annually celebrated on this day, began to be held in greater honor in memory of this event.

The body of Saint Valentine the Bishop, which had rested peacefully for some years buried in the castle of Mayen, was at last around the year of the Lord seven hundred and twenty-three conveyed by Liutprand, king of the Lombards, to Trent; from which afterward Tassilo, duke of Bavaria, son of Odilo, caused it to be honorably transported to Passau on the fourth of the Nones of August, around the year of the Lord seven hundred and seventy-seven, and to be placed between two walls, before the doors of the church of the blessed Protomartyr Stephen, where the bishop's seat is.

For the consecrated woman, lowering her head into her hands, had poured a river of tears upon the table, through which she drew the clear air to rain. Nor did that flood of rain follow long after her prayer; but the harmony between prayer and flood was such that even as she raised her head from the table with the thunder, one and the same moment was both the raising of her head and the descent of the rain. Then the man of God, amid lightning and thunder and the flooding of a mighty rain, seeing that he could not return to the monastery, began to complain in sorrow, saying: May almighty God pardon you, sister: what have you done? She answered him: Behold, I begged you and you were unwilling to hear me; I prayed to my God and he heard me. Now therefore, if you can, go out and, leaving me, return to the monastery. But he, unable to go out of doors, who had been unwilling to remain of his own choice, remained against his will. And so it came to pass that they spent the whole night in vigil, and through the sacred conversations of the spiritual life refreshed one another in mutual exchange.

This holy Pontiff, imitating the mercy of the good shepherd Jesus Christ, showed himself benign also toward those who had lapsed into idolatry out of fear of persecution; but thereby gave offense at the wicked severity of certain men among the clergy, led by one Heraclius. Whose burning zeal boiled over so against Eusebius that they not only harassed him but, by stirring up disorders and discords in Rome, provided the tyrant Maxentius with an occasion, under the pretext of restoring public peace, to exile the holy Pontiff as though he were an author of sedition to Sicily. There, worn out by the hardships of exile, he ended his life on the sixth of the Nones of October. His body was then translated to Rome and deposited in the cemetery of Callixtus on the Via Appia. Pope Saint Damasus afterward added to the tomb of Eusebius a metrical epitaph, in which, commemorating the slanders of malicious men, his exile, and his death, he declared the holy bishop Eusebius a Martyr. He governed the Church for two years, eight months, and sixteen days; and in a single ordination in the month of December he created thirteen priests, three deacons, and fourteen bishops in various places.

He decreed that no faithful person should fast at all on Sunday or on Thursday, because the pagans observed those days as if dedicated to a sacred fast. Likewise he established that the consecrated offerings sent through the Bishop, which were called the fermentum, should be distributed to the churches, lest the Priests, celebrating in their titular churches together with their people, should judge themselves separated from communion with the Bishop. Having suffered much in the persecution of Maximian, he rested at last in the Lord under Constantine, on the fourth of the Ides of December, and was buried in the cemetery of Callixtus on the Via Appia. In a single ordination he created six Priests and five Deacons. Eleven Bishops in various places.

Scholastica, sister of the venerable Father Benedict, as Saint Pope Gregory writes in the second book of the Dialogues, consecrated to almighty God from her very infancy, was accustomed to come to him once a year; and the man of God would go out to meet her not far from the entrance of the monastery property. But on a certain day, when, due to a sudden flooding of rain which Scholastica obtained from God, and with the darkness of night already pressing in, the venerable brother could not go out of doors, it came to pass that they spent the whole night in vigil and, through the sacred conversations of the spiritual life, refreshed one another in mutual exchange. When on the following day that same venerable woman had returned to her own cell, the man of God returned to the monastery. But behold, three days later, as he stood in his cell with his eyes raised to the air, he saw his sister's soul departing from her body and penetrating in the form of a dove the hidden places of heaven. Then Benedict sent brothers to place her body in the tomb he had prepared for himself. Thus it came to pass that those whose mind had always been one in God, their bodies too were not separated in burial.

We must know that, just as a garment is woven on two beams, the upper and the lower, so charity is held in two precepts, namely in the love of God and of neighbor. For it is written: You shall love the Lord your God with your whole heart and with your whole soul, and your neighbor as yourself. In this matter it must be noted that in the love of neighbor a measure of love is set, when it is said: You shall love your neighbor as yourself. But the love of God is bound by no measure, when it is said: You shall love the Lord your God with your whole heart, with your whole soul, with your whole strength. For one is not commanded how much to love, but from what depth, when it is said, From your whole; because he truly loves God who keeps nothing for himself. Therefore whoever takes care to have the wedding garment at the marriage feast must keep the two precepts of charity.

We must know that the name of Angels is a name of office, not of nature. For those holy Spirits of the heavenly homeland are indeed always Spirits, but they cannot always be called Angels; because they are Angels only when some message is announced through them. Hence the Psalmist also says: Who makes his Angels spirits; as if to say plainly: Those whom he always has as Spirits, he also makes Angels when he wills. Now those who announce lesser things are called Angels; but those who announce the highest things are called Archangels. Hence it is that not just any Angel, but the Archangel Gabriel, is sent to the Virgin Mary. For it was fitting that the highest Angel should come for this ministry, who was to announce the highest of all things. They are also designated by individual names, so that their power in operation might be indicated by their names. For Michael means: Who is like God? Gabriel means: Strength of God; and Raphael means: Medicine of God.

The king therefore, foreknowing the future, was aware that death for the sake of justice was imminent; having foretold it, he set out to the church of Saint Alban the Martyr at Odense, as to the place of his contest: and strengthened by the sacraments, he was commending his agony to the Lord. Soon a crowd of conspirators arrived there, and they attempted to set fire to the church, break down the doors, and burst into it. When they could not accomplish this, approaching the windows they did not cease to hurl stones and arrows with great force at the holy king, who was kneeling in prayer for his enemies, until he was struck by the blows of stones and weapons, and finally pierced by a lance, and crowned with glorious martyrdom, fell before the altar with arms extended, in the reign of Gregory VII on the apostolic throne. God afterward illustrated his Martyr by many miracles. For Denmark, oppressed by a severe famine and various calamities, paid the penalty for the committed sacrilege. Several also afflicted with various ailments obtained remedy and soundness at his tomb. And when the queen attempted by night to secretly steal away his sacred body and transfer it elsewhere, she was terrified by a great brightness sent from heaven and abandoned her purpose.

The name of Bede became so quickly illustrious for learning and piety that Pope Saint Sergius thought of summoning him to Rome, namely to work on the definition of very difficult questions that had arisen concerning sacred things. He wrote several books for the correction of the morals of the faithful and for the vindication and defense of the faith, by which he won so great a reputation among all that Saint Boniface, bishop and martyr, proclaimed him a light of the Church; Lanfranc called him a doctor of the English; and the Council of Aachen called him an admirable doctor. Indeed his writings were read publicly in churches even while he was still alive. And when this happened, since it was not permitted to call him a saint, they honored him with the title of Venerable; which title afterward was always considered as his very own even in subsequent times. The power of his teaching was all the more effective in that it was confirmed by holiness of life and religious virtues. For this reason the disciples whom he had many and outstanding to form, he made distinguished by his diligence and example not only in letters and knowledge but also in holiness.

Knowledge is fitting for those who mourn, who have now come to know in the Scriptures what evils hold them bound, which they pursued in ignorance as goods and useful things; of whom it is said here: Blessed are they who mourn now. Fortitude is fitting for those who hunger and thirst: for they labor in their desire for joy from true goods, and in their wish to turn love away from earthly and bodily things; of whom it is said here: Blessed are they who hunger and thirst for justice. Counsel is fitting for the merciful: for this is the one remedy of escaping so many evils, that we forgive as we wish to be forgiven; and that we help others as far as we are able, as we also wish to be helped in what we cannot do ourselves; of whom it is said here: Blessed are the merciful, for God will have mercy on them.

Let us write in the spirit the mysteries, if we wish to speak: let us write the herald of Christ, not on tablets of stone, but on tablets of flesh, that is to say of the heart. For he who speaks of John prophesies of Christ. Let us speak of John, let us also speak of Christ: that our mouth too may be opened, which in so great a priest the reins of a wavering faith restrained as if he were an irrational beast.

But he wrote, saying: John is his name. And here a name is not imposed, but confirmed. And rightly his tongue was at once loosed; because faith unloosed what unbelief had bound. Let us therefore also believe, that we may speak; that our tongue, which is bound by the chains of unbelief, may be loosed by the voice of reason.

He wrote many things, both in prose and in verse, with admirable piety and eloquence; by which, in the judgment of learned and holy men, he so succeeded that nothing in them can be found, nor can anyone rightly call into question, anything that is not in accord with the rule of true piety and the Catholic religion. He was the most ardent champion of the consubstantiality of the Son. And just as no one was placed before him for the praise of his life, so also he easily surpassed all in the gravity of his speech. Leading the life of a monk in the country in those pursuits of writing and reading, he passed to eternal life in old age under the Emperor Theodosius.

Isidore wrote the books of Etymologies, and On Ecclesiastical Offices, and very many others so useful to Christian and ecclesiastical discipline, that Pope Leo IV did not hesitate to write to the bishops of Britain that, just as the sayings of Jerome and Augustine, so also the sayings of Isidore were to be retained, when an unusual matter arose that could not be determined by the Canons. Several sentences from his writings are also found included among the canonical laws of the Church. He presided over the Fourth Council of Toledo, the most celebrated of all the councils of Spain. Finally, having banished the Arian heresy from Spain, and having publicly foretold his own death and the devastation of the kingdom by the arms of the Saracens, after having governed his church for about forty years, he passed to heaven from Seville in the year six hundred and thirty-six. His body, first buried between his brother Leander and his sister Florentina, as he himself had commanded, was bought for a great price from Benavet the Saracen who ruled in Seville by Ferdinand I, king of Castile and Leon, and transferred to Leon, and a temple was built in his honor, where, renowned for miracles, he is venerated with great devotion by the people.

Sebastian, born of a father from Narbonne and a mother from Milan, was dear to Diocletian on account of the nobility of his lineage and his virtue. As commander of the first cohort, he assisted the Christians, whose faith he secretly practiced, with his services and resources; and those among them who seemed to fear the force of torments, he so strengthened by his encouragement that many of them freely offered themselves to the torturers for the sake of Jesus Christ. Among these were the brothers Marcus and Marcellian, who were in custody at Rome in the house of Nicostratus, whose wife Zoë recovered the voice she had lost through the prayer of Sebastian. When these matters were reported to Diocletian, he summoned Sebastian, and after rebuking him most vehemently, attempted by every art to turn him away from the faith of Christ. But when he availed nothing either by promises or by threats, he ordered him to be bound to a stake and shot through with arrows.

But far be it from the hearts of the faithful to say that fate is anything at all. For it is God alone, who created it, who governs the life of man. Nor were the stars made for man's sake, but man was made for the sake of the stars; and if a star is said to be man's fate, man is held to be subject to its ministries. Surely, when Jacob, coming forth from the womb, held with his hand the heel of his elder brother, the elder could by no means have come forth perfectly unless the one following had already begun; and yet, though the mother had brought them both forth at one and the same moment, the quality of life of each was not the same.

But when Eulalius had thrust himself into the City and had provided occasion for public sedition, Honorius, moved by the matter, decreed by rescript that Eulalius was to be expelled from the City, and Boniface to be brought into it; which was confirmed by a full synod of bishops. And so Boniface, having returned, strove with earnest care to restore all to mutual concord, for which he also made provision for the future, lest after his death the Church should be torn by a more grievous schism. He rejoiced in the devotion of most pious emperors, and against the enemies of God's grace, made use not only of apostolic but also of royal edicts; and although he himself was most learned, he nonetheless sought the responses of the blessed Bishop Augustine against the books of the Pelagians; and Augustine deferred to him so greatly that he sent his writings to him not so much to be learned by heart as to be examined and corrected.

But when his disciples saw him lying on his back in prayer in that violent fever, they humbly begged him to turn on his side and rest face downward for a little while, until the force of the illness should abate. But Martin said to them: "Suffer me rather to look up to heaven than to the earth, that my spirit, about to set out on its journey to the Lord, may be directed upward." And when death was now at hand, seeing the enemy of the human race, he said: "What do you stand here for, bloodthirsty beast? You will find nothing in me, you accursed one." At these words, having lived eighty-one years, he rendered his soul to God; and a choir of Angels received it, and many heard them singing divine praises, and among them especially Saint Severinus, Bishop of Cologne.

But since one who does the will of the Father is called the sister and brother of the Lord — on account of each sex that is gathered to the faith — it is not to be wondered at; but it is greatly to be wondered at, how he may also be called mother. For he deigned to call his faithful disciples brothers, saying: Go, tell my brothers. Let one therefore who has been able to become a brother of the Lord by coming to the faith inquire how he may also be a mother.

But when many disciples came to him daily, he built twelve monasteries and fortified them with most holy rules. Afterward he moved to Cassino, where he broke the image of Apollo that was still worshiped there, overturned the altar, and burned the sacred groves; and there he built a chapel of Saint Martin and a small church of Saint John, and instructed the townspeople and inhabitants in the Christian precepts. Wherefore, the divine grace increased in Benedict day by day, so that he also foretold things to come by the spirit of prophecy. When Totila, king of the Goths, heard of this, and wished to test whether it were so, he sent ahead his swordbearer in royal attire and with a royal retinue, to pretend to be the king. But when he saw him, Benedict said: "Put off, my son, put off what you are wearing, for it does not belong to you." And to Totila himself he foretold his coming to the City, his crossing of the sea, and his death after nine years.

But tell us, John, since you are still held within the dark womb of your mother, how do you behold and hear? How do you contemplate divine things? How do you leap and exult? "The mystery that is being accomplished," he says, "is great, and an act removed from human comprehension. Rightly do I renew nature for the sake of him who is about to renew what is above nature. I see, even though I am still in the womb, because I see in the womb the Sun of justice. With my ears I perceive, because I am born the voice of the great Word. I cry out, because I behold the only-begotten Son of the Father clothed in flesh. I exult, because I see the Maker of all things taking upon himself the form of man. I leap, because I consider the Redeemer of the world incorporated. I go before his coming, and in some manner I go ahead of you by my confession."

But as all the rest endured those kinds of torments with a brave and willing spirit, Dionysius, who was more than a hundred years old, was beheaded along with the others on the seventh day before the Ides of October. Of him it is handed down to memory that, after his head was cut off, he took it up and walked, carrying it in his hands, for about two miles. He wrote admirable and truly heavenly books: on the divine names, on the celestial and ecclesiastical hierarchy, on mystical theology, and certain others.

But who could suffice to contemplate how gloriously the Queen of the world set forth today, and with what fervor of devotion the whole multitude of the heavenly legions came forth to meet her; with what songs she was led to the throne of glory; with what a serene countenance, what a calm face, what divine embraces she was received by her Son, and exalted above every creature, with the honor due to so great a Mother, with the glory that so befitted such a Son?
Most blessed indeed were the kisses pressed upon the lips of the nursing Child, as the Virgin Mother cradled him in her virginal lap. But shall we not deem still more blessed those which today, in that blessed greeting, she received from the lips of him who sits at the right hand of the Father, as she ascended to the throne of glory, singing the bridal song and saying: Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth?

But who could suffice to contemplate how gloriously the Queen of the world set forth today, and with what fervor of devotion the whole multitude of the heavenly legions came forth to meet her; with what songs she was led to the throne of glory; with what a serene countenance, what a calm face, what divine embraces she was received by her Son, and exalted above every creature, with the honor due to so great a Mother, and with the glory that so befitted such a Son?

But his Gospel also differs greatly from the others. Matthew, as it were, begins to write of man: The book of the generation of Jesus Christ, the son of David, the son of Abraham; Luke begins from the priesthood of Zechariah; Mark from the prophecy of Malachi and Isaiah. The first has the face of a man, on account of the genealogy; the second the face of a calf, on account of the priesthood; the third the face of a lion, on account of the voice of one crying in the desert, Prepare the way of the Lord, make straight his paths. But our John soars, as it were, on eagle's wings to the heights, and arrives at the Father himself, saying: In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and God was the Word.

But we also learn from the Lord's account that there will be two orders of the reprobate: one of those who have been initiated into the mysteries of the Christian faith but despise the exercise of its works, to whom he testifies at judgment: Depart from me, you accursed, into everlasting fire, which was prepared for the devil and his angels; for I was hungry, and you did not give me to eat. The other of those who either never received the faith and the mysteries of Christ, or who received them and afterward abandoned them through apostasy: of whom he says: But he who does not believe is already judged, because he does not believe in the name of the only-begotten Son of God.

But he also went as far as Pavia and prevailed upon him to cease from the oppression of the Ravennans. He approached Rachis, who was pressing Perugia with a sharp siege, and moved him with such great majesty of prayer, that he both desisted from all attack and, inflamed with love of religion, exchanged royal dignity and the military cloak for the monastic way of life and habit. Consulted by the Franks, he transferred that kingdom from Childeric, a foolish and slothful man, to Pepin, outstanding in piety and fortitude, by apostolic authority. He celebrated many synods and councils for the restoration of ecclesiastical discipline.

But perhaps someone may say to himself in silent thoughts: What, or how much, did either of these fishermen leave at the Lord's word, who had scarcely anything at all? But in this matter, dearest brethren, we ought to weigh the affection rather than the wealth. He leaves much who retains nothing for himself; he leaves much who, however little it may be, forsakes everything. Certainly we both possess what we have with desire, and what we do not have we seek with longing. Much, therefore, did Peter and Andrew leave, since each of them also forsook even the desire of possessing.

But above all, his care was to restore piety among Catholics. The splendor of the temples, the handing on of the catechism, the frequency of sermons and of the sacraments received increase from him. He himself, by opening everywhere schools for the instruction of youth in learning and piety, by founding at Rome a college for Germans, monasteries for women in troubled marriages and for girls in danger, houses for orphans and catechumens of both sexes, and other works of piety, labored without ceasing for the winning of souls for God; and he was heard to say at times that, if the choice were given him, he would rather live in uncertainty of beatitude and in the meantime serve God and work for the salvation of his neighbor, than die at once with the certainty of that same glory. He exercised a wondrous authority over demons. Saint Philip Neri and others beheld his face radiant with a heavenly light. Finally, in the sixty-fifth year of his age, he departed to the embrace of his Lord, whose greater glory he had always had upon his lips and had always sought in all things. Gregory XV, illustrious for his great merits toward the Church and for miracles, enrolled him in the roll of the Saints; and Pius XI, acceding to the wishes of the sacred clergy, appointed and declared him the heavenly Patron of all Spiritual Exercises.

But in what manner of sonship did John become the son of the Virgin, or she become his mother? This is not accomplished by nature, not by conception, not by birth, not by entering the womb to be born anew, not by adoption for the gaining of an inheritance in temporal things, nor by imitation, nor by teaching given. Nor were these things to be expressed in Christ's word; nor was the speech made as if it were a figure, but we read thus said by Christ: Woman, behold your son; so that, all superfluity of words excluded, we might penetrate the secret of the mystery. We understand mystically, therefore, that in John are all the souls of the elect, of whom the Blessed Virgin became mother through love; for "son" in Greek is the name of love. For all the love of Christ passes into love for the Virgin, so that it may rightly be called the love, that is, the son, of the Virgin, and it has the Virgin more truly for mother than she who conceived it from sin, condemned to the world, by receiving seed.

But let us consider what prudence it requires: assuredly that of the serpent. For just as the serpent commits itself wholly, and does not care in the least if its very body must be cut, so long as it keeps its head intact; so too you should care nothing for losing the rest, apart from the faith, whether it be necessary to pour out your money, your body, or even life itself. For faith is the head and the root; and once it is preserved, even if you lose everything, you will recover everything again with greater glory. For this reason he commanded them to be neither merely simple nor merely prudent, but mingled both of these into one, that they might be turned into virtue.

But in the meantime it must be known that the Priscillianist heretics think that every man is born under the constitution of the stars; and in support of their error they assume the fact that a new star appeared when the Lord appeared in the flesh, and they think that the fate of the Lord was that same star that appeared. But if we weigh the words of the Gospel, where it is said of that same star: Until it came and stood over the place where the child was — since not the child ran to the star, but the star, if it may be so said, ran to the child — then not the star was the fate of the child, but it was the child who appeared that was the fate of the star.

But I now clearly see that you did not speak thus as though in indignation or wishing to confound the tender modesty of the Virgin Mother, when you said: What is this to me and to you — since, when the servants came to you at the Mother's command, you without hesitation did what she had suggested. Why then, brethren, why did he respond thus at first? Surely on our account, so that those who have turned to the Lord may no longer be troubled by care for earthly parents, and that such ties may not hinder spiritual exercise. For as long as we are of the world, it is plain that we are debtors to our parents; but once we have left ourselves behind, we are still more free from anxiety on their account. The Lord therefore taught us most excellently not to be anxious about the relatives of our flesh beyond what religion demands, when he replied to his own Mother, and such a Mother: What is this to me and to you, woman?

But the nature of salt is always the same and can never be changed. But since man is subject to change, and blessed is he alone who has persevered in all the works of God to the end: for this reason those who are called the salt of the earth are warned to persevere in the power of the authority entrusted to them, lest, having become tasteless, they season nothing, and they themselves, having lost the sense of the savour received, cannot quicken what is corrupt, and, cast out of the storehouse of the Church, may be trodden underfoot by the feet of those who walk, together with those whom they had salted.

But the things that are hard for those who labor are softened for those who love. For this reason it was brought about by the dispensation of divine mercy, that the inner man, renewed from day to day, no longer placed under the law but already freed under grace from the burden of innumerable observances — which was in truth a heavy yoke, yet fittingly imposed upon a stiff neck — might, with the ease of simple faith and good hope and holy charity, bear lightly whatever the prince who has been cast out might have brought upon the outer man from without.

But since the fragility of human flesh and mind is entangled in inextricable vices through a certain headlong desire of sinning, the future purification of all guilt was prefigured by the eighth day of circumcision, that is, by the age of the Resurrection. For it is this that is meant: Every male that opens the womb shall be called holy to the Lord. For by the words of the law the birth of a Virgin was promised. And truly holy, because without stain. Moreover, that it is he who is signified by the law, the words of the Angel, repeated in the same manner, declare: What shall be born, he says, shall be called Holy, the Son of God.

But who would not be moved by what the Lord replied most graciously to his most holy Mother at those nuptials, saying: What is this to me and to you, woman? What is it to you and to him, O Lord? Is it not what belongs to a son and a mother? Do you ask what pertains to her, when you are the blessed fruit of her immaculate womb? Is she not the one who, with her modesty preserved, conceived you and brought you forth without corruption? Is she not the one in whose womb you dwelt for nine months, at whose virginal breasts you were nursed, with whom, already twelve years old, you came down from Jerusalem and were subject to her? Now therefore, O Lord, why do you trouble her, saying: What is this to me and to you? In every way, greatly.

But since one who does not find his beloved must rise, must go round the city — that is, must traverse the holy Church of the elect in mind and inquiry — and seek him through the streets and the broad ways, that is, must look at those who walk by narrow and broad paths, so that if he can find any trace of him in them, he may seek his footsteps: for there are some even in secular life who have something imitable in the exercise of virtue. But those who seek are found by the watchmen who keep the city: because the holy Fathers who guard the state of the Church come to meet our good endeavors, to teach us by their word or their writing. And when we have passed a little beyond them, we find him whom we love: because our Redeemer, though in humanity he was man among men, was yet in his divinity above men.

But one who wishes to be dismissed, let him come to the temple, let him come to Jerusalem, let him wait for the Christ of the Lord, let him receive the Word of God into his hands, let him embrace him in deeds as with certain arms of his faith: then he will be dismissed, so that he may not see death, who has seen Life. You see the abundant grace poured out upon all through the generation of the Lord, and the prophecy denied to unbelievers, not to the just. Behold, Simeon also prophesies that the Lord Jesus Christ came for the fall and the resurrection of many, that he might discern the merits of the just and the unjust; and according to the quality of our deeds, as a true and just judge, he decrees either punishments or rewards.

But since the soul itself did not know him by whom it was to be healed, and had eyes in the flesh to see bodily things — it did not yet have sound eyes in the heart to recognize God lying hidden. He did what could be seen, so that it might be healed by the one who could not be seen. He entered the place where there lay a great multitude of the infirm, the blind, the lame, the withered.

But since he loved a certain consecrated woman in that same monastery above the rest, Galla at once added: I ask that Sister Benedicta come with me. To which he replied: No, but such a one shall come with you; as for her whom you ask for, she will follow on the thirtieth day. When these things had been accomplished, the vision of the Apostle standing by and speaking with her was taken away. But she at once summoned the mother of the whole community and told her what she had seen and what she had heard. And on the third day she died together with the sister who had been appointed to go; while she whom she herself had asked for followed on the thirtieth day. Which event remains memorable in that monastery even to this day, and the younger consecrated virgins who are there now are accustomed to relate carefully how it was handed down from the preceding mothers, as if they themselves had been present at so great a miracle at that time.

But what need is there to confirm what we say by our own arguments or by the examples of holy men, when it is permitted to bring forward the very words of the Lord in the midst, and by those same words to move the religious and God-fearing soul, by which he openly and without controversy declares: So therefore, every one of you who does not renounce all that he possesses cannot be my disciple? And in another place, having first said: If you wish to be perfect, go, sell all that you have and give to the poor; he afterward added: Come, follow me.

But what precisely is done on this present day, let him know who did it; yet we ought to believe, and not doubt, that whatever it is, it was done for us. For the fact that the Chaldeans, drawn by the rays of a brighter star, came to adore him, is a hope of adoring the true God given to the Gentiles. The fact that the waters were changed in a new order into wine is a foretaste of the new chalice's sacrament given to us. And the fact that the Lamb of God was baptized is the salutary gift of regenerating Baptism dedicated to us.

But we must know that one who is the sister and brother of Christ by believing becomes his mother by preaching. For as it were one gives birth to the Lord, when one has poured him into the heart of a hearer; and one becomes his mother by preaching, if through her voice the love of the Lord is generated in the mind of a neighbor. To confirm this aptly for us, blessed Felicity is here, whose birthday we celebrate today; who, by believing, was a handmaid of Christ, and, by preaching, became a mother of Christ. For she feared to leave her seven sons alive in the flesh behind her — as it is read in the more authentic accounts of her acts — just as carnal parents usually fear to send their children ahead of them in death.

But when the Emperor Constantine obtained health and salvation through the sacrament of Baptism, then for the first time, by a law promulgated by him, it was permitted throughout the whole world for Christians to build churches; and he encouraged them to this sacred building not only by edict but also by his own example. For he both dedicated a church to the Savior in his Lateran palace, and adjoined to it a basilica in the name of Saint John the Baptist, in that place where he himself, baptized by Saint Sylvester, was cleansed of the leprosy of unbelief; and the same Pontiff consecrated it on the fifth day before the Ides of November. The memory of this consecration is celebrated on this present day, on which for the first time at Rome a church was publicly consecrated, and the image of the Savior, depicted on the wall, appeared to the Roman people.

But salvation is reserved for those who persevere to the end; and then, when the apostolic men are dispersed through all parts of the world, the truth of the Gospel will be preached. And when the knowledge of the heavenly mystery has been brought to all, then ruin and end will overtake Jerusalem; so that the punishment of the unbelievers and the fear of the overthrown city may follow upon the faithfulness of the preaching. These things, therefore, were accomplished upon it as they had been foretold; and, the Apostles being stoned, put to flight, and slain, it was consumed by famine, war, and captivity. And then it was worthy to be no more, since, having expelled the preachers of Christ, it showed itself unworthy of God's preaching.

But take care lest it should steal upon you that you wish to destroy yourself, by understanding thus what you ought to hate in this world: your soul. For from this notion certain wicked and perverse men, more cruel to themselves and more criminal than ordinary murderers, give themselves to the flames, plunge themselves in the waters, dash themselves headlong and perish. This Christ did not teach; indeed, he also replied to the devil when he suggested throwing himself headlong: Get behind me, Satan: it is written, You shall not tempt the Lord your God. But to Peter he said, signifying by what death he was to glorify God: When you were young, you girded yourself and walked where you would; but when you are old, another will gird you and lead you where you do not wish. In which words he made it clear enough that one who follows in the footsteps of Christ is not to be slain by himself, but by another.

Callistus held the see for five years, one month, and twelve days. In five ordinations, in the month of December, he created sixteen priests, four deacons, and eight bishops. After long fasting and repeated floggings, he was thrown headlong into a well, and thus crowned with martyrdom under the Emperor Alexander; and he was laid in the cemetery of Calepodius on the Aurelian Way, at the third milestone from the City, on the day before the Ides of October. His body was afterward brought to the basilica of Saint Mary across the Tiber, built by himself, where it is venerated with great devotion beneath the high altar.

He defeated Selim, the Turkish tyrant, who had been exalted by many victories, when he had assembled a great fleet at the Echinades islands — overcoming him not so much by arms as by prayers poured out to God. This victory he knew, at the very hour in which it was obtained, through a revelation from God, and announced it to his household. And while he was preparing a new expedition against the Turks themselves, he fell into a serious illness; and, having endured the most bitter pains with great patience, as he came to his last moments, and having received the sacraments in the customary way, he rendered his soul most peacefully to God, in the year one thousand five hundred and seventy-two, in the sixty-eighth year of his age, having held the see for six years, three months, and twenty-four days. His body is venerated with the greatest devotion of the faithful in the basilica of Saint Mary at the Manger, with many miracles wrought by God through his intercession. These miracles having been duly examined, he was enrolled in the number of the Saints by Clement XI, Supreme Pontiff.

The seven Brothers, sons of Saint Felicity, were put to death in various ways at Rome during the persecution of Marcus Aurelius Antoninus, when the prefect Publius had tried in vain to make them venerate idols, on the sixth day before the Ides of July, their most valiant mother herself exhorting them to martyrdom. Januarius was beaten with leaded whips; Felix and Philip were cudgeled; Sylvanus was hurled headlong from a height; Alexander, Vitalis, and Martialis were beheaded. The mother at last, four months afterward, obtained the same palm of martyrdom. Rufina and Secunda, sisters, Roman virgins, having rejected marriage with Armentarius and Verinus because they had vowed their virginity to Christ, were arrested under the emperors Valerian and Gallienus, and were in no way turned aside from their purpose by the blandishments and threats of the prefect Junius, but were afflicted with various kinds of torments. And since, guarded by Angels, they persevered in their holy purpose, they were beheaded on the Aurelian Way, at the tenth milestone. Their bodies, buried by the matron Plautilla on her estate outside the City, were afterward laid in the Constantinian basilica near the baptistery.

The seven brothers, sons of Saint Felicity, were tried at Rome during the persecution of Marcus Aurelius Antoninus, first by the blandishments and then by the threats of the prefect Publius, to make them renounce Christ and venerate the gods; and, through their own virtue and at their mother's urging, they persevered in the confession of the faith, and were put to death in various ways. Januarius was beaten with leaded whips; Felix and Philip were cudgeled; Sylvanus was hurled headlong from a height; Alexander, Vitalis, and Martialis were beheaded. Their mother obtained the same palm of martyrdom four months afterward: they rendered their spirits to the Lord on the sixth day before the Ides of July.

The following consideration remains: since we have said that the order of this generation, according to the truth of things, is consistent neither in its number nor in its sequence, the reason for this must also be given. For it is no small matter that one thing should be said in the narrative, another should have been in the events; and that one thing should be reported in the total, another held in the number. For from Abraham to David fourteen generations are counted; and from David to the deportation to Babylon, seventeen are found in certain books. But in this there is no fault of falsehood or negligence. For three generations have been passed over. For Joram begot Ahaziah, Ahaziah begot Joash, Joash afterward Amaziah, and Amaziah Uzziah; and in Matthew it is written that Joram begot Uzziah, though he is the fourth from him. This is so because Joram begot Ahaziah from a Gentile woman, namely from Ahab, who had Jezebel for wife.
Serm 41. in Cant.

I, brethren, from the very beginning of my conversion, in place of a store of merits which I knew was lacking to me, took care to bind for myself a bundle gathered from all the anxieties and bitternesses of my Lord, and to place it between my breasts. I will pour forth the memory of the abundance of his sweetness in these things for as long as I live: I will never forget these mercies in eternity, for in them I have been made to live. This saving bundle has been kept for me; no one will take it from me: it will abide between my breasts. To meditate on these things, I have called wisdom: in them I have set the perfection of justice for myself, in them the fullness of knowledge, in them the riches of salvation, in them abundance of merits. From them at times the saving draught of bitterness; from them again the sweet taste of consolation. These raise me up in adversity, restrain me in prosperity, and, as I walk between the joys and sorrows of the present life along the royal road, afford me safe guidance on either side, repelling on every hand the evils that threaten.
Sermo 2 de Nativitate Domini

Jesus Christ our Lord enters these lowly things, descending from his heavenly seat without departing from his Father's glory, born by a new order and a new birth. By a new order: because, invisible in his own, he was made visible in ours; incomprehensible, he willed to be comprehended; remaining before all ages, he began to exist in time. By a new birth was he begotten: conceived of a Virgin, born of a Virgin, without the concupiscence of paternal flesh, without injury to the integrity of the mother; because such a birth befitted the future Savior of men, who should have in himself the nature of human substance, and yet be ignorant of the stains of human flesh. The origin is unlike, but the nature is alike; by human use and custom what we believe is lacking, but it is undergirded by divine power: that a Virgin conceived, that a Virgin gave birth, that a Virgin remained.
Sermo 31, alias 344

He had blood by which he might redeem us; and for this purpose he received blood, so that there might be what he could pour out for our redemption. The blood of your Lord, if you will, was given for you; if you are unwilling, it was not given for you. For perhaps you say: My God had blood by which to redeem me, but now that he has suffered, he has given all of it; what remains to him that he might give even for me? This is the great thing: that he gave it once, and gave it for all. The blood of Christ is salvation for one who is willing, punishment for one who is not. Why then do you hesitate — you who do not wish to die — not rather to be freed from the second death? By which you are freed, if you are willing to take up your cross and follow the Lord; because he bore his own cross and sought his servant.
We praise you, O God: * we acknowledge you as Lord.
All the earth * worships you, eternal Father.
To you all the Angels, * to you the heavens and all the Powers:
To you the Cherubim and Seraphim * cry out without ceasing:
(A bow is made) Holy, Holy, Holy * Lord God of Sabaoth.
The heavens and the earth are full * of the majesty of your glory.
The glorious choir * of the Apostles,
The admirable company * of the Prophets,
The white-robed army * of Martyrs praise you.
The holy Church throughout all the world * confesses you:
the Father * of immense majesty;
Your adorable, true * and only Son;
And the Holy * Paraclete Spirit.
You are the King of glory, * O Christ.
You are the everlasting * Son of the Father.
(A bow is made) You, about to take upon yourself man for his liberation, * did not shrink from the Virgin's womb.
You, about to take upon yourself man for his liberation, * did not shrink from the Virgin's womb.
You, having overcome the sting of death, * opened the Kingdom of Heaven to believers.
You sit at the right hand of God, * in the glory of the Father.
You are believed * to be the Judge to come.
Sermo 5. de eodem Festo, circa medium.

To what end, then, is our praise for the Saints? To what end our glorification? To what end this very solemnity of ours? What are earthly honors to them, when the heavenly Father honors them according to the truthful promise of the Son? What are our proclamations to them? They are full. Truly it is so, most beloved: the Saints have no need of our good things, nor is anything furnished to them by our devotion. Clearly, it is to our benefit to venerate their memory, not to theirs. Do you wish to know how great our benefit is? I sense within myself (I confess it) from this recollection a vehement desire being kindled, and a threefold desire.
Sermo de Aquæductu

The Word was made flesh, and now dwells in us. He dwells in our memory, he dwells in our thought, because he has descended even to our imagination. In what way, you ask? As he lay in the manger, as he reclined in the virginal lap, as he preached on the mountain, as he passed the night in prayer, as he hung on the Cross, as he was pale in death, free among the dead and reigning in hell, or again as he rose on the third day and showed the Apostles the places of the nails — the signs of victory — and finally, in their sight, ascended to the secrets of heaven. Which of these is not truly, devoutly, and holily contemplated?
Sermo Innocéntii Papæ sexti.
In Decreto de Festo Lanceæ et Clavorum Domini.

In the most sacred Passion of our Redeemer the Lord Jesus Christ, we ought so to glory that, numbering all the mysteries of his Passion and its merits, we glory also in each of its saving instruments. Among which, this is to be solemnly recalled: that the Savior himself, his spirit already given up on the Cross, endured to have his side pierced with a lance, so that from the flowing streams of blood and water, there might be formed the one, immaculate, holy, and virginal Mother Church, his bride. O most blessed opening of that sacred side, from which so many and such great gifts of divine mercy have flowed to us! O blessed lance, which merited to accomplish such great goods for us, and to be added to the glory of so great a triumph!
Sermo S. Gregórii Papæ
2. Part Past. c. 1.
Tantum debet ...
Ex Homil. 38. in Evang.

Since the examples of the faithful sometimes convert the minds of hearers more than the words of teachers, I wish to tell you something from nearby, which your hearts may hear with all the more awe, the more closely it concerns them. For we do not speak of things done long ago, but recall things of which witnesses exist, who relate that they were present. My father had three sisters, all three of whom were consecrated virgins; one was called Tarsilla, another Gordiana, another Aemiliana. On a certain night there appeared to this Tarsilla — who among her sisters, by the virtue of continual prayer, zeal for affliction, singular abstinence, and the gravity of her life, had grown venerable in honor and in the heights of holiness — as she herself recounted, through a vision, my ancestor Felix, Bishop of this Roman Church, who showed her a dwelling place of perpetual light, saying: Come, for I receive you into this dwelling place of light. She was shortly afterward seized by a fever, and came to her last day; and as, when noble women and men are dying, many gather to console their nearest of kin, at that same hour of her departure many men and women stood around her deathbed, among them my mother, who was also present: when she, looking upward, saw Jesus coming, and with great intensity began to cry out to those standing by, saying: Stand back, stand back, Jesus is coming! And as she gazed intently at him whom she saw, that holy soul was freed from the flesh; and so suddenly was a fragrance of wondrous perfume diffused that the very sweetness itself showed all present that the Author of sweetness had come thither.

Sermo S. Maximi Epíscopi
We ought not to think it without cause, dearest brethren, that the most glorious princes of the Christian faith, Peter and Paul, endured the sentence of one tyrant on one day and in one place. They suffered on one day, that they might arrive together at Christ; in one place, lest Rome should lack either of them at her side; under one persecutor, that an equal cruelty might bind them both. The day, I believe, was appointed in accordance with their merit, the place in accordance with their glory, the persecutor in accordance with their virtue. And in what place, finally, did they endure martyrdom? In the city of Rome, which holds the sovereignty and headship of the nations; that where the head of superstition had been, there the head of holiness might rest; and where the princes of the Gentiles had dwelt, there the princes of the churches might abide.
Sermo 22.

It is fitting and right, brethren, that after the joy of Easter, which we have celebrated in the Church, we should share our joys with the holy Martyrs; and that we should announce to those who are sharers in the Lord's Passion the glory of the Lord's Resurrection. For those who are companions in reproach ought to be partakers also in joy. For thus the blessed Apostle says: As you are companions of the sufferings, so also you shall be of the consolation; if we endure, he says, we shall also reign together. Those, therefore, who endured evils for Christ's sake, ought also to have glory with Christ.
Sermo sancti Ambrósii Epíscopi.
Serm. 22.

De S. Euseb. 70.6., edit. Rom.

Today we celebrate the depositio of Saint Eusebius. What is a depositio? Not, assuredly, that which is effected by the hands of the clergy, when the remains of the members are buried in the earth; but that by which a man, freed from the bonds of flesh, about to go at liberty to heaven, sets down his earthly body. This is truly the depositio, in which we lay aside concupiscence, cease from wrongdoing, stop sinning, and set down as a burden cast off all that is heavy to our salvation. For this reason this day is observed as a great solemnity, because it is truly the highest festival: to be dead to vices, to live only for justice.
In Luc. cap. 23.

What does it mean that it is not the Apostles, but Joseph and Nicodemus — as John says — who bury Christ? One is just and steadfast, the other was a master in Israel. For such is the burial of Christ: that it should have justice and teaching. The place for evasion is therefore closed off, and the Jews are refuted by domestic testimony. For if the Apostles had buried him, they would have said and argued that he whom they claimed was taken away was not buried. But a just man covers the body of Christ with a linen cloth; an innocent man anoints him with ointment. For we find that these are not distinguished without purpose, because justice clothes the Church, and innocence ministers grace.
Lib. 1. de Virg., cica init.

Since today is the birthday of a Virgin, the love of integrity now invites us to say something about virginity, lest it seem to have been touched upon only in passing, when it is the foremost virtue. For virginity is not praiseworthy because it is found in Martyrs, but because it is itself what makes Martyrs. But who could comprehend it by human genius, when nature itself has not enclosed it within its laws? Or who could embrace in natural speech what is above the use of nature? It sought from heaven what it might imitate on earth. And not without reason did it seek its manner of life from heaven, it who found its Spouse in heaven.
Sermo sancti Ambrósii episcopi
Ex libr. de Virginibus. Lectio iii

Let virginity and the life of the blessed Mary be described for you as in an image, from whom, as in a mirror, the beauty of chastity and the form of virtue shines forth. From her you may take examples of life, where, as in a model, the lessons of goodness are expressed, showing what you ought to amend, what to flee, and what to hold. The first ardor of learning is the nobility of the teacher. What is more noble than the Mother of God? What more splendid than she whom splendor chose? What more chaste than she who begot a body without the contagion of a body?
Sermo sancti Augusini Epíscopi
Sermo 138 de Verbis Dómini

Christ is the good Shepherd. What of Peter? Was he not also a good shepherd? Did he not also lay down his life for the sheep? What of Paul? What of the other Apostles? What of the blessed bishop Martyrs who followed in their times? What also of this holy Felix? Were not all of them good shepherds, not hirelings, of whom it is said: Amen I say to you, they have received their reward? All those then were good shepherds, not only because they shed their blood, but because they shed it for the sheep. For they shed it not out of pride, but out of charity.

Christ is the good Shepherd. What of Peter? Was he not also a good shepherd? Did he not also lay down his life for the sheep? What of Paul? What of the other Apostles? What of the blessed bishop Martyrs who followed in their times? What also of this holy Zephyrinus? Were not all of them good shepherds, not hirelings, of whom it is said: Amen I say to you, they have received their reward? All those then were good shepherds, not only because they shed their blood, but because they shed it for the sheep. For they shed it not out of pride, but out of charity.
Sermo 1 de Innocentibus

At the birth of the Lord, mourning began — not in heaven, but in the world: lamentation was imposed on mothers, exultation on the Angels, migration on the infants. God is he who was born; those innocent ones are owed as victims to him who came to condemn the malice of the world. Lambs must be slain, because the Lamb who takes away the sins of the world was to be crucified. But the mother sheep wail, because they lose their lambs, bleating without a voice. Great is the martyrdom, a cruel spectacle! The sword is drawn out, and no cause intervenes: envy alone hisses, while he who was born does violence to no one. But we behold the mother sheep who mourn over the lambs: A voice was heard in Rama, weeping and loud wailing. They are pledges not entrusted but created; not deposited but exposed.
Sermo 15 de Sanctis

The institution of today's solemnity received from our elders the name "Chair," because the first of the Apostles, Peter, is reported to have taken up the chair of the episcopate on this day. Rightly, therefore, do the churches celebrate the birthday of that seat which the Apostle received for the salvation of the churches, as the Lord said: You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church.
A Sermon of Saint Augustine, Bishop.
Serm. 30. de Sanctis.

I believe you know the passion of the most blessed Martyr Laurence, whose nativity we celebrate today: and I do not doubt that you are able to know how much he endured in the persecution. For such was the glory of his martyrdom that by his passion he illumined the whole world. Laurence truly illumined the world by that light with which he himself was enkindled, and by the flames which he himself endured, he warmed the hearts of all Christians.
Serm. 138 de verbis Domini
Christ is the good shepherd. ...
De S. Cypriano, serm. 12.

So grateful and holy a solemnity requires a sermon, by which we celebrate the passion of the blessed Martyr Silverius. The Church was then, without doubt, sorrowful — not at the loss of one who had fallen, but at the departure of one who was withdrawing — ever longing to see present so good a ruler and teacher. But those whom the anxiety of the contest had afflicted were consoled by the crown of the victor. And now not only without any sorrow, but even with great joy, we recall in reading all that was done then: and on this day we are granted to rejoice, not to fear. For we do not dread him coming terribly, but await him returning joyfully.

A great spectacle, brethren, has been placed before the eyes of our faith. With our ears we heard, with our hearts we beheld a mother wishing that her sons would finish this life before her — desires utterly contrary to the custom of humankind. For all people, as they depart this life, wish to go before their children, not to follow after them; but she desired to die last. For she was not losing her sons, but sending them ahead; nor did she look upon what life they were ending, but what life they were beginning. For they ceased to live where they had been destined one day to die; and they began to live, to live without end. It is a small thing that she was a witness; we marvel rather that she was an encourager. More fruitful in virtues than in offspring: seeing those who strove, in all of whom she herself was striving, and in all who conquered, she herself was conquering.

Thus was it foretold of old: the Mother of Sion says: Man and man was born in her, and the Most High himself has founded her. O omnipotence of one being born! O magnificence of one descending from heaven to earth! He was still carried in the womb, and yet from his mother's womb he was greeted by John the Baptist. He was presented in the temple, and acknowledged by Simeon — that aged, old, proven, crowned elder. Then he knew, then he adored, then he said: Now, O Lord, you dismiss your servant in peace, for my eyes have seen your salvation.
De verbis Dómini 50

Christ is the good shepherd. What of Peter? Was he not also a good shepherd? Did he not also lay down his soul for the sheep? What of Paul? What of the other Apostles? What of the blessed bishop-martyrs who followed in their times? What also of this holy Anterus? Were they not all good shepherds, not hirelings, of whom it is said: Amen, I say to you, they have received their reward? All these then were good shepherds, not only because they shed their blood, but because they shed it for the sheep. For they shed it not out of pride, but out of charity.

When the Lord was born, mourning began — not in heaven, but in the world: lamentation was imposed on mothers, exultation on the Angels, migration on the infants. God is he who was born: those Innocents are owed as victims to him who came to condemn the wickedness of the world. Little lambs must be slaughtered, because the Lamb is to be crucified who takes away the sins of the world. But the mother-ewes howl, because they lose their little lambs bleating without voice. A great martyrdom, a cruel spectacle! The sword is drawn, and no cause intervenes: envy alone rages, since he who was born does violence to none. But we see the mother-ewes mourning over their little lambs: A voice was heard in Rama, weeping and great wailing. These pledges were not lent, but created; not deposited, but exposed.

Whenever, dearest brethren, we celebrate the solemnities of the holy Martyrs, let us so hope, through their intercession, to obtain temporal benefits from the Lord, that by imitating the Martyrs themselves, we may merit to receive eternal ones. For the joys of the feasts of the holy Martyrs are truly celebrated by those who follow the examples of the Martyrs themselves. For the solemnities of the Martyrs are exhortations to martyrdom: that it may not be irksome to imitate what it delights us to celebrate.
But we wish to rejoice with the Saints: and we are unwilling to endure the tribulation of the world with them. For whoever refuses to imitate the holy Martyrs to the extent he can will not be able to attain their blessedness. But the Apostle Paul also proclaims, saying: If we are partners in sufferings, we shall also be partners in consolations. And the Lord in the Gospel: If the world hates you, know that it has hated me before you. He refuses to be in the body who is unwilling to endure hatred with the head.
Sermo 13 de Tempore

Our Lord Jesus Christ, dearest brethren, who is for ever the Creator of all, today, by being born of a mother, has become our Savior. He was born for us today in time by his will, so that he might lead us to the eternity of the Father. God became man, so that man might become God: so that man might eat the bread of the Angels, the Lord of the Angels today became man.
Sermo 18 de Sanctis, qui est 2 de Annunt. Dominica

The longed-for day of the blessed and venerable ever-Virgin Mary is with us, most beloved, and therefore let our land rejoice with the greatest exultation, illumined by the nativity of so great a Virgin. For she is the flower of the field from whom was born the precious lily of the valleys, through whose childbearing the nature of our first parents is changed and their fault is blotted out. In her that sentence of Eve's unhappiness is cut away, whereby it is said: In pain you shall bring forth your children; for she brought forth the Lord in joy.
Sermo 20 de Sanctis

After that most sacred day of the Lord's nativity, we read that no human birth is celebrated, save that of blessed John the Baptist alone. In the other Saints and elect of God, we know that day to be honored on which, after the completion of their labors and the vanquishing and triumph over the world, this present life brought them forth into perpetual eternity. In the others, the merits of the last day are celebrated: in this man, even the first day, and the very beginnings of the man, are consecrated; for this reason, beyond doubt, because through him the Lord willed his coming to be attested, lest men should fail to recognize it when it suddenly arrived unlooked for. For John was a figure of the Old Testament, and bore in himself the form of the law; and therefore John foretold the Savior, just as the law ran before grace.
Sermo 2 de S. Stephano

Christ, the head of the Martyrs, suffered first for us, leaving you an example, that you should follow in his steps. Most blessed Stephen, following in the footsteps of his Passion, and confessing Christ while being stoned by the Jews, merited a crown as if placed for him by his own name. For Stephen in Greek is called corona, that is, crown, in Latin. He already had the name of a crown, and therefore he bore the palm of martyrdom prefigured in his own name. When he was being stoned, he not only did not seek to obtain vengeance from his persecutors, but rather begged God to grant them pardon.

Today, dearest brethren, we honor the nativity of those infants whom the text of the Gospel declares were slain by Herod, that most cruel king. And therefore let the earth rejoice with the greatest exultation, as the fruitful parent of so many heavenly soldiers and such great virtues. Behold, the profane enemy could never have benefited those blessed little ones so much by his service as he profited them by his hatred. For, as the most sacred feast of the present day shows, the more iniquity abounded toward those blessed little ones, the more it poured upon them the grace of blessing.
Sermo 14 de Sanctis

Today this reading from the Acts of the Apostles was proclaimed, in which the Apostle Paul, from a persecutor of Christians, was made a proclaimer of Christ. For Christ cast down the persecutor to make him a teacher of the Church: striking him and healing him; slaying and vivifying: a lamb slain by wolves, yet making lambs from wolves. For thus in a glorious prophecy, when the Patriarch Jacob was blessing his sons — touching those present, foreseeing those to come — what befell Paul had been foretold. Now Paul was, as he himself testifies, of the tribe of Benjamin. And when Jacob, blessing his sons, came to bless Benjamin, he said of him: Benjamin is a ravenous wolf.
Sermo 2 de Epiphania, qui est 30 de Tempore

The Magi came from the East to adore the birth of the Virgin. We celebrate this day today; we discharge the sermon owed to this solemnity. For them this day first shone; for us it returns with an anniversary celebration. They were the firstfruits of the Gentiles; we are the people of the Gentiles. For us the tongue of the Apostles announced this; for them the star, as the tongue of the heavens; and for us the same Apostles, as other heavens, declared the glory of God.
De S. Cypriano, serm. 12
