But those whom the anxiety of the contest had afflicted were consoled by the crown of the victor. And now not only without any sorrow, but even with great joy, we recall in reading all that was done then: and on this day we are granted to rejoice, not to fear. For we do not dread him coming terribly, but await him returning joyfully.

The triumphant day of the blessed Martyr N. returns for us today with its anniversary celebration: as the Church rejoices in his glorification, so she proposes that his footsteps be followed. For if we suffer together, we shall also be glorified together. In his glorious contest, two things are chiefly to be considered by us: namely, the hardened cruelty of the torturer, and the unconquered patience of the Martyr. The cruelty of the torturer, that we may detest it; the patience of the Martyr, that we may imitate it. Hear the Psalmist rebuking malice: Do not vie with evildoers, for like grass they will quickly wither. But that patience must be shown in the face of evildoers, hear the Apostle urging: Patience is necessary for you, so that you may win the promises.
We praise you, O God: * we acknowledge you to be the Lord.
All the earth worships you, * O eternal Father.
To you all the Angels, * to you the Heavens, and all the Powers:
To you the Cherubim and Seraphim * cry out without ceasing:
(A bow is made) Holy, Holy, Holy * Lord God of Sabaoth.
The heavens and earth are full * of the majesty of your glory.
The glorious chorus * of the Apostles,
The admirable company * of the Prophets,
The white-robed army * of the Martyrs praise you.
The holy Church throughout all the world * acknowledges you,
the Father * of immeasurable majesty;
Your true and only Son * worthy of adoration;
And the Holy * Spirit the Paraclete.
You are the King of glory, * O Christ.
You are the everlasting * Son of the Father.
(A bow is made) You, who took it upon yourself to deliver man: * did not abhor the Virgin's womb.
You, who took it upon yourself to deliver man: * did not abhor the Virgin's womb.
You, having overcome the sting of death, * opened to believers the Kingdom of Heaven.
You sit at the right hand of God, * in the glory of the Father.
You are believed * to be the Judge to come.

So grateful and holy a solemnity requires a sermon, by which we celebrate the passion of the blessed Martyr Sixtus. The Church was then, without doubt, sorrowful — not at the loss of one who had fallen, but at the departure of one who was withdrawing — ever longing to see present so good a ruler and teacher. But those whom the anxiety of the contest had afflicted were consoled by the crown of the victor. And now not only without any sorrow, but even with great joy, we recall in reading all that was done then: and on this day we are granted to rejoice, not to fear. For we do not dread him coming terribly, but await him returning joyfully.
Serm. 41. Dom. in Palmis de Pass. Dom.

The day itself reminds us, dearest brethren, of the solemnity of the Lord's Passion — the day in which even the mute elements did not keep silence. Let the light of faith celebrate it with human tongues, that which even the silences of darkness proclaimed. Today our Lord placed on the scales of the Cross the price of our salvation, and by a single death, as the Founder of all, so the Restorer of all, he redeemed the whole world. For let us believe without doubt that he who gave more than the whole world was worth, redeemed the whole world. For the merit of the price paid surpassed the dignity of the distinguished ransom. Between the redeemed and the Redeemer there was dispensation, not equivalence. He therefore who had no sins of his own worthily blotted out those of others. He alone fell as a holy victim for all, that he might raise all; and because he alone owed no debt, he rightly disbursed the interest of mercy for debtors.
A Sermon of Saint Augustine, Bishop
Serm. 1 in Dom. 15. de B. Tobia, qui est 226. de Temp.

Blessed Tobias, who knew how to break his bread for the hungry, prepares a prompt wage for the laboring hired man. We listened patiently to the reading which was just recited, and marveled at the exchange between father and son, as the Angel — whom they thought a mere earthly hired man under his celestial glory — gives counsel. For this purpose he incurred the calamity of blindness: to receive as physician the Angel, who, enkindled by divine torches, breathed after such things. Honest is prayer with fasting and almsgiving. The prayer of the just is the key of heaven. Prayer ascends, and the mercy of God descends. Though the earth be high, and heaven high, yet God hears the tongue of man, if he has a clean conscience. He speaks with the senses, if our groaning be his alone. The rain of tears suffices for his ears: weeping he hears sooner than voices. The prayer of the envious is wont to be driven away from his ears. The soul of father and son was one: while there was a distinction of members, there was in them a singular kinship of souls. Son, he said, let us dismiss this man, adding to the agreed wage, for he has brought us many good things by his labor; and he began to urge the hired man to take the due of his wage. Brother, he said, take what is yours and then go in safety. Receive your wage, for you have shown good mercy to me and to my son. Take, as I said, half the substance which we brought back with my son: for the grace which we owe you cannot be weighed.
Serm. 2. de S. Stephano.

After yesterday's most festive day, on which the Nativity of Christ our Savior shone upon us, this present day is also illumined by the crown of the blessed Martyr Stephen. No part of the world is ignorant of the merits of that Martyr: for he suffered at the very beginning of the Church, that is, in the city of Jerusalem itself. There he ministered as a Deacon: and in the very flower of his youth he adorned the beauty of his age with his blood. His passion is illustrious and most wonderful. We have just now not only heard it as it was read from the book of the Acts of the Apostles, but also beheld it with our eyes.
A Sermon of Saint Basil the Great
Homilia 2 in Psalm. 28

The voice of the Lord upon the waters. What voice? Upon what waters? Let us take as a prophecy what has been said. Remember John, who, when asked by the Jews: Who are you? What answer shall we give to those who sent us? replied: I am the voice of one crying in the desert. Therefore the voice of the Lord is John, the Angel sent by God before the face of the Lord, to prepare for the Lord a perfect people. This voice therefore upon the waters was upon the Jordan, where he was baptizing, preaching the baptism of repentance, and not only in the Jordan but also in Aenon near Salim, because there was much water there.
A Sermon of Saint Bede the Venerable, Priest
Expositio in Luc. 1, 11-20.

The Angel appeared to Zechariah, standing at the right side of the altar of incense. Fittingly the Angel appears both in the temple, and near the altar, and at the right side; for he foretells indeed the coming of the true Priest, the mystery of the universal sacrifice, and the joy of the heavenly gift. For as by the left, present things, so by the right, eternal goods are often prefigured. In accordance with which it is sung in praise of wisdom: Length of days is in her right hand; in her left hand riches and glory. The Angel comforts the trembling Zechariah, because, just as it is of human frailty to be troubled by the vision of a spiritual creature, so it is of angelic benignity to soothe with gentle words those mortals who are afraid at the sight of it. On the contrary, it is of demonic ferocity to shake with ever greater terror those whom it perceives to be terrified by its presence — a ferocity that can be overcome by no better means than by undaunted faith.
A Sermon of Saint Bede the Venerable, Priest
Sermo 18 de Sanctis

Today, most beloved, we celebrate the feast of all the Saints under the one joy of a single solemnity: of whose fellowship heaven exults, by whose patronage the earth rejoices, by whose triumphs the holy Church is crowned; whose confession is as much more glorious in honor as it was stronger in suffering: because, as the struggle grew, so too grew the glory of the combatants, and the triumph of martyrdom is adorned by a manifold variety of sufferings; and through the more grievous torments the rewards were also the more grievous: while the Catholic mother Church, spread far and wide throughout the whole world, was drawn in her very head, Christ Jesus, not to fear reproaches, crosses, and death; strengthened more and more, not by resisting but by enduring, she breathed into all whom the prison of punishment enclosed in its glorious company an equal and like fervor of virtue for waging the contest and the glory of triumph.
Homil. 2 super Missus est, prope finem

Consider what and what manner of man blessed Joseph was: conjecture from the title by which, though by way of dispensation, he merited to be so honored as to be both called and believed the father of God; conjecture also from his own name, which you do not hesitate to interpret as meaning increase. And at the same time remember that great Patriarch of old who was sold and taken to Egypt; and know that this Joseph received not only his name but also attained his chastity, acquired his innocence and grace.
Ex Homil. 2. super « Missus est »

It was fitting that the mystery of the divine counsel should for some time be hidden from the prince of this world: not because God, if he wished to carry out his work openly, feared that he could be hindered by him; but because he who accomplished whatever he willed not only powerfully but also wisely, as he was accustomed in all his works to observe certain fittings of things or of times for the sake of the beauty of order: so also in this most magnificent work of his, namely our restoration, he willed to display not only his power but also his wisdom.
Serm. 52 de divers.

Wisdom, who was of God and was God, coming to us from the bosom of the Father, built herself a house — that is, her own Mother, the Virgin Mary — in which she hewed out seven columns. What is it to hew out seven columns in her, but to prepare her as a worthy dwelling for himself in faith and works? Surely the number three pertains to faith on account of the Holy Trinity, the number four pertains to morals on account of the four cardinal virtues. Now that the Holy Trinity was in blessed Mary — was, I say, by the presence of majesty — there where the Son alone was by the assumption of humanity, is attested by the heavenly messenger who, disclosing the hidden mysteries to her, said: Hail, full of grace. The Lord is with you; and a little later: The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you. Behold, you have the Lord, you have the power of the Most High, you have the Holy Spirit — you have the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit.
Ex Sermóne de 12 Stellis

Most greatly, indeed, dearest, did one man and one woman harm us: but thanks be to God, through one man and one woman nonetheless all things are restored, and not without great increase of graces. And indeed Christ alone would have sufficed: since even now our entire sufficiency is from him; but it was not good for man to be alone. It was more fitting that both sexes should be present for our restoration. And so now that woman herself who is blessed among women will not be seen to be idle: a place for her in this reconciliation will indeed be found. For there is need of a mediator to the Mediator Christ: and none is more useful to us than Mary. Eve was a too-cruel mediatrix, through whom the ancient serpent poured his pestilent venom even into the man himself; but faithful Mary, who administered the antidote of salvation to both men and women. For the one was the minister of seduction, the other of propitiation; the one suggested the transgression, the other brought in the redemption. Why should human frailty tremble to approach Mary? There is nothing austere in her, nothing terrible; she is entirely gentle, offering milk and wool to all. Go through diligently the whole series of the evangelical history: and if by chance any rebuke, if anything harsh, if any sign even of light displeasure should be found in Mary, henceforth hold her suspect, and fear to approach her.

Consider what and what manner of man blessed Joseph was: conjecture from the title by which, though by way of dispensation, he merited to be so honored as to be both called and believed the father of God; conjecture also from his own name, which you do not hesitate to interpret as meaning increase. And at the same time remember that great Patriarch of old who was sold and taken to Egypt; and know that this Joseph received not only his name but also attained his chastity, acquired his innocence and grace.
For indeed that Joseph, sold and led into Egypt out of fraternal envy, prefigured the betrayal of Christ; this Joseph, fleeing the envy of Herod, carried Christ into Egypt. That one, keeping faith with his master, refused to lie with his master's wife; this one, acknowledging his Lady, the mother of his Lord, as a Virgin, and himself continent, guarded her faithfully.
A Sermon of Saint Bernard, Abbot.
Serm. 2. in Epiph. Domini

Go forth, daughters of Sion; to you we speak, daughters of Sion — worldly souls, weak, delicate; daughters, not sons, in whom there is no strength, no virile spirit. Go forth from the understanding of the flesh to the understanding of the mind, from the slavery of carnal concupiscence to the freedom of spiritual understanding. Go forth from your land, and from your kindred, and from the house of your father, and behold King Solomon in the diadem with which his mother crowned him — in the crown of poverty, in the crown of wretchedness; for he was also crowned by his stepmother with a crown of thorns, a crown of wretchedness; he is to be crowned by his family with a crown of justice, when the Angels will go forth and take from his Kingdom all that causes scandal, when he will come to judgment with the elders of his people, when the whole world will fight for him against the senseless. The Father too crowns him with a crown of glory, as the Psalmist says: With glory and honor you have crowned him, O Lord. Behold him, daughters of Sion, in the diadem with which his mother crowned him.
Sermo de duodecim stellis

The martyrdom of the Virgin is commended both in the prophecy of Simeon and in the very history of the Lord's Passion. This child, said the holy elder of the boy Jesus, is set as a sign that shall be contradicted; and a sword shall pierce your own soul — for it was to Mary that he spoke. Truly your soul, O blessed Mother, was pierced. Otherwise it would not have pierced the flesh of your Son unless it had first passed through your soul. And indeed after that Jesus of yours gave up his spirit, the cruel lance which opened his side did not touch his soul, since it was no longer there, but it assuredly pierced your soul. His soul, without doubt, was no longer there; but yours plainly could not be torn away from that place.
In Psalmum Qui habitat

He has given his Angels charge over you. A wonderful condescension, and truly a great love of charity. Who then? to whom? concerning whom? what did he command? Let us carefully consider, brethren, let us diligently commit to memory this so great commandment. Who then gave the command? Whose are the Angels? Whose commands do they obey? Whose will do they follow? Surely it is he who has given his Angels charge over you, to keep you in all your ways. Nor do they delay even to bear you up in their hands. The Supreme Majesty therefore gave commandment to the Angels, and to his Angels gave commandment. To those sublime ones, both so blessed and so closely united to him and truly of his household, he gave charge over you. But who are you? What is man that you are mindful of him, or the son of man that you regard him? As if man were not corruption, and the son of man a worm! But what, do you think, did he command concerning you? To keep you.
Ex Homil. 2 super Missus est, circa finem

And the name, he says, of the Virgin was Mary. Let us speak briefly also about this name, which, when interpreted, is said to mean star of the sea, and is most fittingly applied to the Virgin Mother. For she is most aptly compared to a star, because as a star sends forth its ray without any loss to itself, so the Virgin brought forth her Son without any harm to herself. Nor does the ray diminish the star's brightness, nor did the Son diminish the Virgin's integrity. She is therefore that noble star risen from Jacob, whose ray illumines the whole world, whose splendor shines both in the heights and penetrates into the depths; traversing also the earth, and warming minds more than bodies, it fosters virtues and burns away vices. She, I say, is that illustrious and pre-eminent star raised up of necessity above this great and wide sea, gleaming with merits, giving light by example.
A Sermon of Saint Bernard, Abbot
In Nativ. B. M. V., n. 6

Contemplate, O man, the counsel of God; acknowledge the counsel of wisdom, the counsel of loving devotion. About to water the threshing-floor with heavenly dew, he first drenched the whole fleece: about to redeem the human race, he entrusted the entire price to Mary. Why was this? Perhaps so that Eve might be excused through her daughter, and the complaint of man against woman might henceforth be silenced. Say no more, O Adam: The woman whom you gave me gave me of the forbidden tree; say rather: The woman whom you gave me fed me with a blessed fruit. This is surely a most holy counsel; but perhaps another lies hidden, and this is not all. Look more deeply, therefore, with what affection of devotion he wished her to be honored by us — he who placed the fullness of all good in Mary; so that accordingly, if there be any hope in us, if any grace, if any salvation, we may know that it overflows from her. Therefore with all the marrow of our hearts, with all the affections of our innermost being and all our desires, let us venerate this Mary: for such is the will of him who willed that we should have everything through Mary. This, I say, is his will — but it is for our sake.
In Festo S. Malachiæ, Episc.

Let us rejoice together, brethren, let us rejoice together, as is fitting, for our Bishops: for it is a pious thing to mourn the dead, and more pious still to rejoice with the living. Do they not live? And in blessedness. Surely they seemed to the eyes of the foolish to die, but they are in peace. Already now as fellow citizens of the Saints and members of the household of God, they sing together and give thanks, saying: We have passed through fire and water, and you have brought us to a place of refreshment. They passed through in a manly way, and have passed through happily. They passed through fire and water — those whom neither sorrows could break nor delights detain.
A Sermon of Saint Bernardino of Siena
Ex sermone 9 de visitatione

What mortal man, unless secured by divine oracle, would presume with uncircumcised — nay, with polluted lips to name even slightly or greatly her who is the true Mother of God and of man: she whom God the Father predestined before ages to be a perpetual Virgin, whom the Son chose as his most worthy Mother, whom the Holy Spirit prepared as the dwelling-place of all grace? With what words shall I, a little man, express the loftiest thoughts of the virginal Heart, uttered by that most holy mouth, for which the tongue of all the Angels does not suffice? For the Lord says: The good man from the good treasure of his heart brings forth good things; and this word can itself be a treasure. Who among mere men can be conceived as a better man than she who merited to become the Mother of God, who for nine months received God himself as a guest in her heart and in her womb? What treasure is better than that divine love by which the furnace-hot heart of the Virgin was burning?
A Sermon of Saint Bernard, Abbot
Sermo 1 de Assumpt. B. M. V. n. 1

The Virgin, ascending gloriously to heaven today, has without doubt heaped up abundant increase of joys for the citizens above. For she is the one whose voice of greeting makes even those rejoice with joy whom a mother's womb still encloses. And if the soul of a child not yet born was dissolved when Mary spoke, what, we think, was that exultation of the heavenly ones, when they merited to hear her voice, to see her face, and to enjoy her blessed presence?
But for us, dearest, what is the occasion of solemnity in her Assumption, what the cause of joy, what the occasion of greater gladness? The whole world is illumined by Mary's presence, so that even that heavenly homeland shines more brightly, irradiated by the splendor of the virginal lamp.
Sermon of Saint Bernard, Abbot
Serm. 2 de Festo Omn. Sanct.

Since we celebrate today, most beloved, the festive memory of all the Saints, worthy of all devotion, I think it worthwhile, with the assistance of the Holy Spirit, to address your charity concerning the common happiness in which they now enjoy blessed rest, and the future consummation for which they await. For this is a faithful saying and worthy of all acceptance: that those whom we follow with solemn veneration, we may also follow with a like manner of life; that toward the beatitude of those whom we proclaim most blessed, we may run with full eagerness; and that by the patronage of those whose praises delight us, we may be uplifted.
Sermon of Saint Bernard, Abbot.
Sermo in cap. 12. Apocalypsis, ante medium.

The Lord did a new thing upon the earth, so that a woman would encompass a man — and no other than Christ, of whom it is said: Behold a man, Orient is his name. He also did a new thing in heaven, so that a woman appeared clothed with the sun. Indeed he crowned her, and in turn merited to be crowned by her. Go forth, daughters of Sion, and see King Solomon in the diadem with which his mother crowned him. But this belongs to another occasion. Meanwhile rather enter within, and see the Queen in the diadem with which her Son has crowned her. Upon her head, he says, is a crown of twelve stars.
Serm. 1. de Assumpt. B. M. V.

Today, then, ascending gloriously into heaven, she has without doubt heaped up abundant increase upon the joys of the heavenly citizens. For she it is whose voice of greeting makes even those exult with joy who are still enclosed in their mother's womb. And if the soul of the little one not yet born melted when Mary spoke, what do we suppose that exultation of the heavenly ones must have been, who merited both to hear her voice, and to see her face, and to enjoy her blessed presence?
Sermon of Saint Bernardino of Siena.
Sermo 1 de S. Ioseph.

The general rule for all singular graces communicated to any rational creature is this: that whenever divine grace selects anyone for some eminent state of grace, it bestows all the charisms that are necessary for that person so chosen and for his office, and that richly adorn him. This was most fully verified in Saint Joseph, the putative father of our Lord Jesus Christ, and true spouse of the Queen of the world and Lady of the Angels; who was chosen by the eternal Father as the faithful guardian and custodian of his principal treasures, namely his Son and his Spouse — an office he discharged with utmost fidelity. To him, therefore, the Lord said: Well done, good and faithful servant; enter into the joy of your Lord.
Sermon of Saint Cyril, Bishop of Alexandria
Ap. Metaph. post med.

Blessed Peter, perhaps thinking the time of the Kingdom of God had come, chose to remain on the mountain, and said that three tabernacles should be made, not knowing what he was saying. For it was not yet the time of the consummation of the age, nor are the saints in the present time yet to be sharers of the hope promised to them. Since, then, the dispensation was still in its beginning, and had not yet been brought to completion, how was it fitting that Christ, who had come into the world out of charity, should cease to be willing to suffer for it? Peter, therefore, did not know what he was saying.
Sermon of Saint Cyril, Bishop of Alexandria.
Homilia contra Nestorium.

I see a joyful assembly of all the faithful today, who have gathered with eager hearts, summoned by the holy and God-bearing Mother of God, Mary ever-Virgin. Praise and glory be to you, O holy Trinity, who have called us all together to this celebration. Praise be also to you, O holy Mother of God. For you are the precious pearl of the whole world; you are the lamp of inextinguishable light, the crown of virginity, the scepter of orthodox faith, the indestructible temple containing him who can nowhere be contained, Mother and Virgin; you are blessed among women, the parent of him who came blessed in the name of the Lord.
Sermon of Saint Cyril, Bishop of Alexandria.

I see a joyful assembly of all the saints, who have gathered with eager hearts, summoned by the holy and God-bearing Mother of God, Mary ever-Virgin. Praise and glory be to you, O holy Trinity, who have called us all together to this celebration. Praise be also to you, O holy Mother of God. For you are the precious pearl of the whole world; you are the lamp of inextinguishable light, the crown of virginity, the scepter of orthodox faith, the indestructible temple containing him who can nowhere be contained, Mother and Virgin; through whom he who came in the name of the Lord is named blessed in the holy Gospels.
Sermon of Saint Epiphanius, Bishop
Orat. de Laud. Virg. sub init.

From the root of Jesse sprang King David, and from the tribe of King David came the holy Virgin: holy, I say, and daughter of holy men, whose parents were Joachim and Anna; who indeed pleased God in their life, and brought forth such a fruit — the holy Virgin Mary, both temple and Mother of God. Moreover, Joachim, Anna, and Mary, these three offered openly to the Trinity the sacrifice of praise. For Joachim is interpreted as the Preparation of the Lord, since from him was prepared the Lord's temple, namely the Virgin. Anna likewise is similarly interpreted as Grace, because Joachim and Anna received grace, so that through the coming of their prayers they brought forth such a fruit, having obtained the holy Virgin; for Joachim prayed on the mountain, and Anna in her garden.
Sermon of Saint Fulgentius, Bishop
Ex Serm. 5 qui est de Epiphania, sub initium

God himself, who in the Old Testament commanded the firstfruits to be offered to him, being born as man, dedicated to his worship the firstfruits of the Gentiles. The shepherds were the firstfruits of the Jews; the Magi became the firstfruits of the Gentiles. The former were brought from nearby; the latter were led back from afar. Where, they ask, is he who is born King of the Jews? Sons had already been born of Herod, the king of the Jews. Archelaus was born in a palace; Christ in an inn. Archelaus, when born, was laid in a silver bed; Christ, when born, was placed in a very lowly manger. And yet he who was born in the palace is despised, while he who was born in the inn is sought; the one is not named by the Magi at all, while the other, once found, is humbly adored.
Sermo 3, de S. Stéphano, circa init.

Yesterday we celebrated the temporal birthday of our eternal King; today we celebrate the triumphal passion of his soldier. For yesterday our King, clothed in the robe of flesh and going forth from the chamber of the virginal womb, deigned to visit the world; today the soldier, departing from the tabernacle of the body, has migrated as a conqueror to heaven. The former, preserving the majesty of his eternal Godhead and taking on the servant's girdle of flesh, entered the field of this age to do battle; the latter, having laid aside the corruptible garments of the body, ascended to the palace of heaven to reign forever. The former descended veiled in flesh; the latter ascended crowned with blood.
Sermon of Saint Germanus, Bishop of Constantinople
Oratio 9 post medium

We, who are poor in divine works and virtues, as we behold through you, O Mary, the riches of the divine goodness shown to us, let us say with all our heart: the earth is full of the mercy of the Lord. We, who were exiled from God by the multitude of our sins, sought God through you and found him, and having found him, were made safe. Therefore your help, O Mother of God, is powerful to grant salvation, and such that none other mediator is needed before God. For truly there is no end to your magnificence; your assistance is inexhaustible. There is no number to your gifts. For no one, save through you, O most holy one, obtains salvation. No one, save through you, O most immaculate one, is delivered from evil. No one, save through you, O most chaste one, is granted the gift of pardon. No one, save through you, O most honored one, receives the gift of grace through mercy. Wherefore, who shall not proclaim you blessed? You, I say, the glorious one, you who are to be called blessed, you who have received from your own Son and God great and wondrous things — for which all generations praise you.
Sermon of Saint Gregory Nazianzen
Oratio in sancta Lumina

I cannot restrain the delight of joy, but am lifted up in spirit and moved; and forgetting my own littleness, I strive and am eager to take upon myself the office of the great John, or rather his humble ministry. And though I am not the Forerunner, yet I come from the desert. Christ therefore is illumined — or rather, he illumines us by his own splendor. Christ is baptized; let us also descend together, that we may likewise ascend with him.
2. part. Past. c. 1.

The action of the ruler must surpass the action of the people by as much as the life of the shepherd is accustomed to differ from the flock. For it is necessary that he study carefully to measure himself against the great necessity of maintaining uprightness under which he is bound, when in his estimation the people are called a flock. He must be, then — necessarily — pure in thought, preeminent in action, discreet in silence, profitable in word, near to each one in compassion, exalted above all in contemplation, a humble companion to those who do good, erect against the vices of the erring through the zeal of justice, not diminishing care for internal matters in the occupation of external ones, nor abandoning foresight for external matters in the anxiety for internal ones.
Ex Homilía 3 in Evangelica

Blessed Felicitas, whose birthday we celebrate today, so feared leaving her seven sons alive in the flesh as she departed, in the way that carnal parents usually dread sending their dead on ahead of them. For when she was seized in the labor of persecution, she strengthened her children's hearts by preaching the love of the heavenly homeland; and she gave birth in spirit to those whom she had borne in the flesh, so that by her preaching she might bring forth for God those whom she had borne for the world in the flesh. Shall I then call this woman a martyr? But more than a martyr: she who, having sent ahead seven pledges to the kingdom, transmitted so many dead before her. She came first to punishment, but arrived eighth.
Homilia 25 in Evangelia

Mary Magdalene, who had been a sinner in the city, by loving the Truth, washed away the stains of sin with her tears; and the word of the Truth is fulfilled, which says: Many sins are forgiven her, for she has loved much. For she who had formerly remained cold through sinning, afterward burned mightily through loving. She would not withdraw from the Lord's tomb, even when the disciples withdrew. She sought him whom she had not found; she wept as she sought, and, kindled by the fire of her love, she burned with desire for him whom she believed had been taken away. Hence it came about that she alone then saw him who had remained in order to seek: for without doubt the virtue of a good work is perseverance.
Homil. 34 in Evang. ante medium

We speak of nine orders of Angels, because we know from the witness of Holy Scripture that there are: Angels, Archangels, Virtues, Powers, Principalities, Dominations, Thrones, Cherubim, and Seraphim. For nearly all the pages of Holy Scripture attest the existence of Angels and Archangels. The books of the prophets speak frequently of Cherubim and Seraphim, as is well known. The Apostle Paul also enumerates four orders by name to the Ephesians, saying: Above every Principality, and Power, and Virtue, and Domination. He again, writing to the Colossians, says: Whether Thrones, or Powers, or Principalities, or Dominations. When, therefore, Thrones are joined to those four which he named to the Ephesians, there are five orders; to which, when Angels and Archangels, Cherubim and Seraphim are added, nine orders of Angels are found without doubt.

Mary Magdalene, who had been a sinner in the city, by loving the Truth, washed away the stains of sin with her tears; and the word of the Truth is fulfilled, which says: Many sins are forgiven her, for she has loved much. For she who had formerly remained cold through sinning, afterward burned mightily through loving. She would not withdraw from the Lord's tomb, even when the disciples withdrew. She sought him whom she had not found; she wept as she sought, and, kindled by the fire of her love, she burned with desire for him whom she believed had been taken away. Hence it came about that she alone then saw him who had remained in order to seek: for without doubt the virtue of a good work is perseverance.
We praise you, O God: * we acknowledge you as Lord.
All the earth venerates you, * the eternal Father.
To you all the Angels, * to you the Heavens and all the Powers:
To you the Cherubim and Seraphim * cry out without ceasing:
(A bow is made) Holy, Holy, Holy * Lord God of Hosts.
Heaven and earth are full * of the majesty of your glory.
The glorious choir * of Apostles praises you,
The admirable number * of Prophets praises you,
The white-robed army * of Martyrs praises you.
Throughout the world * the holy Church proclaims you,
Father * of immeasurable majesty;
Your true and only * Son, worthy of all veneration;
And the Holy * Spirit, the Paraclete.
You are the King of glory, * O Christ.
You are the * everlasting Son of the Father.
(A bow is made) You, about to take on man for his deliverance: * did not shrink from the Virgin's womb.
You, about to take on man for his deliverance: * did not shrink from the Virgin's womb.
Having overcome the sting of death, * you opened the Kingdom of Heaven to believers.
You sit at the right hand of God, * in the glory of the Father.
You are believed * to be the Judge who is to come.
Sermon of Saint Gregory Nazianzen
Orátio 20 in Machabæos

Who are the Maccabees? For it is in their name that this feast day is celebrated by the present gathering. Who, though they are not held in honor by many, on the ground that they did not undergo that contest after Christ, are yet worthy to be honored by all, because they showed themselves brave and steadfast for the laws and customs of their fathers. For those who underwent martyrdom before the Passion of Christ — what would they have done, had they suffered persecution after Christ and had before them as a model for imitation his death, undergone for the sake of our salvation? Those whose virtue was so great and so notable even with no example set before them — would they not have descended to the contest all the more bravely, looking upon that example? Indeed there is even a certain mystical and hidden reason, most plausible to me and to all lovers of God: that none of those who were perfected by martyrdom before the coming of Christ could have attained it without faith in Christ.

You, about to take on man for his deliverance: * did not shrink from the Virgin's womb.
Having overcome the sting of death, * you opened the Kingdom of Heaven to believers.
You sit at the right hand of God, * in the glory of the Father.
You are believed * to be the Judge who is to come.
Sermon of Saint Jerome, Priest
De Assumptione B. M. V.

What the blessed and glorious ever-Virgin Mary was, and how great she was, is declared by the Angel from on high when he says: Hail, full of grace; the Lord is with you; blessed are you among women. For it was fitting that the Virgin should be endowed with such gifts, so as to be full of grace: she who gave glory to the heavens, gave the Lord to the earth, poured forth peace, brought faith to the peoples, an end to vices, an order of life, and discipline to morals. And rightly full, because to others grace is granted in part; but upon Mary the fullness of grace poured itself out all at once. Truly full, because though grace is believed to have been present in the holy Patriarchs and Prophets, it was not yet so full; but into Mary came the fullness of all grace that is in Christ, though in a different manner. And therefore it says: Blessed are you among women — that is, more blessed than all women. And thus whatever curse was poured forth through Eve, the blessing of Mary has wholly taken away. Of her, Solomon in the Canticles, as in her praise, says: Come, my dove, my immaculate one. For the winter is past, the rain is over and gone. And then he says: Come from Lebanon, come, you shall be crowned.
Sermon of Saint John Chrysostom
In Epist. ad Rom. cap. 15., serm. 29., circa finem
Christum díliengs, ...
Homilia ad Neophytos

Do you wish to hear of the power of the Blood of Christ? Let us return to his example, and call to mind the earlier type, and recall the ancient Scripture. In Egypt, in the middle of the night, God threatened the Egyptians with the tenth plague, so that their firstborn should perish, because they were detaining his firstborn people. But, lest the beloved people of the Jews should be endangered together with them, since one place contained them all, a remedy of distinction was found. This is a wondrous example, so that you may learn in truth of his power. The wrath of divine indignation was at work, and the deadly angel went about each house. What then did Moses say? Kill, he said, a year-old lamb, and smear your doorposts with its blood. What do you say, Moses? Is the blood of a sheep accustomed to deliver a rational human being? Greatly, he says; not because it is blood, but because by it is shown forth the example of the Lord's Blood.
Sermon of Saint John Chrysostom

Do you wish to hear of the power of the Blood of Christ? Let us return to his example, and call to mind the earlier type, and recall the ancient Scripture. In Egypt, in the middle of the night, God threatened the Egyptians with the tenth plague, so that their firstborn should perish, because they were detaining his firstborn people. But, lest the beloved people of the Jews should be endangered together with them, since one place contained them all, a remedy of distinction was found. This is a wondrous example, so that you may learn in truth of his power. The wrath of divine indignation was at work, and the deadly angel went about each house. What then did Moses say? Kill, he said, a year-old lamb, and smear your doorposts with its blood. What do you say, Moses? Is the blood of a sheep accustomed to deliver a rational human being? Greatly, he says; not because it is blood, but because by it is shown forth the example of the Lord's Blood.

What thanks shall we render to you, O blessed Apostles, who labored so much for us? I think of you, Peter, and am struck with awe; I recall you, Paul, and am overcome with tears, carried out of myself. For what shall I say, or what shall I speak, as I contemplate your afflictions — I do not know. How many prisons did you hallow! How many chains did you adorn! How many torments did you endure! How many curses did you bear! How you carried Christ! How you gladdened the churches by your preaching! Blessed are the instruments of your tongues; your members were sprinkled with blood for the sake of the Church. You imitated Christ in all things. Their sound went forth into all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world.

Sermo 1 de Martyribus, tom. 3.

There is no one who does not know that the glories of the Martyrs are frequented by the people of God by divine counsel for this purpose: that due honor may be paid to them, and that examples of virtue may be shown to us, with Christ's favor; so that, as we perceive these things to be celebrated in this manner, we may know how great a glory awaits in heaven those whose birthdays are celebrated in such a way on earth; and that we too may be provoked by such examples, with equal virtue, similar devotion and faith; so that, with Christ granting it, we may fight and conquer the enemy, and, with victory won, may triumph with those same Saints in the heavenly kingdoms.
Sermon of Saint John Chrysostom.
Apud Metaphrast.

The Son of God chose for himself as his mother not a rich or wealthy woman, but the blessed Virgin, whose soul was adorned with virtues. For since the blessed Mary preserved chastity beyond all human nature, for that reason she conceived Christ the Lord in her womb. Let us, therefore, running to this most holy Virgin and Mother of God, obtain benefit through her patronage. And so, whatever virgins you may be, flee to the Mother of the Lord. For she will preserve for you by her patronage that most beautiful, most precious, and incorruptible possession.
Sermon of Saint John Damascene
Oratio 2 de Dormit. B. M. V., post init.

Today the sacred and living ark of the living God, who conceived her Creator in her womb, rests in the temple of the Lord, which was built by no human hands. And David her parent exults, and with him the Angels lead the choirs, the Archangels celebrate, the Virtues give glory, the Principalities exult, the Powers rejoice together, the Dominations are filled with gladness, the Thrones keep the feast day, the Cherubim praise, the Seraphim proclaim her glory. Today Eden, the paradise of the new Adam, receives her animated form, in whom the condemnation was loosed, in whom the tree of life was planted, in whom our nakedness was covered.

Today the sacred and living ark of the living God, who conceived her Creator in her womb, rests in the temple of the Lord, which was built by no human hands. And David her parent exults, and with him the Angels lead the choirs, the Archangels celebrate, the Virtues give glory, the Principalities exult, the Powers rejoice together, the Dominations are filled with gladness, the Thrones keep the feast day, the Cherubim praise, the Seraphim proclaim her glory. Today Eden, the paradise of the new Adam, receives her animated form, in whom the condemnation was loosed, in whom the tree of life was planted, in whom our nakedness was covered.
Sermon of Saint Athanasius, Bishop
De Assumptione?

Today the Queen stands at the right hand of her Son who reigns everywhere, as in a garment of gold, clothed about with the variety of incorruption and immortality, and is celebrated with sacred and solemn words: not in the sense that she stands only according to spirit, as if without body and flesh, but in the sense that she is clothed — as regards her most holy flesh — with incorruption and immortality. She is clothed about with variety, moreover, as regards the most holy bones that support her flesh. For from her flesh and from her bones, as from the old Adam, this new Adam fashioned for himself, as it were, a rib to fulfill his place — namely this Incarnation — and, once clothed in it, he bears it forever. And accordingly this new Eve is called the mother of life, and remains clothed about with variety as the firstfruits of immortal life for all the living.
Oratio 1 de Virg. Mariæ Nativit., circa principium

Since it was to come about that the Mother of God and Virgin would spring from Anna, nature did not dare in the least to forestall the fruit of grace, but waited until grace had brought forth its fruit. For it was fitting that she who was to give birth to the First-Born of all creatures, in whom all things are held together, should herself be brought forth into the light as firstborn. O blessed pair, Joachim and Anna! All creation is indebted to you. For through you, creation offered to the Creator the most excellent of all gifts — a chaste mother, who alone was worthy of the Creator.
Oratio 2 de Nativ. B. Mariæ, prope finem

Before us is set the chamber of Anna, reflecting at once the form of married life and of virginity: the former in the mother, the latter in the daughter; of whom the one was but recently freed from barrenness, while the other, a little later, was to give birth to Christ — formed by divine workmanship according to the condition of our nature, yet above nature. Rightly, therefore, does Anna, filled with the divine Spirit, resound with joyful and glad heart: Rejoice with me, you who have brought forth from a barren womb the offspring of the promise, and who nourish at my breast, as I had hoped, the fruit of blessing. I have put off the sadness of barrenness, and have put on the glad garment of fruitfulness. Let that other Anna, the adversary of Pheninnah, also rejoice with me today, and celebrate with her own example this new and unexpected wonder that has been wrought in me.
Sermon of Saint John Chrysostom
Serm. de Mart, quod aut imitandi sunt, aut non laudandi. Tom. 3

Whoever admires the merits of the Saints with devout charity, and frequently celebrates the glories of the righteous with abundant praise, let him imitate their holy ways and justice: since whoever delights in the merit of some Saint, ought to delight in a like devotion to the worship of God. Therefore he ought either to imitate, if he praises; or not to praise, if he shrinks from imitating: so that one who praises another may render himself praiseworthy; and one who admires the merits of the Saints may himself be rendered admirable by the holiness of his life. For if we love the just and the faithful for this reason — that we look up to the justice and faith in them — we can also be what they are, if we ourselves do what they do.
Sermon of Saint Leo, Pope
Sermo de Transfiguratione, ante medium

The Lord disclosed his glory before chosen witnesses, and so clarified that outward form which he shared in common with other men with such splendor, that his face became like the brightness of the sun and his garment equal to the whiteness of snow. The chief purpose being accomplished in this Transfiguration was that the scandal of the Cross should be removed from the hearts of the disciples; and that the voluntary humility of the Passion should not trouble the faith of those to whom the hidden excellence of his dignity had been revealed. But with no less providence was the hope of the holy Church being founded, that the whole body of Christ might recognize what manner of transformation it was to receive, that the members might promise to themselves a share in that honor which had shone forth in the Head.
Sermo 1 de ieiúnio décimi mensis, et collectis

If we faithfully and wisely understand the origin of our creation, most beloved, we find that man was created in the image of God to the end that he might be an imitator of his Author; and that this is the natural dignity of our kind — if in us, as in a certain mirror, the form of the divine goodness should shine forth. To this dignity the grace of the Savior repairs us each day, as what fell in the first Adam is raised up in the second.
Now the cause of our restoration is nothing other than the mercy of God: whom we would not love, had he not first loved us, and dispersed the darkness of our ignorance with the light of his truth.
Sermo 1 in natali App. Petri et Pauli

Of all the holy solemnities, most beloved, the whole world is a partaker, and the devotion of a single faith requires that whatever is recalled as having been done for the salvation of all should be celebrated everywhere with common rejoicings. Yet this day's festivity, beyond that reverence which it has merited throughout the whole world, is to be venerated with a special and proper exultation of our City; so that where the glorious departure of the foremost Apostles was glorified, there on the day of their martyrdom the preeminence of joy should reside. For these are the men through whom the Gospel of Christ, O Rome, shone forth upon you; and you, who were a teacher of error, have been made a disciple of truth.
Sermo 1 de Nativitate Domini

Our Savior, dearly beloved, was born today; let us rejoice. For it is not fitting that there be any place for sadness where the Birthday of Life is celebrated: which, having consumed the fear of mortality, fills us with joy at the promised eternity. No one is excluded from sharing in this gladness. There is one common reason for joy for all: because our Lord, the destroyer of sin and death, as he found no one free from guilt, so he came to free all. Let the holy man exult, for he draws near to his crown; let the sinner be glad, for he is invited to pardon; let the Gentile take courage, for he is called to life. For the Son of God, in the fullness of time which the unsearchable depth of the divine counsel disposed, took to himself the nature of the human race to be reconciled to its Author, so that the devil, the inventor of death, might be conquered through the very one whom he had conquered.

If we understand faithfully, dearly beloved, and wisely the beginning of our creation, we shall find that man was made in the image of God in order to be an imitator of his Creator: and that this is the natural dignity of our kind, if the form of divine goodness shines in us as in a kind of mirror. To this image the grace of the Savior restores us daily, while what fell in the first Adam is raised up in the second.
Sermo 4 de Epiphania

It is just and reasonable, dearly beloved, that the true service of piety on the days that proclaim the works of divine mercy should be to rejoice with all one's heart, and to celebrate with honor the things done for our salvation, as the very law of the recurring seasons calls us to this devotion — seasons which, after the day on which the Son of God, coeternal with the Father, was born of the Virgin, brought us in a short interval the feast of Epiphany, consecrated by the manifestation of the Lord.
Sermo 1 de Ss. Apost. Petro et Paulo, ante medium.

When the twelve Apostles, having received through the Holy Spirit the gift of speech in all tongues, had undertaken to instruct the world in the Gospel, dividing among themselves the regions of the earth, the most blessed Peter, the prince of the apostolic order, was appointed to the stronghold of the Roman Empire, so that the light of truth, which was being revealed for the salvation of all peoples, might the more effectively spread from its very head throughout the whole body of the world. For what nation was not then represented in this city? Or what people anywhere did not know what Rome had learned?

A royal Virgin of the lineage of David was chosen, who, destined to bear a sacred burden, was first to conceive in her mind, before her body, the offspring both divine and human; and lest, unaware of the heavenly counsel, she should be alarmed by the unaccustomed greeting, she learned through the angelic colloquy what was to be wrought in her by the Holy Spirit, and she who was soon to be the Mother of God did not believe that her purity would be harmed. For why should she despair at the novelty of the conception, when the power to accomplish it was promised to her from the Most High? The faith of the believing one is also confirmed by the testimony of a preceding miracle. Elizabeth is given an unexpected fruitfulness, so that he who had granted conception to a barren woman would undoubtedly also grant it to a Virgin. The Word therefore, the Son of God, who was in the beginning with God, through whom all things were made, and without whom nothing was made, became man for the liberation of man from eternal death.

Rejoice in the Lord, dearly beloved; again I say, rejoice: for within a brief interval of time, after the solemnity of the Nativity of Christ, the feast of his manifestation has shone upon us; and he whom on that day the Virgin bore, on this day the world acknowledged. For the Word made flesh so ordered the beginnings of his reception among us, that the newborn Jesus was made manifest to believers and yet hidden from those who persecuted him. Already then the heavens declared the glory of God, and the sound of truth went out into all the earth, when both the army of Angels appeared to the shepherds to announce the Savior's birth, and the star led the Magi to adore him: so that from the rising of the sun to its setting the generation of the true King shone forth, since both the kingdoms of the East, through the Magi, came to believe the truth of the event, and the Roman Empire was not left in ignorance.
Sermo 2 de Nativ. Domini

Almighty and merciful God, whose nature is goodness, whose will is power, whose work is mercy, as soon as diabolical malice had poisoned us with the venom of its envy, immediately signified, among the very beginnings of the world, remedies of his loving kindness predestined for the renewal of mortals; announcing to the serpent that a future seed of the woman would crush the pride of that harmful head by his own power — signifying Christ to come in the flesh, at once God and man — who, born of a Virgin, by an undefiled birth would condemn the violator of the human race.
Sermo 1 de Epiphania

After the day was recently celebrated on which an unstained virginity gave birth to the Savior of the human race, the venerable feast of Epiphany, dearly beloved, grants us perseverance in our joys: so that, amid the closely linked mysteries of kindred solemnities, the vigor of exultation and the fervor of faith may not grow cold. For the salvation of all mankind is at stake in the fact that the infancy of the Mediator between God and men was already being declared to the whole world, even while he was still held in a very small town.
In Natali S. Laurentii, post initium

When the fury of the pagan powers was raging against the most elect members of Christ, and fell especially upon those of the priestly order, the impious persecutor burned with rage against the levite Lawrence, who was preeminent not only in the ministry of the sacraments but also in the administration of the Church's wealth, promising himself a double prize from the seizure of one man; for if he could make him a betrayer of the sacred money, he would make him also a stranger to the true religion. Thus a man greedy for money and an enemy of truth armed himself with a twofold torch: with avarice, to seize the gold; with impiety, to take away Christ. He demanded from the spotless guardian of the sanctuary that the Church's riches, for which he greedily gaped, be brought to him. The most chaste levite, showing him where they were laid up, offered him very large flocks of holy poor people, in whose food and clothing he had stored away inalienable wealth, which was all the more safely preserved the more holily it was shown to have been spent.
Serm. 4. de Epiphania

It is just and reasonable, dearly beloved, that the true service of piety on the days that proclaim the works of divine mercy should be to rejoice with all one's heart, and to celebrate with honor the things done for our salvation, as the very law of the recurring seasons calls us to this devotion — seasons which, after the day on which the Son of God, coeternal with the Father, was born of the Virgin, brought us in a short interval the feast of Epiphany, consecrated by the manifestation of the Lord.
Sermo 7 de Nativitate Domini

He is a true worshipper and devout celebrant of this day's feast, dearly beloved, who holds nothing false about the Incarnation of the Lord, nor anything unworthy about his Divinity. For it is an evil of equal danger if either the truth of our nature or the equality of the Father's glory is denied to him. When, therefore, we approach the understanding of the mystery of the nativity of Christ, by which he was born of a Virgin Mother, let the fog of earthly reasoning be driven far away, and let the smoke of worldly wisdom depart from the eye of enlightened faith.
Sermo sancti Máximi Epíscopi
De S. Cypriano Hom. 2.

In the martyrdom of the most blessed Eutychian, dearest brothers, the whole Church of Christ exults with us — the Church which he instructed to all joy both by the teaching of the heavenly word and adorned by the gift of his triumphant blood. For there was in him, as we know well, both a fullness of spiritual wisdom against the errors of the devil, and a tempered steadfastness of the Christian heart against the persecutions of the world. Who would not celebrate such a man with whatever praises he can, whose eloquence, divinely inspired, both taught the churches and refuted the world?
Ex Homilía 59, quæ est 2 de S. Eusebio

Let us now magnify with confidence the merits of the blessed Father Gregory, already placed in safety; who, manfully holding the helm of faith, has set the anchor of hope now in a tranquil harbor, and has laid up in the desired haven a ship laden with heavenly riches and eternal merchandise. Who, against all adversaries, held the shield of the fear of God for so long, until he came to victory. For what was the whole course of his life but a single unceasing combat with a watchful enemy?
Homilia 1 de Epiphania

On this day, dearly beloved, as we are instructed by the account of paternal tradition, we are to rejoice in a manifold festivity. For it is said that today Christ our Lord was adored by the Gentiles, led by a star; or, having been invited to a wedding, turned water into wine; or, having received baptism from John, consecrated the waters of the Jordan, and at the same time purified his Baptist.
Sermo sancti Maximi Epíscopi.
Homilia 3. in Nativ. S. Ioannis Bapt.

The genuine nativity of the venerable John the Baptist has consecrated the feast of the present day, dearest brothers; for he was sent into this world by heavenly providence not only that he himself might be exalted with prophetic glory, but that the proclamations of all the other prophets might also be confirmed through him. Nor do we unworthily venerate him now with special honor, who by a particular grace foretold the Redeemer of the world last among the prophets, precisely in order that he might point him out first. For he is the only one among the prophets who merited to see with his own eyes the Lord Jesus Christ, whom the others foresaw as coming in distant ages, and to announce him as present.
Sermo sancti Maximi Epíscopi
Homilia 1 de S. Laurentio

It is holy, brothers, and pleasing to God, that we venerate the birthday of the blessed Lawrence with exceptional devotion: by whose radiant flames the victorious Church of Christ shines throughout the whole world even to this day. He, while discharging the office of the diaconate in the see of the most glorious Patriarch, joined himself to the fellowship of the Apostles by the purity of his innocent life and the triumph of his most courageous death. Nor do we wrongly proclaim him the equal of the Apostles, to whom both the chastity of soul gave the levitical ministry, and the fullness of faith conferred the dignity of martyrdom.
Sermo sancti Petri Canísii Presbýteri
De Maria Deipara Virgine incomparabili, lib. 15, c. 13

Why, following Damascene, Athanasius, and others, shall we not address the most blessed Virgin Mary by the title of Queen, when both her father David is a celebrated king, and her son the King of kings and Lord of lords reigning without end hold the most excellent praise in the Scriptures? She is moreover a Queen, if she be compared with those who, as kings, have attained the heavenly kingdom with Christ the supreme King, as co-heirs of that same kingdom, and as placed with him on the same throne, so to speak, as Scripture says. She is also a Queen second to none among the elect, but at the same time set above both angels and men by so much greater dignity as nothing can be more sublime and holy than she who alone has the Son in common with God the Father, and who sees only God and Christ above herself, and all else below.
Sermo sanctii Augustíni Epíscopi
Serm. 21 de Sanctis.

Today we celebrate the nativity of Saint John, dearest brothers: which we read was granted to none other among the Saints. For only the birthday of the Lord and of blessed John is celebrated and observed throughout the whole world. For a barren woman bore the one, and a virgin conceived the other: in Elizabeth barrenness is overcome, in the blessed Mary the custom of conception is transformed. Elizabeth, through knowledge of a man, bore a son; Mary believed the Angel, and conceived. Elizabeth conceived a man, and Mary a man; but Elizabeth only a man, while Mary conceived God and man.
Sermo venerabilis Bedæ presbyteri
In Luc. Evang. Cap. I

When the consent of the virgin had been given, the angel immediately returned to heaven, while she set out for the hill country, hastening to visit Elizabeth, not as one incredulous of the oracle, nor in doubt of the example, but as one joyful of desire, reverent in duty, at the same time offering a typical example: that every soul which has conceived the Word of God in the mind should immediately mount the lofty heights of virtues with the step of love, so that it might penetrate the city of Juda — that is, the citadel of confession and praise — and be able to dwell there in the perfection of faith, hope, and charity, as for three months.

Severus, Severianus, Carpophorus, and Victorinus, brothers, in the persecution of Diocletian, openly denouncing the worship of the gods, were beaten with leaded scourges and poured out their lives in stripes for the name of Christ. Their bodies, cast to dogs and left untouched by them for a long time, were taken up by Christians and buried on the Via Lavicana, three miles from the City, in a sandpit near the sepulchre of the holy Martyrs Claudius, Nicostratus, Symphorianus, Castorius, and Simplicius, who had suffered under the same emperor; for, being the foremost sculptors, they could in no way be induced to make statues of idols, and, when led before the image of the sun to venerate it, they declared they would never adore the works of human hands. Wherefore they were cast into prison, and after persisting many days in the same resolve, they were first beaten with scorpions, then, enclosed alive in leaden coffins, cast into a river. There exists in the City a church under the name of the holy Four Crowned Ones, whose names were long unknown and afterwards revealed by divine providence; there not only the bodies of those four but also of these five Martyrs are honorably buried, and their feast is celebrated on the sixth day before the Ides of November.
We praise you, O God: * we acknowledge you as Lord.
All the earth * worships you, the eternal Father.
To you all Angels, * to you the Heavens and all the Powers:
To you the Cherubim and Seraphim * cry out without ceasing:
(A bow is made) Holy, Holy, Holy * Lord God of Hosts.
Heaven and earth are full * of the majesty of your glory.
The glorious * choir of Apostles praises you,
The admirable * company of Prophets praises you,
The white-robed * army of Martyrs praises you.
Throughout the world * the holy Church confesses you:
Father * of immense majesty;
Your true and only * adorable Son;
And the Holy * Spirit, the Paraclete.
You, O Christ, * are the King of glory.
You are the * everlasting Son of the Father.
(A bow is made) You, about to take upon yourself man for his liberation: * did not shrink from the Virgin's womb.
You, about to take upon yourself man for his liberation: * did not shrink from the Virgin's womb.

The sixth step is purity of heart from a good conscience of good works, which has the power to contemplate that supreme Good, which can be seen only by the pure and serene intellect. Last is the seventh step itself, which is wisdom — that is, contemplation of truth — bringing peace to the whole man and receiving the likeness of God, which is thus concluded: Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called sons of God. The eighth, as it were, returns to the head, because it shows and proves what is consummated and perfect. And so in the first and in the eighth the kingdom of heaven is named: Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven; and, Blessed are they who suffer persecution for justice's sake, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven.

But if your hand or your foot causes you to sin, cut it off and cast it from you. It is necessary indeed that scandals come; but woe to that man through whose own fault it comes to pass that what must happen in the world happens through him. Therefore every affection is to be cut off and every close relationship severed, lest under the pretext of piety any one of the faithful be exposed to scandals. If anyone, he says, is so joined to you as a hand, foot, or eye; if he is useful and watchful, and sharp-sighted; but causes you scandal and, by the discord of his morals, drags you into Gehenna: it is better for you to lack both his closeness and the material advantages he brings, rather than, in wishing to gain relatives and dear ones, to have cause for ruin.

If you compare him with the whole Church of Christ, is he not that chosen and special man through whom and under whom Christ was introduced into the world in an orderly and fitting manner? If, then, the whole holy Church is in debt to the Virgin Mother because through her she was made worthy to receive Christ; so surely, after her, it owes this man a singular grace and reverence. For he is the key of the Old Testament, in whom the patriarchal and prophetical dignity attains its promised fruit. Moreover, he alone possessed in a bodily manner what the divine condescension promised to them. He is rightly represented by that patriarch Joseph, who kept the grain for the peoples. But he also surpasses that patriarch, since he nourished not only Egyptians with the bread of bodily life, but all the elect with the Bread from heaven, which bestows heavenly life, with great and devoted care.

If there are twelve thrones there, there is no place for a thirteenth — for Paul the Apostle — to sit, and there will be no way for him to judge; yet he himself said he would judge, not men only but also angels. What angels, if not apostate angels? Do you not know, he says, that we shall judge angels? Let the crowd therefore reply: Why do you boast that you will judge? Where will you sit? The Lord assigned twelve thrones to twelve Apostles; one fell — Judas — and in his place holy Matthias was ordained; the number of twelve thrones was completed. First find a place where you may sit; and then threaten that you will judge. What the twelve thrones mean, let us see. It is the Sacrament of a certain totality; because the Church was to exist throughout the whole world, whence this structure is called to the framework of Christ.

For if, when he was here, he so loved men that, though he desired to depart and to be with Christ, he nonetheless chose to remain here; how much more will he display an even more fervent charity there. And I myself love Rome for that reason too, though I can praise her on other grounds as well — namely for her greatness, her antiquity, her beauty, her multitude of inhabitants, her empire, her riches, and her deeds of valor in war. But, setting all these aside, I call her blessed because Paul, while he lived, was so benevolent toward her people, loved them so much, both in his discourses among them and at the last by laying down his life among them. His holy body they themselves possess. And therefore that city is all the more illustrious by this fact than by all other things; and, as a great and powerful body, it has two shining eyes, namely the bodies of these Saints.

For if, dearest brothers, we desire to dwell in the house of the Lord in the blessedness of the age to come and to praise him for ever, we must assuredly show forth even in this age what we seek in the age to come: by frequenting the thresholds of the Church, and not only singing therein the praises of the Lord, but also in every place of his dominion demonstrating by words and deeds alike the things that redound to the praise and glory of our Creator.

If therefore to love God is to love one's neighbor (for if you love me, O Peter, he said, feed my sheep): if also the love of neighbor causes us to keep the commandments: rightly does he say that the whole law and the prophets hang upon these. And just as above, when asked about the resurrection, he taught more than those who were testing him asked: so in this place, being questioned about the first commandment, he also brought in, of his own accord, a second not much less than the first: for the second is like to the first. Thus he covertly suggested that it was hatred that was spurring them on to question him. For charity, he says, is not jealous.

If therefore we understand the mystery, my brothers, John is a man, Christ is God. Let man be humbled, that God may be exalted, according to what John himself said of the Lord: He must increase, but I must decrease. That man might be humbled, John was born today, the day from which the days begin to grow shorter; that God might be exalted, Christ was born on the day from which the days begin to grow longer. It is a great mystery, dearest brothers. Therefore we celebrate the nativity of John as we do that of Christ, because even this nativity is full of mystery. Of what mystery, if not that of our humility — just as the nativity of Christ is full of the mystery of our exaltation?

If then Nicodemus was one of those many who had believed in his name, let us consider in this Nicodemus why Jesus did not entrust himself to them. Jesus answered and said to him: Amen, amen I say to you, unless a man be born again, he cannot see the kingdom of God. Therefore Jesus entrusts himself to those who have been born again. Behold, those men had believed in him, and yet Jesus did not entrust himself to them. Such are all catechumens: they already believe in the name of Christ, but Jesus does not entrust himself to them. Let your charity attend and understand. If we say to a catechumen: Do you believe in Christ? he answers, I believe, and signs himself with the Cross of Christ: he bears it on his brow, and does not blush for the Cross of his Lord. Behold, he believes in his name. Let us ask him: Do you eat the flesh of the Son of man and drink the blood of the Son of man? He does not know what we are saying, because Jesus has not entrusted himself to him.

When therefore Nicodemus was from among those many who had believed in his name, he came to the Lord; but he came by night; and this perhaps pertains to the matter. He came to the Lord, and he came by night: he came to the light, and he came in darkness. But those who are reborn of water and the Spirit, what do they hear from the Apostle? You were at one time darkness; but now you are light in the Lord: walk as children of light.

But we pray that they may not persist in the pit which they themselves have dug, but that, being lawfully born and converted to the Church of God, Christ may be formed in them, and that they may come to know the Maker and Creator of this universe as the only true God and Lord of all. These things we pray for them, loving them more truly than they think they love themselves. For the love we bear them, since it is true, is salutary to them, if they receive it. It is like a bitter medicine, consuming the more corrupt and excessive flesh of the wound; for it empties out their pride and inflation. Therefore, bearing witness with all our strength that we extend our hand to them, we shall not grow weary.

If you show him a queen adorned with a diadem, he does not prefer her to his mother dressed in worn rags; he would rather see her plainly clad than the queen magnificently arrayed. For what is his own and what is another's he judges not by poverty or riches, but by love; and he requires nothing beyond what is necessary, and as soon as he has had his fill of milk, he moves away from the breast. He is not oppressed by the same anxieties as we are, nor by loss of money and similar things; nor does he rejoice in the same fleeting things as we do, nor does he marvel at the beauty of bodies. That is why it was said: For of such is the kingdom of heaven; that we may do by deliberate will the things that children do by nature.

If the shadow of one who came to visit was so healing, how much more the chain of one who bound? If an empty appearance of a hollow image was able to have in it the power of salvation, how much more did the fetters, pressed by their iron weight upon the sacred limbs, draw forth healing from the body? If before martyrdom he was so powerful in aid of those who prayed, how much more efficacious is he after his triumph? Blessed those bonds, which, changed from manacles and fetters into a crown, and touching the Apostle, made him a Martyr! Blessed the chains, which sent their prisoner all the way to the Cross of Christ, destined not so much to condemn as to consecrate him!

So indeed was the Lord received as a guest, who came into his own and his own received him not; but to as many as received him, he gave power to become sons of God, adopting servants and making them free, redeeming captives and making them co-heirs. Yet let none of you perhaps say: O blessed are they who merited to receive Christ into their own home! Do not grieve, do not murmur because you were born in times when you no longer see the Lord in the flesh. He has not taken from you that dignity. When you did it, he says, to one of the least of mine, you did it to me. These few things, suited to the occasion, we have said about feeding the Lord in the flesh, yet feeding in the spirit.

So also from that lamb it was done: the Jews slew the sheep, and I came to know the fruit from the sacrament. Blood and water from his side. I would not have you, hearer, pass so easily over the secrets of so great a mystery; for I still have a mystical and hidden discourse to offer. I said that the water and blood signify the symbol of baptism and of the mysteries. For the holy Church has been founded through these by the washing of regeneration and renewal of the Holy Spirit. Through baptism, I say, and the mysteries, which are seen to have been brought forth from the side. From his side therefore Christ built the Church, as from the side of Adam his wife Eve was brought forth. For this reason Paul also testifies, saying: We are of his body and of his bones; meaning clearly that side. For just as from that side God caused a woman to be born, so too from his side Christ gave us water and blood, by which the Church is to be restored. Moreover, in the year one thousand nine hundred and nineteen from the redemption of the human race, which the Supreme Pontiff Pius XI willed to be celebrated with a solemn Jubilee above all others for the recalling of so ineffable a benefit; so that the fruits of the most precious Blood by which we have been redeemed, of the Immaculate Lamb Christ, might flow more abundantly upon men, and its memory might be commended to the faithful more vividly, that same Supreme Pontiff elevated the feast of the Most Precious Blood of our Lord Jesus Christ, to be celebrated each year by the whole Church, to the rank of a double feast of the first class.

So indeed the Lord permitted his disciple to doubt after his Resurrection, yet did not abandon him in his doubt; just as before his birth he willed Mary to have a husband who nevertheless did not come to know her in marriage. For thus the doubting and touching disciple became a witness of the true Resurrection, just as the bridegroom of his mother had been the guardian of her inviolate virginity. He touched him, and exclaimed: My Lord and my God. Jesus said to him: Because you have seen me, you have believed. Since the Apostle Paul says, Now faith is the substance of things hoped for, the evidence of things not seen; it is clearly evident that faith is the evidence of things that cannot be seen. For the things that are seen already have not faith, but knowledge.

The order thus established, the holy founders returned to Gaul, and the first monastery of Cervi Frigidi having been built in the diocese of Meaux, Felix remained for its governance; while John returned to Rome with some companions, where Innocent gave them the house, church, and hospital of Saint Thomas of Formis on the Caelian Hill, together with many revenues and possessions. Letters having also been given to the Miramolin, king of Morocco, the work of redemption was begun under happy auspices. Then John set out to the Spains, which were in great part under the yoke of the Saracens, and moved the hearts of kings, princes, and other faithful to compassion for the captives and poor. He built monasteries, erected hospitals, and at great profit of souls redeemed many captives. Finally returning to Rome, and applying himself to holy works, worn down by continual labors, consumed by illness, and burning with the most ardent love of God and neighbor, he came to his last end. Therefore, calling the brethren together and earnestly exhorting them to the work of redemption shown from heaven, he fell asleep in the Lord on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of January, in the year of salvation one thousand two hundred and thirteen; and his body was buried with fitting honor in that same church of Saint Thomas of Formis.

But as we ourselves have experienced, and as our ancestors proved, we believe and are confident that, amid all the labors of this life, we are always to be assisted in obtaining the mercy of God by the prayers of special patrons: so that, to the degree that we are weighed down by our own sins, we may be raised up by the merits of the apostles. Through our Lord Jesus Christ, to whom with the Father and the Holy Spirit belong the same power, one divinity, for ever and ever. Amen.

Sigismund obtained the kingdom upon the death of his father Gunobald, king of the Burgundians. Led by zeal for piety, he built the monastery of Agaunum with devoted care. After the death of his first wife, by whom he had fathered a son named Sigeric, he took another; and she began with all her heart to turn against the son in the manner of a stepmother. Hence the boy, having conceived a similar hatred toward her, was moved one feast day when he saw her adorned in the garments of his deceased mother and said: You were certainly not worthy that these garments should touch your back, which are known to have belonged to my lady and my mother. But she, inflamed with fury at these words, meditated revenge day and night. At last, instructed by the fraud of the devil, she persuaded her husband that Sigeric, desirous of reigning, was plotting wicked plans to destroy him. Urged by these words, the father defiled himself with a wicked parricide. For, after having plied his son with wine in the afternoon, when he was overcome by deep sleep, he strangled him by thrusting a strap under his neck.
