And these signs shall follow those who believe: In my name they shall cast out devils; they shall speak in new tongues; they shall take up serpents; and if they drink any deadly thing, it shall not harm them; they shall lay hands upon the sick, and they shall recover. Is it not so, my brothers, that because you do not perform these signs, you do not believe? But these things were necessary at the beginning of the Church. For in order that faith might grow among the multitude of believers, it had to be nourished by miracles; just as we, when we plant shrubs, pour water upon them until we see that they have already taken root in the earth; and once they have fixed a root, the watering ceases. Hence it is that Paul says: Tongues are a sign not for believers, but for unbelievers.

Silvester, born at Osimo in Picenum of a noble family, adorned his boyhood years wonderfully with letters and good morals. Well formed in sacred letters and made a canon, he aided the people by his example and sacred sermons. At the funeral of a certain deceased nobleman, beholding in the open tomb the disfigured corpse of a handsome man who had been his kinsman, he said: I am what this man was; what this man is, I shall be. And straightway he withdrew into solitude, out of desire for greater perfection, where he devoted himself to vigils, prayers, and fasts. And that he might be more hidden from men, he moved to various places, and at length upon Mount Fano, a place then deserted, he erected a temple in honor of Saint Benedict and laid the foundations of the Silvestrine Congregation. There he shone before the monks in wondrous holiness; he excelled in the spirit of prophecy, in power over demons, and in other gifts, which he always preserved by a profound humility. He fell asleep in the Lord in the year of salvation one thousand two hundred and sixty-seven.

Silvester, a Roman, son of Rufinus, devoted himself from his earliest years to the priest Cyrinus, whose learning and manner of life he imitated excellently. During the raging of persecution he had hidden on Mount Soracte; and in his thirtieth year he was created a priest of the holy Roman Church by Pope Marcellinus. Excelling all the other clergy in that office with every praise, he afterwards succeeded to the place of Miltiades, under the Emperor Constantine, who had previously given peace to the Church of Christ by public law. He had barely taken up the governance of the Church when he earnestly fostered Constantine, already illuminated from heaven by the sign of the Cross and victorious over his enemy Maxentius, in the protection and propagation of the Christian religion. He also, as the ancient tradition of the Roman Church recounts, caused him to recognize the images of the Apostles, washed him with holy baptism, and cleansed him from the leprosy of unbelief.

Excelling all the other clergy in that office with every praise, he afterwards succeeded to the place of Miltiades, under the Emperor Constantine, who had previously given peace to the Church of Christ by public law. He had barely taken up the governance of the Church when he earnestly fostered Constantine, already illuminated from heaven by the sign of the Cross and victorious over his enemy Maxentius, in the protection and propagation of the Christian religion. He also, as the ancient tradition of the Roman Church recounts, caused him to recognize the images of the Apostles, washed him with holy baptism, and cleansed him from the leprosy of unbelief.
To this Emperor, when he had ordered a bath to be prepared for him from the blood of children, by the advice of physicians, for the cure of his leprosy, the holy Apostles Peter and Paul appeared to him in sleep, commanding him that if he wished to be freed from his leprosy, setting aside the horror of that impious bath, he should summon Silvester, who was hiding on Mount Soracte; from whom, refreshed by the saving washing, he should command temples to be built throughout all the territory of the Roman Empire in the Christian manner, and, with the statues of the empty gods removed, should render worship to the true God. Constantine therefore, obeying the heavenly warnings, summoned Silvester when he had been most diligently sought out; from whom, recognizing the images of the Apostles, he was healed by baptism and inflamed to protect and propagate the religion of Christ.

Silvester, a Roman, son of Rufinus, had hidden on Mount Soracte during the raging of persecution; and in his thirtieth year he was created a priest of the holy Roman Church. When Pope Miltiades had departed this life, he succeeded to his place, under the Emperor Constantine, who had previously given peace to the Church of Christ by public law. He so fostered Constantine in protecting and propagating the faith that the emperor erected many basilicas and endowed them most generously. In this Pontiff's time the first Council of Nicaea was held, confirmed by Silvester himself, in which Arius was condemned. Distinguished by holiness of life and kindness toward the poor, he died in peace and was buried in the cemetery of Priscilla.

Silverius, a Campanian, was created Pontiff immediately after Agapitus: whose learning and holiness shone forth in combating heretics, and whose greatness of steadfast spirit was evident in upholding the judgment of Agapitus. For when he was repeatedly asked by the Empress Theodora to restore Anthimus, whom Agapitus had deposed from the bishopric of Constantinople because he defended the Eutychian heresy, he refused. For this reason the enraged woman directed Belisarius to send Silverius into exile. He went into exile on the island of Pontia, from where he is said to have written these words to Bishop Amator: I am sustained with the bread of tribulation and the water of anguish; but I have not left, nor do I leave, my duty. And indeed, being quickly worn down by hardships and afflictions, he fell asleep in the Lord, on the twelfth day before the Kalends of July; his body was brought to Rome and deposited in the Vatican Basilica, and was made illustrious by many miracles. He governed the Church for more than three years, having ordained in the month of December thirteen priests, five deacons, and nineteen bishops in various places.

Silvester, born at Osimo in Picenum of a noble family, immediately adorned his boyhood years wonderfully with letters and good morals. Sent as a youth to Bologna by his father for the study of jurisprudence, when, admonished by God, he had applied himself to sacred letters, he incurred his father's displeasure, which he bore with equanimity for a full ten years. By reason of his outstanding virtue, he was chosen as a fellow in honor by the canons of the cathedral church of Osimo; in which office he aided the people by his sermons, example, and preaching.

Simeon, son of Cleophas, was ordained bishop of Jerusalem next after James. Under the Emperor Trajan, he was accused before the consul Atticus of being a Christian and a kinsman of Christ. For at that time all who were descended from the family of David were being seized. He was accordingly subjected to many torments and suffered the same kind of passion that our Savior had undergone; all marveling that a man worn out by age — for he was one hundred and twenty years old — bore the most bitter sufferings of the cross with such courage and steadfastness.

Simon the Cananean, also called the Zealot, and Thaddaeus, called also Jude the brother of James in the Gospel, the author of one of the Catholic Epistles; the former traversed Mesopotamia, the latter Egypt with the proclamation of the Gospel. Afterwards meeting in Persia, when they had begotten innumerable sons for Jesus Christ and had disseminated the faith among those vast regions and fierce peoples, they together glorified the most holy name of Jesus Christ by teaching and miracles, and finally by a glorious martyrdom.

Simplicius, a native of Tivoli, son of Castorius, received the governance of the Roman Church next after Saint Hilary, and governed it with the greatest vigilance in most difficult times (when the Catholic faith through a great part of the Christian world, because of almost all the princes being infected with heresy, was wavering). He strenuously resisted the Emperor Leo, who petitioned that the privileges granted to the Church of Constantinople by the bishops of the Council of Chalcedon should be ratified, even sending his own legate to Constantinople for that reason. With the same pastoral solicitude he labored greatly so that Timothy Aelurus, the usurper of the Church of Alexandria, who was dwelling freely in Constantinople and striving as much as possible to propagate heresy, and who sought through the efforts of the new Emperor Zeno to have a new council convened, should be sent into exile, and thus the Church of Alexandria restored to its integrity. He also vigorously resisted the attempts of the remaining rebels to have a new synod announced, declaring that new councils were not easily to be convoked, unless something new had arisen in perverse doctrines, or something ambiguous had emerged in the assertion of dogmas.

He had a singular care for the clergy, whom he always attended with fatherly love and many benefactions. Yet his marvelous generosity shone forth especially toward the poor, to whom he distributed the revenues of the Church with a generous hand both during his life and at his death, being firmly convinced that the riches of the Church could not be put to nobler use, and that, passed through the hands of the needy, they were transferred straight to the treasury of eternity with an incredible profit of spiritual interest. At length, after two years and nearly nine months, he came to rest in a holy death, in the year of Christ six hundred and fifty-five, and his body was laid to rest in the basilica of Saint Peter.

With a singular zeal for fostering peace, he directed all his efforts toward settling the disputes between the Pisans and the Lucchese. He had the deepest love for the beauty of the house of God: for he adorned the Liberian basilica with richer decoration, and either restored or enriched with precious gifts very many other churches. Moreover, he gave as a free gift the fourth part of the oblations belonging to him by custom from the Vatican basilica, over and above the tithe already assigned to the Prince of the Apostles by Saint Leo IX. He enrolled the Emperor Henry, a noble example among Catholic princes, in the roll of the saints. At last, at Tivoli, whither he had withdrawn from the City to escape the summer heat, he was stricken with a grave illness and sought the death of the just on the sixth day before the Ides of July in the year one thousand one hundred and fifty-three, after having sat in the Chair of Peter for eight years and four months. His body, brought to Rome, was laid to rest in the Vatican, together with the remains of Saint Gregory III and Blessed Peter the Levite. The sacred veneration already then offered to him, glowing with the splendor of miracles, and flourishing likewise in other regions down to this very age, was ratified and confirmed by the Supreme Pontiff Pius IX, acting on the advice of the Congregation of Sacred Rites.

His singular zeal shone forth in promoting the salutary devotion toward the Most Sacred Hearts of Jesus and Mary, whose liturgical cult to be rendered to them he was, not without some divine inspiration, the first of all to devise; and thus he was regarded as the father, doctor, and apostle of that same cult. Strongly resisting the doctrines of the Jansenists, he kept his obedience to the Chair of Peter unchanged, and prayed to God unceasingly for his enemies as for brothers. Broken more by his labors than by his years, longing to be dissolved and to be with Christ, on the nineteenth day of August in the year one thousand six hundred and eighty, repeatedly pronouncing the sweet names of Jesus and Mary, he expired peacefully. Pope Pius X, having proclaimed him illustrious for many miracles, enrolled him in the roll of the Blessed; and Pope Pius XI, as he shone with new signs, enrolled him among the Saints on the holy year, on the Sunday of Pentecost, and extended his Office and Mass to the universal Church.

Fortified by a singular austerity of life and the protection of all the virtues, through his assiduous contemplation of divine things he frequently endured prolonged and wondrous ecstasies; and so ardently did he burn with love toward God that, when the divine fire could no longer contain itself within him, it seemed to burst forth outwardly and to radiate from his countenance. Wholly intent on the salvation of his neighbors, he was assiduous both in the preaching of the word of God and in the administration of the Sacraments. Thus, enriched by so many merits and inflamed with ardent zeal for the promotion of stricter discipline, he was given by God as a companion to Saint Teresa, so that the primitive observance of the Carmelite order which she had restored among the sisters, the same might with John's assistance be restored also among the brothers. Therefore, sharing with the handmaid of God countless labors in advancing the divine work, he visited one by one the monasteries that had been erected throughout Spain by the care of that same holy Virgin, undaunted by any hardships or perils of life. In these and in many others founded through his efforts, he confirmed the restored observance by propagating it with word and example; so that he is rightly held to be the first, after Saint Teresa, to profess and be the father of the order of the Discalced Carmelites.

Siricius, a Roman, having served as priest of the title of the Shepherd, was raised to the Apostolic See by the acclamation of the entire clergy and people after the death of the holy Pope Damasus, the schismatic Ursinus opposing him in vain, while the Emperor Valentinian above all rejoiced, proclaiming him a great example of innocence and uprightness. At the very outset of his pontificate, he gave to Himerius, Bishop of Tarragona, a decretal letter full of most salutary ordinances, to be communicated to the other churches of Spain, so that the corrupt morals of the clergy might be reformed and the vigor of discipline restored; and when the same discipline was also collapsing in Africa, he took care to repair it by holding a synod of eighty bishops at Rome.

At the very outset of his pontificate, he gave to Himerius, Bishop of Tarragona, a decretal letter full of most salutary ordinances, to be communicated to the other churches of Spain, so that the corrupt morals of the clergy might be reformed and the vigor of discipline restored; and when the same discipline was also collapsing in Africa, he took care to repair it by holding a synod of eighty bishops at Rome.
Countless are the other deeds which he accomplished without wavering in defense of the faith throughout the whole time of his pontificate. He struck the monk Jovinian, enemy of holy virginity and a Christian Epicurus, with anathema at a Roman synod. He likewise condemned Bonosus, Bishop of Sardica, who denied both the divinity of Christ and the virginity of the Mother of God after childbirth. The Manicheans, expelled from the City, he subjected to the coercive power of secular penalties under imperial law; but those who returned to the Church he wished to be confined to monasteries, and to be received back into communion only at the end of life.

May what we bring through you be excusable through you; may what we ask with faithful mind be granted. Accept what we offer, restore what we beg, excuse what we fear: for you are the sole hope of sinners. Through you we hope for pardon of our offenses, and in you is the most blessed expectation of our rewards. Holy Mary, come to the aid of the wretched, help the fainthearted, console the sorrowful, pray for the people, intercede for the clergy, make intercession for the devout female sex: may all experience your help, whoever celebrates your holy Nativity.

Having made his solemn profession, out of his singular devotion to the divine Francis of Assisi, he took the name Francis. Two years later, upon the death of Adorno, he was placed over the whole order, though unwilling; in which office he gave brilliant examples of every virtue. Most zealous for the expansion of his institute, he besought this of God earnestly by assiduous prayers, tears, and continual mortification of the body. For this purpose he went to Spain a third time, clothed in the habit of a pilgrim and begging his food from door to door. Having endured every hardship on the journey and experienced in a wondrous manner the help of the Almighty, he saved by the protection of prayer the ship he had boarded from imminent shipwreck. That he might accomplish his vow in those kingdoms, he labored greatly; and, his reputation for holiness shining before him, and with the most ample munificence of the Catholic kings Philip II and Philip III, having overcome the efforts of his adversaries with singular courage of soul, he founded many houses of his order — an achievement he accomplished with equal success throughout Italy.

It was by the love of God alone that his Only-Begotten came to unite to himself the minds of chosen human beings. Hence John also says: For God so loved the world that he gave his Only-Begotten Son for us. He who therefore came to mankind through charity made known that same charity to be the wedding garment. Every one of you, then, who, placed in the Church, has believed in God, has already entered the wedding feast; but he has not come in the wedding garment if he does not keep the grace of charity. And indeed, brethren, if anyone were invited to a bodily wedding, he would change his garment, he would show by the very elegance of his dress that he rejoiced with the bridegroom and bride, and he would be ashamed to appear among those rejoicing and celebrating the feast in shabby clothes. We come to the wedding feast of God, and we are unwilling to change the garment of our heart. The Angels rejoice when the elect are taken up into heaven. With what spirit, then, do we behold these spiritual festivities, we who do not have the wedding garment, that is, charity, which alone makes us beautiful?

For the holy Lord Jesus alone is holy in every respect among those born of woman: he who, by the newness of an immaculate birth, neither experienced the contagion of earthly corruption nor was subdued by it, but repelled it by his heavenly majesty. For if we follow the letter: how is every male holy, when it is well known that many have been most wicked? Was Ahab holy? Were the false prophets holy, whom the avenging fire of heaven consumed at the prayer of Elijah? But he is holy whom the pious ordinances of the divine law signified in the figure of a coming mystery; inasmuch as he alone would open the fruitful secret of the immaculate virginity of the holy Church the virgin, for the begetting of the peoples of God.

Soter, born at Fundi in Campania, decreed that sacred virgins should not touch the sacred vessels or the altar linens, nor perform the ministry of incense in church. He likewise ordained that the Body of Christ should be received by all at the Lord's Supper, except those who were forbidden to do so on account of grave sin. He sat in the pontificate for three years, eleven months, and eighteen days. He was crowned with martyrdom under the Emperor Marcus Aurelius, and was buried in the cemetery later called that of Callixtus; and, in accordance with ancestral custom, he ordained in the month of December eighteen priests, nine deacons, and eleven bishops for various places.

Caius, a Dalmatian of the family of the Emperor Diocletian, established that one should ascend to the episcopate through the following degrees of orders and offices in the Church: namely, those of Doorkeeper, Lector, Exorcist, Acolyte, Subdeacon, Deacon, and Presbyter. He, fleeing the cruelty of Diocletian toward Christians, lay hidden for some time in a cave; but eight years later, having obtained the crown of martyrdom together with his brother Gabinus, he was likewise buried in the cemetery of Callixtus.

After the death of Stephen, he returned to the monastery of Monte Cassino, and was soon appointed by Nicholas II a Cardinal of the holy Roman Church, and at the same time was blessed as Abbot of Monte Cassino. The same Pontiff and his successors destined him for the management of the most important and most difficult affairs of the Church, without drawing him away from the governance of the monks; for not only did he advance the observance of the holy rule as their number increased, but he also restored the monastery almost entirely from the ground up. Moreover, he so splendidly raised from its foundations the basilica made glorious by the body of the holy father Benedict, and enriched it with precious stones brought even from the shores of the East, with mosaic works and sacred furnishings crafted with wondrous art and at great cost, that it stands as an illustrious monument to his munificence and genius. This basilica was consecrated by Alexander II as a sign of his benevolence toward Desiderius, in the presence of very many Bishops and Cardinals, among whom worthy of memory are Saint Peter Damian and Hildebrand, who later succeeded that same Alexander, having taken the name Gregory VII.

Stephen, king of the Hungarians, brought the faith of Christ and the name of a king into Hungary. Having obtained a royal crown from the Roman Pontiff, and anointed king at his command, he offered his kingdom to the Apostolic See. He established various houses of piety at Rome, Jerusalem, and Constantinople; in Hungary he founded the archbishopric of Esztergom and ten bishoprics with admirable devotion and munificence. He was distinguished by an exceptional charity toward the poor and by an assiduous zeal for prayer. He venerated the Mother of God with the most ardent devotion, built a most magnificent temple in her honor, and established her as the patron of Hungary; and was in turn received into heaven by that same Virgin on the very day of her Assumption, which the Hungarians, following the institution of the holy King, call the day of the Great Lady. Yet his feast is celebrated above all on this day, by the constitution of Pope Innocent XI, on which the most strongly fortified citadel of Buda was valiantly recovered from the Christian army through the help of the holy King.

He established stations in the City, so that the priests — for the sake of those seeking Baptism and penance — of the first region would remain at Saint Paul, those of the third at Saint Lawrence, and those of the seventh at Saint Peter. He dedicated the basilicas of Saint Stephen on the Caelian Hill, of the Apostle Saint Andrew next to Saint Mary, likewise another of Saint Stephen next to Saint Lawrence, and finally another of the Martyr Saint Bibiana within the City near the Licinian palace; and he gave to the Roman Church a great number of both silver and golden vessels. At length, under the Emperor Zeno and Odoacer king of Italy, he passed to the Lord. He held three ordinations in the month of December, in which he ordained fifty-eight priests, fifteen deacons, and thirty-six bishops for various places. He administered the priesthood for fifteen years, five months, and ten days.

Stanislaus, born of a noble family near Krakow, whom his devout parents, barren for thirty years, obtained from God through their prayers, gave proof of his future holiness from his earliest age. As a young man, he made great progress in the sacred learning of canon law and theology. After the death of his parents, he distributed a large inheritance to the poor, out of desire for the monastic life. But, God disposing otherwise, he was made a canon of Krakow and a preacher by Bishop Lambert, and was afterwards, though unwilling, appointed to his place. In this office he shone forth by the praise of all pastoral virtues, and especially by his mercy toward the poor. Having rebuked Boleslaw, King of Poland, many times in vain on account of his corrupt morals, he excluded him from the communion of the faithful. The king, therefore, raging with fury, sent soldiers into the church to cut down the holy bishop; but when they were repelled by divine power, the impious king with his own hand slew the priest of God as he was offering the immaculate Victim at the altar. God declared the holiness of his servant by many miracles after his death, moved by which Innocent IV enrolled him in the number of the Saints.

Stanislaus, born in Poland of a senatorial family of the Kostkas, had been destined for a military career, but the name of Jesus was divinely inscribed in the womb of his mother before his birth. As a boy, he guarded his chastity so jealously that if at his father's table he heard anything said that was less than modest, he would fall senseless with horror. Sent to the seminary at Vienna in Austria for his studies, he was no less an example to his companions than an object of veneration. Forced thence to move into the house of a Lutheran host, and there urged by his brother Paul with every kind of hardship toward a more licentious life, he endured this domestic warfare with the utmost constancy for two full years, affirming that he had been born for eternal, not for perishable things. Thus his only desire was for heavenly things, his conversation with God was unceasing, and his devotion to the Mother of God was so tender that he would call her his sweetest mother.

Stanislaus the Pole, born at Krakow of a noble family and devout parents, who had previously obtained him from God by prayers through thirty years of barrenness, gave proof of his future holiness from his earliest age. As a young man, he applied himself diligently to the liberal arts, and made great progress in the sacred learning of canon law and theology. After the death of his parents, he distributed a large inheritance to the poor, out of desire for the monastic life. But by the providence of God, having been made a canon of Krakow and a preacher by Bishop Lambert, he was afterwards, though unwilling, appointed to his place. In this office he shone forth by the praise of all pastoral virtues, and especially by his mercy toward the poor.

Immediately after making his profession, he was sent to the convent of Saint Anne in the city of Altötting; a place celebrated and most frequented among all the Marian shrines under German rule, so much so that several hundred thousand of the faithful gather there each year. On account of the great concourse to that city, the office of porter in the monastery became exceedingly difficult; and Conrad, to whom this task had been entrusted from the very day of his arrival, retained it until his death and fulfilled it as an apostolate of example. Tireless in labor, sparing in speech, generous toward the poor, prompt in receiving and assisting pilgrims, for more than forty years he bore the burden of doorkeeper with equanimity, to the greatest benefit of the inhabitants and pilgrims alike, in all needs both of soul and of body.

He at once converted his father's house into a monastery and assigned his estates to the same monastery for the use of the monks; but in order to bind the men of this institution to himself by a far greater benefit, having called a synod of the bishops of Italy, he restored by holy laws the discipline of the monks which had been declining. Mellitus, Bishop of London, who had come to Rome to consult the Vicar of Christ on English affairs, attended the synod, and carried its decrees to Britain along with the letters of Boniface.

Stephen brought the faith of Christ and the name of a king into Hungary. Having obtained a royal crown from the Roman Pontiff, and anointed king at his command, he offered his kingdom to the Apostolic See. He established various houses of piety at Rome, Jerusalem, and Constantinople; in Hungary he founded the archbishopric of Esztergom and ten bishoprics with admirable devotion and munificence. His love and generosity toward the poor was equal; embracing them as Christ himself, he never dismissed anyone from his presence in sorrow or empty-handed; but to relieve their need, having disbursed his most ample resources, he also frequently distributed with remarkable kindness even the furnishings of his household. Moreover, with his own hands he was accustomed to wash the feet of the poor, to frequent the hospitals alone and unknown by night, to serve the sick, and to perform the other works of charity. Through the merit of these virtues, his right hand, while the rest of his body dissolved, remained incorrupt.

Stephen the Roman held the pontificate under the Emperors Valerian and Gallienus. He ordained that priests and deacons should never use sacred vestments except in church. He forbade those baptized by heretics to be baptized again, writing back to Saint Cyprian with these words: Let nothing be innovated, except what has been handed down. He also converted many to Christ, among them the tribune Olympius together with his wife Exsuperia and his son Theodulus, likewise the tribune Nemesius with his whole family, after the eyes of his daughter Lucilla were restored; all of whom became Martyrs of Jesus Christ. But, the persecution of the emperors now pressing ever more severely, Stephen, having summoned the clergy, urged his people to martyrdom, and in the crypts of the Martyrs celebrated Masses and councils without ceasing. When at one time he was seized by unbelievers and brought to the temple of Mars to sacrifice there, he freely declared that he had no wish to give to demons that honor which was owed to God alone. At these words, the statue of Mars fell at an earthquake and the temple shook. Wherefore, all those who held Stephen taking to flight, the Pontiff returned to his people in the cemetery of Lucina; and, instructing them in the divine precepts, he gave them Communion in the Sacrament of the Body of Christ; and there, as he was completing the solemnities of the Mass, when the satellites of the emperors arrived again, his head was cut off in his own seat. His body, together with the seat sprinkled with the blood of the Martyr, was buried by the clergy in the cemetery of Callixtus, on the fourth day before the Nones of August. He lived in the pontificate for three years, three months, and twenty-two days. He held two ordinations in the month of December, in which he ordained six priests, five deacons, and three bishops.

Yet Apronianus urges them to worship the gods of the nations, promising that they would thereby recover their lost wealth, the favor of the emperor, and their distinguished betrothal. If they refused, he threatened them with prison, flogging, and the axe. But they, yielding to neither flattery nor threats from the right faith, and ready rather to die than to be defiled by the customs of the pagans, with the utmost constancy expressed their abhorrence of the praetor's impiety. Wherefore Demetria, falling suddenly before the eyes of Bibiana, died in the Lord; and Bibiana was handed over to be corrupted by a most cunning woman named Rufina, who had been trained from the cradle to preserve the Christian laws and the unsullied flower of virginity. Stronger than herself, she overcame the snares of that woman and foiled the cunning of the praetor.

Inflamed by the heavenly fire of charity, which he had once drawn copiously in the Vatican Basilica from the depths of the Heart of Jesus, and intent only on extending the glory of God, it is hardly possible to say how many labors he undertook and hardships he endured for more than forty years in order either to defend several cities and provinces of Germany from the contagion of heresy, or to restore those infected with heresy to the Catholic faith. At the Diet of Regensburg and Augsburg, he stirred up the leaders of the empire to defend the rights of the Church and to reform the morals of peoples; at Worms, he reduced the insolent masters of impiety to silence. Appointed by Saint Ignatius as provincial of Upper Germany, he founded houses and colleges in many places. He labored with all his might to promote and enlarge the German College established at Rome; in the academies, he restored the studies of sacred and humane disciplines, which had fallen into pitiable ruin; against the Magdeburg Centuriators he wrote two outstanding volumes; and he published for the people a summary of Christian doctrine most thoroughly approved by the judgment of theologians and by three centuries of public use everywhere, and many other works highly suitable for the instruction of peoples. For this reason, called the Hammer of Heretics and the second Apostle of Germany, he was plainly held worthy of being regarded as divinely chosen to protect religion in Germany.

But when the day of the Paschal feast came, in the silence of the dead of night, the treacherous Arian father sent a bishop to him, that he might receive from his hand the communion of a sacrilegious consecration, and through this might be found worthy to return to his father's favor. But the man devoted to God reproached the Arian bishop as he came, as was right, and repelled his treachery from himself with fitting rebukes: for even though he lay bound outwardly, yet within himself he stood secure on the high summit of his mind. When therefore the bishop returned to him, the Arian father raged and at once sent his officers to kill the most steadfast Confessor of God where he lay; and this was done. For as soon as they entered, they drove an axe into his brain and took away the life of his body: and in this they had power to destroy only what he himself, who was destroyed, had already resolved to despise. But to manifest his true glory, heavenly signs did not fail. For in the silence of the night, the chant of psalmody began to be heard at the body of that same King and Martyr — and truly a King's, because also a Martyr's.

Martha received him as pilgrims are wont to be received; yet a handmaid received the Lord, the sick received the Savior, a creature received the Creator. She received him, however, to be fed in spirit, while he was to be fed in the flesh. For the Lord willed to take the form of a servant, and, having taken the form of a servant, to be fed in that form by his servants — by condescension, not by condition. For this very condescension was a gift: to allow himself to be fed. He had flesh in which he might indeed hunger and thirst; but do you not know that when he was hungry in the desert, Angels ministered to him? Therefore, what he willed to receive as food, he himself gave to the one who fed him. And what wonder, if he also gave to the widow on account of holy Elijah, whom before that a raven fed? Surely he had not grown deficient in feeding when he was sending Elijah to the widow? By no means; but he was disposing to bless a devout widow through the service rendered to his servant.

Symphorosa of Tivoli, wife of the Martyr Getulius, bore him seven sons: Crescentius, Julian, Nemesius, Primitivus, Justin, Stacteus, and Eugenius; all of whom, together with their mother, were arrested by the Emperor Hadrian on account of their profession of the Christian faith. When their piety, tested by many and varied tortures, remained steadfast, their mother, who had been their teacher in the faith, became likewise their guide to martyrdom. For, with a stone bound to her neck, she was cast into the river; and her body, sought out by her brother Eugenius, was buried. On the following day, which was the fifteenth day before the Kalends of August, the seven brothers, each bound to a stake, were put to death in various ways: Crescentius had his throat pierced with iron; Julian was stabbed in the chest; Nemesius had his heart run through; Primitivus was pierced in the belly; Justin was cut limb from limb; Stacteus was transfixed with javelins; Eugenius was split in two from the chest. Thus eight most pleasing victims were immolated to God. Their bodies were cast into a very deep pit on the Via Tiburtina, nine miles from the City; and afterwards, having been transferred to Rome, they were laid to rest in the church of the Holy Angel in the fish-pond.

For King Herod feared him, when the same Magi announced it to him, even while they were still seeking the infant whom they had known, heaven bearing witness, to have been already born. What will the tribunal of the Judge be, when the cradle of the infant struck terror into proud kings? How much more wisely might kings seek not, like Herod, to slay him, but rather, like the Magi, to delight to adore him; now especially him who, even for his enemies, endured from his enemies the very death which the enemy sought to inflict, and who, being slain, slew that death in his own body. May kings fear devoutly him who now sits at the right hand of the Father, whom an impious king feared while still drinking at his mother's breast.

For such ought to be the pastor in the Church who, after the manner of Paul, becomes all things to all men, so that the sick may find in him healing, the sorrowful joy, the despairing confidence, the ignorant instruction, the doubtful counsel, the penitent pardon and consolation, and whatever at length is necessary for the salvation of each. For this reason, Christ, when he wished to appoint the chief teachers of the world and the Church, was not content to say to his disciples: You are the light of the world; but added this as well: A city set on a mountain cannot be hidden, neither do men light a lamp and put it under a bushel, but upon a lampstand, that it may give light to all who are in the house. For those ecclesiastics are mistaken who think they can satisfy their ministry more by the splendor of their teaching than by integrity of life and the ardor of charity.

He showed himself in the pontificate the same as he had shown himself before his elevation: most devout, most gentle, with a singular devotion toward God, charity toward his neighbor, prudence in the conduct of affairs — a father to the poor and the sick, a defender of the Church, a promoter of divine worship — inasmuch as he diligently accomplished and patiently endured all the greatest things for Christ and the Church.

He wrote so much, with such piety, subtlety, and copiousness, that he most greatly illumined Christian doctrine. Those followed him above all who afterwards transmitted theological learning by way and method. When the Vandals were devastating Africa with war and had already besieged Hippo for three months, he fell into a fever. And so, perceiving that his departure from life was at hand, he had the Psalms of David that concern penance placed before him, and read them with flowing tears. He was accustomed to say that no one, even if he were conscious of no crime, should allow himself to pass from life without penance. Therefore, with his senses intact, fixed in prayer, with the brothers standing by, whom he had exhorted to charity, piety, and all the virtues, he passed into heaven. He lived seventy-six years, and in the episcopate nearly thirty-six. His body was first brought to Sardinia, then redeemed at a great price by Liutprand, king of the Lombards, and transferred to Pavia, where it was honorably laid to rest.

On account of such salutary works, John fell into the most fierce persecution of wicked men, who made every effort to destroy the family he had recently gathered together. But the man of God, bearing all things gladly with equanimity of mind, having obtained from the Supreme Pontiff Gregory XIII the confirmation of his congregation, steadfastly preserved the fruits of his apostolic labor. Many bishops made use of him as counselor and helper in settling difficult affairs, and even the Roman Pontiff himself delegated him to resolve intricate disputes and to reform religious communities. He was at hand to assist Saint Joseph Calasanz and his nearly ruined society. He also devoted no small effort to the affairs of the hospital of the Holy Spirit in Sassia, and to the formation of the Oblate nuns of Saint Frances of Rome.

As to an oracle, from all parts of the world, questions of sacred Scripture to be explained were referred to him. Pope Damasus, and Saint Augustine himself, frequently consulted him on the most difficult passages of Scripture, on account of his singular learning and his knowledge not only of Latin and Greek but also of Hebrew and Chaldean; and because, by the testimony of that same Augustine, he had read almost all authors. He assailed heretics with the sharpest writings; he always took under his protection the cause of the devout and Catholic. He translated the Old Testament from the Hebrew; at the command of Damasus, he rendered the New Testament according to the Greek truth, and in great part explained it as well. He also translated into Latin many writings of learned men, and himself with other monuments of his own genius illumined Christian learning. He, having reached the most advanced old age, illustrious in holiness and learning, under the Emperor Honorius, passed into heaven. His body, buried at Bethlehem, was afterwards transferred to Rome to the basilica of Saint Mary at the Crib.

As if therefore they were about to perish through him, they were rightly troubled; but when they hear, In my Father's house there are many mansions; if it were not so, I would have told you, because I go to prepare a place for you — they are refreshed from their disturbance, certain and confident that even after the perils of temptations they will remain with God in Christ. For even though one is stronger than another, one wiser than another, one more just than another, one more holy than another, in my Father's house there are many mansions. None of them will be excluded from that house, where each one will receive a mansion according to his own merit.

At last, having returned to Viterbo amid the great rejoicing of the citizens, she sought admission to the community of the holy nuns of Saint Mary of the Roses; but when they refused her entry on account of the girl's poverty, she foretold that she would remain with them in that monastery after her death. Returning shortly to her former prison in her own house, after spending two years there she was seized by illness, and, longing for the blessed homeland, full of merits she passed to her Spouse, not yet having completed her eighteenth year of life. Her body, illumined by a wondrous splendor and perfumed with a sweet fragrance, was buried in the church of Saint Mary of the Hill, earth being dug out and heaped over it; until, after about thirty months, it was exhumed at the bidding of Alexander IV, who was then residing at Viterbo and had been warned by her three times in his sleep, and found incorrupt; and on the day before the Nones of September it was solemnly transferred to the aforesaid monastery, which was afterwards called that of Saint Rose; where to this day it is preserved whole and supple, to the greatest admiration of all the world, and it shines with ever new miracles.

Such was the holiness of James's life that people eagerly contended to touch the hem of his garment. For when he was ninety-six years old, having most holily presided over that Church for thirty years, while most steadfastly preaching Christ the Son of God, he was first set upon with stones; then, being led to the highest part of the Temple, he was thrown down from it. And, with his legs broken, lying half-dead, he stretched out his hands to heaven and prayed to God for their salvation with these words: Forgive them, O Lord, for they know not what they do. While he was at prayer, his head was struck with a heavy blow from a fuller's club, and he gave up his soul to God in the seventh year of Nero; and he was buried next to the Temple from which he had been cast down. He wrote one Epistle, which is among the seven Catholic ones.

Such a flame of divine charity burned in his breast that the garment closest to his heart was often seen as if scorched by fire, and two of his ribs were raised up. Especially when celebrating the sacred mysteries, he could not restrain his tears; and he was frequently seen to enjoy prolonged ecstasy, sometimes with a wondrous levitation of the body, his countenance radiant with heavenly light. At times, while he was preaching, a heavenly voice was heard suggesting words to him, or his discourse resounded for many thousands of paces. He shone with the gift of prophecy and of tongues, the discernment of hearts, and power over demons, over sickness, and over the elements. And although he was dear and venerable even to the Supreme Pontiffs themselves, he judged himself to be a useless servant, the most wicked of sinners, fit to be trampled underfoot even by demons. At last, most tenaciously clinging to a most austere manner of life even to extreme old age, in the year one thousand seven hundred and seventy-five, having entrusted his most excellent counsels to his disciples as a kind of legacy of his spirit, refreshed by the Sacraments of the Church and by a heavenly vision, he passed into heaven at Rome on the day he had foretold. Pope Pius IX, Supreme Pontiff, enrolled him among the Blessed, and afterwards, as he shone with new signs, among the Saints.

He was inflamed with such ardor of faith that he longed to undergo death for it, and earnestly besought this grace from God. And so the heretics inflicted on him the death which he had a little before foretold in his preaching. For when he was discharging the office of the holy Inquisition, an impious assassin wounded him twice in the head with a sword as he was returning from Como to Milan; and already almost dead, he pronounced with his final breath the articles of the faith which he had confessed as a child with manly fortitude; and, once more transfixed in the side with a dagger, he passed into heaven to the palm of martyrdom, in the year of salvation one thousand two hundred and fifty-two. Innocent IV, having proclaimed him illustrious for many miracles, enrolled him in the following year in the number of the holy Martyrs.

She burned with so great a fire of divine love that, unable to endure it, she was compelled to cool her breast by pouring water on it. Frequently caught up out of her senses, she endured prolonged and wondrous ecstasies, in which she also penetrated heavenly mysteries and was illumined by most excellent graces from God. Fortified by these, she sustained a long battle against the princes of darkness, dry, desolate, abandoned by all, and vexed by various temptations — God so permitting in order that she might furnish an example of invincible patience and most profound humility.

And so, though they were three, they became one. Three are seen in the beginning, one at the end. For in perfect faith they are one. And furthermore the Lord prays the Father that all may be one. Nor are Moses and Elijah alone one in Christ, but we also are one body of Christ. Therefore those too, as into one body, are received into the body of Christ, because we also shall be one in Christ Jesus. Or perhaps, because the law and the prophets are from the Word: and what began from the Word ends in the Word. For the end of the law is Christ, for justification to every believer.

With your help, nations come to repentance. What more shall I say? Through you the Only-Begotten Son of God, that true light, shone upon those sitting in darkness and the shadow of death. The Prophets foretold you, the Apostles celebrated you with the highest praises. Who could unfold the proclamations of your praises, O Mary, Mother and Virgin? Let us celebrate her, brethren most beloved, adoring her Son, the immaculate Spouse of the Church: to whom be honor and glory for ever and ever. Amen.

Telesphorus, a Greek by birth, from Thurii in Magna Graecia, was created Supreme Pontiff from being a priest of the Roman Church, whose worthy minister he had been. He fulfilled this supreme office in such a way that he seemed to have been chosen as an outstanding successor of Peter. He sat in his chair under the Emperor Antoninus Pius, when the fervor of persecution was raging. Yet this did not prevent him from devoting diligent attention to governing the Church of Christ.
We read that he admirably decreed many things by new enactments pertaining to the morals of the faithful, the liberty of churchmen, and the sacred rites: namely, that he restored by a new decree the Lenten fast, already handed down long since by the Apostles; and commanded that on the Nativity of the Lord the holy sacrifice of Mass should be celebrated three times — at midnight, at the break of dawn, and finally at the third hour after sunrise; and ordained that the angelic hymn, Glory to God in the highest, should be added to the sacred Liturgy.

He will also hold that charity which is surpassing above all gifts, without which every virtue is nothing. For the guardian of chastity is charity; and the dwelling place of this guardian is humility. He will also hold, among all these, the preeminence of chastity: so that a mind dedicated to Christ may be clean and free from every defilement of the flesh. Among these things it will be necessary to exercise care for the poor with diligent stewardship: to feed the hungry, to clothe the naked, to receive strangers, to ransom captives, to protect widows and orphans, to show vigilant care in all things, and to exercise foresight in distribution with discernment. In this also hospitality will be so excellent that he receives all with kindness and charity. For if all the faithful desire to hear those words of the Gospel: I was a stranger and you received me; how much more the bishop, whose house ought to be the lodging of all?

Thérèse of the Infant Jesus was born at Alençon in France of honest and devout parents. In her fifth year, having lost her mother, she entrusted herself entirely to the providence of God under the watchful care of her most loving father and her elder sisters; under whose guidance she rejoiced as a giant to run the way of perfection. At nine years of age she was handed over to be educated by the nuns of the Order of Saint Benedict at Lisieux. At ten years of age, long tormented by a hidden and grave illness, she was miraculously delivered through the help of Our Lady of Victory. Filled with angelic fervor, when she first approached the sacred banquet, she seemed to drink in an insatiable hunger for this food. Desiring to enter the order of the Discalced Carmelites, she encountered many difficulties in embracing the religious life on account of her youth; having overcome these with fortitude, she happily entered the Carmel of Lisieux at fifteen years of age. There she burned with a most excellent charity toward God and neighbor. Following the spiritual way of childhood according to the teaching of the Gospel, she taught others, especially the novices, the same way. Inflamed with the desire to suffer, two years before her death she offered herself as a victim to the love of God's mercy. At twenty-four years of age, on the thirtieth of September in the year one thousand eight hundred and ninety-seven, she flew to her Spouse. Pope Pius XI, Supreme Pontiff, having enrolled her among the Blessed Virgins and two years later, on the occasion of the great Jubilee, having solemnly placed her among the Saints, appointed and declared her the special Patroness of all the Missions.

Thérèse of the Infant Jesus, born at Alençon in France of honest parents, conspicuous for their singular and unceasing devotion toward God, was from her earliest age drawn forward by the divine Spirit, and desired to lead a religious life. She earnestly promised that she would deny God nothing that he seemed to ask of her, and labored faithfully to keep this promise until death. In her fifth year, having lost her mother, she entrusted herself entirely to the providence of God under the watchful care of her most loving father and her elder sisters; under whose guidance, Thérèse rejoiced as a giant to run the way of perfection. At nine years of age she was handed over to be educated by the nuns of the Order of Saint Benedict at Lisieux, where she was seen to excel in the knowledge of divine things. At ten years of age, a hidden and grave illness long tormented her, from which, as she herself relates, she was miraculously delivered through the help of the most Blessed Virgin, who smiled upon her as she appeared to her, and whom she had been zealous to invoke through novenas under the title of Our Lady of Victory. Then, filled with angelic fervor, she took great care to prepare herself most diligently for the sacred banquet, at which Christ is received.

Thérèse, born at Ávila in Spain of devout and noble parents, was even as a little girl inflamed with the desire for martyrdom and, fleeing from home, attempted to make her way to Africa. Brought back home, after the death of her mother, having entrusted herself wholly to the patronage of the blessed Virgin, she made her profession at twenty years of age in the monastery of the nuns of Saint Mary of Mount Carmel. Solicitous for the salvation of souls, having built very many monasteries, she proposed the ancient rule of the Carmelites for women and men to observe. For unbelievers and heretics she continually offered to God voluntary torments of her own body, and, burning with divine love, having made the most difficult vow of always doing what she understood to be more perfect, she merited to have her heart transfixed by a burning dart by an Angel. She wrote many documents of heavenly wisdom, and taught much by word and example, having often on her lips: Lord, either to suffer or to die. Distinguished by her virtues, the gift of prophecy, and other charisms, at Alba she rendered her most pure soul to God in the year one thousand five hundred and eighty-two, the sixty-seventh year of her age, on the Ides of October.

Teresa the Virgin was born at Ávila in Spain of parents illustrious both in birth and in piety. Nourished by them on the milk of the fear of God, she gave a wondrous proof of her future holiness even in her most tender age. For, while reading the acts of the holy Martyrs, the fire of the Holy Spirit blazed up so greatly in her heart that, fleeing from her home, she attempted to cross into Africa, there to pour out her life for the glory of Jesus Christ and the salvation of souls. Called back by her uncle, she compensated her burning desire for martyrdom with almsgiving and other pious works, and deplored with continual tears that the best lot had been snatched from her. After the death of her mother, when she begged the most blessed Virgin to show herself as her mother, she obtained the fulfillment of her pious vow; and she always enjoyed the patronage of the Mother of God as a daughter. In her twentieth year, she betook herself to the nuns of Saint Mary of Mount Carmel. There, for eighteen years vexed by the gravest illnesses and various temptations, she merited with the utmost constancy in the camp of Christian penance, refreshed by none of those heavenly consolations with which holiness is accustomed even on earth to abound.

Nature herself bore witness — she who was fighting on behalf of the Martyrs when the tyrant was casting infants down. The mother was tearing at the hair of her head, she who was losing the ornament of her head. In how many ways she wished to hide the infant, and the little child himself made himself known! He did not know how to be silent, for he had not yet learned to be afraid. The mother fought, and the executioner: he dragged, she held fast. The mother cried out to the executioner: Why do you tear from me the one I bore from my own womb? My womb bore him; he did not remain with me in life, turning my breasts to no purpose with milk. I carried him carefully, and I see him thrown about by your cruel hand. Just now my own body gave him birth, and you dash him to the ground.

The martyr George beareth among the Easterns the title of the holy and glorious Archmartyr. He suffered a glorious death, for Christ's sake, in the persecution under Diocletian. When peace was given to the Church soon after, under Constantine, the memory of the martyr began to be celebrated, and churches were built under his invocation at Lydda in Palestine and at Constantinople. For thenceforth an extraordinary enthusiasm with regard to him grew up among the faithful, first in all parts of the East, and afterwards in the West. Of old time, when Christian armies had been about to fight, they have been used to call as patrons upon holy George, Maurice, and Sebastian. There had been already special honour paid in England to the holy martyr George, and the supreme Pontiff Benedict XIV declared him the protector of the whole kingdom.

The virgin Thecla, born of illustrious parents at Iconium, instructed in the precepts of the faith by the Apostle Paul, is celebrated with wondrous praises by the holy Fathers. At eighteen years of age, having left her betrothed Thamyris, when her parents accused her of being a Christian, she first armed herself with the sign of the Cross and then cast herself into the blazing pyre which had been prepared for her unless she should renounce Christ. But the fire being extinguished by a sudden downpour of rain, she came to Antioch; where, thrown to the beasts and bound to bulls driven in opposite directions, then cast into a pit full of serpents, she was delivered from all of them by the grace of Jesus Christ. Through the ardor of her faith and the holiness of her life, many were converted to Christ. Returning again to her homeland, she withdrew alone to a mountain. Then, distinguished by many virtues and miracles, she passed to the Lord at ninety years of age, and was buried at Seleucia.

Theodore, a Christian soldier, was seized under the Emperor Maximian for having set fire to a temple of idols. When the prefect of the legion offered to remit his punishment if, repenting of his deed, he would renounce the Christian faith, he persevered steadfastly in the confession of the faith and was cast into prison. There, torn with iron hooks while his ribs were being laid bare, he sang joyfully: I will bless the Lord at all times. Thereupon he was thrown into a blazing fire and, in prayer and divine praise, gave up his soul to Christ, on the ninth of November. The matron Eusebia, wrapping his body in a shroud, buried it on her own estate.

Under the rule of the younger Theodosius, when Eudocia his wife had come to Jerusalem to fulfill a vow, she was there favored with many gifts. Pre-eminent among them was the remarkable gift of an iron chain, adorned with gold and gems, which they asserted to be the very one with which the Apostle Peter had been bound by Herod. Eudocia, having venerated the chain with piety, afterwards sent it to Rome to her daughter Eudoxia, who brought it to the Supreme Pontiff. He in turn showed her another chain with which the same Apostle had been bound under the Emperor Nero.

Under the rule of the younger Theodosius, Eudocia his wife received at Jerusalem, pre-eminent above all other gifts, an iron chain which they asserted to be the very one with which the Apostle Peter had been bound by Herod. Eudocia, having venerated the chain with piety, sent it to Rome to her daughter Eudoxia, where it was joined by the Supreme Pontiff with the other chain by which the same blessed Apostle had been bound under the Emperor Nero, and the two were so fitted together that they appeared to be not two chains but one, made by a single craftsman. Thereafter, since the health of the sick and the liberation of the possessed were often obtained by touching these sacred bonds, such honor began to be paid to those holy fetters that on their account the church of Saint Peter in Chains, endowed by Eudoxia, was dedicated on the Esquiline Hill, and a feast day was established in their memory on the first of August, replacing the profane celebrations of the pagans.

The Apostle Thomas, who was also called Didymus, a Galilean, after receiving the Holy Spirit went forth into many provinces to preach the Gospel of Christ: he delivered the precepts of Christian faith and life to the Parthians, Medes, Persians, Hyrcanians, and Bactrians. Proceeding at last to India, he instructed its people in the Christian religion. There, having finally stirred the admiration of all by the holiness of his life and teaching and by the greatness of his miracles, and having aroused love for Jesus Christ, he kindled all the more the wrath of that people's king, a worshipper of idols; condemned by his sentence and pierced with spears, he crowned the honor of his apostolate with the crown of martyrdom at Calamina.

Thomas Aquinas, born of noble parents, while still a young man entered the Order of Preachers against the wishes of his mother and brothers, and was sent to Paris. But his brothers, attacking him on the journey, brought him to the castle of San Giovanni, where the angelic youth drove away a woman who had been introduced to undermine his chastity, using a burning brand. At Paris he devoted himself so earnestly to philosophy and theology that, scarcely twenty-five years old, he publicly interpreted philosophers and theologians with the highest distinction. He never applied himself to reading or writing except after prayer. When he once heard these words of Jesus crucified: You have written well of me, Thomas; what reward will you receive?, he replied most lovingly: No other, O Lord, but you yourself. There was no kind of writing in which he was not most diligently versed. Called to Rome by Urban IV, he composed at his command the Office for the solemnity of Corpus Christi. Sent by Blessed Gregory X to the Council of Lyons, he fell ill at the monastery of Fossanova and there, though infirm, commented on the Song of Songs. He died there at the age of fifty, in the year twelve hundred and seventy-four, on the seventh of March. Leo XIII declared and established him as the heavenly patron of all Catholic schools.

Thomas, born in the town of Fuensalida in the diocese of Toledo in Spain in the year of the Lord fourteen hundred and eighty-eight, received from his excellent parents, from the very beginning of his life, piety and a singular mercy toward the poor, of which he gave many examples even as a boy; most notably, that to clothe the naked, he more than once stripped himself of his own garments. When his boyhood was over, having been sent to Alcalá to study as a student at the major college of Saint Ildefonso, he was called back by his father's death, and devoted his entire inheritance to the support of poor maidens; then immediately returned thither, and having completed the course of sacred theology, excelled so greatly in learning that, bidden to ascend the chair at that same university, he expounded philosophical and theological questions with wonderful clarity, meanwhile most earnestly beseeching the Lord through constant prayer for the knowledge of the Saints and the right norm of life and conduct. Whereupon, moved by divine impulse, he embraced the institute of the Hermits of Saint Augustine.

Thomas, born in the town of Fuensalida in the diocese of Toledo in Spain, received from his good parents at the outset of life piety and a singular mercy toward the poor, of which he gave illustrious examples throughout the entire course of his life. For as a boy, to clothe the naked, he more than once stripped himself of his own garments; as a young man, after his father's death, he devoted his entire inheritance to the support of poor maidens. Having completed the course of theology and embraced, by divine impulse, the institute of the Hermits of Saint Augustine, he was adorned with every virtue, excelling especially in charity toward the poor and sinners, whom he strove to draw out of the mire of vice. His mercy shone forth most especially when, called by obedience to govern the church of Valencia, he fulfilled most vigilantly the role of pastor and distributed the ample revenues of the church to the needy, not even keeping a bed for himself. He fell asleep in the Lord on the eighth of September, at the age of sixty-eight.

Thomas, born in London in England, succeeded Theobald as Archbishop of Canterbury; and he who had previously distinguished himself in the administration of the chancellorship was proved strong and unconquerable in the episcopal office. For when Henry II, King of England, having summoned the bishops and nobles of the kingdom, enacted laws contrary to the benefit and dignity of the Church, Thomas resisted the king's ambition with such steadfastness that, yielding neither to promises nor to threats, and refusing to depart from his position, he withdrew secretly just as he was about to be cast into prison. Thereupon all his relatives of every age were expelled, as were all his friends and supporters — save those whom age permitted — bound by oath to visit Thomas from every side, in case he might perhaps be moved by the pitiful sight of his people's misfortune, who could not be deterred from his holy purpose by private hardships. He did not look to flesh and blood, nor did any human sentiment weaken the constancy of his duty.

Tiburtius, son of Chromatius the prefect of the City, having become a Christian through the work of Saint Sebastian, was brought before the judge Fabianus on that account and preached much to him about the faith of Christ. The enraged judge ordered the pavement to be strewn with glowing coals. Then he said: Tiburtius, you must either sacrifice to our gods, or walk barefoot over those coals. But Tiburtius, fortifying himself with the sign of the Cross and walking boldly upon the embers, said: Learn from this that there is no God but the one whom Christians worship; for the embers seem to me like flowers. When this was attributed to magical arts, Tiburtius was led outside the City and beheaded at the third milestone from the City on the Lavican Way, and was buried there by Christians. On that same day, the most noble virgin Susanna, who had vowed her virginity to God and therefore refused marriage to Galerius Maximian, son of the Emperor Diocletian, was struck with the sword in her own house at the Emperor's command, after many kinds of torments by which her holy virgin resolve had been variously assailed, and she passed to heaven to receive the twofold reward of virginity and martyrdom.

Timothy of Antioch, coming to Rome, under the Supreme Pontiff Melchiades, having preached the faith of Christ there for a year, was cast into chains by Tarquinius, prefect of the City; and after long sufferings in prison he was brought to the idols to sacrifice to them. Having denounced that impiety with the utmost freedom, he was most savagely beaten, and his torn body was drenched with quicklime. Constant amid these and other torments, the Martyr was beheaded. His body was buried on the Ostian Way near the tomb of the blessed Apostle Paul. On that same day, under the Emperor Alexander, Hippolytus, bishop of Porto, was precipitated headlong into a deep pit full of water, with his hands and feet bound, for his illustrious confession of the faith, and was crowned with martyrdom at Ostia on the Tiber, and was buried there by Christians. On the same day also, under the Emperor Aurelian, Symphorianus, a young man of Autun, was variously tortured for the same faith. Veronica de Julianis, previously called Ursula, born in Mercatello, a town of the diocese of Urbino, of devout and honorable parents, gave wondrous signs of future holiness from her very cradle. For as an infant, while she otherwise fed abundantly on milk, on three days of the week she tasted only a few drops in the morning and evening. Scarcely six months old, on the day consecrated to the most holy Trinity, she leapt from her mother's arms onto her own feet. Still very young, she deterred a certain man from injustice with grave words. She enjoyed familiar converse with the child Jesus and the most blessed Virgin, and sometimes the divine Child descended to console her as she wept and prayed; at times she also received him from the Mother of God herself, with the announcement of a spiritual betrothal between her and Jesus, along with a pledge — namely the warfare she was to endure from men and the infernal enemies. To this end Veronica, not yet past childhood, girded herself with the utmost humility and equal obedience, and with a burning desire to imitate Christ our Lord, who suffered and was crucified for us. And in order to pursue this more abundantly, overcoming obstacles at home and abroad, she fled to the Capuchin nuns of Città di Castello, who profess the original rule of Saint Clare.

And as he was being led through Armenia, the holy Martyr Basiliscus, in whose church he had previously prayed, addressed him at night in these words: Brother John, tomorrow the same place will unite us. At his death, a fearful hailstorm fell upon Constantinople, and within four days the Empress departed this life. His body, accompanied by a distinguished procession and a great multitude of people, was carried to Constantinople by order of Theodosius, son of Arcadius, and honorably buried on the sixth day before the Kalends of February; and he also venerated his relics and sought pardon for his parents. Later, when the body was translated to Rome, it was laid to rest in the Vatican basilica. All men marvel at the great number, the piety, and the splendor of his sermons and other writings, as well as at his method of interpretation and the exposition of the sense of the sacred books that clings to the text; and they deem him worthy that the Apostle Paul, whom he wondrously revered, should seem to have dictated much to him as he wrote and preached. This most illustrious Doctor of the whole Church was declared and appointed heavenly patron of sacred orators by Pope Pius X.

But having briefly recalled with due fear and trembling these things, let us rather turn our hearing to the most joyous promises of our Lord and Savior. Let us see what is the grace of such great piety: he promises his followers not only the rewards of eternal life, but also exceptional gifts of the present life. And everyone, he says, who has left house, or brothers, or sisters, or father, or mother, or wife, or children, or lands, for my name's sake, shall receive a hundredfold and shall possess eternal life. For whoever has renounced earthly affections or possessions for the discipleship of Christ, the more he advances in love of him, the more he will find those who gladly welcome him with inward affection and sustain him from their substance.

Yet not even by these things was he made more sluggish, but he obeyed willingly and believed, enduring all tribulations whatsoever with joy. For indeed the merciful God mingles certain joyful things with sorrowful ones. This he does indeed for all the saints, allowing them to have neither tribulations nor joys uninterrupted, but weaving the life of the righteous now with adversities, now with prosperity, as in a wondrous variety. Consider that he did this for him also here.

But while he was shut away in that dark prison, a most brilliant splendor arose and illumined the whole cell; and when this light had filled all who were present with the greatest wonder, the matter was reported by the prison warden to Dacian. He had him brought out and laid on a soft couch, and sought by pleasures to lead where he had failed to move by torments. But the unconquered spirit of Vincent, fortified by faith and hope in Jesus Christ, overcame all things; and having mastered the cruelty of fire, iron, and torturers, flew victorious to the heavenly crown of martyrdom on the eleventh day before the Kalends of February. When his body had been cast out unburied, a raven defended it wonderfully from birds and from a wolf, with talons, beak, and wings. When Dacian learned of this, he ordered it cast into the deep sea; but there too, by divine power, it was cast up onto the shore, and the Christians buried it.

But because the name of mountain sometimes signifies the devil, namely on account of the pride by which he raises himself against God and wishes to be like the Most High, the mountain is lifted from the earth and cast into the sea at the command of those who are strong in faith, when, as the holy teachers preach the word, the unclean spirit is driven from the hearts of those who are ordained to life, and is permitted to exercise the frenzy of his tyranny in the turbulent and bitter minds of unbelievers.

But above all these things is this: to be joined to the companies of Angels and Archangels; to enjoy also the fellowship of Thrones and Dominations, Principalities and Powers, and all the heavenly supernal Virtues; to behold the ranks of the Saints shining more brightly than the stars, the Patriarchs radiant with faith, the Prophets rejoicing in hope, the Apostles judging the world in twelve tribes of Israel, the Martyrs gleaming with the purple crowns of victory, and also to look upon the choirs of Virgins bearing garlands of white.

But when he understood that he was proposing these things to them in vain: Bind, he said, the hands and feet of these men, and rack them with exquisite torments. While his orders were being carried out, Cosmas and Damian nonetheless persisted in their resolve. Wherefore, being bound as they were, they were cast into the depths of the sea. From thence they came out safe and unbound; the prefect attributed the deed to magical arts, gave them over to prison, and the next day, bringing them out, ordered them thrown into a blazing fire; where, when the flame recoiled from them, he wished them tortured in various and cruel ways before being struck with the sword. And so, in the confession of Jesus Christ, they received the palm of martyrdom.

Yet if you look carefully, you will find in Mary not only this, but all the other virtues too to be quite singular, which seemed to be common to others. For what angelic purity would dare to compare itself to that virginity which was worthy to become the sanctuary of the Holy Spirit and the dwelling of the Son of God? How great, and how precious, is the virtue of humility together with such purity, with such innocence, with a conscience altogether without fault — indeed with such a fullness of grace? Whence comes this humility in you, and so great a humility, O blessed one? Truly worthy was she upon whom the Lord would look, whose beauty the King desired, by whose most sweet fragrance that eternal one who lies in the Father's bosom would be drawn to her.

Clothe therefore you also the body of the Lord with his glory, that you yourself may be just. And if you believe him to be dead, nonetheless labor with the fullness of his own divinity. Anoint it with myrrh and aloe, that you may be the good odor of Christ. That just man Joseph sent fine linen — and perhaps it was that which Peter saw let down from heaven, in which were depicted the kinds of four-footed beasts, and of wild beasts, and of birds, in the likeness of the Gentiles. With that mystical nard so precious, therefore, the Church is buried together with him — she who has united the diversity of peoples in the communion of her faith.

With the death of the body close at hand, the pastoral vigilance of the shepherd did not die in his soul; and the care of guarding the Lord's flock was held with sober mind until the very last day of this life. Nor did he shake from his soul the diligence of the most faithful steward, though the hand of the bloody executioner was already near. So truly did he think of himself as a martyr to come, that he did not forget he was a bishop; caring more for the account he would render to the Prince of shepherds concerning the sheep entrusted to him than for what answer he would make to the unbelieving proconsul concerning his own faith. For he loved him who had said to Peter: Do you love me? Feed my sheep. And he fed those sheep, for whose sake, imitating him, he was preparing to shed his blood.

Victor, born in Africa, governed the Church under the Emperor Severus. He confirmed the decree of Pope Pius I, that the sacred Passover be celebrated on the Lord's Day; and in order that this custom might thereafter prevail, councils were held in many places; and finally at the first Nicene Synod it was decreed that the feast of Easter be observed after the fourteenth moon, lest Christians should seem to imitate the Jews. He established that any person, if necessity required, could be baptized with any water, provided it be natural. He expelled Theodotus the Tanner of Byzantium from the Church for teaching that Christ was merely a man. He wrote on the question of Easter and certain other short works. In two ordinations in the month of December he created four priests, seven deacons, and twelve bishops for various places. Crowned with martyrdom, he was buried in the Vatican on the fifth day before the Kalends of August. He held his see for nine years, one month, and twenty-eight days.

When Saint Joseph beheld the Virgin great with child, he fell into the greatest distress; but an Angel suddenly appeared, utterly banishing his fear. Then, seeing the child born, he was filled with the greatest exultation; but again to this joy too a great danger succeeded, when the entire city was thrown into turmoil, the king himself was raging, and seeking the child's death. But this grief also was followed by another joy — namely the appearance of the star and the adoration of the Magi. After this gladness too, danger again, and again dread. Herod, he says, seeks the life of the child, and it is necessary to flee and pass into a distant land.

See that you do not despise one of these little ones who believe in me. He laid a most fitting bond of mutual love, especially on those who had truly believed in the Lord. For the Angels of the little ones see God daily, because the Son of Man came to save what was lost. Therefore both the Son of Man saves, and the Angels see God, and the Angels of the little ones preside over the prayers of the faithful. That Angels preside is an absolute authority. The prayers therefore of those saved through Christ are offered daily by Angels to God. Therefore he is dangerously despised whose desires and petitions are conveyed to the eternal and invisible God by the eager service and ministry of Angels.
