See how our finest vine has blossomed with this rose flower — the crimson Jesus. Look at the whole body, and see if you do not find the flower of the blood-red rose somewhere upon it. Examine one hand and the other: do you not find the rose's flower in both? Examine one foot and the other: are they not rose-red? Look at the opening in his side, for that too lacks not the rose, though that one is more subdued in color, on account of the mingling of water; because, as the Evangelist relates, when one of the soldiers pierced his side with a lance, blood and water came out.

Let us look at what follows. Behold the Lamb of God. This is John speaking. And the two disciples heard him speaking, and they followed Jesus. They did not follow him in the way of already cleaving to him, for it is clear when they cleaved to him, because he called them from the boat. For among these two was Andrew, as you have just heard. Now Andrew was the brother of Peter. And we know from the Gospel that the Lord called Peter and Andrew from the boat, saying: Come after me, and I will make you fishers of men. And from that time they cleaved to him, so as not to depart.

You see from the very beginning how joyful are these things united. But if you are uncertain about those things that pertain to your honor, learn to believe your own from those that are his. For as far as human reason can attain, it is far more difficult for God to become man than for man to be consecrated son of God. When therefore you hear that the Son of God is also son of David and of Abraham, cease now to doubt that you, who are a son of Adam, shall be a son of God. For he would not have so humbled himself, unless he were about to exalt us. He was born according to the flesh, that you might be born of the Spirit; he was born of a woman, that you might cease to be a son of a woman.

You see, O beloved, how new and wonderful is this mystery. He is not yet born, and he speaks by leaps; he has not yet appeared, and he threatens menaces; he is not yet permitted to cry out, and he is heard through deeds; he does not yet live his life, and he proclaims God; he does not yet behold the light, and he points to the Sun; he is not yet brought forth, and he hastens to run ahead. For he does not bear, with the Lord present, to be contained; he cannot sustain waiting for nature's appointed term; but he strives to burst the prison of the womb, and labors to foretell the coming Savior. He who looses bonds has drawn near, he says; why do I sit bound and am held back to remain? The Word comes to establish all things; and do I still remain detained? I will go forth, I will run ahead, and I will proclaim to all: Behold the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world.

You see therefore, dearest brethren, and, as I suppose, you already understand in these two women, who were both pleasing to the Lord, both lovable, both disciples — you see therefore, and you understand something great, all of you who understand; which even those of you who do not understand ought to hear and know: that in these two women two lives are figured, the present and the future, the laborious and the quiet, the full of hardship and the blessed, the temporal and the eternal.

He was never lacking to widows and orphans in money, counsel, and labor; he relieved the oppressed so greatly that he even freed three tribunes who had been condemned unjustly by the Emperor Constantine, and who, on account of the fame of his miracles, had commended themselves to his prayers while he was still alive and far away — appearing to the emperor and terrifying him with threats. And when he was preaching the truth of the Christian faith at Myra against the edict of Diocletian and Maximian, he was seized by the agents of the emperors and led very far away, cast into prison, where he remained until the Emperor Constantine, by whose command he was freed from custody and returned to Myra. He quickly betook himself to the Nicene council, where together with those three hundred and eighteen Fathers he condemned the Arian heresy. Returning thence to his episcopate, not long after, as death drew near, looking up to heaven and beholding the Angels coming to meet him, he pronounced that Psalm, In you, O Lord, have I hoped, as far as the verse, Into your hands I commend my spirit; and so he departed to the heavenly homeland. His body, translated to Bari in Apulia, is there venerated with the greatest solemnity and devotion.

Vincent de Paul, born at Pouy in Aquitaine, showed from boyhood an exceptional charity toward the poor. Called from the keeping of his father's flock to letters, and thereafter initiated into the priesthood, he fell into the hands of Turks who carried him captive into Africa; from there, having led his master back to the faith of Christ, he escaped and returned to Gaul. In the parishes entrusted to him and afterwards in the galleys, he labored diligently for the salvation of souls. He presided with the greatest prudence over the nuns of the Visitation for some forty years. He labored tirelessly to the very point of old age in evangelizing the poor, especially country people, and bound himself and the pupils of the congregation which he founded under the name of the Secular Priests of the Mission by a perpetual vow confirmed by the Holy See. He founded very many confraternities for seeking out and relieving the wretched and for the education of the female sex. Finally, worn out by bodily affliction, labors, and old age, in the year of salvation one thousand six hundred and sixty he fell peacefully asleep in the Lord. Clement XII, who had declared him illustrious by miracles, enrolled him among the Saints, and Leo XIII declared and appointed him the special patron before God of all charitable societies existing throughout the Catholic world and in any way deriving from him.

Vincent, born of an honorable family at Valencia in Spain, at the eighteenth year of his age put on the religious habit in the Order of Preachers; in which, devoting himself assiduously to sacred letters, he obtained the laurel of theology with the highest praise. Soon he began to preach the word of God with such power and efficacy that he led a great multitude of unbelievers to the faith of Christ, and recalled many thousands of Christians from sins to penance. He celebrated Mass with chant every day, gave a sermon to the people every day, never ate meat, settled the quarrels of peoples; and when the seamless garment of the Church was being torn by a dreadful schism, he labored greatly that it might be united and, once united, preserved. Finally, worn down by old age and sickness, and renowned above all for miracles, he died most holily at Vannes in Brittany. Pope Callixtus III enrolled him among the Saints.

Vincent, born at Huesca in Hither Spain, devoted from an early age to study, learned sacred letters from Valerius, bishop of Saragossa; he also undertook Valerius's part of preaching the Gospel, for the bishop, on account of an impediment of speech, was unable to perform the office of preaching. When this matter was reported to Dacian, the most impious prefect, Vincent was brought by him to Valencia; and having endured prison, hunger, the rack, and other kinds of torments, he flew to the crown of martyrdom on the eleventh day before the Kalends of February. Anastasius the Persian, a monk, in the time of the Emperor Heraclius, after visiting the holy land of Jerusalem, endured bonds and stripes at Caesarea of Palestine steadfastly for the religion of Christ. Then, afflicted by the Persians for the same cause with various torments, he was beheaded by the command of King Chosroes together with seventy other Christians. His relics, first taken to Jerusalem and then to Rome, were placed in the monastery of the Aquae Salviae.

Vincent de Paul, a Frenchman by birth, born at Pouy not far from Dax in Aquitaine, showed from boyhood an exceptional charity toward the poor. Called from the keeping of his father's flock to letters, he studied the humanities at Dax, and sacred learning both at Toulouse and at Saragossa. Ordained to the priesthood and distinguished by the laurel of theology, he fell into the hands of Turks who carried him captive into Africa. But while in captivity he led his master back to Christ. Together with him, therefore, escaping from that barbarous shore with the help of the Mother of God, he set out for the Apostolic See. Returning thence to Gaul, he governed most holily first the parish of Clichy, then that of Châtillon. Appointed by the king as the principal minister of sacred affairs in the galleys of France, with what marvelous zeal he labored for the salvation of the officers and the oarsmen! Placed at the head of the nuns of the Visitation by Saint Francis de Sales, he sustained that charge with such great prudence for some forty years as to vindicate in the fullest measure the judgment of that most saintly bishop, who avowed that he knew no priest more worthy than Vincent.

Vincent, born of an honorable family at Valencia in Spain, bore from earliest age a heart grown old in wisdom. While he was reflecting on the fleeting course of this clouded age according to the measure of his talent, he received the religious habit in the Order of Preachers at the eighteenth year of his age; and after making his solemn profession and devoting himself assiduously to sacred letters, he obtained the laurel of theology with the highest praise. He soon obtained permission from his superiors and began to preach the word of God, to refute the perfidy of the Jews, to confute the errors of the Saracens, with such power and efficacy that he led a great multitude of those very unbelievers to the faith of Christ, and recalled many thousands of Christians from sins to penance, from vices to virtue. For, chosen by God to scatter the seeds of faith through all nations, tribes, and tongues, and to show that the day of the last and dreadful judgment was drawing near, he stirred the souls of all his hearers — shaken with terror and torn away from earthly affections — to the love of God.

Vincent, born at Huesca in Hither Spain, devoted from an early age to study, learned sacred letters from Valerius, bishop of Saragossa; he also undertook Valerius's part of preaching the Gospel, for the bishop, on account of an impediment of speech, was unable to perform the office of preaching. When this matter was reported to Dacian, appointed prefect of the province by Diocletian and Maximian, Vincent was arrested at Saragossa and brought in bonds to Dacian at Valencia. There, stretched on the rack and beaten with stripes before many onlookers, since he could not be turned from his purpose by any force of torments or by the severity or mildness of words, he was placed on a gridiron with burning coals heaped beneath it, torn with iron hooks, and seared with red-hot plates of iron; then he was taken back to prison, strewn with shards of pottery, so that his naked body, overcome with sleep, might be tortured further by the sharp points of the potsherds set beneath him.

For it is attachment to earthly things that is our bond; and in order to lead us to its dissolution, hear what Christ says. He who loves his soul will lose it; and he who hates his soul in this world will keep it to eternal life. This saying seems like a riddle, yet it is not; rather it is full of surpassing wisdom. And how does he who loves his soul lose it? By yielding to its perverse desires, by indulging it beyond what is due; just as, conversely, he who hates his soul in this world keeps it — that is, he who does not obey it when it commands what is harmful.

He preserved perpetual virginity, and shameless women who attempted to lay snares for his chastity he not only repelled but even won for Christ. In expounding the divine mysteries, equally with Saint Teresa, by the judgment of the Apostolic See, instructed by God, he composed books on mystical theology full of celestial wisdom. When asked once by Christ what reward he sought for so many labors, he replied: Lord, to suffer and to be despised for you. Most renowned for his power over demons, whom he often drove from bodies, for his discernment of spirits, the gift of prophecy, and the glory of miracles, he was always of such humility that he frequently besought the Lord to grant him to die in a place where he was unknown to all. He obtained his wish. At Úbeda, enduring with the utmost constancy a dreadful sickness and five wounds on his leg oozing with matter, in fulfillment of his longing to suffer — having devoutly and holily received the Sacraments of the Church, in the embrace of Christ crucified, whom he had always borne in his heart and on his lips — after those words: Into your hands I commend my spirit, he fell asleep in the Lord on the day and hour foretold by himself, in the year of salvation one thousand five hundred and ninety-one, in the forty-ninth year of his age. A most brilliant globe of fire accompanied his departing soul; and his body breathed forth a most sweet fragrance; it is still incorrupt and honored at Segovia. Blessed with many signs before and after his death, Pope Benedict XIII enrolled him in the number of the Saints, and Pius XI, by decree of the Congregation of Sacred Rites, declared him a Doctor of the universal Church.

The Virgin is the unspotted lily who brought forth Christ, the unfading rose. O holy Mother of God, the immaculate ewe who bore the Lamb Christ, the Word incarnate from you! O most holy Virgin, who struck the armies of Angels into wonder! Wonderful is the miracle in the heavens — a woman clothed with the sun, bearing the Light in her arms; wonderful is the miracle in the heavens — the bridal chamber of the Virgin possessing the Son of God; wonderful is the miracle in the heavens — the Lord of Angels became an infant of the Virgin. The Angels accused Eve; but now they honor Mary with glory, she who raised up the fallen Eve and sent Adam, cast out from paradise, to the heavens. For she is the mediatrix of heaven and earth, who accomplished the union by nature.

Her husband having become a Cistercian monk and shortly thereafter having died, Birgitta, hearing the voice of Christ in a dream, undertook a stricter form of life. Thereafter many secrets were revealed to her by God. She founded the monastery of Vadstena under the rule of the Holy Savior, received from the Lord himself. She came to Rome at God's command, where she inflamed very many with a powerful love of God. From there she made her way to Jerusalem, and then again to Rome. Falling ill on her return from this pilgrimage and afflicted with serious sicknesses for a whole year, laden with merits and having foretold the day of her death, she passed to heaven. Her body was translated to the monastery of Vadstena; and Boniface IX, who had rendered her illustrious by miracles, enrolled her in the number of the Saints.

Her husband having died, she hastened to the aforesaid house of the Oblates, and there, barefoot, with a rope tied about her neck, prostrating herself on the ground, she humbly begged with many tears to be received into their number. Having obtained her wish, although she was the mother of all, she gloried in no other title than that of servant, of most vile woman, and vessel of uncleanness. This lowly estimation of herself she declared both in word and in deed: for often returning from the suburban vineyard, carrying on her own head a bundle of firewood, or driving through the city a small donkey loaded with the same, she would come to the aid of the poor, upon whom she also lavished generous alms; and visiting the sick in the hospitals, she refreshed them not only with bodily food but with salutary counsel. She labored continually to reduce her body to servitude by vigils, fasts, a hair shirt, an iron belt, and frequent scourgings. Her food was herbs and legumes once a day, her drink was water. These bodily austerities she sometimes moderated slightly at the command of her confessor, on whose word and nod she hung.

Her husband having been slain in the hunt, she formed the resolution of a more perfect life and bound herself by a vow of continence. She bore her husband's death not only with equanimity but, as a public testimony of the pardon she had granted, chose as conqueror of herself to receive at the sacred font the son of the one who had killed him. Content with a small household and modest food and clothing, she converted costly garments to pious uses. Whatever time remained from domestic duties she spent in prayers, pious readings, and labor. She could never be persuaded to enter into a second marriage, however useful and honorable. And lest she should hereafter be moved from her purpose of observing chastity, she renewed her vow and had the most holy name of Jesus Christ branded on her breast with a red-hot iron. Burning ever more ardently in charity from day to day, she had the poor, the abandoned, the sick, and those infected with most loathsome diseases brought to her; and she not only received them with hospitality, consoled and tended them, but also washed their filthy garments, mended the torn ones, and did not shrink from applying her lips to their ulcers flowing with foul matter.

Already mature by austerity of life and holiness for apostolic service, when John III, king of Portugal, requested from Paul III some men of the nascent Society for the Indies, he was chosen at the urging of Saint Ignatius by that same Pontiff for so great a work, with the authority of apostolic nuncio. Having arrived there, he was immediately seen to have been divinely endowed with a knowledge of the very difficult and varied languages of diverse peoples. Indeed, sometimes while preaching in a single tongue to different peoples, each one heard him speaking in its own language. He journeyed through countless provinces always on foot, and often barefoot. He brought the faith to Japan and six other regions. He converted many hundreds of thousands of men to Christ in the Indies; and he purified great princes and several kings with the sacred font. And while he was accomplishing such great things for God, such was his humility that he wrote to Saint Ignatius, his superior at that time, kneeling.

Austere to himself but dear and acceptable to others, especially to the holy Charles and Philip Neri, he was always of great simplicity and innocence. Spending his nights in prayer, he frequently underwent a most sweet ecstasy; and on one occasion he merited to embrace most tenderly the child Jesus reclining in his arms, received from the Virgin Mother. Distinguished for the gift of prophecy and for miracles, he restored to his mother alive even a son who had died. At last, laden with merits in a good old age, on the Monday of Pentecost — as he had foretold — he joyfully departed to the heavenly homeland at the invitation of the Mother of God. His body is venerated with the greatest devotion of the city of Rome in the church of his order, while the Lord honors the holiness of his servant with frequent miracles, for which reason Pope Urban VIII enrolled him among the Blessed, and Pope Clement XI among the Saints.

Most devoted to the religious life, when enrolled among the purple-clad Fathers, he preserved it as an example to others. He declined wealth beyond what was necessary; content with modest servants, simple furnishings, and plain dress; he did not seek the prosperity of his own household, and could barely be moved to relieve their need from time to time. He thought most humbly of himself and possessed a wondrous simplicity of soul. He loved the Mother of God with singular devotion; he gave many hours each day to prayer. Living most sparingly, he fasted three times a week; steadfastly austere to himself, he burned with charity toward his neighbor, and was often called the Father of the poor. He strove earnestly not to stain with even the slightest fault the innocence received at Baptism. Near his eightieth year, he fell into a final illness at Sant'Andrea al Quirinale, which he illumined with the customary radiance of his virtues. As he lay dying, Pope Gregory XV and several Cardinals stood by, lamenting the loss of so great a pillar of the Church. On the feast of the sacred Stigmata of Saint Francis — whose memory throughout the world he had been the author of establishing — he fell asleep in the Lord in the year one thousand six hundred and twenty-one. At his death the whole city mourned, acclaiming him a Saint with one voice. Pope Pius XI, Pontiff, first enrolled him among the Blessed and then among the Saints, and shortly after, by decree of the Congregation of Sacred Rites, declared him a Doctor of the universal Church.

Illustrious in all the virtues, he loved silence above all else. During the day he spent the spare moments of time in a certain small hut near the gate, from which he was able to visit and adore the most holy Eucharist; at night he stole from sleep the hours which he gave to prayer in the brothers' dormitory or in the church. Though he had grown old, he never gave himself over to rest, but continued in labors and devout exercises to the very end. Indeed, one day, having ministered to several bands of pilgrims, he recognized that he was wholly spent in bodily strength; and three days later, on the eleventh day before the Kalends of May, he fell asleep in the Lord in the year one thousand eight hundred and ninety-four, in the seventy-fifth year of his age. This servant of God, illustrious for heroic virtues and miracles, Pope Pius XI enrolled among the Blessed in the year one thousand nine hundred and thirty; and, as new miracles shone forth, the same Supreme Pontiff, four years later, solemnly enrolled him in the calendar of the Saints.
Vitalianus ...

Vitalis and his master Agricola, in the persecution of Diocletian and Maximian, were arrested at Bologna for preaching Jesus Christ. And when Vitalis, the more he was tried with entreaties and threats to change his resolve, the more he professed himself a worshiper and servant of Christ; tortured with various kinds of torment and enduring all things steadfastly, he gave back his spirit to God in prayer. Agricola, however, since the punishment of his slave had been delayed — lest perhaps he, moved by the slave's sufferings, might wish to renounce Christ — was rather confirmed by his example. And so, fixed to the cross, he shared as companion and fellow in the noble martyrdom of the slave Vitalis. Their bodies, which had been buried among the tombs of the Jews, were found by Saint Ambrose and translated to a sacred and renowned place.

Vitalis the soldier, father of the holy martyrs Gervase and Protase, entering Ravenna together with the judge Paulinus, when he saw Ursicinus the physician being led to execution for confessing the Christian faith, and wavering a little in the midst of his torments, cried out: Ursicinus, physician, you who were accustomed to heal others, take care lest you wound yourself with the dart of eternal death. Confirmed by these words, Ursicinus underwent martyrdom bravely. Wherefore Paulinus, inflamed with rage, ordered Vitalis to be seized and, after being stretched on the rack, cast down into a deep pit and buried under stones. When this was done, a certain priest of Apollo who had incited Paulinus against Vitalis was overwhelmed by a demon and began to cry out: You burn me too greatly, O Vitalis, Martyr of Christ! And, tossed about by that burning, he threw himself into the river.

He diligently scrutinized the life and conduct of the clergy and laity of the whole diocese by unceasing visitations. He vigorously defended and preserved the persons, rights, and property of the churches. He wonderfully calmed the disturbances and ravages of wars. With incredible skill he reconciled the souls of the greatest princes torn by discord, and composed a peace between King Otto and his son. He showed himself hospitable and kind to all, and commended himself, sober, holy, and continent, as a pastor according to the teaching of the Apostle. When on a certain occasion he was celebrating the divine mysteries, the hand of almighty power was seen to be present with him, blessing the sacred rites together with him. Having completed fifty years in the episcopal office, a man of wondrous holiness, generosity, abstinence, and watchfulness, knowing the day of his death which he had long desired with great longing, he fell peacefully asleep in the Lord on the fourth day before the Nones of July, in the year of salvation nine hundred and seventy-three, in the eighty-third year of his age, illustrious by miracles in his life and after his death, leaving his noble body — an ornament full of consolation — at Augsburg.

While staying at Viterbo, he received the legates of England, Scotland, Germany, Spain, and France, who professed obedience and homage to blessed Peter in his person; likewise certain bishops of Armenia, who also, in the name of the Metropolitan and their nation, sought his opinion on the weightier affairs of the Eastern Church. Setting out for France, he held councils at Reims and at Trier, in which he condemned the errors of Eon and of Gilbert de la Porrée.

Vitus, still a young child, was baptized without the knowledge of his father; and when his father learned of it, he left nothing untried to turn his son from the Christian religion. He delivered him to the judge Valerianus to be punished with stripes for persisting in this resolve. But Vitus, nonetheless holding to his purpose, was restored to his father. But while his father was devising a harsher punishment for him, Vitus, warned by an Angel, with his companions Modestus and Crescentia — his tutors — departed into foreign lands; and there he gained such renown for holiness that his fame reached the ears of Diocletian, who summoned him to free his son who was tormented by a demon. When the son had been freed, and the ungrateful emperor had been unable to persuade him by the most lavish rewards to worship the gods, he had him sent to prison in chains together with Modestus and Crescentia. When he found them more steadfast than ever, he ordered them cast into a great vessel filled with molten lead, boiling pitch, and tar; in which, as they sang divine hymns after the manner of the three Hebrew children, they were drawn out from there and thrown to a lion, which, prostrating itself, licked their feet. Wherefore the emperor, inflamed with rage because he saw the multitude stirred by the miracle, ordered them to be stretched on a rack and so their limbs to be beaten and their bones torn apart. At that time there were thunders, lightnings, and great earthquakes, by which the temples of the gods fell in ruin and many were crushed. The noble woman Florentia buried their relics, prepared with spices and embalmed with honor.

He lived in the flesh, yet his heart already hung with Christ on the cross; and therefore he said: I have been crucified with Christ; it is no longer I who live, but Christ who lives in me. Far more excellently did the martyr live in this death; for far more excellent is it to die to the world through righteousness than to die through a torment that lasts but a little while.

Scarcely had he begun his pontificate when he applied his mind to bringing the Apostolic See back to the City, to correcting the morals of the faithful, to restoring clerical discipline, to reforming the cloistered orders, to propagating the Catholic faith, and to defending the liberty of the Church.

He called his disciples, he says, and chose twelve of them, to send as sowers of faith throughout the world, to scatter the help of human salvation to the ends of the earth. Observe at the same time the heavenly design: he chose not certain wise men, not the wealthy, not the noble, but fishermen and tax collectors, to send forth; lest it should seem that he had drawn any to his grace by cleverness, or won them over by wealth, or attracted them by the authority of power and nobility; so that the force of truth, not the charm of argument, might prevail.

Elizabeth heard the voice first, but John perceived the grace first. She heard according to the order of nature; he exulted by reason of the mystery. She perceived the coming of Mary; he perceived the coming of the Lord. These speak of grace; those contemplate mysteries. Elizabeth heard with the bodily ear; John exulted with the inward sense of devotion. She recognized the arrival of Mary; he, still enclosed in his mother's womb, rejoiced at the presence of God.

But who do you say that I am? Prudent reader, note that, from what follows and from the texture of the discourse, the Apostles are called not men but gods. For when he had said: Who do men say the Son of Man is? — the Apostles replied, naming men who had spoken of him. But when he said: But who do you say that I am? — Peter, speaking on behalf of all and in the place of all, replied: You are Christ, the Son of the living God.

At last having attained his wish, he made his way first to Chieri and then to Turin, so that, under the blessed Joseph Cafasso as master, he might advance the more keenly both in the knowledge of the saints and in the sacred teaching of morals for the worthy administration of the Sacraments of Penance and the Eucharist. By his example and labors he also drew many young men after him, and later founded the Salesian Society for their formation.

The voice of the Lord breaking the cedars. It can be said that, by preparing for the Lord a perfect people, breaking down and crushing the proud impieties and those exalted against the knowledge of God, he made crooked things straight. For he who removes all obstacles, he who breaks down all arrogance, and through the sweetness of God's word calms all the storms of the spirit, that person makes the crooked straight, levels the rough places.

It is commonly said: What the eye does not see, the heart does not grieve. My eye is my memory; and to think of the Saints is, in a manner, to see them. Thus indeed is our portion in the land of the living; and no small portion, if only we cherish and hold fast what we possess.

Walpurga, daughter of the holy Richard, king of the English, and sister of the holy Willibald and Wunibald, dedicated her virginity to Christ her spouse almost from her very cradle, courageously trampling underfoot all the enticements of this world, and with admirable holiness of life became renowned throughout England. Then, crossing to Germany at the call of Saint Boniface, and spending some years in the monastery of Bischofsheim under the direction of the holy abbess Leoba, she was finally placed at the head of the monastery of Heidenheim, founded by her brother Willibald. There, enriched with the gifts of virtues and miracles, she passed to the heavenly life, and Pope Adrian II enrolled her among the Saints.

Wenceslaus, duke of Bohemia, son of the Christian father Wratislaus and the pagan mother Drahomira, was piously raised by his grandmother Ludmilla, a most holy woman, and was distinguished by every kind of virtue; with the greatest zeal he preserved his virginity undefiled throughout his whole life. His mother, having secured the administration of the kingdom through the wicked murder of Ludmilla, and living impiously with her younger son Boleslaus, aroused against herself the indignation of the nobles; and so, weary of their impious rule, throwing off the yoke of both, they saluted Wenceslaus as king in the city of Prague. He governed his kingdom more by piety than by power, zealous and assiduous in relieving the needy and afflicted. With the deepest reverence he honored priests, sowing with his own hands the grain and pressing the wine to be used in the sacrifice of the Mass. But when the emperor had honored him with the royal insignia, he was killed by his impious brother, at the instigation of his mother, while praying in church. His blood sprinkled on the walls is still visible.

Sixtus, the first of that name, a Roman by birth, of the seventh region of the City, called the Via Lata, born of the father Pastus, was appointed to govern the whole Church in the place of Alexander I, the Roman Pontiff crowned with a most noble martyrdom. He is said to have ordained that the Sanctus be sung during the celebration of Mass. He established that sacred vessels should not be touched by anyone but the ministers of the altar. He decreed that, after the Mass is finished, the bishop would give his blessing to the people. Concerning the Feast of Easter he wrote various letters and established much. He crowned his life with martyrdom and was buried near the body of the blessed Peter on the eleventh day before the Kalends of May. He held his see five years, a month, and twenty-two days.

Sixtus III, the third of that name, a Roman by birth, son of Sixtus, was appointed bishop of the Roman Church upon the death of Saint Celestine, with the wondrous peace and agreement of the whole city. Saint Augustine, while he was still a priest, held him in great esteem as a man of remarkable probity. He himself, made bishop, refuted the Nestorian and Pelagian heresies and labored mightily for the unity of the Church. He built and adorned the great basilica of Saint Liberius, which is also called Saint Mary Major. He redeemed captives, assisted the poor, protected the oppressed, and was most devoted to sacred vigils and prayers. For eight years and nineteen days he governed the Church of God; and resting in the Lord, he was buried on the Esquiline Hill on the fifth day before the Nones of August.

Sixtus II, an Athenian, philosopher turned disciple of Christ, was charged in the persecution of Valerian with publicly preaching Christ; arrested, he was dragged into the temple of Mars, with capital punishment set before him if he refused to sacrifice. But when neither threats nor promises could move him from his resolution, he was sent to prison. After a few days, when the judge had him brought out to behead him, Saint Lawrence the Deacon came to meet him lamenting that he was leaving him behind. To whom he replied: I am not abandoning you, my son; a greater contest awaits you. In three days you will follow me. With Sixtus were also beheaded the deacons Januarius, Magnus, Vincent, and Stephen; and the next day, the deacons Felicissimus and Agapitus. A few days later, Lawrence himself, after enduring various torments, was crowned with martyrdom. Pope Sixtus was buried in the cemetery of Callixtus on the fifth day before the Ides of August.

Zach 13:1-5

1 In that day, there will be a fountain open to the house of David and to the inhabitants of Jerusalem, for the washing of the transgressor and of the defiled woman.
2 And this shall be in that day, says the Lord of hosts: I will disperse the names of the idols from the earth, and they will not be remembered any longer. And I will take away the false prophets and the unclean spirit from the earth.
3 And this shall be: when any devotee will continue to prophesy, his father and his mother, who conceived him, will say to him, 'You shall not live, because you have been speaking a lie in the name of the Lord.' And his father and his mother, his own parents, will pierce him, when he will prophesy.
4 And this shall be: In that day, the prophets will be confounded, each one by his own vision, when he will prophesy. Neither will they be covered with a garment of sackcloth in order to deceive.
5 But he will say, 'I am not a prophet; I am a man of agriculture. For Adam has been my example from my youth.'
Zach 13:6-9

6 And they will say to him, 'What are these wounds in the middle of your hands?' And he will say, 'I was wounded with these in the house of those who love me.'
7 Awake, O spear, against my shepherd and against the man that clings to me, says the Lord of hosts. Strike the shepherd, and the sheep will be scattered. And I will turn my hand to the little ones.
8 And there will be in all the earth, says the Lord, two parts in it will be scattered and will pass away, and the third part will be left behind.
9 And I will lead the third part through fire, and I will burn them just as silver is burned, and I will test them just as gold is tested. They will call on my name, and I will heed them. I will say, 'You are my people.' And they will say, 'The Lord is my God.'
Zach 2:1-5

1 And I lifted up my eyes and I saw, and behold, a man, and in his hand was a measuring line;
2 and I said: Where are you going? And he said to me: To measure Jerusalem, so that I may see how great its width and how great its length may be.
3 And behold, the angel who had been speaking with me departed, and another angel went out to meet him.
4 Jerusalem will be inhabited without walls, because of the multitude of men and beasts of burden in its midst.
5 And I will be to it, says the Lord, a wall of fire all around. And in glory, I will be in its midst.

Zacharias, a Greek by birth, son of Polychronius, upon the departure from this life of Gregory III, was raised to the chair of blessed Peter. He was a man of the most gentle disposition, of wondrous sweetness and grace, beloved by the Roman clergy and people. Endowed with singular wisdom and singular prudence, he governed the Church peacefully and devoutly. He translated the Dialogues of Saint Gregory into the Greek tongue. The King of the Lombards, Liutprand, moved by his holiness and authority, restored to the Roman Church the cities taken from it and ended the war by which he was afflicting Italy. He also turned the Lombards from an unjust war against the Romans. He held a synod at Rome in the church of the Lateran. He held his pontificate for eleven years and a half.

Zacharias, hesitating at the greatness of the promises, seeks a sign by which he may believe — he for whom the very vision or address of the Angel alone should have sufficed as a sign. Wherefore he paid the merited penalty of his distrust in silence: he who had doubted whether what God had promised could come to pass was justly condemned to silence, so that he who had not believed in the word of God might not be able to use human words.

Zeno, bishop and doctor of Verona, converted very many by his teaching, holiness, and miracles from the worship of idols to the true religion of Christ. He freed the only daughter of the Emperor Gallienus from cruel vexation by a demon. Having achieved the liberation of many captives, he was especially diligent in the reception of the poor, in the protection of virgins, and in the assistance of widows. He governed the Church of Verona for many years and fell asleep in the Lord illustrious with holiness and miracles on the twelfth day before the Kalends of May.

Zeno, returning to Verona, when he had obtained from Gallienus the freedom to preach Christ openly, began to preach the faith and to denounce the idols, which the idolaters bore with the most hostile spirit. But in order to make manifest that he did these things by divine power, the holy man confirmed his teaching by a miracle. For calling to himself the corpse of a man that was at the time being carried downstream along the river, he restored life to it to the wonder of all; by which miracle nearly the whole city, casting aside the images of the gods, received the faith of Christ and called the blessed Zeno the father of the fatherland. Finally, having governed the Veronese church with wondrous constancy amid the storms of persecution, he went to heaven as an undaunted martyr of Christ and champion of the faith in the time of Gallienus. The holy Corbinianus was an outstanding venereator of this holy martyr, in whose honor he built and consecrated the church of Saint Valentine at Mayer; from which also the cathedral basilica of Freising venerates him as a secondary patron.

Zephyrinus, a Roman, was appointed to govern the Church under the Emperor Severus. He decreed that those who were to be ordained should at the proper time and in the presence of many clergy and laity be initiated in the sacred rites according to custom; and that men of learning and proven life should be chosen for that service and office. He further decreed that all priests should stand by the bishop while he celebrates the divine sacrifice. He likewise established that a patriarch, primate, or metropolitan should not pass judgment against a bishop unless supported by apostolic authority. He lived in the pontificate for eighteen years and eighteen days. He held four ordinations in the month of December, in which he created thirteen priests, seven deacons, and thirteen bishops in various places. Zosimus, a Greek, son of Abraham, received the episcopate of the Roman Church after Saint Innocent. He appended the decrees of the African Councils against the Pelagian heresy as a support for his own judgment, and armed the right hands of all the bishops with the sword of Peter for the destruction of the impious; for, after these had been approved by him, the Pelagian heresy was condemned throughout the whole world. He also condemned Pelagius himself together with Caelestius, issuing letters on this matter to the universal Church.

Almighty and merciful God, from whose gift it comes that worthy and praiseworthy service is rendered to you by your faithful: grant us, we pray, that we may run to your promises without offense.
Almighty and merciful God, in your mercy keep far from us all that opposes us, so that, unencumbered alike in mind and body, we may freely carry out what pertains to you.
Almighty ever-living God, grant us an increase of faith, hope, and charity, and that we may merit to attain what you promise, cause us to love what you command.
Almighty ever-living God, grant us so to celebrate the mysteries of the Lord's Passion that we may merit to receive pardon.
Almighty ever-living God, make us always bear toward you a devoted will, and to serve your majesty with a sincere heart.
Almighty ever-living God, look graciously upon our weakness, and stretch forth the right hand of your majesty to protect us.

Almighty ever-living God, who in the abundance of your loving kindness both surpass the merits and the desires of those who implore you: pour out upon us your mercy, that you may pardon what conscience fears and add what prayer does not dare to ask.
Almighty ever-living God, who govern heavenly and earthly things alike: mercifully hear the prayers of your people, and grant your peace to our times.

Almighty ever-living God, who have given your servants, in the confession of the true faith, to acknowledge the glory of the eternal Trinity, and in the power of majesty to adore the Unity: we pray that, by the steadfastness of that same faith, we may always be defended against all adversities.

Almighty ever-living God, who have caused our Savior to take flesh and undergo the Cross for the human race, as an example of humility to be imitated: graciously grant that we may hold both the lessons of his patience and merit to share in his Resurrection.
Almighty ever-living God, who have bestowed the Paschal Sacrament in the covenant of human reconciliation: grant to our minds that what we celebrate by our profession, we may imitate in effect.

Almighty ever-living God, who through salutary abstinence heal both bodies and minds: we humbly implore your majesty that, appeased by the devout prayer of those who fast, you may grant us both present aid and future.
O God, founder and ruler of your people: drive away the sins by which they are assailed, that, ever pleasing to you, they may be secure under your protection.
Look graciously upon your people, we pray, O Lord, and mercifully turn away from them the scourges of your wrath.
Look graciously upon your people, we pray, O Lord, and to those whom you command to abstain from bodily food, grant also to cease from harmful vices.
Graciously perfect in us, O Lord, the help of holy observance: that what we have learned must be done by your authority, we may fulfill by your working.
May the ears of your mercy be open, O Lord, to the prayers of those who implore you; and that you may grant the desires of those who ask, make them seek what is pleasing to you.
May the ears of your mercy be open, O Lord, to the prayers of those who implore you; and that you may grant the desires of those who ask, make them seek what is pleasing to you.
Spare, O Lord, spare your people, that, chastised by worthy afflictions, they may breathe again in your compassion.
Grant, O Lord, to your faithful that they may undertake the venerable solemnities of the fasts with fitting devotion, and pursue them with steadfast piety.
Grant us, we pray, O Lord, the help of your grace, that, fittingly intent upon fasts and prayers, we may be freed from the enemies of mind and body.
Grant us, we pray, O Lord, that, instructed by salutary fasts and abstaining also from harmful vices, we may more readily obtain your propitiation.
Grant, we pray, almighty God, that the dignity of the human condition, wounded by immoderation, may be reformed by the practice of healing restraint.
Grant, we pray, almighty God, that your family, which abstains from food by afflicting the flesh, may fast from fault by pursuing justice.
Grant, we pray, almighty God, that we who recall the sacred observances with yearly devotion may please you both in body and in mind.
Grant, we pray, almighty God, that we who trust in your loving kindness in our affliction may always be defended by your protection against all adversities.
Grant, we pray, almighty God, that we who trust in your protection may, with your help, overcome all things that oppose us.
Grant, we pray, almighty God, that we who are incessantly afflicted by our own transgressions may be freed through the Passion of your Only Begotten Son.
Grant, we pray, almighty God, that we who have completed the Paschal feasts may, by your bounty, hold fast to them in conduct and in life.
Grant, we pray, almighty God, that those who abstain from food by afflicting the flesh may fast from fault by pursuing justice.

Grant, we pray, almighty God, that those whom votive fasts chastise may also be gladdened by holy devotion itself, so that, with earthly attachments quieted, we may more readily lay hold of heavenly things.
Grant, we pray, almighty God, that the approaching solemnity of our redemption may both confer upon us the supports of the present life and bestow the rewards of eternal blessedness.
Grant, we pray, almighty God, that, ever meditating on what is reasonable, we may carry out in word and deed what is pleasing to you.
Mercifully hear our prayers, we pray, O Lord, and stretch forth the right hand of your majesty against all things that oppose us.
Mercifully hear our prayers, we pray, O Lord, and guard us, freed from the bonds of sin, from all adversity.
Mercifully hear the prayers of your people, we pray, O Lord, that we who are justly afflicted for our sins may be mercifully freed for the glory of your name.

May your dedicated people, we pray, O Lord, advance in the spirit of devout piety, that, instructed in sacred actions, the more they become pleasing to your majesty, the more they may be enriched with greater gifts.
Be propitious, O Lord, to our supplications, and heal the weaknesses of our souls, that, having received forgiveness, we may always rejoice in your blessing.

O God, protector of those who hope in you, without whom nothing is strong, nothing is holy: multiply your mercy upon us, that, with you as our ruler and guide, we may so pass through temporal good things as not to lose the eternal.
Look graciously upon your family, we pray, almighty God, that, by your bounty, it may be governed in body and, by your keeping, guarded in mind.
Look upon the prayers of the humble, we pray, almighty God, and stretch forth the right hand of your majesty for our defense.
Look upon your family, O Lord, and grant that our mind, which chastises itself by mortification of the flesh, may shine before you in its desire for you.
May the fasts of holy observance, we pray, O Lord, bestow upon us both an increase of devout conduct and the continual help of your propitiation.
Sanctify our fasts, we pray, O Lord, and graciously grant us pardon for all our faults.
Grant us, O Lord, to have perpetually both fear and love of your holy name, for you never fail to guide those whom you establish in the steadfastness of your love.
O God, at this hallowed fast, mercifully enlighten the hearts of your faithful, and graciously give attentive and kindly hearing to the supplications of those to whom you grant a spirit of devotion.
May heavenly propitiation, we pray, O Lord, enlarge the people subject to you and make them always serve your commandments.
May your mercy come to our aid, O Lord, that we may merit by your protection to be rescued from the impending dangers of our sins and by your liberation to be saved.
Guard your people, O Lord, and mercifully cleanse them from all sins, for no adversity shall harm them if no iniquity holds dominion over them.
Defend us, O Lord, by your protection, and keep us always from all iniquity.
May your mercy, O God, both cleanse us from all the corruption of the old ways and make us capable of holy newness.
May your grace, we pray, O Lord, always go before us and follow us, and make us continually intent on good works.

Author of the blessed age,
Christ, Redeemer of all,
Light from the light of the Father,
and true God from God.

Your love compelled you
to take on mortal flesh,
that you, the new Adam, might restore
what the old had taken away.

That same love, gracious maker
of earth and sea and stars,
took pity on the sins of our fathers
and broke our chains.

Let not that power of your glorious love
depart from your Heart:
from this fountain may the nations draw
the grace of forgiveness.

For this your side was pierced with a lance,
for this you endured your wounds:
that with flowing water and blood
you might wash us clean from stain.

Jesus, to you be glory,
who pour forth grace from your Heart,
with the Father and the gracious Spirit,
for ever and ever.
Amen.

The cycle of the year has brought back
blessed joys to us,
when the Holy Spirit the Comforter
descended upon the Apostles.

With vibrant flame of light
he bore the form of tongues,
that they might overflow with words
and be fervent in charity.

They speak in the tongues of all peoples;
the crowds of the Gentiles are amazed
and deem those filled with the Spirit
to be drunk with new wine.

These things were accomplished mystically
when the time of Pascha was fulfilled,
in the sacred round of the days
in which the Law grants remission.

Now, O most gracious God,
we pray to you with prostrate face:
grant us the gifts of the Spirit
descended upon us from heaven.

Long ago you filled consecrated hearts
with your grace:
forgive our sins
and grant us peaceful times.

Glory be to God the Father
and to the Son who rose
from the dead, and to the Comforter,
for ever and ever.
Amen.

The Heart: an ark containing the law
not of the old servitude,
but of grace, of pardon,
and of mercy.

The Heart: the undefiled sanctuary
of the new covenant,
holier than the ancient Temple
and more fruitful than the torn veil.

Charity willed that you be wounded
by an open blow,
that we might venerate the wounds
of an invisible love.

Under this symbol of love,
suffering both bloody and mystical,
Christ the Priest offered
both sacrifices in one.

Who would not love him who loves?
Who, redeemed, would not cherish him
and choose within that Heart
an eternal dwelling?

Jesus, to you be glory,
who pour forth grace from your Heart,
with the Father and the gracious Spirit,
for ever and ever.
Amen.

Behold, how the proud and savage host
of our sins
has wounded the innocent Heart
of a God who deserved nothing of the kind!

Our sins guide the soldier's lance;
the steel of that dread spear
mortal guilt has sharpened.

From the cleft Heart the Church is born,
bride of Christ:
this is the door in the side of the ark,
set for the salvation of the nations.

From here perennial grace,
like a sevenfold river,
flows, that we may wash
our soiled robes in the Blood of the Lamb.

It is shameful to return to the sins
that would wound the blessed Heart:
but let us kindle in our hearts
the flames that bespeak his love.

Jesus, to you be glory,
who pour forth grace from your Heart,
with the Father and the gracious Spirit,
for ever and ever.
Amen.

Christ had now ascended to the stars,
returning whence he had come,
to enjoy the Father's gift
and to give the Holy Spirit.

The solemn day pressed on,
when the mystic sevenfold
cycle turned seven times
marks the blessed season.

When at the third hour of light
the world suddenly thunders
and announces to the Apostles at prayer
that God is coming.

From the Father's light therefore
a gracious and beautiful fire descends
to fill the faithful hearts of Christ
with the warmth of the Word.

Breasts rejoice, filled
with the breath of the Holy Spirit,
and they sound forth diverse voices,
proclaiming the great deeds of God.

Known to all the nations,
Greeks, Latins, Barbarians,
all marveling together,
they speak in the tongues of all.

Then unbelieving Judea,
raving with a sinister spirit,
accuses Christ's faithful, sober as they are,
of being drunk with new wine.

But Peter comes forward
with the miracles performed and teaches
that the unbelievers speak false,
confirming it with Joel as witness.

Glory be to God the Father
and to the Son who rose
from the dead, and to the Comforter,
for ever and ever.
Amen.

Jesus, angelic beauty,
a sweet song to the ear,
a wonderful sweetness on the lips,
a heavenly nectar in the heart.

Those who taste you hunger;
those who drink still thirst;
they cannot desire anything
but Jesus, whom they love.

O my sweetest Jesus,
hope of the longing soul!
Devout tears seek you,
the inmost cry of the heart seeks you.

Stay with us, O Lord,
and enlighten us with your light;
dispel the darkness of the mind
and fill the world with sweetness.

Jesus, flower of the Virgin Mother,
love of our delight,
to you be praise and honor of name,
the kingdom of blessedness.
Amen.

Jesus, sweet memory,
giving true joys to the heart;
but above honey and all things
is his sweet presence.

Nothing is sung more sweetly,
nothing is heard with greater delight,
nothing is thought more pleasantly,
than Jesus, the Son of God.

Jesus, hope of the penitent,
how gracious you are to those who ask!
How good to those who seek you!
But what to those who find you?

Neither tongue is able to tell
nor letter to express:
one who has experienced it may believe
what it is to love Jesus.

Be, O Jesus, our joy,
you who are to be our reward:
let our glory be in you
through all ages for ever.
Amen.

Jesus, admirable King
and noble conqueror,
ineffable sweetness,
altogether desirable.

When you visit our heart,
then truth shines within it,
the vanity of the world grows worthless,
and charity burns within.

Jesus, sweetness of hearts,
living fountain, light of minds,
surpassing all joy
and all desire.

Let all acknowledge Jesus
and seek his love:
seek Jesus ardently,
and in seeking grow ardent.

Let our voice proclaim you, Jesus,
let our lives express you,
let our hearts love you,
both now and for ever.
Amen.

O fortunate village that gave him shelter,
Nazareth, august dwelling,
which cherished and brought forth
the first beginnings of the holy Church.

The sun, which wanders through the lands
with golden light,
has seen through all the ages
nothing more gracious or more holy than this house.

To this place the messengers of the heavenly court
fly in throngs;
they visit, revisit, and honor
this sanctuary of virtue.

With what mind, with what hand
Jesus fulfills the Father's will!
With what joy the Virgin delights
to perform the duties of a mother!

Joseph, a sharer in love
and care for his spouse, is at her side,
bound by a thousand bonds
through grace, the author of virtue.

These two, loving each other,
flow together into the love of Jesus;
Jesus gives to each in turn
the reward of mutual charity.

May it thus be that charity
joins us in an everlasting bond,
nurtures peace in the home,
and tempers the bitter seasons of life!

Jesus, you who were made
obedient to your parents,
with the supreme Father and the Spirit
be glory to you for ever.
Amen.

O blessed light of heaven
and highest hope of mortals,
O Jesus, upon whose birth
domestic charity smiled:

Mary, rich in grace,
O you alone who can
cherish Jesus with a chaste breast,
giving him kisses with your milk:

and you, chosen from ancient fathers
as guardian of the Virgin,
whom the divine Child calls
by the sweet name of father:

born of the noble stock of Jesse
for the salvation of the nations,
hear us as we suppliants
stand before your altars.

As the sun returns at evening
and withdraws luster from things,
we who remain here pour forth
vows from our inmost heart.

The grace of every virtue
that flourished in your dwelling:
grant that we may be able
to reflect it in our domestic ways.

Jesus, you who were made
obedient to your parents,
with the supreme Father and the Spirit
be glory to you for ever.
Amen.

Sing, my tongue, the mystery
of the glorious Body
and of the precious Blood,
which the King of nations,
fruit of a noble womb,
poured out as the world's ransom.

Given for us, born for us
from an inviolate Virgin,
and dwelling in the world
with the seed of the word scattered,
he closed the span of his sojourn here
in a wondrous manner.

On the night of the Last Supper,
reclining with his brothers,
having fully observed the Law
in the legal foods,
he gave himself with his own hands
as food to the twelve.

The Word made flesh, by a word
makes true bread into flesh;
and wine becomes the Blood of Christ:
and if sense is lacking,
faith alone suffices
to confirm a sincere heart.
The following stanza, if Office is celebrated before the Most Blessed Sacrament exposed, is said kneeling.

Therefore so great a Sacrament
let us venerate with bowed heads;
and let the ancient rite
yield to the new:
let faith supply the supplement
for the failure of the senses.

To the Father and to the Son
be praise and jubilation,
salvation, honor, and power too,
and benediction:
to the one proceeding from both
let equal praise be given.
Amen.

The sacred temples now shine,
adorned with lamps,
now the altar is wreathed with garlands,
and the censers smoke and breathe
with the tribute of holy incense.

Shall it delight us to celebrate in song
the royal birth of the Only Begotten of the Most High Father,
or the house of David,
and the honored names of an ancient race?

It is sweeter for us to recall
the humble cottage of Nazareth and its modest life;
it is sweeter to render in song
the hidden life of Jesus.

A stranger from the far shores of the Nile,
guided by an angel, hastening back,
much having suffered, the Child,
arrives safe at his father's threshold,

Jesus grows to youth in hidden years,
to be shaped in the humble craft
at which Joseph labored,
and freely joins himself as partner in that toil.

Let sweat water my limbs, he said,
before they are drenched with scattered blood:
let this penalty too be paid
for the expiation of the human race.

The devoted Mother sits at her gracious Son's side;
the good wife sits by her husband, happy
if she can relieve the weariness of the tired
with a kindly service.

O you who are not strangers to labor and toil,
nor ignorant of hardship, help the wretched
whom pressing need drives
through the sharp trials of life.

Rid of their pride those on whom ample prosperity
shines, give them a mind at peace with things;
whatever number implore your aid,
look upon them with a benign countenance.

To you, Jesus, be honor and power,
you who set before us the lessons of a holy life,
and who reign with the supreme Father
and the gracious Spirit.
Amen.

Let joys be joined to sacred solemnities,
and let praises ring out from the depths of our hearts;
let old things pass away, let all be new:
hearts, voices, and deeds.

The last supper of the night is recalled,
at which Christ is believed to have given
the lamb and the unleavened bread to his brothers,
according to the legal rites
given of old to the fathers.

After the symbolic lamb, the feast completed,
the Body of the Lord was given to the disciples,
whole to all, and whole to each,
as we confess, by his hands.

He gave to the frail a portion of his Body,
he gave to the sorrowful a chalice of his Blood,
saying: Receive this vessel which I hand over;
drink from it, all of you.

Thus he instituted this sacrifice,
whose ministry he willed to be entrusted
to priests alone, to whom it thus befits
that they receive and give to others.

The bread of angels becomes the bread of humanity;
heavenly bread puts an end to figures;
O wondrous thing: the Lord is eaten
by the poor, the servant, and the humble.

We implore you, O threefold and one Deity;
vouchsafe to visit us as we worship you:
lead us by your paths to where we are tending,
to the light that you inhabit.
Amen.

Sower of human salvation,
Jesus, delight of hearts,
Founder of the redeemed world,
and chaste light of those who love:

By what clemency were you vanquished
that you bore our sins?
You, innocent, would undergo death
to raise us from death.

You burst through the darkness of the underworld,
you strike the chains from captives;
a victor in noble triumph
you sit at the right hand of the Father.

May your indulgence move you
to repair our losses,
and to enrich those who behold your face
with blessed light.

You, leader and way to the stars,
be the goal of our hearts,
be the joy of our tears,
be the sweet reward of life.
Amen.

Holy Mother, do this:
fix the wounds of the Crucified
deep within my heart.

Of your wounded Son,
who so deigned to suffer for me,
divide the sufferings with me.

Make me devoutly weep with you,
to share in grief with the Crucified,
as long as I shall live:

To stand beside the Cross with you
and to unite myself to you
in mourning — this is my desire.
Amen.

The sorrowful Mother stood
weeping beside the Cross,
while her Son hung there.

Her sighing soul,
grieving and afflicted,
a sword pierced through.

How sad and afflicted
was that blessed Mother
of the Only Begotten!

She who mourned and grieved,
the devoted Mother, while she saw
the sufferings of her glorious Son.

Who is the man who would not weep,
if he saw the Mother of Christ
in such great torment?

Who could fail to be saddened,
contemplating the Mother of Christ
suffering with her Son?

For the sins of her people
she saw Jesus in torments
and subject to scourges.

She saw her sweet Son
desolate in dying,
as he gave up his spirit.

Ah, Mother, fount of love,
make me feel the power of your grief,
that I may mourn with you:

Make my heart burn
in loving Christ my God,
that I may be pleasing to him.
Amen.

Father of supreme clemency,
who govern the frame of the world,
God, one in substance
and threefold in persons:

Give your right hand to those who rise,
let the sober mind rise also,
blazing, and render to the praise of God
due thanks.

Glory be to God the Father
and to his only Son,
with the Spirit the Comforter,
for ever and ever.
Amen.

Eternal and most high King,
Redeemer of the faithful,
to whom death overcome bestowed
the triumph of supreme glory:

You ascend the orbits of the stars,
whither called from heaven
by power over all things bestowed,
not by human means:

That the threefold frame of creation,
celestial, terrestrial,
and that below the earth,
may now bow the knee in subjection.

The Angels tremble to see
the changed lot of mortals:
flesh sins, flesh atones,
God reigns, the flesh of God.

Be yourself our joy,
remaining the reward in heaven,
you who govern the fabric of the world,
conquering earthly joys.

Hence imploring you we pray:
forgive all our sins,
and lift our hearts on high
to you by heavenly grace.

That, when you suddenly begin
to appear in the cloud of judgment,
you may repel the deserved penalties
and restore the crowns that were lost.

Jesus, to you be glory,
who return as victor to heaven,
with the Father and the gracious Spirit,
for ever and ever.
Amen.

You, Unity of the Trinity,
who govern the world with power,
heed the song of praise
that we sing keeping watch.

The morning star shines in the east
and goes before the sun as herald;
the shadows of night fall:
let the holy Light illumine us.

Glory be to God the Father
and to his only Son,
with the Spirit the Comforter,
now and through every age.
Amen.

The Word of the Father coming forth on high,
not leaving the Father's right hand,
going out to his work,
came to the evening of life.

About to be handed over to death
by a disciple into the hands of his enemies,
he first handed himself over
to his disciples in the food of life.

To them under a twofold kind
he gave flesh and blood;
that of a twofold substance
he might nourish the whole human person.

At birth he gave himself as companion,
at table he gave himself as food,
in dying he gave himself as ransom,
in reigning he gives himself as reward.

O saving Victim,
who opens wide the gate of heaven,
hostile wars press upon us;
give strength, bring help.

To the Lord who is one and threefold
be everlasting glory;
who may grant life without end
to us in the homeland.
Amen.

O foremost Virgin of virgins,
be no longer bitter to me,
but make me weep with you.

Make me bear the death of Christ,
make me a sharer in his Passion
and ponder his wounds.

Make me be wounded by his wounds,
make me be inebriated by the Cross
and by the Blood of your Son.

Lest I be burned and consumed by flames,
may I be defended by you, O Virgin,
on the day of judgment.

Christ, when the time comes for me to depart hence,
grant that through your Mother I may come
to the palm of victory.

When the body shall die,
grant that to the soul may be given
the glory of paradise.
Amen.
The admirable name of Jesus, which is above every name: * Come, let us adore.
Alleluia, Christ the Lord ascending into heaven: * Come, let us adore, alleluia.
Alleluia, the Spirit of the Lord has filled the whole earth: * Come, let us adore, alleluia.
Christ the Son of God, subject to Mary and Joseph: * Come, let us adore.
Let us adore Christ the King who rules over the nations: * Who gives fatness of spirit to those who eat him.
The Heart of Jesus, wounded by love for us: * Come, let us adore.
The true God, one in Trinity and Trinity in Unity: * Come, let us adore.
Recalling the glorious sorrows of the Virgin, the Lord who suffered for us: * Come, let us adore.
Let us come before the face of the Lord: * and in psalms let us sing joyfully to him.
