The name of Jesus, however, is not light alone but also food. Are you not strengthened as often as you call him to mind? What so abundantly nourishes the mind of one who contemplates? What so restores the exercised senses, strengthens virtues, cultivates good and honorable conduct, fosters chaste affections? All spiritual nourishment for the soul is dry if not moistened with this oil; tasteless, if not seasoned with this salt. If you write, I find no savor in it unless I read Jesus therein. If you dispute or converse, I find no savor unless Jesus has sounded there. Jesus is honey to the mouth, melody to the ear, jubilation in the heart. But he is also medicine. Is any among us troubled? Let Jesus come into his heart, and from there leap to his lips. And behold, at the rising of that name, all cloud takes flight and serenity returns. Does someone slip into sin and run on toward the snare of death through despair? If he but invokes the name of life, will he not breathe again unto life at once?

Let no one say, therefore: I have not sinned against God, but against my brother; I have sinned against a man — it is a slight matter or no matter at all. Perhaps you say: It is slight, because it is quickly healed. You sinned against your brother: make satisfaction, and you are healed. Quickly you did a deadly deed, but quickly you found a remedy. Which of us may hope for the kingdom of heaven, my brothers, when the Gospel says: Whoever shall say to his brother, You fool, shall be in danger of the fire of Gehenna? Great is the terror: but look there for the remedy. If you bring your gift to the altar, and there recall that your brother has something against you, leave your gift there before the altar. God is not angry because you delay placing your gift: God seeks you more than your gift.

There is no one, dearly beloved, to whom the fellowship of this glory is denied by reason of the condition of the times, as though the tranquility of peace were empty of opportunity for virtue. For the Apostle proclaims, saying: All who wish to live godly in Christ will suffer persecution: and therefore the tribulation of persecution is never absent, if the observance of godliness is never absent. For the Lord says in his exhortations: Whoever does not take up his cross and follow me is not worthy of me. And we ought not doubt that this word pertains not only to the disciples of Christ, but to all the faithful and to the whole Church, which in those who were present was hearing its saving word universally.

For this Jesus of mine does not carry a name that is empty or void, as did his predecessors: in him there is no shadow of a great name, but the reality. For the name given from heaven is attested by the Evangelist, that it was called by the Angel before he was conceived in the womb. And mark the depth of the word: After Jesus was born, he is called Jesus by men — he who was called by the Angel before he was conceived in the womb. For indeed he is Savior both of the Angel and of man; but of man from the Incarnation, of the Angel from the beginning of creation. His name was called, he says, Jesus, which was called by the Angel. In the mouth of two or three witnesses every word stands firm; and that very name, which in the Prophet is expressed in brief, is read more openly in the Gospel as made flesh.

For not only do those enjoy participation in this priestly office, and the ministry of making satisfaction and offering sacrifice, whom our High Priest Christ Jesus employs as ministers for the offering of the clean oblation to the divine Name from the rising of the sun to its setting in every place; but also the entire people of Christians, called by the Prince of the Apostles a chosen people and a royal priesthood, is bound to offer sacrifice both for itself and for the whole human race — not altogether unlike the manner in which every priest and pontiff, taken from among men, is appointed for men in the things that pertain to God.

For the Gospel does not lie, where we read: And his father and mother were marveling at the things that were said about him. And in another place: His parents went every year to Jerusalem. Likewise a little later: And his mother said to him: Son, why have you done this to us? Behold, your father and I have been seeking you with sorrow. But he, to show that he had, beyond them, a Father who had begotten him beyond a mother, answered them: Why is it that you sought me? Did you not know that I must be about the things that are of my Father? And again, lest it be thought that by this saying he had denied those as parents, the Evangelist added in what followed: And they did not understand the word that he spoke to them; and he went down with them, and came to Nazareth, and was subject to them. To whom was he subject, if not to his parents? And who was subject, if not Jesus Christ, who, though he was in the form of God, did not count it robbery to be equal to God?

For what we know, if we know anything at all, we know not by reason of natural talent or sharpness of mind; but because we are intensely devoted to this man, we never depart from his reading: for those who love know more than all others the deeds of those they love, as being solicitous for them. As the blessed Apostle himself shows, when he says to the Philippians: As it is just for me to think this of you all, because I have you in my heart, and in my bonds, and in the defense and confirmation of the Gospel.

Nor can it be said here, in which matter some deceive themselves, that the eternal fire spoken of does not mean eternal burning. For some suppose that those who die with a dead faith pass through the fire that will be eternal, and on account of that faith they promise them salvation through fire: so that the fire itself would be eternal, but the burning of those within it — that is, the action of the fire upon them — would not be eternal; whereas the Lord, having foreseen this very thing, concluded his sentence by saying: Thus shall they go into eternal burning, but the just into eternal life. Therefore the burning shall be eternal, just as the fire: and Truth declares that those will go into it whose lack was not of faith but of good works.

It was not without reason that the birth of Christ from the Holy Spirit was kept silent among the people, and Joseph was assumed in the place of father; and from this, as is consistent with the truth, he was reckoned as the father of the Child. For had this not been so, the Child would have been thought to be without a father, since his lineage would not have been reckoned from the paternal side. For this reason it was necessary for the distinguished Evangelists to recount the lineage of Joseph. For if, passing over this, they had woven the line of his descent from the maternal side, apart from being unseemly, it would have been contrary to the custom of the sacred Scriptures. Fittingly, therefore, tracing the lineage of Joseph from David for the reason we have stated, they confirm at the same time that the Virgin Mary was also descended from David — inferring the wife's lineage together with the husband's.

For it was not sufficient to have passed beyond all the heavens to glory, nor to stand among the Angels: but he passed beyond the heavens, ascended above the Cherubim, was raised beyond the Seraphim, and did not halt until he had merited the throne of the Lord. Consider how great a space separates heaven from earth — indeed how far the earth is from the lower regions — and how much heaven is separated from the higher heaven, and from the higher heaven what a distance there is to the Angels, even to the higher Powers, and to the very throne of the Lord. Above all these was our nature elevated, so that man, who was held in so lowly a place that he could not descend further, was raised to so lofty a seat that he could not ascend higher.

For Christ is not in the head without being in the body: rather, Christ whole is in the head and in the body. Therefore what his members are, he is; but what he is, his members are not necessarily. For if they were not his members, he would not have said to Saul: Why do you persecute me? For it was not Saul who persecuted him, but his members — that is, his faithful ones — on earth. Yet he did not choose to say my saints, my servants, or, in a yet more honorable way, my brothers; but me, that is, my members, of whom I am the head.

It is therefore not absurd that Matthew, taking by way of others the centurion's coming to the Lord — which could be understood by the multitude — chose to say briefly: The centurion came to him. Nevertheless, the depth of the mystic speech of the holy Evangelist is not to be looked upon carelessly, in accordance with which it is written in the Psalm: Draw near to him, and be enlightened. And therefore, because the Lord so praised the centurion's faith — by which one truly draws near to Jesus — saying: I have not found so great faith in Israel: the wise Evangelist chose to say that he himself had come to Christ, rather than those through whom he had sent his words.

It was therefore no great sin if they sold in the Temple what was purchased in order to be offered in the Temple: and yet he drove them out. What would the Lord do if he found drunkards there — he who drove out even those who were selling things that were lawful and not contrary to justice (for what is honestly bought is not unlawfully sold) — and would not allow the house of prayer to become a house of trade?

There is no doubt that Joseph, to whom the Mother of the Savior was betrothed, was a good and faithful man. Faithful, I say, and prudent servant, whom the Lord appointed as the comfort of his Mother, the nurturer of his flesh, and, finally, the most faithful collaborator on earth in the great counsel. To this is added that he is said to have been of the house of David. Truly of the house of David, truly of royal stock descended this man Joseph, noble by birth, more noble by mind. Plainly a son of David, not degenerate from his father David; altogether, I say, a son of David, not only in flesh, but in faith, in holiness, in devotion; one whom the Lord found, as another David, according to his own heart; to whom he could safely entrust the most sacred and most secret treasury of his own heart; to whom, as to another David, he revealed the hidden and secret things of his wisdom, and granted that he not be ignorant of the mystery which none of the princes of this age knew.

Vices do not rise up, I say, after virtue's parent, sins after the just man, nor can weaknesses and diseases follow the physician. Therefore, if we wish to enter the kingdom of the physician himself, let us first heal our wounds. Let us set in order and preserve within ourselves the condition of both substances; lest our soul — the nobler portion of man, surely — be dragged down to Tartarus by the lower part; but rather, through the sanctified body, a more glorious nature may gain for itself the heavens: with his help who lives and reigns for ever and ever. Amen.

Let this not seem to you a slight example of faith on account of the lowliness of the shepherds' station. Surely the lowlier they are in wisdom, the more precious in faith. The Lord did not seek out gymnasia filled with choirs of the wise, but a simple people, who would not know how to embellish and color what they heard. For simplicity is sought, not ambition.

The Savior therefore does not without purpose excuse himself for having worked no miracles of power in his own homeland; lest perhaps someone should think that we ought to hold a lesser affection for our homeland. For he who loved all could not fail to love his own citizens: but they by their jealousy cast off from themselves the love of their homeland. I tell you truly: there were many widows in the days of Elijah. Not that those were days belonging to Elijah, but days in which Elijah was at work: or because Elijah was making days for those who saw in his works the light of spiritual grace and were turning to the Lord. And therefore heaven was opened to those who saw the eternal and divine mysteries: it was closed, and there was famine, when there was no abundance of knowledge of the divinity. But of this we have spoken more fully when we wrote on the subject of widows.

This ship is not troubled, in which prudence navigates, faithlessness is absent, and faith breathes. For how could it be troubled, when he who presided over it is the very foundation of the Church? There is disturbance, therefore, where faith is little; here there is security, where love is perfect. And if others are commanded to let down their nets, to Peter alone is it said: Launch out into the deep; that is, into the depth of disputations. For what is so deep as to see the height of riches, to know the Son of God, and to assume the profession of divine generation? Which, though the human mind cannot fully comprehend by investigation of reason, yet the fullness of faith embraces.

Sometimes indeed Scripture not only declares to us the virtues of these men, but their falls also become known; so that in the victory of the brave we may see what to seize upon by imitation, and again in the falls what we ought to fear. For behold, Job is described as increased by temptation, but David as prostrated by temptation; so that the virtue of the great may nourish our hope, and the falls of the great may gird us to the caution of humility: while those, joyfully, lift us up, and these, fearfully, weigh us down; and the soul of the hearer, instructed by the confidence of hope from the former and by the humility of fear from the latter, neither grows proud in rashness because it is pressed down by dread, nor, pressed down by fear, despairs, because by the example of virtue it is strengthened toward the confidence of hope.

The faithful know the Body of Christ, if they do not neglect to be the Body of Christ. Let them become the Body of Christ, if they wish to live by the Spirit of Christ. No one lives by the Spirit of Christ except the Body of Christ. Understand, my brethren, what I have said. You are a human being, and you have a spirit, and you have a body. By spirit I mean that which is called the soul, by which you subsist as a human being; for you consist of soul and body. You have an invisible spirit, a visible body. Tell me, what of the two lives from the other? Does your spirit live from your body, or does your body live from your spirit? Everyone who lives answers: my body lives from my spirit. Do you then wish to live by the Spirit of Christ? Be in the Body of Christ.

We, however, dearly beloved brothers, who are philosophers not in words but in deeds; who display wisdom not in dress but in truth; who know the consciousness of virtue rather than its boasting; who speak no great things but live as servants and worshipers of God: let us render that patience which we learn from heavenly teachings, in spiritual service. For this virtue is shared between us and God: thence patience begins, thence its brightness and dignity takes its head. The origin and greatness of patience proceeds with God as its author. This is a thing for man to love, which is dear to God. The good that the divine majesty loves it commends. If God is both Lord and Father to us, let us imitate the patience of a lord and a father alike; for servants too ought to be obedient, and sons ought not to be degenerate.

But we, for whom Christ the Lord is a spirit before our face, live in the shadow of Christ. And therefore the Church says: I longed for and sat in his shadow. That man, therefore, by living luxuriously, consumed all the adornments of his nature. Wherefore you, who have received the image of God, who have his likeness, do not consume it in irrational defilement. You are the work of God: do not say to wood, You are my father; lest you receive the likeness of wood, because it is written: Let those who make them become like them.

But let us understand by the rod from the root of Jesse the holy Virgin Mary, who had no shoot joined to her, of whom we read above: Behold, a virgin shall conceive and bear a son. And by the flower, the Lord our Savior, who says in the Song of Songs: I am the flower of the field and the lily of the valleys.

We truly, if we wish to obtain eternal life, if we desire to have the giver of immortality within us, let us gladly run together to receive the blessing; and let us beware lest the devil set before us a harmful religion as a snare. You speak rightly, says one; yet we know that it is written that one who eats the bread and drinks the chalice unworthily eats and drinks judgment to himself. I examine myself, therefore, and find myself unworthy. When, then, whoever you are who say this, will you be worthy? When will you offer yourself to Christ? For if by sinning you are unworthy, and you do not cease to sin — for who understands his own faults? according to the Psalmist — you will be altogether without this life-giving sanctification.
Osee 1:4-7

4 And the Lord said to him: Call his name Jezreel, for yet a little while and I will visit the blood of Jezreel upon the house of Jehu, and I will cause the kingdom of the house of Israel to rest,
5 and in that day I will crush the bow of Israel in the valley of Jezreel.
6 And she conceived again and bore a daughter. And he said to him: Call her name, Without Mercy, for I will no longer have mercy on the house of Israel, but I will utterly forget them.
7 Yet I will have mercy on the house of Judah, and I will save them by the Lord their God; and I will not save them by bow and sword and battle and horses and horsemen.

9 And he said: Call his name, Not My People, for you are not my people, and I will not be yours.
10 And the number of the sons of Israel shall be like the sand of the sea, which is without measure and cannot be numbered. And in the place where it is said to them, You are not my people, it shall be said to them, Sons of the living God.
11 And the sons of Judah and the sons of Israel shall be gathered together; and they shall appoint for themselves one head, and they shall go up from the land, for great is the day of Jezreel.

4 Yet truly, let no one judge, and let no man be reproved; for your people are as those who contend with the priest.
5 And you shall fall today, and the prophet shall also fall with you. In the night I have made your mother to be silent.
6 My people have been silent because they had no knowledge. Because you have rejected knowledge, I will reject you from exercising the priesthood for me; and since you have forgotten the law of your God, I also will forget your sons.
Osee 4:7-10

7 According to their multitude, so have they sinned against me. I will change their glory into shame.
8 They will devour the sins of my people, and they will lift up their souls to their iniquity.
9 And it shall be as with the people, so with the priest; and I will visit their ways upon them, and I will repay them for their deeds.
10 And they shall eat and not be satisfied; they have played the harlot and have not ceased, for they have abandoned the Lord in not keeping watch.

The way of contempt for death has been shown us, for us to follow: the pattern has been set before us, for us to be conformed to it. Our first duty is to bestow mercifully upon his sheep our exterior goods: our last, if need be, to minister even our very death for those same sheep. And from this first and lesser duty one arrives at that final and greater one. But since the soul by which we live is incomparably far better than the earthly substance which we possess outwardly: one who does not give his substance for the sheep — when will he give his soul for them?

He departed into a far country. What is farther than to withdraw from oneself: to be separated not by regions but by morals; to be divided by pursuits, not by lands; and, as it were, with the swelling tide of worldly luxury flowing between, to stand apart from the saints? For whoever separates himself from Christ is an exile from his homeland, a citizen of the world. But we are not strangers and pilgrims, but fellow citizens of the Saints and members of the household of God. For we who were far off have been made near in the Blood of Christ. Let us not be envious of those returning from a far country: for we too were in a far country, as Isaiah teaches. For thus you read: Those who sat in the region of the shadow of death, upon them a light has arisen. The far country, therefore, is the shadow of death.

And she will bear a Son, and you shall call his name Jesus; for you are not to think, because he is from the Holy Spirit, that you are therefore a stranger to the ministry of so great a dispensation. For even though you have nothing in common in this generation — for the Virgin remained untouched — yet what is proper to a father and in no way diminishes the dignity of the Virgin, this I readily grant to you: namely, that you should give a name to the newborn; for you will be the first to call him. For even though he who is born is not your son, you will nevertheless show toward him the care and solicitude of a parent; and therefore I unite you with him from the very moment of naming. Then, lest anyone should suspect from this that he was his father, he says: She will bear a Son. He did not say, She will bear to you, but set it down as indefinite and open; for she bore Christ not to him, but to the whole world.

The reason is therefore evident why he who had said nothing began by saying: And it came to pass in the thirtieth year: because he joined the word which he brought forth outwardly to the word which he had heard inwardly. He therefore connected the words he uttered to the inner vision, and for this reason begins by saying, And it came to pass. For he appends the beginning of his outward speaking; as though that too were outward which he saw inwardly. But the fact that he received the spirit of prophecy in the thirtieth year indicates something for us to consider: namely, that the word of teaching is not available, according to the use of reason, except in a perfect age. Wherefore also the Lord himself, at the twelfth year of his age, chose to be found sitting in the midst of the doctors in the Temple — not teaching, but asking questions.

Patience it is that commends us to God and preserves us for him: it is patience that tempers wrath, bridles the tongue, governs the mind, guards peace, regulates discipline, breaks the onset of lust, crushes the violence of pride, extinguishes the fire of strife, restrains the power of the wealthy, refreshes the poverty of the poor, guards in virgins the blessed integrity, in widows the laborious chastity, in those joined and married the undivided charity: it makes the humble in prosperity, the strong in adversity, meek against injuries and insults; it teaches to forgive the offending quickly; if you yourself offend, to plead long and earnestly; it repels temptations, endures persecutions, brings sufferings and martyrdoms to their completion. It is patience that firmly fortifies the foundations of our faith.

David sinned, as kings are wont to do; but he did penance, he wept, he groaned, as kings are not wont to do. He confessed his fault, besought pardon, lay prostrate on the ground lamenting his misery, fasted, prayed, and transmitted the testimony of his confession for everlasting ages through his publicly manifested sorrow. What private men blush to do, a king did not blush to confess. Those who are bound by laws dare to deny their sin, and disdain to ask for the pardon which he implored who was bound by no human laws. That he sinned is of human condition; that he made supplication is of correction. The fall is common, but the confession is singular. Therefore, to have fallen into fault is of nature; to have washed it away, of virtue.

Let each of you therefore weigh within himself whether this voice of God has grown strong in the ear of his heart, and whether he recognizes that he is already of God. For there are some who do not even deign to receive the commandments of God with the ear of the body. And there are some who receive them with the ear of the body, but embrace them with no desire of the mind. And there are some who receive the words of God willingly, so as even to be moved to tears of compunction, but after the time of weeping return to iniquity. These surely do not hear the words of God, who disdain to carry them out in deed. Recall, therefore, dearly beloved brothers, your life before the eyes of your mind, and tremble with deep consideration at what rings out from the mouth of Truth: For this reason you do not hear, because you are not of God.

Through this natural unity, the entire Father is in the Son and in the Holy Spirit; the entire Son is in the Father and in the Holy Spirit; and the entire Holy Spirit likewise is in the Father and in the Son. None of these is outside any of the others: for no one of them either precedes another in eternity, or exceeds another in greatness, or surpasses another in power; for neither is the Father, as regards the unity of the divine nature, earlier or greater than the Son or the Holy Spirit; nor can the eternity and immensity of the Son, as though prior or greater, by nature precede or exceed the immensity and eternity of the Holy Spirit.

You know what assembly of the malicious Jews it was, and what was the multitude of those working iniquity. What iniquity? Because they wanted to kill the Lord Jesus Christ. So many good works, he says, have I shown you: for which of these do you wish to kill me? He bore with all their infirm ones, healed all their sick, preached the kingdom of heaven, did not keep silent about their vices — so that the vices themselves, rather than the physician by whom they were healed, might displease them. Ungrateful for all these healings of his, like those raving with a great fever, raging against the physician who had come to heal them, they devised a plan to destroy him: as though wishing to prove thereby whether he was truly a man who could die, or something above man who would not allow himself to die. We recognize their very words in the Wisdom of Solomon: With a most shameful death, they say, let us condemn him. Let us question him: for there will be regard for his words. For if he is truly the Son of God, let him deliver him.

It is also to be noted that Elijah is read to have ascended in a chariot: so that it might be openly shown that a mere man stood in need of another's help. For those assistances were effected and displayed through Angels: since he who was burdened by the weakness of his own nature was not able to ascend even into the lower heaven by himself. But our Redeemer is not read to have been lifted up by a chariot or by Angels: because he who had made all things was borne above all his own creation by his own power. For he was returning to where he was; and was going back from where he remained: because, when through his humanity he ascended into heaven, through his divinity he equally encompassed both earth and heaven.

It is also to be noted that when Jesus is said to draw near to Jericho, the blind man is enlightened. Jericho indeed is interpreted as moon: but the moon in sacred speech stands for the defect of the flesh: because, as it wanes with its monthly changes, it signifies the defect of our mortality. Therefore, when our Creator draws near to Jericho, the blind man returns to the light: because, when the Divinity took upon itself the defect of our flesh, the human race received the light it had lost. For from the source where God suffers human things, man is raised up to divine things. And this blind man is fittingly described as sitting by the way and as a beggar. For Truth itself says: I am the way.

We must also note what it means that the Angel is seen to be sitting on the right side. For what else is signified by the left but the present life; and what by the right, but the life that is everlasting? Whence in the Song of Songs it is written: His left hand is under my head, and his right hand will embrace me. Since therefore our Redeemer had already passed through the corruption of this present life, fittingly the Angel who had come to announce his everlasting life was sitting on the right. He appeared clothed in a white robe: because he announced the joy of our festival. For the brightness of the garment proclaims the splendor of our solemnity. Shall we say our solemnity, or his? But that we may speak more truly, let us say both his and ours. For that Resurrection of our Redeemer was both our festival, because it brought us back to immortality, and the festival of the Angels as well, because by calling us back to heavenly things it filled up their number.

It is to be noted carefully, however, that the side of Christ is said to have been opened, not wounded; for strictly speaking a wound can only be made in a living body. For the Evangelist John says: One of the soldiers opened his side with a lance; so that, with his side opened, we might acknowledge the love of his Heart unto death, and might enter into that ineffable love of his by which he went out toward us. Let us therefore draw near to his Heart — the high Heart, the secret Heart, the Heart that thinks all things, the Heart that knows all things, the Heart that loves, or rather burns with love — and let us understand the open door at least in the vehemence of his love; let us enter, fashioned in the heart, into the secret hidden from eternity, now revealed as it were with side opened in death; for the opening of the side reveals the opening of the eternal temple, where the consummated eternal happiness of all who exist is perfected.

For it is known within what boundaries the kingdom of Solomon was enclosed: and yet in that Psalm we read — to say nothing of other things — He shall rule from sea to sea, and from the river to the ends of the earth; which we see fulfilled in Christ. For from the river he took the beginning of his dominion, when, having been baptized by John, and pointed out by him, he began to be recognized by the disciples, who called him not only Master, but also Lord.

For the Lord knows those who are his: he knows who persevere unto the crown, who unto the flame. He knows the wheat in his threshing floor, and he knows the chaff as well: he knows the harvest, and the tares as well. Already judged is the one who does not believe. Why already judged? Because he did not believe in the name of the only-begotten Son of God. And this is the judgment: that light has come into the world, and men loved darkness more than light, for their works were evil. My brothers, whose works did the Lord find to be good? No one's. He found all works evil. How then did some do the truth and come to the light? For this too follows: But whoever does the truth comes to the light.

There is no Sacrament more salutary than this, by which sins are purged, virtues are increased, and the mind is enriched with an abundance of all spiritual gifts. It is offered in the Church for the living and the dead, that it may profit all for whose salvation it was instituted. The sweetness of this Sacrament no one can sufficiently express: through it spiritual sweetness is tasted at its very source, and the memory is recalled of that most excellent charity which Christ showed in his Passion. Wherefore, that the immensity of this charity might be more deeply engraved in the hearts of the faithful, at the Last Supper, when the Passover had been celebrated with the disciples, as he was about to pass from this world to the Father, he instituted this Sacrament as the abiding memorial of his Passion, the fulfillment of the ancient figures, the greatest of the miracles he himself had worked; and as a singular consolation to those saddened by his departure, he left it behind.

Does my body live from your spirit? Mine lives from my spirit, and yours from your spirit. The Body of Christ cannot live except from the Spirit of Christ. Hence comes what the Apostle Paul, explaining this bread to us, says: We who are many are one bread, one body. O sacrament of devotion, O sign of unity, O bond of charity! Whoever wishes to live has where to live, has whence to live. Let him draw near, let him believe, let him be incorporated, that he may be made alive. Let him not shrink from the fellowship of the members, let him not be a rotten member deserving to be cut away, let him not be a misshapen one to be ashamed of. Let him be beautiful, let him be fitting, let him be sound: let him cleave to the body, let him live for God from God. Now let him labor on earth, that afterward he may reign in heaven.

Now let us consider who they were who, once their error was detected, were cast out of paradise and confined to a village. And you see how those whom death had expelled, life has called back. And therefore, according to Matthew, we read of both an ass and a colt: so that, because in two human beings both sexes had been expelled, in two animals both sexes might be called back. Therefore in the mother ass he figured as it were the Eve of error; but in the colt he expressed the generality of the Gentile people: and therefore the colt of the ass is ridden. And fittingly: one on which no one had yet sat; because no one, before Christ, had called the nations to the Church. Finally, according to Mark you have it thus: On which no man yet had sat.

For now, both by the Lord's own profession and by our faith, it is truly flesh and truly blood. And when received and drunk, they bring it about that both we are in Christ and Christ is in us. Can this not be the truth? Let it not be the truth for those who deny that Jesus Christ is true God. He is therefore in us through the flesh, and we are in him, since that which we are is, with him, in God. But that through the Sacrament of sharing in his flesh and blood we are in him, he himself testifies, saying: And the world will see me no more, but you shall see me; because I live, and you will live; because I am in my Father, and you are in me, and I am in you.

Therefore the infirm one himself nourishes the infirm, like a hen her chicks: for to this he likened himself. How often, he says to Jerusalem, I wished to gather your children together under my wings, as a hen gathers her chicks, and you were not willing. But you see, brothers, how a hen grows weak together with her chicks. For no other bird is known, by the fact that it is a mother. We see any sparrows nesting before our eyes; we see swallows, storks, doves nesting every day: we do not recognize them as parents except when we see them at their nests. But the hen is so weakened in her chicks that even if the chicks themselves do not follow, you may not see the young, yet you understand the mother.

O precious and wonderful banquet, health-bearing and filled with all sweetness! For what can be more precious than this banquet? In it, not the flesh of bulls and goats, as of old in the Law, but Christ true God is set before us to be received. What is more wonderful than this Sacrament? For in it the bread and wine are substantially converted into the Body and Blood of Christ; and therefore Christ, perfect God and man, is contained under the small appearance of bread and wine. He is eaten therefore by the faithful, yet is in no way broken; rather, with the Sacrament divided, he remains whole under each and every part of the division. The accidents, moreover, subsist in it without a subject, so that faith may have place, while the visible is taken up invisibly, hidden beneath an alien appearance; and the senses may be rendered immune from deception, for they judge of the accidents that are known to them.

The guards come out to meet him, and command that the gates be shut fast, so that he might obtain his glory at those very gates. But they do not recognize him, for he is clothed in the soiled garment of our life: whose garments are red from the wine-press of human evils. And so his companions are again questioned by those voices: Who is this King of glory? And the answer given is no longer, Strong and mighty in battle; but, The Lord of hosts, who has obtained the dominion of the world, who has gathered all things up into himself in summary, who has restored all things to their former state: he is the King of glory.

Long ago, when disputing with the Jews, Christ said: Unless you eat my flesh and drink my blood, you will not have life in you. But when they, not having received these words spiritually, went away offended — for they thought he was urging them to eat flesh — there were also in the old testament the loaves of proposition; yet since those belonged to the old testament, they have already come to an end. In the new testament, however, there is the heavenly bread and the chalice of salvation, which sanctify both soul and body. I would not have you regard these things, therefore, as though they were bare and simple bread, bare and simple wine; for they are the Body and Blood of Christ. For even if the senses report that to you, yet let faith confirm you. Do not judge the matter by taste: but let faith render you certain beyond all doubt that you have been made worthy to be a partaker of the Body and Blood of Christ.

Soldiers were posted as guards at the tomb. We give you money, they said; say that while you were sleeping his disciples came and took him away. Truly, those who search out schemes have come to an end. What have you said, O wretched cunning? Do you forsake the light of righteous counsel so utterly, and plunge so deep into the pit of craftiness, as to say: Say that while you were sleeping his disciples came and took him away? One may ask, however, how it is said he was high priest of that year, since God appointed one chief priest, to be succeeded by another upon his death. But it is to be understood that, through ambition and contention among the Jews, it was later established that there should be several, ministering in turn year by year. For this is also said of Zechariah: Now it came to pass, while he was performing the priestly office in the order of his course before God, according to the custom of the priestly office, it fell to him by lot to offer incense, and he entered the temple of the Lord. From this it appears that they were many, and that they had their courses: for it was not lawful to offer incense except to the chief priest. And perhaps even more than one administered for a single year, with others succeeding them in another year, from among whom the lot fell for one to offer incense.

This may be understood simply of Antichrist, or of the image of Caesar that Pilate placed in the temple, or of the equestrian statue of Hadrian, which stood in that very place of the holy of holies even to the present day. Moreover, the Abomination, according to the ancient Scripture, is the name given to an idol; and therefore desolation is added, because an idol was placed in the desolate and destroyed temple.

The Lord had commanded, out of regard either for weakness or age or the poverty of parents, that children should honor their parents, even by ministering to their bodily needs. The scribes and Pharisees, wishing to subvert this most prudent law of God so as to introduce impiety under the guise of piety, taught the most wicked of sons that, if anyone wished to vow to God the things that ought to be offered to his parents — who is the true Father — then the offering to the Lord is to take precedence over the duty owed to parents; or at any rate that the parents themselves, seeing that things had been consecrated to God, would refrain from them for fear of incurring the crime of sacrilege, and so would be reduced to destitution. And thus it came about that the offering of children, under the pretext of the temple and of God, fell as profit to the priests.

The first-fruits are indeed of the same kind and nature as the rest of the fruit, for whose more abundant increase the first-fruits are offered to God as a sacred gift on behalf of all, a kind of pledge, as it were, of nature restored. Christ, therefore, is the first-fruits of those who sleep. But are they the first-fruits of his own who sleep — who are held, as it were, in a sweet slumber, exempt from death — or of all the dead? But as in Adam all die, so also in Christ shall all be made alive. And so, just as the first-fruits of death are in Adam, so too the first-fruits of the Resurrection are in Christ, and all shall rise. But let no one despair, nor let the just man grieve at the common lot of rising, since he awaits the preeminent fruit of virtue. All shall indeed rise, but each one, as the Apostle says, in his own order. The fruit of divine clemency is common to all, but the order of merits is distinct.

He had first said: Prophesy, or drop a word toward the south, toward the southwest, the south, and toward the southern forest. It is surely beyond doubt that Christ, in heaven, did not deny but rather fulfilled and perfected that intimacy, reverence, and most sublime dignity which Joseph showed him while he lived among men, as a son to his own father. Hence it is not without reason that the Lord adds in the word set before us: Enter into the joy of your Lord. And therefore, although the joy of eternal blessedness enters into the heart of man, the Lord chose rather to say to him, Enter into the joy; so that it is mystically intimated that this joy is not only within him, but surrounds him on every side and absorbs him, and, like an infinite abyss, submerges him. Remember us therefore, blessed Joseph, and by the intercession of your prayer plead our cause before your putative Son; and render the most blessed Virgin, your spouse, propitious to us — she who is the Mother of him who lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit for endless ages of ages. Amen.

Indeed these things were done that the Scripture might be fulfilled which says: You shall not break a bone of him. For it had been commanded by the Lord to Moses that in the sacrificial Passover, at the celebration of the immolated lamb, not a single bone should be broken. But in the Lord Jesus, the most innocent Lamb, the truth of the figure was fulfilled. His legs were by no means broken, as were those of the two wicked men hanging with him; but only his side was opened, so that another Scripture might be fulfilled which says: They shall look upon him whom they have pierced. Furthermore, the Lord willed to retain in his own body the wounds' scars, so that they might serve both as an incentive of devotion for the elect and as an irrefutable testimony of damnation for the reprobate. Thus all things were consummated in Christ, proclaimed long before by the oracles of the Prophets, so that the Catholic faith might be fortified both in its own behalf and against the errors of heretics.

The Evangelist recorded that the Angel had brought his name from heaven, in order to show thereby how marvelous was that birth — teaching that his name was conveyed to Joseph both by an Angel and from God. For the very name itself was not placed there without purpose; it surely contains a thousand treasuries of good things. For this reason the Angel also interprets it, encouraging one sorrowing with good hopes; and in this way too he draws him to believe what he is saying. For we are easily moved toward what is favorable, and we give our assent more readily to what is fortunate. For he, it says, will save his people from their sins. From this too the newness of the benefit is indicated. For it is not from visible warfare, nor from the sword of barbarians, but — what is far greater than these — from their own sin that he announces his people are to be freed: which no human being has ever been able to bring about.

For this reason was the first woman made from the side of the sleeping man, and she was called life and the mother of the living. A great good was signified, before the great evil of transgression. This second Adam, with head bowed, slept upon the Cross, so that from thence his spouse might be formed, who flowed from the side of the sleeper. O death, through which the dead are brought back to life! What is purer than this blood? What more wholesome than this wound? And he who saw it, it says, bore witness, and his testimony is true; and he knows that he speaks truly, so that you also may believe. He did not say: so that you also may know, but: so that you may believe. For he who saw it knows, and it is for one who did not see to trust in whose testimony he should believe. It pertains more to faith to believe than to see.

Nowhere, assuredly, does the goodness of grace and the generosity of God's omnipotence shine forth so clearly as in the man who is the Mediator between God and humanity, the man Christ Jesus. For what shall we say, my brothers? I speak to those nourished in the Catholic faith, or won over to Catholic peace. We know and hold that the Mediator between God and humanity, the man Christ Jesus, in as much as he was man, was of the same nature as we are. For our flesh is not of a different nature from his flesh, nor is our soul of a different nature from his soul. He assumed this nature which he judged to be in need of salvation.

Therefore, whatever faithful soul you are, anoint the feet of the Lord with precious ointment, as Mary did. That ointment was justice, and for that reason it was a pound; but it was ointment of pure nard of great price. As for the word pure nard, we should believe that this was a place from which this precious ointment came; yet this too is not without meaning and accords most fittingly with the sacrament. In Greek pistis means faith in Latin. You were seeking to perform justice. The just man lives by faith. Anoint the feet of Jesus by living well: follow in the footsteps of the Lord. Wipe them with your hair: if you have more than you need, give to the poor, and you will have wiped the feet of the Lord — for hair seems to be what is superfluous on the body. You have something to do with your superfluities: they are superfluous to you, but to the feet of the Lord they are necessary. Perhaps the feet of the Lord on earth stand in need.

For I saw iniquity and contradiction in the city. Consider the glory of his very Cross. Now that Cross is fixed upon the brows of kings, which enemies once mocked. Experience has proved its power: it has conquered the world not by iron, but by wood. The wood of the Cross seemed worthy of contempt in the eyes of enemies, and standing before that very wood they shook their heads and said: If he is the Son of God, let him come down from the Cross. He was stretching out his hands to an unbelieving and contradicting people. For if the just man is one who lives by faith, the unjust man is one who has no faith. Therefore what he says here — iniquity — understand as faithlessness. The Lord therefore saw in the city iniquity and contradiction, and was stretching out his hands to an unbelieving and contradicting people; and yet, awaiting even them, he was saying: Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do.

You will seek me and will not find me, and where I am you cannot come. Here he foretold his own Resurrection: for they refused to acknowledge him when he was present, and afterward they sought him, when they saw the multitude already believing in him. For great signs were wrought even after the Lord rose and ascended into heaven. Then great things were done through the disciples — but he himself was acting through them, just as he does through himself: for he himself had said to them: Without me you can do nothing. When that lame man who sat at the gate rose at the voice of Peter and walked on his own feet, so that the people marveled, Peter addressed them thus: that he had not done these things by his own power, but by the power of him whom they had killed. Many, stricken with compunction, said: What shall we do?

One may also ask why, after his Resurrection, the Lord stood on the shore when his disciples were laboring at sea, whereas before his Resurrection he walked on the waves of the sea in the sight of his disciples. The reason for this is quickly grasped if one weighs the very situation that then prevailed. For what does the sea signify, if not the present age, which dashes itself against the tumults of misfortune and the waves of a corruptible life? What is figured by the solidity of the shore, if not that perpetuity of eternal rest? Because, then, the disciples were still amid the waves of mortal life, they were laboring at sea; but because our Redeemer had already passed beyond the corruption of the flesh, after his Resurrection he stood upon the shore.

You ask what free will avails for evil? Recall man as he sins. You ask what God-made-man avails for help? Consider in him grace that liberates. Nowhere could it be shown more clearly how much the will of man, seized by pride and used without the help of God, is capable of — evil could not be expressed more fully or more plainly than in the first man. Behold, the first man perishes — and where would he be, had not the second man come? For because that man is a man, so too is this one a man; and hence the saying is in human terms.

Such people therefore often seek also to persuade men to live well even while not being Christians. They seek to enter by another way — to steal and to kill; not to save and keep safe, as the good shepherd does. There were indeed certain philosophers who treated with great subtlety of virtues and vices, dividing, defining, drawing most acute chains of reasoning, filling books, airing their wisdom with loud-boasting mouths, who even dared to say to men: Follow us, hold to our school, if you wish to live happily. But they did not enter by the door: they wished to destroy, to slaughter, and to kill.

For the things that are signified are actually being stated: they are deemed lies, however, because not the things that are truly signified are understood to have been said, but rather those things are believed to have been stated which are false. To make this plainer by examples, consider what Jacob himself did. He covered his limbs with the skins of kids. If we seek the immediate reason, we shall think he lied: for he did this so that he might be taken for one he was not. But if this deed is referred to the purpose for which it was in truth done to signify something, then by the skins of kids, sins are signified; and by him who covered himself with them, he is signified who bore not his own sins but those of others.

In this matter it is to be considered with what great force of love the mind of this woman had been kindled — she who did not withdraw from the tomb of the Lord even when the disciples had departed. She sought him whom she had not found; she wept while seeking, and, inflamed by the fire of her love, she burned with desire for him whom she believed to have been taken away. Hence it came about that she alone then saw him who had remained to seek — since truly the power of a good work is perseverance, and it is said by the voice of Truth: But he who perseveres to the end, he shall be saved.

How many receive from the altar and die — and die in the very act of receiving! Hence the Apostle says: He eats and drinks judgment to himself. Was not the Lord's morsel a poison to Judas? Yet he received it. And when he received it, the enemy entered into him — not because he received something evil, but because a wicked man received something good wickedly. See therefore, brothers, eat the heavenly bread spiritually; bring innocence to the altar. If your sins are only daily sins and not mortal ones, yet before you come to the altar, take heed of what you say: Forgive us our debts as we also forgive our debtors. If you forgive, you will be forgiven: approach with confidence; it is bread, not poison.

Why is it similar to this? Because the one introduces the other and is in turn confirmed by it. For whoever does evil hates the light and does not come to the light. And again: The fool has said in his heart, There is no God. Then follows: They are corrupt, and have become abominable in their pursuits. And again: The root of all evils is greed; which some desiring, have strayed from the faith. And: He who loves me will keep my commandments — whose head and root is: You shall love the Lord your God, and your neighbor as yourself.

Hence it follows: He who is faithful in a little, that is in earthly things, shall also be faithful in much, that is in spiritual things. But he who is unjust in a little, as one who does not give to brothers to use what was created by God for all — this man will also be unjust in the distribution of spiritual wealth, dispensing the teaching of the Lord not according to need but according to persons. But if, he says, you do not faithfully dispense earthly riches that pass away, who will entrust to you the true and eternal riches of God's teaching?

And although Luke says that Joseph was begotten of Heli, this word ought not to disturb us into thinking something other than that one Evangelist commemorates the natural father, and the other the adoptive father. Nor is it absurd for one to be said to have begotten, not in the flesh but in charity, the one whom he has adopted as a son. Indeed, even we ourselves, to whom God has given the power to become his children, were not begotten by him from his own nature and substance as was his only-begotten Son, but were adopted by his love.

Yet, although in Solomon's time less diligence in wisdom was required than in more ancient ages — for the old Law forbade neither pleasures, nor called it vain to enjoy other superfluous things — still, even in such circumstances as then obtained, it is possible to see how base and subject to vanity these things are. But we have been called to a higher life, have ascended to a more excellent summit, and are trained in greater contests: and what else are we commanded to do but — like those heavenly, intellectual, and incorporeal powers above — to fashion our life accordingly?

For although the flesh desires nothing without the soul, and receives its sensations from the same source whence it receives its movements, yet it belongs to the soul to deny certain things to the substance subject to it, and by an interior judgment to restrain the exterior from what is unfitting — so that, freed more often from bodily desires, the soul in the chamber of the mind may be free for divine wisdom: where, with all the noise of earthly cares falling silent, it may rejoice in holy meditations and in eternal delights.

When, therefore, he hid himself as a man, he is not to be thought to have lost his power, but to have given an example to our weakness. For he was detained when he willed, and killed when he willed. But because his members — that is, his faithful — were yet to come, who would not have that power which he himself had as our God: what he did in hiding, what he concealed as if to avoid being killed, indicated what his members would do — in which members he himself, of course, was present.

How great justice is can be understood from the fact that it makes no exception for places, persons, or times, and is observed even toward enemies: so that if a place or day has been appointed with an enemy for battle, it is held to be against justice to anticipate him either in place or time. For there is a difference between one who is taken in a pitched battle and fierce conflict, and one who is overcome by superior advantage or some chance event. If therefore justice holds in war, how much more must it be maintained in peace?

But as regards that death with which the Lord threatened — the death by which those fathers of theirs died — Moses ate manna, Aaron ate manna, Phinehas ate manna; many who pleased the Lord ate it there, and did not die. Why? Because they understood the visible food spiritually, hungered for it spiritually, tasted it spiritually, so that they might be filled spiritually. For we too today receive visible food; but the Sacrament is one thing, and the power of the Sacrament is another.

Therefore his saying: Father, the hour has come, glorify your Son, shows that all time — what he would do and when, or what he would permit to be done — was disposed by him who is not subject to time, since the things that were to come in each successive moment have their efficient causes in the wisdom of God, in which there are no times. Let it not be believed, therefore, that this hour came driven by fate, but rather that it was ordered by God. Nor did any starry necessity bind the Passion of Christ: far be it that the stars should have compelled the Creator of the stars to die.

If therefore you are also willing to attend diligently to the reading, you will have no need to look further. For the word of Christ is true when he says: Seek and you shall find; knock and it shall be opened to you. For the rest, since many of those who assemble here with us have taken upon themselves the upbringing of children, the care of a wife, and the management of a household, and for that reason cannot give themselves wholly to this labor: at least rouse yourselves to receive what others have gathered; bestowing as much diligence upon listening to what has been said as upon gathering money. For even if it is shameful to require only so much effort from you, yet it will be desirable if you will give at least that much.

I beg you, therefore, to embrace holy thoughts, to live devoutly and holily, and to be partakers of blessing — which, believe me, drives away not only death but all diseases as well. For when Christ dwells within us, he calms the warring law in our members; he strengthens piety, extinguishes disturbances of the soul, heals the sick, restores the broken: and like the good shepherd who laid down his soul for his sheep, he raises us up from every fall.

Therefore, as consecration professes and confirms union with Christ, so expiation both begins that same union by cleansing faults, brings it to completion by sharing in the Passion of Christ, and consummates it by offering victims on behalf of one's brothers. And this was indeed the design of the merciful Jesus when he willed to lay open to us his Heart — displaying the marks of his Passion and showing forth the flames of his love — clearly so that from this source we might conjecture the infinite malice of sin, and from that source, marveling at the infinite charity of the Redemption, we might both detest sin more vehemently and return the ardor of charity more fervently. And truly the spirit of expiation, or rather of reparation, has always held the first and foremost place in the worship rendered to the Most Sacred Heart of Jesus; nothing is more congruent with the origin, the nature, the power, and the endeavors proper to this form of religion, as the record and practice of events, the sacred liturgy, and the acts of the Supreme Pontiffs confirm.

Just as one who sees letters in an excellently written book and does not know how to read praises the hand of the scribe, admiring the beauty of the characters, but does not know what those characters mean or indicate — and is a praiser with his eyes, but no knower with his mind. But another both praises the craftsmanship and grasps the meaning: that man, namely, who can not only see, which is common to all, but also read — which one who has not learned cannot do. So those who saw the miracles of Christ and did not understand what they meant and what they were, as it were, intimating to those who understood, only marveled that they were done; but others both marveled at what was done and attained to what was understood. Such must we be in the school of Christ.

He who did not hold the teaching of the law to charity but to pride swelled up as one puffed up with wealth received; and because words poured forth from him out of knowledge, they fell like crumbs from the table. But, on the other hand, the dogs licked the wounds of the poor man lying there. At times in sacred Scripture, preachers are understood by dogs. For the tongue of a dog, when it licks a wound, heals it; so too holy teachers, when they instruct us in the confession of our sin, touch the wound of the mind as it were with their tongue.

He, therefore, who shines with excessive care for bodily adornment and dress, or for the splendor of other possessions, is easily convicted by the very things themselves of being a follower of the pomps of the world, and deceives no one with the deceptive appearance of holiness. But he who in his profession of Christianity, through unusual slovenliness and squalor, draws the eyes of men upon himself — doing so by will and not enduring it out of necessity — from his other works it can be conjectured whether he does this out of contempt for superfluous adornment or out of some form of ambition: for the Lord commanded us to beware of wolves in sheep's clothing. But by their fruits, he says, you shall know them.

He who knows the hidden secrets of minds — for God does not fail to scrutinize any of the things hidden within a man — commanded a denarius to be brought to him, and asked whose image and inscription it bore. The Pharisees answered that it was Caesar's. To them he said that what belongs to Caesar must be rendered to Caesar; and that what belongs to God must be rendered to God. O answer full of wonder, and perfect resolution of a heavenly saying! So perfectly did he balance everything between contempt for the world and the dishonor of injuring Caesar, that he freed minds devoted to God from all earthly cares and duties, when he decreed that what was Caesar's should be rendered to Caesar.

He who eats my flesh and drinks my blood abides in me, and I in him. This then is what it means to eat that food and drink that drink — to abide in Christ, and to have him abiding in oneself. And therefore he who does not abide in Christ, and in whom Christ does not abide, without doubt neither spiritually eats his flesh nor drinks his blood, even if he crushes the Sacrament of the Body and Blood of Christ carnally and visibly with his teeth; but rather eats and drinks the Sacrament of so great a thing unto his own judgment, since he, being unclean, has presumed to approach the Sacraments of Christ, which no one receives worthily unless he is clean — of whom it is said: Blessed are the clean of heart, for they shall see God.

He who lay dead upon the bier was borne to the tomb by four material elements, yet he had hope of rising again, because he was carried upon wood. And even if this had not profited us before, yet after Jesus had touched it, it began to avail unto life: as a sign that salvation was to be poured back upon the people through the gibbet of the Cross. When, therefore, the word of God was heard, those bitter bearers of death stood still, who were pressing upon the human body with the deadly flux of material nature. For what else do we do but lie as though dead in a kind of bier, that is, in the instrument of a supreme funeral, when either the fire of immoderate desire blazes up, or cold moisture overflows, or the vitality of our souls is dulled by a certain sluggish disposition of the earthly body, or our spirit, thickened by corruption and emptied of pure light, feeds the mind? These are the bearers of our funeral.

Because, therefore, our Redeemer, taken up into heaven, now judges all things and will come at the last as the judge of all, Mark describes him as seated after his Assumption, because after the glory of his Ascension he will be seen as judge at the end. But Stephen, in the midst of the struggle of his contest, saw him standing, who had him as his helper: for that, while Stephen on earth was overcoming the faithlessness of his persecutors, the grace of Christ fought on his behalf from heaven.

Since, therefore, the Ascension of Christ is our advancement, and where the glory of the Head has gone before, there the hope of the Body is also called; let us, dearly beloved, rejoice with worthy joys and be glad with devout thanksgiving. For today we have not only been confirmed as possessors of paradise, but in Christ we have even penetrated the heights of heaven; we have gained more through the ineffable grace of Christ than we had lost through the envy of the devil. For those whom the venomous enemy cast down from the happiness of their first dwelling, these the Son of God, having made them members of his own body, has set at the right hand of the Father: with whom he lives and reigns in the unity of the Holy Spirit, God, for ever and ever. Amen.

Now since the monad multiplied tenfold yields the number ten, and ten multiplied by itself is extended to a hundred, which again multiplied by ten is stretched to a thousand; when we begin from one in order to arrive at a thousand, what is signified here by the name of one, if not the beginning of right living? And what is signified by the amplitude of the number a thousand, if not the perfection of that same good life? To contend with God, however, is to claim for oneself rather than to attribute to him the glory of one's own virtue. But let the holy man take heed: for even he who has already received the highest gifts, if he exalts himself on account of what he has received, loses everything he had received.

These things being so, the cult of the Holy Family has rightly and deservedly been introduced among Catholics at a mature time and gains ever greater increase day by day. This is proved both by the Christian confraternities established under the invocation of the Holy Family, and by the singular honors paid to it, and especially by the privileges and graces imparted by our predecessors to arouse devotion toward it. This kind of veneration has been held in great honor since the seventeenth century, and spreading widely through Italy, France, and Belgium, it has pervaded almost all of Europe; then, crossing the vast expanses of the Ocean, it extended itself in America through the Canadian region and flourished under most auspicious signs. Indeed, nothing more salutary or efficacious than the example of the Holy Family can be conceived for Christian families, since it encompasses the perfection and completion of all domestic virtues. May Jesus, Mary, and Joseph, thus invoked within the household walls, be present with favor, nourish charity, govern conduct, invite to virtue by their imitation, and by alleviating them make the mortal hardships that press in from every side more bearable. — To augment the cult of the Holy Family, Pope Leo XIII prescribed that Christian families be consecrated to the same Holy Family; and Benedict XV extended the Office and Mass to the universal Church.

What does the fig tree signify, if not human nature? What does the woman bent low signify and declare, if not that same nature? She was well planted like the fig tree, and well created like the woman; but having fallen into fault by her own will, she preserves neither the fruit of her action nor the upright stature of rectitude. For falling into sin by her own will, because she was unwilling to bear the fruit of obedience, she lost the upright stature of rectitude. Created in the likeness of God, since she did not persist in her own dignity, she scorned to preserve what she had been planted or created to be. The lord of the vineyard came to the fig tree a third time, because he sought out human nature — awaiting it before the law, admonishing it under the law, visiting it under grace.

But what would there have been worthy of wonder in Joseph, if he had harmed those who harmed him, or loved those who loved him? For this is what most people do. But it is admirable to love your enemy: which the Savior teaches. Rightly, therefore, is he to be admired who did this before the Gospel — that when wronged he spared, when attacked he forgave, when sold he did not return injury but paid back grace for insult: which after the Gospel we have all learned, yet cannot keep. Let us learn also from the Saints' envy, that we may imitate their patience; and let us acknowledge that they were not of a more excellent nature, but of a more observant one; and that they did not remain ignorant of vices, but corrected them. And if envy burned even the Saints, how much more must we take care lest it inflame sinners?

What shall I say of these? Behold, the very Pharisees read, and in what they read they sounded forth Christ, they hoped for him to come, yet they did not acknowledge him when present. They even boasted among those called Seers, that is, among the wise, yet they denied Christ and did not enter through the door. Therefore, if they led any astray, it was to be slaughtered and killed, not liberated, that they led them. Let us leave these aside. Let us look at those who, perhaps, enter through the door themselves — those who glory in the very name of Christ. For there are innumerable ones who not only boast of being Seers, but wish to be seen as illumined by Christ: yet they are heretics.

What shall I say of the Maccabees? But first let me speak of the people of the fathers; who, being ready to fight for the temple of God and for their laws, assailed by deceit on the Sabbath day, preferred to offer their bare bodies to wounds rather than to resist, lest they violate the Sabbath. And so, all of them offered themselves joyfully to death. But the Maccabees, considering that by this example the whole nation might perish, even on the Sabbath, when they themselves were provoked to battle, avenged the slaughter of their innocent brothers. Thereafter the king Antiochus, stirred to anger, when he kindled war through his generals Lysias, Nicanor, and Gorgias, was so ground down with his Eastern and Assyrian forces that forty-eight thousand were laid low in the midst of the field by three thousand.

For what merit is there in calling the Lord, 'Lord'? Surely the Lord will not cease to be Lord unless we call him such? And what sanctity of duty consists in the utterance of a name, when the path to the heavenly Kingdom is to be found by obedience to the will of God, not by uttering his name? Many will say to me on that day: Lord, Lord, have we not prophesied in your name? Even now he condemns the fraud of false prophets and the pretense of hypocrites, who presume for themselves glory from the power of the word, in the prophecy of doctrine, in the expulsion of demons, and in the powers of such works.

What, then, had the mountains of Gilboa done wrong, that at the death of Saul neither dew nor rain should fall on them, and the word of judgment should dry them of every shoot of greenery? But since Gilboa is interpreted as 'downflow,' and through Saul the anointed who died the death of our Mediator is expressed; not without reason are the mountains of Gilboa taken to signify the proud hearts of the Jews, who, while flowing downward in the desires of this world, have mingled themselves in the death of Christ, that is, of the anointed; and because the anointed King dies bodily among them, they themselves are dried of every dew of grace.

What then did his sisters announce? 'Lord, behold, he whom you love is sick.' They did not say: Come; for to one who loves, it was enough merely to inform him. They did not dare to say: Come and heal him. They did not dare to say: Command there, and it will be done here. For why not these women too, if the faith of that centurion is praised for this very thing? For he said: I am not worthy that you should enter under my roof; but only say the word, and my servant shall be healed. None of this from them, but only: Lord, behold, he whom you love is sick. It suffices that you know; for you do not love and then abandon.

What, then, does it mean to say: Blessed is he who is not scandalized in me, unless it is to signify plainly the abjectness and humility of his death? As if he were openly saying: I indeed perform wonders, but I do not disdain to undergo what is abject. Therefore, because in dying I follow after you, men must be most careful lest they despise my death, who venerate my signs.

What, then, is the confession of sins, but a certain breaking open of wounds? For the venom of sin is healthfully disclosed in confession, which was pestilentially concealed in the mind. For wounds of the skin draw the matter of putrefaction to the surface. And in confessing our sins, what else do we do but open up the evil that lay hidden within us? But Lazarus, wounded, longed to be filled with the crumbs that fell from the rich man's table, and no one gave to him: because that proud people disdained to admit any Gentile to the knowledge of the law.

But what does it mean that, spitting, he touched his tongue? For us, the saliva is wisdom received from the mouth of the Redeemer in divine speech. For saliva flows from the head into the mouth. This wisdom, therefore, which is himself, when it touches our tongue, forthwith forms it for the words of preaching. Looking up to heaven, he groaned: not that he himself stood in need of groaning, who gave what was asked; but he taught us to groan toward him who presides over heaven, that both our ears might be opened through the gift of the Holy Spirit, and our tongue loosed through the saliva of his mouth — that is, through knowledge of the divine word — for the words of preaching.

Why should I relate Jonathan his brother, who, fighting with a small band against the royal armies, abandoned by his own men and left with only two, renewed the battle, turned back the enemy, and recalled his fleeing soldiers to share in the triumph? You have military valor, in which there is a considerable form of what is noble and honorable, because it prefers death to servitude and disgrace. But what shall I say of the sufferings of the Martyrs? And lest we wander too far: the Maccabee boys carried off no lesser a triumph over the proud king Antiochus than their own fathers had done; for those conquered armed, these conquered without arms.

What does it mean, then, that he says here: These things I have not told you from the beginning, because I was with you — unless it means that what he speaks here about the Holy Spirit, namely that he will come to them and bear witness, when they are about to suffer those evils, he had not told them from the beginning, because he was with them? The Consoler, therefore, or advocate — for both meanings are conveyed by the Greek word Paraclete — had been necessary at the departure of Christ; and therefore he had not spoken of him from the beginning, when he was with them, because they were consoled by his presence.

To you Cherubim and Seraphim * cry out without ceasing:

the Father * of immeasurable majesty;

Who is it that sows, but our own perception and mind, which, receiving the grain of preaching and fostering the seed, causes it to spring up with the moisture of faith in the field of the breast? The preaching of the Gospel is the least of all disciplines. For at its first teaching, it has no claim to truth when it preaches a God who is man, a Christ who is dead, and the scandal of the Cross. Compare this kind of doctrine with the teachings of the philosophers, with their books, with the splendor of eloquence, with the composition of discourses: and you will see how much lesser than the other seeds is the seed of the Gospel.

Whoever, therefore, is vexed by an unclean spirit — if he but take note of this and use this remedy, namely fasting — the evil spirit, immediately oppressed and fearing the power of fasting, will depart. For demons take great delight in excess and drunkenness and bodily comforts. Great is the power in fasting, and great and illustrious are the things wrought through it. Otherwise, how would men perform such wonders, and signs be done through them, and God grant health to the infirm through them, unless plainly it were on account of spiritual exercises, and humility of soul, and good conduct? For fasting is the food of the Angels: and he who makes use of it is to be reckoned in the order of the angelic.

How much purer, therefore, ought to be the one who enjoys such a sacrifice? How much more radiant than the solar ray ought to be the hand that divides this flesh? The mouth that is filled with spiritual fire, the tongue that is reddened with that most awesome Blood? Consider with what honor you are distinguished, with what table you feast. That which the Angels behold and shudder at, and dare not look upon freely because of the splendor that blazes from it — this is what we are fed upon, this is what we are united to, and we have been made one body with Christ and one flesh. Who will declare the powers of the Lord, who will make all his praises heard? What shepherd feeds his flock with his own blood? And what do I say, shepherd? There are many mothers who, after the pains of childbirth, hand over their children to other nurses. But he himself did not suffer this; rather, he himself feeds us with his own Blood and in every way binds us to himself.

To what end have they brought those scrutinies of theirs, in which they searched and failed — so that even after the Lord was dead and buried, they set guards at the tomb? For they said to Pilate: That deceiver — this was the name by which the Lord Jesus Christ was called, for the consolation of his servants when they are called deceivers — therefore those men said to Pilate: That deceiver said, while he was still living: After three days I will rise again. Command therefore that the tomb be guarded until the third day, lest his disciples come and steal him and say to the people: He has risen from the dead; and the last deception would be worse than the first. Pilate said to them: You have a guard; go, guard it as you know how. And they, departing, secured the tomb, sealing the stone with the guards.

As for the fact that he says: And I told his disciples to cast him out, and they could not; he covertly reproaches the Apostles — though the inability to effect a cure is sometimes attributed not to the weakness of those who cure, but to the faith of those who are to be cured, as the Lord says: Let it be done to you according to your faith. And answering them, he said: O faithless generation, how long shall I be with you? How long shall I endure you? Not that he who is gentle and meek — who did not open his mouth like a lamb before its shearer, nor broke out into words of fury — was overcome by weariness; but as if in the manner of a physician, who, seeing a patient behaving contrary to his prescriptions, might say: How long shall I come to your house? How long am I to waste the labor of my art, when I order one thing and you do another?

Now that this natural unity is in us, he himself testified as follows: He who eats my flesh and drinks my blood abides in me, and I in him. For no one will be in him unless he himself will have been in that person; having received into himself only the flesh of him whose flesh he has taken. But he had already taught above the sacrament of this perfect unity, saying: As the living Father sent me, and I live through the Father; so he who eats my flesh, he also shall live through me. He lives, therefore, through the Father; and in the same manner as he lives through the Father, so we shall live through his flesh.
